articles.title: Chicago lawsuits claim delivery robots collected personal information without authorization — but the defendants say the allegations are 'frivolous'
articles.text:
'Sidewalk surveillance': Illinois residents accuse delivery robots of capturing biometric data without permission
Scan and deliver
- Two new Chicago lawsuits claim unauthorized biometric data collections
- In these cases, the biometrics are face and body scans
- Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics have denied the allegations
The backlash to what's perceived as surveillance technology continues, with two Chicago residents taking robot delivery companies to court over the alleged collection of biometric data while dropping off food and groceries.
As the Associated Press reports, the two men bringing the cases claim that robots from Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics turned up — via DoorDash and Uber Eats respectively — even though robot delivery hadn't been requested in the app.
The key allegation is that when these individuals were unlocking the robot cargo bay to get their orders, their hands and faces were scanned via camera and LiDAR technology, without explicit prior permission. If true, that would put Coco and Serve in breach of the Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) of 2008.
Both class-action lawsuits claim that video and sensor data is being retained by these bots in violation of privacy law, and shared with AI companies for training purposes. Statutory damages of $1,000 per negligent violation or $5,000 per intentional or reckless violation are being claimed through the courts.
Both Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics have denied the allegations. We've reached out to both companies and will update this story if we hear back, but the AP reports Coco as saying the legal action is "frivolous", while Serve says it "does not use data to identify individuals or create biometric profiles".
'Fundamentally misunderstands our technology'
The Coco Robotics privacy policy — last updated in 2022, before it started operating in Chicago — is a little light on data retention policies, but does mention sharing data with third parties and affiliates, though most of this seems to be aggregated and anonymized before it's used.
As for the Serve Robotics privacy policy, it's been updated much more recently. It says data retention periods are determined by "contractual obligations with our delivery partners", and there's the standard vagueness about sharing information with unnamed "service providers and vendors" on occasion. There's also an explicit mention of sharing data "to train AI agents and models".
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
It's obviously impossible for a delivery robot to work without scanning its environment and navigating around sidewalks and pedestrians, and that's the defense being put forward here. The crux of the case will be whether the data collection involved was done without permission, and contravenes the Illinois privacy act.
"This lawsuit fundamentally misunderstands our technology, we have not collected biometric data in Chicago," a Coco spokesperson told the AP. "The data we share is navigational data used to make sidewalks safer for all users."
With complaints around Flock cameras, delivery drones, 'spy' glasses, and other tech on the rise, it does feel there's more privacy scrutiny than ever before — with Redditors describing these bots as "mobile data thieves" and "sidewalk surveillance".

articles.title: Starfall, la mystérieuse capsule de SpaceX, lancée pour la deuxième fois dans l'espace
articles.text:
SpaceX vient de lancer Starfall, une capsule qui doit permettre de fabriquer et de tester des produits en orbite avant de les ramener sur Terre. Mais l’entreprise reste encore très discrète sur son vaisseau.
Ce mardi 20 octobre, une fusée Falcon 9 a transporté la charge utile partagée Bandwagon-5 en orbite. À son bord, 32 dispositifs différents, dont une certaine Starfall. Et si SpaceX a expliqué que le déploiement était terminé quelques heures après le décollage, elle n’en a pas dit plus sur son intrigant vaisseau.
Une capsule en forme de disque
Pourtant, Starfall a volé pour la première fois le 23 juin dernier. SpaceX n’avait alors révélé la présence de la capsule que peu avant le décollage, avec pour seul document une image de synthèse. Mais cette fois, elle figurait noir sur blanc sur la page officielle de la mission, aux côtés des clients payants.
Mais à quoi ressemble ce mystérieux vaisseau ? De la forme d’un gros disque, il mesure 3,1 mètres de diamètre pour seulement 0,75 mètre d’épaisseur. Il pèse environ 2 100 kilogrammes et peut ramener jusqu’à une tonne de charge utile sur Terre. Pas de quoi remplacer une capsule habitée, mais assez pour rapatrier des expériences ou des petites productions.
Son rôle ? » Starfall permet un accès abordable et régulier à un environnement de microgravité, offrant des opportunités uniques pour la fabrication en orbite, la recherche scientifique et les essais », explique SpaceX. Dans une évaluation environnementale publiée en mai, la Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), régulateur américain de l’aviation, décrit l’engin comme une capsule dotée d’un bouclier thermique en fibre de carbone. Elle s’oriente grâce à de petits propulseurs à gaz froid (comme ceux du Tesla Roadster), puis freine sa descente avec des parachutes.
Mais à quoi sert Starfall ?
Starfall serait pensé comme un laboratoire en apesanteur accessible « en tant que service » : une entreprise y enverrait ses expériences ou ses productions, et les récupérerait sur Terre après la rentrée de la capsule. Une fonction très utile à l’approche de la retraite de la Station Spatiale internationale (ISS). L’idée est de faire de la microgravité une prestation courante, comme on loue aujourd’hui un lanceur.
Mais ce n’est pas tout. La capsule pourrait, en théorie, transporter du fret entre deux points du globe en passant par l’espace. Elle pourrait également servir les projets de data centers orbitaux de SpaceX, car ces installations auront besoin, tôt ou tard, d’allers-retours pour remplacer ou réparer des composants.
Il s’agit d’un marché en pleine expansion. Sur ce même lancement, Le Falcon 9 a embarqué la capsule W-7 de Varda Space Industries, une start-up qui vise exactement le même marché. Environ trois fois plus petite que Starfall, elle doit tester si l’apesanteur peut améliorer la solubilité d’un médicament contre le cancer. SpaceX, elle, dispose bien entendu d'un avantage non négligeable : en plus de posséder le vaisseau, elle gère aussi les lancements.
Sources : Space.com, Spaceflight Now
La microgravité désigne un état où tout est en chute libre autour de la Terre, ce qui réduit fortement les effets du poids et de la sédimentation. Cela change la façon dont se comportent les fluides, les mélanges, les cristaux ou certaines réactions chimiques, parfois avec moins de défauts ou une meilleure homogénéité. En R&D, cet environnement sert à observer des phénomènes difficiles à isoler au sol, ou à qualifier des composants dans des conditions proches de l’espace réel (vide, cycles thermiques, rayonnements). L’intérêt industriel est de produire de petites séries à forte valeur ou de valider des procédés avant de les adapter sur Terre. La contrainte principale reste le coût et la logistique du retour des échantillons, qui conditionnent l’intérêt économique.
Un bouclier thermique est un système de protection qui encaisse l’échauffement extrême lors de la rentrée atmosphérique, quand l’air comprimé devant l’engin monte à très haute température. La fibre de carbone est souvent utilisée sous forme de composites capables de résister à de fortes contraintes thermiques et mécaniques, parfois avec des matériaux ablatifs qui se consument pour évacuer la chaleur. Ce n’est pas un simple revêtement décoratif : c’est une partie critique de l’architecture, dimensionnée selon la vitesse de rentrée, l’angle d’attaque et la masse. Si ce système est mal conçu, l’échauffement peut dégrader la structure ou l’avionique. Le choix du matériau influence aussi la réutilisation, les inspections et les coûts entre deux missions.
Des propulseurs à gaz froid expulsent un gaz stocké sous pression à travers une tuyère, produisant une poussée faible mais très contrôlable. Ils ne brûlent pas de carburant : c’est simple, propre et généralement très fiable, au prix d’une efficacité moindre que des moteurs chimiques. Sur une capsule, ils servent surtout au contrôle d’attitude (pointer et stabiliser l’engin) pour présenter correctement le bouclier thermique et gérer la trajectoire de rentrée. Ils sont adaptés aux manœuvres fines où l’on privilégie la précision et la sûreté plutôt que la puissance. Leur limitation principale est la quantité de gaz embarquée, qui impose un budget de manœuvres.

articles.title: Unitree reveals H2-X humanoid bodyguard robot — 'Kung Fu Legend Guardian' packs 8-hour battery and martial arts defense skills
articles.text:
Unitree reveals its H2-X bodyguard robot — a 'Kung Fu' humanoid with an 8-hour battery life and some serious martial arts skills
But don't expect the personal Robocop to go on sale
- Unitree has shown off an impressive demo for its new 'kung fu' robot
- It's based on the company's H2 platform, and is designed for security
- It's unlikely to go on general sale, though, and there are no details on pricing or availability
Humanoid robots are improving at a rapid pace, and the world's biggest robotics manufacturer, Unitree, has just revealed a Robocop-esque new model called the H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian.
A one-minute teaser video released on X and YouTube (below) shows the H2-X in action across a series of slightly bizarre scenarios. The first few clips show the robot unleashing a series of knees and punches to cars in a scrapyard, in scenes reminiscent of a Street Fighter II bonus stage.
Beyond the robot's kung fu credentials, it isn't exactly clear what real-world roles Unitree is trying to showcase there. But the rest of the video shows that the H2-X is being billed as a personal security guard that can jump in front its owner during attempted robberies, or lift cars to release humans trapped underneath.
Unitree hasn't revealed much in the way of specs for the H2-X, with the only specifics being that it's capable of jumping from four-meter high platforms and also standing for "approximately eight hours" between charges.
However, the similar Unitree H2 robot is a 1.8-meter tall humanoid that comes with an optional Nvidia Jetson AGX Thor chip and costs $29,900 (around £22,380 / AU$42,720). We've asked Unitree for some more specifics on the specs and pricing for the H2-X, and will update this story if we hear back.
Not quite ready for security guard duty
It's fair to say that Unitree's H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian video is more of a tech demo than a consumer product showcase, in much the same vein as its rollerblading and iceskating demos earlier this year.
However, that doesn't mean Unitree isn't making big strides in humanoid robots, or what is often billed as "embodied intelligence". At Computex 2026 the trio of Unitree, Nvidia and Sharpa announced a collaboration to create an H2+ blueprint for next-gen robots, with Nvidia supplying the much-needed training data and its Jetson AGX Thor T5000 chip.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian demo appears to be a different project that's focused more on physical prowess. But despite those impressive jumping abilities, the robot would find it nigh-on impossible to clear the global and national consumer certification hurdles necessary for it make it to market as a personal bodyguard.
It's possible that a version of the robot could be designed for industrial or military uses, but Unitree hasn't yet commented on its future plans. What is clear is that Unitree is keen to continue the momentum it's gained after its IPO in August 2026, which started well but then ran into turbulence last month after a 55% slump from its peak.
According to Reuters, that drop has apparently prompted China to put the brakes on a humanoid robot IPO rush, which has seen half a dozen Chinese robotics companies queuing up to follow Unitree's stock-market debut.
Still, Unitree's latest H2-X video at least keeps us dreaming that personal robot safety guards are coming, even if they might dent a few cars along the way.

articles.title: Carros más inteligentes: ahora recordarán correos, mapas y más gracias a la IA de Gemini
articles.text:
Google comenzó a desplegar una de las actualizaciones más ambiciosas para Gemini dentro de los vehículos: la Inteligencia Personalizada, también llamada Personal Intelligence. La función llega a Android Auto y permite que el asistente consulte correos, fotos, citas y rutas guardadas para responder sin que el conductor dé ningún dato adicional.
Hasta ahora, Gemini respondía en el vehículo de la misma manera para todos los usuarios. Con esta actualización, el asistente accede a la misma información personal que ya usa en el teléfono, lo que multiplica el contexto disponible en cada conversación al volante.
Qué es la Inteligencia Personalizada y cómo conecta los datos con el auto
La Inteligencia Personalizada es la función de Gemini que, con autorización del usuario, conecta de forma segura la información de Gmail, Google Calendario, Google Fotos, Google Maps, YouTube y el historial de búsqueda. Si el conductor tiene una cuenta de Google Workspace, el asistente también puede usar esas herramientas para dar contexto adicional.
El sistema combina dos capacidades: recuperar un dato concreto, como una reserva de hotel guardada en el correo, y razonar sobre varias fuentes a la vez para dar una respuesta completa. Esa combinación es la que permite resolver pedidos complejos sin que el usuario tenga que revisar cada aplicación por separado.
Esta función solo se activa cuando el usuario otorga permiso explícito desde la configuración de Gemini, y puede desactivarse en cualquier momento. Mientras permanezca apagada, el asistente sigue funcionando con normalidad para navegación, música o llamadas, aunque sin respuestas adaptadas a cada persona.
Qué se podrá pedirle a Gemini al volante
Los comandos funcionan en lenguaje natural, sin necesidad de especificar datos concretos. Camino al aeropuerto, una pregunta como “¿cuál es mi puerta de embarque y llega a tiempo mi vuelo?” alcanza para que el asistente localice la confirmación en Gmail y revise el estado del viaje en un mismo intercambio.
La función también se integra con la navegación. Decir “llévame a la cita del médico” basta para que Gemini busque el evento en el Calendario, extraiga la dirección y comience a dar indicaciones, sin que el conductor recuerde la calle ni la busque antes de salir.
El asistente incorpora además preferencias personales al sugerir lugares. Ante un pedido como encontrar un restaurante en la ruta, puede priorizar opciones acordes a los gustos habituales del usuario, por ejemplo locales vegetarianos si ese es su patrón de consumo.
Otro escenario es recuperar información visual: pedir que localice “el lavadero de autos de la foto que saqué la semana pasada” y que trace la ruta hacia ese sitio, sin necesidad de revisar el carrete de imágenes ni detener el vehículo para buscar la dirección.
También es posible retomar una conversación anterior. Una frase como “llévame a la cafetería de la que hablamos ayer” permite que el asistente identifique el lugar mencionado en un intercambio previo y arranque la navegación de forma directa.
Cómo acceder a estas funciones de IA en Android Auto
Google diseñó la función con el consentimiento como eje central: ninguna aplicación queda conectada hasta que el usuario decide activarla desde los ajustes de Gemini, y la opción puede revertirse en cualquier momento. En los vehículos con Google built-in, las respuestas personalizadas solo se comparten mientras el teléfono permanece conectado al coche.
Para acceder a la Inteligencia Personalizada en Android Auto es necesario mantener actualizadas tanto la aplicación de Android Auto como la app de Gemini en el teléfono, además de tener activada la personalización desde esa misma aplicación móvil, donde se gestionan los permisos de acceso al correo, al calendario y a las fotos.
El despliegue arrancó esta semana en Android Auto, mientras que los coches con Google built-in recibirán la función en los próximos meses. Según pudo conocer el medio especializado 9to5Google, es probable que la actualización llegue primero a Estados Unidos y después a mercados como España, aunque la compañía no confirmó un cronograma oficial para esa expansión.
Quienes ya tengan habilitada la Inteligencia Personalizada en la aplicación móvil de Gemini la verán activa de forma automática al conectar el teléfono al coche. Quienes no la hayan configurado pueden hacerlo en cualquier momento desde los ajustes del asistente, donde también se revisan qué servicios de Google comparten información con Gemini.

articles.title: China-Aligned Bronze Sandcastle Abuses Sandboxie DLL Sideloading to Deploy Backdoors
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a previously undocumented China-aligned threat cluster known as Bronze Sandcastle that has been observed targeting organizations in Asia and Africa since mid-2025.
"The most distinctive technical marker for Bronze Sandcastle is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading," Sophos security researcher Gabor Szappanos said in a post published Tuesday.
Between August 2025 and August 2026, attacks mounted by the threat actor have resulted in victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely South Korea. Evidence indicates that Bronze Sandcastle is most active in the UTC+8 time zone.
DLL sideloading is a popular adversarial technique that exploits the way Windows loads DLL files, allowing an attacker to trick a legitimate program into loading a malicious DLL.
When an application is launched, it needs to load various DLLs in order to function correctly. If the application does not provide the full path to a required DLL, the operating system looks for it in a predetermined sequence of directories.
An attacker can take advantage of this behavior by planting a malicious DLL with the same name as a legitimate one in a location that Windows searches before the folder that contains the actual DLL. Thus, when the legitimate application starts, it proceeds to load and run the malicious DLL, giving the attacker a way in to the system.
"Because the malicious code is executed by a trusted and often digitally signed application, it is less likely to be flagged by antivirus software and other security solutions," Zscaler noted in an analysis last week.
"If the legitimate application runs with elevated privileges, the malicious DLL will inherit those same permissions, allowing the attacker to perform more sensitive actions on the system."
What's more, the technique enables persistence if the compromised application is configured to automatically run every time a system is rebooted, thereby allowing the attacker's code to execute on the infected host.
Sophos said it observed legitimate Sandboxie executables placed in multiple victim environments, along with a malicious "sbiedll.dll" file, which, in turn, causes the trusted application ("SandboxieWUAU.exe") to load attacker-controlled code during runtime.
Besides Sandboxie, Bronze Sandcastle has been leveraged in seven other DLL sideloading combinations -
- javaw.exe (Java application) - jli.dll
- Krita.exe (Krita digital painting) - Krita.dll
- NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access) - NvdaHelperRemote.dll
- Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper) - Libcef.dll
- Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer) - version.dll
- LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application) - msvcp140.dll
- bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information) - snmpapi.dll
"The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files," Sophos said. "This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims' environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts."
The DLL is designed to load and execute an encrypted payload ("config.ini"), which functions as a backdoor designed to enumerate local network and user accounts, as well as collect system metadata, running processes, keystrokes, and screenshots. Two different versions of the payload have been identified to date: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7.
The payload has also been found to communicate with external sites (e.g., file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io), likely in an attempt to receive additional tasking from its operators. In addition, version 1.1.5 has been observed using dc.cathaypacifice[.]com and net.dpworldto[.]com for command-and-control (C2).
Version 1.1.7 payloads, on the other hand, have been observed communicating with GitHub repositories ("github[.]com/LatonyCharnleyaW") via the API to download encrypted config files. The GitHub account is no longer accessible.
This is not the first time Chinese hacking groups have relied on DLL sideloading, nor is it the first time Sandboxie has been employed in such attacks. In July 2024, the APT41 threat actor leveraged a different executable signed by Sandboxie ("taskhost.exe") to sideload a malicious version of "sbiedll.dll" to deploy a backdoor called MoonWalk ultimately.
"The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective," Sophos said. "Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity."

articles.title: "Des scènes qui ne se sont jamais passées" : Emmanuel Macron s’attaque aux images IA du 17 octobre
articles.text:
En déplacement à Doha, Emmanuel Macron a dénoncé ce mercredi une manipulation étrangère de l’information après les manifestations du 17 octobre. Le président pointe les images générées par intelligence artificielle et s’en prend directement à Donald Trump.
Les images générées par intelligence artificielle qui ont accompagné les manifestations du 17 octobre ont fini par s'inviter au sommet de l'État. Devant la presse ce mercredi 21 octobre à Doha, dernière étape de sa tournée dans le Golfe, Emmanuel Macron a pris soin de séparer ce qui s'est passé dans la rue de ce qui s'est raconté ensuite en ligne, avec notamment la vague d'images IA. Le chef de l’État écarte l’hypothèse d’une ingérence étrangère visible dans les violences elles-mêmes, mais pas dans la manière dont elles ont été racontées en ligne. Il vise au passage plusieurs dirigeants étrangers, Donald Trump en tête.
Depuis Doha, Macron accuse des dirigeants étrangers de relayer des images IA sur la France
Sur les événements récents eux-mêmes, le président Macron dit ne voir « pas d'ingérence étrangère visible ». Pour la suite, donc après les violences et pillages du samedi 17 octobre, c'est une autre histoire. Le chef de l'État dénonce une « manipulation étrangère de l'information », qui a donné lieu à des commentaires « inacceptables autant que stupides », prononcées parfois par ses homologues. Dans son viseur, il y a d'abord des images générées par l'intelligence artificielle montrant « des scènes qui ne se sont jamais passées en France ». Il y a ensuite le récit d'un pays envahi par des « hordes de migrants et d'islamistes », qu'il qualifie de « totalement faux ».
Ces images, nous les décortiquions dès le 19 octobre. Depuis plusieurs jours effectivement, des comptes très suivis sur les réseaux glissent des visuels fabriqués ou retouchés par IA au milieu des vraies photos des manifestations. Le plus loufoque montre par exemple une Panthère rose arrêtée devant un camion de CRS. Il a notamment été relayé par Sprinter Press, un compte régulièrement épinglé pour avoir diffusé de la désinformation russe, et le détecteur SynthID de Google l'a démasqué.
Le plus insidieux, c'est peut-être d'un couple d'octogénaires en sous-vêtements, prétendument dépouillé place de la République. Sa photo, au mieux retouchée par IA, a frôlé le million de vues sur le réseau social d'Elon Musk, X. Au 20 octobre, le parquet de Paris n'avait été saisi d'aucune plainte. Certains de ces visuels ont même été partagés par des élus avides de récupération politique, et même un syndicat de police.
Donald Trump, cible d'un président agacé
Mais Emmanuel Macron ne s'en est pas tenu aux pixels mercredi. « Dans ces moments-là, on voit qui aime la France et qui ne l'aime pas », a-t-il glissé, avant de formellement acquiescer lorsqu'il était fut invité par un journaliste à confirmer que Donald Trump étaient parmi ceux qui « parlent mal de notre pays ». « Ces gens m'indisposent », a-t-il ajouté, visiblement très remonté. Dimanche, sur sa plateforme Truth Social, le président américain assurait que la France « brûle », accusait l'immigration et exhortait Paris à fermer ses frontières. Son vice-président, JD Vance, en a rajouté en reprochant aux progressistes occidentaux d'avoir « importé le tiers-monde » en France. Le Hongrois Péter Magyar et le Salvadorien Nayib Bukele ont, eux aussi, livré leur lecture des événements.
Le chef de l'État français déplore plus largement des dirigeants en campagne, « dans la région ou de l'autre côté de l'Atlantique », qui reprennent « parfois avec crédulité » ce que diffuse l'IA. « Ils font campagne sur notre dos », a-t-il tranché.
En ce qui concerne le maintien de l'ordre, il juge l'état d'urgence inutile à ce stade, sans l'exclure si la situation venait à le justifier. Les préfets peuvent déjà décréter des couvre-feux ou interdire des rassemblements. Les enquêtes se poursuivent et les premières décisions de justice sont tombées. Selon lui, c'est assez pour préserver le calme retrouvé depuis lundi. Signe des temps : une crise se gère désormais aussi image par image.

articles.title: 'I love third-person shooters and guns' – Anomalith producer reveals the origins of the upcoming 'mutating girl' survival game
articles.text:
Anomalith producer reveals that 'liminal spaces, including things like the Backrooms' inspired the upcoming third-person survival shooter
FuRyu's ‘mutating girl’ shooter arrives later this month
Anomalith might be one of the most interesting releases of 2026. A third-person survival shooter set in a twisted, retro vision of Japan, it’s a major departure from publisher FuRyu Corporation’s usual role-playing game (RPG) output.
It looks almost like the company’s take on Resident Evil, with 17-year-old protagonist Reona Minazuki venturing into deadly anomaly zones filled with grotesque creatures at the behest of a shadowy government organization.
Real-time gun combat, managing your small inventory, and keeping track of precious ammunition form a key part of every mission. Each run unfolds in an almost extraction-shooter-like format, and between missions you can use the resources you’ve scavenged to upgrade your gear.
There’s more to Minazuki than meets the eye, though, with the hero able to harness a mysterious set of mutant powers brought on by exposure to these supernatural environments. I spoke to producer Gai Kidokoro over email to learn a little more about how this project took shape and discover some of what’s in store for players.
Expanded arsenal
Anomalith is Kidokoro’s first original project, having joined FuRyu in the company’s anime division, which has helped produce hit titles like Is It Wrong to Try to Pick Up Girls in a Dungeon?, before making the leap to its gaming business to direct some licensed titles. Working on games has “always been an area I was interested in,” he says, adding that his career has been “a little different from that of FuRyu’s other producers.”
It therefore seems only fitting that he is producing quite a unique project, with Anomalith standing apart as FuRyu’s first third-person shooter. Interestingly, Kidokoro says that the genre was chosen because both he and the director “love third-person shooters and guns” and set out to create something based on the things they enjoy.
“Rather than thinking, 'Let’s deliberately challenge ourselves with a completely different genre,' it was really more about wanting to make a game in a genre that we personally love,” he continues.

This fascination with firearms seems evident in the game’s weapon customization system, which lets players “swap out a fairly detailed range of parts,” including a variety of attachments such as “sights, grips, stocks, and more.” These help you personalize the appearance of each gun, but also provide statistical bonuses to help in the field.
The producer is also keen to highlight the player’s ability to scavenge “pieces of equipment called Artifacts that enhance your character’s stats” and change your overall build.
“These include loot-based, hack-and-slash-style elements,” he teases, “and if you manage to equip an Artifact with extremely high values, some skills have the potential to become incredibly powerful.”
The team is well aware that not everyone is going to be interested in tweaking their guns or experimenting with the nitty-gritty of their character’s stats, which is why the game offers a wealth of cosmetic options for players to outfit themselves with – some already available to try in the recent free Steam demo.
“We realized that there are quite a lot of people who don’t necessarily get the same enjoyment we do from firing their favorite, carefully customized gun,” Kidokoro begins. “We thought, 'Maybe adding character outfits and customization would make it more fun for those players,' and that’s why we ended up including such detailed character customization options. Judging from the response to the demo, I’m really glad we added the outfit customization.”
Uncanny valley
The world design is shaping up to be a treat, with plenty of intricate detail to pore over. In fact, Kidokoro highlights this as one part of the experience that he is most excited about. “The development team has put a tremendous amount of effort into designing the Otherworlds,” he explains. “There are many areas where something may initially look like nothing more than an ordinary ceiling, but if you stop and look up, you might find something that gives you a real sense of unease.”
He describes the fundamental concept behind it all as the “anxiety and fear lurking within familiar scenery” and reveals that it was inspired by popular ideas of “liminal spaces, including things like the Backrooms,” referring to the viral meme featuring endless wallpapered corridors that recently inspired a horror film adaptation.
“Within the development team, we often use phrases like ‘give it a liminal-space atmosphere’ when discussing the visual direction.”
This extends to the soundtrack. Aside from the game’s title theme, the music of Anomalith doesn’t feature any vocal tracks. Nevertheless, the producer argues fans “can definitely look forward to the soundtrack” and warns “many of the tracks are quite dark and unsettling.” He jokes: “I recommend listening to them during the daytime.”
Although Anomalith seems very different, long-time FuRyu fans will recognize some common elements shared with the publisher’s past games, such as the focus on a teenage protagonist. Kidokoro thinks the reasons behind this particular motif “would vary” depending on the title, but personally reckons “that it is easier for audiences to emotionally root for younger characters.”
“Watching boys and girls confront unreasonable circumstances and ultimately overcome them can also feel more hopeful and moving than a story centered on adults,” he continues. “Of course, we have been influenced by other games. However, we try to keep those influences as references rather than simply copying them. Our main criterion is always whether a particular element is necessary for players to enjoy the world and experience of Anomalith.”
We will be able to find out whether this formula pays off when Anomalith launches for Nintendo Switch 2, PC, and PlayStation 5 on October 29, 2026.

articles.title: Lista de celulares que perderán WhatsApp el 31 de octubre de 2026
articles.text:
La lista de celulares que perderán WhatsApp el 31 de octubre de 2026 incluye modelos antiguos de Samsung, Motorola, LG y Sony que no alcanzan los requisitos mínimos de la aplicación.
La pérdida de acceso no implica que las cuentas desaparezcan de forma automática. El problema afecta al dispositivo que ya no puede ejecutar una versión compatible del sistema operativo. Quien conserve su número, su copia de seguridad y su cuenta podrá restaurar sus conversaciones en otro teléfono que cumpla las condiciones técnicas exigidas por WhatsApp.
WhatsApp exige Android 6.0 y iOS 15.5 como mínimo
La aplicación de mensajería establece que los equipos con Android deben operar con Android 6.0 o una versión posterior. En los teléfonos de Apple, el requisito señalado es iOS 15.5 o una edición más reciente del sistema. Los móviles que no puedan actualizarse hasta esos niveles perderán la capacidad de instalar nuevas versiones o de mantener el funcionamiento del servicio.
La medida alcanza, sobre todo, a dispositivos lanzados hace más de una década. Muchos ya dejaron de recibir actualizaciones oficiales de sus fabricantes, una situación que limita el acceso a herramientas actuales y reduce las opciones de seguridad. El fin de la compatibilidad responde a la necesidad de que WhatsApp incorpore funciones nuevas sobre sistemas que aún reciben soporte técnico.
No todos los teléfonos antiguos quedarán fuera por la misma razón. Algunos mantienen una versión de Android o iOS cercana al mínimo requerido, mientras que otros ya no admiten ningún tipo de actualización. Por ello, la fecha no debe interpretarse como una baja general para todos los móviles veteranos, sino como un aviso para verificar cada modelo y su software instalado.
Estos son los modelos que podrían perder el acceso
Entre los equipos mencionados como posibles afectados aparecen varios teléfonos de Samsung, Motorola, LG y Sony. La lista incluye modelos que tuvieron amplia presencia en el mercado, pero que ya no cuentan con actualizaciones capaces de llevarlos a los requisitos actuales de la plataforma.
Los dispositivos son los siguientes:
- Samsung: Galaxy S3, Galaxy S4 Mini, Galaxy Note 2, Galaxy Core, Galaxy Trend y Galaxy Trend Lite.
- Motorola: Moto G de primera generación, Moto E de primera generación y Droid Razr HD.
- LG: Optimus G, Optimus L5, Optimus L7, Optimus F7, Lucid 2, Nexus 4 y G2 Mini.
- Sony: Xperia Z y Xperia SP.
La presencia de un equipo en esta relación no sustituye la revisión individual. Algunas variantes, actualizaciones disponibles según el país o modificaciones previas del sistema pueden alterar la versión instalada. La clave consiste en comprobar si el teléfono ejecuta Android 6.0 o superior, o iOS 15.5 en el caso de los iPhone.
Cómo comprobar la versión del sistema operativo
En un móvil Android, el procedimiento comienza en Ajustes. Después hay que entrar en “Acerca del teléfono” y buscar “Información de software” o “Versión de Android”. Si la cifra mostrada es inferior a Android 6.0, conviene revisar si el fabricante ofrece alguna actualización. Si no existe una versión posterior, el teléfono podría dejar de utilizar WhatsApp.
En los iPhone, se debe abrir Ajustes, seleccionar General y entrar en Información. Allí aparece la versión de iOS instalada. También resulta conveniente acceder a “Actualización de software” para comprobar si hay una edición más reciente compatible con el dispositivo. Instalar la última versión disponible puede prolongar el uso de aplicaciones que aún admiten el modelo.
Las actualizaciones no solo determinan el acceso a la mensajería. También corrigen problemas de seguridad, mejoran la estabilidad y permiten utilizar herramientas recientes. Un equipo que ya no recibe soporte puede mantener funciones básicas, pero acumula limitaciones frente a aplicaciones que modifican sus requisitos con el paso del tiempo.
La copia de seguridad permite conservar los chats
Si el teléfono no cumple las condiciones, será necesario migrar a otro equipo compatible. Antes de hacerlo, es importante crear una copia de seguridad de conversaciones, fotografías y documentos. En Android, WhatsApp permite guardar ese respaldo en Google Drive. En iPhone, la alternativa es iCloud.
Para realizar el proceso, hay que abrir WhatsApp, entrar en Ajustes, seleccionar Chats y pulsar en Copia de seguridad. Después, el usuario podrá restaurar la información desde el nuevo teléfono con la misma cuenta y el mismo número. La incompatibilidad afecta al móvil antiguo, no elimina la cuenta de WhatsApp, siempre que el respaldo se haya creado antes del cambio.

articles.title: Generative AI Is Erasing Behavioral Tells, Weakening Behavior-Only Detection, Proofpoint Reports
articles.text:
Generative AI has changed what a malicious email looks like. Messages that once gave themselves away through clumsy wording, generic pretexts, and reused templates now arrive fluent, personalized, and unique to each recipient, and the behavioral signals email filters have relied on for years are fading as a result.
Proofpoint shared several examples of the shift at its Protect 2026 conference. In one, a single threat actor contacted more than 30 real estate agents at the same company, each from a different account, about a different property, and in different words, before closing every thread with the same request: join a video meeting.
Federal data points the same way. The FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center counted more than 22,000 complaints involving AI in 2025, with nearly $900 million in associated losses, and logged 24,768 business email compromise (BEC) complaints with about $3.05 billion in reported losses, according to its 2025 Internet Crime Report.
What AI Changed
Email filters were built for attackers who had to cut corners. Researching a target, writing convincingly in a second language, impersonating a supplier, and producing enough variants to defeat signatures all took time, so attackers reused templates and infrastructure, and that reuse left patterns. Behavioral detection learned to spot them: new infrastructure, awkward language, odd timing, and requests that did not fit the conversation.
Generative AI removes those constraints:
- Language. Fluent, localized text in any language, with no typos or translation artifacts.
- Context. Replies that fit the thread, the recipient’s role, and the timing.
- Persona. Matched writing style, signature blocks, and fully fabricated conversation histories.
- Variation. A unique message for every recipient, generated in seconds, so there is no template to match.
The result, Proofpoint argues, is that behavior has become a weakening signal. When AI lets attackers make every message look normal, the analysis has to change too, from asking whether a message looks unusual to asking what it is trying to do.
Thirty Conversations, One Ask
The real estate campaign shows what that looks like in practice. Writing 30-plus distinct, plausible property enquiries, each tailored to a different listing and a different agent, is exactly the kind of work generative AI now does in seconds. The opening questions were mundane: whether a property was still open for inspection, what the price guide was, whether a viewing was possible that week. The sender mailboxes were real, and replies landed in threads the agents were already answering.
| Figure 1. Different properties, senders, and wording, with the same final ask in every thread. | 
In one thread, an inspection enquiry sent at 2:58 a.m. turned into a meeting invitation 13 minutes later, complete with a branded template and a claim that the meeting required the agent’s “immediate attention.” The join link was a genuine google.com redirect, so reputation checks read clean, while a parameter in the URL handed the click to an unrelated site.
Because each sender was making first contact, behavioral filters had no history to compare against, and because every message was different, there was no repeated content to match. What the messages shared was not how they looked but what they were trying to get the recipient to do.
AI makes it easy to run this pattern against any business that depends on hearing from strangers, including clinics taking new patients, firms signing new clients, banks opening accounts, and insurers quoting policies, Proofpoint said. A variant aimed at insurance agents used quote requests, neighbor referrals, and coverage questions to build trust before sending a spoofed conference invitation that delivered the payload.
AI-Powered Disruption
AI has also made it easier to run campaigns that aim to disrupt rather than steal. Proofpoint described hostile communications campaigns in which hundreds or thousands of senders write to the same executives, each on a topic tailored to the target’s industry. Some messages carry derogatory language; others carry AI-generated or manipulated images that mock the recipient.
| Figure 2. Hostile communications campaigns carry no payload. The signal is the pattern. | 
These messages have no link to detonate and no credential to harvest, and any one of them could pass for a single angry correspondent. Scoring messages one at a time will not catch them. The analysis has to recognize disruptive intent across the whole set, and read text and imagery together, since the hostility may sit in an AI-generated picture.
Legitimacy on Demand
The same shift applies to phishing infrastructure. One phishing-as-a-service kit Proofpoint highlighted presents a single flow behind four different disguises: a court access portal, a document-signing request, an identity check, and a finance report library. Each page displays a verification code and directs the victim to a legitimate sign-in page to paste it. Because the attacker generated the code, entering it authorizes the attacker’s session, a technique known as device-code phishing.
| Figure 3. Four pretexts in front of one device-code flow. | 
Swapping the disguise is trivial for the operator, so the visual and linguistic fingerprints defenders might match change from one campaign to the next while the objective stays fixed.
BEC shows AI’s effect on context most clearly. In another example, a single email contains a quoted thread in which an impersonated audit vendor and an executive at the target appear to agree on an invoice, a 50 percent loyalty rebate, and a payment date. The attached invoice itemizes audit phases, hours, and rates, and the closing line asks for payment that day to a remittance address that differs from the actual sending address.
| Figure 4. A single BEC message with a fabricated thread and invoice. Names and domains are anonymized. | 
Writing both sides of that exchange and building a believable invoice once took research and hours of work. A language model drafts all of it in seconds, which removes the effort that used to limit how many targets received this kind of attention.
Changing the Analysis: From Behavior to Intent
If AI lets attackers control how a message looks, the signal that remains is what the message is trying to accomplish. Proofpoint’s approach evaluates that objective, whether it is plausible given the relationship and conversation, and what technique is being used to pursue it. The company announced its Nexus Intent-Based Detection Model in September as part of what it calls the Agentic Collaboration Security system.
A bank-detail change request illustrates the approach. The message comes from a known supplier’s real mailbox, inside a real thread, with a clean reputation, and its language is exactly what AI makes easy to produce. Read for intent, however, five details line up:
- It is the supplier’s first banking change in years.
- The request does not match the invoice-confirmation thread it replies to.
- The deadline is tied to a specific payment run.
- The sender asks to keep the exchange off the thread and deal with one person.
- Verification is closed off in advance with a claim that the finance mailbox is “mid-migration.”
| Figure 5. A bank-detail change request read for intent. | 
AI can polish the wording of a request like this. But the intent must match the attacker’s path to success, whether that’s the user clicking a link, entering credentials or joining a meeting. That’s why intent holds up where behavior is a less reliable indicator.
Proofpoint positions intent analysis as a third layer rather than a replacement. Traditional detection, built on rules, signatures, infrastructure reputation, and indicators of compromise, still clears known threats quickly and at scale. Modern detection, built on threat actor intelligence and behavioral baselines, still catches known actors and senders that deviate. Intent reasoning targets the AI-crafted messages that pass both.
| Figure 6. Three layers of detection, each answering a different question. | 
Defenders are using AI here too. Because running deep language-model analysis on every message would be too slow for mail flow, the model is split into three tiers that match depth to ambiguity:
- Tier one (flash models) evaluates all mail in under 500 milliseconds using machine learning, threat intelligence, computer vision, and language models.
- Tier two (extended thinking) handles fewer than 1 percent of messages in seconds to minutes, adding sandboxing, topic and tone analysis, and an organizational graph.
- Tier three (deep thinking) handles fewer than 0.01 percent in minutes, adding multi-stage language model analysis, voice and video, and profiles of privileged individuals.
| Figure 7. Multi-tier reasoning: most mail is resolved in milliseconds, and only the most ambiguous reaches deep analysis. | 
A message one tier cannot resolve moves to the next, and a malicious verdict can come at any tier. The organizational graph is designed to surface campaigns like the real estate example, where AI-varied requests land across one company but no single mailbox sees more than one.
Investigating at Machine Speed
AI has also compressed attacker timelines. Automated campaigns can generate and adapt hundreds of messages in the time an analyst triages one, so a missed detection is rarely a single email; it is often a campaign that already includes replies, sign-ins, and mailbox changes. Proofpoint argues that investigation has to change as well, from analyst-driven, ticket-by-ticket review to agentic investigation that keeps pace with the attacker.
Its Threat Investigation Agent is designed to run one investigation across email, identity, messaging, browser, and supplier activity, map the blast radius, and feed findings back into detection. Use cases include account takeover, abuse mailbox triage, advanced campaigns, false positive and false negative feedback, and third-party investigative requests.
| Figure 8. A sample account takeover case in the Threat Investigation Agent, with automatic actions, pending approvals, and an event timeline. | 
In an example case, an RFP-themed credential-phishing lure led to the takeover of a finance user’s account. The attacker signed in from New York and then Dallas, added a mailbox rule to hide replies, and sent about 100 phishing messages to 42 internal recipients. The agent contained the incident four minutes after the trigger, retrieving 92 outbound messages, deleting the rule, blocking the URL, and restoring the user’s settings.
Four higher-consequence actions, including a credential reset and 14 days of outbound inspection, were held for human approval. The case also lists what the agent could not determine, such as who clicked a link that sat inside a PDF and was never rewritten, and records failed actions, such as quarantine attempts that did not complete.
Defending Against What Attackers Want, Not How They Look
The examples Proofpoint shared point to the same conclusion: generative AI has changed the threat landscape faster than behavior-based analysis can keep up. Attackers can now make every message fluent, plausible, and unique, run campaigns that look like ordinary business, and adapt them at machine speed. The behavioral tells that filters once depended on are disappearing.
A changed threat calls for changed analysis: keeping traditional and modern detection for what they still catch well, adding intent-based reasoning that asks what a message is trying to achieve, scaling that reasoning across tiers so it keeps pace with mail flow, and investigating incidents at the same speed attackers now operate.
Learn more about Proofpoint’s approach to AI, and see a demo, at Proofpoint Nexus.

articles.title: Microsoft pensait en avoir fini avec ce bug VPN sur Windows 11, raté !
articles.text:
Le correctif était annoncé, l'incident classé comme résolu. Une semaine plus tard, Microsoft fait marche arrière : le bug d'Always On VPN perturbe toujours les connexions professionnelles sur Windows 11.
Depuis septembre, certaines configurations VPN rencontrent des difficultés pour établir ou rétablir leur connexion au réseau de l'entreprise, privant parfois les salariés de leur accès distant aux ressources professionnelles. Microsoft pensait avoir réglé le problème avec les mises à jour de sécurité du 13 octobre, avant de reconnaître, une semaine plus tard, que le correctif annoncé n'avait pas fonctionné. Le 20 octobre, l'éditeur a donc modifié les notes de version de KB5127648 et KB5127646 pour en retirer la correction du bug, toujours en attente d'une solution définitive.
La sélection automatique des protocoles toujours en cause
Pour rappel, le bug concerne plus précisément les configurations d'Always On VPN qui sélectionnent automatiquement un protocole de connexion ou tentent d'en utiliser un autre en cas d'échec, par exemple en passant d'IKEv2 à SSTP. Dans ces conditions, la connexion peut rester bloquée sur « Connexion en cours », multiplier les tentatives infructueuses ou afficher le message « Le port spécifié est déjà utilisé ».
Dans une communication adressée aux administrateurs informatiques, référencée WI1482218 et relayée par The Register, Microsoft a ramené le statut de l'incident à « atténué » et présenté ses excuses pour avoir annoncé sa résolution prématurément. Les entreprises concernées doivent donc continuer d'appliquer le contournement préconisé par l'éditeur, qui consiste à désactiver la sélection automatique et à imposer un seul protocole de connexion.
Microsoft prévoit (à nouveau) de publier un véritable correctif dans les prochaines semaines, sans avancer de date précise. En attendant, ne désinstallez pas les mises à jour d’octobre, qui corrigent d’autres bugs pénalisants et s’inscrivent dans un Patch Tuesday ayant traité plus de 1 400 failles de sécurité.

articles.title: ‘It's our mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more’: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlines what businesses need to conquer the AI frontier ecosystem
articles.text:
‘It's our mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more’: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlines what businesses need to conquer the AI frontier ecosystem
Don’t be overwhelmed by AI, Satya Nadella says
- Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella extols virtues of "frontier ecosystem" for AI
- AI can do great things for human workers, but there still needs to be some control
- Microsoft reveals new research showing a divide between bosses and employees over the future of AI in the workplace
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has urged businesses to embrace AI even further to push on and succeed, but urged caution around giving such systems too much control in everyday work tasks.
"When I think about what keeps us grounded every day at Microsoft, it's our mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more,” Nadella told the company’s Frontier Tour London event.
Looking at what he called the "frontier ecosystem", Nadella identified three key pillars which need to be tackled - including recapturing individual empowerment, as although AI is taking charge of the dullest parts of our jobs, there is still need for a human to have control.
Frontier AI
Nadella also highlighted "the reverse information paradox" - with a digital learning system which is constantly improving itself, the challenge is for organisations to "capture that knowledge and keep it locally to yourself...in other words, you have to own the knowledge that gets created, both with the human capital that you have, as well as the token capital that you generate"
The final challenge concerns trust, as Nadella noted, “our scaling laws are producing even more powerful models that are less and less trustworthy…you need to treat these models as new forms of insiders, and create a zero-trust architecture around it.”
The speech came as Microsoft unveiled new research revealing something of a divide between bosses and employees over the future of AI in the workplace.
It found the vast majority (84%) of business leaders believe the UK can become a world-leading AI economy within five years, compared with just 41% of employees.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
But it also noted that workers are becoming increasingly concerned about the impact on jobs and opportunities for young people, with over half (57%) of employees using AI at work afraid it will reduce opportunities for young people, while 35% fear for their own job security.
For bosses, the future was a bit brighter, with 90% of leaders claiming they had a clear AI strategy in their business, while 84% of those in organisations already adopting AI say they’ve already experienced moderate or significant changes to how their work gets done.
“Bending the curve changes what the UK can achieve, increasing productivity, business growth, better public services, and the measure of that progress is the difference that people feel in their everyday lives,” noted Darren Hardman, Microsoft UK CEO.
“We will not bend the curve unless people see a place for themselves in what comes next…the question is no longer whether you have a strategy, it’s whether AI is actually changing how work gets done.”
“For organizations here, the challenge is to turn AI's potential into improvements that people can feel in the work they do, the services they use, and the opportunities that are open to them...our role at Microsoft to bring intelligence and trust together in AI that puts your organization's knowledge to work helping people achieve more while providing the safeguards and visibility to stay in control.”

articles.title: PHP2Shell: What Actually Protects You Before the 14:00 UTC PHP RCE Patch, and What Doesn't
articles.text:
You cannot fully block the two critical PHP flaws called PHP2Shell before today's fix, and the one setting being passed around as a workaround is not enough on its own, the security firm that suggested it now says.
PHP will release the fix at 14:00 UTC on October 21 for two flaws it rates 9.2 out of 10, and has given no workaround of its own. Until you can install it, what lowers your risk is taking exposed PHP off the internet or behind access controls, cutting what a compromised server can reach, and having the update ready to apply the moment it lands.
Cloudflare says it is seeing early attempts to exploit the flaws, and has pushed emergency rules for sites behind it that it calls a stopgap until you patch. No compromise has been confirmed, the public exploit code going around has not been shown to work, and neither flaw is in CISA's catalog of known exploited flaws. PHP has not said which versions are affected, which part of PHP is involved, or whether any setting changes the risk; it says the full details and the fixed versions come with the release.
At the time of writing, that release was not yet out. So nobody outside the group that found the flaws can test whether a given defense works, which is why the advice below is about lowering risk, not promising safety.
The setting you were told to change is not protection
The workaround spreading on social media and security blogs is one line in a PHP configuration file: session.upload_progress.enabled=0. It turns off Session Upload Progress, a PHP feature that's enabled by default, which records how far a file upload has progressed so another request can check on it.
GMO Flatt Security, a Tokyo security firm, suggested setting it early on October 21, saying it could not be sure the change fully addresses the flaws but thought it would help with some probability.
Later the same day, the firm walked that back. In an update timestamped 14:00 Japan time (05:00 UTC), it said the setting alone is not a complete fix and that attacks getting around it are expected. It told administrators to prepare their update, watch for attack traffic before the release, and apply the fix as soon as it is out.
Two people from the PHP project said the same thing more bluntly. Replying to someone who suggested the upload-progress setting might patch the flaw, Gina Peter Banyard, a PHP core developer and documentation writer funded by the PHP Foundation, wrote: "The only thing I can say is that the only mitigation is patching / upgrading PHP. I sadly know too much." Joe Ferguson, the release manager for the coming PHP 8.6, put it shorter: "ini settings won't save you."
The setting cannot be relied on for two reasons. GMO Flatt expects a way around it but has not said what that is. And the whole idea that the flaw lives in Session Upload Progress is a guess: PHP has not confirmed it, the firm itself said it holds only so far as its own research matches PHP2Shell, and an independent code audit argues the specific bug others describe in that feature does not exist in released PHP. That audit is from an anonymous account and PHP's own code will settle it, but it is one more reason not to treat the setting as a shield.
Not everyone agrees. One vendor, Upwind, still lists the setting as an immediate mitigation, passing along another researcher's analysis rather than its own tests. watchTowr, which reproduced one of the flaws, says there is "no confirmed patch or workaround at this time."
If you already set it
No one is telling you to undo the change. The instruction is only not to count it as protection. PHP's own manual already advises turning the feature off where an application does not use upload progress bars, because the stored file names and field names "are not validated and may contain PHP code." If you turned it on by mistake somewhere that needs it, the only cost is that upload progress bars stop working.
Check that the change is actually in effect on the process that serves web traffic, not on the command line. The setting is INI_PERDIR, so it can be set in php.ini, .htaccess, or .user.ini.
A .user.ini file is read only by the CGI and FastCGI versions of PHP, not by the Apache module, and PHP re-reads it only every 300 seconds by default, so a change there can take five minutes to apply.
Under the Apache module, use .htaccess or the server config. Confirm the value on PHP-FPM or mod_php, whichever serves your site, not on php -i at the shell.
If you can patch at 14:00 UTC
Get ready now. GMO Flatt's advice is to confirm your update steps and the checks you run afterward, rehearse any config change, and line up the people and approvals for a possible emergency restart. When the fix lands, update the runtime that serves web requests, which is PHP-FPM, mod_php, or CGI, not the application on top of it.
PHP issues fixes only for its four supported branches, 8.2 through 8.5. Which exact versions carry the fix and how far back the flaws extend will be announced with the release.
The Hacker News reported the branch support and the wider background in its earlier coverage of the disclosure.
If you cannot patch at once, or run an unsupported version
Where an immediate update is not possible, CERT-EU advises organizations to "consider isolating internet-facing applications from public networks until a fix can be applied." Banyard put the same point from inside the project: turning a server off for a day "might be the most sensible thing to do. But that is far from a reasonable thing to demand for most people." Short of shutting down, restrict reach: put the site behind a VPN, allowlisted clients, or authenticated access at the edge, and check that traffic cannot reach the origin directly around those controls.
Shrink what an attacker gets if the server is taken over. GMO Flatt's other steps are to reduce the data stored on the server, reduce its privileges, remove stored credentials, including cloud roles, and ensure logging is enabled and kept in a secure location so you can investigate later.
Branches older than 8.2, including 8.1, 7.x, and 5.x, are end-of-life and receive no PHP fixes. For those, upgrade, take the system offline, or isolate it; a Linux distribution or hosting provider may backport a fix on its own schedule.
A web application firewall is a stopgap here, not a fix, and Cloudflare says so itself. It has pushed emergency rules for the known exploit paths, free tier included, which its CTO calls "a STOPGAP only" ahead of patching. Such rules only see traffic that passes through Cloudflare, and they can miss new attack paths as they appear.
If someone else runs your PHP
Updating WordPress, Laravel, or another application does not update the PHP runtime underneath it; that comes from your server package, host, or container image. On managed or shared hosting, ask your provider when a fixed PHP build will land and have them stand by.
Hosting providers build their packages only after PHP ships the fix: CloudLinux, for one, says its updated packages depend on the upstream release and will be posted when ready.
What to check when the release lands
Exploitation is early and unconfirmed. Cloudflare reports emerging attempts; watchTowr says it reproduced one flaw but has not reported attacks; the public exploit code going around has not been shown to work; and neither flaw was in CISA's catalog of known exploited flaws when it was last checked on October 21.
A researcher has posted a video said to demonstrate the exploit chain, and the audit above states that the circulating proof-of-concept code does not fire against released PHP. Treat all of this as a snapshot that can change by the hour.
When the fix ships, check the fixed version for your branch, which versions PHP lists as affected, whether PHP confirms or rejects any setting as a mitigation, and whether the session code changed, which also answers the dispute over where the flaw lives.
The fixed versions and the advisory will appear on php.net and through PHP's GitHub security advisories, where the project assigns its own identifiers. After updating, review your logs for anything that happened before you patched.

articles.title: Netflix superó las expectativas de ganancias, pero sus acciones cayeron por el temor a perder audiencia
articles.text:
Netflix reportó sus ganancias del tercer trimestre por encima de lo previsto, pero sus acciones cayeron con fuerza en las operaciones posteriores al cierre de Wall Street tras recortar la proyección de ingresos publicitarios y reconocer dudas sobre el crecimiento de las horas de visualización.
La compañía facturó USD 12.870 millones entre julio y septiembre, un 12% más que un año antes, en línea con lo que esperaban los analistas. La ganancia por acción llegó a 87 centavos, por encima de los 82 previstos y de los 59 centavos del mismo trimestre de 2025.
Pese a esas cifras, el mercado castigó al título: las acciones de Netflix cayeron cerca de un 6% en las operaciones posteriores al cierre, según informó CNBC. La compañía redujo su previsión de ingresos publicitarios para 2026 de USD 3.000 millones a USD 2.700 millones, algo que atribuyó a demoras en el despliegue de nuevas herramientas para anunciantes.
Netflix también achicó el rango de su proyección de ingresos anuales a USD 51.100 millones, en el extremo más bajo de lo que había anticipado y por debajo del consenso de Wall Street, según el portal especializado Deadline. Los mayores gastos, entre ellos los vinculados a despidos recientes, también presionarán los márgenes operativos del último trimestre del año.
La audiencia que no termina de crecer
El reporte llegó después de que la empresa despidiera, la semana pasada, a unos 1.000 empleados, el 6% de su plantilla global y el recorte más profundo desde 2022, según Deadline. Los despidos golpearon sobre todo a las áreas de producto, tecnología, legales y recursos humanos.
El trasfondo es una preocupación persistente por el tiempo que la gente pasa mirando Netflix. Según estimaciones del banco Jefferies, el promedio mensual de horas vistas por usuario cayó de 66 horas en la primera mitad de 2023 a 49 horas en el mismo período de 2026, una baja de alrededor del 26%.
La firma de medición Apptopia agregó que la cancelación de suscripciones en Estados Unidos subió 16,6% interanual en el tercer trimestre, el doble de ritmo que en los tres trimestres anteriores, mientras que las descargas de la aplicación en Estados Unidos y Canadá bajaron 20%.
YouTube, de Google, es hoy el destino de streaming más visto en Estados Unidos desde hace tres años y casi duplica el tiempo de consumo de Netflix, de acuerdo con datos de Nielsen citados por Reuters.
En su carta a los accionistas, la compañía admitió la inquietud de los inversores: “sabemos que hay cierta preocupación de los inversores sobre nuestro crecimiento en horas de visualización”, aunque sostuvo que el compromiso de los usuarios “sigue siendo saludable”.
Un recambio completo en el área creativa
La presión sobre la audiencia ya había provocado un recambio en la cúpula creativa. Bela Bajaria dejó la dirección de contenidos y será reemplazada por Peter Rice, exejecutivo de Disney, a partir del 26 de octubre. También salieron el jefe de cine Dan Lin, su segundo Doug Belgrad y la directora de series originales Carolina Garcia.
El codirector ejecutivo Ted Sarandos había anticipado el malestar semanas antes, en la cumbre Screentime de Bloomberg, al admitir que la plataforma “no está creciendo tan rápido” como él quisiera. Su socio al mando, Greg Peters, calificó de todas formas el nivel de compromiso de los usuarios en Estados Unidos como “sólido”.
No todas las señales fueron negativas. Netflix destacó que el consumo de contenido no hablado en inglés ya supera un tercio del total, frente a menos del 10% hace unos años, impulsado por series como la surcoreana Plastic Beauty y la india Lock Upp, que ayudó a que el país sumara su mayor cantidad de altas pagas en un trimestre.
El próximo movimiento concreto llegará el 26 de octubre, cuando Rice asuma oficialmente como jefe de contenidos con la tarea de revertir la desaceleración que la propia compañía reconoció ante sus inversores.

articles.title: Navigateur : Proton vient de sanctionner Chromium, mais son patron l'a presque adopté
articles.text:
Proton vient tout juste de publier un petit comparatif des navigateurs Web misant sur la confidentialité. L’entreprise note moins bien ceux basés sur Chromium, le moteur de Google. Pourtant en début de mois, Andy Yen semblait bien moins alarmé.
La présence de Chromium dans un navigateur doit-elle être sanctionnée quand on adresse le sujet de la vie privée ? Il semblerait y avoir une discordance sur le sujet chez Proton.
Un critère d’indépendance qui n’empêche pas Brave de gagner
Le comparatif note cinq navigateurs sur 10 pour trois critères : l’indépendance vis-à-vis de Google, la protection contre le fingerprinting et la facilité d’usage. Sont passés en revue : Brave, Vivaldi, Firefox, Zen et LibreWolf.
Rappelons que le fingerprinting, c’est l’empreinte matérielle d’une session d’un internaute. Un site peut reconnaître un navigateur particulier grâce à un ensemble de détails (résolution d’écran, polices installées, réglages, extensions installées, langues…), sans avoir besoin de cookies.
Côté indépendance, le moteur de rendu, le composant qui affiche les pages, compte beaucoup. Brave et Vivaldi utilisent Chromium, le projet open source à l’origine de Chrome. Pour ce segment, ils obtiennent la note de 4/10. Proton reconnaît que Brave ajoute ses propres protections, mais précise qu’il « s'appuie toujours sur une technologie développée au sein de l'écosystème de Google ». Firefox, qui repose sur son propre moteur (Gecko), reçoit 7/10, car Mozilla a historiquement touché des revenus conséquents de Google pour que son moteur de recherche soit proposé par défaut. De leur côté, LibreWolf et Zen, dérivés de Firefox, grimpent à 9/10.
Les notes sont ensuite additionnées, sans pondération. Brave l’emporte avec 23/30, porté par son 10/10 en fingerprinting (il modifie certaines caractéristiques du navigateur d’une visite à l’autre pour brouiller l’empreinte) et son 9/10 en usage. LibreWolf et Zen suivent avec 22, Firefox avec 21. L’indépendance de Google représente donc un tiers du total, et un navigateur Chromium peut gagner malgré son 4/10.
Interrogé par nos soins en début de mois, le PDG de Proton Andy Yen, lui, relativise cette dépendance. Dans notre interview, il résume ainsi le problème :
"Ce que les gens reprochent à Chromium, au fond, c’est Google, non ? Si on retire Google de l’équation, c'est en réalité du très bon code."
Il n’exclut pas que Google puisse un jour polluer le code du projet, voire rendre son utilisation par des tiers plus difficile. Mais il voit « suffisamment d'acteurs construire par-dessus Chromium » et dans un tel scénario, « une communauté assez large se mobiliserait pour rendre un fork possible ». Cela inclurait donc tous les éditeurs actuels utilisant le code, parmi lesquels Opera, Brave, Vivaldi, Samsung ou Microsoft.
Le PDG de Proton a botté en touche sur un éventuel navigateur développé en interne. Mais l’offre d’emploi publiée cet été pour un ingénieur logiciel intégrant « notre équipe produit navigateur, pour contribuer à construire un navigateur internet pensé d'abord pour la confidentialité, utilisé par des millions de personnes dans le monde », ne laisse pas trop de doute.
Reste que si Proton appliquait sa propre grille, un navigateur construit sur Chromium recevrait donc la même note que Brave et Vivaldi sur l’indépendance. Il devrait par ailleurs surpasser Brave et Firefox en matière d’ergonomie pour se placer en tête.
- Respect et protection de la vie privée
- Interface et ergonomie soignée
- Le plus rapide du marché

articles.title: I played Dawn of War 4, and it took me back to LAN parties, replaying campaigns repeatedly, and building massive armies for map domination just as I did in the first game over two decades ago — and I simply must have more
articles.text:
I’ve been watching my Dawn of War 4 armies dominate enemies, completely cover maps, and take more resource points than you can shake a Gretchen at, and it’s reminded me why I fell in love with the first game all those years ago
It’s been a long time since I’ve poured so many hours into Warhammer 40,000, but playing a bunch of the Dawn of War 4 campaign has absolutely captivated me, and almost made it feel like I was playing from my living room floor 30 years ago all over again.
After seeing a glimpse of the game last summer, I knew it was on the right track, but after a couple of weeks with Dawn of War 4, it’s safe to say that the series’ rip-roaring, gritty action, and moreish strategic map play is back with a vengeance, and channels all that made the first game brilliant.
My time with the chunky preview build has shown that King Art Games are an incredibly safe set of hands for the next Dawn of War game.
Going back to Kronus
The planet of Kronus provides the setting for Dawn of War 4, and while a part of me wonders whether it might have been more exciting to go for a brand new setting and premise, the familiar planet is still superbly executed by the new developer.
Each map is extremely well detailed and feels alive with wind-blown sand and tumbleweeds across barren landscapes, blinking lights and crumbling epic architecture in urban maps, and wonderfully icy and snowy maps providing some of the best backdrops.
No matter where you are, though, you’re always cheered on by some mega, epic battle music, and the individual unit audio from ambient mechanical whirring, distinct machine clunking, and furious fighting are all absolute chef's kiss level.
Underneath the aesthetic excellence, there is a real meaty campaign here. My preview build dived in and out of a few armies’ storylines, and the branching narrative is interesting and genuinely compelling, with twists that you can make decisions to impact through mission selection and choices (from what I’ve seen), while the accompanying cutscenes are also fantastic.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Even the in-game story moments help to give me the feeling of those excellent battle write-ups in the old White Dwarf magazines that I remember poring over for hours at a time.
Unrivaled units and chaotic combat
Moving your forces around that campaign is the true highlight: this is a properly meaty and fabulous strategy experience, and a 40K experience.
Taking control of the Orks or Adeptus Mechanicus in my preview, it really does feel like the perfect real-time recreation of seeing your miniatures on a tabletop. The action can be slower and methodical; or you can embrace some chaos and have fights on multiple fronts as you aim to use speed to your advantage over the battlefield.
There were multiple times in both scenarios where managing large masses of a mix of units was a genuine thrill, with each resource point captured, the mowing down of enemy infantry, or the blowing up of tanks with grenade barrages more satisfying than the last.
If you remember the best thing about moving units across maps in the Dawn of War games of yesteryear, then you’re in for a treat. Orks feel as wild and chaotic as they should; and the Adeptus Mechanicus have wonderful machine-focused units as well as biomechanic infantry that can pack more of a punch than you think, especially from cover.
However, Dawn of War 4 simultaneously feels more modern, and there’s an effort to streamline some controls to make things more straightforward. You can drag over a whole heap of enemies, and your units will automatically attack the ones most vulnerable to their attack type; and you can right-click on any unit’s ability so it will automatically trigger during missions.
Engaging with the units — be you a more casual player, or a really experienced one — is superb, and starts with them being a treat for the eyes. Units really look the part, and every combat encounter does too. King Art Studio’s attention to detail, with bespoke combat animations for every combination (it seems) that look genuine, and plenty of blood splatter and rag doll physics on show. Even the armor and weaponry of all units look radiant and detailed, down to the lustre on metals.
The machine endures
There’s a good mix of missions that keep things interesting and elevate the branching campaign, too. That’s a really great thing in a particular way, as my one ‘gripe’, if you can really call it that, is that Dawn of War 4 continues the series’ trend of sometimes being purely a numbers game.
Especially in base-building missions; if you can pace your play a bit, secure your territory, and build an army that’s massive, you’ll rarely fail. This can offset the nuances and ‘other’ factors to think about too when managing Orks and the WAAGH! that fuels them in battle, and the Adeptus Mechanicus and the Nosphere links that strengthen buildings and open up more development options.
That’s why the mix of missions is welcome: while those base- and army-building ones are heavily present, there’s usually a gauntlet or defence mission around the corner to mix things up — and I’ve probably enjoyed the latter two more on the whole.
Not that dominating a map is unenjoyable, of course. The power fantasy is real in Dawn of War 4 and can feel fantastic, but the game is also wonderfully successful at creating those ‘If I can just make it to that resource point’ or ‘if I can just hold off this enemy encounter’ or ‘if I can just create a couple of units quickly ot turn the tide here’ kind of moments, which are a thrill.
I could talk about more of the individual features in the game that make it shine, but the most important thing about my time with the game for preview is that everything adds up to an authentic Dawn of War experience and really captures the feeling and the essence of the series — as well as translating the turn-based tabletop game into a real-time action setting once again.
Dawn of War 4 successfully takes me back to early 2000s LAN parties, devouring campaigns over and over again, and building massive armies to crush my foes as I did in the first game over two decades ago — and now I just want more.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. Make sure to click the Follow button!
Rob is the Managing Editor of TechRadar Gaming and Streaming, a video games journalist, critic, editor, and writer, and has years of experience gained from multiple publications. Prior to being TechRadar Gaming's Managing Editor, he was TRG's Deputy Editor, and a longstanding member of GamesRadar+, being the Commissioning Editor for Hardware there for years, while also squeezing in a short stint as Gaming Editor at WePC just before joining TechRadar Gaming. He is also a writer on tech, gaming hardware, and video games but also gardens and landscapes, and has written about the virtual landscapes of games for years.
