articles.title: The Harness Is the Hard Part of Agentic Pentesting
articles.text:
An AppSec team can point an AI agent running on a general-purpose model at its own web apps with little setup. Sure, the model writes the attacks. But everything that makes those attacks safe to run against production and worth acting on afterward lives in the harness around the model. The harness is where the engineering in AI pentesting sits. The Hugging Face intrusion OpenAI disclosed in July showed what happens when that harness gives way, even inside an OpenAI evaluation built to contain the agents.
Why Each Control Takes Rigorous Engineering
Let’s take a closer look at the attack different stages and the role AI agents can take there
Scope
A pentesting agent makes thousands of decisions about where to send its next request, and the model judges each one against a rule written in plain language. A web app’s real boundary often extends past one domain through redirects and calls to outside services. Enforcing scope means code that inspects every request before it leaves, and OWASP’s 2026 guidance routes privileged actions through a deterministic policy engine that checks them at execution time, outside the model.
Credentials
Finding exposed credentials is part of what a pentest does, so the agent regularly comes across working keys outside its assignment. Which of those it may use, for what, and when a person gets involved are policy decisions that the code around the model applies on every attempt.
Prompt Injection
Every page and API response the agent reads, including hidden fields, metadata and comments a user never sees, can carry content written by anyone who can post to the app. A single product review is enough to plant malicious instructions. OWASP ranks prompt injection the top risk for LLM applications and notes that no reliable prevention exists today. The design question is not whether the model gets fooled, but how much damage it can do if and when it does. That comes down to two things: how tightly each action is constrained and which actions require further inspection and human sign-off. Neither is simple. OWASP warns that approval fatigue degrades reviewer judgement at scale, so routing everything to a human simply shifts the failure point down the line.
Proof
In October 2026, Google stopped accepting product vulnerability reports to its open-source bug bounty program after a surge in automated submissions, the majority of which it said were not valid. A finding a developer can’t reproduce is just another ticket to close. Producing one worth acting on means running the exploit, capturing what it reached, and packaging the result so anyone can replay it, all within the limits of the other controls set.
None of this is built once. Every model upgrade can change how the agent behaves, and every release changes the app whose security it tests. And around the controls sit the systems a production agent depends on, including change-triggered testing, routing findings to the developers who own the code, strictly controlling what customer data reaches a model provider, and connecting what the agent finds in the app to the rest of the environment.
Across all of it, the pattern is the same. The model reasons about what to try, and deterministic code decides what runs, records it, and stops it when needed.
How Pentera Apps Implements the Harness
This separation of reasoning and execution is how we approach building Pentera Apps. Instead of letting an AI model send requests directly into an application, Pentera Apps pairs an AI that decides what to test with a deterministic harness that controls what runs. Every action is logged and any test can be paused or stopped at any time. It's the same safety discipline Pentera has applied to production testing for nearly a decade, across thousands of global customers.
The harness also produces the proof. Every finding ships with a replayable exploit script, a CVSS 3.1 score and CWE mapping, so developers can reproduce the attack themselves instead of taking it on trust. Once the fix lands, the exact same attack can be re-run to confirm the path is closed. Tests run on demand or on a schedule, with change-triggered testing in CI/CD coming next, so validation stays inline with development.
The surrounding systems follow the same discipline. Only minimal, redacted data reaches the LLM, with zero retention and no training on customer data, and data stays in the customer’s region. Every test starts with context from reconnaissance across the customer’s attack surfaces, findings from their security stack, and live threat intelligence signals. That context lets Pentera trace an exploit in a web app be traced into network, cloud, and identity on one platform.
In agentic pentesting, the harness determines the results. Pentera Apps builds it in, so security teams get validated findings without building one themselves.
Note: This article has been expertly written and contributed by Assaf Regev, AVP Product Marketing at Pentera. Security teams can sign up for early access to Pentera Apps, Agentic Web App Pentesting.

articles.title: Un juez obligó a Meta a revelar qué ejecutivos aprobaron piratear libros para entrenar su IA
articles.text:
Un juez federal de California ordenó a Meta identificar a todos los ejecutivos y mandos que autorizaron descargar libros pirateados mediante BitTorrent para entrenar sus modelos de inteligencia artificial, luego de que la empresa intentara responsabilizar solo a empleados técnicos.
La orden, firmada el 19 de octubre por el juez federal Thomas Hixson, obliga a Meta a nombrar a cada persona que haya tomado, autorizado o aprobado la decisión de obtener material de las bibliotecas piratas Anna’s Archive y LibGen, incluidas las decisiones sobre si distribuir esos archivos a otros usuarios mientras se descargaban.
El fallo forma parte de dos demandas que avanzan en el Distrito Norte de California: una demanda colectiva de autores, entre ellos Richard Kadrey y la comediante Sarah Silverman, y otra presentada por la editorial Entrepreneur Media.
Un tribunal ya había resuelto antes que entrenar modelos de IA con esos libros constituye un uso legítimo bajo la doctrina de fair use. Lo que sigue en disputa es si la forma en que Meta obtuvo ese material, mediante torrents que también distribuyen archivos a terceros, implicó una infracción adicional de los derechos de autor.
Según los demandantes, Meta descargó en conjunto unos 116,3 terabytes de contenido entre 2022 y 2024: alrededor de 80,6 terabytes provenientes de LibGen y 35,7 terabytes de Anna’s Archive.
Meta había argumentado que no podía identificar a nadie que hubiera aprobado “formalmente” la decisión de usar BitTorrent, porque, según la empresa, se trató de elecciones técnicas tomadas por consenso entre equipos de ingeniería. También dijo que la obtención de datos de Anna’s Archive pasó por una revisión legal interna a comienzos de 2024.
El juez Hixson rechazó ese argumento. Consideró que la pregunta de los demandantes no se limitaba a decisiones formales y que las respuestas de Meta se habían enfocado en el uso de los datos, no en cómo fueron obtenidos. “Si una decisión es atribuible a un grupo o un equipo, todos los que participaron en tomarla deben responder a este requerimiento”, señala la orden.
El registro interno que complica la defensa
Un empleado que participó en las descargas ya había declarado que la posibilidad de compartir archivos durante el proceso se discutió internamente y que se tomaron medidas para limitarla.
Un cuaderno de registro interno de Meta, citado en la presentación de Entrepreneur Media, muestra que al menos un empleado evaluó evitar los torrents antes de una descarga de Anna’s Archive: “Se decidió optar por subidas directas de archivos sin usar torrents, porque eso implicaría compartir el contenido hacia afuera, lo que legalmente no estaría bien”, dice la anotación.
Para Entrepreneur Media, esa nota contradice la versión de la empresa. “Bajo esa construcción, nadie en Meta decidió torrentear nada, y sin embargo Meta torrenteó bibliotecas piratas repetidamente entre 2022 y 2024”, argumentó la editorial ante el tribunal.
Los montos en juego y un contrato que quedó expuesto
La ley de derechos de autor de Estados Unidos permite indemnizaciones de entre USD 750 y USD 30.000 por obra, y de hasta USD 150.000 por obra si el tribunal determina que la infracción fue deliberada. Como referencia, Anthropic acordó pagar cerca de USD 1.500 millones por unas 500.000 obras en un litigio similar, lo que equivale a unos USD 3.000 por obra.
La misma orden reveló además la existencia de un acuerdo de licencia entre Meta y Fox Corporation para usar contenido de esa cadena en el entrenamiento de sus modelos de IA. El juez mantuvo en reserva el monto pagado por esa licencia por considerarlo información comercialmente sensible.
El tribunal también le dio a Meta un plazo de siete días para entregar documentos de su catálogo interno de datos de entrenamiento, que serán revisados de manera confidencial por el juez antes de decidir si deben incorporarse como prueba en el caso.
El litigio continúa en etapa de descubrimiento de pruebas, por lo que los nombres de los ejecutivos señalados todavía no se conocen públicamente y dependen de que Meta cumpla con la orden en los próximos días.

articles.title: ChatGPT s’installe un peu plus dans Google Chrome et prend les commandes de votre navigateur
articles.text:
Comparer des produits sur plusieurs sites, remplir des formulaires ou organiser ses recherches sans jongler entre les onglets… OpenAI donne de nouvelles capacités à son extension pour Chrome. Un gain de temps appréciable, à condition de bien surveiller les informations auxquelles l’IA peut accéder.
Passer d’un onglet à l’autre pour comparer des prix, récupérer des informations ou remplir un formulaire pourrait bientôt devenir une corvée du passé. OpenAI fait évoluer son extension pour Google Chrome afin de permettre à ChatGPT de travailler directement dans le navigateur. L’assistant peut désormais consulter plusieurs pages, recouper leurs contenus et effectuer certaines manipulations sans que vous ayez à intervenir à chaque étape.
Une évolution intéressante, mais qui suppose aussi de lui ouvrir les portes de votre navigateur, y compris celles des services auxquels vous êtes déjà connecté.
ChatGPT ne se contente plus de lire vos pages Web
Jusqu'ici, les assistants intégrés aux navigateurs servaient surtout à résumer des articles ou à répondre à des questions sur une page. Avec cette nouvelle version, OpenAI veut aller beaucoup plus loin.
Vous pouvez, par exemple, ouvrir trois fiches produits de PC portables chez différents marchands et demander à ChatGPT d’en comparer les caractéristiques dans un tableau. L’extension peut également remplir des formulaires, intervenir dans des documents en ligne ou réorganiser vos onglets.
Certaines opérations peuvent même se poursuivre en arrière-plan pendant que vous continuez à naviguer.
Sous Chrome, vous pouvez maintenant lâcher ChatGPT dans tous vos onglets personnels. ©Nicolas Guyot pour Clubic
Pour en profiter, il suffit d’installer l’extension, puis de l’autoriser à accéder aux pages concernées. Depuis ChatGPT sur le Web, la mention @Chrome ou le bouton + permettent ensuite de sélectionner les onglets à utiliser. Pas besoin d’installer l’application de bureau et ça fonctionne parfaitement en France (cf. Captures d’écran ci-dessus).
- Chat dans différentes langues, dont le français
- Générer, traduire et obtenir un résumé de texte
- Générer, optimiser et corriger du code
Des autorisations à ne pas accorder les yeux fermés
Cette autonomie a évidemment une contrepartie. Pour manipuler les pages, l’extension peut demander des autorisations étendues, notamment sur leur contenu, l’historique, les favoris ou certaines fonctions de débogage de Chrome.
OpenAI a toutefois prévu plusieurs garde-fous. Par défaut, ChatGPT réclame votre accord lorsqu’il doit accéder à un nouveau site. Vous pouvez lui ouvrir la porte pour une seule utilisation, pour un domaine entier ou pour tous les sites. Cette dernière possibilité est naturellement la moins prudente.
L'entreprise précise également ne pas conserver un historique exhaustif distinct de votre navigation. En revanche, les informations et captures récupérées dans les pages puis intégrées à une conversation restent soumises aux règles de confidentialité de ChatGPT.
Il faut aussi compter avec les injections de prompt, ces instructions malveillantes dissimulées dans une page Web pour tenter de détourner le comportement d’un assistant. Mieux vaut donc conserver les autorisations au cas par cas, particulièrement sur les sites contenant des données personnelles ou professionnelles.
- Navigation rapide
- Écosystème d'extensions très riche
- Synchronisation multi-appareils fluide
Google, Anthropic et Mistral avancent aussi sur ce terrain
La bataille des assistants se joue désormais directement dans nos navigateurs. Google intègre Gemini à Chrome, avec la possibilité d’exploiter le contenu de l’onglet consulté. Cette fonction n’est toutefois pas encore disponible en France.
Anthropic propose de son côté une extension Claude réservée aux abonnés payants, capable de naviguer, cliquer et remplir des formulaires. Là encore, l’accès aux pages peut exposer des informations sensibles.
Mistral participe également à cette évolution en fournissant notamment son modèle Mistral Small 4 à Firefox Smart Window, dont la bêta est accessible en France. Mozilla indique que les conversations ne sont pas enregistrées sur ses serveurs par défaut et que les fournisseurs partenaires s’engagent à ne pas les conserver.
OpenAI rejoint donc une course déjà bien engagée, où les assistants ne veulent plus seulement répondre à nos questions, mais agir directement dans nos outils.
Sources : Chrome Web Store via Cybersecurity News

articles.title: The iPhone Duo is a foldable phone in the most Apple way possible — and that's a very good thing
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Apple iPhone Duo arrives as a fully realized folding smartphone from a company that, perhaps smartly, sat back and watched a category stumble, grow, develop, and solidify into a desirable form factor. As such, it avoids most of its predecessors' missteps while delivering exquisite engineering, a vibrant, virtually crease-free screen, and a compelling design. Even so, when compared to its chief rival, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, it isn't a slam dunk, and Samsung's lighter, thinner, and slightly cheaper passport-sized foldable remains compelling. But, for Apple fans who've been eagerly awaiting the Cupertino tech giant's entry into the folding space, there is no other or better choice.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent design
- + Best folding hinge ever?
- + Flat, matte folding screen that hides the crease
- + Excellent performance
- + Split-screen multitasking
Reasons to avoid
- - Cover screen loses too much space to the dock placement
- - No telephoto camera
- - Needs more third-party app support
- - Missing Face ID
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Apple iPhone Duo: Two-minute review
In the early days of the iPhone, seeing one in the wild, usually in a brave early adopter's hands, was like spotting a unicorn. The excitement was palpable. Over the years, though, as every smartphone has become a glass and metal slab, making it difficult to tell one iPhone release from another, the excitement has diminished. Where I used to keep my 'regular' iPhone review units out of sight, I now casually carry them around in a case, and no one is any the wiser.
That, though, is not the case with the iPhone Duo. In my effort to spend as much time using the new folding iPhone as possible, I carried it everywhere, including to a wedding party for my friend's son. My iPhone Duo test unit was somewhat disguised by being clad in a Taupe Folio with a Kickstand case, but as I held it aloft to photograph the newlyweds, the bride's eyes grew wide.
"Is that...?!"
My eyes darted from her to the phone in my hand, and I considered stuffing it back in my pocket, but I was intrigued by her reaction. I hadn't seen this level of interest and excitement in years.
I nodded wordlessly; the newlyweds started peppering me with questions, and as I folded and unfolded it, and they glimpsed the inner display, the bride's jaw dropped. She asked if I liked it. I mumbled, "Yes, I think so," without offering much more information.
I was determined to use the iPhone Duo's two external 48MP cameras to photograph the event, which meant this scenario repeated itself more than once.
It was obvious that, unlike every other iPhone of the last decade or so, the iPhone Duo could not travel incognito; people were, it seemed, intensely interested in Apple's first truly new iPhone form factor in basically forever.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The interest is warranted.
The iPhone Duo is not simply an iPhone folded in half. I'd argue it's only marginally an iPhone and more of a hybrid, splitting the difference between a sub-sized smartphone and a slightly larger, 8-inch iPad mini.
From the highly polished titanium frame to the curves and pitch-perfect tolerances, the iPhone Duo's design is Apple at its best, and while it doesn't reinvent the genre, the nano-texture finish on the main display cannily solved the chief folding phone complaint: that darn crease. It's not that the crease is completely gone, but in daily use it's virtually invisible. As an added bonus, that matte finish kills reflectivity in bright sunlight, and makes almost everything look better.
Apple includes four cameras, three of which are powerful enough to produce high-quality photos across a range of styles. I saw excellent color accuracy and low-light performance, and the ultra-wide camera feels expansive. The inner-display camera is, it appears, just 4MP, but it does a good job with casual selfies and FaceTime calls.
Apple has almost stuck the landing here, but there is a slight step backwards. I'm fairly certain its decision to move the status bar and dock to the right side of the 5.4-inch outer screen, and therefore shrink the width of most apps, will divide opinion. I like how this makes it easy to tap an app with your right thumb, but the remaining screen real estate makes some app experiences look and feel cramped.
Then there's the lack of Face ID on the cover screen, which means this is the first iPhone in ages that I have to use my finger to unlock.
I'm also less than thrilled that a nearly $2,000 / £1,999 phone starts with just 256GB of storage; although, to be fair to Apple, the $1,899.99 / £1,699 Galaxy Z Fold 8 also starts with the same amount.
Those small nits are like pointing out the missing eyelashes on the Mona Lisa, though. Overall, this is a fantastic entry into the folding phone space, offering the dual capabilities of a glanceable and attractive iPhone that fits in any pocket or hand, and a versatile 7.6-inch tablet.
Not everyone needs two screens in one device, or wants to pay as much as they would for a home appliance for their next smartphone; but for those who feel confined by the boundaries of a typical iPhone and want to do more in less space, the iPhone Duo, which starts out smaller than your average smartphone but unfolds to reveal an almost twice-as-large tablet display, is well worth your consideration.
Apple iPhone Duo review: Price and availability
- From $1,999 in the US
- From £1,999 in the UK
- From $3,499 in Australia
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo, its first folding phone, as its "one more thing" during the Surprise and Shine event on September 9, 2026.
The list price is $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499 for the 256GB model, which is in line with most of its folding competitors from Samsung, Huawei, Motorola, and Oppo. It's available in storage configurations up to 2TB for $3,199 / £3,199 / AU$5,899.
The iPhone Duo is the most expensive iPhone Apple has ever made, but we should put this in context. Like most foldables, this is a two-in-one device: a pint-sized smartphone with a 5.4-inch 4:3 screen, and a 7.6-inch tablet. Unlike the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a similar passport-style shape, and even the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, which is a more conventionally sized and shaped foldable, the iPhone Duo's larger main screen supports digital pen input (this wasn't available for my testing period, but it's expected by November).
You may also be able to soften the price blow a bit with a trade-in; or you might want to look at Apple's leasing program, which will run about $57-to-$83 / £47 to £66.63 / AU$97.19 to over $161 a month for the base model.
In total, the iPhone Duo is probably better value than you think.

Samsung Galaxy Fold 8 review: Design
- Polished titanium
- Exquisitely engineered hinge and folding operation
- Unfolds flat
- IP68
- Thicker and heavier than nearest competition
- No Face ID
'Satisfying' is the best way to describe the feeling of repeatedly opening and closing the iPhone Duo. It's as if Apple inadvertently created a digital fidget spinner — the more I carried around the iPhone Duo, the more I found myself absentmindedly folding and unfolding the phone.
Apple's exceptional engineering makes it possible to unfold the phone initially, with almost no effort (it almost springs open at the slightest intentional touch), before the internal torque kicks in to allow for the Duo to be opened to almost any angle between zero and 180 degrees (flat).
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
While you can't see the work that went into making this hinge, the effort is evident in every single touch and move. Inside are hundreds of magnets and other components that keep the phone securely closed, but never get in the way of an easy opening. More so than with any folding phone I've tested, the hinge essentially disappears when the iPhone Duo is unfolded flat.
At 5.2mm thick, the fingerprint-attracting polished titanium iPhone Duo is the thinnest iPhone ever. At least that's how Apple markets it, but that's in tablet mode; I do like the sound of a 5.2mm-thick tablet. The 7.6-inch device is thinner than the 8-inch iPad mini (6.3mm). Folded, the iPhone Duo is 11.3mm thick, almost 2mm thicker than the folded Galaxy Z Fold 8. And at 254g, the iPhone Duo outweighs the Galaxy Z Fold 8 by a noticeable 53 grams. It's even slightly heavier than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, which weighs 249g.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
The upshot of all this is that while the 4.64-inch by 3.31-inch folded iPhone Duo fits in even the smallest pocket, you will feel its heft, especially if you pop, say, a Folio with Kickstand case on it.
The iPhone Duo stands out in a way few iPhones have in recent years. Folded, it's closer to square than rectangular in shape, resembling a squat iPhone Pro Max. Plus, the asymmetry — flat and square on one side and curved on the other when folded — means the Duo cuts a unique profile among smartphones.
It does feel good in the hand, though the wider body might take some getting used to. I like the Ceramic Shield 2 front and back, especially the matte-finished back, which makes the Duo almost slip-from-your-hand-proof. The large dual-camera array bump is reminiscent of the iPhone Air, though the similarities end there.
The volume buttons live on the top edge, another departure from the traditional iPhone, and indeed from smartphone design in general — I'm not sure I love that decision. On the right is the long Touch ID-enabled power/sleep/Siri AI button, and below that is the Action button. I often forget that last button exists on my iPhone 18 Pro Max, and I wonder if it was truly necessary here.
I appreciate the inclusion of Touch ID (I registered my index finger and thumb), but the lack of Face ID is frustrating — I had no idea how much I relied on it for quickly unlocking my phone until it wasn't there. Multiple times I've stared at the iPhone Duo's cover screen waiting for something to happen, forgetting that I have to intentionally touch the Touch ID button. A nearly $2,000 device lacking Apple's most powerful biometric security feature is close to unforgivable — I'll probably set up a workaround so that I can unlock the Duo via my Apple Watch.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Along the bottom edge are the USB-C port (the phone ships with a charging cable but no power adapter), the speakers, and the mics.
Unfolded, the iPhone duo feels like a thin, compact tablet — I hesitate to say 'iPad' since the operating system is essentially iOS with some small adjustments for the new form factor.
Remarkably, Apple comes out of the folding gate flourishing an IP68 rating, which means the iPhone Duo is protected against dust and even water. Naturally, I submerged the Duo under a running faucet, and it was none the worse for the experience.
Overall, I like the design and form factor, but it's different from a traditional iPhone, so it does take some getting used to. I struggled, for instance, to figure out the best way to hold the phone for photography. Do I need to turn it into landscape mode, or should I just hold it the way I hold a 'regular' iPhone? I do wonder how many will choose to unfold the phone, and shoot pictures in the same way they might with their iPad.
- Design score: 4.5 / 5
Apple iPhone Duo review: Displays
- Adorable and unusually shaped 5.4-inch cover display
- Industry-leading 7.6-inch foldable internal display
- Crease is canily hidden via a combination of expert engineering and a nano-etched display
- Bright, sharp, fluid screens
Credit to Apple for not skimping on either of its iPhone Duo displays. Both the 5.4-inch outer and the 7.6-inch flexible inner screens are Super Retina XDR-class OLED panels, both with variable refresh rates up to 120Hz, always-on functionality, and up to 3,000 nits of brightness.
Both displays look impressively sharp, and actually offer slightly higher resolutions than the comparable displays on the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8.
The iPhone Duo's 5.4-inch cover display has a 2034 x 1398 resolution (compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 8 cover display's 1972 x 1248), and the 7.6-inch Inner display is 2670 x 1878 (compared to the Z Fold 8's 2448 x 1848 main display).
At first glance, the iPhone duo Cover screen is instantly recognizable as an iPhone, but close scrutiny reveals some interesting adjustments for the relatively short and wide display. First, the pill-shaped Dynamic Island sits in a vertical space along the right side, and when you look at the home screen, the dock is stacked vertically below the time and a status button (a single tap on it expands it to show connectivity and battery, and also drops down the full Control Center).
The Duo takes that right-hand space and rarely gives it up, which means that websites can look cramped in Safari, and some apps like TikTok, and even Apple's native ones, like Sports, can feel a bit squeezed. There are exceptions, like when you use the screen as a viewfinder in the Camera app, or look back at images in the Photo Gallery. In those cases, the imagery fills the entire screen.
I'm less conflicted about the glorious main screen. It's big, it's responsive, and the matte, nano-texture covering almost completely hides the crease by dispersing any light bouncing off it, instead of directing it right back to your eyes. The display looks and feels perfectly flat, plus that matte covering kills all reflections, and makes every image look almost magazine-quality. It could be argued that a tiny bit of visual punch is lost in the texture, but I really enjoyed everything I viewed and did on the screen. It feels wonderful to the touch, and I had fun playing games like PUBG, browsing the web on a big screen, watching Netflix, reviewing and editing my photos, and multi-taking (more on that later).
Unlike the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra, the iPhone Duo's inner display supports a stylus, specifically the USB-C Apple Pencil. That support is not yet live, but I can't wait to start drawing on the Duo. I did attempt some Procreate Pocket sketches with my finger, and it didn't go well, which is mostly a me problem. However, I had slightly better luck with an analog stylus (see below).
Apple hides the 4MP inner FaceTime camera behind a handful of pixels, but they don't appear to have the exact same mix of matte and pixel density as the rest of the display, and as such are easy to spot. I wonder if Apple should have just gone with a standard, albeit smaller, cutout.
As on the cover display, Apple has positioned the status and dock vertically on the right side of the main display. I wonder why, in Tablet mode, Apple didn't simply copy the iPad and put this bar at the base of the screen. Still, I noticed that the dock disappears when you're in apps like Safari.
There's more to say about app compatibility with this platform, which I'll get into later in the Software section of this review.
I especially like the redesigned Standby feature, which takes advantage of the Duo's multiple displays and foldable nature. You can prop up the phone like a tent and have the Standby display appear in landscape mode. If you flip the phone up so it's standing on your desk like an open book, the Duo knows to switch Standby to the inner display. At one point I popped the Duo onto my old Belkin MagSafe charger, and used it as a nightstand clock. It's so smart and useful.
What we have here are two excellent displays with a wide array of capabilities in one device. It's both a tiny iPhone and a mini tablet, with two screens that should please both the iPhone and iPad crowds. I have my reservations about the cover screen, but as an overall multi-display package, I'm impressed with the Duo.
- Display score: 4.5 / 5
Apple iPhone Duo review: Cameras
- Two strong 48MP cameras
- Excellent 12MP Center Stage camera
- Inner camera is lower-resolution but effective for FaceTime
- No telephoto camera
It's been a long time since I've reviewed an iPhone on which camera considerations come second to design and mechanical engineering, but the excitement revolving around the iPhone Duo is about its folding capability, creaseless inner screen, and unique-among-iPhones form factor.
Even so, there's no indication that Apple has skimped on three of the four cameras. Yes, the inner camera is just a 4MP shooter that's primarily devoted to FaceTime calls, but the rest of the lenses — 48MP f/1.6 Main, 48MP f/2.2 ultra-wide, and 12MP f/2.2 Center Stage — are all excellent.
While I haven't had a lot of time with the iPhone Duo, I have managed to shoot in a variety of conditions and situations, pushing the cameras on speed, image quality, color, and low-light performance.
The two external cameras default to shooting at 24MP, which means each photo has effectively twice as much information per pixel (the process is called binning).
I was particularly impressed by the level of detail in the main-camera shots — just look at the specks of pollen on the marigold flower in the gallery below. That same image shows an exceptional balance of shadows and light; the sunlight bleed on the right does not overwhelm the exposure of the rest of the image.
In a challenging social-club environment, the main wide and ultra-wide cameras acquitted themselves nicely, making exposure adjustments to capture the moment without too much grain. Obviously, there was some motion blur, but I think it added to the emotional weight of the event.
With the iPhone duo, Apple has introduced Smart Take, which I liken to your own personal fashion photographer. The setting lives under the grid menu (drawer) in the Camera app, and once it's on, you can set the phone folded at 90 degrees on a desktop, start posing in front of the camera, and Smart Take will capture the 'best shots.'
When I used it, I noted that while I was trusting the phone to take some decent photos of me, I couldn't see a display to keep track of what it was capturing (Smart Take is not supported on the 4MP inner camera). Still, I started striking poses, assuming that the camera would deem those best. It kind of worked, though I think Smart Take would work best if you're able to put the iPhone Duo up on a tripod or shelf to make sure the camera is closer to eye level.

Similar to what we've seen on other foldable phones, Apple has included a camera mode, Duo Preview, that lets you use the best main or ultra-wide camera while still using the cover display as a viewfinder. It's a useful table-stakes feature that I'm glad Apple included, especially since the inner camera is so underpowered.
Apple says you get 2x effective optical zoom on the main camera, but that's a sensor crop. Yes, the pixels and image information will be real, but I prefer a proper zoom lens. To be fair, the iPhone Duo camera array is quite similar to the 50MP pair on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which also lacks a telephoto lens.
I also used the cover screen Center Stage camera to shoot some portrait-mode selfies. They were, as you might expect, impressive (not the subject, just the brilliant bokeh).
The iPhone Duo's trio of high-quality cameras meets, in my estimation, the high watermark set by lenses on previous iPhones, including the iPhone 17 Pro (the 18 Pro models come with a variable aperture).

Apple iPhone Duo review: Software
- An iOS tablet hybrid that somehow works
- Dock position will split some
- Split screen for multitasking
- Third-party app support is a work in progress
With the iPhone Duo, iOS officially means multiple things. Where it was once a smartphone platform, it's now a multi-hardware-configuration operating system that can, depending on where it's installed, fork appropriately.
Instead of the iPhone Duo unfolding and converting into an iPad, it remains steadfastly an iPhone with tablet-like capabilities. This has resulted in some odd decisions on Apple's part, like hiding some of the ever-present status-bar information, including battery life, and rotating and moving the dock. Even the iPad doesn't put the dock on the right-hand side.
On the cover screen, the status bar and dock placement cut into screen real-estate for some apps and browser experiences; this is less of an issue on the larger inner screen.
Since this is not pure-play classic iOS, there is some discontinuity in third-party app support. During my testing, Gmail and LinkedIn didn't look great. The former is stretched wide but doesn't fill the full depth of the display; LinkedIn floats in the middle.
For unoptimized apps, I did have the option of using the very iPad-like 2x zoom icon, which stretched the app to fit more of the screen. In some instances, apps appeared to work, but some features were broken. When I played Asphalt Legends on the inner display, tilt-to-steer was broken, though it worked perfectly on the cover display.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Some third-party apps, including Netflix (clips looked pretty good on the Cover display), and first-party apps like Safari and Messages, look great, and effectively use all the 7.6-inch display's real estate. There are even some apps that are already custom-designed to take advantage of the dual-display setup.
One of my favorites is a game called Toastie. On the inner screen, you butter your bread, add cheese and other ingredients, then hit grill, at which point you fold the phone closed, and it gently pulses for each second of cooking. You have to decide when to stop. To see your grilled cheese sandwich, you open the phone — I did this a half dozen times before I had a virtually edible sandwich.
Deck-Man is also a cute concept; this turns your iPhone duo into a classic cassette tape player, complete with the static you hear when the player is on but not playing a tape. When the iPhone is open, you choose a cassette and virtually put it in the player, then you close the phone to access the player controls. I especially liked how "rewinding" the tape reproduced the classic sounds of a physical tape rewinding in an old-school player.
I also played Battle Fleet, which is a Battleship knockoff, and works well when you set up the phone in 90-degree opened desktop mode.
These are all clever apps, though I wouldn't argue that any are the Duo's 'killer app.'
The 7.6-inch inner display is also a good canvas for multitasking. You split the screen by swiping up from the bottom of the display and slowly dragging an app left or right. Inside each pane, you can swipe up to choose a different app. I used this to have Messages and Safari side-by-side, and also for the drawing app Procreate on one side and a reference image from Safari on the left.
Unlike on the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you can't run three apps, though the iPhone Duo will let you add picture-in-picture video on top of two apps you have open.
The iPhone Duo is a good showcase for Apple's growing AI ambitions. Siri AI now knows more about me and my smartphone, so when I ask if there are any emails I should know about, it automatically accesses 'Priority Mail' in the Mail app, and quickly starts reading off the first crucial message. Siri AI is better at maintaining context, so I don't have to restate myself, but it's still not foolproof. I asked Siri where I had been yesterday, and it showed me a picture of myself and listed my age. Siri AI should, though, get better as it continues to index my system.
In general, iOS 27, which is more customizable that ever, has useful widgets and more powerful AI features, and is the perfect platform for Apple's biggest iPhone design leap. It may not have all the design elements right, and the app support is lagging a bit behind, but these are all minor, and I think easily adjustable or fixable, issues.
- Software score: 4.5 / 5
Apple iPhone Duo review: Performance
- Powerful A20 Pro CPU
- 12GB RAM
- Smooth performance across the board
Apple smartly put the same CPU, the 2-nanometer A20 Pro, in the iPhone Duo as it did in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. As a result, the performance on its first foldable device is equally impressive. In Future Labs benchmark tests, the A20 Pro on an iPhone Duo beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8's Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy in Geekbench 7 single- and multi-core tests, and it also edged out the Qualcomm chip in most of our graphics tests. None of this was by a wide margin, and I'd challenge anyone to notice the difference in real-world scenarios. Still, it's nice to know that the Duo is cooking with gas, just like its Pro counterparts.
In my experience, the iPhone Duo is fast and fluid. Speaking of which, it's fun to start with some third-party apps on the cover screen, and then flip open the iPhone Duo to see the virtually seamless graphics handoff from the smaller display to the larger one. It's both a software and performance feat that nothing stutters or stalls in the handoff process.
The larger inner screen will probably encourage many to try even tougher tasks, like editing 40K 60fps video. I used CyberLink PowerDirector to do so, and while the system and app handled the task fine, the non-optimized app couldn't properly fill the 7.6-inch display.
The back of the phone, near the camera bump, can get a little warm during gaming and other CPU-intensive operations, like recording the aforementioned 4K video, but not uncomfortably so.
Apple's A20 and the 12GB of RAM on board seem well suited to local tasks like photo editing in Cleanup, and both realistic and fanciful image creation in Image Playground.
The iPhone Duo starts with 256GB of storage, which matches the Galaxy Z Fold 8. At this price, though, I think it should start with double that. You can expect strong connectivity across the board from the iPhone Duo. Inside is Apple's C2 modem for better 5G connectivity. Plus, there's support for WiFi 7, Bluetooth 6, and Messages via Satellite.
Apple iPhone Duo benchmark scores

| Geekbench 7.1 multi-core | 11363 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme Unlimited | 7171 | 
| 3DMark Wild Life Extreme (fps) | 45.3 | 
| 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited | 16496 | 
| 3DMark Solar Bay Unlimited (fps) | 6.3 | 
- Performance score: 5 / 5
Apple iPhone Duo review: Battery
- Solid all-day battery life
- Fast wired charging
Apple reportedly squeezed a fairly large, almost 5,000mAh, battery into the iPhone duo, and is promising some pretty impressive battery-life numbers based on fairly specific types of usage. Video playback, which doesn't rely all that much on energy-draining resources, can, Apple claims, go for an eye-watering 44 hours, or 31 hours on the larger inner display.
In more varied use, Apple is claiming a full day of battery life on a charge. In my real-world tests I got around 14 hours, and in our more stringent Future Labs tests, we got 13 hours. That's commendable performance, but not as good as what the same Future Labs tests show for the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which managed 14.33 hours.
I still think the iPhone Duo's numbers are good, especially because my experience was easily cruising through a full day of phone activities, without any concern that I needed to plug in.
The phone supports fast charging and, with a 45W charger, I charged to 60% in 30 minutes. The MagSafe back also supports fast wireless charging.
- Battery score: 4.5 / 5
Should you buy the Apple iPhone Duo?
Apple iPhone Duo scorecard
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
| Value | Most expensive iPhone ever but it's truly a two-in-one device and few will pay the full price upfront anyway, especially with the new leasing option. | 4 / 5 | 
| Design | Beautifully designed and engineered foldable that makes the hinge and, virtually, hinge disappear. Wish it was thinner and lighter. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Displays | Sharp cover dsispl;ay and brilliant inner display that hides the crease and offered a beautiful matte finish. Everything looks good on it | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Camera | Two strong 48MP lenses and an above average Center Stage selfie camera that all produce top-notch images. The inner camera is best for FaceTime only and we miss a true telephoto. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Software | Apple shows how iOS can also be a tablet platform without losing its iPhone essence. Siri AI is starting to live up to its promise. We need more app support and not a huge fan of Status and Dock placement. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Performance | An excellent A20 Pro CPU helps the iPhone Duo live up to its promises. There are zero lags, even when playing console-level games | 5 / 5 | 
| Battery | All day battery life is virtually assured. | 4.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You've been waiting for Apple to enter the folding race
The iPhone Duo is pretty much everything you want or could dream of from a folding iPhone
You want two screens but also cuter and pocketable
The iPhone Duo might be thicker and heavier than a Galaxy Z Fold 8, but it's right-sized for small hands and smaller pockets, and while the Galaxy Z Fold line is all flat edges and sharp corners, the iPhone Duo has curves.
You don't want to see a crease
Apple now holds the crown for best crease concealer, hiding it under nano texture finish that makes it almost impossible to spot the crease unless you really look for it.
Don't buy it if...
You want an affordable smartphone
The iPhone Duo is not just the most expensive iPhone; it's more expensive than the Galaxy Z Fold 8. Either way, think carefully before buying; not everyone needs two displays in one device.
You want a telephoto camera
The iPhone Duo's main camera promises 2X optical equivalent zoom, but that's a sensor crop, which means there's no dedicated telephoto camera.
Apple iPhone Duo review: Also consider
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
Samsung has adapted familiar elements to make a phone that's ready to fit your lifestyle with its practical size, excellent screens, and plenty of software and performance potential. It’s still costly, and the lack of some features seems extra disappointing given the price, but what’s here gels together in a wonderfully cohesive way.
Read our full Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 review
Motorola Razr Plus 2026
This is currently our best flip-style foldable pick, and it might be the better device for you if you're looking for a foldable that can go the distance with its battery, and don’t mind only having a standard-sized phone screen when you open it up.

articles.title: Attackers Hijacked Over 300 Tor Exit Relays to Intercept SSH Connections
articles.text:
Attackers took control of more than 300 Tor exit relays in early October and used them to redirect SSH connections to servers that stole login passwords, a researcher found.
Exit relays are the last hop in a Tor circuit, where traffic leaves the network for its destination. Only a password login to an SSH server made through Tor between October 1 and 5, after accepting the interception server's host key, could have been captured.
The Tor Project began flagging relays on October 4, and by October 5, none remained in the consensus, the list of relays that Tor clients use. At the peak on October 4, the relays carrying the attacker's exit policy made up 7.46% of Tor's exit capacity, measured by consensus weight, according to an analysis of public Tor directory data posted to the tor-relays mailing list.
The researcher, who publishes as kaba, scanned all of Tor's roughly 3,000 exits on October 2 and found 333 redirecting SSH to the same 12 interception servers. The directory-data analysis counts 377 relays run by 59 operators that switched to the attacker's exit policy between October 1 and 4, which it calls "a policy match, not proof of compromise."
How the Hijacked Exits Intercepted SSH
An exit relay only carries traffic to the ports its exit policy allows. The attackers rewrote that policy in the relays' torrc configuration files to allow port 22 (the SSH port), enabling SSH on 342 relays that had blocked it. Another 24 relays that had not been exits at all became exits.
"It seems the attacker is gaining access to Linux based hosts and when these machines are running non-exits they are editing the torrc file and turning them into exits to be able to carry out the SSH attack," the Tor Project's network health team wrote in its October 5 notice to relay operators. Most of the affected relays were already exits, the directory data shows.
The same change closed the encrypted mail ports, IMAPS and POP3S, and on most relays opened the plaintext-capable ones, POP3 and IMAP.
A Tor client only picks an exit that allows the destination port, so these relays stopped carrying encrypted mail and started carrying SSH, Telnet, and, on most of them, plaintext mail. Why the encrypted mail ports were closed is not visible in the data, the analysis says.
With port 22 open, an SSH connection through one of these exits went to one of 12 interception servers instead of its destination, kaba found. When a server intercepted the connection, it presented its own host key. A user who already knew the real server's key saw OpenSSH's warning that the remote host identification had changed, and a user connecting for the first time saw the usual prompt to accept a new key.
In the October 2 scan, about a dozen exits were serving a fake host key, and the other 300 or so redirected through the same servers without altering the key.
A user who accepted the key and typed a password handed it to the interceptor. The interceptor connected to the real server, so the session worked, and every command could be watched and separately logged in with the stolen password to check for sudo and run a base64-encoded Perl installer. In kaba's honeypot, the installer took the same form as the command that put Ebury, a backdoor that hides inside OpenSSH, on one of a relay operator's servers, as described below.
A key-based SSH login could not be relayed this way. Under the SSH authentication protocol, , the client's signature includes an identifier unique to each session, so a signature made for the interceptor's session is useless against the real server. The interceptor could still accept a key login itself and show a fake shell, but it could not reach the real server with it.
A password, by contrast, travels inside the encrypted session and can be read by the server at the other end, which here was the interceptor.
Who Was Exposed, and What to Do If You Were
To be exposed, someone had to connect to an SSH server over Tor between October 1 and the afternoon of October 5, land on one of the hijacked exits, have the connection intercepted rather than passed through, accept the interceptor's host key, and log in with a password. No count of victims exists.
If you accepted an unfamiliar or changed host key over Tor in that window, treat the password you typed as stolen, change it, and check that server for the Ebury signs listed below. An OpenSSH client that accepted the key saved it in known_hosts.
The server that intercepted kaba's connection used an ED25519 key with the fingerprint SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, though the other interception servers may have used different keys.
How It Was Found and Stopped
Kaba encountered the attack on the morning of October 2, when an SSH connection over Tor returned a changed-key warning. He then used exitmap, a scanning tool that the Tor Project's network health team also uses, to open an SSH connection from one of his servers to another via each exit in turn.
One end checked whether the host key was correct, and the other whether the connection originated at the exit or from an interception server. He reported the results to the health team that evening.
The health team also spotted the policy change through its own monitoring. On October 4, it contacted Zimmer, who ran the Quetzalcoatl relay family, the largest group of affected relays, and Zimmer confirmed the change was not his, asked for the relays to be marked bad, and stopped Tor on the server running them.
Directory authorities began voting the BadExit and MiddleOnly flags on affected relays at 18:00 UTC that day, and the flags were in the consensus by 21:00. BadExit tells Tor clients never to use a relay as an exit.
On the morning of October 5,, a scripted restart swept through 55 of Quetzalcoatl's hosts, with the policy still in place. Who ran it is not known. The directory authorities were by then rejecting affected relays from the network, the Tor Project said in its notice, and the two relays Zimmer had stopped were refused when they tried to rejoin, he wrote.
By 17:00 UTC on October 5, no relay with the attacker's policy was in the consensus, and none had returned as of October 9, the directory-data analysis found. Forty-one relays, nine of them Quetzalcoatl's, were still publishing the policy at that point but were not listed.
Tor Metrics' count of relays carrying the Exit flag fell by about 370 between October 3 and October 5, matching the number of affected relays, and had not recovered by October 18.
Ebury, and How the Attackers Got In
Zimmer described his side in a post-mortem on the list on October 7. Two of his servers were running Ebury version 1.8.3: a management server at Contabo that served as the family's VPN gateway and SSH jump host, and a FranTech VPS he calls Switzerland2 that ran two of the exits.
Ebury is a backdoor and credential stealer for OpenSSH that has been active since 2009, according to ESET, which estimated in 2024 that it had infected 400,000 servers, with more than 100,000 still infected in late 2023.
The attacker logged in to the management server on August 28 with the operator account's password on the first try, gained root within five minutes, installed Ebury, then reached Switzerland2 a little over an hour later and installed it there too.
"The root cause was ours: one password reused for SSH login, sudo and the backup passphrase, stored in plaintext on both servers, plus SSH password authentication left enabled on the internet-facing management server," Zimmer wrote. Where the attacker got that password is unknown.
Ebury's backdoor logins leave no record. On October 2, the exits' configuration files were rewritten with no login, sudo command, or cron job in the logs, and the two relays published the attacker's policy at 09:34 UTC. It stayed live for about 52 hours on two relays moving roughly 3.4 TiB a day.
A routine reboot on October 4 killed the attacker's hidden tools, but Ebury came straight back.
The family's "offline" master keys "were not offline: copies sat in the workstation backup on the management server, encrypted with the password the attacker already had," Zimmer wrote. He retired every relay and the bridge in the family and deleted both servers.
This Ebury is a single setuid library file, /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, with the libkeyutils.so.1 symlink pointed at it. The packaged library is untouched, so dpkg -V and debsums do not catch it, and sshd, sudo, and PAM pass their package checks. Version 1.8.3 is newer than ESET's public indicators, which stop at 1.8.2, and ESET's published detection script, read on October 21, lists no socket name for it.
Marc-Etienne M. Léveillé, who co-wrote ESET's 2014 Ebury paper, wrote its 2024 report and has since left the company, replied that version 1.8.3 has been around since at least June 2026 and posted an updated copy of the script that covers it. "Given how many servers had Ebury between 2009 and 2023 (400 000!), there are most likely other compromised Tor relays out there," he wrote.
How the other 58 operators' hosts were entered is the main open question. Among their relays listed on October 1, 71 of the 101 hosted on FranTech Solutions, the network behind the BuyVM hosting brand, switched to the attacker's policy, against 13 of 9,054 hosted elsewhere, the directory-data analysis found.
Forty relays of 21 operators changed within five and a half minutes on October 1, most by a configuration reload, which the analysis reads as one actor already holding access to all 40.
Léveillé's best guess for the password was a login from a host already running Ebury, with a compromised hosting provider as another possibility. ESET has seen providers whose management servers ran Ebury and whose customers' virtual servers ended up infected, he wrote.
Kaba counted 26 of the 27 compromised servers outside the Quetzalcoatl family at FranTech/BuyVM and asked on the list: "Could they have compromised those servers at the hoster level?"
Quetzalcoatl's own compromise ran through its Contabo management server, and 225 of its 273 affected relays sat on other networks.
Who is behind the campaign is unknown, and so is how many of the affected hosts ran Ebury: Zimmer examined two of his, and the directory data shows only the policy. A fake uppercase CRON daemon and NAT rules redirecting port 22 were among the signs other operators reported to the Tor Project. Zimmer's servers had neither, and whether the cases share one actor is open.
On Zimmer's relays, the port changes meant any mail retrieval could only happen in plaintext, he wrote, and a hidden process named snf ran on Switzerland2 for most of the window. What it did is unknown.
What Relay Operators Should Check
The Tor Project's notice asks Linux relay operators to check Relay Search for an Exit flag or exit policy they did not set, and to look through torrc and any included files for changed ExitRelay, ExitPolicy, ContactInfo, MyFamily or Nickname lines.
It also lists NAT rules on port 22, unknown listening processes or outbound connections, new users, authorized_keys entries, cron jobs and systemd units, and a tor binary that fails its package check. Zimmer's servers showed none of the host-level signs on that list, only the changed exit policy, so a clean host check does not rule out this Ebury.
The signs of the implant, from Zimmer's post, are:
- File: /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libkeyutils.so.1.10.2, setuid and owned by no package (63,368 bytes on his servers, with a hash that differs on every server)
- Symlink: libkeyutils.so.1 pointing at that file
- Socket: abstract UNIX socket @event-0YsOG9WSOE
- Process: a fake /sbin/rsyslogd (earlier systemd-udevd or arpd) running inside the ssh.service cgroup
- IP: 185.225.226[.]62, the source of the August 28 login
- SSH key: RSA SHA256:dvACokMYcXJ2om4wuS+TvdtjrAgPK7rC7ZQHDgvBHzk, used to log in to Switzerland2
- SSH keys embedded in the implant: RSA SHA256:KlICz/B59619CpuQdGzgmmvzWBfTMUJ77EwihTYobuo and ED25519 SHA256:OfLY0uF9SwOW9xVjiMXZGDfk6Atmz6CbHy4epknLm8Y
- Interceptor host key: ED25519 SHA256:6baCZCPsl+AfQuujUS81fMEE/C7UeJ+AwjrImqmDB3E, seen on kaba's connection
Check from a rescue system or an offline disk image if you can. On a live server, log in with a key. "Never type a password into a server you suspect, because Ebury will capture it," Zimmer wrote.
Start a shell with H=1 I=1 LD_PRELOAD=":" LD_DEBUG=":" bash to get past the userland rootkit before running Léveillé's updated script or the commands in Zimmer's post.
If you find it, the Tor Project's steps are:
- take the relay offline
- preserve the disk and logs before wiping
- reinstall rather than clean up
- generate a new relay identity and treat the old keys as stolen
- rotate every credential that was on the host
Reinstalling matters because the implant survived a reboot on Zimmer's server. Report to bad-relays@lists.torproject.org, and if your IP address was blocked during the incident, write to the same address once your host is clean to have the block lifted, Georg Koppen of the Tor Project said in a follow-up.

articles.title: El banco más grande de India confirmó un ciberataque que expuso datos de casi 4.000 clientes
articles.text:
El Banco Estatal de la India (SBI), la entidad financiera más grande del país, confirmó este miércoles que sufrió un ciberataque que expuso en la red oscura (dark web) información personal de casi 4.000 clientes, cinco días después de que un grupo de hackers asegurara haber robado cientos de miles de registros.
El banco lo informó en una presentación ante la Bolsa de Bombay, exigida por la ley de valores de la nación asiática cuando ocurre un incidente con impacto potencial en los inversores. Según el documento, el 16 de octubre recibió alertas de su proveedor de inteligencia de amenazas, de la Agencia de Ciberdefensa del país y del equipo nacional de respuesta a incidentes CERT-In sobre una posible filtración de datos.
El análisis preliminar de SBI revisó unos 375.000 registros disponibles en la red oscura y confirmó que 3.897 de ellos contenían información personal identificable de clientes. Entre los datos expuestos figuran números de teléfono, fechas de nacimiento, nombres, géneros, direcciones de correo electrónico, domicilios y códigos internos vinculados a préstamos.
El banco precisó que no se identificaron contraseñas, claves de seguridad ni códigos de un solo uso entre la información filtrada, y que no se reportaron pérdidas de dinero de los clientes. También aseguró que el incidente no tuvo impacto material en sus operaciones centrales ni en su continuidad de negocio.
La filtración salió a la luz el 16 de octubre, cuando un grupo que se identifica como Siriusim publicó en el foro de la red oscura BreachForums que poseía unos 375.000 registros en formato de planilla y 2.722 documentos en PDF, entre ellos solicitudes de préstamos y formularios de apertura de cuentas.
SBI dijo que activó sus protocolos de respuesta y contención ante incidentes cibernéticos y que contrató a una firma de ciberseguridad independiente, habilitada por CERT-In para determinar el origen y el alcance real de la exposición.
Una firma duda sobre la respuesta del banco
La Internet Freedom Foundation, una organización india de derechos digitales, cuestionó que la presentación del banco no aclare si los clientes afectados fueron notificados de manera directa. Entre la alerta inicial y la confirmación pública pasaron cinco días.
La organización pidió a SBI que avise a cada cliente afectado por mensaje de texto, correo electrónico y carta, en inglés, hindi y el idioma local, con una explicación de qué datos quedaron expuestos y qué pasos seguir. También reclamó un canal de consulta específico para las víctimas.
Además, exigió que el banco precise si los 2.722 documentos filtrados incluyen comprobantes de identidad como el número de Aadhaar o el pasaporte, y que explique cómo se produjo la filtración, incluida la posibilidad de que haya salido a través de un proveedor externo.
La fundación también pidió al Banco de Reserva de India, el regulador financiero del país, que fije un plazo obligatorio para que las entidades avisen a sus clientes ante una brecha de datos mientras no entre en vigencia la nueva ley de protección de datos personales del país.
Antecedentes de brechas en la banca india
No es el primer caso del sector bancario indio este año. En julio, el estatal Bank of Baroda reconoció una filtración que expuso información vinculada a cuentas de clientes y documentos internos, tras detectarse en la red oscura un paquete de datos de aproximadamente un terabyte.
En julio de 2025, el SBI ya había reportado una vulnerabilidad de su seguridad en Yono, su aplicación de banca móvil usada por decenas de millones de personas en India y por parte de su numerosa comunidad en el exterior, reportó Cyber Security News, destacado portal ligado a la ciberseguridad. La entidad bancaria aclaró que el fallo correspondía a una versión antigua y que la actualización ya no presentaba dicha fragilidad.
El banco dijo que continúa evaluando el incidente y que irá aplicando medidas preventivas y correctivas a medida que avance la investigación independiente sobre la autenticidad y el alcance real de los datos filtrados.

articles.title: Perplexity Computer peut désormais tourner en local sur Mac, mais il faut une machine musclée
articles.text:
Perplexity Computer peut désormais exécuter ses tâches directement sur un Mac, sans confier systématiquement les données de l’utilisateur à des serveurs distants. Une évolution intéressante pour la confidentialité, qui demande toutefois une configuration généreuse et un abonnement payant.
Confier ses documents professionnels, ses mails ou ses tableaux financiers à un agent IA, pourquoi pas. Mais savoir que toutes ces informations peuvent transiter par des serveurs distants a de quoi refroidir les plus prudents. Perplexity tente de répondre à cette inquiétude avec une nouvelle version de Computer, son assistant capable de réaliser des tâches dans les applications du Mac. Jusqu’ici, l’essentiel du travail reposait sur le cloud. Désormais, l’entreprise propose de faire tourner toute la mécanique directement sur votre ordinateur, du modèle d’intelligence artificielle à l’exécution des actions demandées.
Le modèle et l’agent tournent tous deux sur le Mac
Dans une annonce publiée le 20 octobre, Perplexity présente un mode entièrement local pour Computer, son agent IA disponible sur macOS depuis le printemps. La différence avec la version que nous vous présentions en mai dernier est importante. À l’époque, l’assistant pouvait déjà accéder aux fichiers et aux applications de l’ordinateur, mais déléguait une grande partie de son traitement aux serveurs de Perplexity.
Avec cette mise à jour, le modèle d’IA, la planification, le raisonnement et le traitement des fichiers s’exécutent directement sur le Mac. Même les opérations utilisant du code ou des outils sont réalisées dans des environnements isolés, avec des autorisations d’accès aux données.
L'utilisateur peut choisir entre deux modèles locaux : Qwen 3.6 et PPLX Pro, une version de Qwen adaptée par Perplexity. Concrètement, Computer peut consulter des notes, parcourir des messages, analyser des documents ou préparer un tableau dans Numbers. Il peut aussi travailler avec Mail, Excel ou Keynote, sous réserve des autorisations nécessaires.
Selon Perplexity, les informations personnelles peuvent ainsi rester sur l’ordinateur pendant toute la réalisation d’une tâche. Une promesse intéressante, même s'il faudra vérifier de plus près les échanges réseau de l’application pour s'en assurer.
Plus de confidentialité, mais 36 Go de RAM requis
Faire travailler une IA directement sur son ordinateur présente un avantage évident : les documents confidentiels n’ont plus besoin d’être systématiquement transmis au cloud. Mais cela demande des ressources. Perplexity recommande au moins 36 Go de mémoire unifiée sur un Mac équipé d’une puce Apple Silicon. Il s’agit bien d’une configuration recommandée : l’entreprise ne précise pas le minimum permettant d’activer ce nouveau mode. Les Mac moins puissants peuvent toujours utiliser Hybrid Compute, qui combine traitement local et modèles distants. Cette formule fonctionne à partir de 24 Go de mémoire unifiée, avec macOS 15 ou une version ultérieure.
Autre nuance importante : entièrement local ne veut pas dire systématiquement hors ligne. Computer peut réaliser des tâches sans connexion Internet lorsque les ressources nécessaires sont présentes sur le Mac. En revanche, rechercher des informations récentes, utiliser certains services connectés ou solliciter l’un des modèles avancés disponibles dans le cloud nécessite un accès au réseau. L’utilisateur doit autoriser ce recours aux serveurs distants.
Enfin, le mode local est réservé aux abonnés Perplexity Pro, Max et Enterprise. Il est proposé dès maintenant dans la dernière version de l’application Mac, avec téléchargement du modèle choisi lors de la configuration.
Pour les utilisateurs disposant déjà d'un Mac suffisamment équipé, voilà une manière de confier davantage de tâches à une IA sans lui ouvrir systématiquement la porte de ses données personnelles. À condition, bien sûr, d’accepter de payer l’abonnement.

articles.title: Microsoft Scales Back Copilot Integration in Windows 11, Removes Eight File Explorer Actions
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 21st 2026
Microsoft Scales Back Copilot Integration in Windows 11, Removes Eight File Explorer Actions
Microsoft is officially cutting back on forced AI adoption that has been troubling Windows 11 users by working to simplify AI use across its operating system. According to a report by Windows Latest, Microsoft is removing Copilot actions related to OneDrive in File Explorer. This means that a simple right-click to open the context menu and then selecting the OneDrive icon will no longer present a long list of tasks that Microsoft's Copilot LLM would perform on the file. These tasks included summarizing, comparing, and asking questions, which provided minimal value on their own. Instead, Copilot features like these can be accessed through "Ask Copilot" or other less intrusive methods. This change is part of a OneDrive update aimed at reducing eight AI actions and keeping them available for those who wish to use them. Image below is a courtesy of Windows Latest, which shows how these actions look like.
MicrosoftAs part of this change, we're retiring the OneDrive Copilot Summarize, Create FAQ, Compare Files, Ask a question, Explain image, Explain images, Compare images, Extract text actions from the File Explorer context menu... Users can still access Copilot features via right-click "Ask Copilot," the File Explorer Home icon, or the OneDrive activity center.
According to Windows Latest, Microsoft is rolling out these simplified actions in stages, with plans to fully implement them by mid-November this year. The wait of a few weeks is worthwhile for those eager to see fewer forced AI integrations, suggesting that other areas may receive similar treatment. Hopefully, this simplification and reduction of AI integration will extend to other parts of Windows 11, but we will have to wait for the mid-November update to find out.

articles.title: Criptomonedas: cuál es su precio en el mercado este miércoles 21 de octubre
articles.text:
Las criptomonedas son un activo digital innovador que han experimentado un crecimiento monumental en los últimos tiempos debido a varios elementos que contribuyen a ello, entre ellos que algunos gobiernos hayan decidido darles una oportunidad como moneda de curso legal; no obstante, también han sufrido descalabros que han puesto en duda su viabilidad, como el más reciente episodio conocido como el "criptoinvierno".
Pese a este panorama, cada vez más personas han empezado a adquirir criptomonedas para poder invertir en algo "seguro" y "fiable" tanto a corto como a largo plazo, a pesar de los niveles extremos de inestabilidad que sufre constantemente.
Sin embargo, invertir o comprar en criptodivisas es más fácil de lo que parece. Hay que recordar que se trata de monedas virtuales, por lo que serán controladas en carteras o monederos que comparten esa particularidad, pues a diferencia del dinero corriente, no tienen un soporte físico.
El precio de las criptomonedas hoy
Esta es la cotización de las criptodivisas más destacadas en este momento.
El Bitcoin, cotiza a 82.734,19 dólares, lo que implicó un cambio de -0,249% en las últimas horas.
La segunda criptomoneda más popular del mercado, Ethereum, ha mostrado un movimiento de -0,187% en las últimas 24 horas, por lo que su valor se ubica en 2.442,16 dólares.
En el caso de TetherUs, su precio es de 1 dólares, por lo que en el último día tuvo un movimiento de -0%.
Por su parte, BNB, tiene un valor de 743,49 dólares, con un cambio de 1,71%, en cambio el Litecoin cotizó a 61.523 dólares, tras una variación de 3.132767.
Finalmente, el Dogecoin, una de las monedas virtuales que fue impulsada por Elon Musk, tiene un valor de 0,08 dólares tras presentar un cambio de 2,54% en las últimas 24 horas.
Qué pasa con las criptodivisas
Luego de que en las primeras semanas de mayo del 2022 se viviera el "criptocrash" o "criptoinvierno" que dejaron al descubierto la enorme volatilidad de estas monedas digitales, ha llegado un nuevo periodo de relativa estabilidad.
Bitcoin, ethereum y BNB han mostrado variaciones "controladas", puesto que no se han disparado los precios como en semanas previas. Por ejemplo, a inicios de agosto, las mencionadas anteriormente tuvieron un cambio menor del 2%.
Por otra parte, algo que esta llamando la atención en el mundo de las criptomonedas es que China está ablandando sus restricciones y podría comenzar a permitir su uso. Específicamente sería Hong Kong en donde este cambio se haría presente.
Sumado a ello, la plataforma de transacciones digitales PayPal anunció su propia stablecoin llamada PayPal USD (PYUSD), que cuenta por el respaldo de depósitos en dólares, bonos del Tesoro de Estados Unidos a corto plazo y activos equivalentes.
La compañía ha afirmado en su declaración que permitirá la transferencia de fondos a monederos digitales de terceros y proporcionará detalles sobre cómo integrar su servicio en exchanges centralizados y descentralizados, con el objetivo de ser utilizado en Finanzas Descentralizadas (DeFi, por sus siglas en inglés). Por lo tanto, es muy probable que se utilice ampliamente en la industria Web3.
Su avance en Latinoamérica
Criptomonedas en México: el Banco de México (Banxico) ha determinado que ninguna de las instituciones que participan en el sistema financiero nacional podrá hacer uso o deberá permitir operaciones de ninguna clase a través de este medio de pago.
En territorio mexicano el empresario Ricardo Salinas Pliego, uno de los más ricos del país, ha mostrado interés en las criptomonedas y ha asegurado que varios de sus negocios aceptarán bitcoin en el futuro, incluido su banco; hasta el momento una de sus tiendas más populares ya lo hace.
Criptomonedas en Perú: el Banco Central de Reserva del Perú (BCR) ha dejado en claro que su misión no es ser el primero ni el segundo banco central que regule el uso de las criptomonedas, ello debido a la inestabilidad que las caracteriza. Sin embargo, hace días el presidente del (BCR) aseguró que el BCR trabajaba en un proyecto de moneda digital propia.
Criptomonedas en Colombia: en la nación sudamericana hay más de 500 sitios donde es permitido pagar con criptodivisas. Colombia ocupa el puesto 14 entre 26 países de adopción de criptomonedas, según el informe de Finder.
Criptomonedas en Centroamérica: en el gobierno de El Salvador, el bitcoin, que en septiembre de 2021 se convirtió en moneda de curso legal, ha perdido oficialmente este estatus en este enero del 2025 tras una reforma aprobada por la Asamblea Legislativa del país. Según informó la prensa local, la modificación de la Ley Bitcoin fue impulsada por el gobierno del presidente Nayib Bukele y respaldada por la mayoría oficialista en el órgano legislativo. Este cambio marca el fin de una política que había colocado al país centroamericano en el centro del debate global sobre las criptomonedas.
¿Cómo crear una criptomoneda?
Al momento de crear una criptomoneda es importante primero determinar qué se desea tener: una moneda o un token. La primera usa su propia blockchain, mientras que la segunda se basa en una red preexistente.
De acuerdo con el sitio de Binance, para crear una criptomoneda se necesita de un gran equipo de desarrolladores y expertos; mientras que para el token sí se requieren conocimientos técnicos pero es posible crearlo en minutos a través del uso de otras blockchains como Ethereum o BNB, que son las más populares.
Los costos de creación, el tiempo requerido y el uso de fuerza de trabajo dependerá de si se opta por hacer una moneda virtual o un token. En éste último caso también se puede usar un código establecido para crear tokens o pagar para usar un servicio de creación de monedas.
Es importante saber que antes de crear una criptomoneda se debe considerar su utilidad y estado legal.
En el caso de elegir crear una criptomoneda, entonces se debe elegir una blockchain, posteriormente se debe hacer un plan acorde al funcionamiento y la funcionalidad de la blockchain para diseñar los nodos y la interfaz.

articles.title: Trump says data centers should pay locals to get them on side — but last time they offered $10,000 and the residents called it a bribe
articles.text:
Trump says data centers should pay locals to get them on side — but last time they offered $10,000 and the residents called it a bribe
Data center developers could end up paying residents for approval
- President Trump says data center developers should offer a 'dividend' to get local community approval for campuses
- Nebius CRO says the company is "100% in principle" considering some form of local investment
- Paying local residents to approve a local data resident didn't go so well in Hazle, Pennsylvania
President Trump has told data center companies that one way to get local residents to support new developments is to “make deals” with local residents.
Trump suggested offering communities a “dividend,” adding, “I have watched the process closely, and Data Centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area, have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.”
“MAKE DEALS, and get them built!!! GREAT FOR THE U.S.A.,” the President wrote on Truth Social. But as one town has already demonstrated, these payments are viewed as a bribe that threaten to turn communities against each other.
Dividend or bribe?
As the November 2026 midterm elections draw closer, data centers have become a make-or-break topic for some candidates. Data center developers and AI companies have been channeling millions of dollars into political action committees in an effort to get a more favorable view of data centers.
Multiple states are considering enacting moratoriums on AI data center development, which if approved could cost developers and AI companies billions in lost investment. Environmental concerns and issues relating to noise and light pollution are high on the list for residents protesting against local developments.
NorthPoint Development is currently seeking to build an AI data center in Hazle, Pennsylvania, and offered each household $10,000 in an attempt to convince residents to get on board with having the campus approved. But the residents did not react as planned, calling the payment a bribe and turning it down over fears it could split the community in two - those who live near the campus and declined and those who live further away and took the payment.
When questioned by Trump’s proposal, Marc Boroditsky, CRO of Nebius told CNBC that the company is “100% in principle” having discussions about potential investments in local communities.

I could see something like a benefit of some sort that’s more direct economic opportunity for the community as well,” Boroditsky said. “A dividend is being paid in different forms — investing in education, job development, overall economic development. The concept that the president identified... it’s not crazy to consider something like that"
