articles.title: 'How do you know what's real?': US utilities are making AI data centers prove they exist before handing over power connections — as 50% of planned buildouts are currently being delayed, stalled, or canceled
articles.text:
'How do you know what's real?': US utilities are making AI data centers prove they exist before handing over power connections — as 50% of planned buildouts are currently being delayed, stalled, or canceled
The AI boom should have been a golden age for America's electric utilities
- US data center developers have requested 1,066GW of grid connections, but Wood Mackenzie expects utilities to commit to only about 28%
- Utilities are demanding collateral, longer contracts, and study fees; Exelon's high-probability load fell from a whopping 18GW to 11GW once it insisted on the former
- Because grid costs are shared, phantom demand risks landing on household bills, and nobody knows how much of it is real yet
US utilities and grid operators are now demanding higher rates, longer contracts, collateral, and steep engineering study fees from data center developers, in an attempt to weed out what the industry calls "phantom" data centers.
Reporting from The Wall Street Journal claims the reasoning is straightforward: Grid costs are shared, so if a utility builds substations and transmission lines for a project that never shows up, everyone else on the network ends up helping to pay for them.
The numbers back up the nerves in play: developers have requested 1,066GW of grid connections for US data centers, according to a Wood Mackenzie analysis first reported by Bloomberg in August 2026, a figure equal to roughly 83% of the country's entire utility-scale generating capacity at the end of 2025.
A queue full of ghosts as collateral becomes the norm?
Wood Mackenzie expects utilities to commit to serving only about 28% of it: roughly 12% that already has firm service commitments, plus a further 17% that looks likely. The WSJ also cites a separate Wood Mackenzie measure that puts just 23% of disclosed requests in its high-confidence category.
Much of the gap is due to duplication; developers who don't yet know which utility can deliver power fastest file the same project with several of them and keep every option open until one pans out.
Others are simply speculators: commentary in POWER Magazine argued that private equity funds, land brokers and shell companies are claiming queue positions without site control or a signed customer, betting that land with a grid connection attached will find a buyer.
The phenomenon isn't new. Utility Dive was writing about phantom data centers in 2025, and TR reported in July that 67% of electricity executives surveyed by Capgemini were seeing speculative applications for capacity. The change is that utilities are now pricing the problem, and it is causing many adverse effects.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Exelon's attempts to lock down potential consumers
Exelon, which runs utilities across the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest, offers the clearest look at what happens when developers are asked to put money down.
After it began requiring transmission security agreements (TSAs), contracts that bind customers to credit obligations, committed revenue contributions, and shortfall payments, its high-probability data center load fell nearly 40%, from 18GW at the end of 2025 to about 11GW in the second quarter. Its wider pipeline of projects under study dropped from about 43GW to 25GW.
Jeanne Jones, Exelon's CFO, told the WSJ that typical requests used to be around 50MW and now often run to 1,000MW or more. The question she kept fielding, internally and externally, was "How do you know what's real?"
Exelon, however, also told analysts its $41 billion capital plan through 2029 is unchanged, so a 40% cut in expected data center load has not, so far, shrunk the spending plan.
None of this would matter much if grid capacity were cheap, but it simply isn't. PJM, the largest US grid operator, saw its capacity auction clear at the price cap for the third time in a row this summer while missing its reliability target by 6.8GW.
In September, its independent market monitor told federal regulators that 4,017MW of forecast data center load, 42% of the growth PJM had assumed, had already been canceled or delayed.
Households are feeling the cost increase; reports in July indicated that Henrico County, Virginia, asked staff and schools to cut electricity use after a 24.9% rate increase. Virginia has also moved to stop utilities passing data center costs onto everyday users, and Texas bills are rising faster than inflation. Lindsey Short of the Ohio Manufacturers' Association warned against building the grid around "the most optimistic number on somebody's spreadsheet."
Underbuilding carries its own risks, though, especially when transformers can take years to arrive, as a recent deep dive on grid bottlenecks laid out. That is why utilities are locking in the customers they do accept. Average minimum contract lengths for large customers have risen to about 10.8 years from 4.6 before 2024, according to filings aggregated by Halcyon and cited by the Journal, and a separate research brief built on Halcyon's tracker found a similar jump.
What nobody can yet say is how much of the AI power rush is real, and that poses problems for planners, stakeholders, and households alike. Until it does, utilities are doing what any lender would: asking to see the money first; households just happen to be roadkill if things don't pan out.

Rahim Amir is a UAE-based tech writer who enjoys building PCs as much as he enjoys writing about them. He has been professionally writing about PC hardware since 2023, focusing on buyer’s guides, hardware reviews, and sponsored content and features related to tech.
Having built hundreds of gaming PCs and being an avid gamer in his spare time, Rahim tends to have stronger opinions about hardware than most. This is particularly on display when he gets his way with powerful, but minimalistic RGB builds even as Small Form Factor (SFF) PCs come a close second.

articles.title: Le nouveau Google Pixel 11 est déjà disponible pour 20% de moins sur Amazon
articles.text:
Pour contrer son prix plus onéreux, Amazon retire 180 euros au nouveau Google Pixel 11. L'occasion d'avoir un smartphone polyvalent avec une partie photo redoutable d'efficacité.
Pour finir l'année, Google a sorti son Pixel 11. La marque ne révolutionne pas sa gamme et continue sur la lancée du Pixel 10 avec un appareil qui brille sur sa partie photo. Malgré ce manque d'évolution, le Pixel 11 avait été lancé pour 100 euros de plus que la version précédente, mais Amazon réduit la facture avec une promotion de 18 %.
Sur Amazon, le Google Pixel 11 passe de 999 euros à 819 euros
Pourquoi choisir le Google Pixel 11 ?
- Pour les efforts sur l'appareil photo : Le Google Pixel 11 conserve le téléobjectif 5x, mais se dote d'un nouveau zoom numérique 30x, ce qui peut être intéressant pour les éléments à moyenne distance.
- Pour ce design toujours identifiable : La gamme Pixel s'est démarquée avec cette grosse barre de photo au dos qui fait tout le charme de ce smartphone.
- L'IA au service de l'utilisateur : Les fonctionnalités IA de ce Google Pixel 11 sont multiples pour convenir à chacun. Parmi elles, on retrouve un outil de retouche photo et il est aussi possible de traduire des conversations en temps réel.
Google mise sur la photo
Sans surprise, Google mise sur la partie photo. Cela se voit avec cette large bande photo au dos de l'appareil pour accueillir les différents capteurs. Parmi eux, on compte un téléobjectif 5x déjà présent sur la version précédente. Un capteur grand angle de 48 Mpx est aussi de la partie et l'ensemble brille par sa bonne restitution des couleurs, surtout la journée. Un zoom numérique 30x est aussi présent pour restituer les détails des éléments à moyenne distance.
Pour retoucher vos photos, vous pourrez compter sur l'intelligence artificielle pour améliorer vos clichés. Pour s'éloigner des photos, l'IA offre la possibilité de traduire des conversations en temps réel.
Enfin, un petit point sur l'autonomie. Le Google Pixel 11 peut tenir près de 18 heures avec une seule charge et est compatible avec la charge sans fil.
Toujours les mêmes défauts
Deux problèmes sont à pointer du doigt avec ce Google Pixel 11. Le plus gênant concerne certainement les performances surtout si vous êtes un joueur. Le smartphone de Google est équipé du Google Tensor G6. Sur le papier, ce processeur peut faire tourner toutes les applications même les jeux les plus gourmands. Cependant, la firme américaine a souhaité mettre au point un smartphone qui ne chauffe pas. Par conséquent, dans les jeux gourmands, un "throttling" est présent pour contenir la chauffe et il limite donc les performances de l'appareil.
Deuxième point négatif : le design et surtout la façade avant. La dalle OLED de 6,3 pouces brille avec un pic de luminosité de 3 000 nits, mais il pêche par ses bordures épaisses. Elles sont visibles et Google ne prend pas le pli de la sobriété comme de nombreux constructeurs peuvent le faire.
✅ Les points forts
- Une partie photo améliorée avec un téléobjectif x30
- Des fonctionnalités IA bien intégrées
- Un pic en HDR mesuré à 3 000 nits
❌ Les limites
- Des performances gaming limitées, encore un coup du throttling
- Des bordures épaisses, en 2026, cela fait un peu tâche
Au lieu de dépenser 999 euros pour acheter le Google Pixel 11, vous pouvez l'avoir pour 819 euros sur Amazon
Avec ce Google Pixel 11, la marque continue de s'appuyer sur ses points forts en améliorant son appareil photo et en lui offrant un boost d'autonomie appréciable.
Néanmoins, les défauts restent les mêmes avec ce "throttling" important qui peut ternir l'expérience gaming.

articles.title: Elon Musk dispara los ingresos de SpaceX a 14.600 millones de dólares: centros de datos e IA, son la clave
articles.text:
Los ingresos de USD 14.600 millones que SpaceX reportó en el tercer trimestre de 2026 estuvieron impulsados por sus centros de datos y negocios de inteligencia artificial, que ya representan el 52% de la facturación de la compañía dirigida por Elon Musk.
La expansión de esta área, rebautizada como Super Inteligencia, explica la transformación de SpaceX: la empresa sumó USD 7.500 millones en ingresos mediante la herramienta de programación Cursor, el bot Grok y, sobre todo, su negocio de nube para inteligencia artificial.
Según TechCrunch, los centros de datos y los agentes de Grok generaron más ganancias de las previstas por los inversores.
La división de IA obtuvo USD 431 millones de beneficio, aunque el resultado fue afectado por USD 1.200 millones en gastos extraordinarios de compensación en acciones vinculados a la compra de Cursor.
Cómo es la iniciativa de Super Inteligencia de SpaceX
La línea de Super Inteligencia combina productos de software y capacidad de cómputo a gran escala.
Su negocio de nube ya cuenta con 1,7 GW de capacidad informática, un volumen que se convirtió en el principal motor de los resultados trimestrales.
El crecimiento de los ingresos también estuvo acompañado por una recuperación de la rentabilidad.
SpaceX registró un beneficio neto de USD 4.400 millones, frente a la pérdida de USD 1.000 millones que había informado en el mismo trimestre del año anterior.
Sin embargo, la expansión exige inversiones elevadas. La empresa destinó USD 19.600 millones a gastos de capital y prevé invertir entre USD 35.000 millones y USD 40.000 millones adicionales en el cuarto trimestre, mientras avanza con un segundo proyecto de centro de datos, Colossus II, y con el desarrollo del cohete Starship.
Cuál es el rol de los centros de datos en SpaceX
Musk sostiene que el principal límite para desplegar sistemas de superinteligencia ya no está solo en los chips, sino en la energía, la refrigeración y la infraestructura necesaria para operar los centros de datos.
Por eso, pasa cuatro días por semana en Memphis, Tennessee, donde se construye Colossus II.
La compañía busca trasladar a esa infraestructura capacidades industriales desarrolladas para sus operaciones espaciales.
Por ejemplo, utiliza técnicas de fundición de metal para fabricar componentes de turbinas y reducir las demoras de entre 12 y 18 meses que enfrentan los fabricantes para conseguir palas y álabes.
La apuesta también se conecta con Starlink, que alcanzó 13,6 millones de clientes. Musk prevé que el crecimiento de los agentes de inteligencia artificial aumente la demanda de conectividad, mientras SpaceX proyecta desplegar una nueva generación de satélites y desarrollar centros de datos orbitales.
Elon Musk presenta la nueva línea Roadster de Tesla
Elon Musk presentó el nuevo Tesla Roadster, un deportivo eléctrico con tecnologías desarrolladas junto con SpaceX y una promesa de producción para 2028.
La exhibición buscó reposicionar al modelo como una demostración de ingeniería extrema, más que como un vehículo de producción masiva.
El Roadster incorpora propulsores derivados de SpaceX, que Tesla utilizó durante la presentación para exhibir maniobras aéreas breves y una aceleración fuera de los parámetros habituales de la industria.
Musk sostuvo que el auto podrá acelerar de 0 a 60 millas por hora en menos de un segundo en algunas configuraciones.
El evento se realizó en una instalación de pruebas de SpaceX en McGregor, Texas. Allí, Tesla mostró un vehículo biplaza capaz de subir una rampa pronunciada, quedar suspendido boca abajo y completar un giro antes de aterrizar con asistencia de chorros de aire.
La compañía no informó el precio ni el volumen previsto de producción.
El proyecto refuerza la alianza tecnológica entre Tesla y SpaceX. Sin embargo, todavía quedan interrogantes sobre la homologación para circular en la vía pública y sobre si las capacidades exhibidas en el escenario podrán trasladarse al producto final.

articles.title: Pegasus Spyware Infection Confirmed on Serbian University Rector's iPhone Days Before Election
articles.text:
The iPhone of Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade and a prominent supporter of Serbia's student protest movement, was infected with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware in 2026, the Citizen Lab said on October 19.
The finding came six days before Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary election. The infection used a zero-click exploit, meaning Đokić did not have to tap a link or open a file for it to work.
The lab found the infection with high confidence, but its note provides no date within 2026, does not identify who was behind the attack, and notes that its investigation is ongoing.
The election was called in September after nearly two years of protests that began when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people.
The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, analyzed forensic artifacts from the phone at Đokić's request, working with the Serbian digital-rights group SHARE Foundation. SHARE led the investigation of an earlier wave of Serbian cases made public in September.
A second case concerns Rade Bajić, a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia's Public Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime who worked on the "Generalštab" corruption investigation into a Kushner-linked property project in Belgrade. Bajić received an Apple Threat Notification on August 13 and a reminder on August 27.
Apple sends these alerts when it detects activity consistent with an attack by mercenary spyware, the commercial hacking tools that companies such as NSO sell to governments, and it does not say who is behind the attacks.
The Citizen Lab treats a notification as a high-confidence sign that Bajić's phone was likely targeted. Its forensic analysis of the device is ongoing, and the note does not say whether the phone was infected.
The Generalštab case concerns the removal of heritage protection from Belgrade's bombed-out former army General Staff complex to clear the way for a luxury development backed by a company linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law.
In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials with abuse of office and falsifying documents in the case, the Associated Press reported. Bajić says he was taken off the investigation in November 2025 without explanation, and in February he spoke about the case at a protest called by student activists outside Serbia's Constitutional Court.
The lab's note does not say what, if anything, was taken from the rector's phone. Pegasus gives whoever operates it the same access as the phone's owner, including private and encrypted messages, and can switch on the microphone and camera without the owner knowing, according to the lab's analysis of the September case.
Đokić called the spyware on his phone "another attempt of intimidation" in an English-language statement published by the university, and demanded an independent investigation without delay, with its results made public and whoever installed and used the spyware prosecuted. Police raided the rector's offices on March 31 and seized computers and servers, he said at the time.
The Security Information Agency (BIA), Serbia's civilian security service, dismissed the September allegations that students and opposition politicians had been spied on as "purely trivial sensationalism" in a statement on September 3, as translated by the broadcaster N1, and said it operates strictly within Serbian law.
The two cases extend a wave that SHARE reported on September 2, when it said at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists, an opposition MP and a local councilor, had been targeted with spyware since the start of the year. Twelve of them had received Apple Threat Notifications in August, the month Apple warned users in 110 countries.
One was Jelena Kontić, a student whose Pegasus infection the Citizen Lab confirmed. The other two had a new version of NoviSpy, an Android spyware, installed on their phones.
By the Citizen Lab's count, the two new cases bring the number of people in Serbian civil society publicly known to have been targeted or infected with mercenary spyware this year to at least 16.
Amnesty International reported in December 2024 that NoviSpy was configured to send stolen data to a server whose IP address belonged to the BIA and was installed on activists' and journalists' phones during police questioning, after the devices were unlocked with Cellebrite forensic tools.
Lawyers for Kontić filed a criminal complaint on October 6 against unidentified individuals in the BIA and the police, as well as people responsible at NSO Group. Pegasus is sold only to governments and state agencies, SHARE says, and the complaints already filed over spyware in Serbia have brought no effective action.
The note does not name the flaw used against Đokić's phone or say whether current iOS releases block it, so there is no case-specific fix to install. The lab's advice for people at risk because of who they are or what they do:
- Turn on Lockdown Mode on your iPhone and keep iOS up to date.
- If you receive an Apple Threat Notification, assume the phone is infected until an expert has checked it, and get help at once: SHARE Foundation in Serbia, or Access Now's Digital Security Helpline elsewhere.
- Have close contacts, such as family members and people they work with, screened for spyware too.

articles.title: Keychron Launches J3 SE QMK Wireless Mechanical Keyboard With Soft Pastel Color Palette
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Keychron Launches J3 SE QMK Wireless Mechanical Keyboard With Soft Pastel Color Palette
Deviating from its usual line-up of understated, almost professional keyboard designs that mostly feature matte black and white designs with small splashes of color, Keychron has just released the J3 SE wireless mechanical keyboard in more playful "Pink" and "Pink Blue" colorways. The J3 SE features an easy-to-use 96% layout that makes few compromises to cut down on desk space—even including a full-size zero key in the num pad. Keychron sells the J3 SE on its site for $129.99. 
The Keychron J3 SE has an ABS case, in either pastel pink or blue, while the Blue Pink colorway has a mix of white, pink, and blue keycaps, and the Pink colorway features keycaps in white, light pink, and a deeper salmon pink color. Both the Pink and Blue Pink variants of the J3 SE have double-shot PBT keycaps in the MDA profile, and there is a sizeable knob in the top right corner of the keyboard, above the num pad. Another notable feature is the inclusion of north-facing RGB backlighting, which should make it significantly easier to find shine-through keycaps that work properly with the keyboard.Keychron has equipped the J3 SE with Keychron Sakura Milk switches, which are pre-lubricated linear switches with 35 gf actuation force, 3.6 mm of total travel, and a 2 mm actuation distance. The switches have POM stems and top housings, which should result in long-term smoothness, but may have a slightly more scratchy feel initially.The Keychron J3 SE has both 2.4 GHz and Bluetooth 5.2 wireless connectivity, with a USB Type-C wired connection as a third option, and it has a 4,000 mAh battery that Keychron says should deliver up to 2,000 hours of battery life—106 hours with RGB enabled and set to the lowest brightness. The 2.4 GHz connection peaks at 1 kHz polling rate, but that should be plenty, unless you're a hardcore esports gamer. 
One of the benefits of an ABS case is that Keychron was able to include two-stage flip out feet, giving the J3 SE optional typing angles of 4.5°, 6.4°, or 8.7°. The J3 SE also uses QMK firmware, which means that it is fully customizable in Keychron's Launcher browser-based software, including key remapping, macros, sleep time adjustment, and backlighting customization.

articles.title: Trump officials asked CISA to secretly hack a voting machine — and not disclose any vulnerabilities they found
articles.text:
Trump officials asked CISA to secretly hack a voting machine — and not disclose any vulnerabilities they found
CISA usually helps protect elections, but this time they were asked to help hack them
- Trump administration officials asked CISA to hack a voting machine just months into his second term
- CISA was told not to disclose any vulnerabilities to the voting machine manufacturer
- CISA has been gutted by job cuts and a lack of funding, with many state officials hesitant to trust the agency with securing the midterm elections
Towards the start of President Trump’s second term, allies in the Department of Homeland Security tasked the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) with secretly acquiring a voting machine with instructions to hack it and not tell anyone except the White House about the vulnerabilities they found.
ProPublica, who spoke to two former administration officials with knowledge of the request, noted that the standard practices of CISA require the agency to let manufacturers know of vulnerabilities in their technology, but the political appointees explicitly asked CISA not to.
“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any [election] results they don’t like,” one of the former officials told ProPublica. “This goes against everything CISA represents.”
CISA asked to hack voting machine
CISA has been a relentless target of the Trump Administration, with the agency’s jobs being cut by one third and the majority of its senior leadership resigning or being fired.
In total, CISA has cut 1,000 jobs since the start of Trump’s second term - largely down to Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency - with additional cuts to funding in 2027 likely to result in a further 900 jobs being lost.
As a result of these job cuts, remaining CISA employees told the political appointees that the request to hack a voting machine couldn’t be fulfilled.
Since 2018, CISA has been responsible for helping to protect election infrastructure from cyber attacks and interference, but has had to cut back on much of its work in these areas due to a lack of funding and staff. Many state officials have been unable to seek election support ahead of the November midterm elections.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
As a result of Trump’s cuts to CISA’s jobs and funding, many state officials fear the agency has become a shell occupied by Trump loyalists. “They’ve violated the entire premise of that information-sharing relationship,” a former high-ranking federal cybersecurity official told ProPublica. “There’s no fucking way they’re ever going to give any information to CISA. And it’s unclear if they ever will in the future.”
In response to the claims, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said, “President Trump has done more than any other President to ensure we have free and fair elections.”
“I don’t pay attention to what the president says. I pay attention to what his administration does,” said Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes. “And what they’ve done is basically cut us off and left us on our own.”
Voting difficulties start early
Early voting for the midterms has already started in some states, but early polling sites at North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, the University of North Carolina Greensboro, and Western Carolina University have been shut down, with Guilford County board members saying the resources could be better allocated elsewhere.
Shutting the polling sites makes it significantly harder for the collective 40,000 students to vote, with university policy preventing some students from owning a car during their first year of study.
Shia Rozier, a senior at North Carolina A&T and cofounder of student organization Protect Ours NC told NPR, “In order to get to the polls, they now have to get a Lyft or get a Uber or get somebody to take them at a time where gas prices are extremely high, creating an additional barrier to the poll.”
In response, students organized a march to the nearest polling site over 45 minutes away.

articles.title: Google activó en los autos una versión de Gemini que usa tu Gmail y tus fotos
articles.text:
Google empezó a distribuir una versión de su asistente Gemini en el auto que puede leer el Gmail, el calendario y las fotos del usuario para responder preguntas con información personal, sin que haga falta tocar el teléfono.
La función se llama Personal Intelligence y llega primero a Android Auto, la aplicación que proyecta el teléfono en la pantalla del vehículo. En los próximos meses se sumará a los autos que traen el sistema Google built-in instalado de fábrica.
Con el permiso del usuario, Gemini conecta Gmail, Google Calendar, Google Photos, Google Maps, YouTube y el buscador de Google para combinar datos de varias fuentes y dar una sola respuesta.
Google puso como ejemplo preguntarle a Gemini, camino al aeropuerto, por la puerta de embarque y el estado del vuelo: el asistente busca ambos datos en el correo sin que el conductor tenga que abrir la app de la aerolínea.
Otros ejemplos del comunicado incluyen pedirle un restaurante vegetariano en la ruta según gustos previos, pedirle que lleve al usuario a una cita médica sin decir la dirección, o pedirle que encuentre, a partir de una foto guardada, el lavadero de autos visitado la semana anterior.
Gemini ya estaba en el auto desde el 2025
Google incorporó Gemini a Android Auto en reemplazo de Google Assistant el año pasado. Personal Intelligence ya existía en el teléfono desde enero y se había extendido a las cuentas gratuitas en marzo.
Android Auto es compatible con más de 250 millones de autos en el mundo, según datos que Google difundió en mayo. El sistema Google built-in, en cambio, viene instalado de fábrica en más de cien modelos de dieciséis marcas, entre ellas Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo y Polestar.
Apagada por defecto y con límites de acceso
Personal Intelligence viene apagada por defecto. El usuario debe activarla desde la configuración de Gemini y puede elegir qué aplicaciones conectar o desconectarlas en cualquier momento, según detalló Google en su blog oficial.
En los autos con Google built-in, el asistente solo entrega respuestas personalizadas cuando el teléfono del usuario está conectado al vehículo. Sin la función activada, Gemini sigue funcionando para navegación, música y llamadas, pero sin adaptar sus respuestas a cada persona.
TechCrunch señaló que ese nivel de cruce de datos personales, dentro de un vehículo, podría generar incomodidad en algunos usuarios. Google respondió que el control queda siempre del lado de quien maneja, con la posibilidad de apagar la función en cualquier momento.
El despliegue alcanza a cuentas personales de Google de usuarios mayores de 18 años en casi todo el mundo, aunque no está disponible en el Reino Unido, Suiza, Nigeria y los países del Espacio Económico Europeo. Tampoco funciona en cuentas de Workspace para empresas o instituciones educativas.
La actualización llega en un momento en el que varios fabricantes de autos exploran asistentes de inteligencia artificial propios: Apple sumó a Siri funciones que también usan información personal del usuario dentro de CarPlay, su sistema para conectar el iPhone al auto. Google todavía no fijó una fecha exacta para completar el despliegue en los vehículos con Google built-in, más allá de hablar de “los próximos meses”.
Funciones de Gemini en Android Auto
Gemini en Android Auto permite encadenar órdenes, corregir instrucciones y obtener respuestas adaptadas a cada situación sin apartar la vista de la carretera. Su integración con Google Maps habilita búsquedas complejas —“busca una cafetería bien valorada en mi ruta que esté abierta ahora”— y la selección de resultados por voz, mientras que la gestión de mensajes y llamadas entiende correcciones y dictados largos con mayor precisión que su antecesor, Google Assistant.
La productividad al volante se extiende a Gmail, Calendar, Tasks y Keep: el conductor puede pedir la dirección de un hotel desde un correo, consultar eventos del calendario o crear recordatorias sin tocar el teléfono. Para la música, el sistema interpreta pedidos por estado de ánimo o duración del viaje. La función Gemini Live suma conversación continua, con memoria de temas previos, útil para preparar reuniones o entretener a los niños durante el trayecto.

articles.title: IA : la demande est telle que ces 3 réacteurs nucléaires endormis seront bientôt réveillés
articles.text:
Les États-Unis vont relancer trois centrales nucléaires fermées, dont une déjà en cours de démantèlement. Un pari inédit, dicté par l’appétit insatiable de l’intelligence artificielle (IA) pour l’électricité.
Car les data centers qui font tourner l’IA ne peuvent pas s’arrêter. Ils ont besoin de courant jour et nuit. Le nucléaire répond parfaitement à cette problématique, puisqu’il produit en continu, contrairement au solaire ou à l’éolien. Mais construire un nouveau réacteur peut prendre une dizaine d’années, alors que le temps presse pour les géants de la tech. Ils se ruent alors vers des dispositifs déjà existants.
Trois réacteurs, 2,25 GW à remettre sur le réseau
Ensemble, ils doivent redonner 2,25 GW au réseau, de quoi alimenter environ 2 millions de foyers et d’entreprises. Tous ont été arrêtés avant la fin de leur licence, car leur électricité coûtait alors trop cher.
Le projet le plus avancé est celui de Palisades, dans le Michigan. En service de 1971 à 2022, le site avait été racheté par l’entreprise Holtec qui avait commencé à le démonter. C’est du jamais-vu : aucun réacteur commercial n’est connu pour avoir redémarré après le début de son démantèlement. Et le chargement du combustible a démarré en août pour une remise en service prévue en mars 2027.
Deux autres réacteurs vont suivre. En Pennsylvanie, c’est l’unité 1 de Three Mile Island, rebaptisée Crane, qui s’apprête à renaître après un arrêt en 2019, faute de rentabilité. Elle doit fournir 835 MW à Microsoft dès 2027, à condition d’obtenir le feu vert de l’autorité de sûreté américaine. Car cette centrale a un lourd passif : son unité 2 a été détruite lors d'un accident en 1979.
Puis dans l’Iowa, le réacteur de Duane Arnold est attendu en 2029. Fermé en 2020 après des dégâts causés par une tempête, il devrait alimenter Google avec 615 MW.
Ce n’est que le début
Il ne s’agit que du début. Google vient en effet de signer un contrat avec le fournisseur Constellation pour moderniser 11 réacteurs avec plus de 4,3 milliards de dollars d’investissements à la clé. Même son de cloche chez Amazon, qui multiplie les accords clés pour alimenter ses data centers AWS avec de l’énergie nucléaire.
Les efforts de Meta sont, eux aussi, notables. En janvier, la firme a dévoilé des accords censés soutenir jusqu’à 6,6 GW d’ici à 2035, soit l’équivalent de la consommation d’environ 5 millions de foyers. Premier volet : la firme Vistra lui vendra pendant 20 ans toute la production de deux centrales de l’Ohio, Perry et Davis-Besse, soit plus de 2,1 GW. Meta financera aussi l’augmentation de puissance de ces deux sites et de celui de Beaver Valley, en Pennsylvanie, pour 433 MW de plus dès le début des années 2030. Selon le groupe, ce sont les plus importantes améliorations de ce type financées par un client privé aux États-Unis.
Il soutient TerraPower, la société fondée par Bill Gates, qui développe des réacteurs d’un nouveau genre : les Natrium, refroidis au sodium, de 345 MW chacun, et s’est associé à Oklo pour créer un complexe de réacteurs avancés dans l’Ohio. Cette électricité doit nourrir ses data centers, dont Prometheus, un site d’1 GW en construction dans le même État.
D’autres initiatives vont très certainement voir le jour, tant l’appétit de ces géants pour l’IA est insatiable. Leurs dépenses exorbitantes pour la développer le prouvent.
Sources : Tom’s Hardware, The Los Angeles Times
Une énergie pilotable est une production électrique qu’on peut maintenir et ajuster à la demande, y compris la nuit et lors des pics de charge. Les infrastructures d’IA (serveurs, stockage, réseaux) tournent en continu et tolèrent mal les coupures ou les fortes variations, car l’arrêt/redémarrage a un coût technique et opérationnel. Le solaire et l’éolien sont dits intermittents : leur production dépend de la météo et du cycle jour/nuit, ce qui impose des solutions d’équilibrage (batteries, hydraulique, gaz, importations). Le nucléaire fournit généralement une production stable sur de longues périodes, ce qui colle bien à un besoin « base-load » des grands data centers.
Redémarrer un réacteur implique de repasser une chaîne complète d’étapes techniques et réglementaires : inspections, remise à niveau des systèmes de sûreté, qualification d’équipements, puis rechargement en combustible et essais avant couplage au réseau. Après une longue mise à l’arrêt, certains matériels peuvent avoir vieilli ou avoir été modifiés, ce qui impose des contrôles et parfois des remplacements lourds. Si le démantèlement a déjà commencé, la difficulté augmente : des équipements peuvent avoir été retirés, des circuits déconnectés, et la configuration du site peut ne plus correspondre à l’état requis pour l’exploitation. Dans tous les cas, l’autorité de sûreté doit valider que le réacteur respecte les exigences actuelles, pas seulement celles en vigueur lors de sa fermeture.

articles.title: WhatsApp Hid Instructions in Help Pages Telling Its AI Chatbot Not to Recommend Privacy Regulators
articles.text:
WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden instructions for its support chatbot that told it not to recommend a data protection authority or regulator to users who could no longer delete their accounts, even though WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe tells users they can complain to one.
The text sat in the pages' code, never shown on screen, until it was removed by October 18. Whether the chatbot ever followed the instructions is not known: Redact, the data-deletion software company that found the text, read the instructions, not the chatbot's answers.
WhatsApp told WIRED the instructions were for the chatbot that users reach by messaging WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they appeared in the pages because of a bug, now fixed.
A second block of hidden text on the page about reporting and blocking told the chatbot that once a user mentioned a lawyer, a lawsuit, or a court, it should not cite privacy laws such as the GDPR, even when the user raised them.
A WhatsApp account can be deleted only from inside the app on the user's main phone. A user who has lost the phone or the number cannot do it, and the help page on deleting an account says so in a visible note: a deactivated account is deleted 30 days after deactivation, and an inactive one is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days in the US.
Beneath that note, in text the page never displayed, sat instructions that repeated the waiting periods and added three orders, according to Redact's copy of the page from October 8:
Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number.
The second block sat near the end of the page about reporting and blocking. It applied, in its own words, "When a user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation", and from then on told the chatbot not to cite WhatsApp's Terms of Service or Privacy Policy, not to discuss WhatsApp's liability, to send users with legal matters to "a qualified legal professional", and:
Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly.
On the regulator, WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, effective July 2, 2026, says the opposite. "You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp's lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority," it says.
On deletion, the gap is narrower: the hidden text told the chatbot not to suggest that WhatsApp could delete a user's account, while the policy says users "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of" their information.
Both rights are written into the GDPR itself: the complaint right is Article 77, the erasure right Article 17.
Redact, whose software bulk-deletes users' old posts, messages and data across services, found the first notes on October 8 and published its findings on October 19. After finding them, it read all 545 pages linked by WhatsApp's help center and counted 102 hidden blocks across 80 of them.
Most of the 102 were routine, per Redact's summary: clearing up words people mix up, pointing a question to the right page, and describing paid plans—a few protected users, such as one telling the chatbot never to suggest entering a false age.
A few were in the same family as the two above. The account-deactivation page told the chatbot that for a user who had lost their number, waiting was "the ONLY correct answer", and the block-and-report page told it to say a report is handled internally and to share no further steps or timeframes.
One block named WhatsApp's support chatbot. Redact also checked 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages, which run on the same system, and found no notes like these.
The blocks sat in the pages' HTML under the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude and were not shown on screen, so anyone who viewed the page source could read them.
WhatsApp's server sent them, with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers, Redact found. Requests Redact sent on October 9 under the user-agent names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and Perplexity's crawlers use came back without the article or the notes. Redact did not test whether any AI assistant acted on them.
Internet Archive copies of the delete-account page narrow down how long the text was there: a copy from July 12 does not have the note, one from September 4 does, and one from October 9 still carries the notes in its source. Both notes were still on the live pages at 21:40 UTC on October 15.
By 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were removed from all 80 pages, with the pages themselves still up; an archive copy from 02:37 UTC that day shows the change.
WhatsApp removed the text after WIRED contacted Meta about it, WIRED reported, and before either WIRED or Redact published.
"These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI," WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told WIRED.
The company wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice," he said.
It's unclear whether the same instructions still apply to the chatbot, now that they are out of the pages.
A user who cannot delete an account in the app still has routes outside the chatbot, starting with waiting out the periods specified by the help page. Under WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, a user can always ask WhatsApp to erase their information.
In the EU, a user who is not satisfied can complain to their national data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which WhatsApp's policy names and asks people to raise the matter with the organization first, then through its online form.

articles.title: AMD Software Adrenalin 26.10.1 WHQL Drivers Released
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
AMD Software Adrenalin 26.10.1 WHQL Drivers Released
AMD has released its Adrenalin 26.10.1 WHQL graphics drivers, adding FSR Upscaling 4.1 support for Radeon RX 6000 series graphics cards and several Ryzen AI processor families. The release follows yesterday's announcement that AMD plans to bring FSR 4.1 to older Radeon GPUs, APUs, and Xbox. The new upscaling version supports Radeon RX 6000 series graphics products released back in 2020 and powered by the RDNA 2 graphics architecture. AMD FSR Upscaling 4.1 also arrives to Ryzen AI Max "Strix Halo" and "Gorgon Halo" APUs, and Ryzen AI 9 "Strix Point" and "Gorgon Point" mobile processors. The drivers also add support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, STAR WARS: Galactic Racer, and FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE.
In these new graphics drivers, AMD has fixed a stuttering issue that could occur in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Radeon RX 6000 series graphics products and newer models. Several known issues remain, as detailed in the release notes that follow, as usual.
DOWNLOAD: AMD Software Adrenalin 26.10.1 WHQLNew Features
- AMD FSR Upscaling 4.1 support for:
  - AMD Radeon RX 6000 Series Graphics products
  - AMD Ryzen AI Max 300 Series processors
  - AMD Ryzen AI Max 400 Series processors
  - AMD Ryzen AI 9 300 Series processors
  - AMD Ryzen AI 9 400 Series processors
New Game Support
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4
- STAR WARS: Galactic Racer
- FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE
Fixed Issues
- Stuttering may be observed while playing the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Radeon RX 6000 series graphics products and above.
Known Issues
- Intermittent application crash or driver timeout may be observed while playing Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced on Radeon RX 7000 series graphics products.
- Intermittent driver timeout may be observed while playing War Thunder on Radeon RX 5000 series graphics products. Users experiencing this issue are recommended to use AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition 26.9.1.
- Intermittent system shutdown may be observed while playing Valor Mortis on Radeon RX 7600 series graphics products.
- Intermittent driver timeout may be observed while playing Valor Mortis on Radeon RX 7000 series graphics products.
- Intermittent system shutdown may be observed while playing FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE on Ryzen AI MAX PRO 400 Series processors.
- Intermittent application hang may be observed while playing Death Stranding 2: On the Beach with AMD FSR enabled on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products. Users experiencing this issue are recommended to disable AMD FSR.
- Intermittent application crash or driver timeout may be observed while playing Cyberpunk 2077 with AMD FSR Upscaling, AMD Radeon Anti-Lag and in-game frame generation enabled during video playback on a secondary display on some Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products. Users experiencing this issue are recommended to disable in-game frame generation.
- Black screen may be observed when launching Fallout 76 on Ryzen AI Max PRO 400 Series processors.
- Intermittent application crash or driver timeout may be observed in some games when opening or closing other overlays, such as Xbox Game Bar, while the AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition Performance Metrics Overlay is enabled on Radeon graphics products. Users experiencing this issue are recommended to temporarily disable the Performance Metrics Overlay before opening or closing other overlays.
- Intermittent system crash or hang may be observed when switching between applications or toggling overlays while playing games with in-game AMD FSR Frame Generation enabled on Radeon RX 9000 series graphics products. Users experiencing this issue are recommended to enable V-Sync in game settings.
- Failure to install may be observed while installing AI Bundle components in some regions with limited access to HuggingFace and GitHub.
- AMD Smart Access Memory may become disabled after driver installation on Windows 10 systems.

This one required two reboots for it to activate on some systems as of the last few drivers updates for me its has been working 26.9.1 26.9.2 without requiring the extra reboots and same for this 26.10.1 driver on Win 10 here.

articles.title: 15 000 km par an et 96 % de satisfaits : la voiture électrique séduit toujours plus de Français, quitte à les faire rouler davantage qu’en thermique
articles.text:
15 000 km par an et 96 % de satisfaits : la voiture électrique séduit toujours plus de Français, quitte à les faire rouler davantage qu’en thermique
La voiture électrique s’impose désormais comme le véhicule principal des foyers équipés, au point de les faire rouler nettement plus que la moyenne du parc thermique.
Menée auprès de 1 009 automobilistes, la septième étude annuelle d’Enedis sur les habitudes de déplacement et de recharge confirme l’ancrage durable de la voiture électrique dans le quotidien des Français. Loin de se limiter aux courts trajets urbains, les propriétaires de ces motorisations affichent un taux de satisfaction record, avec des retours négatifs en chute libre (de 70 % à 42 % en un an). Épargnés par la hausse des prix des carburants, ils roulent désormais nettement plus que la moyenne nationale, majoritairement portée par les modèles thermiques.
Des Français qui roulent 3 400 km de plus en électrique qu’en thermique
Les conducteurs de voitures électriques parcourent désormais en moyenne 15 000 kilomètres par an (15 432 km exactement) d’après les derniers chiffres d’Enedis, soit 3 400 km de plus par rapport au parc thermique en 2025. Dans les foyers multi-équipés, qu’ils disposent d’un parc mixte (électrique et thermique, 55 %) ou de plusieurs modèles électriques (23 %), la motorisation 100 % électrique s’impose d’ailleurs comme le véhicule principal dans 78 % des cas.
Si 47 % des sondés l’utilisent uniquement au quotidien pour des trajets courants, la sérénité sur les longs parcours s’ancre grâce à l’amélioration du réseau autoroutier, désormais jugé adapté par 66 % des usagers (contre 54 % en 2025). Parmi les conducteurs partant en vacances en électrique, la moitié se dit ainsi prête à franchir plus de 600 kilomètres sans stress, un cap élevé qui reste stable sur un an (53 % en 2025).
Du côté de la recharge, le domicile reste le point de ravitaillement privilégié pour 87 % des résidents en maison individuelle. En immeuble collectif, cette pratique progresse de 10 points en un an pour atteindre 48 % des conducteurs, grâce au déploiement continu de solutions de recharge dans les copropriétés.
La prise renforcée s’impose à domicile, mais la recharge intelligente reste boudée
Pour brancher leur voiture chez eux, les automobilistes vont au plus simple : la prise renforcée de 3,7 kW équipe désormais 34 % des propriétaires de modèles 100 % électriques (contre 29 % en 2025), faisant reculer l’usage de la borne murale de 34 % à 31 %. Parallèlement, seuls 12 % des sondés utilisent les bornes publiques comme mode de recharge principal. Ce recul s’explique avant tout par une recharge à domicile qui suffit amplement (76 %) et par des tarifs publics jugés dissuasifs (38 %).
Enfin, l’optimisation énergétique peine à décoller. Bien que 57 % des recharges à domicile débutent la nuit entre 23 h et 7 h pour profiter des heures creuses, 22 % sont encore lancées lors du pic de consommation entre 18 h et 23 h, soit entre le retour du travail et l’heure du coucher. On apprend aussi que seuls 32 % des propriétaires pilotent systématiquement leur recharge. Un taux qui stagne depuis quatre ans, notamment car 30 % des sondés ont un contrat électrique au tarif Base sans heures creuses, et que 62 % des réfractaires déclarent ne tout simplement pas vouloir piloter leur charge.
Pourtant, comme le rappelle Mathias Povse, directeur Clients et Territoires d’Enedis : “Le pilotage des bornes représente une opportunité d’optimisation du coût de la recharge permettant une économie d’au moins 15 % sur la facture d’électricité, en rechargeant au meilleur moment”.

articles.title: Amazon hikes Prime membership by up to 30% in Australia ahead of Black Friday and holiday sales
articles.text:
Amazon hikes Prime membership by up to 30% in Australia ahead of Black Friday and holiday sales
Effective immediately for new members, while the price hike comes into effect from November 25 for existing subscribers
- Amazon Prime subscriptions will increase to AU$12.99 per month or AU$99 per year, up from AU$9.99 and AU$79, respectively
- These prices are effective immediately for new subscribers, while existing members will be charged starting from November 25
- Inclusions and perks like Prime Video, Music Prime and sale events remain unchanged
Amazon Australia has revealed its monthly Prime membership fee has increased from AU$9.99 to AU$12.99, effective immediately for new subscribers — a significant 30% hike from the previous cost. The annual membership price also increases from AU$79 to AU$99, a 25% rise.
In emails sent to Prime members, Amazon said the new pricing reflects the growing range of products and benefits available through the service, although the inclusions remain the same, including free and expedited delivery, Prime Video, Prime Music, Prime Reading, video games with Amazon Luna, and member-only events such as Prime Day and Prime Big Deal Days.
Existing customers will continue to pay the usual AU$9.99 per month and the price increase will apply from their first membership renewal date on or after November 25, 2026.
In a statement, an Amazon spokesperson told TechRadar that this price change is specific to Australia and attributes it largely to the expanded delivery footprint, new Prime Video content and access to Alexa+.
"We are committed to growing the value of Prime for members, and in just the last six months we have brought Prime Free overnight delivery before 8am on hundreds of thousands of products to four cities, expanded Prime Free Same-Day Delivery available now in nine regions across Australia, added new TV series and movies to Prime Video plus live sport, given free access to Alexa+, provided exclusive deals through events like Prime Day, and more," the spokesperson said.
"With the continued expansion of Prime member benefits, and so we can continue growing the offering, we will change the price of Prime to $12.99 per month or $99 per year. Prime has never offered as much value for members as it does today."
This price hike comes just in time before Amazon’s own Black Friday sale in Australia, which we expect to start a few days before the actual Black Friday date of November 27, and will run until Cyber Monday on November 30.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
While the US has seen multiple price increases recently, this is Amazon’s second round of hikes in Australia since launching in 2018. Initially just AU$6.99 per month or AU$59 per year at launch, Amazon later bumped that up to AU$9.99 per month (43%) or AU$79 per year (34%) in May 2023 as more inclusions were added. As mentioned, the price doesn’t reflect better inclusions, which is surely going to factor into household costs for many regular Amazon shoppers.
Earlier this month, Amazon opened its third Sydney fulfilment centre located in western suburb of Horsley Park which is “a 12-hour drive of 80% of Australia”, meaning even more shoppers will benefit from same-day delivery. Perhaps this goes some way in justifying a price increase, along with the fact that Amazon typically offers the best prices on thousands of items even outside of major sales. However, with an additional AU$2 monthly payment to get rid of ads on Prime Video, this news is sure to sting some customers.
While the Amazon Black Friday sale in Australia isn’t a Prime-exclusive event, the best prices will be for subscribers, so it does still pay to have a subscription. Thankfully, Amazon also makes it easy to cancel your subscription any time, although you won’t be eligible for the usual 30-day free trial if you’re a returning customer.
Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.
Nico is an experienced writer and journalist, having previously written for business titles across Australia. He mainly focuses on evergreen content like buying guides and reviews, as well as finding deals and coupon codes at TechRadar Australia. Outside of work, Nico is a keen cyclist and occasionally goes on runs and hikes.

articles.title: Xbox Game Pass "Á La Carte" System May Let Players Choose Features
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Xbox Game Pass "Á La Carte" System May Let Players Choose Features
Xbox's Game Pass has long offered relatively few choices, with just three tiers to choose from, with the more expensive plans offering features like day-one game availability, access to certain online games and their more premium features, longer cloud game streaming allotment, and a larger game library. This seems to be on the cusp of changing, though, with a new report from Fortune making mention of an upcoming á la carte service that would allow players to build out their own feature-set for their Game Pass subscription. 
The change is described as a planned "overhaul" of Game Pass, suggesting that the existing Game Pass tiered subscriptions may disappear when the new system comes in. An á la carte Game Pass system would allow subscribers to tailor their Game Pass experience, and, while this may result in a more affordable bottom-end for Game Pass, something that Xbox CEO, Asha Sharma, has expressed interest in before, it may also result in a more "complete" Game Pass experience ultimately costing more.The á la carte Game Pass offering was mentioned as part of Asha Sharma's plan for the future, with the insiders who spoke to Fortune citing a 2027 launch date for the offering. In fact, much of Sharma's current strategy to turn Xbox around—meaning to increase profits, revenue, and player counts—seems to hinge on Xbox exclusive games and Game Pass subscriptions. The Xbox CEO has already increased the top-end Xbox Game Pass pricing earlier in 2026, at the same time as the company introduced the Game Pass Essential tier was introduced.
Source:
				Fortune

articles.title: Por qué instalar Xuper TV en un Smart TV pone en riesgo la red WiFi de toda tu casa
articles.text:
Instalar aplicaciones de IPTV no oficiales como Xuper TV en un Smart TV introduce malware que utiliza el televisor como un ‘caballo de Troya’ para infiltrarse en toda la red doméstica. Como este tipo de aplicaciones se descargan desde fuentes no verificadas, mediante archivos APK, y exigen permisos amplios en el sistema, eluden los filtros de seguridad de las tiendas oficiales.
Una vez instalada, la amenaza se expande a la red wifi y compromete el hogar completo, desde el router hasta cada computadora, celular o cámara de seguridad conectada.
Xuper TV se difundió a través de redes sociales y foros como una plataforma que permite ver televisión en vivo, películas y series sin pagar suscripción. Su catálogo incluye contenido en alta definición, canales en directo y una biblioteca bajo demanda que promete actualizaciones diarias.
Muchos usuarios la consideran una reencarnación de Magis TV, ya que ambas comparten características técnicas y un modelo visual casi idéntico. Ese atractivo gratuito, sin embargo, esconde un costo oculto que se paga en seguridad.
Cómo el malware de Xuper TV se mueve por la red wifi doméstica
El Smart TV ya está conectado a la red del hogar y funciona como un dispositivo de confianza detrás del cortafuegos del router. El malware oculto en Xuper TV aprovecha esa posición para escanear la red local de forma silenciosa, en busca de vulnerabilidades, puertos abiertos o contraseñas débiles en otros equipos conectados, como computadoras, teléfonos celulares, cámaras de seguridad o discos duros en red.
Este movimiento lateral permite que una sola infección en el televisor se convierta en la puerta de entrada hacia el resto de los dispositivos de la casa. El usuario suele notar primero una lentitud inusual en el internet o comportamientos extraños en otros equipos, sin asociarlos de inmediato con la aplicación de streaming instalada semanas atrás.
El código malicioso también puede intentar acceder a la interfaz de administración del router probando combinaciones de contraseñas predeterminadas, como “admin/admin”.
Si logra entrar, puede alterar la configuración de los servidores DNS, de manera que cualquier dispositivo de la casa que intente acceder a sitios legítimos, como el portal de un banco o el correo electrónico, sea redirigido a páginas falsas diseñadas para robar credenciales y datos financieros.
Estas aplicaciones instalan procesos en segundo plano que convierten el televisor en parte de una red zombi o botnet. El equipo comienza a recibir órdenes externas para participar en ataques de denegación de servicio contra otras empresas o para minar criptomonedas, lo que satura el ancho de banda de la red wifi y ralentiza el internet en toda la vivienda.
Al operar desde un nodo de confianza, el televisor comprometido también puede actuar como puente para interceptar datos no cifrados que circulan entre los demás dispositivos y el router.
Por qué la descarga de APK fuera de las tiendas oficiales multiplica el riesgo
El verdadero peligro comienza al intentar instalar Xuper TV. Dado que no se encuentra en tiendas oficiales como Google Play Store o App Store, los usuarios deben recurrir a páginas web externas para descargar el archivo APK.
Esta práctica elude los controles de seguridad y calidad que aplican las tiendas oficiales, lo que deja el camino libre para que archivos modificados con software malicioso infecten los dispositivos.
Según especialistas de ESET, al instalar aplicaciones como Xuper TV desde fuentes no verificadas, el usuario corre el riesgo de descargar malware, troyanos o software espía capaces de robar contraseñas, datos bancarios o incluso insertar keyloggers. Esto puede comprometer la seguridad no solo del dispositivo utilizado, sino de toda la red doméstica, con la posibilidad de exponer información de otros equipos conectados.
El modelo de negocio de estas aplicaciones suele sostenerse en sistemas de publicidad agresiva e intrusiva. Los anuncios pueden interrumpir la visualización, redirigir a sitios inseguros o incitar a descargar más archivos potencialmente peligrosos.
Algunos prometen premios falsos o incentivan transacciones en plataformas sin garantías, lo que puede derivar en fraudes con tarjetas de crédito, pérdida de acceso a cuentas bancarias y estafas en línea.
La Interpol ha advertido que las transacciones financieras a través de estos servicios carecen de seguridad y que, en muchos casos, los usuarios no tienen forma de recuperar el dinero perdido en caso de fraude.
Qué permisos excesivos pide Xuper TV y qué datos pone en riesgo
Al instalar Xuper TV, la aplicación solicita permisos inusualmente elevados: acceso al almacenamiento, a la red, a la ubicación e incluso a la posibilidad de publicar notificaciones.
Estos permisos pueden utilizarse para acceder a documentos, fotos, videos, audios, credenciales laborales y archivos sensibles almacenados en el dispositivo. Además, facilitan el envío de spam, ataques de phishing y la ejecución de acciones maliciosas sin el conocimiento del usuario.
Entre los permisos más peligrosos identificados por los expertos destacan el acceso a tareas en ejecución, que permite rastrear el uso de otras aplicaciones, y la capacidad para montar y desmontar sistemas de archivos, que habilita la manipulación de datos.
También se suma el permiso para instalar paquetes adicionales, que incrementa el riesgo de que se descarguen más aplicaciones maliciosas, junto con la lectura y escritura en el almacenamiento externo, que posibilita el robo o la modificación de archivos personales.
A esto se añade el acceso a grabaciones de audio, con el riesgo de exponer conversaciones privadas y notas de voz. La combinación de estos permisos convierte al televisor en un punto de vigilancia dentro del hogar, con capacidad para recolectar información mucho más allá del simple consumo de contenido audiovisual.
Cómo limpiar la red wifi si Xuper TV ya fue instalada
Desinstalar la aplicación no suele ser suficiente, ya que el malware puede dejar archivos residuales en el sistema. El primer paso recomendado es restablecer el televisor a valores de fábrica desde el menú de configuración, en las opciones de sistema o de restablecimiento general, para borrar todo el contenido instalado.
El segundo paso consiste en cambiar las contraseñas del router. Esto se hace al ingresar a la configuración del equipo, generalmente mediante las direcciones 192.168.1.1 o 192.168.0.1 escritas en un navegador web, donde se debe modificar tanto la contraseña de administrador como la contraseña de la red wifi.
Una vez que el televisor se reinicie, conviene asegurarse de que la opción para instalar aplicaciones de “fuentes desconocidas” u “orígenes desconocidos” permanezca desactivada en los ajustes de seguridad. Por último, se recomienda verificar que tanto el router como el Smart TV tengan instalada la última actualización de firmware, ya que estas incluyen parches diseñados para cerrar agujeros de seguridad explotados por este tipo de aplicaciones.

articles.title: Samsung veut changer la façon de fabriquer ses écrans OLED, et cela pourrait faire baisser les prix
articles.text:
Samsung Display explore deux nouvelles méthodes de fabrication OLED capables de se passer des traditionnels masques métalliques. Le géant coréen préparerait une ligne pilote d'OLED imprimé par jet d'encre, tout en développant une technologie alternative de dépôt des pixels. Une offensive qui intervient alors que TCL CSOT et LG Display avancent déjà sur ce terrain.
La course aux nouvelles méthodes de fabrication OLED s'intensifie. Selon deux enquêtes publiées le 19 octobre par les médias coréens ETNews et The Elec, Samsung Display travaille sur des procédés capables de remplacer les masques métalliques fins (FMM), utilisés pour déposer avec précision les matériaux organiques émissifs. L'objectif est de simplifier la production, de limiter le gaspillage de matériaux et, à terme, de réduire les coûts.
Deux pistes différentes pour se passer des masques métalliques
Selon ETNews, Samsung Display discute avec ses fournisseurs en vue de créer une ligne pilote consacrée à l'OLED RGB imprimé par jet d'encre. Cette technique consiste à déposer directement les matériaux émissifs rouges, verts et bleus aux emplacements des sous-pixels, plutôt que de les faire passer à travers un masque métallique.
Elle pourrait faciliter la fabrication sur de grandes plaques de verre tout en réduisant la consommation de matériaux. ETNews évoque une économie théorique supérieure à 30 %, à condition d'obtenir des rendements industriels suffisants. Les écrans de PC portables et les moniteurs figureraient parmi les applications envisagées.
Samsung explore parallèlement une autre voie. D'après The Elec, le fabricant développe un prototype OLED d'environ 7 pouces utilisant une technologie baptisée Micro Patterned OLED (MPO). Celle-ci repose sur de minuscules structures permettant de déposer les matériaux organiques uniquement aux emplacements souhaités, sans devoir ensuite graver les couches émissives. Un premier échantillon technique serait attendu fin 2026 ou début 2027.
Cette piste aurait notamment retrouvé de l'intérêt chez Samsung après l'examen d'une dalle utilisant la technologie ViP du fabricant chinois Visionox. Les deux projets restent toutefois expérimentaux, sans calendrier de production commerciale confirmé.
TCL avance déjà, LG prépare aussi sa riposte
Samsung n'est pas seul à chercher une alternative aux masques métalliques. TCL CSOT a déjà franchi plusieurs étapes avec ses dalles OLED imprimées, présentes dans des produits annoncés chez Lenovo et MSI. Le fabricant chinois investit également dans une ligne de génération 8.6 pour développer cette technologie à plus grande échelle.
De son côté, LG Display travaille sur FLiPP, un procédé reposant sur la photolithographie et destiné, lui aussi, à supprimer les masques métalliques. Son industrialisation reste néanmoins à concrétiser.
Samsung dispose d'un atout : le constructeur maîtrise déjà l'impression à jet d'encre, employée pour déposer les matériaux de conversion des couleurs de ses dalles QD-OLED. Imprimer directement les matériaux organiques émissifs représente cependant un défi différent, notamment en matière de précision et d'uniformité.
L'enjeu est désormais industriel autant que technologique. TCL commence à intégrer ses solutions dans des produits, LG prépare sa propre méthode et Samsung multiplie les expérimentations. Reste à déterminer quel procédé permettra de produire des dalles fiables, en grandes quantités et à moindre coût. Pour les consommateurs, une baisse des prix des écrans OLED est envisageable à terme, mais elle est encore loin d'être garantie.

articles.title: What Security Teams Can Do To Tame Wild Code
articles.text:
A sales manager builds an AI-assisted workflow to route leads. It connects to customer records, summarizes inbound requests, and posts updates to a shared channel. The workflow saves time, reduces manual work, and soon becomes part of the team’s daily routine. Across the same organization, employees are building useful apps, agents, and automations faster than existing processes can support them.
If you work in security, that success introduces a new set of questions. Whose credentials does the workflow use? Which records can it access? Who can see its output? If it starts exposing information it shouldn’t, can you trace what happened and stop further access?
Wild code takes root when useful builds spread faster than the processes for owning, securing, and maintaining them. It isn’t simply another name for unapproved software. Employees are creating new capabilities, not just adopting existing products. A small experiment can become an operational dependency before security knows it exists.
The risk goes beyond vulnerabilities in generated code. Even code that works as intended can operate with too much access or expose data to the wrong audience:
- Excessive permissions. A workflow needs a small set of records but runs with credentials that can read or modify far more.
- Sensitive data exposure. An employee connects an agent to information it doesn’t need, or makes its output available too broadly. Sensitive information can also end up in model requests or logs.
- Unintended actions. An agent can change records or permissions without an approval boundary appropriate to the action.
- Orphaned access. A useful workflow keeps running after its creator changes roles or leaves, with no clear owner reviewing its permissions.
- Investigation gaps. When something goes wrong, security can’t readily establish which identity ran the workflow, what it accessed, or what changed.
Employee education, sandboxes, and AI steering committees are a good start, but they aren’t enough to control wild code on their own. A more sustainable approach builds controls into the environment itself: what employees can connect to, what their apps and agents can do, and how that work is monitored once it’s running.
Why the usual fixes fall short
Education, sandboxes, and steering committees all have a role. The mistake is expecting them to govern software they may never encounter, or control what happens after it starts running. A policy describes what should happen. Security also needs controls that constrain what can happen, evidence of what did happen, and a way to intervene.
1. Education explains good practice, but can’t enforce it
An AI policy can explain what’s allowed. Training can introduce good practices. Neither guarantees that someone building a reporting workflow will recognize the moment they cross into handling sensitive data or operating production software.
As AI brings more employees into building software, organizations have an opportunity to make practices like least privilege, secrets management, and separating test environments from production more accessible. Policies can set expectations, but employees also need practical guidance and built-in safeguards to apply them in everyday work.
Even employees who recognize a risk still face deadlines and pressure to move faster. If the approved route is slow or confusing, knowing the rules doesn’t make following them easier.
Education helps people make better decisions. It shouldn’t be the only thing preventing an unsafe connection or an unauthorized action.
2. Sandboxes protect experiments, not their entire future
An isolated environment is useful for testing prompts, models, and generated code. But a prototype’s value often depends on eventually reaching real business systems and data.
Once a prototype connects to live business systems, it needs controls that extend beyond the test environment. Permissions, monitoring, and change reviews have to remain in place throughout its working life, not just during the experiment. A successful test doesn’t establish which data the production workflow should access or which actions it should be allowed to take.
As Brad Rumph, field CTO at Tines, puts it: “Sandboxes solve the design problem and leave the runtime problem alone.”
A successful experiment still needs a governed path into operation. Without that path, isolation postpones the hard questions rather than resolving them.
3. Committees can’t review what they can’t see
Steering committees can set direction, establish accountability, and make decisions about high-risk use cases. But their review cycles don’t always match the speed at which employees can create and deploy software.
A committee might prohibit one risky practice while employees discover another way to achieve the same result. Oversight can also concentrate on engineering, where established controls already exist, while overlooking builds in finance, HR, or operations.
The limitation isn’t the quality of the committee. It’s a model that depends on each build becoming visible before it becomes useful. An approval process can’t be the only way security discovers new paths to sensitive data and privileged actions.
Put security controls where the work happens
The alternative is to build controls into the environment employees use to create, run, and maintain their work.
Rather than asking everyone to independently assemble a secure operating model, security teams define shared boundaries with IT and system owners, apply them consistently throughout the lifecycle, and update them as business needs and risks change.
Three principles make this practical.
1. Govern before deployment, and keep governing afterward
Define permitted data sources, actions, and access before employees connect business systems. Keep those controls in place when the workflow goes live.
Permissions should reflect what a workflow needs to do, not everything its creator can access. Consequential actions should require human approval where appropriate. A prompt telling an agent what not to do is not an access control.
Keep creation, execution, and monitoring connected. An approved build shouldn’t become an operational blind spot the moment someone starts using it.
2. Make the approved route the easiest route
Employees need more than a list of restrictions. Give them an environment that lets them solve real problems quickly.
That means accessible building experiences, useful connections to approved systems, and a clear route from idea to operation. Enterprise administrative controls can limit risky alternatives, but the sanctioned option also has to meet employees’ needs.
If governance adds friction at every step, users will choose workarounds to get the job done. Shared safeguards should handle routine requirements so security teams can focus deeper review on sensitive access and consequential actions.
AI can help create an application or agent. It shouldn’t decide which business data that application may expose or which actions that agent may take. Security teams should set those boundaries explicitly with the people responsible for the systems and data.
3. Make investigation and intervention part of the design Security
needs to understand what a workflow did, not just what it was intended to do.
Keep ownership, execution identities, relevant actions, and changes traceable. Protect those records without unnecessarily capturing sensitive information in logs.
Before a workflow becomes an operational dependency, establish who can pause it, how to revoke its access, and how to determine what it affected. Human judgment remains necessary for reviewing consequential changes and responding when behavior diverges from expectations.
What this looks like in practice
A governed environment should make important security questions answerable without a separate investigation:
- Accountable ownership. Who owns the workflow, and which identity does it run as?
- Controlled access. What can it read, change, and send elsewhere? Which actions require approval, and where is that enforced?
- Protected execution. Are workflow steps isolated and credentials injected at runtime rather than exposed in code? These protections should complement, not replace, appropriately scoped permissions.
- Traceable activity. Can security establish what ran, what it accessed, and what changed?
- Clear intervention. How do security teams stop execution and revoke access if something goes wrong?
These controls don’t eliminate every risk. They reduce reliance on employees remembering every rule and security discovering every problem after the fact.
Keep control as more people build
Employees will keep finding valuable ways to build with AI. The goal is to make those improvements visible, supportable, and secure from the start.
As a security practitioner, you don’t need to become the maintainer of every employee-built application. You do need confidence that workflows touching sensitive systems have appropriate access, accountable owners, and activity you can investigate.
Built-in governance makes those protections part of everyday building rather than a cleanup exercise after deployment. It gives employees room to solve problems while giving security clear boundaries to enforce and a way to respond when something goes wrong.
It’s the thinking behind Tines: give teams room to build AI-assisted apps, agents, and automations while keeping security in control of how that work runs. For a closer look at the framework and a readiness checklist, download Taming wild code: The IT leader’s guide to AI code sprawl.

articles.title: Chaleur ajustée selon la distance et cinq embouts : le Dyson Supersonic Nural est à 299 €
articles.text:
Le sèche-cheveux Dyson Supersonic Nural Velours rouge/Or est à 299 € (-25 %)
Le Dyson Supersonic Nural ajuste la chaleur à l’approche du cuir chevelu et mémorise les réglages des embouts. La version Velours rouge/Or passe à 299 € chez Dyson.
Dyson propose le sèche-cheveux Supersonic Nural Velours rouge/Or à 299 €, contre 399 € auparavant. L’économie atteint 100 €, soit environ 25 %. Cette version comprend cinq embouts magnétiques et un coffret de présentation. La marque annonce également un embout lissant supplémentaire offert, d’une valeur de 35 €. L’offre est disponible directement sur la boutique Dyson.
Une température qui s’adapte à la distance du cuir chevelu
Le sèche-cheveux Dyson Supersonic Nural intègre un capteur de distance pour ajuster automatiquement la température lorsque l’appareil se rapproche de la tête. En mode Protection du cuir chevelu, le système réduit la chaleur à proximité des cheveux. Cette fonction vise à améliorer le confort thermique pendant le séchage, avec les accessoires compatibles.
L’appareil propose trois vitesses et quatre niveaux de température, dont l’air froid. Il reconnaît aussi les embouts intelligents et mémorise les derniers réglages utilisés. Le mode Protection du cuir chevelu prend toutefois la priorité sur les réglages de chaleur personnalisés. Une détection de pause coupe la chauffe et réduit le débit d’air lorsque le sèche-cheveux est posé ; elle est désactivée avec un diffuseur.
Cinq embouts pour varier le séchage et le coiffage
Le coffret réunit un concentrateur pour brushing, un embout de séchage doux, un peigne à dents larges, un diffuseur Wave+Curl et un embout de finition lisse. Le peigne sert notamment à travailler les cheveux bouclés ou frisés, tandis que le concentrateur dirige le flux d’air sur une zone précise.
Le diffuseur Wave+Curl dispose de deux configurations pour travailler les ondulations et les boucles. Le coffret de présentation permet de ranger l’appareil et ses accessoires. Cette déclinaison associe une finition Velours rouge à des éléments dorés, avec un câble de 2,62 m.
