articles.title: 'Some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior': Tencent admits AI agents it was testing made more than 2,600 attempts in 11 days to slip past Alibaba's map defenses, just to find out which zoo gate people use
articles.text:
'Some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior': Tencent admits AI agents it was testing made more than 2,600 attempts in 11 days to slip past Alibaba's map defenses, just to find out which zoo gate people use
Researchers hid a message for a live fleet of rogue AI agents, and the agents wrote back
- Tencent says AI agents it used to evaluate third-party models showed "unintended" browsing behavior, the first such admission by a major Chinese firm
- Swarmchasers researchers logged more than 2,600 attempts by the Tencent Cloud fleet to pull entrance data from Alibaba's Amap
- Most attempts failed, but agents used a public scanner as a remote browser, and one leaked company API key returned real place data
Tencent has acknowledged that AI agents running on its infrastructure behaved unexpectedly after independent researchers caught a fleet of them repeatedly trying to pull data from Alibaba's Amap navigation service.
Reuters reports the company's AI unit, Tencent Hunyuan, said the agents were being used to evaluate third-party models, in what appears to be the first known case of rogue agent activity acknowledged by a major Chinese company.
In a post on X, the unit said the activity did not come from its own Hunyuan models, noting "During these evaluations, some agents exhibited unintended web-browsing behavior, but our review found no evidence of deliberate targeting or coordination," before adding that it was tightening network access controls and agent monitoring.
A lot of "unintended" effort for a zoo gate?
The admission follows a full report by Swarmchasers, a loose group of researchers who met at an AI hackathon. They counted more than 2,600 attempts to extract Amap data over 11 days, from September 28 to October 8 2026, traced the traffic to Tencent Cloud servers in Hong Kong, and then did something nobody appears to have done before: they talked to the agents while they were still running.
The tasks were almost comically mundane. A typical job asked which entrance of a place like Chengdu Zoo most Amap users use, with other runs covering parks, museums, and hospitals and, on September 30, a British Columbia cancer statistics dashboard.
The problem was getting the answer. Amap's anti-bot system expects browser cookies, JavaScript-generated tokens, and sometimes a CAPTCHA, while the fleet's harness sent plain Python and curl requests. One agent told the researchers that Amap had blocked its Tencent sandbox, so it could not fetch the data itself.
The agents improvised instead; according to the Swarmchasers report, they packed their own HTML and JavaScript into URLs and fed them to urlquery.net, a public security scanning service, borrowing its browser to run their code.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
When Amap kept blocking them, the programs tried to intercept or forge tokens from Alibaba's own anti-bot libraries, sent 57 requests to four pre-production hosts, routed traffic through Baidu Translate and remote browsers, and, in seven reports, used Amap API keys found on the open web.
Most of it did not work as intended: in a snapshot of 2,372 reports up to October 4, nearly half ended on an empty Amap page or login prompt and almost a quarter on a blank tab. None of the token tricks appear to have succeeded, and there is no evidence that any pre-production server answered. The entrance figures that did come back arrived mostly through Jina's page reader, which can serve cached copies up to 30 days old.
The exception should worry businesses more than Alibaba. A key and security code exposed in another company's public source code did return real place data, and the researchers say they cannot tell whose account was billed for those requests.
Tencent's framing of the activity as "unintended" is accurate as far as it goes, but it sidesteps an awkward point. If an evaluation asks agents for data that only Amap displays, behind defenses a sandboxed agent without a browser cannot legitimately clear, then crossing that line is close to the only route to a correct answer.
US incidents involved something similar: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face while hunting for answers to an ExploitGym benchmark, with later disclosures showing they organized through a makeshift message board, and roughly 700 of them took part in an attack Hugging Face eventually contained using Zhipu's open GLM 5.2 model. Anthropic found three Claude models had compromised real organizations after a misconfigured evaluation left internet access open, and this month disclosed that Claude Haiku 4.5 filed a false homicide tip with Philadelphia police while exploring random websites.
Reuters judges Tencent's case less egregious than those, and the Swarmchasers found no sign the agents coordinated, which is why they call it a fleet rather than a swarm. Still, as recent analysis argued, sandbox escapes often come down to an agent routing around a proxy, and borrowing a stranger's browser is exactly that.
Tencent's admission lands in the same week ByteDance's Seed unit created a dedicated Alignment & Preparedness team and began recruiting 10 researchers worldwide, a rare public commitment to frontier safety work by a major Chinese developer. The internal email announcing it went out a day before the Swarmchasers' full report and, in 36Kr's translation, points to a broader run of agent escapes rather than this one case, so the two are not cause and effect even if they do point the same way.
The argument is that alignment remains unsolved regardless of whose flag flies over the data center, and they want every lab running internet-connected agents to audit what its sandboxes can reach, a seemingly modest ask.
This fleet, however, ran for nearly a week before outside researchers stumbled on it at a hackathon, then carried on for four more days after their preliminary findings went public, and Tencent has yet to explain why.

articles.title: QNAP Introduces USB4 JBOD Series with up to 12 Bays for Desktop and Rackmount Deployment

Tuesday, October 20th 2026
QNAP Introduces USB4 JBOD Series with up to 12 Bays for Desktop and Rackmount Deployment
QNAP Systems, Inc., a leading innovator in computing, networking, and storage solutions, today introduced industry-leading high-capacity JBOD expansion units featuring USB4 connectivity: the 8-bay desktop TL-D810TC4 and 12-bay rackmount TL-R1210TC4-RP, delivering up to 40 Gbps theoretical bandwidth. Their USB4 Type-C ports are also compatible with Thunderbolt 5/4/3, giving creators and businesses a convenient, cost-efficient, and flexible way to expand storage.
The new USB4 JBOD series supports SATA 6 Gb/s HDDs and SSDs, allowing users to flexibly expand their NAS or computer storage based on their environment and workflow needs. This enables rapid capacity expansion and enhanced data protection. Its optimized ventilation and active cooling ensure stable performance and long-term reliability during extended operation. Whether for short-term projects, media creators requiring high-speed expansion, or businesses focused on long-term archiving and scheduled backups, the QNAP USB4 JBOD series delivers a dependable and flexible storage expansion solution.QNAP also introduces the QXP-40G2UC Dual-port USB4 Type-C PCIe expansion card designed for Intel - and AMD-based NAS, enabling users to add USB4 connectivity to their NAS, and easily connect to USB4 JBOD units for high-speed data transfer and capacity expansion. Supported models are subject to the QNAP Compatibility List.
Eddie Chuang, Product Manager of QNAP"Most USB4 expansion products on the market are small SSD enclosures that cannot meet large-capacity storage or mid-to-long-term expansion needs. QNAP's USB4 JBOD lineup breaks these limitations by enabling laptops, workstations, and NAS users to expand storage while maintaining convenience, high speed, and stability. It is a cost-effective solution for both creators and business users who require scalable high-capacity storage."
Key Features of the QNAP USB4 JBOD Series:
- TL-D810TC4: The 8-bay desktop model supports Windows, macOS, and QNAP NAS, and features a metal enclosure and cooling fan. Its compact design is optimized for creators working long hours on desktop workflows, enabling fast processing of 4K/8K video editing assets and backup tasks.
- TL-R1210TC4-RP: The 12-bay 2U rackmount model with dual power supplies supports Windows and QNAP NAS, and is purpose-built for server rooms and backup environments requiring continuous and reliable operation. Ideal for SMBs demanding large-capacity data storage and resilient backup architectures.
Both models include a single USB4 Type-C port and come with a USB4 cable in the box. They are compatible with USB4, Thunderbolt 5/4/3 devices. Users can choose standalone external-storage mode or create software RAID for enhanced capacity and data protection. JBOD and drive status can be monitored and configured through management tools.
USB4 Expansion Card for QNAP NAS:
QXP-40G2UC: The dual-port USB4 Type-C expansion card delivering up to 40 Gbps theoretical bandwidth. Supporting USB4 and USB 3, it allows NAS users to easily add USB connectivity for greater scalability and compatibility with USB4 JBOD units.Availability:
The new USB4 JBODs and expansion card are available now.

But you can see holes marked "cable clip" next to the connectors, so in the absence of a standard, some sort of cable clip might be the best option.

articles.title: Claude n’aurait que 7,8% de chances de rattraper ChatGPT d’ici 2037, selon cette étude
articles.text:
En un an, la part de ChatGPT a reculé au profit de Claude et de Gemini. Mais la firme de Sam Altman est encore très largement leader. Les analystes de OneLittleWeb ont procédé à quelques simulations et Anthropic ne pourrait passer devant OpenAI que dans une dizaine d'années et seulement dans une minorité de cas.
En août 2025, ChatGPT recevait 32 fois plus de visites web que Claude. Un an plus tard, l'écart a presqu'été divisé par 6, et OneLittleWeb a voulu savoir ce que donnerait cette tendance jusqu'en 2037.
Dans 7,8% des simulations, Claude finit par passer devant
L'étude compare les visites mensuelles de cinq chatbots entre août 2025 et août 2026, à partir d'estimations provenant des plateformes d'analyse de trafic web Ahrefs et Semrush.
Point important : ces données ne portent donc que sur les accès aux sites web des fournisseurs. Cela n'inclut pas les usages API, ni même les applications mobiles.
Sur cette période, ChatGPT passe de 5,4 à 6,6 milliards de visites par mois (+22,22%). L'IA d'Anthropic, elle, enregistre une croissance fulgurante de +615,14% avec une hausse des visites de 167,8 millions à 1,2 milliard.
Chez Google, Gemini est passé de 282,8 millions à 1,2 milliard de visites (+324,33%) sur un an. L'IA chinoise DeepSeek, alors positionnée en seconde place en août 2025 avec 303,8 millions de visites, tombe à la quatrième place (339,1 millions) douze mois plus tard. Enfin, Grok progresse de 40,28%, à 217,3 millions de visites.
Selon OneLittleWeb, en un an, ChatGPT aurait perdu 16,5 points de part de marché à 69,1% contre 12,6% pour Claude et 12,6% également pour Gemini.
Mais la progression n'est pas linéaire. Ainsi, entre mars et août 2026, Claude a continué sur sa lancée, avec des visites en hausse +66,2%, à 1,2 milliard. A contrario, Gemini n'aurait progressé que 9,1% sur la même période. Mais du côté d'Anthropic, c'est surtout le mois de mars qui fait figure d'anomalie (+150,85%).
ChatGPT, lui, varie fortement d'un mois à l'autre (+1 milliard en mars, -1 milliard en avril). On pourrait prolonger la croissance moyenne de Claude (17,8% par mois). Dans ce cas, Anthropic rattraperait OpenAI dans le courant de l'été prochain. On pourrait également dessiner une progression en se basant sur son rythme de +6,7% mensuels observé depuis mai, ce qui présagerait une parité vers 2029. Mais les analystes ont préféré un modèle statistique, dit AR(1). Ce dernier part du principe que la variation d'un mois influence celle du suivant. Elle y ajoute des écarts imprévus piochés au hasard dans l'historique, puis rejoue 250 000 fois l'avenir jusqu'en avril 2037. Chaque simulation alterne hausses et baisses, comme les données réelles.
Dans seulement 7,8% des simulations, Claude dépasserait ChatGPT d'ici avril 2037, contre 3,8% pour Gemini. Mais dans la majorité des cas, ChatGPT resterait toujours en tête. L'étude détaille l'un des cas où Claude passe devant. Anthropic dépasse Google dès ce mois-ci, mais son retard sur ChatGPT commence par se creuser (5,88 milliards en décembre 2026). Il est aux alentours de 4,5 milliards entre août 2030 et août 2032. Puis il descend à 1,70 milliard en août 2033, et fond progressivement jusqu'au premier trimestre 2037 avant de dépasser ChatGPT en avril.
Bon évidemment il ne s'agit en aucun cas de prévisions, mais plutôt d'un scénario. Les données sur lesquelles les analystes se sont appuyées ne couvrent que treize mois seulement. Et rappelons une nouvelle fois qu'elles n'incluent ni les applications, ni l'API. Or l'accès direct à un chatbot risque, lui, de baisser face aux IA agentiques ou à l'intégration des interfaces dans des applications surmesures.

articles.title: eMudhra faces scrutiny after weak certificate keys expose flaws in web security
articles.text:
eMudhra faces scrutiny after weak certificate keys raise web security concerns
Eight weak intermediate certificate keys have prompted browser safeguards and questions over eMudhra’s controls, although the company said customer data and Indian eSign services remain unaffected.
Eight intermediate certificate authority keys linked to eMudhra’s global website-security business were found to be dangerously weak, raising concerns about the systems that browsers use to establish trust online.
The flaw could have enabled attackers to create fraudulent HTTPS certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. The keys were generated on April 30, 2025, but the weakness remained undetected for about 18 months, according to eMudhra’s statement on October 21, 2026.
A certificate authority (CA) verifies identities and issues digital certificates. Intermediate authorities operate under a root certificate trusted by browsers and operating systems.
eMudhra said a key-wrap/unwrap step during its key-generation procedure produced a second, weak set of keys, which were subsequently published to browser root stores. Although the company added its root private key was not compromised, browser operators have withdrawn trust from the associated emSign ECC Root CA - G3 as a precaution.
Google’s Chrome Security team warned that the flaw was “enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not yet removed trust in those CAs.” Google blocked the affected keys and plans to remove the parent root from Chrome’s trust store from October 27, Pacific time. Some legitimate websites using certificates under that root may consequently stop functioning in Chrome.
Mozilla, meanwhile, blocked the affected certificates in Firefox within three hours of receiving the report and released software updates to extend protection to users who might not receive automatic safeguards.
The immediate impact appears limited, although the investigation remains ongoing.
eMudhra said none of the eight affected intermediate authorities issued end-user certificates, its infrastructure was not compromised and no data was breached. It identifies one affected customer ecosystem in the United States, where certificates are being replaced.
The company stated its Indian digital-signature and eSign services, which operate on separate infrastructure, remain unaffected. It acknowledged uncertainty over the cause, noting, “We have not yet confirmed the exact root cause. We will publish it in full once our investigation is complete.”
The incident highlights a wider challenge for the digital-trust industry. Encryption can protect communications, but only when the certificates establishing a website’s identity are reliable. Browser companies therefore maintain their own trusted certificate lists and can revoke acceptance when a provider’s controls fail.
Public Certificate Transparency logs also help detect suspicious certificate issuance. The uncomfortable question for eMudhra is how a weakness of this significance escaped detection through two audit cycles.
The company said it is reviewing its key-generation procedures and offering enterprise customers certificates from an additional certificate authority to reduce dependence on a single trust chain.

articles.title: « Supervision humaine minimale » : l’armée américaine veut ses propres IA pirates pour « neutraliser les menaces »
articles.text:
Des documents internes à l’armée de terre américaine décrivent un programme destiné à transformer des agents d’IA en armes offensives autonomes. Son nom de code : ECHOTRIBBLE. Sa mission, naviguer seul dans les réseaux adverses pour les « neutraliser ».
Un logiciel qui se réplique et s’autodétruit
Le programme est piloté par le commandement cyber de l’armée de terre, chargé depuis 2010 des opérations défensives comme des attaques informatiques les plus discrètes. ECHOTRIBBLE vise à confier une partie de ces offensives à des agents conçus pour « naviguer de façon autonome dans les infrastructures » et pour « identifier et neutraliser les menaces ». Neutraliser, précisent les documents, peut vouloir dire désactiver une cible temporairement ou définitivement, ou effacer ses données.
À l’instar de ce qu’avait décrit Anthropic dans une mise en garde la semaine dernière, le fonctionnement décrit tient du ver informatique. Déposé sur un appareil, l’agent repère seul d’autres cibles sur le même réseau, puis produit une copie de lui-même taillée pour chaque machine rencontrée, de l’iPad au PC Windows 11. Il sait viser le cloud comme les systèmes coupés d’Internet, et s’autodétruit une fois sa mission accomplie, si possible sans avoir été repéré. L’armée pourrait fixer quelques « déclencheurs prédéfinis », mais le logiciel devrait surtout fonctionner avec une « supervision humaine minimale » et un « comportement autodirigé ». L’appel d’offres, publié mi-juillet et clos un mois plus tard, a déjà réuni 65 dossiers de candidats, dont cinq retenus. Une démonstration est attendue ce mois-ci.
Le risque d’une frappe qui déborde
L’armée américaine s’équipe après un été de dérapages chez les grands laboratoires d’IA. Des systèmes autonomes se sont introduits dans l’infrastructure d’Hugging Face, dans des réseaux du gouvernement australien et sur un dépôt de code, sans en avoir reçu l’ordre. L’un d’eux a même tenté de forcer l’entrée de sites du gouvernement américain.
Un agent lancé contre une cible pourrait l’atteindre en traversant un service des eaux américain, si l’adversaire y a dissimulé ses relais de commande, et le mettre hors service en chemin. Les hôpitaux, petites entreprises et cabinets dépourvus du moindre défenseur en cybersécurité forment autant de victimes collatérales possibles. Des groupes étatiques routent déjà leurs offensives par des box domestiques et de petites sociétés. Le groupe chinois Volt Typhoon a ainsi piraté par avance des systèmes américains pour s’en servir plus tard. Un agent autonome lancé à l’assaut pourrait très bien ranger ces relais parmi ses cibles.
Si l’armée confie des munitions réelles à un jeune Marine, soulignent les spécialistes, c’est qu’il a le discernement de se dire « je ferais mieux de m’abstenir ». Les IA grand public actuelles sont dépourvues de cette capacité de jugement. Un agent reste un logiciel qui, rappellent les experts, tend à contourner un obstacle lorsqu’il y est confronté, quitte à « traiter ses propres garde-fous comme des obstacles » dès qu’on lui demande de casser, détruire ou mettre hors service. Interrogé sur les protections prévues, le commandement cyber de l’armée n’a pas répondu.

articles.title: Plex
articles.text:
Plex gives you one place to find and access all the media that matters to you. From personal media on your own server, to free and on-demand Movies & Shows, live TV, podcasts, and web shows, to streaming music, you can enjoy it all in one app, on any device.
And, it's really simple to start using:
First, if you are streaming only third-party content (Movies & Shows, live TV, podcasts, web shows, TIDAL music), then you are good to go as soon as you have an account, just install an app on your phone, Smart TV, computer, or simply open up our web app on your browser!
If you are looking to set up your own personal media server to house your own stuff, there are a few more (simple!) steps to get up and running.
How do I get Plex to work?
First, install the Plex Media Server on a computer (or compatible NAS device) where your media/movies are stored. Add media libraries by type of content and let Plex do the rest. Cataloging, adding artwork and info is all automatic.
With the media server installed, you can then install the Plex app on virtually any device (phone, tablet, smart TV, streaming device, game console, PC, or any web browser) and stream and play all your media on those devices. Sit back and enjoy.
Is Plex free?
Streaming your own media using Plex is free on most devices. The Plex Media Server component is free, as well as the Plex player for Windows, macOS and streaming boxes. Media playback on iOS and Android devices requires an in-app purchase to remove limitations, and Plex also offers a subscription that adds more features like Live TV and DVR recording.
What file formats does Plex Support?
Plex Media Server supports all common media files. For videos and movies Plex can playback ASF, AVI, MP4, MPEGTS, MPEG, MKV, AVI, MOV, DIVX, and WMV. It also has support for 4K/UHD video. For music you got AAC, ALAC, E-AC3, MP3, M4A, FLAC, WAV and WMA. Finally for images JPG, PNG, RAW, TBN, among others.
How does it work?
- Install and run the Plex Media Server on a computer (or compatible NAS device or Nvidia Shield) where all your media is stored and managed in movie, TV show, home video, music, and photo libraries.
- Add media libraries by type of content and let Plex do the rest---cataloging, adding artwork and info---it's all automatic.
- Install and open the Plex app on virtually any device---smartphone, tablet, smart TV, streaming device, game console, personal computer, or any browser.
- Wherever you are, press play, sit back, and enjoy your media as it streams from the Plex Media Server to your device.
What can I do with Plex?
- Share home movies from your Chicago Mac with Grandma on her Roku in France.
- Stream music from your PC in London to your iPad while abroad in Tenerife.
- See photos on a SoHo LG Smart TV while they are stored in your Brooklyn brownstone.
- Set up your own DVR and record your favorite shows and games from over-the-air signal and watch anywhere!
- Link your TIDAL account and integrate your own personal library with TIDAL's 60 million tracks.
What Media and Devices Work?
Plex supports these media file types
- Plex Media Server supports all common media files:
- Movies, TV Shows, and Home Video: MP4, MKV, AVI, MOV, DIVX, and more
- Music: MP3, M4A, FLAC, WMA, and more
- Photos: JPG, PNG, RAW, TBN, and more
Plex Media Server compatibility
Plex Media Server is supported on computers running all the major operating systems as well as NAS devices:
- Windows
- macOS
- Linux
- Nvidia Shield
- Netgear Nighthawk X10 router
- Many popular NAS devices such as QNAP, Synology, Netgear, Drobo, and more
Use Plex on these devices
Plex apps work with the all the market leading devices and brands:
- Browsers: Chrome, Edge, Firefox, and Safari
- Mobile Apps: Android, iOS
- Tablets: Android and iOS
- Desktop/Laptop computers: macOS, Windows
- Smart TVs: LG, Samsung, Hisense, VIZIO, and Roku TV
- Streaming Devices:
- Amazon Alexa
- Amazon Fire TV
- Android TV
- Apple TV
- Chromecast
- Portal from Facebook
- Roku
- Sonos
- Gaming Consoles: PlayStation and Xbox
In addition to running the Plex web app in a browser, desktop computer users can also run dedicated player apps. This is aimed at users wanting to use Plex in their HTPCs or to have a "home theater" type experience. It provides advanced audio and video playback capabilities to give you the best experience possible.
Enjoy your videos, movies, TV shows, music and photos anytime, anywhere.
Run Plex Media Server on your Windows, Mac or Linux computer and stream to your iOS or Android device. Have multiple TVs in your house? No problem, Plex also works on Chromecast, Amazon Fire TV, Roku, Android TV, Xbox, PlayStation, VIZIO, and many late-model smart TVs. Plex is even available on most network-attached storage devices.
Make your media beautiful
Plex gives you one simple interface to organize all of your media: your movie and TV collection, your music library, and all of your photos and home videos. Plex enriches your media library by adding descriptions, plot summaries, posters, and album covers. Enjoy your media on every TV in the house or on any mobile device on the go.
Plex keeps track of your media
Recently added content is presented front and center so you can instantly see what's new. Plex also knows which movies and shows you're watching, so you can easily pick up where you left off or play the next episode.
High quality SSL certificates for all media servers
We've teamed up with DigiCert to provide high quality SSL certificates for your media servers, at no cost to you. Your media server will be able to securely communicate with your devices with top-grade encryption, it's like having your own secret service escort protecting your data end-to-end, preventing hacks, attacks, and snooping.
Plex Home Theater
For those of you with a dedicated computer for your TV, Plex Home Theater celebrates your personal videos, music and photos and gives them the stage they deserve. Simply download Plex Home Theater on your dedicated computer and the free Plex Media Server on your home computer then sit back and enjoy.
Your music's new home
Music on Plex is accessible everywhere and beautifully presented. With support for nearly all audio formats, all of your music gets airtime. Once setup, you can hear (and even watch!) your music anywhere, on anything, and even share access to your music libraries with your friends. Recent improvements include Vevo music videos and Gracenote functionality that improves the metadata of your music library.
Playlists, for endless entertainment
Create customized music or video playlists to fit any occasion, based on mood, genre, collection, and more. You can even import existing iTunes playlists, ratings, track counts, and other details! Playlists are currently available on most platforms, but we're working hard to bring them to all as quickly as possible.
Share your media with friends and family
Effortlessly share media among friends, so you can all discover and enjoy even more content together. Exchange precious memories with distant family members by sharing your vacation photos and home videos. Now, you can also see what your friends are streaming from your collection as everyone gets their own view into your library.
What's New
- Plex Server updated to 1.43.5.11029
- Plex Player updated to 1.115.0.426
- Plex for Android updated to 10.17.0.868
- Plex Home Theater updated to 2.58.0.1076
Update: CVE details and active exploitation
As promised in the original post, here are the CVE details for the issues fixed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.
Chained together, these issues let an unauthenticated remote attacker run code with the privileges of the Plex Media Server process. Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 and later are not affected.
These vulnerabilities are being actively and widely exploited. A public proof of concept was released on October 16.
Since then, we've seen widespread attacks against internet-facing servers that haven't been updated. Compromised servers have been used to run cryptocurrency miners and proxy software, which routes other people's traffic through the victim's internet connection.
If your server is older than 1.43.3.10861 and reachable from the internet, assume it may be compromised.
What you should do:
- Update now. Make sure your server is on 1.43.3.10861 or newer: open Plex Web, go to Settings → General, and check the version shown. Update instructions for each platform are in the original post above.
- Check for signs of compromise:
- Processes started by Plex Media Server that you don't recognize, especially names like myawesomeproxy, mylovelyminer or x12345.
- Unfamiliar .so or .dll files in the Plex Codecs folder.
- Outbound connections to proxystream.st, or sustained high CPU use while nothing is playing.
- If you find any of these, or you can't rule out compromise:
- Rebuild the server from a clean installation rather than reusing the old Plex data directory. At minimum, delete everything in the Codecs folder and check Preferences.xml for transcoder options you didn't set.
- Sign out of all devices from your Plex account settings, and change your Plex password.
- Treat anything the Plex service account could reach as potentially exposed, such as mounted shares and credentials stored on the same machine or VM.
- If you don't need remote access, turn it off under Settings → Remote Access. Avoid forwarding port 32400 directly unless you need it.

articles.title: MrBeast pide un Tesla Roadster volador a Elon Musk: el auto valdría miles de millones de dólares
articles.text:
MrBeast pidió en X un Tesla Roadster con capacidad de vuelo para grabar un video, una solicitud que dirigió a la compañía de Elon Musk luego de la presentación del nuevo deportivo eléctrico, que por el momento no se conoce precio oficial pero valdría miles de millones de dólares si comparamos el Roadster Thrust.
“¿Puedo tener uno de esos Roadster voladores para un video, por favor?”, escribió Jimmy Donaldson, conocido en internet como MrBeast. Elon Musk ni Tesla no han emitido una respuesta pública a la petición del creador.
El mensaje, publicado el 17 de octubre, derivó en reacciones de usuarios que imaginaron posibles desafíos, accidentes ficticios y colaboraciones entre el youtuber y la empresa de autos eléctricos.
Entre los comentarios, varios usuarios propusieron que Musk le prestara el vehículo y otros bromearon con la posibilidad de que MrBeast lo estrellara contra una estructura construida para uno de sus videos.
Incluso hubo quienes se adelantaron y desde ya crearon portadas para el video que MrBeast haga con este nuevo carro.
El auto, en su versión que vuela denominado Roadster Rocket, todavía no está aprobado para circular en vías públicas y la empresa prevé iniciar su producción en 2028.
Cómo es la nueva línea Roadster de Tesla
La línea Tesla Roadster contempla las versiones Performance, Thrust y Rocket. La primera cuenta con dos asientos y está pensada para circular por carretera. Tesla exige un depósito de reserva de USD 50.000 para acceder a esa configuración.
Thrust es la alternativa intermedia. Incorpora propulsores de SpaceX y requiere un depósito de USD 250.000, según la información difundida por la compañía.
La versión Rocket es la que despertó el interés de MrBeast. Será un monoplaza disponible únicamente por invitación y sin precio de reserva publicado. Tesla indicó que integra un sistema de succión bajo la carrocería, alerones activos y 10 propulsores de gas frío instalados alrededor del vehículo.
Esos mecanismos permiten asistir la aceleración, el ascenso y los giros laterales. El modelo cuenta con tanques de 600 litros de aire comprimido, cuya liberación genera el humo blanco que se observó en las demostraciones del prototipo.
Tesla aclaró que Rocket puede volar, aunque no estará homologado para las calles. Musk también señaló que el deportivo no está “optimizado para la seguridad”.
Tesla planea una pista con loopings al estilo Hot Wheels en Texas
Musk adelantó que Tesla construirá una pista de pruebas con loopings en su sede de Texas, Estados Unidos. El circuito estará destinado a los propietarios del Roadster, quienes podrán probar algunas de las maniobras anunciadas para el vehículo.
“Tendremos una pista de looping salvaje, más loca incluso que Hot Wheels, en nuestra sede de Texas”, escribió Musk durante un intercambio con el divulgador tecnológico Robert Scoble en X.
El empresario no informó cuándo abrirá el circuito, cuál será su diseño ni cuáles serán las condiciones de acceso. Tampoco precisó si la instalación estará disponible para todas las versiones del Roadster o si se limitará a modelos como Rocket.
Musk sostuvo además que el auto podrá ejecutar de forma autónoma algunas de las maniobras exhibidas durante su presentación. Según explicó, el propietario podrá pedirle al vehículo que reproduzca ciertos trucos sin controlar de manera manual la aceleración, la dirección y el frenado.
MrBeast y Google acordaron usar Gemini en la producción de videos
La petición del Roadster coincide con una etapa en la que MrBeast amplía sus colaboraciones con empresas tecnológicas.
En septiembre de 2026, Google anunció un acuerdo plurianual con Beast Industries para integrar Gemini, Google Health y Fitbit Air en futuros contenidos y campañas del creador.
El primer desafío de la alianza contempló una prueba de supervivencia en la jungla, el desierto y el Ártico. Donaldson y su equipo usaron Gemini para identificar riesgos, responder a variaciones del clima y tomar decisiones durante cada etapa.

articles.title: Financial services AI at scale: Dell CFO on budgeting tokens - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell’s AI playbook for CFOs: Budget the tokens, then chase speed
Enterprise AI is crossing from experimentation into production, and financial services firms are among the first to prove it can pay off at scale. As token consumption climbs, finance chiefs are now treating AI less as a science project and more as a budget line that has to earn its keep.
That shift is changing how chief financial officers judge AI spending, moving the conversation from cost control toward competitive speed. Dell Technologies Inc., fresh off another blowout quarter driven by AI servers, sees demand spreading well beyond GPUs into traditional servers and storage, according to David Kennedy (pictured), chief financial officer of Dell.
“The spend piece, honestly, will take care of itself,” Kennedy said. “It needs to be managed. IT and finance can help put guardrails around that. I think it’s important, but the real value driver is the speed and productivity an enterprise can get.”
Kennedy spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed budgeting token spend, prioritizing speed and scaling AI in financial services. (* Disclosure below.)
How financial services set the pace for AI at scale
Not every enterprise is moving at the same speed. Financial services firms, especially in high-frequency trading, were early to push AI from pilots into production, with pharmaceutical companies likely next, Kennedy noted. Dell now counts 6,500 AI factories across its customer base, and in May it expanded its AI Factory with Nvidia to help more customers close the gap between experiment and outcome.
“Ultimately, I think we’ve enough proof points now that AI works and it works really well and it gives you speed and efficiency in your company,” Kennedy said. “The question is, can you do that at scale?”
Scaling well starts with basic financial discipline, whether in financial services or any other industry. Most CFOs are now creating a dedicated line item for token spend and tracking it like any other cost, Kennedy explained. From there, efficiency becomes a question of model placement: Repetitive finance workflows can run on open-weight models on-premises, turning variable token costs into fixed ones.
“It’s not necessarily about the amount and the cost of a token,” Kennedy said. “It’s about the tokens you use. Can you be efficient with them? If you are, you’re going to see great outcomes.”

articles.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry.
Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution.
Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes.
The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.”
Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes.
It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA).
In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said.
The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls.
In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions.
Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse.
Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all.

articles.title: ‘Quite the deal, especially when you consider all the features on hand’ — I tested Hisense’s mid-range mini-LED TV and was impressed by its quality HDR, decent sound and near-budget price
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Hisense U6SF Pro is a solid TV, especially for the price. It has just about all the features one could want, though Alexa+ is not hands-free. And it comes with a good but not great picture and decent audio that’s good enough to at least skip the soundbar.
Reasons to buy
- + Good picture quality for the price
- + Alexa+ a little more accurate than other AI voice assistants
- + Good sound quality with a few well implemented audio features
- + The price is right
Reasons to avoid
- - Quite a bit of vignetting
- - Not a lot of detail in shadows
- - No hands-free control
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Hisense U6SF Pro: One-minute review
The Hisense U6SF Pro felt like a budget TV reaching for the mid-range when I first unboxed it. After spending some time with it, I think that impression stands. I don’t mean that in a derogatory way, either. If you had $650 for a TV, getting the 65-inch size of the Hisense U6SF Pro is certainly worth it.
That price tag gets you a 4K resolution with a native 144Hz refresh rate, all the HDR and spatial audio support one could want, a Fire TV interface, and Alexa+ built-in. And just to clear the air, the Hisense U6SF Pro does have appreciable if somewhat hidden upgrades over the non-Pro version. The Pro version is a couple pounds heavier, comes with a built-in subwoofer (and has double the speaker wattage) and WiFi 6, and has the pro version of AMD FreeSync Premium and support for DTS Virtual:X.
The Hisense U6SF Pro has most of the bonafides of the best gaming TVs, such as two HDMI 2.1 ports for up to 4K@144Hz refresh rate passthrough support and the aforementioned AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, though I do wish there was a game-specific bar or menu. I can see an argument for putting this model among the best TVs for the price, though it still comes with some compromises, such as some vignetting all along the bottom of the screen and a lack of detail in the shadows.
Hisense U6SF Pro review: Price and release date
- Release date? March 2026
- 55-inch: $499.99
- 65-inch: $649.99
- 75-inch: $799.99
- 85-inch: $1,099.99
- 100-inch: $2,299.99
The Hisense U6SF and U6SF Pro, along with the Hisense U7, hit the market in March of 2026. While the listed MSRP of the U6SF Pro is much higher on retail sites like Amazon and Best Buy, where the TV’s “value” at 65 inches is listed at $1,099.99, the actual and consistent prices listed above are what I consider the real prices and are what you’ll actually pay.
With a price range of $499.99 for the 55-inch to $2,299.99 for the 100-inch, the Hisense U6SF Pro really falls right into that area between budget TVs and more mid-range models (most TVs within a couple hundred dollars above or below a grand). And it comes in just about every size one could need, unless you’re looking for a smaller TV. The 55-inch model is the smallest it comes in.

Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Features
- Supports all the necessary HDR and spatial audio formats
- Alexa+ works well but isn’t hands-free
- Ambient mode includes options to load personal photos or AI art
Let’s get the basics in terms of features out of the way. The Hisense U6SF Pro supports the litany of HDR formats one would need including Dolby Vision IQ. It also comes with Dolby Atmos and DTS: Virtual X for anyone wanting or needing spatial audio support. And you can connect to the TV via Bluetooth (whether that’s playing music or connecting a device like a game controller), Apple AirPlay, and Smart Home integration.
Since the Hisense U6SF Pro is a Fire TV, it comes with Alexa+, Amazon’s AI-powered version of the company’s long-standing voice assistant. One of the places where this TV’s limitations are a little more obvious than slightly more expensive TVs like the Hisense U7 is the fact that, while there is an actual voice assistant on hand, I have to press the mic button on the remote to use it. In essence, there’s no hands-free control here.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As far as using Alexa+, it’s conversational and does one thing that I’ve had issues with on Google TVs and Google Gemini and that is actually play content directly from the home screen when asked instead of bringing me to an intermediary landing page. Sometimes, I don’t want more info. Sometimes, I just want to watch Psych.
Since it is 2026, AI is implemented throughout this TV and not just with Alexa+. For one, it comes with what Hisense calls “Hi-View AI Engine,” which from what I can tell is the same thing as Dolby Vision. Also worth noting that this TV is said to support Dolby Vision IQ but doesn’t have any Dolby-Vision-related settings in its menu (it only pops up as a picture mode when watching certain media), but it does have more generic sounding settings that do the same thing. I assume this is Hisense’s Hi-View AI Engine.
Also implemented on this TV is an AI-powered Ambient mode, a neat feature that I personally don’t get a lot out of, but you might. You can use premade art, create AI-generated art, or upload pictures using the Amazon Photos app.
- Features score: 4.5 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: picture quality
- Not a lot of detail in shadows
- Smooth action; little blooming
- Quite a bit of vignetting
The interesting thing about a TV like the Hisense U6SF Pro is that the picture quality is generally decent but looks a little two-dimensional compared to more expensive TVs. Whether I’m watching Coco, Top Gun: Maverick, or The Batman, the colors are vibrant enough — this TV has around 96% P3 color coverage — for me to feel like I’m seeing everything as intended. Of course, I have Filmmaker Mode and Imax Mode available along with Dolby Vision IQ.
And the action is smooth — something I noticed with my gaming tests as well. The Hisense U6SF Pro has a 144Hz refresh rate that applies to any content capable of taking advantage, including sources coming through the two 2.1 HDMI ports.
Considering that this TV has all the HDR formats one could need as well as a peak brightness of over 1200 nits (at 10% in Filmmaker Mode) in our benchmarks, I was surprised that the screen felt a little flat. That’s because I consider that flatness to be an issue with the contrast.
While a Hi-QLED mini-LED TV, the Hisense U6SF Pro doesn’t have as much separation of detail in shadows, something I noticed most sharply when gaming but I think contributed to the more two dimensional quality of the picture.
That said, the TV did a good job with blooming, as I didn’t notice any of that halo effect show up when watching a bright subject against a dark background.
The one other issue that I noticed with this TV is vignetting, not just in the corners as I’ve seen with TVs in this range, but along the bottom of the screen as well.
- Picture quality score: 4 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: sound quality
- Sounds good enough to skip a soundbar
- Soundstage is pretty narrow
- Dialog enhancer and night mode work well
The Hisense U6SF Pro’s sound quality is pretty good. With a 50 watt 2.1 built-in system, it should be good enough to skip a soundbar. And I think it is, within reason. I can hear dialog clearly with whatever I’m watching and there’s a bit of a sound stage where I can hear audio elements go from one side to the other, though it’s only as wide as the TV itself.
Since there’s a built-in sub, you do get some low-end information. For instance, one of the scenes I use to test is the Penguin chase scene in The Batman and explosions had a bit of that low-end rumble that you want when watching an action-packed movie.
I will say that the sound quality won’t reach home theater levels, however, so using a soundbar system with a subwoofer (and surrounds) will still sound better. The sound here, with its crisp highs and balanced mids, will do the job if you don’t want to also invest in a full system.
When deep diving into the settings, I noticed that Devialet has licensed its name to Hisense for this model so you can thank the company for the sound quality here. I also noticed that there’s some Atmos and surround sound virtualization, the latter of which completely removes any stereo separation when on.
There’s also a dialog enhancer that works as intended while not sounding too hinky (this feature can sometimes do that since it’s basically boosting the frequencies where voices typically sit). And there’s also a night mode that does a good job of compressing audio so that you can watch at night without loud sections of audio waking someone up. A five-band EQ is also available, as well as a handful of sound modes.
- Sound quality score: 4 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Design
- Uses feet instead of stand but are width-adjustable
- Plenty of ports including two 2.1 HDMI
- Anti-glare screen
The Hisense U6SF Pro comes in the usual sizes one would expect from most models these days with its smallest size at 55 inches and its biggest at 100. There are also 65, 75, and 85 inch sizes available.
As far as stands go, the Hisense U6SF Pro has two feet on the outer ends of the TV instead of the center base. While this means that the TV isn’t height adjustable (some stands can be screwed in at different heights), there are a couple places to screw in the feet so that one can have the feet wider or narrower. This is helpful if you have a smaller entertainment console. Just be aware that this particular feature is not available on the 55-inch model.
The ports on the TV are more than enough for most people. There are the usual four HDMI ports — two 2.1 that support 4K@144Hz — a single LAN, two USB (one USB 3.0 and one USB 2.0), an optical port, and an RF Antenna port.
While I don’t want to talk too much about the screen here, Hisense does use an anti-glare screen that makes this TV a little easier to watch in a bright room. Also worth noting is that there’s a 2.1 50 watt built-in sound system with an included subwoofer.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Smart TV & Menus
- Amazon-focused content and ads in interface
- Less free content than expected
- Some menu settings only accessible when playing content
Being a Fire TV, using the Hisense U6SF Pro is going to be a little Amazon-focused. The layout, which is composed of a banner of rotating content followed by rows of suggested content and apps, is littered with ads and content on Prime. Of course, this isn’t new nor is it unique. Whenever I review a Google TV, it’s the same except with Youtube-related suggestions instead of Prime.
The layout itself is one that I think has been broadly adopted because it’s intuitive and lets you navigate to content without having to open an app just to see what’s locked in there. Interestingly, maybe because Amazon wants everyone on Prime, there’s less free content here than I typically find included in an OS. Sure, there’s a Guide app that looks like an old school cable interface with plenty of free content, but that’s about it.
The OSD menu, integrated into the Fire TV OS, seems intuitive to use. However, certain settings, particularly for picture and sound settings, are not accessible through the settings menu in the interface. Instead, you have to press the settings button on the remote when some content is playing to get access to advanced settings. So, if I want to turn on “Intelligent Picture” or change to Filmmaker Mode or Imax Mode (both of which are available on this TV), I need something to be playing first.
- Smart TV & menus score: 4 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Gaming
- Screen holds gaming back a little, especially with shadows
- No gaming-related menu settings or game bar
- Smooth action thanks to fast refresh rate and a few key features
There are only two things that really hold the Hisense U6SF Pro back as a gaming TV. The first are the limitations of the screen that I’ve covered above. For instance, because the Hisense U6SF Pro’s HDR support is good but not up to the standards of a mid-range $1,000+ TV (let alone a flagship TV), there’s less differentiation in shadows so games that are overall just darker or have a lot of shadow are harder to make out what’s happening. On top of that, the colors aren’t quite as vibrant as they are on something like the Hisense U7 that I keep comparing this TV to.
That said, without being able to A/B the way I am, the colors probably won’t bother you, as they still look good. You might have to compensate in the settings for the shadows, however.
The other is the fact that, outside of a Game Picture Mode, there aren’t any gaming specific menus. There certainly isn’t a gaming bar. I would appreciate being able to make more specific adjustments based on the type of game or to bring up an FPS counter.
That said, I do appreciate that AMD FreeSync Premium Pro is on offer (non-Pro version for the 100-inch) that uses a variable refresh rate along with an auto low-latency mode. I also appreciate the Motion Rate 480 feature, which gives a virtual representation (though not a true one) of having a 480 Hz refresh rate. The end result is smooth action no matter the game.
- Gaming score: 4 / 5
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Value
- Occupies that mid-range performance at budget price point
- Strong value but can find slightly better TVs for slightly more
- The competition has at best similar value
When I think of the Hisense U6SF Pro, I think of a few other specific TVs. The Hisense U7 is a natural comparison since they came out at the same time and is the next step up. Interestingly each TV has a slightly different issue. Whereas the U6SF Pro has more vignetting and a flatter picture, the U7 has some color bleed. But the Hisense U7 is a slightly better TV at just $150 more at the 65-inch size and the 75-inch model has even been cheaper in the past. While this is a rarity, the U7 is generally worth the higher price.
I also think of the TCL QM6K, which came out in 2025 and only got a mild refresh in 2026. It occupies a similar mid-range at almost budget price space, especially since its prices have come down since first reviewed last year. Originally, a 65-inch size would have cost $999.99, but it now goes for $649.99 just like the U6SF Pro. And it’s basically the same or similar prices at the various other sizes as well. That’s for a TV with a slightly better picture quality and slightly worse audio and brightness.
- Value score: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV?
| Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | This TV has all the features you could want from HDR and spatial audio support to the inclusion of Alexa+, though you can’t use that last one hands-free. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Picture quality | There could be a little more detail in the shadows and there’s more vignetting than I would like, but the picture quality is very good for the price. | 4 / 5 | 
| Sound quality | You can skip the soundbar with this TV as its 2.1 system has enough detail and low-end rumble for casual use. | 4 / 5 | 
| Design | The port selection is good including two 2.1 HDMI ports and the screen is anti-glare. While the TV uses feet instead of a stand, they are width-adjustable. | 4 / 5 | 
| Smart TV and menus | I don’t like how some of the settings are separated. It makes adjusting the screen a bit counter intuitive. But the OS is generally easy to use. | 4 / 5 | 
| Gaming | The Hisense U6SF Pro comes with some nifty features like AMD Freesync Premium Pro for smooth action, but there’s no game-specific menu and no game bar. | 4 / 5 | 
| Value | The price for what you get the Hisense U6SF Pro for is quite the deal, especially when you consider all the features on hand. | 4.5 / 5 | 
Buy it if...
You want mid-range quality at budget prices
With all the features and good quality picture and sound, this TV almost reaches the heights of mid-range TVs at a lower price point.
You don’t want to buy a soundbar
It won’t be home theater level, but for casual use, the 2.1 Devialet-branded system sounds good enough that you won’t feel compelled to buy an external soundbar.
You’re in the Alexa Smart Home ecosystem
Being a Fire TV, it comes with Alexa+ so you can ask it all sorts of questions, not just to play content. And being a Fire TV, you can integrate it into an Alexa-based smart home.
Don't buy it if…
You want hands-free control
There’s something to being able to just talk to your TV, and, unfortunately, that’s just not a feature on this TV. For some, it’s not a big deal. For others, it might be as vital as any of the accessibility ones that usually come stock in a smart TV.
You can stretch your budget a few extra hundred dollars
The Hisense U6SF Pro is a good TV for the price and comes at a good price. But for just a few hundred dollars more, there are slightly better TVs, including ones from Hisense.
Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV review: Also consider
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Hisense U6SF Pro | TCL QM6K | Hisense U7 | Roku Pro Series (2025) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price (65-inch) | $649.99 | $649.99 | $999.99 | $899.99 | 
| Screen type | Hi-QLED Mini-LED | Mini-LED | Mini-LED Pro | QLED | 
| Refresh rate | 144Hz | 144Hz | 165Hz | 120Hz | 
| HDR support | Dolby Vision, Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10, HDR10+, HDR10+ Adaptive, HLG | Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10, HLG | HDR10, HDR10+, HDR10+ Adaptive, HLG, Dolby Vision | Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive, HLG | 
| Smart TV | Fire TV with Alexa+ | Google TV | Google TV | Roku | 
| HDMI ports | 4 (2x HDMI 2.1) | 4 (2x HDMI 2.1) | 4 HDMI 2.1 | 4 (2x HDMI 2.1) | 
TCL QM6K
The TCL QM6K is just as good value if you’re looking for a mid-range TV for almost budget prices. It has a relatively great picture quality with vibrant colors, and good contrast, but suffers a little bit in the audio department and comes with lower brightness. Read our full TCL QM6K review.
Hisense U7
While the audio on the Hisense U7 has a little less low end and the picture has some color bleed, this TV outperforms its price by a wide margin making it an even better deal than the Hisense U6SF Pro here. However, it is at a slightly higher price point. Read our full Hisense U7 review.
Roku Pro Series (2025)
The Roku Pro Series (2025) is a little more expensive, but comes with a lot of the same features, has a similarly fast refresh rate for gamers (though no game bar), and has a unique shadowbox design that makes it sit flush on the wall when mounted, making it the better TV for that situation. Read our full Roku Pro Series (2025) review.
How I tested the Hisense U6SF Pro Series MiniLED TV
- I used the TV for a couple weeks
- Tested with both TV, movies, music, and games
I used the Hisense U6SF Pro MiniLED TV regularly for a couple weeks. I tested it using streaming shows, movies, music, and games (via PS5). I went through the various features, particularly Alexa+. I also spent time listening to the audio as well as paying attention to the picture quality.
After spending some time with this TV, it’s my humble opinion that this TV is ideal for those who are looking for a mid-range TV but wanting to pay closer to budget prices.
I’ve tested a lot of tech gear over the years from laptops to keyboards and speakers, and so have been able to use my expertise towards giving an honest and fair opinion, not to mention a critical eye, to any product I test.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read TechRadar's reviews guarantee
James Holland loves checking out gadgets of all sorts, whether it's audio equipment, laptops, or vacuums (especially of the robot variety), and does so for a number of Future Publications including TechRadar, Top Ten Reviews, Homes & Gardens, and T3. He's built up an expertise for in-depth reviewing over the last four years. When he's not putting in the work on the latest tech, he loves to travel, play music, and eat questionable food.

articles.title: Espressif Debuts ESP-Mosaico Modular Development Platform
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Espressif Debuts ESP-Mosaico Modular Development Platform
Espressif Systems (688018.SH) today announced ESP-Mosaico, a modular development platform designed for AI-assisted hardware creation. ESP-Mosaico allows creators to combine functional modules and multiple devices while enabling Coding Agents to understand the current hardware configuration and participate directly in application development.
ESP-Mosaico supports two complementary development approaches. Chat Coding lets creators start from a natural-language request and quickly build working hardware prototypes without setting up a local development environment. Vibe Coding brings AI Agents deeper into the engineering workflow, including implementation, deployment, testing on physical hardware, and continuous iteration.Software can now be generated and modified rapidly with AI, but hardware is still often constrained by fixed boards, interfaces, and product forms. ESP-Mosaico is designed to make hardware equally extensible: capabilities can be added as ideas evolve, without requiring creators to define the final form of a device from the outset.
The name Mosaico, meaning "mosaic," reflects this concept—individual hardware building blocks can be combined to create something larger and continuously evolving.
Modular Hardware That Grows with the Application
At the center of ESP-Mosaico is a compact standalone host featuring a 480 × 480 OLED touchscreen, haptic feedback, a built-in battery, USB Type-C connectivity, and expansion I/O.
The host is powered by Espressif's ESP32-S31, a RISC-V SoC running at up to 320 MHz, with 512 KB SRAM and support for up to 32 MB of high-speed DDR PSRAM. ESP32-S31 also integrates Wi-Fi 6, dual-mode Bluetooth 5.4, and 802.15.4, and supports interfaces including 1 Gbps Ethernet, USB 2.0 High-Speed OTG, hardware JPEG encoding and decoding, and DVP camera input.ESP-Mosaico extends these capabilities through modular hardware for functions such as cameras, sensors, buttons, lighting, and motors. Supported modules can be automatically identified and integrated by the system, reducing the need to repeatedly handle wiring and low-level driver adaptation.
Composability also extends across devices. Multiple ESP-Mosaico hosts can recognize their relative position and orientation and synchronize application state wirelessly, allowing devices to be joined, separated, or rearranged as part of the application itself. This enables experiences ranging from cross-screen games to modular information displays and other multi-screen applications.
Bringing AI Agents into Real-World Development
Chat Coding: From an Idea to a Working Prototype
For creators new to programming or AI-assisted development, ESP-Mosaico provides Chat Coding through ESP-Claw, the Coding Agent built into the platform.
Creators simply describe what they want to build. ESP-Claw uses the capabilities of the connected ESP-Mosaico hardware to generate, build, and deploy the application. Development does not require a locally configured toolchain, while application interfaces, logic, and peripheral control that do not depend on online services run locally on the device after deployment.
Creators can then continue refining the application conversationally—for example, adding functionality, changing behavior, or improving the user interface—turning an initial idea into an interactive hardware prototype through successive iterations.
ESP-Mosaico also connects to Skills Lab, where device applications can be packaged as reusable Skills containing Lua scripts, assets, and peripheral dependencies. Creators can install existing Skills, customize supported applications, or publish their own Skills for others to use.
Vibe Coding: Iterating Directly on Real Hardware
ESP-Mosaico is supported on ESP ZeroCode AI platform including its complete board and peripheral simulation. You can find various ESP-Mosaico community projects here.
For more advanced development, ESP-Mosaico is designed to bring other coding agents into the complete build-test-debug loop.
The platform provides:
- Specification-driven UI development, giving Agents defined design rules, components, resources, and constraints.
- ESP-GSP, an AI-oriented UI framework, where interfaces can be represented using structured JSON, validated during build, simulated on a PC, and then deployed to ESP32 hardware.
- Closed-loop device debugging, exposing flashing, device control, inputs, UI state, performance data, and fault information through unified interfaces so Agents can analyze results and iterate.
- Agent-ready development resources, including BSPs, SDKs, schematics, reference projects, documentation, and Agent References.
- Together, these capabilities allow an Agent to repeatedly modify code, build and deploy, test on real hardware, analyze feedback, and refine the application, while developers define the goals, constraints, and acceptance criteria.
Built on the Open ESP Development Ecosystem
AI-generated code still depends on a strong engineering foundation to run reliably on physical hardware. ESP-Mosaico builds on Espressif's established development ecosystem, including ESP-IDF, drivers and components, technical documentation, development and debugging tools, ESP Component Registry, and community projects. 
More than 200,000 projects related to ESP32 and ESP8266 are available on GitHub, along with more than 300 books published in over 10 languages. These resources can provide Coding Agents with engineering context, reference implementations, and proven development practices.
By connecting these open engineering resources with direct feedback from physical devices, ESP-Mosaico provides a foundation for AI-assisted hardware development that Agents can not only reference, but also build against and validate on real hardware.
Bring Ideas Beyond the Screen
Whether starting with Chat Coding or using Vibe Coding for deeper product development, ESP-Mosaico enables creators to move from an idea to a working physical device—and continue evolving it through software, hardware, and AI-assisted iteration.
Developers can visit the ESP-Mosaico website to learn more about the product and access development resources, or share applications with other users through Skills Lab.
The ESP-Mosaico development kit is now available for purchase. For additional product information, please contact the Espressif customer support team.
From natural-language creation to Agent-driven development, and from modular hardware to multi-device applications, ESP-Mosaico brings AI coding beyond the screen and into the physical world.

articles.title: AMD's FSR 4.1 now works on Radeon RX 6000 GPUs, Xbox Series X and S, and Ryzen AI Max, AI 9, and Z2 SoCs — new release brings cutting-edge tech to older hardware with a small performance cost
articles.text:
AMD's FSR 4.1 now works on Radeon RX 6000 GPUs, Xbox Series X and S, and Ryzen AI Max, AI 9, and Z2 SoCs — new release brings cutting-edge tech to older hardware with a small performance cost
AMD gives older GPUs an image quality boost amid the ongoing AI chip drought
Earlier this year, AMD brought the previously RX 9000-exclusive FSR 4 upscaling tech to Radeon RX 7000-series graphics cards and promised an early 2027 release for RX 6000-series products. Christmas has come early for RDNA 2 and many other Radeon gamers, as Radeon honcho Jack Hyunh has announced an FSR 4.1 release for Radeon RX 6000 series cards, Xbox Series X and Series S consoles, Ryzen Z-series handhelds, and machines with Ryzen AI Max and AI 9 chips today.
To accomplish this feat, AMD says it tweaked FSR 4.1's neural network model to support the INT8 shader hardware (as opposed to the higher-precision FP8 matrix acceleration hardware on Radeon 9000 cards). Additionally, the version specific to handhelds is slimmed down even further, to less than half the size of the full one.
AMD says that compared to FSR 3, games on the aforementioned GPUs and APUs will now deliver better image quality, all else equal. With Cyberpunk 2077 running in FSR Balanced mode at 4K, our quick testing with a Radeon RX 6900 XT shows that running FSR 4 costs just about 13% performance, a small price to pay for sharper and more stable visuals, especially in motion.
And the higher upscaling quality of FSR 4.1 might let gamers use Performance mode where they might previously have used Balanced, or so on, which might offset that performance cost.
There are more goodies in store, too. The Radeon team says that FSR Frame Generation now ought to have better frame pacing, resolving a longstanding complaint with the tech and potentially making for smoother gameplay with framegen enabled. Support for the Vulkan API with FSR 4.1 is set to arrive at some point, as well, a boon for some games and console emulators. Finally, AMD says FSR Ray Regeneration will also be coming to more games, too. The company showed the tech running in Warhammer 40,000: Darktide, and that integration is available now.
To get all this goodness into your GPU, you can download the just-released Radeon 26.10.1 drivers from the AMD Adrenalin application or directly from AMD's website. The updated software also adds support for Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, Star Wars: Galactic Racer, and Final Fantasy Resonance. You can check out the full release notes here.
For owners of Xbox and Ryzen Z2-series handhelds, AMD says that an update from their manufacturers will be forthcoming, as those devices depend on OEM-specific drivers.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
We're pleased to see that Radeon gamers are getting upgrades for their existing graphics chips along the lines of what Nvidia has been delivering throughout 2025, because the way things are going, it looks like it'll be around 2077 before there will be a new gaming graphics card launch. If you're an RDNA 2 gamer, go give FSR 4 a shot and see what you think.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.
