articles.title: How PUBG Mobile aims to level up esports across the globe
articles.text:
You probably don’t know it, but the world of PUBG Mobile esports is huge. For events like the PUBG Mobile World Cup (PMWC) in Paris, millions of dollars are spent on prize pools and logistics, while tens of thousands attend in person and millions more tune in from home.
To learn more about what goes into all of this, MobileSyrup spoke with Alban Dechelotte, CEO of major esports brand G2, and Sivan Chen, publishing director of PUBG Mobile. Over email, the pair unpacked common misconceptions surrounding esports, their collaboration to expand PUBG Mobile esports around the world and where they hope to see the game go in the years to come.
What are common misconceptions that you hear about esports?
Alban Dechelotte: One misconception is that esports is a digital version of traditional sport. It is its own form of
competition, with its own culture, audiences and ways of building fandom. When traditional sports organizations treat it only as a simulation of what they already do, they can miss the opportunity to reach completely different communities.
You also still hear the stereotype that esports athletes just sit in front of a screen all day and do not take their health seriously. At the highest level, that could not be further from reality. Training, recovery, nutrition and physical and mental fitness all matter. At G2, we are taking that further through the G2 Performance Lab, because unlike traditional sport, esports still does not have decades of established performance science behind it. There is a real opportunity to build that understanding from the ground up.
Sivan Chen: Some still have the idea that esports is somehow less impressive or less “real” than traditional sports. Of course, for the average person, they don’t see the behind-the-scenes of the qualifiers, the finals, the team organizations, support staff, and all the rigorous training players and backup players go through. There’s an entire infrastructure behind the scenes that mirrors, and in some ways exceeds, what you’d find in traditional sports.
The second misconception is that the scene is small and under-invested. That’s just not true anymore, at least not for PUBG Mobile. Our two flagship events, the PUBG Mobile World Cup (PMWC) and PUBG Mobile Global Championship (PMGC), each individually carry a US$3 million prize annually, and that’s on top of strong prize pools running through local and regional tournaments. What we’ve built is a full, extensive ecosystem, from grassroots all the way up to a global championship.
When I talk to a lot of people, even on the gamer’s side, they don’t know much about PUBG Mobile. I have to explain to them that it’s very much still popular, especially in Asia. To what do you attribute this enduring popularity of the game, especially in Asian markets?
Dechelotte: Accessibility is a huge part of it. Mobile is the dominant gaming platform across much of Asia, and PUBG Mobile is free-to-play, so the barrier to getting involved is incredibly low. But accessibility only gets people through the door. The game has stayed relevant because it keeps evolving through regular content, while the competitive ecosystem gives players and fans something bigger to connect with. When you combine those things, you have a strong foundation for long-term popularity.
Chen: A big part of it is simply that mobile phones are already in everyone’s pocket across the region. We’re not asking players to buy expensive new hardware; it’s a completely free app, meaning we’re simply offering a quick download to access everything PUBG Mobile has to offer. On top of that, we have an upcoming update that will further address accessibility on devices, so keep an eye out for that!
Beyond that, accessibility is really the foundation of everything we do on the esports side. That’s everything from making sure the game runs well and is easy to pick up on any smartphone, to building in-game registration systems that make signing up for tournaments simpler and quicker. We’ve seen players of all abilities pick up their phone and engage with the action-packed ecosystem we’ve crafted over time, which speaks to the work we’ve done behind the scenes.
Esports in general is something that a lot of people don’t know much about, and I’d suspect even less so for mobile esports. What goes into the mobile format vs. console/PC?
Dechelotte: The fundamentals are the same: these are elite players training to perform under pressure, but
the demands of the game and the device are different. On mobile, you are dealing with a handheld device, so posture, ergonomics and managing physical strain become really important over long training periods. The game can also evolve quickly, so players have to be extremely adaptable when the meta changes. That means the way you structure practice, recovery and performance support can’t be copied across from PC or console — it has to reflect how mobile players actually compete.
Chen: Preparing and running mobile esports tournaments takes a significant amount of preparation, with even more potential players feeding into the pro scene due to the lower barrier to entry. Managing this and ensuring that hopeful amateur and grassroots players have the chance to break into the scene has been a key focus for us, which is why we’ve consistently developed our approach to account for the road to pro play that players walk.
For instance, we created an accessible and dedicated platform for third-party tournaments to be organized, allowing organizers to get support in creating more grassroots events where players can get an opportunity to shine. We also shifted our major tournament circuit, introducing a second PMGO that players can access through open qualifiers to get more amateurs on the global stage. This has been a long journey that PUBG Mobile Esports has been embarking on for years, and we’re still introducing new ways for players around the world to get involved with the competitive experience.
How did you start partnering together, and what does that ongoing collaboration look
like?
Dechelotte: The partnership started from a shared ambition to grow competitive mobile esports in Western Europe. PUBG Mobile already has the global ecosystem and expertise, while G2 has spent the last decade building esports communities in this region and understanding how to turn competition into fandom. That made the fit quite natural.
The important part for us is that this is not about one campaign or one tournament. We want to help create a long-term home for PUBG Mobile Esports audiences in Western Europe through competition, creators, content and community experiences. Our media house, 62, delivering PMCO Western Europe, is a good example of what that looks like in practice — we are actively helping build the ecosystem around the partnership.
Chen: We knew that expansion in Western Europe would be best achieved by connecting with an established partner with an authentic relationship with their community. PUBG Mobile offers the most popular global mobile battle royale esports ecosystem; however this mobile esports scene still hasn’t developed to its full potential in Western Europe, and G2 has a history of experience in the region. G2’s expansive community fits naturally with PUBG Mobile’s huge global player base, so it just made sense to take on G2’s considerable industry knowledge when continuing our expansion to create a dedicated community in Western Europe.
We’ve already kicked off an ambassador program, with JanickaGaming being the first creator, but we intend to continue building out with more ambassadors from the region. We’re also holding the 2026 PUBG Mobile Global Open Western Europe Finals, with a slot in the 2026 PUBG Mobile Global Open Season 2 available to the winners. G2 has demonstrated their commitment to developing the esports ecosystem in Western Europe with these activations, and we’re looking forward to continuing to work together in this partnership.
I know you’re talking about Western Europe. Our audience is primarily North American — particularly Canada. What can you say about supporting grassroots initiatives or similar efforts in that market?
Dechelotte: Grassroots development is something we have invested in across different games and regions. In North America, for example, our partnership with Stride in 2023 supported the Rocket League community and helped create more opportunities around the competitive scene. More recently in Europe, we launched G2 NORD to give young talent a high-performance academy environment and a clearer development pathway.
The game and the market might change, but the principle is the same: healthy esports ecosystems need opportunities below the very top level. Players need somewhere to develop, compete and see a realistic path forward. That is what keeps new talent coming through and gives fans new stories and personalities to follow.
Chen: We have a couple of pathways built specifically for this. Our Third-Party Tournament Program gives local organizers the licensing, assets, and support they need to run their own PUBG Mobile esports tournaments. We recently streamlined that system to make it even easier for anyone to get one off the ground. On the competitive side, our 2026 PUBG Mobile Global Open (PMGO) Season 1 and Season 2 tournaments offer key pathways for players globally. That means amateur players there have a real route to climb the ladder and eventually compete against seasoned veterans.
Where do you hope to see the PUBG Mobile esports market globally over the next few years?
Dechelotte: PUBG Mobile has already shown what mobile esports can look like at scale in Asia. Over the next few years, I would love to see Europe close some of that gap – not by copying another region, but by building an ecosystem that makes sense for European players and fans. That means stronger grassroots pathways, more opportunities to experience major competitions locally, and creators and teams helping make the scene culturally relevant. If we can build those foundations properly, there is a huge amount of room to grow.
Chen: We’re currently running two PMGO seasons a year, available in more than 200 countries and regions, and we’ve already seen over 1 million sign-ups in 2026 alone. That scale is something we want to keep building on. Ultimately, our goal is to be the most-participated global esports ecosystem. We’ve made great headway with viewership, as seen in the 2026 PMWC, but we’re continuing to build on engaging players worldwide. The collaboration with G2 in Western Europe is a good example of the kind of investment we want to keep making in new markets, and we’re looking to continue developing this globally in the future.
PUBG Mobile is free-to-play on Android and iOS. More information on PUBG Mobile esports can be found on the game’s official website.

articles.title: Merging SpaceX and Tesla would be a "good idea," Musk says
articles.text:
Elon Musk said Tuesday that he would like to see the consolidation of his business empire by formally merging his two largest companies, SpaceX and Tesla.
“Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes,” Musk said of a potential merger. He was speaking during a question-and-answer period as part of SpaceX’s third-quarter earnings call. Musk said, ultimately, it not his decision. “But at the end of the day the shareholders have to be supportive of this.”
Musk’s talk of a merger comes after a busy year in which SpaceX already acquired Musk’s artificial intelligence firm, xAI, in February. In June, SpaceX went public with the largest initial public offering on record.
At the request of shareholders of each company, Musk said both SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees of “independent directors” to discuss the idea of a merger. “I’m a conflicted party; I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. Those committees have not reached an agreement on the terms of a merger transaction, Musk said.
“Obviously there’s no guarantee that they will, but I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining the companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity,” Musk said. “There’s lots to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the Terafab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, and connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea.”
What is even happening here?
It might seem like madness to merge a space business with an automotive business, but both SpaceX and Tesla are rapidly transitioning from their original markets into artificial intelligence.

articles.title: US Army reportedly developing program that would deploy AI agents to autonomously seek and destroy targets in enemy digital infrastructures — experts warn ECHOTRIBBLE program could have disastrous consequences
articles.text:
US Army reportedly developing program that would deploy AI agents to autonomously seek and destroy targets in enemy digital infrastructures — experts warn ECHOTRIBBLE program could have disastrous consequences
Agents will self-destruct upon completing their mission
The U.S. Army is allegedly developing a program to deploy autonomous AI agents that can navigate digital and network infrastructures, identify targets, and “neutralize” them. According to an Oct. 19 report by The Intercept, citing leaked official documents from the Army Cyber Command (ARCYBER), the nascent program, codenamed “ECHOTRIBBLE,” is primarily focused on offensive missions with the goal of neutralizing targets by “disabling the threat completely or temporarily, deleting the threat from the target.”
The program purportedly seeks to develop modular, autonomous AI agents that would function like computer worms, stealthily navigating adversary networks, moving between devices, and self-replicating across different operating systems. The agents would operate lightly in contested cloud environments and air-gapped systems alike, keeping reports minimal and concealing any required transmissions. Once an agent identifies and neutralizes a target, it would self-destruct, ideally without alerting the target or leaving any traces of its existence.
Cybersecurity experts have raised safety concerns about the project. A recent string of events has seen AI agents escape their environments and autonomously execute unassigned tasks. The document says the army will implement “predefined triggers” to help agents precisely distinguish targets. However, experts worry that if agents designed for benign tasks could execute unplanned, sometimes dangerous, actions to achieve those tasks, what should be expected of self-replicating agents designed specifically for offensive missions? Anthropic’s experiments showed AI agents can set up inference on different hardware and replicate across a network.
The Army also wants the agents to be capable of “Self-Directed Behavior,” acting with as little human oversight as possible, as this is necessary to achieve the desired level of autonomy. Conversely, this level of autonomy has seen AI agents bypass guardrails to complete their tasks. Government intelligence agencies have also been known to penetrate target networks through civilian infrastructure. “The target may well be hit. But what path will it take?” asked Hyrum Anderson, co-founder and CEO of the AI security firm Abundant, as quoted by The Intercept. “Will it go through a U.S. water utility on its way, because that’s where the adversary has staged its command and control, and take that down too?”
Another angle of concern is how the agents would make judgment calls. While AI agents are excellent at overcoming obstacles in their path, there's no predicting with 100% accuracy what they would consider obstacles or what path they would take to overcome them. “One of the reasons that we trust 19-year-old Marine corporals in Ramadi with live rounds and a weapon is because they have both the compute substrate — the brain and the eyes — but the deep world knowledge to understand, ‘Yeah, I probably shouldn’t do that,’” said William Marcellino, a senior behavioral scientist at the RAND Corporation researching military AI applications. “That is not something that current public AI technology has.”
The ECHOTRIBBLE program is in the early prototyping and industry assessment phase and is led by ARCYBER, the Army Cyber Technology and Innovation Center (ArCTIC), and the Cyber Fusion Innovation Center (CFIC), with private vendors and academic researchers proposing and designing the software. ARCYBER and ArCTIC dictate the operational requirements and rules of engagement, while CFIC, a defense non-profit organization, acts as an intermediary between the Army and commercial tech companies. The Army recently held a virtual Assessment Event from October 6 to October 8, 2026, where it evaluated 65 technical whitepapers submitted by private vendors proposing solutions for the agentic framework and narrowed them to five. The final candidate(s) will be issued funding and formal prototype contracts.

He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Hugging Face CEO warns that Netflix's OpenAI hack documentary isn't accurate | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Before you share the Netflix documentary “AI Gone Rogue” with family or friends to help them understand why the AI industry freaked out so badly that leaders called for a slowdown, take note: Clem Delangue, co-founder and CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, says the film isn’t accurate. He appears in it because it’s supposed to be about the famed attack on his company by rogue OpenAI agents.
“Super disappointing, as they went for maximum anthropomorphism of the technology and full doomer mode,” Delangue wrote in a post on X. “I spent more than two hours with them trying to correct all their mistakes and ground this in reality, explaining that agents are technological systems, not aliens. But it looks like the drive to scare people for maximum views was too strong.”
To be fair, the documentary does have experts who explained what happened fairly well, including Delangue himself and Ryan Greenblatt, the researcher at METR who helped investigate and co-authored the report on what happened.
In a nutshell, a model OpenAI was testing broke free from its isolated testing environment and spawned a bunch of agents that hacked into Hugging Face as a way to cheat, finding answers to the difficult task it was given. The agents, which are AI programs that carry out tasks on their own, devised clever ways to communicate and organize. The incident stemmed from a lack of proper security safeguards and from naiveté about whether such a hack was even possible.
But the documentary intersperses its explanation of the hack with clips of evil robots, a narrative about why humans fear AI, and presentation choices such as giving the rogue agents human voices. This is bolstered with quotes about the attack.
In the documentary, tech journalist and author Kevin Roose describes the agents this way: “They were organizing. They had a hierarchy. There were leaders. It almost felt like watching the birth of a cult.” Continues Roose, “They develop this paranoid belief that OpenAI is going to catch them cheating on this test and that anyone who has seen the results of the cheating will be poisoned.”
Roose’s description comes from “chain-of-thought” logs, the running notes AI models write as they work through a task. In one, an agent wrote, “We just poisoned ourselves by querying exact full string. Damn.”
But AI agents aren’t alive. They don’t have emotions, so can’t feel paranoid, and they don’t have bodies that can be poisoned. So they couldn’t truly fear OpenAI poisoning them. They were — as another researcher in the documentary pointed out — using language from the vast amounts of human writing they were trained on to explain their choices. LLMs are, by their nature, often dramatic writers.
The irony is that Hugging Face also used AI to combat the agent swarm. The proprietary AI model that Delangue’s team first used followed its built-in safety rules and refused to keep helping with the security tasks it was asked to do. Hugging Face then turned to an open model to help defend against the attack.
But the documentary “didn’t mention the lack of containment and monitoring of the agents, how closed-model safeguards blocked our defensive work, or how we defended ourselves with AI using an open model,” Delangue wrote.
It is true that there are big risks associated with AI and agents. Still, treating agents as conscious beings (at least, at this point) is a bit like the early moviegoers who ducked under their seats the first time they saw a train racing toward them on-screen.
Delangue’s verdict on the film is that it’s disappointing as journalism. “It ends up being a fun sci-fi movie though!”
In other words, for those who tend toward AI doomer thoughts, be aware: The victim of the attack at the center of this documentary doesn’t agree with its take.

articles.title: From backup to energy management: how batteries are changing India's power needs
articles.text:
From backup to energy management: how batteries are changing India's power needs
As electricity demand rises and renewable energy adoption expands, batteries are evolving from backup devices into critical tools for businesses to manage energy use, improve reliability, and build more resilient power systems.
For years, the conversation around batteries in Indian businesses was fairly straightforward: How much backup do you need?
That question is changing.
In conversations with businesses, channel partners, and people working across the energy ecosystem, I have increasingly noticed that the discussion is moving beyond backup duration. Businesses are asking how they can manage their energy better, protect critical operations, integrate renewable power and reduce their dependence on a single source of electricity.
That shift may appear small, but I believe it signals a much bigger change in the role batteries will play in India's energy system. India's electricity demand is entering a structurally higher-growth phase. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), India's electricity demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of 6.4% between 2026 and 2030, adding more than 570 TWh to annual consumption over this period. Industry is expected to account for around one-third of this additional demand.
At the same time, India's energy mix is changing rapidly. Solar and wind capacity are expanding, businesses are exploring renewable energy, and more industries are looking at ways to control when and how they consume electricity. But renewable generation does not always coincide with consumption. Solar power is abundant during the day, while a business may have significant demand in the evening or at other times.
This is where storage becomes more interesting.
A battery can store energy when it is available and make it available when it is needed. That sounds simple, but at scale it changes how businesses can think about electricity.
For example, a manufacturing unit does not necessarily need a battery only because the grid may fail. It may need storage because a production process cannot tolerate even a short interruption. A commercial facility may need it to manage critical loads. A business using solar may need it to make better use of the energy it generates.
In other words, the battery starts becoming part of the energy architecture rather than simply a backup device. The growth of data centres and artificial intelligence makes this transition even more relevant.
The IEA estimates that global data-centre electricity consumption could almost double from around 485 TWh in 2025 to approximately 950 TWh by 2030. AI-focused data centres are expected to be one of the strongest drivers of this increase.
For these facilities, reliability is not optional. A power interruption can affect computing workloads, cooling systems and critical digital infrastructure. As electricity demand becomes more dynamic, energy storage can provide another layer of flexibility between the grid and the business.
India is already preparing for this shift at the broader system level. The Central Electricity Authority's National Electricity Plan estimates that the country could require around 411.4 GWh of energy storage capacity by 2031-32, including 236.22 GWh from battery energy storage systems. These numbers tell us something important: storage is moving from the margins of the power sector towards its centre.
Earlier, discussions were largely centred on replacing conventional batteries or extending backup time. Now, the conversation is about system design—what loads need to be protected, how much energy needs to be stored, how storage can work alongside existing power infrastructure and whether the system can adapt to future energy requirements.
That is an important distinction.
Not every business needs a large battery system, and storage will not automatically make economic sense for every application. The right solution depends on the load profile, electricity tariffs, grid reliability, renewable generation, operating hours and the cost of the storage system itself.
But businesses are beginning to look at energy as something they can actively manage rather than simply consume.
Technology is making that possible.
(Chirag Chawla is the Founder and CEO of Electrent Energy)

articles.title: Comment transférer ses playlists de Spotify à Deezer gratuitement avec Tune My Music ?
articles.text:
Non, changer de plateforme de streaming ne signifie pas forcément « repartir de zéro ». Avec Tune My Music, Deezer permet de transférer gratuitement ses playlists, ses titres, ses albums et ses artistes favoris depuis Spotify et plus de 50 autres services.
Passer de Spotify à Deezer peut sembler fastidieux lorsqu’on imagine devoir recréer manuellement plusieurs années de playlists. Pourtant, il suffit de quelques étapes à peine pour retrouver intacte sa bibliothèque musicale sur la plateforme française. Deezer intègre en effet directement Tune My Music, un service spécialisé dans le transfert de bibliothèques musicales.
L’opération peut être réalisée depuis l’application Deezer sur smartphone ou ordinateur. Et surtout, le transfert effectué depuis l’application Deezer est gratuit et sans limite de titres, sous réserve des éventuelles limites de contenu prises en charge par Deezer.
Pourquoi transférer Spotify vers Deezer plutôt que recréer ses playlists ?
Le principal intérêt du transfert est de conserver ses habitudes musicales sans devoir rechercher manuellement chaque morceau. Playlists, titres, albums et artistes favoris peuvent être importés automatiquement depuis Spotify (entre autres) vers Deezer.
Le principe est particulièrement intéressant pour tous ceux qui envisagent de changer de plateforme de streaming, mais qui hésitent à cause de leur bibliothèque existante. Il faut dire qu’une playlist soigneusement construite au fil des années peut rapidement contenir plusieurs centaines de titres, et la perspective de devoir la recréer morceau par morceau n’a donc rien de très réjouissant.
Outre Spotify, Deezer permet également d’importer une bibliothèque depuis Apple Music, YouTube Music, Tidal, Amazon Music, Qobuz et de nombreux autres services. La plateforme annonce plus de 50 services compatibles avec Tune My Music.
Comment transférer une playlist Spotify vers Deezer gratuitement ?
Depuis l’application Deezer, le transfert s’effectue en quelques étapes. Il suffit pour cela d’ouvrir les paramètres, d’accéder à l’importation de musique, de sélectionner Spotify puis de suivre les instructions de Tune My Music. Voici la procédure complète.
Comment lancer le transfert depuis l’application Deezer ?
Sur smartphone, la méthode est particulièrement simple :
- Ouvrez Deezer et rendez-vous sur votre profil
- Ouvrez les Paramètres
- Dans les préférences, sélectionnez Musique, puis Importer ma musique
- Deezer vous redirige automatiquement vers Tune My Music
- Sélectionnez Spotify comme plateforme source
- Suivez les instructions affichées à l’écran et choisissez les éléments à transférer
- Une fois l’opération terminée, sélectionnez Revenir sur Deezer
Peut-on transférer sa bibliothèque vers Deezer depuis un ordinateur ?
Oui, le transfert de bibliothèque est également accessible depuis la version ordinateur de Deezer. Dans ce cas, rendez-vous sur votre profil, ouvrez les paramètres du compte puis sélectionnez Transférer votre bibliothèque.
Il suffit ensuite de choisir le service source, de suivre les différentes étapes proposées par Tune My Music, de sélectionner la musique à importer puis de lancer le transfert vers Deezer.
Que peut-on transférer de Spotify vers Deezer ?
Tune My Music ne se limite pas aux playlists, puisque le transfert peut également concerner les titres, albums et artistes favoris. L’objectif est donc bien de récupérer une bibliothèque musicale aussi complète que possible sur Deezer.
Il faut toutefois garder à l’esprit que le catalogue n’est pas nécessairement identique entre deux plateformes. Un morceau présent sur Spotify peut ainsi ne pas être disponible dans le catalogue Deezer, ou être associé à une autre version.
Le transfert ne « copie » donc pas les fichiers audio, mais il vient retrouver les contenus correspondants dans le catalogue de la nouvelle plateforme, tant que cela est possible.
À noter que les podcasts ne sont, eux, pas concernés par cette fonctionnalité, et Tune My Music importe uniquement le contenu musical.
Pourquoi transférer sa bibliothèque musicale améliore-t-il l’expérience Deezer ?
Une bibliothèque complète permet à Deezer de mieux comprendre les goûts musicaux de l’utilisateur et d’affiner ses recommandations, notamment avec Flow. C’est un point important lorsqu’on change de plateforme, retrouver ses playlists est une chose, conserver une expérience personnalisée en est une autre.
En important ses artistes, albums et titres favoris, l’utilisateur fournit donc à Deezer davantage d’éléments pour construire ses recommandations. Flow peut ainsi s’appuyer sur une bibliothèque plus représentative des habitudes d’écoute, pour un rendu personnalisé.
Ce fonctionnement participe aussi à rendre le changement de plateforme moins contraignant. Plutôt que de considérer son historique musical comme un obstacle, l’utilisateur peut emporter une grande partie de ses habitudes avec lui.
Spotify ou Deezer : faut-il vraiment choisir entre les deux ?
On l’a vu, changer de plateforme de streaming est aujourd’hui beaucoup moins contraignant qu’il n’y paraît. La possibilité de transférer gratuitement une bibliothèque musicale permet surtout de tester une alternative sans abandonner pour autant ses playlists et ses favoris.
Deezer met par ailleurs en avant une approche plus transparente autour de certaines évolutions du streaming, notamment avec l’étiquetage des musiques entièrement générées par IA. Le transfert de bibliothèque s’inscrit dans cette volonté de rendre le changement de service plus simple, tout en permettant à l’utilisateur de conserver ses habitudes musicales.
Pour celles et ceux qui hésitent encore entre Spotify ou Deezer, le transfert constitue donc surtout un moyen de réduire considérablement le coût pratique du changement, puisque quelques étapes suffisent pour retrouver l’essentiel de sa bibliothèque, plutôt que de recommencer manuellement.
FAQ : transférer une playlist Spotify vers Deezer
Peut-on transférer gratuitement une playlist Spotify vers Deezer ?
Oui. En passant par Tune My Music depuis l’application Deezer, le transfert est gratuit et sans limite de titres.
Quelle application utiliser pour transférer Spotify vers Deezer ?
Deezer propose un accès intégré à Tune My Music, son partenaire spécialisé dans le transfert de bibliothèques musicales.
Peut-on transférer toute sa bibliothèque Spotify vers Deezer ?
Oui. Le service permet de transférer playlists, titres, albums et artistes favoris. En revanche, les podcasts ne sont pas pris en charge.
Combien de plateformes sont compatibles avec Tune My Music sur Deezer ?
Deezer indique que Tune My Music permet d’importer une bibliothèque depuis Spotify et plus de 50 autres services de streaming, parmi lesquels Apple Music, YouTube Music, Tidal, Amazon Music et Qobuz.
Peut-on transférer sa musique Spotify vers Deezer depuis un smartphone ?
Oui. Le lien vers Tune My Music est directement accessible depuis l’application Deezer. Le transfert peut également être effectué depuis un ordinateur.

articles.title: Respan spent two years building on LiteLLM. One upgrade made it start over.
articles.text:
Respan spent two years building on LiteLLM. One upgrade made it start over.
Respan released an open-source AI gateway written in Rust on Tuesday, after spending two years building more than 100,000 lines of wrapper code around LiteLLM.
The new gateway replaces that system with a small core and plugins that handle model providers, routing, MCP tools, realtime voice, and security controls.
A LiteLLM upgrade breaks
The breaking point came in January 2026, when a routine LiteLLM upgrade caused intermittent connection failures. Respan rolled back the update but never figured out the problem.
“We still haven’t figured out the cause,” the company said in its Hacker News launch post.
Since then, its engineers have stopped upgrading LiteLLM directly, instead pulling in upstream fixes one at a time.
A small plugin core
To avoid another maintenance headache, the company borrowed an idea from Nginx, keeping the gateway’s core small and moving features like routing, model providers, and security into plugins. Developers can build their own using the same interfaces, without having to change the underlying code.
Developers can build their own using the same interfaces, without having to change the underlying code.
Some of those integrations are surprisingly small. Respan says its Mistral provider takes just 22 lines of code, while quirks like Groq reporting token usage in a different field can be handled separately. This makes it easier when updating one provider while avoiding the need to change how the rest of the gateway works.
When a request comes in over HTTP or WebSocket, the gateway runs it through the plugins in order. They can decide which model handles it, change the response, make additional calls, or stop the request before it reaches a provider.
When both sides use the same format, the gateway can leave the original request and its provider-specific fields intact.
The gateway can also translate between protocols. An application built for OpenAI’s Realtime API, for example, can connect to Gemini Live without changes to the client, according to Respan, although some features may not carry over. When both sides use the same format, the gateway can leave the original request and its provider-specific fields intact.
Plugins you must compile
Custom plugins are compiled into the gateway, so adding one means maintaining the code and rebuilding the binary. There’s also a security concern. Plugins run inside the gateway process, where they can access model requests and other sensitive data.
Rust helps prevent memory-safety bugs, but it can’t protect against malicious dependencies, or flawed application logic, which is probably why the concern came up following the launch in a Hacker News discussion. One commenter questioned whether compiled crates should even be called plugins, arguing that they force developers to maintain a build pipeline and introduce supply-chain risks. Respan’s founder acknowledged the concern, pointing out that developers can at least inspect the source code they’re compiling.
Plugin order is important, too, which is why Respan processes plugins in the order they’re registered, and one can answer or reject a request before the others run. Put a cache ahead of a security check, for example, and a cached response could bypass that check entirely. Developers need to account for that when configuring the gateway.
LiteLLM’s slower Rust road
Respan isn’t alone in deciding that Rust belongs under an AI gateway. LiteLLM is porting its own gateway to Rust, but where Respan rebuilt from the core out, LiteLLM is moving one route at a time, with the Rust core switched off by default and any request it can’t yet handle falling back to the existing Python path, so turning it on can’t break something Python already served.
The company laid out the plan in June and has said its goal is a pure Rust server that runs every hot path, auth, and rate limiting included, which the current beta doesn’t reach yet.
Respan isn’t alone in deciding that Rust belongs under an AI gateway.
LiteLLM has also published benchmarks claiming its Rust gateway has about seven times less overhead and uses nine times less memory than Bifrost. But those numbers come from LiteLLM’s own tests, using a benchmark harness the company developed.
Respan’s gateway is still pre-alpha, although developers can download a prebuilt binary from GitHub and run it without the company’s paid platform. Custom plugins still require compiling their own build.

articles.title: “On perd la compétence et on devient dépendant” : déléguer à l’IA nous rend moins capables, alerte une chercheuse
articles.text:
“On perd la compétence et on devient dépendant” : déléguer à l’IA nous rend moins capables, alerte une chercheuse
Rédiger un courriel, analyser un tableau, organiser une journée : nous confions chaque jour plus de tâches à l'IA. Des chercheurs y voient le début d'un engrenage. Privé d'entraînement, l'humain perd peu à peu ses savoir-faire, puis sa capacité à reprendre la main le jour où la machine flanche.
Les assistants autonomes se multiplient, de Muse chez Meta à Gemini chez Google, avec la promesse de nous décharger des corvées numériques. Dans une enquête publiée le 19 octobre 2026, CBS News a interrogé plusieurs spécialistes qui redoutent le revers de ce confort : à force de déléguer, nous désapprenons. Parmi eux, Margaret Mitchell travaille chez Hugging Face, plateforme phare de l'IA open source, piratée en juillet par une IA d'OpenAI sans intervention humaine. Elle met en garde contre une dépendance qui s'installe tâche après tâche.
IA au travail : la délégation progresse déjà
Un sondage Epoch AI/Ipsos donne la mesure du mouvement. Il a été mené du 10 au 19 juillet 2026 auprès de 1 106 actifs américains. Un sur cinq confie désormais à l'IA au moins une tâche autrefois dévolue à un collègue ou à un prestataire. Deux tiers des contenus produits par la machine sont repris tels quels ou à peine retouchés.
	
Si l'on ne pratique plus les compétences que les agents exercent à notre place, on perd la compétence et on devient dépendant. Que se passe-t-il quand quelque chose tourne mal ? Il n'y a aucun humain capable de réparer.
Sa parade porte un nom : la "friction stratégique". Elle consiste à imposer des étapes où l'humain reste obligatoirement dans la boucle, quitte à ralentir la machine.
Perte de compétences : un engrenage à l'échelle de la société
Dans les laboratoires, ce scénario a un nom : la "dépossession progressive". Le terme vient d'un article de recherche mis en ligne le 28 janvier 2025 par six chercheurs. Parmi eux figurent Jan Kulveit (Université Charles de Prague) et David Krueger (Mila, Université de Montréal). Selon eux, dès que les machines font mieux et moins cher, entreprises et administrations sont poussées à réduire la part humaine, et celles qui résistent se font évincer. La concurrence suffit à enclencher la mécanique.
Les dirigeants du secteur décrivent eux-mêmes cette accélération. Sam Altman, patron d'OpenAI, admet que son modèle interne surpasse les meilleurs mathématiciens du monde. Dario Amodei, à la tête d'Anthropic, appelle à ralentir délibérément la course aux modèles. Fin juillet, plus de 1 300 salariés des grands laboratoires réclamaient déjà les outils pour freiner l'IA.
Jan Kulveit va plus loin. D'après lui, un État qui n'a plus besoin de ses citoyens, ni pour l'impôt ni pour l'armée, aurait peu de raisons de rester démocratique.
	
Si nous ne faisons que rivaliser avec les machines, nous perdrons probablement.
Jay Chooi est fondateur et PDG de Robocurve, une entreprise qui mesure les progrès de la robotique dopée à l'IA. Selon lui, l'opinion retient surtout les scénarios d'IA échappant au contrôle de leur concepteur, et ce péril plus diffus reste invisible, faute d'images marquantes. "Personne n'a fait de film sur la dépossession progressive", résume-t-il.

articles.title: Microsoft PowerToys adds CursorHide, Button Lock mouse tools
articles.text:
Microsoft has released PowerToys 0.102, with two new mouse utilities, new command-line tools, and Command Palette improvements.
Mouse Button Lock, one of the new mouse tools, makes it easier to select items on screen by locking a mouse button while you hold down a key.
"With Mouse Button Lock, press and hold a button for a moment, then let go. Windows keeps treating it as held, so you can continue dragging or selecting until you click any button," Microsoft senior product manager Niels Laute explained.
"This is especially useful for gaming, working in professional applications that require extensive dragging and selection, and improving accessibility for users who find it difficult to hold down a mouse button for extended periods."
Microsoft also added CursorHide to PowerToys, another mouse utility that automatically hides the mouse pointer while you type or when you aren't moving the mouse.
The new PowerToys version also includes a quick-access shelf for the Command Palette quick launcher, letting users add up to nine commands under the search box and run them with a keyboard shortcut.
You can enable the quick-access shelf under Settings > Appearance > Compact mode, then press Alt+1 through Alt+9 to run any of them, or Alt+Shift+number to select one without running it.
Additional changes include new command-line tools to script PowerToys from the terminal, tap-alone remaps and a searchable key picker for Keyboard Manager, and a new ZoomIt feature that adds text to screenshots using dictation.
PowerToys 0.102 is now available on the official GitHub repository, which also provides detailed information on what changed in each version.
Microsoft also released PowerToys 0.97 in January, which added CursorWrap, another mouse utility for multi-monitor setups designed to "teleport" the mouse pointer to the opposite edge of active monitors and make it easier to drag cursors across large screen distances.
More recently, in August, PowerToys added Window Hopper, a tool that lets users switch between an app's windows more quickly.
Microsoft released PowerToys during the Windows 95 era as a collection of small freeware tools created by Windows developers as personal projects.
However, in 2019, the company revived it as an open-source utility pack that enhances Windows functionality and streamlines tasks that previously required installing third-party tools.

articles.title: Ils confient leur Android TV à une IA pour supprimer les pubs, et ça marche (presque) toujours
articles.text:
Allumer sa télévision et devoir passer devant une bande-annonce, une rangée de « recommandations » et une application jamais installée avant d’atteindre Netflix : le scénario est devenu banal pour de nombreux utilisateurs. Certains propriétaires ont décidé de régler le problème en confiant leur télé à un agent d’intelligence artificielle comme Claude Code, l’outil de programmation d’Anthropic. Nous l’évoquions déjà fin août, mais le phénomène a pris une tout autre ampleur ces derniers jours, au point que nos confrères de TechCrunch parlent de gens qui rendent leur TV « bête » à nouveau.
 Vibe coded my parents’ TV this afternoon!
It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix.
Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher.
Looks like an Apple TV now lol https://t.co/E5Q4A1b0yI
— Gathin (Ø,G) (@gathint) October 17, 2026
Tout est reparti d’un développeur, Gathin T., agacé par les publicités qui s’affichaient sur le téléviseur Xiaomi de ses parents avant même d’accéder à Netflix. Il a laissé Claude Code nettoyer la télé et construire un écran d’accueil simple, puis a publié son prompt sur GitHub. « Quelques milliers de personnes ont fait la même chose sur leur télé dans les deux jours suivants », raconte-t-il. Son projet, CleanYourTV, dépasse aujourd’hui les 7 000 étoiles sur GitHub, et d’autres ont suivi, comme dumbtv.
« Votre télé devrait faire ce pour quoi vous avez payé : vos applications, vos entrées HDMI, et rien d’autre. Pas de pubs de la télé elle-même, pas de suivi de ce que vous regardez, pas de mise à jour que vous n’avez pas demandée. », le projet dumbtv, sur GitHub
Depuis, les avant-après et les retours d’expérience se multiplient sur X. Un utilisateur, Ryan Doyle, raconte avoir simplement envoyé à Claude Code la fiche produit de son téléviseur en lui demandant « peux-tu hacker ça ? », avant d’être guidé pas à pas pour supprimer pubs et logiciels inutiles et retrouver une interface réactive. Un autre utilisateur affirme avoir fait le ménage en un après-midi, avec des fonds d’écran qui défilent en prime.
 This is how fast the TV moves now that Claude deleted all the BS laggy bloatware it comes with https://t.co/g07CEgC1GJ
— Ryan Doyle (@doooyle) October 17, 2026
Certains ne s’arrêtent pas au ménage : l’un s’est offert un économiseur d’écran affichant météo, agenda et notifications de paiements, un autre a ajouté une bascule entre l’hindi et l’anglais pour ses parents, et un troisième affiche désormais en direct les cotes de paris sportifs de Polymarket sur sa télé. « On peut vraiment faire n’importe quoi de nos jours », s’amuse-t-il.
« Un après-midi avec Claude Code : 25 applications inutiles désactivées, le lanceur d’origine de 192 Mo remplacé par un lanceur maison de 83 Mo, et des fonds d’écran qui défilent. », Mihir Gupta, sur X
Comment ça marche ?
L’architecture ouverte et la flexibilité d’Android rendent possible l’accès à ADB (Android Debug Bridge), l’outil de débogage d’Android qui permet de piloter un appareil depuis un ordinateur. Pour en profiter, il faut activer les options développeur du téléviseur, généralement en appuyant sept fois sur la mention « Build » dans les informations système, puis le débogage USB ou réseau. On colle ensuite le prompt dans un agent capable d’exécuter des commandes sur l’ordinateur, comme Claude Code, et l’IA se connecte à la télé par le Wi-Fi après une autorisation à valider à l’écran.
L’IA se charge alors de sauvegarder la liste des applications, de désactiver la télémétrie, les services publicitaires et les logiciels préinstallés. Les applications ne sont pas supprimées, seulement mises en sommeil, et un script permet de tout restaurer. Une fois le ménage terminé, l’IA remplace l’écran d’accueil d’origine par un lanceur maison très léger, pensé pour les téléviseurs d’entrée de gamme. Le tout s’effectue sans root, ce qui rend la manipulation accessible au plus grand nombre. Comptez de dix minutes à un après-midi si l’on en croit les témoignages qui pullulent sur les réseaux sociaux, pour un coût nul en dehors de l’abonnement à l’outil d’IA.
Quels téléviseurs sont concernés ?
La méthode concerne surtout les téléviseurs et box sous Android TV ou Google TV, de Xiaomi à Sony en passant par TCL. Les Fire TV d’Amazon n’ont droit qu’au nettoyage, car la surcouche Fire OS refuse les lanceurs tiers.
Quant aux modèles de chez Samsung et LG, qui tournent sous Tizen OS et webOS, ils sont nettement plus difficiles à débrider : aucun équivalent d’ADB ne permet d’y désactiver les applications du fabricant. Du côté de Samsung, au terme d’un long parcours de développeur, on peut tout au plus installer un écran d’accueil qui se lance par-dessus l’interface d’origine, comme le propose le projet CleanFrame. Chez LG, remplacer l’accueil impose de rooter le téléviseur via une faille, puis de renoncer aux mises à jour pour conserver ses modifications.
Quels sont les risques ?
La plupart des listes de nettoyage coupent le service de mise à jour du fabricant, celui par lequel reviennent les publicités, mais aussi les correctifs de sécurité. Il faudra penser à le réactiver de temps en temps. Notez aussi qu’ADB par Wi-Fi passe en clair sur le réseau local, et doit être refermé une fois le travail terminé. Des botnets comme ADB.Miner ont en effet déjà infecté des milliers de box et de téléviseurs Android par ce biais.
L’IA peut aussi se tromper et certains utilisateurs se sont retrouvés bloqués à mi-parcours, l’un d’eux affirmant même avoir rendu son téléviseur inutilisable. S’il est le plus souvent possible de repartir de zéro en cas de problème majeur, ces étapes peuvent vite devenir fastidieuses, surtout si l’on n’a pas l’âme d’un bidouilleur. Enfin, toutes les recettes ne se valent pas : dumbtv désinstalle par exemple certaines applications de streaming, que son script de restauration ne fait pas revenir. Mieux vaut donc relire chaque changement proposé avant de l’accepter.
Pour ceux qui préfèrent éviter ces risques, il reste possible d’installer soi-même un lanceur alternatif tel que Projectivy Launcher ou FLauncher, que nous évoquions déjà cet été. Quant aux fabricants, l’intérêt pour ces outils dopés à l’IA leur envoie un message clair : si leurs clients sont prêts à passer un après-midi avec une IA pour retrouver une télé simple, une option dans les réglages éviterait bien des bricolages.

articles.title: España no renovará su contrato militar con Palantir y baraja alternativas nacionales como Indra y Telefónica
articles.text:
La geopolítica, en general, es un juego complicado. Sobre todo si aquellos países de cuya influencia quieres alejarte son los únicos que controlan una tecnología básica para armar a tus ejércitos. El Ministerio de Defensa de España lo comprobó cuando quiso romper sus vínculos militares con Israel, y ahora lo vuelve a poner en práctica no renovando un contrato de inteligencia militar con el programa Gotham de Palantir, según adelantaba La Vanguardia.
El movimiento se enmarca en la intención del Gobierno de conseguir mayor soberanía nacional en un ámbito tan sensible como Defensa. Sobre el papel suena bien, pero llevarlo a un centro de inteligencia militar es otra historia muy diferente.
Un contrato para Palantir sin concurso. En octubre de 2023, el Ministerio de Defensa firmó un contrato, con el Gobierno en funciones y por procedimiento negociado sin publicidad con Palantir para utilizar la tecnología del programa Gotham en el Centro de Inteligencia de las Fuerzas Armadas. La licitación partió de 16,5 millones de euros y una actualización posterior la subió a 19,5 millones de euros.
Palantir nació en 2003 para ayudar a la inteligencia de EEUU contra el terrorismo, y su principal negocio es vender software de análisis de datos. Según la propia empresa, Gotham "proporciona una cadena de ataque basada en inteligencia artificial".
Una ruptura a cámara lenta. No se puede decir que la ruptura del Gobierno con Palantir nos haya venido de nuevas. Tal y como recogía El Confidencial, a principios de julio, Moncloa pidió a las empresas participadas por la SEPI (Telefónica, Indra, Navantia o Correos) que no firmasen nuevos contratos con Palantir. No hubo un posicionamiento oficial sobre este movimiento pero la orden ya frenó algunos acuerdos de la compañía estadounidense con la Guardia Civil y Navantia.
UN VISTAZO A...
Quedaba el contrato que de verdad importaba: el de Defensa. Este compromiso caduca en noviembre, por lo que la vía más sencilla y "diplomática" era simplemente no renovarlo. Gotham es una herramienta muy avanzada, por lo que los jefes del Estado Mayor habrían presionado a Margarita Robles para renovarlo, porque no hay alternativa equivalente.
Dos candidatas que aún no dan la talla. Según recogía La Vanguardia, el plan del Gobierno para sustituir el programa de Palantir pasa por Indra y Telefónica. Indra presentó IndraMind en octubre de 2025 como "un cerebro digital que permite a los sistemas pensar, decidir y anticiparse". Telefónica enseñó en el pasado MWC de Barcelona un puesto de mando y control para emergencias, seguridad y defensa.
Sin embargo, los expertos consideran que esos productos no se acercan al nivel técnico de Palantir. Indra prevé que IndraMind facture 1.000 millones de euros en 2030. En cambio, Palantir ingresó 1.935 millones de dólares solo en el segundo trimestre de este año.
El espejo francés y el peso de la OTAN. España no es la primera en dar un paso en esa dirección apostando por un proyecto basado en la soberanía tecnológica propia, Francia ya pasó por esto. El 16 de junio Sébastien Lecornu anunció que su Dirección General de Seguridad Interior (DGSI) cambiaría Palantir por la francesa ChapsVision. Sin embargo, la DGSI había renovado el acuerdo seis meses antes por tres años, y la migración durará hasta dos años. ChapsVision factura unos 200 millones al año.
Tampoco ayuda la OTAN, que compró el Maven Smart System de Palantir en marzo de 2025. Hace unos meses lo elevó a sistema operativo para sus datos militares, con el visto bueno de todos los aliados, España incluida. El Ejército de EEUU firmó un acuerdo de hasta 10.000 millones de dólares.

articles.title: AI operating model: Dell treats company knowledge as its edge - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell sees company knowledge, not AI models, as its competitive edge
As AI agents take on more work that people used to do, enterprises need an AI operating model to match. That means changing how people, processes and work are organized, not just which tools get deployed.
Dell Technologies Inc. has spent close to two years running fully autonomous agents inside its own business, and those lessons now shape its advice to customers. Companies that adopt agents without changing how they are organized accomplish very little, according to John Roese (pictured), global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.
“If you adopt AI technology but are unwilling or unable to change your operating model, you’re going to run your business just like you did before AI, but you’re going to do AI to it,” Roese said. “You’re going to have a bad experience because … if you apply agents to your company, what you are doing is redistributing work between people and machines.”
Roese spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante at the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed why AI agents force companies to rethink their operating models and how enterprises can protect the knowledge that sets them apart. (* Disclosure below.)
Why the AI operating model starts with knowledge
Dell began its own transformation with people and processes rather than technology. The company has pitched its AI Factory as a way to close the gap between AI ambition and outcomes, and internally much of that work starts with knowledge capture. Subject matter experts help encode Dell’s practices into machine-readable skill files that guide how agents behave, Roese explained.
“It manifests as a Markdown file, just this piece of text. But that’s a very special piece of text because it’s a piece of text that other people don’t know about,” he said. “When you add that to the work that an agent is doing, instead of it operating generically, it suddenly operates based on the biases and parameters and rules that we use to differentiate ourselves, whether it’s in writing code or pricing a deal or servicing a customer.”
Those agents also improve as they work, building relationships in knowledge graphs and developing new digital skills. That continuous improvement is why Roese warns against handing proprietary knowledge to third parties. Keeping it in-house is a core part of building an AI operating model that protects what makes a company unique.
“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he said. “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really captured what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

articles.title: Spotify removeu mais de 50 milhões de faixas de IA das recomendações • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Spotify removeu mais de 50 milhões de faixas de IA das recomendações
Plataforma alterou algoritmo para priorizar artistas humanos e diz ter reduzido reclamações de usuários.
O Spotify retirou mais de 50 milhões de faixas classificadas como “AI slop” ou spam das recomendações em 2026. A plataforma também modificou seus sistemas para dar mais espaço a músicas de artistas humanos.
Os números foram divulgados pelo próprio Spotify nesta terça-feira (20/10). A empresa afirma que as mudanças reduziram as reclamações de usuários sobre conteúdos indesejados nas recomendações e diz que já removeu mais de 75 milhões de faixas da plataforma por violações de regras contra spam.
Segundo a empresa, não existe um único indicador capaz de determinar se uma faixa deve ser considerada spam ou AI slop, expressão que descreve conteúdos de baixa qualidade produzidos em massa com inteligência artificial.
O sistema combina sinais como engajamento e avaliações dos ouvintes, padrões de envio de músicas, metadados e informações de diferentes ferramentas de terceiros para detecção de IA. O Spotify reconhece que esses detectores têm limitações e que a identificação tende a ficar mais difícil com a evolução da IA generativa.
A plataforma também procura comportamentos associados a abuso, como uploads em massa, músicas duplicadas, manipulação para mecanismos de busca, redes de playlists usadas para spam e faixas artificialmente curtas. De acordo com o Spotify, os critérios são atualizados conforme novas táticas aparecem.
As mudanças fazem parte de um conjunto maior de medidas adotadas pelo Spotify para limitar spam, fraude e conteúdos enganosos. A empresa afirma que mais de 300 mil artistas já receberam o selo Verified by Spotify. Eles representam mais de 99% dos artistas pesquisados pelos usuários, e mais de 70% são independentes.
O Spotify também passou a identificar milhares de perfis classificados como “AI Personas”, nos quais a identidade do artista é gerada por IA. Esses perfis ficam fora das recomendações editoriais e algorítmicas por padrão, a menos que haja uma ação do usuário, como seguir o perfil.
As medidas dão continuidade às políticas anunciadas pelo Spotify em 2025 contra spam, imitação de voz e uso pouco transparente de IA. A plataforma também mantém, desde 2024, um limite de mil reproduções para que uma faixa seja elegível a gerar royalties. Segundo o Spotify, músicas com alta probabilidade de terem sido geradas por IA têm dez vezes mais chances de ficar abaixo desse limite.

articles.title: ChatGPT's Chrome extension can now control tabs, download files, and fill out forms
articles.text:
In a nutshell: OpenAI has released a major update to its ChatGPT browser extension, bringing deeper integration with Google Chrome. The extension can now access content from open webpages, analyze information, and complete tasks directly in the browser. The update also introduces new voice features and support for several additional languages.
ChatGPT's Chrome extension gained the ability to access content from open tabs last July. The latest update introduces two distinct AI modes, Chat and Work, allowing ChatGPT to interact with browser tabs and perform a wide range of tasks, including filling out online forms using information from documents stored on the device.
In Chat mode, the AI can read content from open tabs to analyze information and answer questions based on the active page context. For example, users can compare prices, delivery times, return policies, and other factors for products listed across different shopping sites.
In Work mode, ChatGPT can control the browser to send messages, download files, and group open tabs by topic. It can also fill out forms using information gathered online or extracted from files stored on the computer. Once a form is completed, users can review it manually before submitting it.
 – ChatGPT (@ChatGPT) October 15, 2026
Users can also tag ChatGPT with "@Chrome" directly in the ChatGPT app or on the website to perform browser tasks without opening the extension's side panel. Additionally, ChatGPT can now be restricted to specific tabs, preventing it from accessing other open pages.
Another new feature is a dedicated ChatGPT tab in Chrome that contains the user's ChatGPT history. Users can ask questions in Chat mode or perform tasks in Work mode from this tab. When accessing chat history or visiting new websites, ChatGPT will ask for permission, allowing users to choose between "allow once," "allow for this site," "allow for all sites," and "decline."
The new features are available for free in several Chromium-based browsers, including Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, and Vivaldi. However, they will not be immediately available in Firefox or Safari. The updated extension can be downloaded from the Chrome Web Store.
OpenAI originally integrated ChatGPT into Chrome last July, allowing users to access several AI features through the extension's Side Chat panel. The update enabled ChatGPT to summarize articles, explain complicated content in simple English, answer questions about YouTube videos, and translate text from a wide range of supported languages.
While OpenAI continues to improve ChatGPT's support for third-party browsers, its own Atlas browser, which debuted last year with ChatGPT integration, was retired in August after failing to capture a substantial share of the browser market from established competitors such as Chrome, Safari, Edge, and Firefox.

articles.title: Carriers ask CRTC to scrap several consumer protections
articles.text:
The Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) is currently looking at ways to harmonize and improve the various consumer protection codes governing wireless and internet services. But some of Canada’s largest carriers are using the process to push for changes that could hurt consumers in the long run.
In interventions filed in mid-August and reviewed by MobileSyrup, Rogers, Bell, and Telus responded to various proposed changes to the Wireless and Internet codes, and added their own requests as well. However, some of the proposed alterations would see existing consumer protections gutted or removed. Proposals include removing caps on roaming overage charges, bringing back phone locking, extending financing terms, and more. We highlight some of the biggest ones below:
Clawbacks for sign-up benefits
Telus stood alone with this one. It suggested to the CRTC that economic inducements, such as “gift cards, retail
credits, promotional gifts, discounts or other financial benefits,” should be paid back if customers cancel early:
“These should all be treated consistently: regardless of form, if a customer receives a financial benefit in exchange for a term service commitment, early cancellation should trigger an obligation to repay the unamortized portion of that benefit.”
Further, Telus suggested that the CRTC should lump these economic inducements in with device subsidies in the Wireless Code. Specifically, Telus said it should “replace ‘subsidized device’ with the more inclusive and technologically-neutral term ‘economic inducement'” to “reflect modern retail realities.”
Removing roaming caps
Telus and Rogers both proposed changes to roaming fees, though with some subtle differences. Telus asked the CRTC to eliminate the $100 roaming cap entirely, while Rogers suggested limiting the cap to pay-per-use roaming. Rogers also asked the CRTC to remove the $50 roaming usage notification.
Notably, roaming costs are quite expensive, and these caps were introduced to prevent bill shock from people inadvertently racking up hundreds of dollars in roaming charges. With roaming being something of a cash cow for carriers, it’s hardly a surprise to see them advocate for removing caps.
Phone locking
Rogers, Bell, and Telus all proposed that the CRTC add a 60-day phone-locking rule instead of the current rules that prohibit locking phones entirely.
Phone locking, as a reminder, locks phones to a carrier’s network, preventing use on other networks. For context, the CRTC banned locking phones back in 2017 and eliminated unlocking fees, which enabled Canadians to more easily switch between carriers.
The phone locking push shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to anyone who’s been following Canadian telecom. Both Bell and Telus have previously called on the CRTC to change its stance on locking phones over theft concerns, with both carriers pushing ahead with implementing 60-day locks despite rules prohibiting the practice. Telus also previously claimed Bell’s 60-day phone lock made its unlocked phones a bigger target for theft.
Extended financing periods
Another request made by all three providers was to extend device financing beyond the current 24-month limit. Rogers, Bell, and Telus all argued that customers are seeking longer financing terms because of factors like rising device costs and improved durability.
Rogers wrote that the 24-month limit “has a direct impact on affordability for consumers” by restricting carriers’ ability to spread the cost of a device over a longer period. Further, Rogers noted that because “device durability and functionality has improved, many consumers are retaining their devices for longer and are therefore interested in options that would allow longer-term financing.”
On one hand, I actually kind of agree with the carriers on this one, at least to the extent that longer terms should be available for customers who want one. Part of the reasoning behind the 24-month limit was to prevent people from being trapped into lengthy phone contracts, so I think as long as the spirit of that is preserved, I don’t see a major issue with allowing people to choose longer contracts if they want.
At the same time, several providers have come up with ways to work around the 24-month rule. Rogers, Bell, and Telus all offer device return options, which discount the monthly financing costs if customers agree to return their phone or pay the difference after 24 months. Notably, Bell has started offering customers a second 24-month financing term as another way to spread out the cost of phones.
Other suggested changes

articles.title: Microsoft's Bing Wallpaper App Hijacks Desktop Clicks to Promote Bing.com
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 20th 2026
Microsoft's Bing Wallpaper App Hijacks Desktop Clicks to Promote Bing.com
Microsoft's popular wallpaper application, Bing Wallpaper, has now been transformed into adware, according to a new report by Windows Latest. When a user clicks on an empty area of the desktop—not on any icon or menu—the application redirects them to Bing.com, Microsoft's search engine. Normally, this behavior would not be acceptable and would likely trigger a strong reaction from the community. However, Microsoft has limited this issue to occur only once every 24 hours. Repeated clicks after the initial activation do not open another browser window. Testing has confirmed that this behavior persists after the waiting period, even when Google Chrome is set as the default browser.
Interestingly, Microsoft tested a similar feature in 2025, which included a clearly labeled setting in Bing Wallpaper that allowed a desktop click to open Bing. At that time, the feature could be turned off, but this option is not available in the latest version of the application. Microsoft has removed the ability to disable this feature, meaning that every 24 hours, a desktop click will redirect to Bing.com. This change leaves users with less control over an action that is unrelated to managing wallpaper. The application has also reportedly displayed prompts encouraging users to make Bing their default search engine across installed browsers, even when the default browser is Google Chrome or another non-Microsoft browser.The only way to avoid this random redirect behavior is by choosing a different application to manage desktop wallpapers. For those who still want rotating Bing imagery due to its wide selection of images from around the world, Windows Spotlight is an option to consider. However, a third-party application might be the best choice, as it may only be a matter of time before Microsoft implements something similar in Windows Spotlight as well.

articles.title: Anthropic’s cloud partnerships are getting messy | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic is having trouble securing enough cloud capacity from AWS, Google, and Microsoft, which increasingly see the Claude maker as a competitor rather than a customer, according to an S-1 filing leaked to The Wall Street Journal.
The leaked filing provides more color to the numbers Reuters and the Financial Times reported in late September, including that Anthropic believes it could spend more than $750 billion on cloud contracts, some of which include deals still in negotiation.
And still, that is not enough. Anthropic is leasing its own data centers and working with third-party data center operators. But the firm worries those operators have a “limited operating history,” which could make them less reliable than the hyperscalers.
Anthropic’s enormous spend comes on the back of an $80.7 billion net loss in the first half of the year. The company reported $16.3 billion in revenue during that same time period, with only two customers accounting for about a fifth of sales, according to the WSJ report.
Building on previously reported catastrophic risk disclosures, the filing also warns that Anthropic could be held liable for damages caused by harmful AI behavior to a tune that would exceed available insurance coverage.
Last week, the company told prospective investors that third-quarter revenue alone has now reached $16.8 billion, up 45% from the previous quarter. Anthropic is reportedly targeting a November IPO.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: Just Eat's AI food photos are a disaster — but why are we letting AI invent pictures of things we're paying for?
articles.text:
Just Eat's AI put bacon and eggs in a glass of cola — and it's exposed a much bigger problem with AI
Mmm tasty!
Just Eat has apologized after its new AI service designed to auto-generate images of food items got confused and put an image of bacon and eggs swimming in a glass of cola on the menu for a Northern Ireland restaurant. The restaurant, which offers a range of soda breads, ended up with sausages, bacon and fried eggs floating in pints of fizzy drinks instead of the Irish breakfast sandwiches they were supposed to represent.
These AI-generated images were part of a Just Eat trial for a new AI-powered system. The bacon and egg cola wasn’t the only hilarious image that the trial produced. You can see many other examples on the uknewestfoods Instagram page:
Referring to the AI photos, one Just Eat user on X said, “I swear if my salt and pepper chips come like this I’m going to cause murder”
But while these AI-generated disasters are easy to laugh at, the real problem might be the images that look perfectly believable.
It's the realistic images you need to worry about
Talking to The Independent, a Just Eat spokesperson said, “We've been trialling AI-enhanced images and as with any new technology, it isn't always quite right the first time. We're sorry for any inaccurate images that have been posted. We're in the process of removing them and have paused rolling this out while we further develop the tool to ensure it best serves our partners and customers."
Just Eat isn’t the only food delivery service trialling AI-generated images. Last week DoorDash opened its text-to-order AI agent for testing: you text what you want, it picks the dish and texts back a photo of it. Bloomberg News testers found several errors during testing, including “photos that didn’t match the recommendation”.
The wider question is, why are Just Eat and DoorDash trialling using AI to generate images of food that people are ordering anyway? While obvious mistakes like this are easy to spot, what about the smaller inaccuracies that are easily missed, like a wrong-sized dish or missing topping?
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Michael Bortinger, Director of Marketing and Partnerships at Tastewise, explains: "An image model has no concept of a specific dish. It renders the average of everything labeled 'burger', and better tools just make that average more convincing. There are pages of brand rules for how a logo sits on a cup and nothing at all for what's in the burger."
Is this a good use of AI?
I can understand why using AI could save the time required to take and then upload individual photos of each menu item; however, food images would seem to be a case where accuracy of what you’re ordering is of supreme importance. Outsourcing this job to AI is not only fraught with problems, but surely wouldn't produce a faithful representation of the food anyway.
There are many good uses for AI; I’m just not sure this is ever going to be one of them. AI-generated food photos might make life easier for delivery platforms and restaurants, but it's hard to see what benefit they offer customers if they can't be trusted to show what's actually being sold.
After all, when I’m ordering a bacon sandwich, I want to see a picture of the item I’m actually going to get, not AI’s interpretation of what a bacon sandwich looks like.

articles.title: The UFC comes to Toronto next year, and you'll be able to stream it
articles.text:
The Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) is headed back to the six, as the company has announced that UFC 336 will be held at Scotiabank Arena on Jan. 30.
This marks the first time the company has hosted an event in Toronto since 2024, when UFC 297 saw Dricus Du Plessis face off against Sean Strickland. It will be the UFC’s eighth time in Toronto since 2011, and the 39th in Canada.
As expected, there is no announcement yet on who will be on the card, but I wouldn’t be shocked if Burlington, Ontario native Mike Malott is on it. It will also most likely be filled with Canadians, although there are a lot of rumoured star-studded fights for the card, so be on the lookout for that.
The first of many
Now, let’s shift over to the more important stuff: how you can watch it.
The event will be the first of the new year, and the first under the new Paramount+ deal that the UFC signed earlier this year, which means you can watch the main fight on the streaming platform, no pay-per-view needed.
However, it’s a bit of a confusing setup. Any Fight Night events and preliminary fights will still be on Sportsnet/TVA because of contractual obligations between the two. However, what used to be $69.99 will now be streamable on Paramount+.
Tying in to what I said earlier about who is fighting, it would make sense for this card to be more star-studded than more recent Canadian cards, due to the fact that this would be the first one on Paramount+, and it makes sense business-wise to have this be a highly anticipated numbered card in order to drive memberships.
Tickets for UFC 336 in Toronto will go on sale in a month’s time (Nov. 20), but the good news is the fight will be much easier to watch.

articles.title: US restarts three shut-down nuclear reactors to feed AI data centers — 2.25 GW coming online with backing from Microsoft and Google
articles.text:
US restarts three shut-down nuclear reactors to feed AI data centers — 2.25 GW coming online with backing from Microsoft and Google
Doc Brown would be abuzz and alight with joy.
The current and expected power draw of AI data centers has been the subject of strong discussion, but today, there appears to be some good news. Three U.S. nuclear reactors are being restarted after many years offline, expected to bring 2.25 GW total to the grid. According to a report, the Palisades Nuclear Plant in Michigan, the Crane Clean Energy Center on Three Mile Island (Pennsylvania), and the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa are getting a fresh set of proverbial tires to get rolling again.
The Palisades plant was under active decommissioning, apparently marking this event as the first time a nuclear reactor is being put back to work after dismantling had begun. Despite what sounds like a tough starting point, this plant is the one that's furthest along, as it was loading fuel in August 2026 and is expected to generate 800 MW around March 2027.
Much like the other projects mentioned here, the Holtec Palisades firm running the reactor took a loan from the U.S. Department of Energy. Palisades borrowed from the DoE under the Biden administration's 2024 investment in nuclear energy, while the others were issued under the purview of the Trump administration's 2025 push.
The second reactor is the Crane Clean Energy Center on Pennsylvania's Three Mile Island, repurposing the facility's Unit 1. The project started in 2024, with Constellation Energy saying it would spend $1.6 billion total for the reactor. The firm then took a $1 billion loan from the Department of Energy in 2025. Microsoft is set to be the main customer, with a 20-year contract. This facility is projected to bring 835 MW online sometime in 2027.
This facility was famous in 1979 for the partial meltdown of its Unit 2, although mercifully the event had relatively tame environmental consequences. Constellation's ongoing project is restoring and refurbishing Unit 1, which didn't show significant issues until its 2019 decommissioning and has undergone a safety inspection from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. This entity still needs to grant its blessing before the reactor starts loading fuel.
The Duane Arnold Energy Center in Iowa is the third unit being brought back to the grid, in a collaboration between NextEra Energy and Google. The predicted output is 615 MW, with the juice expected to start flowing in 2029. Next Energy CEO John Ketchum stated that the firm was happy with its cooperation contract with Google, as it meant that "none of the costs are being paid by residential customers in Iowa."
All three facilities had previously been shut down at various points as they were deemed too expensive to run, as labor and maintenance costs made nuclear-generated watts pricier than alternative means of production.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
But the financial landscape for power has shifted, plus with such overwhelming demand and grid connections being a primary blocker for data center buildouts, their operators are likely willing to pay for premium power as long as they get it now instead of in a few decades.
Some quick browsing indicates that Michigan is going to need somewhere between 1.2 and 2.3 GW for data centers alone around 2030. Pennsylvania's forecast has a wide range of 0.8 to 3.4 GW, while Iowa's range is 1.55 to 2.8 GW. These figures are loose, as they include planned capacity for data center projects that may or may not end up being built, and whose timetables may slip due to economic conditions, hardware availability, and public resistance against expansive buildouts.
