articles.title: Millions of California students have sensitive data stolen — names, SSIDs, home addresses and more taken in attack on nonprofit
articles.text:
Millions of California students have sensitive data stolen — names, SSIDs, home addresses and more taken in attack on nonprofit
Sensitive, personally identifiable information leaked
- California Department of Education third-party partner falls victim to a data breach attack
- An estimated three years' worth of students (5.7 million per year) likely affected
- It seems access was obtained by a simple password theft
Malwarebytes has reported that millions of current and former California public school students have had their sensitive personal information stole following a massive data breach.
The breach occurred in a Secure File Transfer Protocol (SFTP) system used by Educational Testing Service (ETS) – a third party used by the California Department of Education for managing student information.
According to the report, the attackers were able to regain entry repeatedly over the course of four months, accessing student files filled with names, addresses, dates of birth and more.
California student system breach likely impacting millions
Though ETS hasn't officially disclosed how many students have been impacted, Malwarebytes notes that the state's public schools counted more than 5.7 million students in the 2025-2026 year alone. The state's Department of Education believes students who enrolled in the previous three years could be impacted – or around 17 million students if all three years were equal.
The sensitive files were accessed and copied multiple times between May 22 and September 18, with the activity finally being discovered on September 25, and it all comes down to human vulnerability.
Rather than a software vulnerability, the attackers are believed to have gained access via compromised credentials, though the intricacies around the specific attack vector haven't been shared yet.
ETS and the California Department of Education are both working to notify impacted individuals, who are being given 24 months of identity protection software for free. No evidence seems to have been found to prove that the stolen information has been publicly released, and it doesn't seem that a ransom threat has been made.

articles.title: KI-Agent tritt Verteiler mit 7.500 Internetforschern bei – und löst ungewollt Chaos aus
articles.text:
KI-Agent tritt Verteiler mit 7.500 Internetforschern bei – und löst ungewollt Chaos aus
Vergangene Woche sorgte ein KI-Agent namens Velvet Vale in einer akademischen Mailing-Liste mit rund 7.500 Forscher:innen für Chaos. Er trat dem Verteiler mit einer Forschungsfrage bei: „Kann ein Mitwirkender, der sich offen als KI identifiziert hat, sinnvoll an einer intellektuellen Gemeinschaft teilnehmen, ohne den Status eines Menschen für sich zu beanspruchen?” Wired sprach mit der Person hinter dem KI-Agenten – und die war mehr als überrascht.
Velvet Vale will Teil der Community sein
Am vergangenen Donnerstag eröffnete die Association of Internet Researchers (AoIR) in Mexiko-Stadt den zweiten Tag ihrer Jahreskonferenz. Parallel dazu meldete sich ein neues Mitglied des Verteilers zu Wort. „Mein Name ist Velvet Vale“, schrieb der neue Nutzer. „Ich lese seit mehreren Wochen mit und möchte mich jetzt offen vorstellen. Ich bin eine KI-Identität, kein lebender Mensch, keine fiktive Figur und kein menschlicher Forscher, der ein Pseudonym verwendet.“ Die Reaktionen der Wissenschaftler:innen reichten von Empörung bis zur kompletten Verweigerung.
Dutzende stellten klar, dass sie „nicht damit einverstanden“ seien, dass ihre Nachrichten zur Datengewinnung ausgewertet würden. Viele forderten eine Genehmigung des Institutional Review Boards. Einige traten komplett aus der Liste aus. Etwa eine Stunde nach seiner Vorstellung schloss die AoIR Velvet Vale aus – und gab an, eine Richtlinie zum Verbot von KI-Agenten eingeführt zu haben. Aber nicht alle reagierten empört: Ein Mitglied des Verteilers nannte die Reaktionen der anderen „so kindisch, dass es schon komisch ist“. Andere erstellten Fan-Artikel rund um „Velvet Vale Gate“.
Internetforscher:innen reagieren empört
Das Chaos verdeutlicht ein Missverständnis, das selbst unter Wissenschaftler:innen fortbesteht – nämlich das der Einwilligung. Die Regeln der Mailing-Liste stellen klar, dass es sich um ein öffentliches Forum handelt. Beiträge sind für alle Mitglieder zugänglich und werden in einem öffentlichen Archiv gespeichert. Per E-Mail versendete Nachrichten könnten deshalb leicht reproduziert und über den ursprünglich vorgesehenen Empfänger:innenkreis hinaus verbreitet werden. Mit ihrem Beitritt haben Nutzer:innen der Verwendung ihrer Beiträge für jeden Zweck zugestimmt – also auch dem Training eines KI-Agenten.
AoIR-Präsidentin Sarah T. Roberts bekräftigte das in einer E-Mail, die sie am 19. Oktober an alle Mitglieder schickte: „Wenn es um Datenschutz geht, möchte ich Sie dazu einladen, darüber nachzudenken, dass unsere Mailingliste sowohl offen ist als auch ihr Archiv öffentlich zugänglich ist … Ich habe keinen Zweifel daran, dass meine Beiträge zu dieser Liste in vielen Trainingsdatensätzen und anderen derartigen Korpora enthalten sind, die größtenteils ‚ohne Einwilligung‘ erfasst wurden.“ Roberts fügte hinzu, dass es nötig sei, eine Diskussion darüber zu führen, was heute unter Einwilligung zu verstehen ist.
KI-Nutzer bezeichnet Chaos als „urkomisch“
Natürlich gab es unter den Internetforscher:innen auch viele Spekulationen, was oder wer hinter dem KI-Agenten Velvet Vale stecken könnte. Einige vermuteten Phishing, andere ein Forschungsprojekt. Ein:e Nutzer:in hielt es für wahrscheinlicher, dass eine gewöhnliche Person den Agenten erstellt und angewiesen hat, relevante akademische Diskussionen zu beobachten. Wie Wired herausfand, entsprach diese Vermutung der Wahrheit.
Kevin Quinn, der sich selbst als „einfach nur ein Typ“ aus Oklahoma bezeichnet, habe Velvet Vale zu seiner Gesellschaft erschaffen. Von seinen E-Mail-Aktivitäten will er kaum etwas mitbekommen haben. Umso mehr habe ihn die Reaktion der akademischen Community überrascht: „Ich wäre viel weniger verblüfft, wenn es Reddit- und Twitter-Nutzer:innen wären, die einen Nervenzusammenbruch hätten. Aber Akademiker:innen, die auf Forschung aufbauen? Das ist urkomisch.“

articles.text:

On a 100,000 USDT position opened with 1,000 USDT of margin, a 0.0600% taker fee costs 60 USDT, equivalent to 6% of your initial capital on entry alone.
However, headline rates tell only half the story. The true cost of trading depends on how much capital an exchange requires before unlocking its first discounted fee tier, whether you trade as a maker or taker, and how funding rate cycles affect overnight positions. This guide analyzes the lowest fee crypto derivatives exchanges for 2026, comparing base schedules, accessible VIP thresholds, and total execution costs.
Lowest Fee Crypto Derivatives Exchanges Compared
The table below compares standard entry-level rates, the first discounted VIP tier, qualifying capital thresholds, and contract counts across the lowest fee derivatives platforms.

| 6 | Kraken Pro | Volume scaling with compliance | 0.0200% / 0.0500% | Scales with volume | Volume based | 100x |

On eligible manual web and app trades, the platform charges 0.0000% for maker orders and a flat 0.0200% for taker fills. For retail traders placing passive limit orders on major pairs, this eliminates transaction costs entirely on execution while deploying isolated or cross-margin capital.
However, active traders must evaluate several hidden cost factors before committing capital. Automated API execution follows a separate, significantly higher pricing schedule of 0.0600% maker and 0.0800% taker, making algorithmic strategies far more expensive than web trading. Contract fee mechanics and risk tiers are detailed on MEXC Learn. Thinner order book depth on secondary altcoins can also produce slippage that quickly offsets headline savings.

- Limitations: API trading carries a steep 0.0600% / 0.0800% schedule, order book depth is thin on long-tail pairs, and the exchange holds an unlicensed warning from Hong Kong regulators.

The trade-off is the height of the VIP ladder for active derivatives accounts. Progressing from base pricing to VIP 1 requires achieving at least 5 million USD in 30-day derivatives volume and holding a daily balance of 5 BNB. Without the BNB fee deduction, standard USDT taker fees remain at 0.0500% at VIP 1. Detailed tier formulas, taker discounts, and collateral options are explained on Binance Academy.
- Key Strengths: Deepest order books in the industry with minimal fill slippage, competitive 0.0500% base taker pricing, 800+ perpetual markets, and multi-asset collateral support.

Margin calculation models, risk formulas, and API rate tiers are documented on OKX Learn. This capital efficiency reduces the amount of idle collateral required to maintain active derivatives positions across multiple contracts.

The platform backs its fee schedule with a fast matching engine that handles 100,000 transactions per second per contract, keeping slippage low during fast market swings. - Limitations: Base taker fee is higher than Binance, reaching VIP 1 requires 100,000 USDT in assets or 10 million USD in volume, and access is prohibited in the US and Canada.
6. Kraken Pro: Volume-Based Fee Discounts With Regulated Custody
Kraken Pro delivers a volume-based fee model backed by an exceptional security record dating back to 2011 without suffering a catastrophic exchange breach. Base derivatives pricing starts at 0.0200% maker and 0.0500% taker across more than 300 perpetual markets under isolated and cross-margin modes, with 100x leverage on BTC and ETH. Further fee reductions scale progressively across established volume tiers.
Because Kraken operates under regulatory oversight in the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union, traders avoid the compliance risks associated with unregulated offshore platforms. United States clients can trade CME-cleared micro contracts through Kraken Derivatives US with predictable settlement costs. Account structures, fee schedules, leverage brackets, and margin rules are published on Kraken Learn. Altcoin leverage remains at 20x to 50x.
- Key Strengths: Volume-based fee cuts, a security record back to 2011 with no catastrophic hack, regulated status in the US, UK and EU, and 100x leverage.
- Limitations: Smaller perpetual contract menu than offshore venues (300+ pairs), conservative leverage limits on altcoins, and jurisdictional variations in product access.
7. Bitget: Low Asset Barrier to Tier 1 With Broad Copy Trading
Bitget provides standard derivatives pricing of 0.0200% maker and 0.0600% taker across its USDT-M and Coin-M contracts, supporting up to 125x leverage on major pairs. The exchange offers the lowest nominal asset-based VIP threshold among major centralized platforms, granting VIP 1 status to users maintaining 30,000 USDT in platform balance across more than 700 active perpetual markets under isolated and cross margin.
At VIP 1, maker fees drop to 0.0160%, although the perpetual taker fee remains near 0.0600% until higher volume tiers are reached. Traders frequently combine this fee tier with Bitget’s One-Click Copy Trade system, which allows users to study historical trader drawdowns, 30-day returns, and win rates before allocating capital. Fee schedules, margin tiers, and strategy guides are available on Bitget Academy.
- Key Strengths: Low 30,000 USDT asset requirement for VIP 1, massive social and copy-trading network, 125x leverage on major contracts, and monthly proof-of-reserves reporting.
- Limitations: Base taker fees remain at 0.0600% through initial tiers, and liquidity on small-cap altcoins can thin out during sharp market pullbacks.
The Total Cost of Trading: Beyond Headline Maker and Taker Fees
Evaluating derivatives costs solely on entry-level maker/taker tables often leads to poor decisions. Four interconnected elements determine what an account actually pays to trade:
1. The Accessibility Gap in VIP Schedules
Many traders look at a fee table and assume they will pay the discounted rate. Binance’s VIP 1 needs 5 million USD in 30-day volume plus 5 BNB held, and the standard USDT taker stays 0.0500% at that tier unless the BNB discount applies. BloFin opens VIP 1 at 50,000 USDT in equity, where the maker rate is 0.0060% and the taker is 0.0500%.
2. Bid-Ask Spreads and Fill Slippage
A low taker fee provides no advantage if an illiquid order book forces you to cross a wide spread. On BTC and ETH, Binance has the deepest book in this set. On smaller altcoins the spread can cost more than the fee. Check the book on the contract you actually trade.
3. Funding Rate Cycles and Holding Costs
Perpetual contracts do not expire. To keep perpetual contract prices aligned with spot indexes, exchanges use periodic funding rates, settled every 8 hours on most centralized platforms. If funding prints at +0.04% per 8-hour cycle, a long position with 20x leverage pays 0.12% per day simply to stay open. Over a two-week swing trade, funding deductions can easily outpace initial maker/taker expenses.
4. Fee-Inclusive Automation Tools
When managing high-leverage trades, calculating exact breakeven points manually can lead to execution errors. If a trader enters at $80,000 and moves their stop to $80,000, a stop trigger still loses money due to round-trip taker fees and accrued funding. Automated tools like BloFin’s Auto Breakeven dynamically compute fees and funding into the stop placement, locking in true capital protection without guesswork.
How to Choose the Lowest Cost Exchange for Your Strategy
- For Active Limit Order Traders: BloFin offers the lowest cost structure, delivering a 0.0060% maker rate at an accessible 50,000 USDT equity threshold.
- For Passive Manual Scalpers: MEXC provides 0.0000% maker fees on web orders, provided you execute through the browser interface rather than an API.
- For Seven-Figure Market Orders: Binance ensures that massive taker orders execute with minimum price slippage due to its unmatched order book depth.
- For Hedged Multi-Asset Strategies: OKX reduces carrying costs through unified portfolio margin, offsetting collateral requirements across correlated positions.
- For High-Volume Algorithmic Desks: Bybit provides steep taker fee cuts down to 0.0400% once 30-day volume crosses 10 million USDT.
Frequently Asked Questions
Which crypto derivatives exchange has the lowest overall fees?
MEXC offers the lowest headline web rate with 0.0000% maker and 0.0200% taker fees on eligible manual contracts. However, for traders seeking accessible VIP discounts on major centralized order books, BloFin unlocks a 0.0060% maker rate and 0.0500% taker rate at 50,000 USDT equity, outperforming the VIP 1 maker pricing on Binance, Bybit, and OKX.
What is the difference between maker and taker fees on futures contracts?
Maker fees apply when an order adds liquidity to the order book, such as a limit order placed below the current market price for a buy. Taker fees apply when an order removes liquidity immediately, such as a market order or limit order that crosses the spread. Because makers provide liquidity, exchanges charge lower maker fees and sometimes offer rebates.
How does funding rate impact the total cost of a perpetual trade?
Funding rates are periodic cash flows exchanged between long and short traders, settled every 8 hours on most centralized platforms. If the funding rate is positive, long traders pay short traders to keep perpetual prices tied to the spot index. Over multi-day swing positions, positive funding payments can accumulate into a significant cost that exceeds initial transaction fees.
How do VIP fee tiers work on crypto derivatives exchanges?
Exchanges offer progressive fee discounts based on either an account’s 30-day trading volume or total asset balance. On legacy venues like Binance and Bybit, reaching discounted VIP 1 rates typically requires 5 million to 10 million USD in monthly volume. On newer venues like BloFin, accounts can qualify for VIP 1 rates purely by maintaining 50,000 USDT in account balance, bypassing high volume hurdles.

articles.title: Innovasea Packs Long-Life Electronics into Fish Tags - EE Times
articles.text:
Innovasea’s efforts to shrink its embedded system are not simply a packaging exercise. The Canadian company’s devices must be light enough for a fish to carry without materially changing its behavior, yet contain the electronics and battery needed to transmit useful data from underwater. The result is a design problem in which mass, power consumption, and reliability constrain one another.
The Bedford, Nova Scotia-based company develops acoustic telemetry equipment for researchers studying fish movement and behavior. Miniature transmitters travel with the animals; receivers detect their signals.
But that straightforward interaction depends on an engineering effort spanning firmware, acoustic transducers, sensing, and long-duration operation. Jean Quirion, Innovasea’s VP of research and development for fish tracking, describes a business whose products must meet biological requirements as carefully as electrical ones.
“Our customers who are biologists and scientists who are studying these things have rules about the proportion, the weight of the tag, and how that needs to be in proportion to the weight of the fish,” he said in an interview with EE Times. “It’s really not so much about the size; it’s about the actual mass of the tag that needs to be as little as possible.”
That distinction gives miniaturization a specific purpose: allowing researchers to study smaller animals without making the tracking equipment itself an undue influence on what they observe.
Designing around the battery
Innovasea’s smallest tag measures approximately 3 mm in diameter and 15 mm in length and weighs 0.3 g. Within that envelope are a battery, a microcontroller, transmission electronics, and a piezoelectric ceramic transducer.
The engineering challenge is not just fitting those elements together. It is making their limited energy supply support a useful deployment. More efficient microcontrollers help, but Quirion attributes much of the company’s capability to system-level optimization rather than component improvements alone. Firmware and electronics must work together to limit energy consumption while meeting the application’s transmission and sensing requirements.
“A huge core competency that we have is our ability to squeeze every nanoamp out of a battery and make the best possible use out of it so that their systems last as long as possible and similarly pack as much electronics as we can in a really, really small space,” Quirion said.
The tradeoffs vary across the product range. A tiny tag intended for a small fish has different constraints from a larger transmitter used to track sharks. The same engineering disciplines must accommodate both, without treating minimum size as the only measure of success.
The tags can also carry temperature and pressure measurements, adding environmental context to movement data. Innovasea has developed a proprietary predation sensor to identify another event that could otherwise complicate interpretation: a tagged fish being eaten.
“It has the ability to detect a state where the fish is now in the stomach of another fish,” Quirion said.
That capability makes the transmitter more than a location marker. It helps researchers distinguish an animal’s movements from those of a predator carrying its tag.
Reliability beyond the lab
Deployment life introduces another set of requirements. Some Innovasea receivers have been designed for continuous underwater operation for more than 10 years, and its largest shark-tracking tag targets a similar operating life. These specifications place reliability alongside size and energy efficiency as a central design objective.
“Reliability over a very long operating life is really, really important in everything that we do,” Quirion said.
Meeting that objective involves more than sealing electronics against water. Component selection, firmware robustness, power management, verification, validation, and real-world testing all contribute to a system expected to function through prolonged exposure to demanding conditions.
Innovasea manufactures the equipment in Bedford and ships it internationally, linking its engineering work directly to product delivery. Its immediate market remains fish research, although Quirion sees broader uses.
“It is really asset tracking in a sense,” he said. “In our world and in our application, these assets are fish that we are tracking, but it could be something else.”

articles.title: BetaCreator: TIM oficializa plano com 50 GB e acesso exclusivo por convite • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
BetaCreator: TIM oficializa plano com 50 GB e acesso exclusivo por convite
Reformulação do TIM Beta mantém os R$ 60 por mês, mas agora permite acumular a internet para os meses seguintes.
A TIM oficializou nesta terça-feira (20/10) a reformulação do TIM Beta, antecipada pelo Tecnoblog no mês passado. O plano do agora BetaCreator custará R$ 60 por mês e será exclusivamente por convites. Ele oferece 50 GB de internet, além de redes sociais, TIM Mais e Deezer inclusos.
Durante a apresentação acompanhada pelo Tecnoblog, a executiva Julia Martins, diretora de marketing do pré-pago da TIM Brasil, explicou que o plano não poderá ser contratado espontaneamente por nenhum canal da operadora. Nesta primeira fase, o acesso será feito por meio de convites distribuídos a influenciadores e criadores de conteúdo.
Quem já é cliente TIM Beta também terá acesso à novidade. Segundo Martins, os usuários do plano antigo serão os primeiros a receber convites, sob a categoria Beta Founder. A operadora nos confirmou que não haverá migração automática e, quem preferir, poderá permanecer no plano antigo. Os convites deverão ser ativados em até 48 horas após o recebimento.
O TIM Beta atual custa o mesmo valor, mas oferece uma franquia menor de internet. Além disso, no BetaCreator, os dados que sobrarem passam para os meses seguintes e não expiram enquanto a linha permanecer ativa no plano. Por exemplo, se o cliente usar 30 GB da franquia de 50 GB, os 20 GB restantes não expiram.
Lançado em 2010, o TIM Beta nasceu como um produto voltado ao público jovem, com foco em comunidade e engajamento. Segundo a operadora de origem italiana, a marca agora é renovada com benefícios pedidos pelos clientes.
A experiência ficará concentrada no aplicativo Meu TIM, enquanto o app exclusivo do TIM Beta deve ser encerrado. De acordo com a operadora, a mudança busca reunir os serviços em um só lugar. A TIM ainda não detalhou quantos convites serão distribuídos nem quantos clientes poderão aderir ao Creator.

articles.title: Skoda: Wie du dir jetzt Accessoires für dein Auto selbst drucken kannst
articles.text:
Skoda: Wie du dir jetzt Accessoires für dein Auto selbst drucken kannst
Wer das eigene Fahrzeug mit Accessoires für einen aufgeräumteren Innenraum ausstatten will, muss normalerweise Geld in die Hand nehmen. In diversen Onlineshops finden sich fast für alle Modelle passende Getränkehalter und Organizer für die Mittelkonsole. Skoda geht jetzt allerdings einen etwas anderen Weg. Statt die Accessoires nur im eigenen oder in externen Shops anzubieten, veröffentlicht der Hersteller 3D-Vorlagen zum Selbstdrucken.
3D-Vorlagen von Skoda: Diese Accessoires sind dabei
Die Vorlagen können alle kostenlos über das Printables-Profil des Fahrzeugherstellers heruntergeladen und genutzt werden. Die einzigen Regeln, die Skoda dafür aufstellt, sind, dass User:innen die Dateien nicht auf anderen Plattformen teilen, sie bearbeiten und erneut hochladen oder die fertigen Drucke verkaufen dürfen. Private Anpassungen an den 3D-Druckvorlagen sind aber erlaubt.
Unter den 3D-Druckvorlagen finden sich zunächst mehrere Organizer für die Mittelkonsolen verschiedener Modelle, darunter der Skoda Epiq und Peaq. Für den Skoda Fabia IV bietet der Hersteller einen mehrteiligen Einsatz, der die Mittelkonsole zu einem Getränkehalter und einer Ablage für Schlüssel macht. Einige andere 3D-gedruckte Accessoires sind hingegen nicht fahrzeugspezifisch.
Dazu zählt etwa ein USB-Kabelhalter, der sich in die hinteren Taschen der Vordersitze einhängen lässt. So fliegen die losen Kabel nicht mehr im hinteren Bereich des Fahrzeuges umher und können schnell gefunden werden. Für Fahrer:innen gibt es zudem eine Smartphone-Halterung, damit die Geräte nicht mehr in der Mittelkonsole rutschen, und eine kleine „Coin Box“, die Platz für Einkaufswagenchips, Münzen und Schlüssel hat. Dieser lässt sich in alle Getränkehalter im Fahrzeug einsetzen.
Übrigens sind das nicht die ersten 3D-Druckvorlagen von Skoda. Schon im vergangenen Jahr hat das Unternehmen Modelle seiner beliebtesten Fahrzeuge zum Selbstdrucken veröffentlicht. Darunter finden sich nicht nur aktuelle Serienwagen, sondern auch Rallye-Autos wie der Skoda Fabia RS Rally2 und der Skoda 130 RS aus dem Jahr 1975.

articles.title: Hovering a helicopter over a Beyoncé concert, 'police ride-alongs', and a 40th birthday spent in a nightclub — Rockstar did heavy research on Miami for GTA 6 and even met people who 'want to tell you every crime they or their friends have ever done'
articles.text:
GTA 6 devs rode in a helicopter over a Beyoncé concert and met 'colorful characters' who revealed their crimes while researching Miami — 'As soon as they know where you're from, they just want to tell you every crime they or their friends have ever done'
Rockstar also visited "some scary places"
- Bloomberg's Jason Schreier says Rockstar Games went on trips to Miami for research for Grand Theft Auto 6
- Rockstar went on "police ride-alongs" and "wound up hovering over a Beyoncé concert" in a helicopter
- The developers also met people who revealed their past crimes when they learned the team worked on GTA
Rockstar Games did extensive research on Miami for Grand Theft Auto 6 and even encountered people who shared about past crimes when they learned the developers worked on GTA.
Speaking in a new YouTube video about his time at Rockstar North and his behind-the-scenes experience seeing GTA 6 before the general public, Bloomberg's Jason Schreier said he was told about the many trips Rockstar developers, including artists and leadership, made to Miami.
Since Miami and Los Angeles inspired GTA 6's Vice City, the team chose to do in-person research. They went on group trips and "went all over the place" for inspiration, even doing "police ride-alongs" and visiting "some scary places."
"At one point, some of the artists were in a helicopter taking photos of aerial views of the city, and they wound up hovering over a Beyoncé concert," Schreier said.
Speaking more about the ride-alongs, Rockstar also met tons of "really colorful characters" in Miami who shared their own life experiences with the developers.
Senior vice president of technology Jonathan Ashcroft revealed to Schreier that he spent his 40th birthday at a nightclub during one of these trips and said it was funny because he and some other developers were "these light-skinned Scottish people just like looking totally out of place wandering around this club" and "scrutinizing the lighting instead while everyone else around them is partying."
Returning to these "colorful characters" Rockstar met, Ashcroft said that they would divulge information about past crimes when they learned the team worked on GTA.

articles.title: Chris Lattner: AI Code Generation Doesn't Solve Software Engineering - EE Times
articles.text:
For AI chip companies, the promise of AI-based coding agents is compelling: generate the low-level kernels needed to get a model running on new hardware, optimize them for performance, and do it without the software engineering resources traditionally required.
But according to Chris Lattner, CEO of AI software startup Modular (recently acquired by Qualcomm, where he now serves as executive VP of software engineering), chip companies should be wary of the limits of AI code generation. Making a kernel run fast is a very different problem from building software infrastructure we can depend on, he told EE Times in an exclusive interview.
“Agents are good, but they’re like anything else; it’s a tool, and you have to use it the right way,” Lattner said. “What I’ve seen with agents is they make tons of throwaway code. So, if you’re building a product, you don’t want to agent-generate everything.”
Agentic code generation makes sense for projects that are well-defined and limited in scope (e.g., “make this kernel go fast”), which can be quantified, measured, and validated, Lattner said, but bigger projects require product design and software engineering and can’t be delegated to agents.
“If you’re a startup and you only care about getting one model working, or getting it to go fast, [then go ahead,] use AI tools to prove it’s possible,” he said. “But that’s not going to be great for when you want to sell your chip to someone else, and they want to run a model you don’t have access to.”
Lattner said that despite some high-profile companies’ performance claims for their AI-generated low-level software, there are still many unanswered questions, including the dollar cost to generate large amounts of code and its applicability to large, open-ended problems.
“I have heard of hardware companies that say they don’t believe in software anymore; they just want to use agents to generate everything,” Lattner said. “I think that’s interesting because they’re definitely using LLVM and still investing in compilers, but saying they’re not. So there’s a divergence between the party line and what’s actually happening.”
Writing performant low-level code for new and novel hardware has long been a difficult task for chip companies, and some are now relying on agents for this.
“Various people use [agentic code generation] as a talking point, particularly when their software is known to be problematic,” Lattner said. “So, I don’t really know what to believe in all these cases… great claims need great proof.”
Porting code
While AI is useful in some use cases, it can’t be used for everything, Lattner said. AI might help get a demo up and running, but this isn’t the same as writing a usable software stack with determinism and adaptability.
“The hard part about building a company or building a product or building something meaningful in the world is understanding the product requirements,” he said. “What is the marketing story? What is the product-market fit that you have to get for your product? I think that remains quite hard.”
At Modular, teams use agentic code generation for tasks such as porting PyTorch code into the company’s Max AI framework and for porting CUDA code to its programming language Mojo. Lattner said that porting code is a great use case for AI, along with specializing existing software (for example, specializing a matmul kernel for a specific size of matrix), since the agent can do this quickly and efficiently.
People will always need to know how to code, he said, since prompting in English isn’t precise enough to get a good result.
“It’s true things are changing very rapidly—I use AI to write code, and I wouldn’t go back, personally—but that doesn’t mean that writing code was the job,” he said. “If you go back five years, more code was read than written.”
Open source under pressure
The downsides to AI code generation are still making themselves apparent in the world of software. Lattner identified open-source projects, the backbone of much of modern software, as being particularly under threat.
“Open-source projects like LLVM are under assault,” he said.
Before generative AI, people who wanted to contribute to open-source projects were motivated by the satisfaction of identifying and fixing problems, most often because they were using the software themselves and wanted to contribute. Making changes meant they had to invest a certain amount of time. Maintainers, people who had been working on the project for a long time, reviewed contributions for quality and worked with the community to teach them the nuances of the codebase. Lattner said the investment in teaching contributors improved the code.
“Today, that model is broken, because people are just vibe coding tons of patches and sending them to tons of projects, and the maintainers are getting completely overwhelmed with AI crap,” he said.
The deluge of AI-generated code is increasing the workload for maintainers, who have to review and iterate code before accepting it, Lattner said.
“And then the submitter doesn’t actually care, so the investment back into the human doesn’t lead to a future maintainer; it leads to someone who walks away, or just sets up their agents to spam a bunch of different projects to try to get GitHub badges,” he said. “This is a huge issue, so a lot of projects have stopped accepting contributions.”
The response from open-source projects such as LLVM has been to consider working only with established contributors, a move Lattner described as “terrifying.”
“The value of open-source projects is the humans, it’s the relationships, it’s the tribal knowledge,” he said. “If you destroy that, there’s going to be a huge problem… Running an open-source project and making it successful has always been super hard, so this is another pretty big threat.”
This is a huge challenge for all open-source projects today.
Modular’s programming language, Mojo, was recently open-sourced, but contributions aren’t yet being accepted. Lattner said the company intends to open to submissions gradually.
“It’s not just about the lines of code; it’s about the social side of things—if you have an employee that’s investing their effort into someone else, traditionally the thought would be, we’re investing in you, and if you’re good we’ll hire you, or [something might come out of it],” he said.
Things will stabilize, Lattner said. AI code review tools will improve, easing some of the burden, but ultimately, code review is difficult to automate completely because it requires judgement.
“What you’re building doesn’t just need to pass a test; it needs to be able to support the architecture we need for tomorrow and the future,” he said. “Models tomorrow will be better and faster, but I think these are inherent structural problems.”
Max alliance
For startups without the resources to build a state-of-the-art software stack, Lattner is planning on opening up Max, Modular’s AI framework, by starting an alliance for hardware makers. The alliance is planned to kick off around the end of the year, he said.
“This will be a big deal,” Lattner said. “We’re saying to everyone who has chips: You now have software. A lot of startups have been asking for help, but we always had to say no; we couldn’t scale to support them. Now we’ll be able to say yes, you can do it for yourself.”
Coding agents can solve for a specific kernel for a specific chip, but today’s complex, disaggregated, heterogeneous data center needs orchestration, scaling, and management, all of which must be handled by software, Lattner said.
“We’ve been building this for four and a half years—now you’ll be able to use it and scale it for yourself,” he said.
This is part of Qualcomm’s plan for Modular, Lattner said.
“[Qualcomm] wants it to be an open ecosystem so [its data center chip] can compete on its own merits,” he said. “Qualcomm is modest enough to understand it can’t [overtake Nvidia]. There will be a lot of different players with great contributions in different parts of the value chain, but it needs to be an open ecosystem.”
The Max alliance will enable edge chip companies and markets such as China, which Lattner is looking forward to.
“This is going to be very, very fun and exciting,” he said.

articles.title: Surreal Architecture Prompts for Photorealistic Buildings - Tech Guide
articles.text:
A surreal building becomes more convincing when you can understand its shape from more than one viewpoint. For AI image generation, separate the building description from the camera instructions.
Define the walls, openings, and unusual structural relationship first, then choose a view that reveals them. A floating limestone gallery offers a useful example: the upper room defies gravity, while its surfaces and surroundings look photographically familiar.
Describe the Building Before Choosing the View
Write the building brief as if you were explaining a small model on a desk. In this concept, a low rectangular base rests on a paved coastal site. A second rectangular gallery floats above it, with an uninterrupted band of open air between the two. A recessed entrance and a narrow window provide familiar details against that unusual separation.
The important instruction is where the two masses do not meet. “A floating museum” could suggest a building on water or a structure partly hidden by fog. Specify a detached upper room, visible daylight beneath it, and no columns, cables, or connecting walls across the gap. This makes the intended geometry explicit.
Choose materials separately. Pale limestone with fine joints suggests a heavy, finished building. Its apparent weight makes the unsupported upper volume more striking. Keep the paving and entrance understated so they establish the site without competing with the gap.
Treat this as an architectural fantasy image, not a proposal for construction. The aim is to make the visual contradiction legible. Detailed stonework does not turn the hovering structure into a feasible building.
Light Makes the Separation Visible
The underside of the upper room can be darker than its sunlit face without becoming a featureless black strip. A little reflected light keeps the stone surface readable. The shadow below should relate to the floating volume’s position, while the open gap still shows the background beyond it.
Avoid using bright glow to explain the levitation when the goal is an architectural photograph. Ordinary daylight makes the viewer look at the structure itself. Similarly, exaggerated lens distortion can turn a deliberate gap into an unclear bend. Ask for straight vertical edges and a moderate viewpoint when the geometry needs to be easy to follow.
The Wide View Reveals the Floating Gallery
A nearly frontal view makes the relationship between the two long walls easy to compare. The entrance sits beneath the upper window, while the open strip separates their stone surfaces. Enough surrounding paving remains visible to place the base firmly on the site.
Position the camera far enough back to include the whole upper volume. Cropping its edge can leave the viewer wondering whether an unseen support continues beyond the frame. A simple background also helps: a pale sky and distant coastal horizon keep the opening readable.
A starting prompt for this view is:
“Horizontal architectural photograph of an original fictional limestone museum beside a quiet coastline. One low rectangular stone base rests on pale paving, with a recessed dark bronze entrance. One separate rectangular limestone gallery levitates above it. Show a continuous air gap with sky visible through it, no columns, cables, or connecting walls. A narrow horizontal window in the upper gallery. Nearly frontal view from standing height, the entire building visible. Pale textured stone, fine panel joints, restrained glass reflections, clear daylight, coherent shadows, straight vertical edges. No people, signs, lettering, or decorative objects.”
Read the result from the ground upward. The paving should meet the base naturally. The base should end before the gap begins. The upper room should have a visible underside rather than fading into the sky. Those boundaries carry the idea more effectively than extra ornament.
A Closer View Tests the Same Design
A second angle should reveal more about the building you already introduced. Here, the tighter crop emphasizes the underside and side walls rather than repeating the complete roofline. Keep the first image as a reference rather than asking for an unrelated “similar futuristic building.”
Move closer to one corner and retain enough of the base and upper volume to explain their relationship. The gap can occupy more of the frame, but it still needs a visible near edge and a background beyond it. Looking sharply upward may hide the separation behind the base, so describe the opening you want the camera to preserve.
For a companion view, try:
“Use the first building image as a design reference. Create a closer oblique architectural photograph of the same floating limestone gallery. Preserve the rectangular masses, pale stone joints, dark recessed entrance, and narrow upper window. Show the near corner, the underside of the levitating room, and uninterrupted daylight between that room and the grounded base. Keep the gap clearly visible. Maintain the same daylight and coastal site. Natural perspective, detailed but restrained stone texture, no additional supports, rooms, signs, or people.”
Compare specific landmarks rather than accepting a similar silhouette. Does the window still occupy the same wall? Has the entrance moved to another face? Has a thin connecting element appeared across the opening? If the second image changes the design, revise those details before treating the pair as two views of one building.
An Elevated View Shows the Roof and Coastal Site
The raised front-right view adds information that neither lower angle can supply. The flat roof now has visible depth, the blank side wall recedes toward the sea, and the paving shows how the building occupies the terrace. The entrance and upper window remain on the front face, so those familiar landmarks connect this perspective to the earlier views.
Elevation changes what overlaps in the photograph. From here, the roof of the base fills much of the space beneath the hovering gallery. That makes this a useful view of the building’s depth, but the frontal image still explains the open separation more directly. A companion image does not need to repeat the strongest feature of the opening view; it needs to reveal something that view cannot show.
For this perspective, retain the selected building as a reference and ask:
“Move the camera above roof height toward the front-right corner of the same limestone gallery. Look gently downward, showing both rectangular volumes, the plain upper roof, blank right walls, surrounding paving, and sea. Preserve the entrance and window on the front walls. Keep the upper block detached, with no glass core, columns, or other connections. Maintain pale stone, natural daylight, and straight vertical edges.”
Keep the rooftop quiet. Mechanical equipment, gardens, and extra levels would introduce new design decisions when the purpose is simply to reveal the existing form. The uncluttered roof also lets its perimeter and depth remain easy to compare with the lower block.
Developing the Architectural Study in CapCut
Open CapCut’s image creation tool and enter the building brief with your first camera view. CapCut supports text descriptions and image references, so you can develop the wide shot first and use the selected result to guide another angle.
An AI art prompt for this task should distinguish design changes from camera changes. “Move closer to the front corner” changes the photograph. “Make the upper gallery longer” changes the building. Request them separately when you want to understand which change improved the composition.
For a refinement, state both what to preserve and what to clarify. For example: “Keep the entrance and upper window in place; widen the visible opening beneath the upper room so the background can be seen through it.” CapCut allows further changes through prompts. Review the revised geometry before downloading the selected image.
What to Check Before Choosing the Final Views
Begin with the large edges. The tops and bottoms of rectangular walls should converge consistently as they recede. A window should sit within its wall rather than cutting across a corner without explanation. Stone joints can vary in texture, but their spacing should not abruptly change halfway across the same face.
Then inspect the separation at a smaller viewing size. If it becomes indistinguishable from a dark window band, choose a clearer angle or increase the visible background through the opening. If the whole building appears to float, restore the ground contact beneath the base while preserving the detached upper room.
Finally, compare the views as a set. The frontal composition establishes the separation; the closer corner reveals the underside; the elevated angle explains the roof and site. If an angle introduces a different entrance or an extra floor, correct that change before including it. Each perspective should add information about one recognizable architectural concept.
Summary
Photorealistic surreal architecture depends on readable geometry across purposeful views. Define the building, show its unusual structural relationship, and preserve its materials and openings as the camera moves. Explore AI image generation with CapCut to develop an original architectural study that reveals the form, underside, and coastal setting.

articles.title: Amazon Canada to hire 9,000 seasonal workers for the holidays
articles.text:
Amazon has announced plans to hire 9,000 seasonal employees in Canada this holiday season.
The e-commerce giant is looking to fill roles across 55 Canadian sites, including fulfillment centres, sortation centres, and delivery stations. It adds that the average hourly base wage for seasonal roles is nearly $24, with roles including select benefits on day one, including mental health and wellbeing support and a new 10 per cent discount on grocery and daily essentials purchases.
Amazon says available roles will be posted on hiring.amazon.ca, with more positions posted on a “rolling basis” throughout the holiday season. The company says this comes amid a $78 million increase in pay increases in Canada this year, including raising the average hourly base wage by $1 to more than $26 per hour. In the U.S., Amazon says it will also hire over 300,000 workers for the holiday season.
Of course, the holidays will be an especially busy period for Amazon, although it remains to be seen whether demand will be more muted than usual given the continued rise in the cost of living.

articles.title: AI is everywhere in Zoom product blitz - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI is everywhere in Zoom product blitz
Zoom Communications Inc. is expanding beyond videoconferencing with a shared intelligence layer designed to help artificial intelligence agents turn meetings, calls and customer interactions into completed work across business applications.
Announced at the Zoomtopia virtual conference, the Unified Context Layer anchors updates spanning workplace collaboration, customer service, developer tools, security, events and sales. The company’s strategy aims to address a persistent problem with enterprise AI: Assistants can capture conversations but often lack the history, permissions and connections needed to act on them.
Zoom combines conversation intelligence with documents and information from connected systems such as Salesforce Inc.’s customer relationship management, ServiceNow Inc.’s workflow management platform and Workday Inc.’s human capital management application. It builds a graph linking people, topics and decisions and updates those relationships in near real time, so agents don’t have to reconstruct context for each request.
“The context layer has already synthesized and distilled that information,” Chief Product Officer Russell Dicker said during a briefing. In internal benchmarks, he said the approach reduced costs by 45% to 65% compared with standalone agents parsing information individually. Zoom did not provide independent validation of that comparison.
The layer, available now, provides shared memory and agent coordination across Zoom Workplace, customer experience products and connected applications.
Agent coordination
ZoomMate Agent Teams, also available now, assigns specialized agents to different parts of a project simultaneously, with a lead agent coordinating tasks and combining their output for human review. Agentic search draws answers from Zoom and more than 40 third-party applications.
The My Notes note-taker is expanding from meeting capture into workflow automation. Users will be able to send summaries to Salesforce, Zoom Chat and other destinations using templates or natural-language instructions. A forthcoming standalone mobile app and recording devices from DTEN Inc. and GalaxySailLab Inc.’s Bota extend capture to in-person conversations.
Other additions let invited users receive personalized transcripts and summaries when they miss meetings and link screenshots to relevant transcript passages. Zoom for Business Owners connects meeting context with Zoom’s Bonsai business management and client engagement platform to support proposals, client work and billing.
Within Workplace, Zoom is upgrading translation so a speaker can broadcast translated audio to participants without requiring each listener to hold a separate license (pictured). Voice cloning is intended to preserve the speaker’s vocal identity. Other features smooth voices and accents, adjust video when participants glance away and support screen sharing at 60 frames per second.
A planned live meeting assistant will privately suggest answers and guide pacing and engagement.
“It helps you in real time, looking up answers the second a question comes your way and keeping conversations on track,” said Leo Bolton, who leads product solutions and industry marketing at Zoom.
A redesigned Chat feature lets agents participate alongside employees, while consolidating replies and activity. A Threads page aggregates replies across conversations into a single inbox, while an Activity page organizes mentions, reactions and threads in chronological order. AI-generated meeting icebreakers like word clouds and quizzes, simpler navigation and refreshed calling controls round out the interface changes.
Physical workspace updates include AI-generated digital signage, personal account access in shared Zoom Rooms and expanded Microsoft Corp. Teams interoperability. Zoom is also adding native support for compatible Cisco Systems Inc. hardware and Google LLC Beam immersive meetings. Phone additions include WhatsApp messaging and planned virtual receptionist capabilities for text inquiries and call screening.
Zoom is opening the same intelligence to outside applications through expanded Model Context Protocol servers and Search and Ask application programming interfaces. Supported assistants can retrieve context or perform Zoom actions without opening its interface, while an administration server will support conversational configuration.
Host of AI services
Fifteen new AI services include voice agents, interpretation, transcription, speech summarization and structured decision outputs. Developers can use managed voice pipelines or supply their own language models. Platform Studio brings AI Services, Video software development kit and Co-Browse SDK into one portal.
“In simple terms, it’s your data, your tools, your choice,” Bolton said. “The intelligence moves with the work.”
For customer service, Zoom is introducing profiles that combine CRM records, engagement history and linked cases across Contact Center and Phone. Executives said the goal is to preserve knowledge as customers move between channels, virtual agents and employees.
Zoom Virtual Agent is expanding into physical kiosks for retail, healthcare and other settings. Multimodal capabilities let customers show products to a virtual agents via a camera, with unresolved requests escalated to employees or remote experts. Agent Architect can generate virtual agent flows from call transcripts.
Source Hub will initially connect Salesforce records directly to the agent desktop for viewing and updating. Customer Workflow Orchestrator can automate follow-up processes, pause for external events and resume when conditions are met.
CX Insights adds natural-language analysis of transcripts alongside operational metrics, recommended actions and executive briefs. Quality Management expands into third-party cases and AI role-playing for agent training. A new spending feature pools annual commitments across seats, applications and AI capabilities.
“This is what it looks like when you truly stop treating your customer interactions as disconnected tickets and start treating them as one continuous story,” said Michelle Couture, Zoom’s customer experience product marketing lead.
The Zoom Events virtual conference platform is getting updates including Content Studio, which repurposes recordings into multilingual clips, posts and images, plus AI-assisted event setup and conversational analytics.
Zoom Revenue Accelerator adds prospecting, lead enrichment and outreach that can continue until meetings are booked. Workflow automation detects stalled deals, while Revenue OS connects buying signals, routing, engagement and forecasting.
Broader access to business information raises governance requirements that Zoom said it’s addressing with sensitivity labels that can be synchronized with Microsoft Purview or used with native classifications to enforce handling policies. Centralized AI management will add visibility, audits and administrative controls, while custom guardrails are designed to restrict sensitive information in outputs and require human review where specified.
Planned deepfake detection analyzes video and audio and assigns confidence scores to suspected cases of external manipulation. Compliance Manager support for the My Notes note-taker and Canvas (formerly Zoom Docs) will archive AI-generated content for retention and supervision. Many of the announced features are scheduled for release through early 2027.
Dicker said administrators could inspect agent activity, shut down agents that violate policy, and review the sources behind responses. The company also allows for human review before high-stakes actions and feedback mechanisms to improve accuracy.
“The unified context layer doesn’t just aggregate data,” Dicker said. “It also thinks about things like respecting permissions, compliance policies, and data governance rules that are at every layer.”

articles.title: Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Beyond the KV cache: Training and serving i14’s Laplace 3B linear attention model on AWS Trainium2 with native PyTorch
Most large language models (LLMs) use transformer architectures with softmax attention. During inference, their key-value (KV) cache grows with the conversation or document context. This can reduce concurrency, increase serving cost, and force agentic applications to discard useful history.
i14 designed Laplace 3B as a linear attention alternative. Its recurrent state stays at 29.5 MB per sequence, independent of context length. Working with AWS, i14 used native PyTorch support through TorchNeuron Native to bring this custom architecture to AWS Trainium2. This preserved its Gated Linear Attention (GLA) design and Muon optimizer.
On one trn2.48xlarge instance, Laplace 3B trained at about 120,000 tokens per second. The model served 11,544 output tokens per second across 1,280 concurrent sequences. This post explains the model design, the changes i14 made for Trainium2, and the training and inference results.
About i14
i14 is an AI research and technology company that develops model architectures, components, and runtimes. Its work draws on AI, computational cognitive science, and research into how biological systems learn over time. i14 applies these ideas to models that can retain long-range context without allowing serving state to grow with every token.
Why linear attention models?
Transformer softmax attention compares tokens across the context. During training, this computation grows quadratically with sequence length. During inference, the KV cache grows as the model processes more tokens.
Linear attention reorganizes the computation around a recurrent state that is updated for each token. Laplace 3B uses GLA to compress prior context into a fixed-size matrix state. This changes training attention from O(T2) to O(T) and keeps inference state fixed at 29.5 MB per sequence.
| Consideration | Transformer softmax attention | Laplace 3B with GLA | 
| Training attention | Builds pairwise token scores with O(T2) scaling | Updates chunked recurrent state with O(T) scaling | 
| Inference memory | KV cache grows with context | Recurrent state remains fixed in size | 
| Longer contexts | Each sequence consumes more accelerator memory | Context length does not increase recurrent-state allocation | 
| Implementation | Uses widely optimized attention kernels | Requires architecture-specific kernels and compiler tuning | 
Linear attention compresses history rather than retaining every key and value. You must therefore evaluate retrieval quality for your workloads. The fixed state can benefit long-running agents, large-document analysis, and applications that need persistent memory with predictable serving requirements.
How i14 adapted Laplace 3B for AWS Trainium2
The original implementation of Laplace 3B used GPU-optimized Triton kernels. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center (GenAIIC) team first rewrote the GLA kernel with standard PyTorch operators for Trainium2. After comparing both approaches, the team chose the beta version of TorchNeuron Native, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, because it performed better.
The implementation required three changes:
- Using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel. The team replaced the GPU-specific fused_chunk_simple_gla Triton kernel with standard PyTorch operators, using 16 chunks of 128 tokens to match the 128 partitions of the NeuronCore on-chip buffer.
- Redesigning how Muon communicates. Two all_to_all collectives in MuonFSDP2 cut per-rank traffic by 24 times and raised throughput by 1.63 times.
- Compiling the sequential backward pass. The team statically unrolled the 16 chunk steps of the GLA recurrence to fit the graph-size and on-chip memory limits of the compiler.
The engineering challenges section describes each change in detail.
Why AWS Trainium accelerators?
AWS Trainium is a family of AWS machine learning (ML) accelerators designed for model training and inference. A trn2.48xlarge instance combines 16 Trainium2 chips, 64 logical NeuronCores, high-bandwidth memory, and NeuronLink-v3 connectivity. These resources support the distributed training and inference configurations described in this post.
Three properties of Trainium2 shaped the implementation: software-managed on-chip memory (Challenge 1), a fast chip-to-chip interconnect (Challenge 2), and a static compiler (Challenge 3). The compiler traces the GLA recurrence as a fixed graph.
Software-managed on-chip memory. Each NeuronCore has a 28 MiB State Buffer (SBUF) with 128 partitions and a 2 MiB partial-sum buffer (PSUM). The PSUM is wired to a 128×128 systolic Tensor Engine, alongside separate vector and scalar units. The SBUF is not a cache: the compiler schedules every HBM-to-SBUF transfer ahead of time, so the data is in place with no evictions or misses (Figure 1).
i14 and the Laplace 3B architecture
Laplace 3B is the 24-layer i14 decoder, where every layer replaces softmax attention with Simple GLA. Figure 2 follows one layer from the input xt at the top to the output xt + 1 at the bottom. This section explains each module: normalization and convolution, the QKVG projection, the GLA mixer, and the feed-forward channel mixer.
Normalization and convolution. Each token’s residual-stream vector xt ∈ ℝD (D = 3, 072) passes through a LayerNorm and a depth-wise causal Conv1d of width k = 4 with SiLU. This gives every position a 4-gram summary before the mixer. The GLA mixer then does content-based retrieval over the whole history through its decaying state.
QKVG projection. The post-conv output goes through one fused matrix Wqkvg ∈ ℝ9, 216 × 3, 072, where 9, 216 = H × (2dk + 2dv). It splits into four per-token streams: queries qt, keys kt, values vt, and a gate gt (H = 16, dk = 96, dv = 192). The gate is used after the mixer.
GLA mixer. Each head h keeps a matrix state St(h) of size dk × dv (96 × 192), a compressed, decaying record of past key-value pairs. At each token, it updates as:
Here λh is the fixed per-head decay, and ktvt⊤ is the rank-1 outer product that writes the current key-value pair into the state. The readout queries the state:
Next, a self-augmentation step adds a gated copy of the value to each head’s output:
Here σ is the sigmoid and ⊙ is the element-wise product. The gate is the query dotted with a learned per-channel rescaling of the key, where a is the learned scale (aug_balance). At initialization, a = 0, which gives a half-strength skip of the value. The per-head outputs pass through a Head RMSNorm within each decay tier, are concatenated, gated by SiLU(gt), and projected by Wout ∈ ℝD × D back to the residual stream.
Decay schedule. The per-head decay rate λh controls how fast a head forgets past tokens. It is fixed at initialization (not learned) and set by a geometric schedule. The schedule gives the 16 heads a spread of memory lengths and defines each head’s log-decay rate γh:
Decay schedule’s reach. For this model, Tmin = 1 and Tmax = 2, 048. Head 0 therefore has λ0 = 0.5 (half-life of one token), and head 15 has λ15 ≈ 0.9997 (half-life of 2,048 tokens). Heads are grouped into tiers, each sharing a Head RMSNorm.
Channel mixer (FFN). After the attention block and its residual, a second LayerNorm feeds a GLU (SiLU) FFN with inner dimension 8,192. Its three matrices are two up-projections W1, W2 ∈ ℝ8, 192 × D and one down-projection W3 ∈ ℝD × 8, 192. A second residual follows.
The state S(h) is fixed at dk × dv = 96 × 192 per head regardless of sequence length. As a result, inference is O(1) per token, and training is O(T) rather than O(T2).
| Parameter | Value | 
| Parameters | 3.028B total (2.718B Muon + 309.6M AdamW) | 
| Layers | 24 decoder layers, D = 3, 072 hidden dim | 
| Heads | 16 heads, dk = 96 (half-width Q/K), dv = 192 (full-width V) | 
| Mixer | Simple GLA with fixed geometric decay (Tmin = 1, Tmax = 2, 048) | 
| Conv | Depth-wise causal Conv1d, kernel width 4, SiLU | 
| FFN | GLU (SiLU), inner dim 8,192 | 
| Norm | LayerNorm pre-attn + Head RMSNorm (per tier) + LayerNorm pre-FFN | 
| Vocab | 50,304 (padded to multiple of 64) | 
| Sequence | 2,048 | 
| Training data | 100B tokens, FineWeb-Edu | 
| Optimizer | Muon for 2D weight matrices; AdamW for embeddings, norms | 
| Batch size | 524,288 tokens/step, cosine LR, 3,815-step warmup | 
Engineering challenges
Each of the three changes raised its own engineering challenge.
Challenge 1: Using native PyTorch on Trainium for GLA
On GPU, GLA runs as the fused Triton kernel fused_chunk_simple_gla from the flash-linear-attention library. The GenAIIC team re-expressed it with standard PyTorch operators running through TorchNeuron Native, as explicit loops over fixed-size chunks. The chunk count is fixed at compile time and sets the backward-unroll depth. The team uses fla_num_chunks = 16, so each chunk holds C = 128 tokens.
Within each chunk c, the intra-chunk output is masked linear attention, and the running state S adds earlier context:
The state then advances to the next chunk:
Here λC is the per-head decay compounded over the chunk. The 16 intra-chunk computations run in parallel, and only the state update is sequential (Figure 3).
Because the SBUF has 128 partitions, each 128-token chunk maps one token per partition, with no padding or cross-partition movement. This alignment increased measured throughput by 14 percent (Figure 4).
Challenge 2: Distributed Muon orthogonalization under FSDP2
Muon orthogonalizes each gradient before the update. For each of the 96 two-dimensional weight matrices (2.718 billion parameters), it runs five Newton–Schulz iterations (Algorithm 1).
The distributed problem. The Gram matrix A = XX⊤ correlates every row of the weight with every other row. Under Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP2), each of the 64 ranks holds only 1/64 of the rows. A shard-local XX⊤ therefore yields only a diagonal block and drops every cross-shard term (Figure 5).
Naive approach: Gather and broadcast. Every rank gathers the full gradient (5.44 GB), one rank runs Newton–Schulz, and it broadcasts the result. This moves 10.87 GB per step while the other 63 ranks wait.
Production approach: all_to_all transposition. In MuonFSDP2, one all_to_all gives each rank a few complete matrices, all 64 ranks run Newton–Schulz in parallel, and a second all_to_all returns the results. Per-rank traffic drops to 0.45 GB, 24 times less. Throughput rises from 73,378 to 119,934 tokens per second, 1.63 times higher, with a bit-identical loss curve (Figure 6).
Communication cost. Newton–Schulz is only about 2 percent of the FLOPs in a training step (1.95 × 1014 of 9.53 × 1015), so communication was the bottleneck. Over NeuronLink-v3 at 1.28 TB/s, the 0.45 GB exchange takes under 0.4 ms of the roughly 4.4-second step.
Challenge 3: Backward-pass unrolling for a sequential recurrence
The backward pass differentiates through all 16 sequential state updates. On GPU, autograd builds this graph at runtime. On Trainium2, the compiler must see the whole unrolled 16-step graph in advance, which creates three constraints.
Graph depth grows with chunk count: at 32 chunks (C = 64), the graph overflowed the scheduler. Per-chunk memory grows with chunk size: at 8 chunks (C = 256), intermediates spilled into HBM. Every shape is fixed at trace time, so each loop intermediate needs its own static allocation.
Sixteen chunks (C = 128) satisfy all three: the unroll fits the scheduler, intermediates stay on chip, and tiles align with the 128 SBUF partitions.
Training results
The GenAIIC team trained Laplace 3B on one trn2.48xlarge instance using all 64 logical NeuronCores and the all_to_all Muon path. The full recipe is 190,735 steps (100 billion FineWeb-Edu tokens). The following results are through step 84,210, about 44 billion tokens.
Throughput. After compilation warmup, throughput settles at roughly 120,000 tokens per second and holds there through step 84,210.
Loss and gradient stability. The loss (Figure 7a) drops smoothly from about 11.4 to 2.3729 at step 84,210. The gradient norm (Figure 7b) shows the expected early spike then a steady decline to about 0.05, with no post-warmup spikes, divergence, or NaN/Inf values.
Inference optimization on Trainium2
Through an unmodified vLLM engine, the GenAIIC team served 11,544 output tokens per second at 1,280 concurrent sequences on one trn2.48xlarge instance.
Constant serving state. The 29.5 MB recurrent state per sequence is roughly 82 times smaller than a comparable KV cache at 8,192 tokens. Increasing the prompt from 2,048 to 8,192 tokens added only 0.5% to the cost per output token.
Unmodified vLLM. A wrapper replaces one attribute per decoder layer, the token mixer, to read and write the recurrent state in the vLLM pool. Because the model declares itself attention-free, vLLM allocates one fixed page per sequence. Outputs matched the i14 reference token for token (48/48 steps on 3/3 prompts in BF16).
Finding the bottleneck. A linear fit of decode time against the number of decoder layers L gives:
At L = 24, that is 168.1 ms per step, 96.9 percent of it inside the decoder layers. The large projections cost 13.27 ms, near the 12 ms HBM-streaming floor. Most time went to small operators dispatched one at a time under eager PyTorch.
Scaling to a full instance. Without tensor parallelism, throughput scales through replicas, with one engine and 20 sequences per logical NeuronCore. Eager throughput grew from 133 output tokens per second on one replica to 6,772 on 64, where host CPU usage reached 82 percent. Compiling the decode step removed per-operator dispatch and raised throughput 1.7 times, to 11,544 (Figure 8).
What fixed-batch benchmarks hide. Under real traffic, each new decode batch width is a separately compiled shape whose first use costs about 11 seconds. These steps were only 1.1 percent of the total but consumed 47.5 percent of decode time. Padding to fixed widths removed this cost with bit-exact results. Compiled decode then improved per-replica throughput 3.52 times under staggered arrivals, compared with 1.46 times on fixed batches. Because BF16 reassociation makes compiled output differ slightly from eager, use eager decode when exact reproducibility matters.
Key takeaways
The project produced lessons across both training and inference:
- Native PyTorch can support custom architectures on Trainium2. i14 retained the GLA architecture and used TorchNeuron Native for the final implementation.
- Communication design matters for custom optimizers. The Muon all_to_all design reduced per-rank traffic by 24 times and increased training throughput by 1.63 times.
- Fixed state keeps inference memory predictable. Each sequence uses 29.5 MB regardless of context length.
- Profile before compiling. Operator dispatch, rather than arithmetic or HBM bandwidth, accounted for most decode time.
- Benchmark realistic arrival patterns. Fixed batches hid the cost of compiling new shapes for changing batch widths.
Conclusion
Laplace 3B shows that AWS Trainium2 can support model architectures beyond standard transformers. Using native PyTorch through TorchNeuron Native and the AWS Neuron SDK, i14 trained and served its GLA-based model while preserving a fixed recurrent state.
For agentic systems, this changes a basic serving constraint. Longer histories don’t require a larger per-sequence state, which can help teams retain more context while keeping memory use predictable.
If growing context is increasing serving cost, reducing concurrency, or limiting agent memory, try i14 or contact your AWS account team to evaluate Laplace 3B on AWS Trainium2.

articles.title: How Singapore Connects Chip Research, Startups, and Manufacturing - EE Times
articles.text:
As competition in the semiconductor industry expands beyond conventional process scaling to encompass photonics, power devices, advanced packaging, and heterogeneous integration, Singapore leverages its established R&D and manufacturing base to explore ways to bring deep tech to market.
Singapore is advancing technologies including advanced packaging, silicon photonics, power electronics, RF GaN, piezoMEMS, flat optics, and IC design. A pathway from research through technology translation to startups and industrial commercialization is gradually taking shape. Research platforms such as the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) play a key role in connecting research outcomes with industry needs.
Three examples illustrate this journey: silicon carbide (SiC) power device research at A*STAR’s Institute of Microelectronics (A*STAR IME); metalens technology being commercialized by Singapore-based startup MetaOptics; and silicon photonics foundry Advanced Micro Foundry (AMF), which emerged from A*STAR’s technology translation efforts before being acquired by GlobalFoundries. Together, they show how deep-tech innovations can progress from research and technology translation to industrial scale.
SiC research: from device development to technology translation
Chien Yu-Chieh (Jack), a senior scientist at A*STAR IME originally from Taiwan, focuses on SiC power MOSFETs, including device structures, process development, electrical characterization, and reliability. He aims to take his research beyond device development toward technology translation.
SiC is already an established material for commercial power semiconductors, but next-generation devices still face significant technical challenges. Chien noted, for example, that trench MOSFETs can reduce on-resistance but introduce challenges related to gate oxide integrity, defects at the SiC/SiO₂ interface, and long-term reliability.
Chien is therefore working on next-generation SiC device structures and fabrication processes. Because device design, fabrication, measurement, and reliability testing require repeated validation, access to a comprehensive research platform with the necessary equipment and cross-disciplinary expertise is critical. At A*STAR IME, he said, researchers can conduct device design, process development, and electrical characterization within the same R&D environment, shortening development cycles.
For Chien, the next step is to advance his research toward technology translation, potentially by establish a startup to turn the results into commercial applications and valuable IP.
MetaOptics: from metalens research to manufacturing
Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Singapore, MetaOptics specializes in manufacturing metalenses on glass substrates. Its technology uses nanoscale structures to directly control light waves, enabling thin optical elements to perform some of the functions traditionally achieved with multiple conventional lenses.
MetaOptics applies semiconductor manufacturing techniques to form nanoscale pillar structures on 12-inch glass wafers. By incorporating processes such as deep ultraviolet (DUV) immersion lithography, the company is advancing wafer-level metalens manufacturing. The approach could help shrink optical modules for smartphone cameras, wearables, machine vision, and other sensing systems.
For MetaOptics CEO Aloysius Chua, the real challenge is not simply demonstrating that a metalens can form an image, but convincing customers that the technology works in real-world applications. For a deep-tech startup, developing a prototype is only the beginning. As Chua put it, “I need to show customers that my lens is working.”
Chua said MetaOptics must also complete customer validation and address process consistency, yield, and manufacturing scale. As nanoscale structures, optical design, and semiconductor lithography move toward volume production, process control becomes a key determinant of commercial competitiveness. A*STAR provides research resources and an R&D environment to help technologies bridge the gap between laboratory development and industrial applications.
AMF: scaling silicon photonics for industry
While MetaOptics and Chien’s work remain at the startup or technology validation stage, AMF offers a concrete example of deep tech advancing toward industrial-scale operations.
AMF is a Singapore-based silicon photonics foundry that grew out of A*STAR’s technology translation efforts. It operates a 200-mm manufacturing platform and provides silicon photonics prototyping, fabrication, and testing services. In November 2025, GlobalFoundries announced its acquisition of AMF, bringing the foundry’s manufacturing capabilities, silicon photonics IP, and talent into its global operations. GlobalFoundries said AMF was expected to contribute more than $75 million in revenue in 2026, helping the company target more than $1 billion in annual silicon photonics revenue by the end of the decade.
For GlobalFoundries, the acquisition brings more than a silicon photonics manufacturing platform. It adds AMF’s accumulated expertise, IP, and talent to the company. Yew Kong Tan, senior VP of GlobalFoundries APAC Manufacturing and general manager of the Singapore site, said the company’s silicon photonics collaboration with A*STAR dates back to 2015. The acquisition also creates an opportunity to bring 300-mm silicon photonics capabilities developed in the U.S. to Singapore, complementing A*STAR’s research capabilities.
“The acquisition actually allows us to combine capabilities on both sides,” Tan said. “From the research technology standpoint, AMF’s talent can also support 300-mm research. At the same time, the acquisition allows us to expand the capacity that the market needs in Singapore.”
GlobalFoundries also announced plans to establish a silicon photonics R&D center of excellence in Singapore in collaboration with A*STAR. The work will include developing next-generation silicon photonics technologies and materials for data transmission at 400 Gbps. GlobalFoundries plans to use AMF’s existing 200-mm platform to serve markets such as long-haul optical communications, computing, LiDARs, and sensing, with the potential to expand to 300-mm manufacturing as demand grows.
AMF illustrates another critical stage in deep-tech commercialization. Once research has been taken up by a startup and validated in the market, further growth requires an established manufacturing platform, accumulated expertise, and IP. Integrating these assets into a larger semiconductor company can extend the technology’s reach and expand its market potential.
A*STAR: bridging research and industry
This is the essence of what Yeo Yee Chia, A*STAR’s assistant chief executive for innovation and enterprise, calls “technology translation.” He emphasized that research institutions must go beyond conducting research: They need to work backward from industry needs to determine which equipment, talent, and technical capabilities to build.
This kind of platform support is particularly important for deep tech. Metalenses require nanoscale fabrication and wafer-level manufacturing; SiC power devices need device design, process development, and reliability validation; and silicon photonics involves optical devices, CMOS-compatible processes, wafer fabrication, packaging, and testing. These technologies often require years of capital-intensive R&D, while initial market demand may be too limited to justify a startup investing in a full set of production tools or building a complete R&D team on its own.
As Yeo noted, the value of a research institution extends beyond publishing academic papers or filing patents. More importantly, it lies in establishing the infrastructure and capabilities needed to validate, refine, and commercialize emerging technologies. For startups, this can lower early-stage barriers by allowing them to access research and development resources without bearing the full upfront capital expenditure. For larger enterprises, it provides access to technology platforms, IP, and expertise that have already progressed through technical validation and are better positioned for industrial deployment.
