articles.title: Spotify: Teilen des Familienabos wird schwieriger
articles.text:
Der Streamingdienst Spotify geht mit einer QR-Code-Verifizierung gegen geteilte Familien- sowie auch Duo-Abos vor. Mitglieder einer Gruppe sollen damit beweisen, dass sie tatsächlich im selben Haushalt leben wie die Person, die das Abo verwaltet. Das Teilen über den eigenen Haushalt hinaus ist bei beiden Tarifen eigentlich ohnehin untersagt – alle Nutzer:innen sollen dieselbe Anschrift haben. Doch daran halten sich viele User:innen nicht.
Bisher reichte eine Adresse
Das bisherige Verfahren war simpel: Wer dem Premium-Familienabo (22 Euro) beitrat, das sich bis zu sechs Personen teilen können, oder dem Duo-Tarif für zwei (18 Euro), musste lediglich die vollständige Adresse angeben und bestätigen, mit dem Hauptnutzer zusammenzuwohnen. Spotify erklärt dazu, man verfolge den Standort nicht, sondern prüfe die Adresse nur zur Verifizierung. Praktisch konnte so auch jemand am anderen Ende der Welt Teil des Abos sein.
Laut Spotifys Support-Seite müssen Mitglieder eines Familien- oder Duo-Abos künftig „unter Umständen“ einen QR-Code scannen. Der Code erscheint auf dem Smartphone der Person, die das Abo verwaltet. Das Mitglied scannt ihn mit der Handykamera – beide müssen sich dafür am selben Ort befinden. Zu finden ist der Code in der Mitgliederverwaltung der App: erst auf das Profilbild tippen, dann auf „Dein Abo“ und anschließend auf „Verwalten“. Verpflichtend ist das Verfahren offenbar derzeit nicht, das könnte aber kommen.
Kein Scan, zwölf Monate Sperre
Wer die Aufforderung erhält, hat sieben Tage Zeit, den Code zu scannen. Verstreicht die Frist, kann die Person zwölf Monate lang keinem anderen Family- oder Duo-Abo beitreten – bleibt also nur ein eigenes Abo oder die kostenlose Version.
Damit niemand einfach einen Screenshot weiterschickt, erneuert sich der QR-Code nach Angaben von Spotify alle paar Sekunden. Ganz dicht ist das System trotzdem nicht: Ein Nutzer berichtet auf Reddit, er habe die Prüfung per Bildschirmfreigabe in Microsoft Teams bestanden. Spotify könnte letztlich auch verlangen, dass die Mitglieder der Familiengruppe die gleiche Geoposition haben, wenn der QR-Code gescannt wird. Dazu müsste man der Firma aber erlauben, diese sensiblen Informationen auszulesen.

articles.title: How Neo San is processing non-recyclable waste where it is generated
articles.text:
How Neo San is processing non-recyclable waste where it is generated
Neo San builds compact thermal processing units for dry reject, sanitary, and biomedical waste, reducing the need to transport it to distant disposal sites.
Indian cities generate large volumes of non-recyclable dry waste every day, much of which municipal collection systems struggle to manage. Conventional waste management relies on trucks to transport rubbish to distant landfills, dumpsites, and open incinerators. As collection and transport systems struggle to keep pace, large quantities of sanitary, medical and reject waste go untreated, ending up in open burning pits, water bodies or soil as toxic liquid.
Bengaluru-based Neo San is trying to address this problem by processing non-recyclable waste where it is generated, using compact thermal treatment units.
Founded in 2022 by CEO Dhwaj Bagrecha, the cleantech startup grew out of his experience working in urban planning and waste infrastructure. Bagrecha, who holds a degree in Economics and Finance from Jain University in Bengaluru, affiliated with Bangalore University, saw how rising consumption was outpacing municipal waste management systems. This led him to develop equipment that could treat waste on-site.
Processing waste at source
Neo San's product range includes the Neo-X, a wall-mounted unit designed for washrooms and standalone commercial buildings that can process up to 25 kg of waste a day. The Neo-XT handles 150 kg a day and is intended for tech parks, small hospitals, and commercial complexes. Its third model, the AX, is designed for industrial manufacturing plants processing 500 kg or more a day.
The technology uses rapid, high-temperature electric heating based on induction principles. According to the startup, the system reaches 1,200 degrees Celsius within two minutes while consuming minimal electricity.
The thermal process reduces waste to what the company describes as sterile, non-toxic ash. Neo San is also developing hub facilities to collect the residue and convert it into building briquettes.
The startup has two granted patents for its thermal processing technology, with another 13 patent applications pending.
Bagrecha says that on a lifecycle basis, on-site treatment cuts emissions by 98% compared with collection and landfilling. “The savings come from our patented thermal process and from not trucking the waste away,” he says.
Neo San manufactures its hardware in-house and provides software tools for housekeeping staff. It operates as a managed service, maintaining the equipment and sending regular tracking reports to clients' sustainability teams.
Customers can either purchase the machines outright or pay a monthly service fee. The startup serves corporate offices, healthcare facilities, government bodies and commercial real estate clients.
Neo San describes itself as a seed-to-growth-stage startup and has raised Rs 26 crore in total funding. Its clients include Taj, Embassy, and the Government of Karnataka, along with factories and data centres, the startup says.
Over the next year, the company plans to expand its service operations into four additional states and launch a specialised version of the Neo-XT for biomedical waste processing.
Neo San is part of YourStory's Tech30 cohort—a showcase of India's most promising startups of 2026, unveiled at TechSparks Bengaluru.

articles.title: Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, análisis: tener una pantalla 'Plus' por 200 euros menos tiene truco (y bastante sentido)
articles.text:
La saga Fan Edition nació con una misión sencilla: acercar las bondades de la primera línea de Samsung a un público que no quería, o no podía, romper la barrera de las cuatro cifras. El año pasado, el Galaxy S25 FE demostró que la versatilidad pesaba más que el rendimiento, consolidando una fórmula reconocible. En esta ocasión, el Samsung Galaxy S26 FE aterriza manteniendo ese mismo ADN, eso sí, aunque en un escenario bastante más hostil.
He pasado las últimas semanas con el Galaxy S26 FE en el bolsillo y las sensaciones son tan familiares como reveladoras. Es un dispositivo bien rematado, solvente y con empaque de gama alta que busca servir de alternativa asequible al Galaxy S26+ por su diagonal de 6,7 pulgadas. El dilema no está en lo que hace, sino en entender su papel: en un año complicado por el encarecimiento de componentes, este FE defiende una brecha frente al precio de salida de sus hermanos mayores. La experiencia lo sitúa en un terreno muy interesante, eso sí, no es perfecto. Te cuento por qué.
✅ Cómpralo si…
- Buscas la experiencia de un Galaxy S26+ sin pagar más.
- Priorizas una pantalla AMOLED excelente y un software con siete años de actualizaciones.
- Quieres entrar al ecosistema de Samsung (en la gama alta) sin romper la barrera de las cuatro cifras
❌ No lo compres si...
- Prefieres un móvil compacto que se maneje bien con una sola mano (para eso está el Galaxy S26 base).
- Buscas la máxima versatilidad en fotografía con zoom y ultra gran angular sin importar pagar más.
- La potencia y los juegos pesados a una alta tasa de frames son tu máxima prioridad.
Lo esencial en 30 segundos
El Samsung Galaxy S26 FE es un teléfono digno de la gama alta que no defrauda en lo fundamental. Está bien construído, hereda el diseño de sus hermanos mayores y ofrece una pantalla de 6,7 pulgadas que resulta un placer para consumir contenido o jugar. No se siente un móvil barato ni recortado a la ligera; Samsung domina este formato a la perfección.
Su reto es defender esta subfamilia en un momento complejo. Con un precio de partida de 799 euros, logra mantener una distancia razonable respecto al Galaxy S26 base y una rebaja aún mayor frente al S26+. A cambio de ese ahorro, exige concesiones como montar el Exynos 2500 en lugar del 2600 (o un Snapdragon Elite) o renunciar a sensores fotográficos más ambiciosos. Pero si lo que buscas es una pantalla grande, soporte a largo plazo y la fiabilidad de One UI, la ecuación encaja.
8,4
A favor
- Construcción y acabados que transmiten sensación de gama alta en mano.
- La cámara principal ofrece un nivel de detalle y balance de blancos sobresaliente.
- One UI 9 sobre Android 17 vuela y otorga siete años de soporte oficial.
En contra
- Los 799 euros de partida pesan dadas las concesiones en chip y cámaras secundarias
- El teleobjetivo y el ultra gran angular quedan por detrás del sensor principal.
- La trasera atrapa las huellas con facilidad.
Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, 256 GB, Color Pistacho | Teléfono Móvil con Galaxy AI, Cámara 50MP, Batería 4900mAh, Garantía del Fabricante 3 Años + 1 Año Extra (Versión Española)
Nuestra experiencia con el Samsung Galaxy S26 FE
El empaque de la gama alta en un cuerpo familiar. Nada más sacarlo de la caja, el Galaxy S26 FE deja claro de dónde viene: es un calco de los Galaxy S26 y S26+. Se siente bien construido, sólido y con ese tacto noble que Samsung lleva años perfeccionando.
Con sus 193 gramos y un perfil de 7,4 milímetros, es algo pesado pero sin caer en lo excesivo; tiene la densidad justa que transmite solidez sin fatigar la muñeca. Para mi gusto personal sigue siendo un teléfono un pelín grande debido a sus 6,7 pulgadas, pero es una cuestión de preferencias de tamaño más que un defecto.
Ergonomía y construcción. Una de las quejas que tuvimos en la generación anterior eran unos laterales afilados que podían llegar a molestar al rato. En este S26 FE, Samsung parece haber tomado nota: los cantos se notan pulidos, con una transición suave que hace que sujetarlo a pelo sea placentero.
La cruz de la moneda está en la trasera de cristal. En la unidad de color azul que he estado probando, las huellas y su grasilla se quedan marcadas a la mínima, obligando a limpiarlo cada poco. Lo mejor: ponerle una funda.
Un panel AMOLED disfrutable que sabe a lo que juega. En el frontal me he encontrado un panel de 6,7 pulgadas con resolución FullHD+ de notable. En estas diagonales no he extrañado nunca más resolución: la nitidez es muy buena y se ve de cine.
La calibración de fábrica llega con ese punto colorido y vibrante que uno busca en un panel AMOLED, pero con la madurez suficiente para no caer en la saturación tan exagerada de antaño.
En exteriores responde con soltura para responder un mensaje o consultar el mapa, si bien es cierto que cuando el sol aprieta con fuerza toca forzar el brillo al tope; cumple bien, aunque sin llegar a los picos de los modelos más caros de la surcoreana.
Un sonido digno para el día a día. El apartado de audio acompaña la experiencia: su pareja de altavoces ofrece un volumen generoso y limpio que he disfrutado tanto para escuchar música de fondo por casa como para devorar podcasts sin necesidad de ponerme auriculares. La separación de canales y la claridad de las voces están conseguidas, aunque puesto a ser exigente, he echado en falta un punto extra de pegada y contundencia en los graves, algo que hubiese redondeado el conjunto.
Un rendimiento solvente al que se le notan las costuras. El cerebro que mueve este S26 FE es el Exynos 2500 que debutó en el Galaxy Z Flip7. Tras estas semanas, debo decir que se desenvuelve genial en la inmensa mayoría de escenarios típicos: navegación web, redes sociales y consumo multimedia van sobre ruedas.
Sin embargo, no puedo ignorar que se siente un pelín más perezoso si lo comparo directamente con la experiencia que tuve mismamente con el Galaxy S25 base. Aunque este chip rinde de forma más que digna, no juega en el top del mercado y eso se traduce en pequeños tirones, muy esporádicos pero perceptibles al esperar transiciones más inmediatas. Cumple con lo esperado, aunque una optimización más afinada le habría sentado de lujo.
One UI 9, en plena forma. En el apartado del software, Samsung vuelve a dar una lección de madurez. Su capa, corriendo sobre Android 17, se mueve con una velocidad y una fluidez exquisitas; las animaciones acompañan y visualmente luce de diez.
Por mis hábitos y necesidades no suelo recurrir al paquete de Galaxy AI, pero al ponerlo a prueba —tras haberlo exprimido en su día en el Galaxy S24 Ultra— da buenos resultados: son herramientas orientadas a un público nicho, pero ejecutadas con un nivel altísimo. Entre ellas, la función de intérprete sigue coronándose como la más práctica y mejor resuelta.
Biometría: rápida y fiable, pero con tecnología óptica. A la hora de desbloquear este S26 FE nos topamos con un sensor óptico, claro, bajo la pantalla. Viniendo de los ultrasónicos se nota la diferencia: la zona de lectura es algo más reducida y la animación de desbloqueo tarda una milésima más.
Dicho esto, está lejos de ser un mal sensor; es rápido, no me ha fallado, así que poco se le puede reprochar. En cuanto al reconocimiento facial por cámara frontal, se mantiene en la tónica del mercado: es instantáneo cuando la luz acompaña, pero en cuanto cae la iluminación o estamos a oscuras muestra sus limitaciones frente a un sensor dedicado.
Un sensor principal que saca pecho y dos secundarios que se desinflan. A la hora de sacar fotos, me he encontrado dos realidades muy distintas. La cámara principal de 50 megapíxeles rinde como debería: me ha gustado mucho la definición que consigue, el balance de blancos es muy certero y la apertura contiene el ISO para no meter ruido cuando la escena se complica.
El contraste llega al cambiar de lente. Tanto el teleobjetivo de 8 megapíxeles como el ultra gran angular de 12 MP entregan colores bastante más apagados y acusan una pérdida de detalle, evidente por su menor resolución.
Ahora bien, el telefoto, para la mayoría de fotos retrato, es insuperable frente al gran angular. Aisla muy bien al sujeto del fondo y aplana la perspectiva por su focal equivalente.
Este mismo teleobjetivo salva los muebles de día, pero flaquea en cuanto cae la noche. Con todo, es un conjunto solvente y polivalente, aunque en esta categoría Samsung debería haber dado un paso adelante en estas cámaras secundarias.
Sobre la grabación de vídeo, cumple: permite un máximo de 8k30 o 4k 60 fps. El clip de abajo está grabado precisamente en esta resolución y tasa de fotogramas, sin que sea posible cambiar al ultra gran angular o al telefoto por estar limitados a 4K 30 fps.
Una autonomía que cumple con su tamaño. Con 4.900 mAh —la misma cifra que monta el Galaxy S26+—, la batería se comporta decentemente. Como he dicho anteriormente, marcado por la crisis de componentes, Samsung ha logrado mantener el tipo, también en autonomía: estando de viaje, en jornadas más relajadas me ha aguantado día y medio, y en días exigentes con GPS, 5G y fotos alcanza las seis horas de pantalla activa para llegar a la noche con un pelín de margen. No marca récords frente a las baterías de silicio-carbono que empiezan a poblar los móviles chinos, pero para el usuario medio está bien. Además, carga a 45 W, que con la citada pila, devuelve el 100% en apenas una hora.

|---|---|

| PANTALLA | AMOLED de 6,7 pulgadas Resolución FullHD+ 120 Hz de tasa de refresco 1.900 nits de brillo máximo Corning Gorilla Glass Victus | 
| PROCESADOR | Exynos 2500 |

| BATERÍA | 4.900 mAh Carga rápida a 45 W por cable Carga a 15 W inalámbrica Compatible con carga inalámbrica inversa | 
| CÁMARAS TRASERAS | Principal: 50 MP con f/1.8 y OIS Telefoto: 8 MP con f/2.4, zoom óptico 3x Gran angular: 12 MP con f/2.2 | 
| CÁMARA FRONTAL | 12 MP, f/2.2 | 
| SISTEMA OPERATIVO | One UI 9 basado en Android 17 | 
| SONIDO | Doble altavoz estéreo |

Samsung Galaxy S26 FE, la opinión de Xataka
El Samsung Galaxy S26 FE es un teléfono notable que cumple con dignidad la papeleta de acercar la experiencia de la familia Galaxy S a un precio inferior. Está bien rematado, su pantalla de 6,7 pulgadas es un disfrute para consumir multimedia (o jugar), el sensor principal rinde bien y One UI 9 demuestra por qué Samsung sigue marcando el ritmo en estabilidad y soporte.
Sin embargo, sus sombras no vienen tanto de sus recortes como de su etiqueta y el calendario. Con el Exynos 2500 mostrando algún pequeño titubeo y una trasera bonita pero sucia, este Galaxy vuelve a exponerse al gran reto de los Fan Edition: convencer al usuario de que el ahorro compensa sus renuncias.
¿Te lo recomiendo?
Sí. Si buscas un smartphone con pantalla generosa, la madurez de One UI 9 y un soporte que garantiza años sin pagar los precios de la primera línea, este S26 FE es una compra sensata. La única duda es de formato: si tu prioridad es la ergonomía, el Galaxy S26 base sigue siendo la referencia; pero si lo tuyo son las 6,7 pulgadas para jugar y ver mucho vídeo, este Fan Edition da una experiencia digna del modelo 'Plus' por bastante menos dinero.

articles.title: Galaxy S26 Ultra com câmera de 200 MP sai mais barato no Mercado Livre • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy S26 Ultra com câmera de 200 MP sai mais barato no Mercado Livre
Galaxy S26 Ultra (256 GB) tem tela à prova de curiosos e câmera wide de 200 MP; topo de linha da Samsung recebe desconto competitivo frente às ofertas pré-reajuste
O Galaxy S26 Ultra de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 6.546 no Pix no Mercado Livre. O atual celular de ponta da Samsung, equipado com câmera principal de 200 MP e tela AMOLED de 120 Hz com recurso exclusivo de privacidade, recebe desconto de 45% sobre o preço oficial de R$ 11.999.
Este mês, os celulares da linha Galaxy S26 sofreram reajuste de preços, e o S26 Ultra ficou mais caro (antes era R$ 11.499 oficialmente). Contudo, a oferta de hoje ainda compete facilmente com os menores preços mais recentes. Mas fique atento: esta oferta é válida apenas para o modelo na cor Branca.
O Galaxy S26 Ultra traz um versátil kit traseiro de câmeras que filma em 8K. Ele inclui wide de 200 MP exclusiva, ultrawide de 50 MP, telefoto de 10 MP com zoom óptico de 3x e periscópica de 50 MP e 5x, que fazem capturas em nível profissional. A frontal de 12 MP tira ótimas selfies e filma em 4K a 60 fps.
Seu chip Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy e os 12 GB de RAM nem suam ao rodar apps pesados em multitarefa e soluções do Galaxy AI localmente. Nos nossos testes, o gadget tirou de letra tarefas como edição de imagens, games pesados e gravação de vídeo prolongada, sem engasgar.
A tela LTPO AMOLED Dinâmico 2X de 6,9″ conta com uma exclusiva tecnologia de privacidade, que bloqueia “espiadinhas” de curiosos posicionados nos lados do usuário. A taxa de 120 Hz e o brilho de até 2.600 nits entregam cores vibrantes, alta fluidez e visibilidade garantida em qualquer lugar.
O corpo de alumínio do S26 Ultra é revestido pelos vidros Gorilla Glass Armor 2 (tela) e Victus 2 (traseira), resistentes contra acidentes diversos. A certificação IP68 adiciona proteção contra poeira intensa e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 5.000 mAh resiste a até 31 horas de vídeo, segundo a Samsung. O carregamento rápido de 60 W via USB-C e sem fio de 25 W permite usar o celular por um dia inteiro, um recurso ideal para usuários sem tempo a perder com tomadas e powerbanks.
O Galaxy S26 Ultra de 256 GB (R$ 6.546 no Pix) será atualizado até o Android 23 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0 e NFC.

articles.title: Europe's four largest carriers want to build a Starlink rival, but they don't have satellites
articles.text:
In brief: In another sign of Europe's continuing push away from reliance on US tech, four of the continent's biggest mobile operators are considering joining forces to create a Starlink competitor. The proposed service would connect phones directly to satellites, helping fill coverage gaps while giving European carriers an alternative to Elon Musk's network.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica, and Vodafone have signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for Mobile Satellite Services spectrum in Europe. The agreement, announced on Monday, is an early step toward offering direct-to-device connectivity through their existing mobile networks.
The aim is to reach areas where conventional mobile infrastructure falls short. Starlink already offers similar coverage through partnerships with carriers including T-Mobile in the US and O2 in the UK.
There is, however, a fairly significant piece of the plan missing: the satellites. The four operators don't intend to invest directly in a constellation themselves. Instead, they would build ground infrastructure and establish coordination and monitoring operations in Europe, with a satellite partner providing the orbiting hardware. That partner has yet to be selected.
The companies say other mobile operators would also be able to access the service on equal terms. They want the project to improve coverage in underserved areas, protect critical communications, and make public networks more resilient. Existing satellite partnerships would remain in place.
The European Commission has proposed reserving some of the 2 GHz satellite spectrum for European operators.
Earlier this month, SpaceX secured FCC approval for 15,000 Starlink Mobile satellites. A separate waiver allows it to offer satellite wireless services without leasing spectrum from a terrestrial carrier, opening a way to competing directly with established operators. The planned mobile upgrade also goes beyond emergency messages and basic data, with support for native calls, streaming, browsing, and more demanding apps. It means Starlink could become both a useful partner and a serious rival for traditional carriers.
Europe's effort to reduce its dependence on American technology have been gaining pace in recent times. France plans to move government systems from Windows to Linux, alongside a broader shift toward European software and services. Control over essential infrastructure is becoming a recurring theme.
There was also a German state's plans to replace Windows and Microsoft Office with Linux and LibreOffice for 30,000 government employees. More recently, Switzerland launched an $11 million pilot to move 3,000 federal workstations to openDesk, an open-source alternative to Microsoft's productivity tools.
The Netherlands is trying to break from Microsoft with its DAWO project, an independent IT environment built around NixOS that would offer public institutions alternatives to US desktop software, office applications, and cloud services.

articles.title: JustWatch, which tackles streaming fragmentation, launches own streaming service
articles.text:
Since launching in 2015, JustWatch has helped people navigate the growing number of streaming services by providing a guide on where to find movies they want to stream. Now JustWatch has its own streaming service and wants people to subscribe.
Launched today, JustWatch TV offers some movies available for free with ads that aren’t free on any other streaming service, including Green Room (2015), Locke (2013), and Sing Sing (2023). Other free movies include Fiddlin’ (2018), Friday the 13th (1980), and Hotel Mumbai (2018). I could play movies available for free on JustWatch TV without creating an account.
JustWatch TV also has movies you can rent.
The streaming service also sells a subscription for people who don’t want to watch JustWatch’s library with ads. It’s currently $4 per month or $50 for a lifetime subscription. The latter is only available for a “limited” time, a company spokesperson told Ars Technica. The rep was unable to confirm how long JustWatch will sell the lifetime subscription.
Upon my perusal, JustWatch TV’s library seems limited and somewhat dated. That’s not necessarily a bad idea. Howdy, a Roku-owned streaming service with a similarly lackluster library compared to other services that costs $3/month without ads, reportedly had 1 million subscribers six months into launch.

articles.title: Assess the entire inference stack — not just open model benchmarks
articles.text:
Assess the entire inference stack — not just open model benchmarks
Impressive benchmark results should make it easy for engineers to select the right open model for the outcome they are tasked with developing. However, that is not the case.
Benchmarks indicate an open model’s optimal performance, but in production, a model must work repeatedly. The challenge is that in production, other factors matter, such as the information provided to the model and its accuracy. So benchmarks can’t tell an engineer whether the AI they are developing will complete the task accurately, or even at all. This is especially important for long-horizon AI tasks.
Ryan Hanrui Wang, SVP of Applied AI at AI cloud provider Nebius, tells The New Stack it is important to measure an open model by the industry benchmarks in conjunction with internal benchmarks and harnesses to ensure you get the inference outcomes the organization requires, something he says the Amsterdam, Netherlands-based company always does in partnership with its clients.
Wang joined Nebius when it acquired Eigen AI, the inference-optimization startup he co-founded and led as CEO, in a roughly $643 million deal announced in May; Nebius sells inference through its Token Factory platform.
“Customers often have their own benchmarks, so we can use their agent workflow and its traces to see the level of success we can work with. We always work closely with them to define the benchmarks.”
Wang goes on to add: “The public benchmark may not cover the multi-domain tasks that an engineer wants inference to do in the actual production environment.” He says this can misalign agent tasks with the true cost of inference calls. “The workflow is not tested by the benchmark design. There needs to be in-context learning.”
Engineers and organizations should therefore not spend too much time selecting the open model; they should look at the entire inference stack. Model selection should depend on whether the engineer needs a lower-cost, flexible open-model stack or a frontier model for inference.
For those who need lower cost, Wang says Nebius evaluates open models such as Kimi and DeepSeek, as well as lighter “flash” models, to see whether they can meet inference accuracy needs and whether fine-tuning is required.
Those who want superior accuracy and quality usually narrow it down to two or three large open models and then fine-tune them to improve accuracy. Wang says open model selection is only the first step; after selection, they need to ensure long-context tasks and cached inputs deliver the expected outcome.
Inference and post-training
In post-training, Wang says the organization uses its data to improve accuracy and task fit, while the serving layer, quantization, batching, caching, and kernel optimization drive inference speed. In addition, engineers should develop the cache system for production traffic, ensuring the hit rate is maximized for the workload so repeated inputs hit the cache rather than being recomputed.
“The other important thing is throughput, the measure of how many tokens are generated in a certain time span, as they are a major trade-off against interactivity,” Wang adds. Engineers need to balance better utilization and cheaper tokens with acceptable interactivity– per-user speed.
Getting concurrency right ensures the organization uses the open model effectively; it is a fine balancing act for engineers. If compute isn’t fully utilized, token cost is high. But high utilization with increased concurrency can reduce end-user token-per-second speed.
Engineers also need to watch tail latency, not just averages. “P95 and P99 are important metrics for the per-user token speed and time to first token (TTFT); the time they need to wait needs to be below five seconds for some of our customers,” Wang says. A system can post a great average response time and still be unusable if one request in twenty stalls.
Modeling for accuracy
Engineers need to be careful when considering benchmark results and accuracy. Benchmarks may test reasoning on a mathematical problem, which isn’t very useful if the engineer is developing an AI agent for customer support, where high emotional intelligence (EQ) matters more. “So there is a misalignment between the different benchmarks and actual production,” Wang says.
On cost per successful task, Wang says engineers must remember that cheap tokens are useless if the model is inaccurate.
Engineers need to consider the end-to-end process the AI will perform. This lets engineers select the right-sized open model for the AI task. Wang gives the example of a specialized assistant agent where Nebius gathered 6,000 traces to refine a small model and improved accuracy by 11% while executing 22% fewer tool calls.
He raises this point because it counters the tendency to think bigger is better, but accuracy gains from increasing model size diminish. “There is typically a tipping point for this kind of task,” Wang says. For a task like customer support, he says, 10 billion parameters could be enough, while 100 billion or even a trillion parameters yields only minimal accuracy gains. “What we want to do is find the sweet spot.”
Engineers can use large models as a reference point, then tune the reasoning with their organizational data to find an open model with the right accuracy and size for the task.
“We typically do a sweep of several models, using the largest model as a reference to know where the sweet spot for model size is,” Wang says. “For a complicated task, we can dissect the complex task into smaller subtasks, working with the customer, which connects workflows and can then use smaller models.”
Wang describes this process as a division of labor, referencing the famous economist Adam Smith.
This approach shows the course of AI engineering maturity. Like every sector in technological and engineering history, the initial gold rush targets bigger-is-better. As the engineering matures, it focuses on outcomes and engineering excellence, and therefore on working with partners who understand how to achieve them.
Sometimes that is a bigger model; other times a small niche development is best.

articles.title: SBI finds 3,897 customer records on dark web after hacker’s claim
articles.text:
SBI finds 3,897 customer records on dark web after hacker’s claim
SBI is investigating a suspected data breach after alerts from CERT-In and the Defence Cyber Agency, disclosing the probe in a stock exchange filing.
State Bank of India (SBI) has disclosed a suspected customer data breach, saying it found 3,897 records containing personal information on the dark web. The country’s largest public sector lender confirmed the findings in a stock exchange filing on Wednesday and has launched a detailed cybersecurity investigation.
The bank said it received alerts from its threat intelligence service provider, the Defence Cyber Agency and the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), all pointing to a possible exposure of customer information. In a preliminary review of around 3.75 lakh records circulating on the dark web, SBI identified 3,897 records containing personally identifiable information.
The disclosure follows a claim made last week by a threat actor using the name “Siriusim”. In a post on BreachForums, a site known for trading stolen data, the actor claimed to possess 3.75 lakh customer records and 2,722 PDF documents linked to SBI. The claim was flagged on October 16 by the X account CyberPulse56.
The listing described the data as a CSV file containing 3.75 lakh rows, along with the PDF documents. The poster also shared four sample records as evidence. The Free Press Journal examined the samples and found that the phone numbers were real. Most of the data appeared to relate to loans, while some entries concerned savings account applications and customer acquisition.
Following the alerts, SBI activated its cyber incident response protocols and engaged an independent cybersecurity agency empanelled with CERT-In. The agency will verify the authenticity of the leaked records, trace the source of the potential exposure and assess the associated security risks. The bank said it was implementing preventive and corrective measures.
Several questions remain unanswered, including how the data was obtained and how old it is. The listing did not specify whether the records were recent or linked to an earlier incident. SBI has not yet disclosed how many of the 3,897 records could be linked to current customers.
The nature of the information reportedly contained in the samples adds to the seriousness of the case. The records included identity verification documents, making the potential exposure more consequential than a typical leak of names and phone numbers. Unlike a stolen password, a compromised identity document can be difficult to replace and may carry longer-term risks.
The case also puts banks’ legal obligations around data protection under scrutiny. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, organisations are required to implement reasonable security safeguards and notify authorities of personal data breaches. Violations of certain obligations can attract penalties of up to Rs 250 crore.
This is not the first time SBI has faced questions of this kind. In 2019, the bank rejected a TechCrunch report about an unprotected server, saying its own investigation showed there had been no breach.
This story will be updated as the investigation progresses.

- Modèle toujours plus puissant.
Points faibles
- Îlot photo vraiment très épais.

articles.title: Un SUV chinois éligible à l’aide de 6 000 euros : un tour de magie qui fait mal à l’industrie européenne
articles.text:
Affiché à 31 400 €, le Leapmotor B10 est un SUV chinois relativement classique. Il n’est pas mémorable à conduire, ni même à regarder. Son équipement est en contrepartie plutôt riche mais ses possibilités de personnalisation bien limitées. Il se montre en revanche assez confortable et tout à fait pratique. Bref, assez quelconque en somme… Sauf qu’il revient aujourd’hui sur le devant de la scène en brandissant une nouvelle fois l’argument prix.
En étant désormais produit à l’usine Stellantis de Saragosse, en Espagne, le B10 s’affranchit des droits de douane imposés par l’Union Européenne sur les véhicules électriques importés de Chine. Surtout, il pourrait être éligible à la Prime Coup de Pouce récompensant les modèles à batterie fabriqués en Europe. Un avantage indéniable qui lui permettra d’abaisser significativement son tarif pour aller chercher à coup sûr de nouveaux clients.
Pourquoi produire en Europe devient indispensable pour les marques chinoises
Pour établir ce plan d’attaque, l’usine de Saragosse n’a pas été choisie au hasard. Le site possède en effet une forte capacité de production pouvant accueillir la fabrication d’un nouveau modèle. Le B10 sera ainsi assemblé aux côtés des Peugeot 208, Opel Corsa et Lancia Ypsilon. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans la stratégie FaSTLAne 2030 du géant automobile, qui souhaite renforcer fortement sa compétitivité industrielle.
C’est ainsi que la politique européenne peut se transformer en opportunité selon Silvia Vernetti, porte-parole de Stellantis : « la transition électrique doit aussi être une transition industrielle. Si notre partenariat constitue notre stratégie, Saragosse est la preuve que nous pouvons conjuguer technologie mondiale, compétitivité et capacités industrielles européennes ». Cela fait bien les affaires de Leapmotor, qui espère se développer en Europe.
Que change ce virage industriel pour les clients français ?
C’est ce que confirme Jiangming Zhu, PDG de la marque chinoise : « nos racines sont en Chine et notre ambition est mondiale. L’Europe est un élément stratégique de cette ambition, et la production à Saragosse nous permet de rapprocher notre technologie des marchés et des clients européens ». Faire les yeux doux à l’Europe est aussi synonyme d’une avance cruciale sur les autres constructeurs chinois.
La taxe de 30,7 % s’appliquant habituellement aux modèles électriques chinois importés dans l’Union Européenne devrait logiquement sauter. Mieux, la Prime Coup de Pouce, dont le montant oscille entre 3 600 et 6 100 €, pourrait tomber pour le SUV électrique. S’il valide tous les prérequis exigés par l’Union Européenne, le B10 verrait son prix de départ tomber potentiellement à 25 300 €. Imbattable pour un modèle familial offrant 361 km d’autonomie !

articles.title: Los 10 mejores videojuegos de Super Mario en 3D: desde Odissey hasta Mario 64
articles.text:
Super Mario en 3D no es un único videojuego, sino el nombre que reúne a las entregas de la saga de Nintendo diseñadas en tres dimensiones.
A diferencia de los títulos clásicos en 2D, donde Mario avanza principalmente de izquierda a derecha, estas aventuras permiten recorrer escenarios con profundidad, altura y libertad de movimiento de 360 grados.
El juego Super Mario Odyssey y Super Mario 3D World + Bowser’s Fury están disponibles en Nintendo Switch; Super Mario 3D Land fue lanzado para Nintendo 3DS; Super Mario Galaxy y Super Mario Galaxy 2 llegaron a Wii, mientras que Super Mario 64 debutó en Nintendo 64.
Existe Super Mario 3D All-Stars, una colección para Nintendo Switch que reúne versiones remasterizadas en alta definición de Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine y Super Mario Galaxy.
La selección combina juegos de exploración libre con otros de niveles más lineales, aunque todos conservan el salto y el movimiento tridimensional como eje de la experiencia.
Los mejores juegos de Super Mario en 3D
- Super Mario Odyssey.
Encabeza la lista por su estructura de exploración libre. Mario viaja por distintos reinos a bordo de la nave Odyssey para rescatar a la princesa Peach. Su principal novedad es Cappy, un sombrero vivo que permite capturar enemigos y objetos para usar sus habilidades. Fue lanzado en 2017 para Nintendo Switch.
- Super Mario 3D World + Bowser’s Fury.
Combina niveles de plataformas lineales con un modo cooperativo para hasta cuatro jugadores. El traje de gato permite a Mario trepar paredes y modificar su desplazamiento.
La edición de Nintendo Switch incorpora Bowser’s Fury, una expansión de exploración abierta en la que Mario recorre un archipiélago junto a Bowsy.
- Bowser’s Fury.
Merece un lugar propio por su cambio de formato dentro de Super Mario 3D World + Bowser’s Fury. La expansión lleva a Mario a un entorno más abierto, con islas conectadas y desafíos distribuidos en el escenario. El enfrentamiento con Furia Bowser marca el ritmo de la exploración.
- Super Mario 3D World.
Lanzado originalmente para Wii U, trasladó el diseño de plataformas con meta final a un espacio tridimensional. Su cámara más fija acerca la experiencia a los juegos clásicos en 2D, pero mantiene la libertad de movimiento en cada nivel y potencia el juego cooperativo.
- Super Mario Galaxy 2.
Llevó de nuevo a Mario al espacio y profundizó la fórmula basada en planetas pequeños, superficies curvas y cambios de gravedad. Su diseño propone niveles construidos alrededor de desafíos concretos, con saltos y recorridos que aprovechan la física de cada escenario.
- Super Mario Galaxy.
Presentó ese concepto en 2007. Mario viaja entre galaxias y planetas de distintos tamaños, donde caminar por una esfera o saltar hacia otra superficie modifica la dirección del recorrido. La gravedad se convirtió en una de las mecánicas centrales de la aventura.
- Super Mario 3D Land.
Adaptó las plataformas tridimensionales a Nintendo 3DS. El juego combina niveles breves, límite de tiempo y un banderín de meta, con una cámara pensada para ordenar la acción y facilitar los saltos.
- Super Mario Sunshine.
Cambió el Reino Champiñón por una isla marcada por pintura y suciedad. Mario utiliza la mochila de agua A.C.U.A.C. para limpiar escenarios, atacar enemigos y planear durante los saltos.
- Super Mario 3D All-Stars.
No es una aventura inédita, sino una recopilación que permite jugar en Nintendo Switch a tres clásicos: Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine y Super Mario Galaxy.
- Super Mario 64
Cierra la lista como el pionero de la saga. Lanzado en 1996, estableció las bases del control de Mario en entornos tridimensionales: correr, saltar, nadar y explorar el castillo de Peach para conseguir Estrellas.

articles.title: Agents are breaking AI economics, and the fix starts in the data layer - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Agents are breaking AI economics, and the fix starts in the data layer
When companies talk about the cost of artificial intelligence, the conversation almost always starts with models: which one to use, what it costs per million tokens, and whether a smaller model is “good enough.” That made sense when AI meant a chatbot.
It makes much less sense now that agents are doing real work in production. A single agent task can fire off dozens of queries, pull context from several systems, call a model several times and write results back. What a task costs and how fast it runs are increasingly determined by everything that happens around the model.
During a pre-briefing ahead of this week’s expansion of the company’s AI Data Plane, Tim Finley, Couchbase Inc.‘s senior vice president of AI, highlighted a key trend. The company announced native Amazon Bedrock integration with semantic caching, a fully managed Agent Memory and Model Context Protocol server on Amazon Web Services, and vector search in its analytics engine, now called Operational Insights.
The more interesting part is the reasoning behind the release, which points to a problem most information technology leaders haven’t fully accounted for.
Agents are a different kind of user
Finley opened with queuing theory to explain the problem. As load rises, latency grows faster than traffic, and agents quickly drive upload. Finley cited a Cisco Systems Inc. study finding that agents generate 450% more traffic per task than humans performing the same work, along with Cloudflare data showing that machine traffic surpassed human traffic on the web in June, about 18 months earlier than forecast.
“Capacity plans built for human growth curves are likely to break,” Finley said. He described agents as “probably the nastiest, most demanding user that you can ever imagine when it comes to running a system.” I think this is the most underappreciated risk in agentic AI. Most production databases were sized for people who click, wait and click again. Agents fan out into parallel tasks, need current and historical data in the same loop, and never sleep. Treat them as “just more users,” and the data tier becomes the bottleneck, usually right after a successful pilot convinces the business to scale.
Companies are downgrading intelligence to pay the bill
The pre-briefing comment that should concern IT and business leaders was the trade-off between model choice and capabilities. “Customers are actively sacrificing intelligence by downgrading models because of the bill once they hit scale,” Finley said. That matches what I hear from IT leaders.
The pilot runs on a frontier model, the results look great, then finance sees the inference bill at production volume, and the team falls back to a cheaper model, degrading the results that justified the project. Often, that trade-off isn’t necessary because much of the spend is waste: the same questions sent repeatedly, bloated prompts,and agents that start every session from scratch.
This is where Couchbase’s announcements can help mitigate the tradeoff. Semantic caching serves similar queries without calling the model again, and the company says it cuts large language model calls by 40% to 60%. It also claims Agent Memory reduces token usage by 33% to 45% compared with alternatives on the LoCoMo, or long-term conversational memory, benchmark, and that vector-based context retrieval produces prompts about 70% smaller than those from full-context approaches.
These are Couchbase’s own numbers, and results will depend heavily on how repetitive a workload is. But the direction is right: most organizations have more room to cut token waste than to improve model quality.
Convergence versus consolidation
During the briefing, Finley explained the difference between convergence and consolidation. The latter reduces the number of tools you pay for. With the former, “a converged system is greater than the sum of its parts” because every capability shares a single copy of the data.
The vector search in Operational Insights is a good example. Finley walked through a phone manufacturer’s use case to determine which factories are linked to the most positive battery-life reviews. Typically, that involves a relational database, a key-value store, a vector database, an ETL pipeline and a warehouse.
Couchbase says it answers it in one SQL query, using “cluster by” much like “group by,” then writes the result back so agents can read it. “There has been a fallacy for a long time with analytics that a really great insight was the finish line,” Finley said. “We think it’s the action.”
Every hop between systems adds latency, introduces a sync job that can fail, adds another security model and creates another place where data can go stale. An agent working from stale data can be confidently wrong. Fewer moving parts matter as much for AI speed and accuracy as they do for cost.
The competitive picture
Snowflake Inc. and Databricks Inc. have both bet on Postgres, and Postgres with pgvector is the default for many AI teams because it’s free and familiar. Finley, who came from AWS’ database business, didn’t discount this value, but he argued that it strains at Fortune 2000 scale once vector counts reach the hundreds of millions. Couchbase also points to deployments at LinkedIn, Amadeus and telecom software provider Mavenir.
Brandon Larson, senior vice president and general manager of Cloud, AI & IMS Business Strategy, explained, “Couchbase has been a key component in achieving high availability in Mavenir’s voice solutions for years,” explained Brandon Larson, senior vice president and general manager of Cloud, AI & IMS Business Strategy. “Now we’re creating new AI voice services that require getting reliable context fast, and Mavenir is building that context layer with Couchbase because of their proven performance in production.”
Recommendations for IT leaders
Model agent load, not user load. Rebuild capacity plans around parallel fan-out, many queries per task and sustained bursts. Load-test the data tier with simulated agent traffic before scaling a pilot. If latency climbs faster than request volume, the queuing effect is at work.
Measure cost per task before downgrading models. Find out how many prompts are near-duplicates, how much context is resent each turn, and how often agents rebuild state they already have. Caching, memory, and better retrieval should be the first levers. Switching to a cheaper model should be a quality decision, not a budget one.
Count the hops in your agent loop. Map every system and sync pipeline an agent touches to complete a typical task. Each hop is a latency cost, a failure point and a governance gap. Whatever vendor you choose, that map shows where convergence pays off.
Treat caches and memory like production data. Semantic caches and agent memory store customer context and model outputs. Apply retention policies, user-level isolation, access controls and audit trails from day one. A cache that returns a “similar” answer to a genuinely different question poses a correctness risk, so tune and monitor similarity thresholds.
Insist on proof at your scale. Vendor benchmarks are a starting point. Test at your data volumes, concurrency and vector counts, and check both recall and throughput. What works at 10 million vectors may not at a billion.
Keep the memory layer portable. Agent frameworks are evolving quickly. Choose memory services that work across LangGraph, CrewAI, LlamaIndex and other frameworks, so switching frameworks doesn’t require rebuilding the most valuable part of the stack.
Final thoughts
The industry has spent two years arguing over models. The next two will focus on the cost and reliability of running agents at scale, and much of that will be decided in the data layer. Couchbase is right that agents are a fundamentally different kind of user, and its focus on token economics speaks to the conversation chief information officers are having with chief financial officers right now. Its challenge is winning the architectural argument before customers default to the Postgres-plus-point-tools stack they already know.
Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

articles.title: Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Work management context for AI agents with Smartsheet MCP on AWS
AI agents are most useful when they can act on the real work happening across your organization. Work management involves complex, cross-functional tasks such as updating project timelines, reassigning tasks, and surfacing status. AI agents can support you with these without anyone switching tools. Smartsheet, the work management platform for managing projects, portfolios, and operations, has launched a generally available Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server.
With the Smartsheet MCP Server, AI assistants can read, write, and manage Smartsheet data through a standardized protocol. The protocol spans more than 40 tools for exploring, creating, and managing sheets, rows, columns, and automations. You can update task statuses, create rows, and modify project structure directly through natural language.
In this post, we walk through two ways you can connect it to your existing workflows. Amazon Quick is an agentic AI workspace built for business users, project managers, and operations teams. They can ask questions, update sheets, and build dashboards through natural language without writing code. Kiro is an agentic IDE where developers connect to Smartsheet through MCP to reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.
Architecture overview
The following diagram shows how the Smartsheet MCP Server sits as the central integration layer connecting to AWS services. Amazon Quick and Kiro connect directly as MCP clients.
Amazon Quick serves knowledge workers, project managers, and operations teams who want to query, update, and automate Smartsheet through natural language. With Kiro, developers can reference project specs, update task status, and track dependencies without leaving their coding workflow.
The following architecture diagram illustrates these integration paths: the Smartsheet MCP Server in the center, with Amazon Quick and Kiro as MCP clients on the left, and Smartsheet’s API and data layer on the right.
Sprint management with Amazon Quick and Kiro
Consider a software engineering team that tracks their sprint in Smartsheet. Tasks, owners, statuses, and blockers all live in a project sheet. Here’s what each path looks like for the same team:
When a user such as a project manager wants to check which sprint tasks are blocked this week, they can ask Amazon Quick through natural language. The Amazon Quick chat agent queries the Smartsheet MCP Server, pulls the relevant rows, and surfaces a summary with owner names and due dates. The response is generated from live Smartsheet data without building a report or dashboard.
For developers who are fixing bugs or working through features, they can ask Kiro to pull the current sprint sheet and show them the open backend tasks assigned to them. Kiro queries Smartsheet through MCP and surfaces the list inline. When the fix is committed, a Kiro hook automatically updates the corresponding row status to Complete.
Prerequisites
Smartsheet MCP Server delivers precisely structured context, including row relationships, column types, cell history, and comments. This produces token-efficient payload sizes rather than returning raw API payloads. This engineering decision compounds into reduced cost and improved latency at scale when running hundreds of AI-assisted queries across a project portfolio. To learn how Smartsheet built their remote MCP server on AWS, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS.
Before connecting the Smartsheet MCP Server to Amazon Quick and Kiro, verify that you have the following in place:
- An active AWS account with appropriate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for the service you’re connecting (Amazon Quick, or Kiro)
- A Smartsheet account on a Business, Enterprise, or AWM plan.
- A Smartsheet Personal Access Token, or OAuth credentials if your client supports the OAuth flow.
- For Amazon Quick: Author or higher permissions in your Amazon Quick account.
- For Kiro: Kiro IDE installed from kiro.dev with Node.js available in your environment.
The Smartsheet MCP Server is available at three regional endpoints. It uses Streamable HTTP transport (MCP spec versions 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26) and is authenticated with either OAuth 2.0 or a Personal Access Token.
- Commercial US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
- EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu.
- AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au.
Both options expose the same Smartsheet toolset. The right choice depends on where your work gets done:
Choose Amazon Quick if you need a fully managed, organization-wide solution your whole team can use: no app registration, only pre-built OAuth, and it scales across knowledge workers in your enterprise.
Choose Kiro if you’re a developer who wants something lightweight: no infrastructure, only a config file and a personal access token, scoped to your own workflow.
Amazon Quick integration
Amazon Quick includes Smartsheet as a pre-built connector in its directory. That means reading project status, updating rows, creating discussions, and surfacing risks, all in the same interface your business users already work in.
Amazon Quick makes that integration available across the organization, from project managers and operations teams to business users who manage work in Smartsheet.
To add the Quick integration:
- In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors and find Smartsheet in the directory.
- Select the Smartsheet connector tile.
- Enter the following integration details: 
         
  - Name – Descriptive name for your Smartsheet integration.
  - Keep the Connection type and Auth configuration settings as is.
  - Base URL – https://mcp.smartsheet.com.
  - Client ID – App client ID from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
  - Client Secret – App secret from your Smartsheet Developer Tools app registration.
  - Token URL – https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token.
  - Auth URL – https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize.
- Choose Next.
- On the Manage Tools & Permissions page, you see a list of available tools. Choose Next.
- On the Publish page, choose who can access this connection, and then choose Publish.
- Choose Next.
After you’re connected, your Amazon Quick chat agent can work with Smartsheet data through natural language:
- “What projects in our portfolio are currently At Risk?”
- “Update the status of the authentication task in the Backend API sheet to Complete.”
- “Create a summary of all overdue items across the Q3 Roadmap and send it to the team.”
Kiro integration
Kiro is the right path when developers want Smartsheet project context available directly in their development environment, alongside their code, without context-switching.
Kiro is built around spec-driven development. It turns high-level prompts into structured specs, then into working code, docs, and tests. MCP servers are how Kiro gets real-world context by connecting to documentation, databases, APIs, and enterprise systems to ground its agent in live data rather than training-time knowledge.
A Kiro feature called powers is a one-click installable bundle that packages a curated MCP server with steering files and hooks. It gives the Kiro coding agent a new capability out of the box. For Smartsheet, configuring the connection takes a single JSON configuration block and from that point, the Kiro agent can reference live project data as part of a development workflow.
To connect the Smartsheet MCP Server to Kiro, add it to your Kiro MCP configuration (.kiro/settings/mcp.json for workspace scope). For a full walkthrough, see Getting Started with Kiro and MCP Servers:
This configuration uses the Personal Access Token (API key) approach. For production deployments, OAuth is recommended.
Set SMARTSHEET_API_TOKEN to your Smartsheet Personal Access Token in your environment. Kiro loads MCP servers as background processes on startup. After it’s initialized, Smartsheet tools are available to the Kiro agent across all modes: chat, spec planning, and hooks-based automation. Full details in the Smartsheet MCP Server Documentation.
From there, Kiro can reference Smartsheet data as part of development workflows:
- “Check the Backend API project sheet for any open bugs and generate a prioritized fix list.”
- “Pull the Q3 Roadmap sheet and create a spec for the features marked In Progress.”
Enterprise governance
For builders deploying in regulated or enterprise environments, the Smartsheet MCP Server security model is built on the same infrastructure and permissions layer as the Smartsheet REST API. It’s not a new trust boundary:
- OAuth 2.0 and Personal Access Token authentication: choose the auth method supported by your MCP client.
- User-level permission enforcement: agents can only access data the authenticated user has permission to see. No privilege escalation through natural language prompts.
- Organization-level AI controls: system administrators can turn on or off AI features globally. Write-tool access is configurable by user group.
- Streamable HTTP transport: firewall allowlisting is done by fully qualified domain name (FQDN) (mcp.smartsheet.com), not IP address.
For compliance architects, the MCP Server doesn’t store prompts, and prompt content stays between the AI client and the model. Smartsheet sees only the structured tool calls and their results.
Clean up
If you followed this walkthrough and want to remove the integration afterward, here’s how to undo each path:
Amazon Quick
- In the Amazon Quick console, navigate to Connectors.
- Select your Smartsheet connector.
- Choose Delete to remove the connection. This revokes the OAuth token and stops agent access to Smartsheet data.
Kiro
- Open your MCP configuration file (.kiro/settings/mcp.json).
- Remove the smartsheet-us entry from the mcpServers object.
- Restart Kiro to unload the server.
Next steps
For background on how the server works, see How Smartsheet built a remote MCP server on AWS. After you’ve connected the Smartsheet MCP Server to your system of choice, here are four actions we recommend trying:
You can ask the chat agent to monitor your active project sheets, identify rows marked Blocked or At Risk. You can also ask to annotate projects with a discussion comment, and deliver a structured summary to your team through your preferred channel. This would be an example workflow that chains get_sheet_summary, search, and create_discussion_on_row.
The agent can also retrieve data through the Smartsheet MCP Server to reconcile task statuses between your issue tracker and your Smartsheet project plan. It can flag drift between the two, and update the affected rows, using get_sheet_summary, get_columns, update_rows, and create_discussion_on_row in sequence.
You can also try to aggregate project health signals across your reports and dashboards. You can use it to produce a structured briefing without manual data gathering, drawing on list_reports, get_report, list_dashboards, get_dashboard, and search.
Lastly, you can use the agent to follow every write with a discussion comment explaining what changed and why. This creates a human-readable audit trail inside Smartsheet through the combination of update_rows and create_discussion_on_row.
All four patterns work across the preceding paths: Amazon Quick for business-user-facing workflows, and Kiro for developer-initiated actions.
Building something with Smartsheet MCP and AWS? Share what you’re working on in the comments, or connect with us in the Smartsheet Developer Community.

articles.title: China’s tech giants drop $35 billion on export-compliant Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 workstation GPU orders to power AI ambitions, according to reports — ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent order 3 million cards despite warnings that only 10% of orders are fulfillable
articles.text:
China’s tech giants drop $35 billion on export-compliant Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 workstation GPU orders to power AI ambitions, according to reports — ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent order 3 million cards despite warnings that only 10% of orders are fulfillable
Surging demand for Nvidia's chips in China isn't stopping
Chinese technology giants ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly spent over $35 billion on orders for more than 3 million Nvidia RTX Pro 5500 workstation GPUs. The huge order for the RTX Pro 5500, fully compliant with U.S. restrictions on exports of AI-capable GPUs to China, is reportedly far beyond Nvidia's planned production for this card. As a result, Nvidia has, according to sources who spoke to Reuters, told its customers that it isn't in a position to fill the orders as it far outstrips its planned production for this GPU.
The RTX Pro 5500 is a workstation GPU with the same number of CUDA cores as its flagship RTX 5090 GPU, but with 84GB of GDDR7 memory attached, making it a good option for AI applications. The RTX Pro 5500 is a popular choice at the moment for Chinese buyers as exporting it isn't currently restricted by the U.S. government. It's less powerful than the H200 and B300, Nvidia's AI-focused GPUs for the enterprise market, but those GPUs remain either banned or heavily restricted. As China competes with the U.S. in the race to produce newer, better AI models, GPUs like the RTX Pro 5500 continue to be indispensable.
The report reveals some interesting data about the Chinese tech firms orders. Two of its sources revealed that the cards are priced at around $11,400 each, reaching a total order value of $35 billion. Meanwhile, another source suggested that Nvidia has informed its partners that it may only be able to deliver enough cards to meet between 5% and 10% of the demand. Meanwhile, Nvidia is reportedly in a position to only produce 3 million RTX Pro 5500 cards globally in 2027.
Neither Nvidia nor the three Chinese companies have confirmed any of this on the record. However, an Nvidia spokesman told Reuters that demand from the Chinese market for these chips has faced "unprecedented growth since 2022" since export restrictions were introduced. "U.S. firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated U.S. export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly half a decade ago, and China's own limits on U.S. imports."
While trade hostility between the U.S. and China shows no sign of abating, demand for Nvidia's GPUs hasn't slowed down, despite U.S. attempts to restrict Nvidia's ability to export to China. Meanwhile, export-restricted Nvidia AI chips continue to reach China despite the restrictions, bypassing the Trump administration's efforts in the process.

articles.title: Huawei et DeepSeek s’allient pour concevoir une puce IA capable de rivaliser avec NVIDIA
articles.text:
La Chine continue son chemin vers la fin d'une dépendance aux GPU de NVIDIA. Et ça pourrait notamment passer par une alliance entre Huawei et Deepseek.
Aujourd'hui, les acteurs chinois de l'IA ne peuvent toujours pas se passer de NVIDIA pour se doter des composants les plus puissants pour entraîner leurs IA. Mais il y a de l'amélioration ces derniers temps, avec l'ascension de Huawei dans le domaine des accélérateurs IA. Et le géant pourrait faire encore mieux à l'avenir avec ce partenariat avec l'un des plus grands noms de l'intelligence artificielle dans l'empire du Milieu.
Deepseek et Huawei vont travailler ensemble sur la conception de puces IA plus performantes
Huawei et Deepseek sont dorénavant partenaires dans la conception de puces IA, selon le média The Information. Des ingénieurs de Huawei ont ainsi déjà été dépêchés dans les locaux de Deepseek.
Ils peuvent ainsi intégrer les retours faits du côté du spécialiste de l'intelligence artificielle. Ensemble, ils souhaitent aussi mettre en place un écosystème open source intégrant notamment un modèle IA local qui prendra en charge l'ensemble de la pile logicielle et de l'architecture matérielle.
Encore du chemin avant d'arriver à se passer de NVIDIA ?
Deepseek pourra ainsi transmettre à Huawei les éventuels problèmes rencontrés par les données de calcul lors de l'exécution d'un modèle IA. Huawei de son côté veut notamment améliorer l'efficacité de la bande passante mémoire de ses puces.
Dans ce partenariat, il y a aussi un aspect commercial, avec Deepseek qui voudrait utiliser les puces Huawei Ascend 950 DT d'ici la fin d'année. En 2027, Deepseek voudrait par ailleurs donner la priorité à la génération suivante Ascend 960 DT, qui va sortir lors des premiers mois de l'année prochaine.
Reste qu'il faudra voir à quel moment ces deux grands noms pourront réussir à produire des composants à la hauteur de ce que fait NVIDIA. Car, pour rappel, aujourd'hui, le GPU NVIDIA B300 affiche des performances en moyenne sept fois supérieures dans les calculs d'IA standards par rapport à la Huawei Ascend 950.
Source : Huawei Central

articles.title: CISA: SafePay ransomware hit over 600 critical infrastructure orgs
articles.text:
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) says the SafePay ransomware gang has breached over 600 critical infrastructure organizations worldwide since 2024.
In a joint report with the FBI, the U.S. Secret Service (USSS), Germany's Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz, and the UK's National Crime Agency and North West Regional Organised Crime Unit, the federal agency added that paying ransoms does not guarantee recovery of files encrypted in ransomware attacks and urged victims to report incidents to law enforcement.
"SafePay is one of the most active ransomware groups and have affected businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe, and Australia—including at least 600 organizations from multiple critical infrastructure sectors since August 2024," CISA said.
"SafePay threat actors gain initial access through a variety of means, including credential exposure, brute force password attacks, and exploiting virtual private network (VPN) access—particularly the IP addresses of VPN provider 'Mullvad'."
The co-authoring agencies advised network defenders to secure their networks against the ransomware group's attacks by restricting administrative tools and privileges to block lateral movement after compromise and implementing multifactor authentication (MFA) and identity, credential, and access management (ICAM) policies for better account security.
Security teams should also keep systems updated, focusing on flaws affecting VPNs, firewalls, and other edge devices added to CISA's catalog of actively exploited vulnerabilities because they're often targeted in SafePay attacks for initial access to victims' networks.
"They also use phished account profiles to infiltrate networks and exploit common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs) for edge devices and other internet-exposed systems through automated scripts," CISA added. "SafePay actors may disrupt recovery operations by deleting shadow copies and resetting network-attached storage devices containing backups."
The advisory also includes indicators of compromise (IOCs) and tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to previous SafePay ransomware activity observed between November 2024 and August 2026 during FBI, USSS, and Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz investigations.
Unlike similar operations, SafePay emerged in August 2024 as a private ransomware group that doesn't work with affiliates.
It has since added hundreds of victims from North America, South America, Europe, and Australia to its dark web leak site, but the actual number of victims it has breached and attempted to extort is higher, since it lists only those who don't pay on its leak platform.
This ransomware group is also known for double-extortion tactics, stealing sensitive documents before encrypting the victims' systems and threatening to leak all the stolen data online if a ransom isn't paid.
Since the start of 2025, SafePay has slowly filled the gap left by BlackCat (ALPHV) and LockBit ransomware, becoming one of the most active ransomware operations.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Steam Next Fest : les joueurs réclament un filtre pour repérer les jeux générés par IA
articles.text:
Après avoir longtemps interdit les jeux générés par IA, Valve a finalement assoupli sa politique sur Steam et autorisé leur publication sur son store, à condition que les développeurs signalent l’utilisation de cette technologie. Une mention qui apparaît sur la page du jeu, mais qui serait insuffisante pour certains joueurs.
À l’occasion du Steam Next Fest, des millions d’entre eux se retrouvent sur la plateforme pour découvrir les prochaines nouveautés marquantes du jeu vidéo. Cependant l’événement se serait transformé en « vitrine de jeux bon marché produits par une IA », rapporte RespawnFirst. De quoi alimenter la colère des joueurs, qui réclament un moyen plus simple de repérer ces titres.
Une demande d’identification claire
Sur Reddit, de nombreux joueurs PC expriment leur mécontentement face à la multiplication des jeux générés par IA sur Steam. Certains dénoncent la qualité des miniatures générées, tandis que d’autres regrettent de ne pas pouvoir exclure ces titres de leurs recherches. « À quoi bon exiger l’utilisation et le balisage de l’IA si l’on ne peut pas la filtrer ? », s’interroge un utilisateur.
En effet, si certains jeux affichent bien une mention signalant l’utilisation de l’IA, il n’est actuellement pas possible de s’appuyer sur cette information pour les filtrer directement dans les résultats de recherche.
Pour le moment, Valve n’a pas répondu à ces demandes. Il existe néanmoins une solution alternative. Les joueurs peuvent se tourner vers l’extension navigateur open source « AI warning for Steam », rapporte RespawnFirst. Une fois installée, elle permet de flouter, dans les résultats de recherche, les titres ou les contenus pour lesquels l’utilisation de l’IA a été détectée. Loin d’être aussi pratique qu’un filtre intégré, cet outil permet déjà de faire un premier tri.
