articles.title: AI is an Amplifier: Scale High Performance, Not Dysfunction
articles.text:
Transcript
Nathen Harvey: For those of you that are unfamiliar with DORA, I just want to level set on which Dora we're talking about here. There are quite a few. There's the small child, Dora. She is one of my favorites. How many of you have watched that show ever, Dora the Explorer? The beautiful thing about Dora is every transformational journey she goes on, she has a map in her backpack and she completes it in three steps. Now, Swiper's always there trying to set her off course. I'm here to tell you that your AI adoption journey is going to be just like that. It's three easy steps with just a little bit of Swiper in the way. Of course, we're here in Europe, so we also have DORA, the Digital Operational Resilience Act. I do assure you that if you and your team get better at delivering and operating software and doing this in an automated fashion, that's going to make those regulators from the Digital Operational Resilience Act happy because you'll be more resilient.
Where I come from in the United States, there are a few states within the United States that have a specific set of legislation. They call it Designated Outdoor Refreshment Areas. This means that you can walk around with a beer as long as you stay within the Designated Outdoor Refreshment Area. That, I have to admit, is probably my second favorite DORA in the world. There are others, but I can't take you through all of them. What I am here to talk about is this research program, DORA, that's been running for well over a decade now. This is really research into how do teams get better at doing the technology? How do we get better at IT? How do we get better at software delivery? How do we get better not just with the technology, but as teams, as people? How do we drive our businesses forward and really serve our customers?
DORA used to be an acronym, but we've deacronymed it. DORA now stands for nothing, which doesn't quite sound right either. We have a tagline, that's what DORA stands for. It stands for get better at getting better. The interesting thing is, and we'll get to this at the end of the talk, I'm actually starting to question our tagline. I'm worried that it's not going to serve us right, right now. More on that ahead.
The 2025 DORA Research
If you know anything about DORA, you might know that we run a survey. We run a giant survey every year, and maybe you've participated in that survey. If you have, thank you for sharing your data and your insights with us. It's really helpful. Last year, we had nearly 5,000 people take our survey. We augment that with additional qualitative research. Qualitative research is basically a qualitative researcher sitting down and having interviews with practitioners, with leaders, really trying to get a little bit more context around what's actually happening.
I'm going to share some data from our most recent survey. There is a little footnote on this slide here that you'll see. This global survey was conducted between June 13th and July 21st, 2025. I'm going to tell you some things about how AI adoption is going. Do you think it's accurate? I might be lying to you. We'll leave that for you to sort out. Last year we published this report, the State of AI-Assisted Software Development. You can download the 2025 report here, dora.dev/dora-report-2025. You can grab that report there and read it. It's 140 pages long, so I'm going to summarize it for you. I am going to test you now because I'm putting up another QR code. This one, I really want you to participate in this one. I want you to answer this question for me. What is stopping you? You just generated something with an AI, or maybe one of your colleagues just generated something with an AI.
What's stopping you from shipping it to production right now? Why not go directly to production? Let's just see what we're thinking here. What's stopping you? Trust. You don't trust the solution. Governance, security, quality, uncertainty. Being fired, someone put in there. It's good. It's interesting because might you be fired if you're not using the AI also? It's interesting. You can keep throwing some answers in there. I think they're fascinating. Fear. I don't know how. We are a bank. Stop using that as an excuse, you could still do better.
AI Adoption and Use
I want to talk about AI adoption and use and what our data found. Remember, how do we collect our data? Surveys. Ninety percent of people tell the truth on surveys, 10% lie. This slide was, how many of you are using AI professionally at work? Ninety percent of our survey respondents said yes, and 10% said I'm not allowed to, so I better say no. Remember, this was June and July of last year. We're not going to ask this question again. Because, like I said, we've been doing this research for 10 years. Never once have we asked, do you use a computer at work? From this point forward, we can stop asking, do you use AI at work? Because, yes, you do. We're using it. How much do you rely on it? I think these numbers have probably changed. Reliance on something is different than just using a thing.
Like, if I rely on something and it goes away, that's problematic. What we see here is that about 35% of our respondents say I rely on it a little or not at all. A majority of our respondents are saying, yes, I rely on using that AI for that particular task or set of tasks that I'm doing. I think that's really interesting. Is it helping? We'll get to that. This one is also really fascinating to me. We asked, think back to a recent work day, about how many hours did you interact with AI? Now, stop. I get it, though. I'm falling back into these bad marital patterns. I'm sitting at home and I'm working out something with the AI and it's getting close to dinner time, and my wife is ready for me to stop working. I know like, just one more prompt. Just one more, I'll be there in a minute.
One more prompt. Please, not the 12 hours. If you're the long tail in this chart, please get up, walk away. If you're sitting here in this talk, close the laptop, stop with the AI. Just listen to me for a minute. That'll make me feel better. It will be better for your long-term health, I promise you. The interesting thing here is the median hours, median of two hours working with AI. There are other studies, not our studies and not studies that I will quote, but there are good studies, nonetheless, that ask this question about, how much time a week does a software engineer typically spend actually writing code? The ranges vary pretty wildly, but 10%, 15%, 30% at the high end. How much is two hours in an eight-hour day? It's about 30. You're probably using AI to help you write code. Also, this is, I think, a bit of a challenge for us, are like how people perceive us as software engineers. AI is coming to take your job because it's going to write all of the code for you. It's going to take away that thing that you do 10% of your time, so therefore we don't need you anymore. That math doesn't math to me either. It doesn't work.
Is it helping you? How do you feel about using this? Your perceived impact on individual productivity, it's going up. You feel more productive. I feel like I'm getting more done. I feel more engaged with the work that I'm doing. I feel like I'm spending more time on good work, valuable work, maybe less time on toil. About 5%, slightly decreased, moderately decreased, or extremely decreased my productivity. I've certainly had those days working with AI as well. I've definitely had those days. This is really interesting. We've got high levels of reliance. We're using it a lot. We feel like it's really helping us improve. What about code quality? How's the quality of the codebase that you're working with? Also, improving. With about 10% saying it's actually a little bit worse now that we're using AI. Our codebase is a little bit worse off. This is a really hard question, like, how is it impacting code quality?
What do you mean by code quality? This is one of our challenges as researchers. We don't know. We want you to tell us what do we mean by code quality. You just answer this question, we'll do the data. Here's the thing, how much do you trust the quality that AI is generating? How much trust do you have in whatever it is that it's generating? Whether it's code or that email that you're about to send off to your boss, or a prospect, or the financial plan that you've built for your family. How much do you trust that? Thirty percent trust it a little or not at all. I got to tell you, I'm on team somewhat, right there in the middle. I want to sit down and have coffee. If you were part of the 11%, that say you trust it a great deal or you trust it not at all, if you fall into either of those buckets, you're both wrong.
You should not trust it a great deal. Those are probably the ones I want to talk to most. I want to understand that. How? What are you doing? The not at all, don't you feel the FOMO? You've got to start working with these skills. That great keynote, we've got to start learning in public and leaning in to these new ideas.
If I summarize that entire 2025 report for you in three slides, I'm going to do it right now. AI's primary role in software development is that of an amplifier. The greatest returns on your investments in AI are going to come from a strategic focus on the underlying organizational system. Without that foundation, AI has a tendency to create localized pockets of productivity that are often lost to downstream chaos. I saw a post on LinkedIn, someone lamenting the fact that they can now build something in hours, and it takes six weeks still for that thing to make it into the hands of a customer, to get into production. We've accelerated part of the system, but we're not yet as an industry thinking about the entire system in a holistic manner. That's exactly what we're seeing in our data as well.
Exploring AI's Relationship to Key Outcomes
We do like to report what you're telling us with DORA, we also try to understand and make some sense of the complexity that is your organization, that is these technology tools that we're working with. What is AI's relationship with key outcomes? I promise I'm only going to do this once with one chart. I'm going to teach you how to read this chart really quickly. What we do is we collect a bunch of data, we build a little model, and this tells us the shape of the world. Then, as researchers, we have this amazing capability. We can say, here's the shape of this complex world. Let's change just one thing and see what happens. I encourage you to go back to your organizations and try to change just one thing and see what happens. Because you can't. It's impossible. You can't do that. Our data, what we do, we build up this model.
We say, let's change one thing. What thing are we going to change? We're going to change the score that you achieved for AI adoption. We're going to ramp up AI adoption, change nothing else, and then run a bunch of simulations across our model. What happens? If the score that you receive for this outcome on the vertical bar stays the same, your dot will show up on that dash line, which represents zero. To the right of the dash line, that thing increased. To the left of the dash line, it decreased. Individual effectiveness increased the most. Software delivery instability increased. Just want to be super clear. It's probably not what you wanted. Organizational performance, time spent doing valuable work, code quality, product performance, software delivery throughput, it's probably do what you want, and team performance all improved. Burnout and friction, they basically stayed at zero. Those little bars that come out from the middle of that dot, that's our certainty rate.
We call those error bars. It's not just we that call them that, that's what they're called. The wider the bar, the less certain we are about this. The tighter it is, the more certain we are about it. If you look at burnout and friction, they're both pretty close to zero, and their error bars definitely overlap zero. For burnout, this probably makes sense in June or July. I'm going to maybe counter that. Imagine, you're at work, and it sucks. You feel burnt out. You question everything that you're doing. Your manager comes over and says, here's some AI. Guess what? Work still sucks. You still hate what you're doing. Like, that's not helping your burnout at all. Just handing you a new tool isn't going to help. We see that. The positive spin on this was, it didn't hurt, it didn't make it worse. I do worry right now, today.
How many of you are managing a fleet of agents right now? Maybe a fleet sounds too many, like three or four. If you're trying to do work with three or four agents, and they're all doing very different things, you might find yourself now bouncing from task to task to task. It's ok. It's cool. Because we are all, as humans, super good at multitasking, there's research that shows this. No, wait, it's the other way around. We're all shit at multitasking. It's cool. We'll just give it all to the agents. I've certainly found myself like, I told this agent the thing that I meant to tell that agent. The cognitive overload that we're taking on, I think we don't yet understand it. I worry that in this year's research, we're going to find very different results.
When we think about some of these things. Some are getting better. Some, like software delivery instability is getting worse. In DORA, the way that we measure software delivery instability is we look at how frequently are your pushes into production resulting in what I call the, oh, expletive moment. You've all been there. Push a change to production and you or someone around you shouts out an expletive. What are we going to do? We have to act right now. Like we're going to roll that back. We're going to push forward a hot fix. That's bad. That's software delivery instability. With AI, we see that going up. In 2024, so in the previous year's research, we saw software delivery instability going up and we saw software delivery throughput going down. This year, we see that it's improving. We're seeing changes over time. A lot of these changes have to do with the J-Curve of transformation of taking on anything new.
Anytime you take on something new, your organization will likely go through this pattern. You're going to bring in a new tool. There's going to be some low-hanging fruit. You're going to go pick that fruit. You're going to eat it. Things are going to look really good. Then all the low-hanging fruit will be consumed. Now you've got to get to the hard stuff. That's when it sucks. It gets hard. Software delivery instability starts to go up. You dip into this trough. Today, I would talk about that trough as there's a couple of things. There's software delivery instability. There's the trust that you don't have. With that trust comes a lot of verification of the tools. With that verification comes maybe the changing of your job. I'm a software engineer. I write code. No, I just review it. I just read other people's code, and it's not even people that are creating it anymore.
That's going to drop you down into this dip, the instability tax, the verification tax. There is another side. We've seen this all before. DORA's been researching, as I said, for over a decade. We were there as the cloud just started taking hold. Guess what happened in every organization when they brought on the cloud? Things got a little bit better. Then they got a lot worse. Then we figured out how to use this technology. The same thing with SRE practices. We've seen this in our data modeled over time. We know that this is what's happening. What we don't yet know, because all of this is so new and because the technology is changing so fast, how do you get there? How do you get to the other side? Collectively, we're learning that right now. We're all learning that together.
Team Performance - A Look at Seven Team Profiles
With DORA, we also want to look at how are teams performing? How are you doing? We've oftentimes looked at just software delivery performance, and published benchmarks on software delivery performance, and given names to things like low performers and elite performers. How many of you show up to work to be a low performer? I didn't think so. Some of you silently raised your hands, but you're sitting next to your manager, so I get it. I see you. We're engineers. We're supposed to be low performers. Like, let the computers do the things. We looked at more than just software delivery performance. In fact, we wanted to understand how are teams doing across these eight different factors: team performance, product performance, effectiveness, friction, burnout. Remember, we found that at least 90% of the people in our survey are using AI. What we also found were that there were seven unique team profiles when looked across those eight different characteristics.
The first thing that that tells us is it's not because of AI. If everyone's using AI and we're seeing vastly different, highly variable performance levels, it's not either the AI's fault or the AI that's making that happen. What do these seven team profiles look like? First, because we had seven, we couldn't just use low, medium, high, and elite. We had to come up with way more creative names. Some of these names, just by looking at the name, you might find yourself. You might find your team. Let's look at a chart, shall we? No, let's look at seven charts. No. You can't see anything here. These things are really hard to read. We did, you could call them crimes with this spider chart or this radar chart. They don't act the way that they should. We're not going to look at these charts because you can't see them anyhow.
Let's look at two of the different groups here. Constrained by process. Teams are running on a treadmill. Despite working on stable systems, their effort is consumed by inefficient processes, leading to high burnout and low impact. How many of you feel seen right now? You can see here, burnout is high. Friction is high, or I'll tell you because it says so there. Individual effectiveness is low. The time I'm spending doing valuable work is low. My software delivery instability, actually pretty good. It's lower than everyone else's. My throughput is a little bit lower than everyone else's as well. It's not the perfect team to be on. It's not terrible. We've seen worse. We're not really delivering a whole lot of value. Let's contrast that with harmonious high achievers. Now when you go back to work, you can tell boss, we're a harmonious high achiever. Like this is what excellence looks like, we think.
We've got a virtuous cycle, stable, low-friction environment, empowered teams delivering high-quality work sustainably and without burnout. We have to think about these things. Can we deliver quality sustainably? Can we do that with low levels of friction across the organization without burning our people out? These are really important considerations. Here's the thing. If we have everyone using AI and wild variance in the levels of team performance, how do we overcome that? What are some of the signals here? I have a question for you about just that. What one thing would you need to change in your environment to confidently trust the solutions that AI generates? We just had that question about what's stopping you. Let's explore that a little bit differently. What's stopping you? What's one thing you could change right now that would unlock some of that gate? Same QR code, new answers: guardrails, tests, testing, a harness, management, competency, end-to-end test, automated testing. There's one I'm looking for in particular, validation. My manager. That's real. Observability. Education. Access to better models. Governance. This is great.
DORA AI Capabilities Model
If it's not that you're using AI, maybe it has something to do with how you're using AI. We've seen this before. When we investigated the cloud years ago, we saw some teams that were getting a lot of great value out of cloud. Some teams that were like, it's slower and more expensive. Why did we move to the cloud? It wasn't because you had the cloud or not. It was how you used it. Dr. Nicole Forsgren talks about this a lot as having a membership to the gym. How many of you have a membership to the gym? How many of you go regularly? Just having the membership isn't enough. It's not going to make you fit. You have to do the work. We investigated this. We wanted to understand, are there specific things that help some teams get more value out of AI than others? What we identified were seven capabilities that when combined together with adoption, drive better outcomes.
You've probably heard a couple of themes. There was one talk talking about AI adoption, and AI deployment, and AI value. You don't get adoption just by buying the tools. You don't get value just by having adoption. You can't have impact without adoption. Frankly, this leads us to a lot of challenges. I was talking with Blanca around measurement. How do we know that it's working? Let's go measure it. I want you to be very careful with measurement. One of the most important things with measurement is to understand what is the question that we're trying to answer. I was talking to someone else, and we were talking about what's happening in their organization. They happen to sit on the board. They go to board meetings. The people on the board are like, what are we doing with AI? Are we using AI? Are we using it? Is everybody using it?
The only question they have is adoption. Tell them that you're adopting, show them the numbers, and stop. That's not enough. It is enough to answer their question today. That's all the measurement that you need to answer that question. Next year they might ask, you all adopted all this stuff, what is our return? Now we have a different question. I can guarantee you can't get to the returns if there is no adoption. You got to start there. Measuring adoption, we all know, is not enough. It's not enough. For the love of whatever you view as good and holy, stop measuring how many lines did the AI generate. How many of you as software engineers loved being measured on how many lines of code you wrote? Why is it different for an AI? It's a stupid metric. Stop. What does matter? These seven capabilities. Having these capabilities and conditions in your team, within your organization, will help take the adoption that you're so focused on and let it drive through to real outcomes that we care about.
We've got a clear and communicated stance. If you don't make it clear how, when, where, what AI you can and can't use within your organization, this will cause all kinds of friction for your employees. If I don't know if I'm supposed to use it, one of two things will happen. I simply won't use it, and I'll be fine with that. I'll blissfully work without AI. Or I'll know the power because I've used it at home and I'm going to bring it into work and I'm going to use it anyhow. Then I'm going to worry about getting caught and getting fired for that. Make sure that your stance is clear and communicated. Next up, we have a healthy data ecosystem and access to that internal data. You want the AI to do better for you? Make sure it understands what are the policies that your organization has?
Who are your customers that you're trying to feed? Let's make sure that all of that is accessible to the AI. The next two are two that really have nothing to do with AI. Strong version control practices. The AI can go down a really crazy path if you don't have the confidence that you can roll back those changes very easily. I've talked to so many people who've said, I find myself committing to version control much more frequently. To which I say, what are you talking about? Why weren't you committing to version control every two minutes? Why is this new? It is. It's time. Learn those version control practices. All you need to know how to do really is commit and to roll back. If you can safely and confidently do those, you'll be in a better place. The next one is also super important, working in small batches.
If DORA has found nothing else, it's that if you want to improve software delivery throughput, and software delivery instability, the best way to get there is through shipping smaller changes. When you work in small batches, you can reason about what you're changing. When something goes wrong, you can reason about how to undo that, how to fix that thing. When you roll out changes, try not to roll them out to everyone all at once. Do we have progressive delivery? Can we slowly roll things out? Working in small batches is a powerful thing. Unfortunately, the bots came along, and they're like, "I see your small batches. I'm going to raise you this 50,000-line PR. Here's a small batch for you. Ship it." Even the bots do better if we give them smaller, well-defined tasks. It just makes sense.
Then two that I want to dig into a little bit further, user-centric focus and quality internal platforms. Having a user-centric focus, every piece of software that we create is made for humans. Even if the consumers of that software are bots, we're creating it for humans. The end goal is that this software makes someone's life better. That's why we're here. AI, maybe it's a forcing function for us. As software engineers, our job is not to write code. Our job is to solve problems. Our job is to understand who our users are and build the things that they need, the things that are going to improve their lives. This is fundamentally changing the work that we do. I, personally, I'm optimistic that this is helping us get closer to our users, better understand and have empathy for them, and build better solutions for them. One of the things that we found in our research, in the data, was that when you have a user-centric focus, your team performance improves.
The other thing that we found that was really interesting was when you don't have a user-centric focus, your team performance actually decreases. This is really powerful. I think when it comes to AI, there's a really fascinating thing that we can do now. Yes, AI can generate that 50,000-line PR in the time that it would have taken you to create a 10-line PR. It can do things a lot faster. What else does this do for us? This really unlocks optionality. Now I can prototype five things in less time than it took me to prototype one thing. You know what we're really bad at? Is understanding exactly what our user wants. Let's go build six things. Let's go build 10 things and try them out. Let's debate them as a team. Let's bring in some users to talk about them before we invest in actually productionalizing one of them and shipping it off to production.
Wait, but why just one? We've been building A/B test frameworks forever. Why not A-B-C-D-E-F-G? How many different things can we be actually running in production, getting real user feedback on to help us make better decisions? If you have the capability to enable your product development team to help you build higher fidelity prototypes that we can then explore lots of different options, we can converge on the best choice. We can put some of those best choices in front of users, take feedback from them, feed that back into the cycle. We're building this really tight connection with our users. This is really awesome. Let's get there.
The other thing that probably isn't a surprise that really helps is quality internal platforms help turn your AI adoption into real value for your organization. When I think about quality platforms, there's the obvious things. A platform helps us scale a capability, a technology across an organization because we centralize some of those capabilities, make them available to everyone. Another thing that if you've spent any time near platform engineering, I'm sure you've heard the phrase, treat your platform as a product. Have you heard that phrase before? One of the things about products is they have customers. Who's the customer of the platform? Before AI, who was the customer of the platform? It was other software engineers. It's other developers. I have a lot of empathy. I understand the pain that they have. I know what they're going through. Now it's changing. It's not just other developers I'm building for, I'm also building for the bots.
I need to improve my developer experience. I also need to improve the agent experience. It turns out that some of the things we do for one are good for the other. When we have better documentation, that can help our developers. It can sure help our agents. I know this because now you're all writing documentation. Everyone is writing documentation. DORA has researched it for years and said, "We see documentation is like sunshine, it unlocks all of these capabilities within an organization." Everyone's been like, yes, but writing docs sucks. How many agent files have you written or skills have you written? You are writing documentation now. What's changed? As a senior engineer, I'm not writing documentation to help a junior. I will write documentation to help a bot. Let's be honest, that's messed up. Why? Because when I write the documentation to help the junior, it takes a year or more for them to progress.
The feedback cycle on did I write good documentation or not is really long. When I write documentation for an agent, I get that feedback right away. I changed the agent and I re-ran the prompt and I saw the results from that. It's really fascinating. There was a research paper that they did a little bit of research into like, do these agents files actually help produce better output? Their finding was, no, not so much. I think the interesting thing was, as the user, do I have more confidence in the output because of the agent file? I feel like I have more control, maybe that gives me better trust. We do know, and this is true everywhere, that trust begets adoption, begets trust. The more you use something, the more you trust it. The more you trust it, the more you use it. While maybe it's not helping the bots right now, maybe it is helping me. Maybe that's good enough.
Here's the other thing about AI. We talked about internal platform. We start with developer experience. Now we have to think about agent experience. I want to go back to that very first question. What's stopping you from YOLOing that thing that the AI just generated into production? Because now everyone in your organization is a builder. We go from developer experience to agent experience to builder experience. How do I help Jane from accounting ship that application that she dreamed up last night and built with an AI? That sounds scary, doesn't it? Maybe that's the new job. Maybe that's the new platform engineering. How do we make it safe for there to be more builders across our organization? That's scary. Maybe that's what we have to do. Because otherwise what's the flip side to that? Shadow IT, shadow AI. That's always been a label, in my perception. You might not agree with this.
I feel like shadow IT is a label that we, technologists, have used to denigrate the other side of the house. Those business people, and their shadow IT. Why do you think they're doing that? So that you could stay employed. They're getting their business problems solved. Shadow IT, we should feel bad when there's shadow IT. That's a signal to us that there's a real business problem, it's so bad that they're willing to work around working with us. We need to go enable that. I think a platform team, and this idea of platform, maybe more of your engineering capacity should shift toward enabling builders, and less should go toward shipping that next feature. Just something to think about.
DORA AI Capabilities Model in Action
I want to show you the DORA AI capabilities model in action. If you go to dora.dev, you can do that or you can just watch here. I'm going to click on this little AI guy. I want to show you this capabilities model. We're going to explore it a little bit here. Let's say that you're part of the legacy bottleneck. One of the challenges that the legacy bottleneck has is product performance is low. You decide as a team, we want to improve our product performance. You can come out here to the model and you can click on product performance, and it will show you which capabilities together with AI adoption drive product performance. From this model, you can figure out like, wait, product performance? What does that even mean? How did we assess it? You can click on this how to assess button. Working in small batches, AI accessible internal data, clear and communicated stance.
What do those things mean? You can figure out how to assess them and you can learn more about them. The way that this model works though, you're doing AI adoption. You want to drive an outcome or multiple outcomes. You want to improve these things. How do you do so and make sure that the AI adoption is happening? Follow those arrows backwards with these capabilities and conditions in place. Your AI adoption is more likely to have an impact on those things on the other side, on those outcomes.
Continuous Improvement vs. Radical Change
A bad system will beat a good person every single time. That's from W. Edwards Deming. The one quote I remember to cite. Think about that. When it comes to adopting AI and changing how you work, there's two different approaches that you might take. If you're a fan of the Toyota Production System, you might know the terms Kaizen and Kaikaku. Augmenting, where we look at a current system and we try to make it a little bit better. This is continuous improvement. That's Kaizen. Then evolving. Evolving is like, maybe we throw everything out. Maybe we start from fresh and design the systems that are going to be completely different. That's Kaikaku. That's radical change. When I go back to that slide, the question that I asked you all, what's one thing you would change in order to make it safer, to trust that code that the AI generated, you could ship to production?
Not one of you said code reviews. How many of you feel like code reviews are the new bottleneck? I think it's time. I am a big proponent of Kaizen and continuous improvement, not Kaikaku, radical change. Maybe it's time code reviews go away. Maybe it's time they go away. How uncomfortable does that make you? Pretty uncomfortable. Why do we have code reviews? To validate that there are missing tests. Why else do we have code reviews? To learn. Give me one more reason why we have code reviews. Two brains think better than one. Share the knowledge. How many of you have walked up to a brand-new codebase with an LLM at your side and learned about that codebase very quickly? We can share the knowledge a lot faster. How many of you have written tests to validate that you have tests for this thing or have other ways of validating that without asking a human to look at this thing to validate that there are tests there?
How many of you sit down and do pair programming? You know what's better than asynchronous code review? Synchronous code review. Write that together. We've got four eyes looking at the code as we go. It's better. Maybe it's time to throw out code reviews. Every bit of engineering capacity that we're investing in code reviews would be better invested in better guardrails and better understanding of the intent of what we're trying to build. I know, it's radical. They don't call it radical change for no reason. I think it's time. We need to think about this as an industry. I mentioned that that 2025 report was not the latest report. This is the latest report, the DORA AI Capabilities Model Report, dora.dev/dora-aicmr. This came out in December. It goes into those seven capabilities, talks a little bit more about each one of them. How do you measure them? How do you put them in practice within your organization? All of this. I highly encourage you to download that report and check it out as well.
From Insight to Action
I want to close out with some final thoughts. The first final thought is probably the most important thing that I will say all day today. Don't believe me. Don't believe our research. The way that DORA does research is we go out and we research the world. We get as many inputs as we possibly can. None of you work for the world. Some of you, there is the world, the program, like maybe you're on that program. You don't work in the world. You work at the organization that you work at, and in its context and with its customers. Even within your organization, you don't probably work for the whole organization. You work for a business unit or an application. You've got to contextualize what we've found. Take our findings and use them as your hypothesis. DORA found that when we have a clear and communicated stance, AI adoption leads to better outcomes.
Let's go try that out. Also, you cannot do this alone. No one can improve alone. Look around you. These are your peers. We're all learning together. Also, if you join the DORA community, you can join thousands of other practitioners and leaders and researchers around the world who are taking some of these ideas and trying to figure out what does it mean when we put them into practice.

articles.title: Bungie could be making Star Wars Battlefront 3 instead of longtime series developer DICE
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Star Wars video games have performed surprisingly well recently, and many fans believe it's about time for another Battlefront game. If the latest rumors from an Electronic Gaming Monthly tribute issue are to be believed, Disney agrees but hasn't settled on a developer. DICE is the most obvious choice, but Disney may be exploring alternatives.
Outside of DICE, which revived Star Wars Battlefront in 2015, Bungie might be the top contender to develop a new entry, according to EGM and prominent leaker Jeff Grubb. If accurate, the news suggests the project is years away, potentially resulting in the longest release gap in the franchise's history.
Disney has not yet greenlit Star Wars Battlefront 3 but is searching for potential development partners. While no one has fully committed to the project yet, DICE and Bungie are the two most likely bidders to express interest. Having developed the last two titles, DICE is the clear favorite, with Bungie as a potential backup.
The news comes from the Quartermann section of Electronic Gaming Monthly issue 265, part of a compendium to commemorate the legendary gaming magazine, which ceased publication in 2014 with issue 264. Giant Bomb's Jeff Grubb, who contributed to the compendium, read the section in a recent episode of the outlet's Game Mess Mornings podcast.
A new Star Wars Battlefront could be an interesting fit for Bungie, the company behind Halo, Destiny, and Marathon, especially as it begins to recover from repeated layoffs. However, Bungie might be busy with its recently announced new direction, which involves reversing its decision to sunset Destiny 2 and bringing significant changes to Marathon after its lukewarm commercial performance.
EA's apparent abandonment of Star Wars Battlefront has baffled fans. The 2017 first-person shooter retains an active modding community, and last year's player count spike dwarfed its performance when it arrived on Steam in 2020. By the time a new installment arrives, the series will likely have experienced a longer release drought than the decade between Pandemic Studios' Battlefront II in 2005 and DICE's revival of the franchise in 2015.
Disney may be aiming to capitalize on the strong reviews recent Star Wars games have received, which contrasts sharply with the disastrous box office performance of Star Wars: The Mandalorian and Grogu. While 2024's Star Wars Outlaws was moderately successful, this year's Star Wars Zero Company is well reviewed, and Star Wars: Galactic Racer opened with the highest Metacritic rating for a Star Wars game since Knights of the Old Republic, 23 years ago.

articles.title: Meta drops the word "train" from its commercial TOS after AI backlash
articles.text:
Hoping to quell criticism, Meta has dropped the word “train” from its “streamlined” commercial terms of service that kick in on October 30.
Last week, Meta faced backlash after legal experts warned that the tech giant’s sweeping new commercial terms of service seemed to give Meta permission to endlessly scrape websites linked on business pages. Talking to Nieman Lab, experts suggested that Meta could possibly use the policy to avoid millions in licensing fees from news organizations by requiring all business users to share a wealth of AI training data simply for running a business page.
A Meta spokesperson confirmed that Meta did not alert users to the changed language following backlash. This potentially only adds to confusion ahead of the policy rollout. In response to backlash, Meta’s spokesperson provided a statement to Ars, acknowledging Nieman Lab’s initial report but not its follow-up report reiterating experts’ concerns:
“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”
The same experts who sounded the initial alarms were not impressed by Meta’s updates, which they told Nieman Lab do not go far enough to protect business page users from invasive scraping. Matt Topic, a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy, told Nieman Lab that “publishers should remain concerned.”

articles.title: Galaxy Watch 9 com Snapdragon tem redução de preço com cupom • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Watch 9 com Snapdragon tem redução de preço com cupom
Galaxy Watch 9 BT (40 mm) tem chip Snapdragon e novos recursos de saúde; smartwatch da Samsung recebe desconto de 31% no Pix no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy Watch 9 Bluetooth de 40 mm está saindo por R$ 2.069,10 no Pix no Mercado Livre. O novo smartwatch da Samsung, que traz chip Snapdragon e novos recursos para monitorar a saúde do usuário, atinge o menor preço desde o lançamento com desconto de 37% sobre o original de R$ 2.999.
O novo Galaxy Watch 9 é o 1º smartwatch da Samsung equipado com um chip Snapdragon, o Wear Elite SW6100, substituindo os Exynos. Aliado a 2 GB de RAM e 32 GB de armazenamento interno, ele permite a instalação e execução local de aplicativos com alto desempenho.
Seus sensores avançados suportam várias atividades esportivas e trazem novos recursos de qualidade de vida ausentes no Galaxy Watch 8, como o Sinais Vitais, que cruza dados de frequência cardíaca, oxigenação, temperatura da pele e frequência respiratória, e a Pontuação de Saúde do Coração.
A tela Super AMOLED de 1,34″ do Galaxy Watch 9 possui brilho de até 3.000 nits e reproduz imagens com cores realistas, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer ambiente. O vidro Cristal de Safira protege o display contra pancadas e arranhões.
O corpo de alumínio Armor de 40 mm recebe as certificações IP68 e militar MIL-STD810H, e resiste a até 5 atmosferas de pressão (5 ATM+), podendo ser usado também em esportes aquáticos em águas rasas. A pulseira redesenhada é 25% mais leve e flexível do que a da geração anterior.
Este wearable ainda pode salvar a vida do usuário em uma situação crítica: no caso de uma emergência médica, ele pode ligar para contatos específicos e números como 190 (polícia) e 192 (ambulância), desde que pareado a um celular.
O Galaxy Watch 9 Bluetooth de 40 mm (R$ 2.069,10 no Pix) roda Wear OS 7 e sua bateria de 390 mAh garante até 40 horas de autonomia, segundo a Samsung. O smartwatch possui conectividade Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 6, NFC e GPS multibanda, que determina a posição do usuário em tempo real.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Spotify vérifie avec qui vous partagez votre abonnement Famille : voici ce que vous risquez
articles.text:
Partager un abonnement Spotify Famille avec ses parents ou ses amis permet de réduire la facture. Encore faut-il vivre ensemble : l’offre est réservée aux membres d’un même foyer. Pour vérifier que cette condition est respectée, Spotify peut demander à certains utilisateurs de scanner un QR code sur le téléphone de la personne qui gère leur abonnement.
Des témoignages sur Reddit, relayés notamment par Android Authority le 19 octobre 2026, ont remis ce dispositif en lumière. Celui-ci figure également sur la page d’aide française de Spotify.
Contactée par Numerama, l’entreprise confirme procéder à des vérifications : « Dans le cadre de nos efforts constants pour améliorer la qualité et la valeur de l’offre Premium, nous mettons en place des mesures visant à garantir une utilisation appropriée des comptes Spotify. Cela inclut un examen des abonnements ‘Famille’, afin de s’assurer qu’ils sont utilisés uniquement par les titulaires du compte principal et par les personnes résidant à la même adresse, conformément à nos conditions générales. »
Spotify laisse 7 jours pour scanner le QR code
La procédure nécessite deux téléphones. Le gestionnaire ouvre le QR code dans l’application Spotify, depuis sa photo de profil, puis « Votre abonnement Premium » et « Gérer ». Le membre concerné le scanne avec l’appareil photo de son téléphone. Spotify précise que les deux personnes doivent se trouver au même endroit et que le code change toutes les quelques secondes.
À compter de la notification, le membre dispose de 7 jours pour effectuer la vérification. S’il échoue ou dépasse ce délai, il ne pourra pas rejoindre un autre abonnement Famille ou Duo pendant 12 mois. Il conserve la possibilité de souscrire une autre formule, notamment individuelle.
Spotify procède également à des vérifications d’adresse : « Si nous ne parvenons pas à confirmer l’adresse d’un membre, nous lui envoyons un courriel pour la revérifier. Il dispose de 7 jours à compter de la réception de ce courriel pour saisir son adresse complète », précise la plateforme sur la page d’aide dédiée. En cas d’échec ou si le délai de 7 jours est dépassé, l’abonné perd l’accès à l’abonnement et passe à la version gratuite.
L’obligation de résider à la même adresse existait déjà. Des témoignages décrivant la vérification par QR code remontent par ailleurs à fin 2025 : il ne s’agit donc pas nécessairement d’un dispositif tout juste lancé.
Dans sa réponse à Numerama, Spotify ne précise ni sa date d’introduction, ni les pays concernés, ni l’existence d’une extension récente des contrôles. Les membres d’un même foyer peuvent évidemment toujours utiliser l’offre Famille, chacun avec son propre compte.

articles.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio to beef up its biotech business | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced on its website. Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug-discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.
OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind, its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results. OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna and Novo Nordisk.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma. In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors. In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

articles.title: Air Canada now charges you $30 fee for phone bookings
articles.text:
Air Canada has started charging customers a $30 fee for booking flights over the phone.
As spotted by CP24, the change went into effect on Oct. 15, per Air Canada’s website. On the page, the airline notes that this $30 (plus applicable taxes) charge will apply to each passenger on new bookings made by phone. It adds that the booking fee will continue to apply for Aeroplan flight reward bookings.
Fliers will still be able to call Air Canada for support with existing reservations, travel disruptions and other inquiries without paying any fees.
In an FAQ on its site, Air Canada says the reason it has introduced this fee is to push its self-serve digital tools.
“Air Canada’s website and mobile app make it easy to book and manage your travel,” writes the airline. “Using these digital tools for everyday travel needs helps reduce wait times and allows our Contact Centre agents to focus their expertise on situations that require personalized support. ”
It should be noted that other Canadian airlines WestJet and Flair already charge for phone bookings, although their prices are $25 each.
While most people likely book their flights online anyway, it’s always annoying to see more fees added onto services, especially when, in this case, it’s literally for the purposes of giving money to Air Canada. If nothing else, charging people for speaking to an agent isn’t as bad as Cineplex, which for the past couple of years has charged a $1.50 booking fee for online purchases where it saves money because it’s a self-serve process where you don’t even deal with any actual humans.

articles.title: Du hast Angst vor einer Beförderung? Dann liegst du voll im „Ladderdodging“-Trend
articles.text:
Nach Quiet Quitting kommt Ladderdodging: Warum Fachkräfte Titel und Führungspositionen meiden
Lange galt die Beförderung für Arbeitnehmer:innen als ultimatives Karriereziel. Das hat sich inzwischen geändert: Immer mehr Menschen lehnen den beruflichen Aufstieg heute bewusst ab. Die Gründe dafür sind vielfältig, oft steht dahinter aber der Wunsch, zusätzlichen Stress zu vermeiden. Für diesen Trend hat Rohit Bhargava, Gründer der Non-Obvious Company, jetzt einen neuen Begriff geschaffen: „Ladderdodging“. Diese Wortneuschöpfung beschreibt Menschen, die das Erklimmen der Karriereleiter lieber meiden.
„Ladderdodging“ als neuer Karrieretrend
In seinem neuen Buch 100 Future Words, das er gemeinsam mit Henry Coutinho-Mason geschrieben hat, definiert Bhargava diesen Trend als „das Ablehnen oder das bewusste Nicht-Anstreben einer Beförderung oder einer Führungsposition, um den zusätzlichen Druck, das Risiko und die Einsamkeit zu vermeiden, die oft mit Führungspositionen einhergehen“. Nicht jeder sei bereit, neben der Arbeit auch die zwischenmenschliche Dynamik der Mitarbeiter:innen zu managen, so Bhargava gegenüber Fast Company.
Für ihr Buch haben er und sein Co-Autor neben „Ladderdodging“ noch 99 weitere Wörter definiert, die in Zukunft eine noch wichtigere Rolle spielen könnten. Laut Bhargava hätten sie diese auf Basis neuer Forschungsergebnisse und Erfahrungsberichte aus der Zusammenarbeit mit Führungskräften aus der Wirtschaft erarbeitet. Das Ziel des neuen Buches sei es, Diskussionen anzuregen. Gleichzeitig wollen die beiden Autoren eine neue Sprache anbieten, um bestehende oder sich abzeichnende Trends zu beschreiben.
Beförderungen verlieren an Attraktivität
Auch in Deutschland ist der „Ladderdodging“-Trend zu beobachten. Laut der Talent-Trends-Studie 2026 der Personalberatung Michael Page nennen nur 18 Prozent der Beschäftigten in Deutschland eine Beförderung als ihr wichtigstes Karriereziel – deutlich weniger als im europäischen Vergleich. Anders sieht es in Südeuropa aus: So nennen zum Beispiel in Portugal 48 Prozent der Befragten eine Beförderung als ihr größtes Ziel. Paradoxerweise geben auch in Deutschland viele an, sich beruflich weiterentwickeln zu wollen. 49 Prozent möchten neue Fähigkeiten erwerben, 44 Prozent wollen sich weiterbilden oder zusätzliche Qualifikationen erlangen. Und 36 Prozent wünschen sich, ihre Expertise im aktuellen Tätigkeitsbereich zu vertiefen.
Warum ist also gerade der berufliche Aufstieg dabei nicht mehr so wichtig? Für viele geht die Rechnung schlichtweg nicht auf: Laut Michael Page würden 65 Prozent der Beschäftigten in Deutschland eine Beförderung samt Gehaltserhöhung ablehnen, wenn ihr Wohlbefinden darunter leidet. Der Titel ist ihnen der zusätzliche Stress also offenbar nicht wert. Michael Baier, Geschäftsführer von Michael Page, sieht deshalb auch die Unternehmen in der Pflicht: „Fachkräfte investieren gezielt in ihre Expertise, nicht in Titel. Dieser Trend prägt den Arbeitsmarkt, und Arbeitgeber:innen müssen ihn ernst nehmen, wenn sie Talente gewinnen und halten wollen. [Sie] sollten ihre Aus- und Weiterbildungsangebote klar sichtbar machen.”
Unternehmen müssen hinter den Trend blicken
Früher war es für viele undenkbar, eine Beförderung abzulehnen. Aktuelle Studien deuten allerdings darauf hin, dass genau das heute zur Norm geworden ist – besonders bei jüngeren Arbeitnehmer:innen. Dem Gefühl, das manche bei einem beängstigenden oder unerwünschten Beförderungsangebot empfinden, einen Namen zu geben, könne sich aber auch auf ihr Verhalten auswirken, so Bhargava. Ähnlich wie beim Quiet Quitting könnten Menschen den Begriff als Vorwand nutzen, um sich dem Trend anzuschließen. Trotzdem sieht auch er die Verantwortung bei den Arbeitgeber:innen. „Kluge Unternehmen sind diejenigen, die ein solches Wort als Hinweis auf einen Trend betrachten”, sagte er gegenüber Fast Company. Sie sollten seiner Meinung nach hinter die Fassade blicken und sich fragen, warum Mitarbeiter:innen einer Beförderung wirklich aus dem Weg gehen.

articles.title: Chrome détecte les arnaques ClickFix que des arnaqueurs vous font copier
articles.text:
Des pirates vous font exécuter une commande malveillante sur votre ordinateur, au détour d’un faux test « Je ne suis pas un robot ». Google vient de doter Chrome d’une parade contre ce piège ClickFix, mais vous devrez envoyer davantage de données à ses serveurs pour l’obtenir.
La commande affichée à l’écran n'est souvent pas la même que celle que les pirates glissent en douce dans votre presse-papiers. Dès que vous la collez dans la fenêtre Exécuter de Windows et validez, PowerShell ou cmd.exe sont lancés, deux outils installés d’origine. Le logiciel malveillant est ensuite téléchargé hors du navigateur, donc hors de portée des protections de Chrome, reconnaît Google. Avec Paste Protect, Opera bloque depuis juillet la copie d’une commande suspecte à partir de règles intégrées à son navigateur. Google confie ce tri à ses serveurs et le réserve aux utilisateurs de la Protection renforcée de Chrome. Activer ce mode revient à laisser partir vers Google une partie de ce que vous copiez.
Le presse-papiers et le texte des pages analysés par Google
Dès que vous copiez une commande suspecte avec la Protection renforcée activée, son contenu est expurgé des informations personnelles identifiables, puis transmis aux serveurs Safe Browsing de Google. Si l’entreprise conclut à une commande dangereuse, vous recevez un avertissement dans Chrome. Google promet un tri très précis, afin de ne pas gêner les développeurs qui copient des commandes légitimes.
Google a aussi déplacé vers ses serveurs la détection d’arnaques par Gemini. Avec Gemini Nano, installé dans Chrome en 2025, l’entreprise repérait les arnaques au faux support technique, et seulement sur les appareils compatibles. Grâce au modèle hébergé sur ses serveurs, Google propose cette détection à tous les utilisateurs de la Protection renforcée et l’élargit aux faux antivirus et aux fausses mises à jour de navigateur. La marque affichée sur la page et la probabilité d’une arnaque sont évaluées par Gemini, puis croisées avec la réputation du domaine avant le verdict de Safe Browsing.
Google n’envoie le texte d’une page à ses serveurs qu’en cas d’indices d’arnaque très probables, et indique que ce contenu n’est « jamais journalisé, conservé ni utilisé pour entraîner des modèles ». Dans son billet, cet engagement est rattaché au texte des pages, et seul un retrait des données personnelles avant l’envoi est mentionné pour le presse-papiers. Pour Android Authority, la protection anti-arnaques de Chrome est devenue « meilleure, et plus intrusive ».
- Multimodalité texte, voix et fichiers
- Intégration poussée aux services Google
- Applications Web, mobile et bureau
Un « dix fois plus sûr » mesuré en alertes affichées
D’après Google, les utilisateurs de la Protection renforcée sont dix fois mieux protégés de l’hameçonnage et des arnaques que ceux de la protection standard. Pour arriver à ce chiffre, l’entreprise a comparé le nombre moyen d’avertissements affichés dans les deux modes, et non le nombre d’infections évitées. Google dénombrait plus d’un milliard d’utilisateurs de ce mode en 2025, cinq ans après son lancement.
Avec la Protection renforcée, Google recevait les adresses des sites que vous visitez et un échantillon de leur contenu, et il récupère maintenant les commandes suspectes que vous copiez. Si vous ne copiez jamais de commande depuis une page web, vous gagnerez peu avec cette nouveauté, et il suffit de retenir une règle simple. Aucune vérification anti-robot légitime ne se valide en collant une commande dans Windows, et les pirates repérés par SentinelLabs avec de faux CAPTCHA piégés comptaient justement sur votre lassitude devant ces tests répétés.
Vous copiez souvent des commandes depuis GitHub ou une documentation technique ? Une commande PowerShell parfaitement légitime peut alors ressembler à celles des pirates et être envoyée pour analyse à Google, qui promet surtout d’éviter les fausses alertes aux développeurs. Sur un poste professionnel, mieux vaut demander à votre service informatique s’il autorise ce réglage. Vous pouvez l’activer dans les paramètres de Chrome, rubrique Confidentialité et sécurité, puis Sécurité.
Google réserve en priorité ses nouvelles protections contre les arnaques à la Protection renforcée, et invite les internautes à l’activer pour les recevoir les premiers.

The startup, which develops specialised AI tech for frontline-intensive industries, will use the funds for building AI infrastructure, product development, and go-to-market expansion.

In today’s newsletter, we will talk about
- Amazon’s bet on agentic AI to power enterprise ops
- Marketing AI tool: Is it driving profit or just noise?

TechSparks
Amazon bets on agentic AI to power enterprise ops
Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Rajeev Rastogi, Vice President of Machine Learning at Amazon, highlighted the rise of agentic AI in the entire enterprise operating layer, marking a transition from static software to autonomous systems capable of understanding natural language instructions.
“Agents prepare plans dynamically to solve a problem... and invoke the appropriate tools,” Rastogi explained during a fireside chat at the 17th edition of YourStory’s flagship tech-startup event.
Driving transformation:
- Instead of relying on human intervention at every step, these autonomous agents evaluate queries, formulate a sequence of actions, and call specialised digital tools to complete complex tasks end-to-end.
- Within Amazon, this operating layer is active in systems like Rufus, a conversational shopping assistant that parses customer requests, applies price filters, invokes search engines, and guides users through product comparisons and checkout journeys. Similarly, autonomous seller assistants pre-fill product listings, monitor inventory levels, and guide small businesses through international export compliance.
- According to Rastogi, eventually the industry will advance towards genuine world models that possess an internal understanding of physical spaces and environmental behaviour, establishing a practical, cost-effective framework for enterprise automation.
TechSparks
Is your marketing AI tool driving profit or just noise?
At TechSparks 2026, Anand Jain, Co-founder and Chief Marketing Officer of CleverTap, a customer engagement and marketing automation platform, explained why marketing teams must move beyond basic generative AI productivity tools and adopt autonomous, real-time decisioning systems that drive genuine business profit.
Key takeaways:
- In a masterclass on marketing strategy, Jain urged leaders to look beyond simple shortcuts, and move from using AI for fun and games to generating actual business results.
- While creating content using AI makes the job faster and saves time, Jain questioned whether it truly drives growth. “Is it actually going to impact business results or is it just more of the same?”
- Instead of broadcasting generic promotions to large groups, modern marketing engines should interpret live customer actions to match individual needs. This approach marks a shift towards the highest level of AI maturity, known as ‘real-time decisioning’.

articles.title: Google SynthID Detector Simplifies Watermark Detection and Expands Support to Other AI Providers
articles.text:
Google DeepMind announced the global availability of SynthID Detector, a tool designed to help identify AI-generated content, including media created using AI tools from SynthID partners such as OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Kakao, with Apple support expected soon.
Before the introduction of SynthID Detector, users could identify content AI-generated only by asking Gemini, which was limited to content generated by Google AI. Identifying content from other AI providers required instead using their respective detection tools.
The SynthID.com website simplifies the process by allowing users to upload an image, audio, or video files to have it checked across all SynthID partners, including OpenAI, NVIDIA, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. The tool provides a yes or no outcome, albeit Google also points out that when "no confident signal" is found, a negative outcome does not necessarily mean the content is not AI-generated:
This is not a general AI detector. We can only detect media from the above companies, who have adopted SynthID technology. We are continuously working on extending our partnerships to allow detecting more generated media.
Namely, SynthID does not cover content generated using Meta's or Microsoft's AI, which uses a different watermarking technology. In addition, extensive modifications can also degrade SynthID's watermark signal, resulting in false negatives. In such cases, users need to apply a more comprehensive approach involving additional tools. Despite these limitations, SynthID was included in TIME's Best Inventions of 2026 list, which recognized its approach to AI-content detection over AI detectors.
Commenting on the announcement, Reddit user Chicano_Ducky expressed a negative sentiment about the efficacy of this approach:
[T]hey never worked in the first place, the false positives are unacceptably high on videos their own models made which is in the article [...] They are trying to put the genie back in the bottle and they can't.
User Bulky-Employer adds yet another dimension to this discussion emphasizing that:
A removal node is easily created. You just run a low denoising pass on the image. You can already test this on OpenAI and Gemini's outputs.
SynthID is just a speed bump against people who want to defraud using AI images. It's a good thing that it exists.
A complementary approach to watermarking AI-generated content is C2PA metadata, which records information about a file’s origin and editing history to help establish its authenticity. Harry G argues on LinkedIn that this is the only "approach that actually scales", as "trying to detect synthetic content after the fact turns into an arms race". However, C2PA metadata however can be lost when content is uploaded and does not carry over to screenshots.
Launched in 2023 by Google DeepMind, SynthID is a cryptographic watermarking and detection solution for AI-generated images, audio, video, and text. It embeds an invisible watermark directly into the content by altering audio frequency probability distributions or pixel/token patterns using a secret key.

articles.title: Stolen UpdraftCentral keys used to backdoor WordPress sites
articles.text:
A threat actor breached TeamUpdraft's website, a developer of popular WordPress backup and security plugins, potentially compromising UpdraftCentral connection keys that can send commands to connected websites.
TeamUpdraft detected unauthorized access to its infrastructure over the weekend and believes that the hacker accessed the customer database.
The developer offers several WordPress tools for backup, storage, and site management:
- UpdraftPlus: website backup and restoration plugin with more than 4 million downloads
- UpdraftCentral: for managing multiple sites remotely
- UpdraftVault: for cloud backup storage
- UpdraftClone: for creating staging websites
"Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorised access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in an advisory yesterday.
"Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected."
The vendor says it believes the threat actor accessed its customer database, which included details about the customer and billing, order history, as well as more sensitive information:
- password hashes
- two-factor authentication settings
- connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone services
The vendor said it did not store any payment details and noted that UpdraftPlus plugin files and downloads remain unaffected. Self-hosted UpdraftCentral instances are not impacted.
Even if backups in customers' own remote storage are unaffected, the company recommends that users rotate storage credentials and reauthorize connections if they accessed their site through UpdraftCentral.
Massive blast radius
An estimated 10% of sites using UpdraftPlus have an UpdraftCentral or Migrator key, potentially exposing around 400,000 websites to the attack.
According to Patchstack lead researcher Oliver Sild, attackers have begun using stolen access keys to backdoor sites connected to UpdraftCentral, saying the campaign may be more severe than the "wp2shell” attack.
The WordPress plugin security company says that the attacks started on October 18 at 15:32 UTC to execute arbitrary code and add accounts with full administrator privileges.
The researchers logged at least 99 malicious backdoor plugins with distinct names disguised as WordPress maintenance and optimization tools, such as “Site Health Cache.”
Although Patchstack describes an early variant of the backdoor plugin that is broken due to a coding error, a report from web application security firm Nethemba documents a newer version that lets attackers create privileged accounts or log in as existing administrators.
Nethemba says three of its own WordPress websites were targeted through UpdraftCentral, with malicious plugins successfully installed on two of them.
“All three sites ran the current WordPress 7.1.3 and UpdraftPlus 2.26.11, which is patched against the June vulnerability CVE-2026-10795,” Nethemba says.
“The attacker did not break into our servers and did not exploit any weakness in our configuration. The attacker came in through the UpdraftCentral remote management channel and signed the commands with valid private dashboard keys”
Nethemba reports that the vendor's initial 1.26.12/2.26.12 release was meant to remove UpdraftCentral Cloud keys, but a bug prevented it from doing so.
Users are recommended to update UpdraftPlus to 1.26.13 (free) / 2.26.13 (Premium) or later.
After updating, it is recommended to log into each WordPress site and delete the UpdraftCentral connection keys from Settings → UpdraftPlus Backups → Advanced Tools → UpdraftCentral → Manage existing keys.
Administrators should inspect logs and files for indicators of compromise provided by TeamUpdraft, Patchstack, and Nethemba.
If compromise is confirmed, it is recommended to restore sites from clean backups, change the TeamUpdraft account password, revoke all sessions, and reset the two-factor authentication protection method.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Las pateras de última generación desbordan a la Guardia Civil en Murcia y Baleares: "No tenemos velocidad para interceptarlas"
articles.text:
El 2 de septiembre, frente a Cabo Cope (Águilas), una lancha de unos 10 metros y 2 motores ignoró las órdenes de la Guardia Civil. Un agente hizo dos disparos disuasorios. La lancha, en vez de frenar, embistió a la patrullera por un costado y dejó a 3 agentes con heridas leves. Sus ocupantes tiraron garrafas de gasolina al mar y a correr. Llevaban 28.
Detrás de esa escena hay una cifra a destacar: un fueraborda de 350 CV rinde unos 400 Nm, y estas lanchas montan hasta 4. Cruzan de Argelia a Murcia en 3 o 4 horas. Una patera clásica, con 115 o 150 CV, tarda entre 8 y 48. No estás en Motorpasión pero esto te interesa. Al fin y al cabo, todo es física y tecnología.
Persecuciones fracasadas. El secretario de la AUGC en Murcia lo resume en tres palabras: “Nos falta velocidad”. Lo que pide son interceptoras de 55 a 60 nudos, de 102 a 111 km/h. Suena a queja sindical pero es que en el mar es pura aritmética: sin alcance no hay abordaje, ni identificación, ni detenciones, así que se dan a la fuga.
El problema viene de lejos. La barca de madera con un motor que va tosiendo comparte agua con las planeadoras semirrígidas de 10 a 15 metros. Descargan en la playa, giran y vuelven a por el siguiente grupo. El método, según el coronel Pulido, lleva unos 10 años en Murcia. Lo que cambia, dice la AUGC, es la capacidad: hasta 60 o 70 personas por viaje.
Quién va a bordo. Más gente por viaje implica más gente a merced de quien manda la lancha. Dos días antes, en Calblanque (Cartagena), la Guardia Civil localizó a al menos 63 migrantes en la playa. Según sus testimonios, habían pagado varios miles de euros.
Aquello fue atroz: los patrones los golpearon para que mantuvieran la cabeza agachada y, al acercarse a la costa, los amenazaron con un machete y espray de pimienta. A quien no sabía nadar, le ordenaron saltar igual. La lancha de 15 metros de ese caso montaba 4 motores. Y para entender por qué esos motores mandan en la persecución, toca hablar de mecánica. Es más sencilla de lo que parece.
Qué es un CV. No hablo del currículum: un caballo de vapor equivale a 735,5 vatios. Un motor de 350 CV rinde 257 kW. El Verado 350 de Mercury sirve de ejemplo: 6 cilindros en línea, 2,6 litros, sobrealimentado y 303 kg, con la máxima a 6.100 rpm. La nota de la Guardia Civil cita lanchas con varios motores de hasta 350 CV cada uno.
Por otro lado, el par es la fuerza de giro del motor, en newton-metro (Nm). La potencia es ese par multiplicado por las revoluciones. Con 350 CV a 6.100 rpm, la cuenta da unos 400 Nm en el régimen de máxima potencia.
Por ejemplificar, un Golf GTI entrega 245 CV y 370 Nm: par similar pero 100 CV más. La reductora de la pata, de 2,08:1 en el V10 de la gama, duplica ese giro sobre la hélice. Un coche rara vez pisa el acelerador a fondo. Una travesía a todo gas obliga a estos motores a vivir cerca de ese régimen.
Por qué es crucial. El par ayuda a sacar el casco del agua y la potencia sostiene la velocidad. Tengamos en cuenta que el agua es unas 800 veces más densa que el aire. La resistencia crece con el cuadrado de la velocidad y la potencia necesaria, con el cubo. En términos generales, doblar la velocidad exige 8 veces más caballos. Con 4 motores de hasta 350 CV, una lancha de 15 metros suma hasta 1.400 CV.
De hecho, del escenario con el que abríamos el artículo cabe apuntar que no fue nada para lo que podría haber pasado: a 60 nudos, un impacto libera cuatro veces la energía que a 30. Hablamos de energía al cuadrado. Por eso interceptar a velocidades cada vez más altas no es solo un problema de motores.
Dos viajes. Así eran los viajes de antes: lentos y largos. Una patera de 6 metros y 115 CV transportaba a 15 personas a Formentera en 2025. Otra, rígida y de 150 CV, tardó 20 horas en una travesía prevista de 8. La Fiscalía de Baleares cifra en 30 a 48 horas las travesías, según el tipo de barco.
Las planeadoras han conseguido reducir esa espera a 3 o 4 horas hasta Murcia, según la AUGC. En Baleares, ese salto es puramente teórico: a 70 nudos, un Argel–Ibiza saldría en poco más de 2 horas. La crónica local ya ha advertido que esa velocidad no está acreditada en la ruta.
Quién persigue a quién. La cuestión de fondo es que la Guardia Civil juega con desventaja. Sus tres Aister para Almería, Murcia y Baleares montan 2 Mercury de 350 CV y declaran 450 millas de autonomía a 30 nudos (y ojo, porque cada una de las H60 cuestan 2 millones de euros). Son 700 CV frente a un posible 1.400. Así que buscan atajos. En 2022 licitaron cambiar los 2 diésel de 440 CV de dos patrulleras por fueraborda Yamaha de 300 CV, sacados de narcolanchas incautadas. Las Río Flumen y Río Corneja, en Algeciras y Huelva, rozan los 60 nudos con 2 motores de 1.800 CV. A Murcia llegó el río Ulla: 17 metros y 2 de 1.480 CV. Menudo bicho.
Narcolanchas, mismo drama. El problema ya existía con otro cargamento. El 14 de octubre, frente a Mazagón (Huelva), una narcolancha huyó a gran velocidad y con maniobras bruscas. Un helicóptero y la interceptadora Río Tiétar la alcanzaron y permitieron abordarla. Ocho detenidos, 76 fardos con 3.040 kilos de hachís y una semirrígida con 4 motores. Durante la huida, hicieron lo mismo de siempre: aligerar peso como un globo tirando petacas de gasolina al mar.
El portavoz de Jucil, Agustín Domínguez, lo explica así: “Muchas de las actuaciones terminan en catástrofe”. Según ese relato, dos guardias civiles murieron en una persecución reciente. Dos años antes, otros dos habían muerto arrollados por una narcolancha en Barbate. Lo que pretenden los agentes, más que alcanzarlas, es frenarlas. Y este reto se hace imposible con las condiciones actuales.
Qué les espera a los patrones. La Guardia Civil detuvo a cuatro patrones por los dos casos de Murcia: dos en cada uno. Según una información del 2 de julio, la Fiscalía Antidroga dio una instrucción interna: documentar “con el máximo detalle” los ataques a patrulleras desde lanchas del narcotráfico. Quiere estudiar si, además de agresión o lesiones, pueden juzgarse como piratería (artículo 616 ter del Código Penal).
Hasta ahora, el delito habitual de patronear una patera es el que protege los derechos de los ciudadanos extranjeros, y las condenas varían mucho. En Almería, por ejemplo, 4 años y 3 meses, firmes, para el patrón de una patera con 15 argelinos (uno menor). Cada uno pagó hasta 7.500 euros y el patrón se embolsó mil de comisión, iba sin pericia ni luces, con sobrecarga y garrafas. En Formentera, le cayeron 2 años y 10 meses a cada uno de dos patrones, por conformidad. La Fiscalía pedía 5 para cada uno (eran migrantes que patronearon para huir de la pobreza, iban 19 personas a bordo).
A día de hoy, Baleares suma en 2026 6.673 personas en 366 embarcaciones. 2025 cerró con 401 embarcaciones y más de 7.300 personas. Cada cifra de caballaje acaba en lo mismo.

articles.title: WhatsApp s'attaque à Safari avec un navigateur intégré sur iOS
articles.text:
Une version de test de WhatsApp pour iPhone, repérée le 19 octobre, embarque un navigateur intégré capable d’ouvrir tous les liens partagés dans les discussions. La fonction existe depuis l’an dernier pour certains liens d’entreprises ; elle s’étendrait désormais à l’ensemble des conversations. De quoi éviter le détour par Safari ou le navigateur par défaut de votre iPhone.
Tous les liens, sans quitter la discussion
Le chantier se cache dans la bêta 26.41.10.72, distribuée via TestFlight. Un réglage dédié apparaît dans les paramètres des discussions, pour activer ou couper le navigateur intégré à tout moment. À la première utilisation, un écran détaille le fonctionnement de l’outil. Les pages s’ouvrent ensuite directement dans WhatsApp, sans bascule vers une autre application. L’approche rappelle celle d’Instagram ou de X, qui gardent déjà les liens entre leurs murs.
Depuis iOS 14, chacun peut remplacer Safari par Chrome ou Firefox comme navigateur par défaut de son iPhone. Les applications gardent toutefois la main sur leurs propres liens, une latitude dont les réseaux sociaux usent massivement.
La navigation s’effectue dans une session isolée du reste de la messagerie, assortie d’une commande pour effacer cookies, cache et données en un geste. Un menu permet aussi de renvoyer la page vers le navigateur habituel. L’application, chiffrée de bout en bout, assure ne voir ni les liens partagés dans les conversations, ni ceux que vous ouvrez.
Aucune date de déploiement n’accompagne la découverte, et la fonction reste pour l’heure inaccessible, même aux testeurs. Elle prolonge un premier essai lancé en mai 2025 avec la bêta 25.14.10.72, limité aux liens de comptes professionnels et aux adresses sécurisées en HTTPS.
Le précédent Instagram pèse encore
En août 2022, le développeur Felix Krause démontrait qu’Instagram et Facebook sur iOS injectaient du code JavaScript dans les pages consultées via leur navigateur intégré. De quoi suivre, en théorie, chaque pression sur l’écran et chaque texte saisi, coordonnées bancaires comprises. Son outil en ligne, inappbrowser.com, permettait à chacun de mesurer l’ampleur du dispositif. La démonstration prouvait une capacité de collecte, sans établir qu’elle était exploitée. Meta avait alors justifié ce script maison par le respect du dispositif anti-pistage d’Apple.
L’affaire a durablement entamé la confiance dans les navigateurs intégrés, conçus d’abord pour retenir l’utilisateur dans l’application. Chaque minute gagnée en vaut une de plus pour la publicité, premier revenu de Meta. Les garde-fous mis en avant par WhatsApp répondent point par point à cet épisode : session cloisonnée là où Instagram injectait son code, effacement des traces là où rien n’était prévu. La promesse de ne rien voir devra toutefois se vérifier une fois l’outil entre toutes les mains : le script de 2022 était lui aussi passé inaperçu, jusqu’au regard d’un développeur extérieur.
