articles.title: Apple cambia las condiciones para comprar el iPhone Duo: ahora solo se pueden reservar dos
articles.text:
Apple estableció un máximo de dos iPhone Duo por cliente en su tienda en línea de Estados Unidos. El límite incluye todas las variantes del teléfono: si el comprador intenta añadir una tercera unidad, la tienda le pide que reduzca la cantidad antes de continuar con el pedido. La restricción también aparece en la aplicación Apple Store.
La compañía no ha explicado públicamente el motivo de esta decisión. El cambio se produce, sin embargo, después de una preventa con alta demanda: los pedidos del iPhone Duo comenzaron el viernes 16 de octubre y las unidades con entrega prevista para el lanzamiento se agotaron en pocos minutos. Apple anunció que el dispositivo estará disponible a partir del 23 de octubre.
Algunos pedidos llegarán en enero de 2027
El aumento de los tiempos de espera fue rápido. Durante las primeras horas de la preventa, las estimaciones de entrega empezaron a trasladarse a noviembre y diciembre. Para algunas configuraciones, la fecha disponible en la tienda de Apple llegó a enero de 2027. Los plazos varían según el país, el color y la capacidad de almacenamiento elegidos, y pueden cambiar a medida que se procesan los pedidos.
La demora no afecta únicamente a una variante. En Estados Unidos, las estimaciones de envío de las distintas opciones de almacenamiento y color se extendieron hasta enero pocas horas después de abrirse la preventa, según reportes de medios tecnológicos.
El límite de dos unidades es relevante para quienes planeaban comprar más de un dispositivo en la misma operación. La página de compra permite seleccionar el modelo y la capacidad, pero bloquea el pedido si se supera el máximo. En otros mercados, Apple ya había mostrado restricciones similares durante el proceso de reserva, aunque las condiciones pueden variar entre tiendas nacionales.
Cuánto cuesta el iPhone Duo
En la tienda estadounidense de Apple, el precio depende de la capacidad de almacenamiento. El modelo de 256 GB cuesta 1.999 dólares; el de 512 GB, 2.199 dólares; el de 1 TB, 2.599 dólares, y el de 2 TB, 3.199 dólares. Estos precios corresponden a Estados Unidos y no incluyen impuestos; el costo puede cambiar en otros países por los impuestos locales y las condiciones de cada mercado.
El plegable se vende en los colores Night Sky y Star White. Apple lo presentó como su primer iPhone con pantalla plegable: tiene un panel interior de 7,6 pulgadas y una pantalla exterior de 5,4 pulgadas. El equipo incorpora una estructura de titanio grado 5 y una bisagra de precisión, dos elementos que la compañía destaca en la presentación del producto.
Qué se sabe sobre la compra en tiendas físicas
La disponibilidad en las Apple Store físicas es otra de las dudas para quienes no alcanzaron una fecha de entrega cercana. Apple anunció que el iPhone Duo estará disponible en sus tiendas y en distribuidores seleccionados desde el 23 de octubre, pero eso no garantiza que haya unidades para comprar sin reserva en cada local.
La cantidad disponible puede depender de la tienda, la configuración y el país. Por ello, quienes busquen el dispositivo para recogerlo en persona deberán revisar la disponibilidad local antes de desplazarse. La Apple Store permite consultar opciones de recogida cuando se selecciona un modelo, aunque el inventario puede agotarse.
Por ahora, la compañía mantiene el límite de dos unidades por cliente en su tienda estadounidense y los pedidos siguen sujetos a las fechas que muestra cada configuración. La combinación de una demanda elevada y una disponibilidad inicial limitada hizo que algunos compradores tengan que esperar varios meses para recibir el iPhone Duo.

articles.title: US bans DeepSeek from federal agencies, prompting angry response from China
articles.text:
What just happened? DeepSeek might be one of the most popular non-US AI companies right now, but it's being shown the door across US federal civilian agencies. Washington has ordered the removal of the Chinese firm's AI products from government IT systems and blocked future purchases, and the restrictions include third-party tools built using its technology. Beijing, unsurprisingly, isn't happy.
The Department of Homeland Security's notice was made public on October 19, ahead of today's Federal Register publication. The underlying order dates back to late July, according to AP, making this a public disclosure of an earlier decision rather than a ban signed this week.
The directive covers DeepSeek, its affiliates, and products and services developed using DeepSeek implementations. That last part means the directive is more than just blocking access to the company's chatbot. Agencies also have to consider what powers the software they buy.
DHS invoked the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018. Its stated concerns include DeepSeek's servers being located in China and the possibility that Chinese authorities could access sensitive US information. The order added that DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors." It also warned of potential malware and other security flaws, pointing to publicly available research that found several critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning hit back on Tuesday, accusing Washington of stretching national security arguments and politicizing technology and trade. Ning added that China will "will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies." DeepSeek did not immediately respond to AP's request for comment.
Executive agencies have 60 days from the order's issuance to submit a written justification to DHS seeking an exception, including more time to comply.
This is familiar ground for the Chinese firm. In January 2025, the US Navy warned personnel against using DeepSeek. However, the military branch subsequently clarified that the message reflected existing restrictions on publicly accessible generative AI for official work, which also covered ChatGPT. It wasn't a newly invented policy aimed solely at one Chinese chatbot.
American AI companies have faced restrictions, too. The House of Representatives banned Copilot in April 2024 over concerns about congressional data reaching unapproved cloud services. That position changed in September 2025, when the House announced a Copilot rollout with additional legal and data protections. There's also the whole Anthropic saga.
While DeepSeek isn't facing a nationwide ban, the directive does affect companies selling AI software powered by its models to US federal civilian agencies.

articles.title: Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.
articles.text:
Your Kubernetes dashboard is green. Your users are seeing red.
In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response.
Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure?
To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran, who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software.
Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards.
Earlier stories in this special series:
Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it.
Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap
The illusion of cluster health
Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic.
Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements.
“Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says.
“Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times.
“The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”
Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period.
Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise
Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment.
“HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.”
“When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.”
However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward.
“It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”
A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown.
A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment.
“An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.”
Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure.
OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers:
- Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces.
- Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers.
- Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware, Nutanix, and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks.
- Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity.
Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster
Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model.
When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.”
To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown.
Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload. Synthetic checks provide evidence at the service boundary; they do not reveal the provider’s internal root cause or automatically distinguish every external delay from an internal one. Teams should also identify who owns each dependency and who can investigate when access or instrumentation stops at that boundary.
Telemetry also needs security controls. In AI workloads, prompts, responses, and retrieved documents can appear in logs and traces. Teams should decide what to collect, where that information goes, and who can access it. Design cross-layer visibility alongside existing access and data-handling policies.
Alerting philosophy: From static dashboards to agentic copilots
As environments grow more complex, interpreting telemetry across multiple dashboards becomes difficult. Determining which metrics warrant a real-time alert versus passive monitoring is an ongoing operational challenge.
“Deciding which signals deserve an alert is where science and technology meet domain art,” Ramachandran says. “There is no magic formula. It requires encoding explicit and tacit human operational knowledge into the monitoring platform so the system understands what actually impacts user experience.”
Curated dashboards remain useful for predefined views of system behavior, while AI assistants offer another way to explore operational data. HPE OpsRamp Software includes an AI-powered operations copilot that lets operators explore complex telemetry through natural language.
HPE describes capabilities for investigating incidents, correlating evidence, and recommending next steps. Those capabilities depend on the data available to the platform and the features enabled in the customer’s deployment.
Looking ahead, Ramachandran sees an even more fundamental change in cloud-native operations. He frames machine-led interpretation as a direction for increasingly complex environments, with safeguards still needed before operational changes.
“We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”
“Today, human operators remain the primary first point of interpretation for telemetry,” Ramachandran tells TNS. “But as stack complexity increases with more moving parts and dynamic interactions, expecting a human to digest all these signals first becomes intractable. We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.”
AI-assisted analysis and autonomous changes are separate operational decisions. Ramachandran cautions that AI outputs can be nondeterministic while IT operations often require repeatable behavior.
He recommends retaining human oversight and establishing reliable safeguards before allowing AI findings to trigger operational changes. Teams need to validate a diagnosis and confirm the effect of any response, even when an assistant helps assemble the evidence.
The foundation is instrumentation: Collect the necessary telemetry, establish workload-specific baselines and thresholds, and verify improvements against the user’s experience.
Green cluster indicators are a useful starting point, but application measurements determine whether the service delivers what users need.

articles.title: Blackwall raises $100M at $2.2B valuation to scale its web traffic optimization and management platform - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Blackwall raises $100M at $2.2B valuation to scale its web traffic optimization and management platform
Blackwall, a global web infrastructure company building a web traffic management ecosystem, today announced it raised $100 million in a Series C funding, valuing the company at $2.2 billion.
The firm is a cybersecurity and web-traffic management company headquartered in Estonia. It develops tools that help web-hosting companies, cloud providers and managed service providers protect websites from bots, agents and other malicious traffic.
The company’s flagship product, GateKeeper, inspects incoming traffic by filtering malicious bots, application-layer distributed denial-of-service attacks, and brute-force login attempts before they reach client applications. Blackwall’s broader service also includes firewalls, load balancing, and optimization tools to distinguish legitimate and artificial intelligence traffic from potential attackers.
“The web is becoming more automated, more distributed and more complex, but the infrastructure that powers it remains highly fragmented,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Nikita Rozenberg. “Our ambition is to build the traffic management ecosystem that brings those worlds together.”
The company’s name, Blackwall, changed from BotGuard in March 2025 alongside its Series B funding round, references Cyberpunk 2077, a science fiction video game published by CD Projekt Red. In the game, the Blackwall is a digital barrier that protects the Net from terrifying rogue artificial intelligences that would destroy humanity’s corporate and information infrastructure.
Rozenberg said the new funding will help the company expand globally and deepen its platform, giving hosting and infrastructure providers the technology to participate in the next generation of the web.
AVP led the funding round, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures.
“Blackwall has built something rare: a security company that grows with the internet itself,” said AVP General Partner Warda Shaheen. “It is already the layer in front of millions of websites, and as more of the web’s traffic comes from agents, the company in that position becomes indispensable. That’s why we’re leading this round.”
Blackwall partners with web hosting and cloud providers to catch unwanted traffic, cut operating costs and speed up traffic. Its modular nature also boosts customer-facing web security features, which customers can pick and choose, package and bundle as their own products, generating revenue without building or maintaining the technology themselves.
The web hosting market hit $150 billion in 2025, according to a report from Grand View Research Inc., and is projected to reach $178 billion by the end of this year. The same report estimates that the market will reach $506 billion by 2033. Blackwall supports this market by providing cybersecurity resilience for providers that add its services to their own offerings. According to Grand View, the market is driven primarily by growth in startups and small-business activity online.

articles.title: From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
From data to decisions: Conversational supply chain intelligence with Amazon Quick and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Giving supply chain teams direct access to the systems behind their decisions.
Every supply chain generates constant signals: orders in approval, shifting lead times, slowing ports, drifting prices, disruptions. The problem isn’t scarce data. It’s the distance between the data and the decision-maker.
Answering “which top-revenue SKUs are exposed to the current port closure, and what will it cost?” used to mean knowing which system held each piece and stitching them together by hand while the domain expert waited.
Could that manager instead ask in plain language and get an actionable, cross-system answer in seconds? Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is the intelligence layer, exposing enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers as a composable tool layer. Amazon Quick turns that into action for personas with no setup. Answers come from live systems of record and grounded documents, not model recall, and every change waits for a named human. In this post, we walk through this pattern end to end, from a conversational walkthrough in Amazon Quick to the AgentCore tool layer behind it, and we show you how to deploy it yourself.
The problem: Data-rich, insight-poor
Each question needs its own tool: inventory from the enterprise resource planning (ERP) system, disruptions from email or news, a request for quotation (RFQ) from procurement, and compliance from a checklist. Correlating is manual.
A day in the life
A manager’s morning traditionally spans the ERP (inventory exceptions), monitoring tool (alerts), procurement (alternatives), email (RFQ), and a tracker: 45–60 minutes across five systems with a dozen-plus context switches.
Conversationally it’s three prompts in one tool, “Any critical disruptions affecting my top-revenue SKUs?” → “Assess the TechComp halt and issue an emergency RFQ to approved alternatives” → “Looks good. Send it.”, in minutes.
Deep dive: Supply chain scenario walkthrough
The following five steps follow one disruption from detection to an approved emergency RFQ, all in a single Amazon Quick conversation.
Step 1: Discovery – “What tools do I have?”
The user asks “What supply chain tools do I have?” and Amazon Quick lists the supply chain MCP servers published in AWS Agent Registry. Because an administrator has turned on the registry integration, the four business MCP servers already appear as connector cards, with connection details pre-populated and no URLs to enter by hand. The orchestration agent is added as its own MCP connector.
Step 2: Querying – “Show me active disruptions”
“Check active supply disruptions” calls the Disruption Alerts MCP (assess_disruption_impact): three disruptions with severity, region, and SKU counts. How we solve it: Quick routes the request through AgentCore to the MCP server, which queries backend monitoring and returns a structured result, no dashboard or export.
Step 3: Drill-down – “Assess the critical one”
The user opens the TechComp Production Halt. assess_disruption_impact(disruption_id="DISR-002") correlates order, customer, and inventory data: $750K at risk, 23 orders, three days of supply. How we solve it: one MCP tool call fans out across systems of record, so the manager gets a consolidated impact read without touching the ERP.
Step 4: Action – “Get mitigation recommendations”
The user asks for mitigation. recommend_mitigation(disruption_id="DISR-002") chains the Governance MCP (verify approved alternatives) and Quoting MCP (contract-aligned quote), one flow from one request. How we solve it: the agent plans and sequences the calls, so a single ask spans disruption, governance, and quoting with no manual hand-offs.
Step 5: Automated follow-up
The user then sets up proactive monitoring (“Alert me every morning if there’s a new critical disruption”). The same flow can run unattended from an inbound supplier email. How we solve it: the same agent and tools run on a schedule or email trigger, posting review-ready cards to the Activity Feed for a person to approve.
Put end to end, those five steps are a single runtime sequence:
Solution architecture
That’s the experience. Here’s how it is built: the pattern separates the intelligence layer from the interface layer, so each evolves independently, with Amazon Quick as the interface and AgentCore as the intelligence.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: The intelligence layer
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a modular agentic platform for building, deploying, and operating agents securely at scale. It offers more than we use here. Four of its services are relevant to this pattern:
- Runtime – Serverless hosting for MCP servers and agents, with session isolation and built-in identity.
- Gateway – Turns APIs, AWS Lambda functions, and services into MCP-compatible tools behind a secure managed endpoint, standardizing tool access. Reasoning is the calling agent’s.
- Identity – Authentication and credential management, compatible with existing identity providers.
- Policy – Deterministic authorization rules, authored in natural language or Cedar, that intercept every tool call before execution, keeping an agent in its lane on procurement and financial data.
The MCP protocol: How tools communicate
MCP is an open standard for how AI models interact with external tools. Each server exposes tools with typed parameters:
This means:
- AI clients (Quick, custom agents, other MCP apps) can consume the same servers.
- Backends (SAP, Oracle, custom microservices) can be wrapped as an MCP server.
- Tool discovery is automatic. Clients query the registry for schemas at runtime.
AWS Agent Registry: The discovery layer
The registry is the governed discovery layer: a publisher submits a record, a curator approves it, and only then is it discoverable through hybrid search, browsing, or the registry’s MCP endpoint. One scale reality worth noting: because schemas are discovered at runtime, treat each as a contract, versioning new alongside old for breaking changes.
Multi-step orchestration
The reasoning layer is an agent on AgentCore Runtime, an agent record at its direct invocation URL through a Custom MCP connector, with no Lambda or gateway. Here, it’s the Order Fulfillment Agent. Given one request it plans which tools to call and in what order:
Security and governance architecture
Every tool call passes through the same AgentCore control set before it reaches a backend.
The MCP servers in this pattern
| MCP server | Capabilities | Example queries | 
| Quoting Engine ( sc-quoting-gateway) | Quote generation, pricing rules, validation | “Contract-aligned quote for 500 units of SKU-A” | 
| Governance Engine ( sc-governance-gateway) | Supplier approval, budget authority, regulatory compliance, policy rules | “Is SupplierCo on our approved vendor list?” | 
| Invoice Processing ( sc-invoice-gateway) | Invoice approval routing, AP aging, payment schedules | “What invoices are pending approval this week?” | 
| Disruption Alerts ( sc-disruption-alert-gateway) | Active disruptions, severity, impact assessments, mitigation | “Critical disruptions affecting our APAC suppliers?” | 
| Order Fulfillment Agent ( sc-order-fulfillment-agent) | Multi-step orchestration across all four business MCPs (AgentCore Runtime, direct invocation URL) | “A supplier went down, find alternatives, check compliance, issue an RFQ” | 
Amazon Quick: The enterprise AI assistant
Amazon Quick puts AgentCore tools before business users through chat, agents, the Activity Feed, and automated workflows, with no technical setup.
Key components used
| Component | Role in this pattern | How it works | 
| Agent Registry connection | Surfaces MCP servers as connectors | Admin links the registry once. Records become connector cards | 
| Quick Agent | One SC agent that adapts to role | Tailors to persona (manager, procurement, analyst) | 
| MCP connectors | Expose MCP tools in chat | A card connector exposes tools across Chat, agents, schedules | 
| Activity Feed | Proactive alerts and actions | Agents post cards. The user acts | 
| Schedules | Recurring natural-language automation | For example, “every morning” | 
| Outlook Integration | Email into the feed | Supplier replies parsed and validated | 
| Structured data connectors | Query operational records | Quick queries Space datasets (orders, inventory, suppliers, contracts) for the MCP rule check | 
| Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) knowledge base | Retrieval over documents | Invoices, contracts, policies in an S3 knowledge base, grounding answers through Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) | 
| CRM connector (optional) | Reads customer records (optional) | CRM (for example, Salesforce) accounts, opportunities, contacts. Can also load into datasets | 
Automated Activity Feed and proactive monitoring
The Activity Feed is the proactive surface of Amazon Quick, a unified inbox where agents post results, alerts, and recommendations. Feed items are:
- Actionable, each carries context and next-step actions.
- AI-triaged, with priority indicators (Reply needed, Follow up, Deadline).
- Cross-source, spanning email, schedules, agent runs, and external systems.
- Human-in-the-loop, where agents propose and humans decide.
How automated monitoring works
AgentCore tools plus the proactive capabilities of Amazon Quick give two paths, time-based and email-driven, through a common trigger → agent → output pipeline.
Use case: Validate supplier responses from email
Suppliers reply to an emergency RFQ by email with pricing. The agent validates each (approved supplier? within guidelines?) and stages the result. It does not author a quote, pick a winner, or issue a purchase order (PO).
Phase 1: Setup (one-time, approximately 5 minutes)
- Connect Outlook: in Amazon Quick, choose Settings → Connections → Add Outlook.
- Configure Activity Feed: turn on email monitoring in feed preferences.
- Create SC Agent: build an agent with these instructions:
- Create Schedule: “Every 2 hours during business hours, check for new supplier replies and validate them.”
Phase 2: Runtime (fully automated)
The feed card carries the validation results and decision-relevant facts:
| Supplier Response: Ready for Review | Details | 
| Supplier | TechSupply Co, ✅ approved vendor | 
| SKU / Qty / Price | MCU-7200 · 10,000 units · $2.45/unit | 
| Price check | ✅ within purchasing guidelines | 
| Actions | Select for PO · Compare responses · Reject | 
Phase 3: Human-in-the-loop
The reviewer compares validated responses and either selects a supplier and issues the PO, or rejects with a logged reason. Selection and the PO stay with a person.
Use case: Proactive disruption monitoring
Schedule-triggered, the same pattern applies: a daily 8:30 AM agent checks for new critical or high-severity disruptions, assesses impact, flags anything under seven days of supply as URGENT, and posts an alert card with an Issue Emergency RFQ action.
Where this fits alongside traditional BI
| Dimension | Traditional business intelligence (BI) / dashboards | AgentCore + Amazon Quick | 
| Access model | Navigate, log in, find the dashboard/report | Ask in natural language. The system finds the source | 
| Time to insight | Minutes to hours (find → filter → export → correlate) | Seconds (ask → answer with cross-system context) | 
| Multi-system correlation | Manual: 3-4 tabs, copy-paste | Automatic: the agent orchestrates across MCP servers from one query | 
| Action gap | Insight in one tool → switch → act in another | Insight → action in the same conversation | 
| Setup cost | Weeks/months (dashboard design, ETL, permissions, training) | Minutes to connect, once your MCP servers exist | 
| Run cost | Fixed: pipelines cost the same whether or not anyone asks | Usage-based: serverless scales to zero, cost tracks questions (Lambda + agent tokens) | 
| Trust & accuracy | As fresh as the last ETL load | Computed live from systems of record and grounded docs, every write human-gated | 
This isn’t a “replace everything” argument. Dashboards remain superior for trend visualization, collaborative analysis, regulatory reporting, and exploratory analysis. Use conversational AI for real-time operational decisions and BI for strategic analysis. They complement, not compete.
Personas and use cases
One Quick Agent serves all three personas: the manager maintains continuity, procurement sources with compliance-awareness, the analyst correlates signals. Persona also bounds reach, through row/column-level security and per-persona MCP-tool scoping, so procurement does not see finance data.
| Persona | Use case | Tools invoked | Outcome | 
| SC Manager | Morning disruption check | Disruption Alerts MCP | Disruptions, revenue at risk, days of supply | 
| SC Manager | Emergency procurement | Governance → Quoting MCP | Verified alternatives + RFQ, one flow | 
| Procurement | Supplier verification, budget authority | Governance MCP | Approval, compliance, limits | 
| Procurement | RFQ generation and response validation | Quoting MCP | RFQ issued + responses validated | 
| Ops Analyst | Cross-system correlation | SC Operations Agent | Multi-MCP reasoning, one query | 
| Ops Analyst | Payment queue, audit, disruption trends | Invoice / Governance MCP | AP aging, audit log, patterns | 
Getting started
Deploying the pattern takes three phases: provision the infrastructure, connect Amazon Quick to your data and the registry, and turn on monitoring.
Prerequisites
Before you begin:
- An AWS account with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and AWS Agent Registry.
- AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2, AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) CLI, and Docker (the agent runs as an arm64 container).
- Python 3.12 or later, with Boto3 1.43.94 or later for the registry step.
- Active credentials with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions to deploy and register (aws sts get-caller-identity returns the target account).
- Data layer: a database (Snowflake, PostgreSQL/RDS, or a SQLAlchemy engine), an Amazon S3 bucket, optionally a Salesforce org.
- Amazon Quick set up for your organization.
- (Optional) An Outlook account for email automation.
Setup uses two surfaces, so each of the following steps names where it happens: the Amazon Quick web console in a browser (Amazon Quick Sight permissions, Agent Registry linking, connectors, and agent settings) and the Quick Desktop App (connecting Outlook for email automation). The conversational experience in the Desktop App comes last, once setup is done.
Deploy the infrastructure
Everything is open source and scripted: clone the quick-for-supply-chain example in the aws-samples/sample-amazon-quick-suite-knowledge-hub repository and follow its README.md, or point a coding agent like Kiro at it.
The README.md covers three phases. Phase 1 deploys the AgentCore stack: the identity layer (an Amazon Cognito user pool and app client, authorization-code OAuth flow, plus a test user), four business-rule MCP servers (each an AWS Lambda function fronted by its own AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using CUSTOM_JWT authorization), the gateway targets mapping the tools of each Lambda function, and sc-order-fulfillment-agent on AgentCore Runtime as a container, with least-privilege IAM roles. Phase 2 uploads the synthetic dataset to Amazon S3. Phase 3 verifies gateways and runtime are Ready. Six Agent Registry records are approved.
Grant Amazon Quick access to your data
In the Amazon Quick web console (browser): grant Amazon Quick access from the Amazon Quick Sight admin page (Manage Quick Sight → Security and permissions) to both the S3 bucket and Amazon Athena, since each table is served through an Athena source over an AWS Glue database. Without the Athena grant, dataset creation fails.
Link the registry and create connectors
Linking the registry is one-time and administrator-level. Creating a connector is per-user. Both happen in the Amazon Quick console. See the AWS Agent Registry integration guide.
Link the registry (administrator, one-time)
An administrator links one Agent Registry to the Quick account. In the Amazon Quick web console (admin): go to Manage account → Permissions → AWS Agent Registry and turn on the registry (sc-supply-chain-registry, one per account). Only registries in your account and Region, agent-registry namespace, AWS_IAM (SigV4) authorization, and READY status appear. The Quick-managed service role links it.
Create a connector
After the registry is linked, approved MCP server records become connector cards: the four business MCPs as cards, the order-fulfillment agent added manually. At scale, federate connector authentication through your identity provider and provision connectors to groups, with the Cognito user pool as the seam.
In the Amazon Quick web console (per user): the four cards appear on the Connectors page (sc-quoting-mcp, sc-governance-mcp, sc-invoice-processing-mcp, sc-disruption-alert-mcp). Authenticate through the OAuth authorization-code flow (OAUTH2_AUTHORIZATION_CODE) with client ID, secret, and token, authorization, and redirect URLs from the deploy script. Sign in as the test user, turn on tools, create and share.
Registry-sourced connectors are Custom MCP connectors (relevant for custom permissions). Removing the link later doesn’t delete connectors already created.
Add the order-fulfillment agent connector
In the Amazon Quick web console: because it is an agent record, create its connector manually (Connectors → Create for your team → Model Context Protocol → Create new): name it sc-order-fulfillment-agent, point it at the AgentCore Runtime direct invocation URL from the deploy script, complete the same OAuth sign-in, create and share.
Attach the connectors to your agent
The deployment creates the Supply Chain agent: a Quick Space, imported datasets and S3 knowledge base, and the agent with instructions, starter prompts, and welcome message. What remains is attaching the connectors.
In the Amazon Quick web console (agent settings): open the deployment-created Supply Chain agent (default id sc-supply-chain-agent) and attach all five connectors (four business MCPs plus sc-order-fulfillment-agent), or pass the five connector IDs to the setup script.
Set up proactive monitoring
To make it proactive, Quick runs the same agent on a schedule or on incoming email and posts results to the Activity Feed. Both paths reuse the agent and tools you configured.
In the Quick Desktop App (Settings → Connections): connect Outlook and turn on email monitoring. Then, in Quick Chat, create two natural-language schedules, time-based (“Every morning, check for new critical disruptions”) and email-driven (“Every two hours in business hours, check supplier replies and validate”). The agent extracts pricing, runs the checks, and posts a card.
Try it in Amazon Quick
With the agent and connectors ready, ask in natural language in Amazon Quick Chat. Each prompt shows the data-then-rules pattern.
| Ask Amazon Quick | What you get | 
| “What supply chain tools do I have?” | The five MCP connectors (quoting, governance, invoice, disruption alerts, order-fulfillment agent), with status. | 
| “Show me active supply disruptions.” | Active disruptions with severity, region, SKU counts (Disruption Alerts MCP). | 
| “Assess the impact of the TechComp production halt.” | Revenue at risk, affected orders, days of supply, from your datasets. | 
| “Is this supplier an approved vendor, and do we have budget authority for a $72,000 PO?” | An approval from the Governance MCP (vendor status, budget authority, compliance). | 
| “Generate a contract-aligned quote for 1,000 units for this customer.” | A contract-aligned quote from the Quoting MCP, as a branded document. | 
| “A supplier just went down. Find alternatives, verify compliance, and issue an emergency RFQ.” | The Order Fulfillment Agent chains disruption, governance, and quoting MCPs into one recommendation. | 
Conclusion
AgentCore and Amazon Quick are a repeatable enterprise-AI pattern: separate intelligence from interface. AgentCore turns fragmented backends into a composable, governed, AI-accessible layer through standard MCP interfaces. Amazon Quick democratizes access in natural language.
The gain is the collapsed decision chain: detect, research, decide, act, and log once spanned five tools, now one conversation. The AI researches, correlates, validates. The person decides. Every call is authenticated, authorized, policy-checked, and audited, and a 45-60 minute routine across five systems can collapse to minutes.
That is the shift from data-rich, insight-poor to data-rich, decision-ready. Start with one MCP server and one persona. The registry grows and the experience stays the same.

articles.title: Galaxy Watch Ultra cai 59% para quem busca relógio para aventuras • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Watch Ultra cai 59% para quem busca relógio para aventuras
Galaxy Watch Ultra tem corpo de titânio e monitora diversos esportes; smartwatch da Samsung sai por menos da metade do preço original, no Pix no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy Watch Ultra LTE de 47 mm está saindo por R$ 2.068,64 no Pix no Mercado Livre. O smartwatch da Samsung lançado em 2025, que possui corpo de titânio e sensores que suportam diversos esportes, recebe desconto de 59% sobre o preço original de R$ 4.999.
O Galaxy Watch Ultra é um dos melhores smartwatches da Samsung, equipado com o mesmo kit de sensores do novo Ultra 2. Ele oferece suporte a diversas modalidades esportivas, como corrida e ciclismo, e traz funções de qualidade de vida, como eletrocardiograma (ECG), monitores do sono e da oxigenação do sangue.
Seu corpo em titânio de 47 mm resiste a até 10 atmosferas de pressão (10 ATM) e traz certificações IP68 e militar MIL-STD-810H, podendo assim ser usado em esportes aquáticos em águas rasas, enquanto resiste a altas temperaturas.
Graças à conectividade 4G/LTE, este wearable pode salvar a vida do usuário em uma situação de risco. No caso de uma emergência médica, ele pode disparar alertas para contatos pré-programados e ligar para números como 190 (polícia) e 192 (bombeiros), sem depender de um celular.
A tela Super AMOLED de 1,5″ com brilho de até 3.000 nits do Watch Ultra pode reproduzir imagens nítidas com cores vibrantes e oferece visibilidade garantida em qualquer lugar. O vidro Cristal de Safira protege o display contra arranhões, pancadas e quedas.
O gadget traz o chip Exynos W1000, 2 GB de RAM e 64 GB de espaço interno, um kit interno que o permite instalar e rodar apps localmente. Sua bateria de 590 mAh resiste até 100 horas de uso no modo economia de energia, segundo a fabricante, podendo ser usado por um dia inteiro sem descarregar.
O Galaxy Watch Ultra de 47 mm (R$ 2.068,64 no Pix) suporta redes Wi-Fi 5, Bluetooth 5.3, o já mencionado 4G/LTE e GPS multibanda, que determina a posição do usuário em tempo real, recurso essencial para a prática de esportes e outras aventuras.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Gemini's Personal Intelligence is coming to cars
articles.text:
Google kicked off 2026 with the addition of Personal Intelligence to Gemini, allowing its AI to pull in more of your data to formulate answers. It started as a paid feature but eventually came to all Gemini users. However, this feature wasn’t available in the car until now. Google is rolling out Personal Intelligence to Android Auto and Google Built-in, and it is still, thankfully, an optional feature.
As Google points out, a generative AI’s outputs are better “when it knows the world and knows you,” which is correct in an uncomfortable sort of way. The more context you can provide to a model, the better the output will be at the end of the token shuffle. Since Google has so much of your data already, it sees Personal Intelligence as a differentiator versus other AI systems. You don’t have to provide the AI context because it already has it from apps like Gmail and Calendar.
Personal Intelligence is beginning its rollout in Android Auto today, and it will come to vehicles with Google built-in in the next few months. As an aside, “Google built-in” is questionable branding, but it refers to cars that run Google software in the infotainment system rather than projecting an interface from your phone. Very few vehicles have Google built-in, but Google often releases new car features on them first. This time, it’s the other way around.
Google says Personal Intelligence is a natural fit for the car, allowing you to focus on the road instead of providing detailed instructions to your digital assistant. For example, you can say “take me to my doctor’s appointment,” and Gemini can get that data from your connected calendar. It can also leverage visual analysis to find locations in your photos to begin navigation.

articles.title: Modern software is built on the backs of low-paid maintainers, opening the door to potential threats — report details critically underfunded projects that remain understaffed or unfunded
articles.text:
Nearly half of critical open-source software relies on just one or two low-paid maintainers, opening the door to potential threats — report details critically underfunded projects that remain understaffed or unfunded
Welp, time to bring out that xkcd comic out again.
Modern computing systems and devices typically require pieces of crucial open-source software, typically maintained by unpaid or low-paid volunteers. Recently, a report collated a list of critical open-source projects, noting which of them are chronically underfunded and/or understaffed. The information is sobering: 11 out of 23 of the listed projects currently only have one or two maintainers, and funding is generally scarce and sometimes nonexistent.
The Data Drop's report on open-source maintainers identifies that having only one or two sets of eyes on critical pieces of software means that sooner or later something breaks — and it tends to do so in spectacular fashion, given its ubiquity. So, what happens when these projects, which are widely used across software, go underfunded or understaffed?
Lessons from the past
In 2014, the same year as Heartbleed, Shellshock made waves: a vulnerability in the Bash shell that's present in Linux, macOS, and Unix-type systems. The problem was traced back to a line of code present since 1989, displaying how even software that's thought to have all the bugs hammered out of it can still fall prey to attacks. A quick look at Bash's commit history shows it's almost exclusively maintained by Chet Ramey.
In 2016, ImageMagick was exploited, providing attackers with remote code execution. This library is used for image manipulation across a wide range of software, in webpages, mobile apps, and more. A 2020 analysis revealed that hundreds of security issues had been found over the years in its extensive codebase. Nearly every code contribution in the past couple of years has been done by an individual named Dirk Lemstra.
Contemporary examples include 2021's Log4Shell exploit, a critical vulnerability in the Apache Log4j logging library used in millions of servers. The libwebp image-handling library saw a zero-day vulnerability in 2023, and the xz compression library used across Linux and iOS was compromised in 2024.
Thankless work
Key points in the report mention specific repos, which might be under threat. Somewhat unsurprisingly, the low number of overall maintainers and the unpaid nature of the work make it unattractive to perform.
The main time-zone file used across Linux-based operating systems is maintained pro bono by Paul Eggert, a UCLA teacher. Core-js, a piece of support software that lets new JavaScript work in old browsers and is estimated by the author to be used in half of the busiest websites in the world, is handled by Denis Pushkarev. He once had to endure criticism from the community because he added a command-line message to the library's installer asking for help or a job.
The HarfBuzz library developed by Behdad Esfahbod is a cornerstone in ligatures and text shaping in Middle Eastern languages. In those writings, a letter changes shape and/or orientation according to what's around it. Esfahbod handles that vast majority of the project's code, and doesn't mention public or corporate funding.
Libjpeg-turbo handles JPEG images on Android, Firefox, LibreOffice, and every Chromium-based browser. It's kept ship-shape by D.R. Commander aka DRC, who occasionally is contracted for library-specific work, though at arguably modest values of "3-4 figures rather than 6 or 7." Libxml2, just like the label says, handles XML reading and writing across numerous applications and operating systems. Nick Wellnhofer, the original maintainer, stepped down in September 2025, after years of work with little income.
The SQLite project provides a one-file database that's exceedingly easy to integrate into most software, instead of complicated, resource-heavy databases, while still retaining standard SQL language and accouterments. Thanks to its ease of use, it found its way into an astonishing number of applications. Examples include WhatsApp, Dropbox, Android, Windows, and all major browsers.
The project estimates that there are about a trillion instances of SQLite in use. Just four people keep this critical project together, and they've gone to the length of removing their names and photos from the project's page, as "there are a lot of crazy people in the world who might misuse that information." The project is funded by the offering paid support via the founder's company, though there's no word on effective income, especially when it presumably needs to feed four mouths.
Funding is there, but scarce
It's not all doom and gloom, though. Take curl (the software), for example. Almost every developer has used it, thanks to its URL-fetching abilities and extensive scripting options. The project was started by Daniel Stenberg, who is now paid to work full-time on it. The team has now grown to 11 and has received funding through Open Collective and Germany's Sovereign Tech Agency, among others.
Likely due to the lessons learned from their past respective debacles, both the Log4j and OpenSSL projects are likewise funded by the Sovereign Tech Agency, as are the FFmpeg video file handler and the OpenSSH secure shell software that's ubiquitous in Linux servers.
All things considered, it's easy to argue that the critical importance of all the aforementioned software merits sizable investments from industry players, especially those whose commercial products benefit the most from the community's efforts. Plus, even if the firms feel no moral obligation to contribute, in the day and age where AI agents are finding exploitable vulnerabilities in hours, donations to these open-source projects could also be considered investments.
Bruno Ferreira is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. He has decades of experience with PC hardware and assorted sundries, alongside a career as a developer. He's obsessed with detail and has a tendency to ramble on the topics he loves. When not doing that, he's usually playing games, or at live music shows and festivals.

articles.title: Zoom's new Unified Context Layer unlocks all of your company's complex conversations and video calls for AI agents to use
articles.text:
Zoom's new Unified Context Layer unlocks all of your company's complex conversations and video calls for AI agents to use
UCL tackles one of the biggest data siloes companies face
- Zoom is packaging up conversations and calls into a Unified Context Layer
- APIs mean third-party AI agents can get direct access to this source of data
- Humans can now spend less time explaining context to AI agents
In recognition that increasingly siloed and complex systems are making it harder for companies to keep track of all their data, making it difficult to deploy effective AI on top of existing tech stacks, Zoom has launched its Unified Context Layer (UCL).
UCL works by bringing together meeting conversations, chats, documents and other business data into one connected system, which it hopes will make it easier for AI agents to work across.
This marks an important step in the company's much broader transition from the video conferencing platform we grew to love during the now-distant pandemic to a full productivity suite that spans both human and agentic users.
Zoom's Unified Context Layer
"This new layer brings together conversations with near real-time activity across Zoom and connected third-party applications, giving people and AI agents access to business context that might otherwise be lost or siloed," the company said in an announcement.
But in a world of increasing interoperability, the company is also adding new APIs to allow external AI tools to query its Unified Context Layer directly, which means ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Muse and other AI agents can see straight into the core data that Zoom holds.
The biggest impact is on productivity, where human workers will need to spend far less time fetching different parts of context to give an AI agent the best chances of success.
Of course, Zoom isn't the first platform to be introducing a Unified Context Layer, but being that the software is still primarily used for communications both within organizations and with external clients, Zoom's UCL should be able to unlock some pretty serious unstructured data for future AI agents.

With Zoom now betting on conversations as a vastly underused source of intelligence, its early adoption of a UCL should play an integral role both in its own roadmap, but also how enterprises benefit from agentic AI on the whole.
