articles.title: Distributed Spring Batch Without a Message Broker
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- Spring Batch can scale horizontally without a message broker by using the relational database it already requires as the coordination plane. It fits the small-to-medium clusters many teams run.
- The pattern solves the problems a broker otherwise handles for you: sizing work to the live node count, assigning per-execution master responsibility with no standing coordinator, and claiming partitions with compare-and-set writes so no partition is silently lost.
- Node failure is handled by heartbeats and a two-phase recovery. It marks a stale node as unreachable, then after a grace period window, removes it and reassigns its incomplete, transferable partitions.
- Correctness is an explicit contract. Transferable work runs at least once and must be idempotent; nontransferable work runs at most once and is failed rather than moved. A partition is never silently lost.
- Database coordination fits where operational simplicity and cost matter most. Its ceiling is database contention and past that point, at very large clusters or sub-second latency, a broker remains the better choice.
Introduction
Spring Batch has been the default framework for batch processing on the JVM for more than a decade. Jobs are built from steps, such as chunk-oriented readers, processors, and writers, with a metadata repository that makes runs restartable. For the nightly extract, transform, load (ETL), financial reconciliation, and data-validation workloads on a single machine, it is hard to beat.
The pressure appears when one machine is no longer enough. A reconciliation run that once fit inside its window grows with the business until it does not and the natural response is to spread the work across nodes. The established answer from Spring Batch is remote partitioning. A manager step divides the work into partitions and dispatches them to workers over a message broker such as Apache Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a JMS provider, via Spring Integration.
Remote partitioning is a proven approach. When a broker is already part of the platform it is the right one. But a broker is an extra operational tier and many teams would otherwise never run one. They already operate a well-managed relational database (Spring Batch requires one for its job repository regardless). Teams have little appetite for standing up, securing, and monitoring a messaging cluster solely to fan out batch partitions.
This article describes an alternative for that common case: coordinating a distributed, fault-tolerant Spring Batch job across a small-to-medium cluster using only the shared database. It is not an argument against brokers, but an account of what it takes to remove one from this job, where the approach’s boundaries lie and where a broker is still the better tool.
Where Single-Node Batch Ends and the Broker Question Begins
If you reduce the distributed batch to its essentials, four questions need to be answered through whatever your coordination.
First, how is the work divided and across how many workers? Split too coarsely and nodes sit idle; split too finely and overhead grows for nothing. The right number depends on how much capacity exists when the job starts.
Second, who is in charge of a given run? Something has to split the work, track it to completion, and finalize the job. In broker-based partitioning, that is the node running the manager step.
Third, how does a worker take ownership of a partition without a second worker also running it? Run it twice and you can corrupt data. Run it zero times and the job is silently incomplete.
Fourth, what happens when a node dies mid-run? Its in-flight work has to be detected and, where safe, recovered automatically, without violating the third requirement.
A broker answers some of these questions for you. Its queue hands each message to a single consumer and dispatch is decoupled from execution, so a slow or dead worker does not stall the producer. Take the broker away and every question has to be explicitly answered, in SQL, against a store built for durable shared state rather than message dispatch. The rest of this article is about answering them well.
Structuring Database-Coordinated Partitioning
The design treats the database Spring Batch already needs as the sole coordination plan without broker or coordination service such as Apache ZooKeeper and no deployment platform. Every piece of cluster state lives in ordinary SQL tables, so the whole cluster is inspectable with a SELECT statement.
Three tables augment Spring Batch’s own schema. The BATCH_NODES table is the node registry, having one row per node, with its status (active or unreachable), its last heartbeat timestamp, and its current load. The BATCH_PARTITIONS table tracks the partition lifecycle, having one row per partition and keyed by that partition’s own step-execution ID (each partition is itself a Spring Batch StepExecution, distinct from the manager step that scopes the run), with its assigned node, its status (pending, claimed, completed, or failed), and whether or not it may be transferred to another node on failure. The BATCH_JOB_COORDINATION table binds each job execution to its master node and manager step, with a status of its own. What matters here is the shape of these three tables, not their full column lists.
One thing this design does not remove is the need for a shared, persistent job repository, but that requirement is intrinsic to distributed partitioning, not something added by this pattern. A partition’s payload, the execution context describing its slice of work, is written by the master and read back by whichever node executes it. The master then reads the result back to be aggregated. That handoff is a cross-JVM exchange of Spring Batch metadata, so the store has to be shared and durable. Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning imposes the same requirement. There, the broker carries only a pointer to the partition, never its data. What this design removes is the broker, not the repository. The one shared database serves as both the metadata store and the coordination plane.
Coordination is decentralized by design. There is no standing master elected for the whole cluster. That approach would reintroduce the leader-election machinery and single point of failure that dropping the broker avoids. Instead, the node that launches a job becomes that job’s master, for that execution only (a later section walks through what it does). Two jobs launched on two different nodes have two different masters running at the same time. Because mastership is scoped to a single job execution, losing a master affects only that one job, never the cluster. There is no coordinator to elect and none to lose.
Reusing Spring Batch’s Partitioning Hooks: The Entry Point
For a Spring Batch developer the first question is practical: Where does my code plug in and how much of it changes? The answer is almost none, which makes the approach usable. That simplicity falls out of an extension point Spring Batch has always had.
Spring Batch already splits a partitioned step into two independent responsibilities. A Partitioner interface decides how work is split. It produces a set of named ExecutionContext objects, one per partition, each describing a slice of the input. A separate PartitionHandler decides how those partitions are executed. The built-in TaskExecutorPartitionHandler runs them in local threads, while Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning swaps in a MessageChannelPartitionHandler that ships them over a broker. The manager step is assembled from these two pieces plus a StepExecutionAggregator that combines the results:
new StepBuilder("reconcileStep.manager", jobRepository)
    .partitioner("reconcileStep", clusterAwarePartitioner) // how work is split
    .partitionHandler(clusterAwarePartitionHandler)         // how partitions are distributed
    .step(reconcileStep)                                    // the ordinary worker step
    .aggregator(aggregator)
    .build();
That partitionHandler(...) line is the whole seam. Because Spring Batch treats partition distribution as a pluggable strategy, this approach supplies its own PartitionHandler, one that writes partition rows to the database and monitors them in the slot the broker-backed handler would otherwise occupy. The partitioner is a subclass of Spring Batch’s own Partitioner. Nothing else moves. The worker step (reconcileStep above) is an ordinary chunk- or tasklet-based step, results aggregate through the standard StepExecutionAggregator, and a restart works through the standard JobRepository. A developer comfortable with local partitioning writes the same manager step and changes exactly two beans, the Partitioner and the PartitionHandler.
That covers the manager. Turning the same deployable into a cluster member is configuration, not code. A single flag enables the behavior with auto-configuration registering the node, starting its heartbeat, and starting a poller, without either a broker client or extra beans. A few intervals tune that behavior, including heartbeat cadence, worker poll cadence, per-node concurrency, and the two heartbeat-age thresholds that drive failover, with production-sane defaults (a node is marked as unreachable at about ten seconds and removed at about thirty seconds).
From then on, every node, master and workers alike, runs one loop. On startup it inserts itself into the BATCH_NODES table and heartbeats on the configured interval, publishing its current load, which is the number of partitions it is running right now. On each poll, it scans the BATCH_PARTITIONS table for rows assigned to it, claims them with the compare-and-set update shown later, and then does the one thing that keeps the programming model intact: It looks up the worker step by name and runs it. That name is not arbitrary. It is the name passed to the .partitioner("reconcileStep", ...) method on the manager, recorded in the coordination row, so the worker resolves the same Spring Batch step bean and executes it with the partition’s ExecutionContext. Each node runs up to a configured number of partitions at once and when a step finishes it records it as COMPLETED or FAILED.
So the coordination lives behind extension points Spring Batch already asks you to implement, turned on by configuration rather than new code.
Implementing It on a Spring Batch Cluster
Figure 1. Architecture, a per-job master and worker nodes coordinating through the shared database. (Source: created by author.)
Figure 1 shows the runtime shape. A standing set of peer JVM nodes each register in the BATCH_NODES table and heartbeat. When a job is launched on one of them, that node acts as master for that run. It queries the live nodes, sizes the split to them, writes the partition rows, and monitors to completion, while every node, master included, polls for and executes the partitions assigned to it.
How the Master Step Drives the Run
The master step is not exotic. It is an ordinary Spring Batch partitioned (manager) step, running on whichever node launched the job. What makes that node the master is where the PartitionHandler runs. When Spring Batch executes the manager step, it calls the handler’s handle(...) method on that node, and the database-backed PartitionHandler blocks there until the whole distributed run is finished.
Inside that single call, the master does four things in order. First it records the run, writing a new row in the BATCH_JOB_COORDINATION table that ties this job execution to the manager step’s execution ID as the run’s identity and marks it as STARTED. Then it writes one PENDING row per partition into the BATCH_PARTITIONS table, each tagged with the node to which it is assigned. Then it runs a monitor loop, waking on a short interval to reassign any partitions orphaned by a removed node (their assigned node is gone from the BATCH_NODES table) and to check whether any partition is still PENDING or CLAIMED. Finally, when nothing is outstanding, it fails the manager step if any partition ends as FAILED, otherwise it marks the coordination row as COMPLETED, hands the workers’ step executions to the StepExecutionAggregator, and finishes the job.
Notice what is absent. Workers never call the master and the master never calls the workers. Every decision the master makes, it makes by reading and writing these rows. That is why losing a master is contained rather than causing a cluster outage. Its state is in the database, not in the memory of a coordinator.
Enterprise Scenario
Consider nightly financial reconciliation across dynamically provisioned cloud nodes. The dataset is large enough that if one node misses the batch window, a well-managed relational database is already in place. The operations team has no appetite for a broker purely for this workload. The same shape recurs in mid-sized ETL and in data-validation jobs where each partition is a slice of input that must be recoverable if a node dies. These are the conditions this pattern targets.
Sizing Work to the Live Cluster
Standard remote partitioning splits work before it knows how much capacity exists to run it. The grid size is chosen blind, often as a fixed constant, and the pieces are dispatched into the broker to be picked up as capacity frees. Without a broker, you have to face this issue directly. Before splitting, the master asks the database which nodes are currently alive and passes that count into the partitioner. The partitioner exposes one method that takes this live node count and returns the partitions, so the split is sized to the cluster that actually exists at that instant.
Each partition is expressed as a Spring Batch ExecutionContext, the framework’s key-value carrier for a partition’s input. The parameters that define one slice of work (a row range, a file name, and an ID window) go in and the worker step reads them back to know what to process. Because the partitioner is handed the live count, it can choose the partition count for the cluster at hand, using either one or two per live node or whatever the workload calls for.
An assignment strategy then maps those partitions onto nodes: round-robin for even distribution and fixed-node-count to confine a job to n nodes, or least-loaded, which places each partition on the node reporting the lowest current load and steers work toward the nodes that are most idle. Because assignment is both capacity-sized and load-aware, the split matches the cluster that exists instead of a number fixed in advance. Assignment is fixed at that point. It is placement, rather than runtime rebalancing, so a node that finishes early does not pull partitions from a slower peer and only node failure moves work. That runtime rebalancing is one thing a broker’s pull semantics give for free and this trades away.
Claiming Work Without Double-Execution
Once partitions are written and assigned, each worker independently polls for its PENDING partitions and transitions them to CLAIMED before executing. That transition is the correctness-critical moment, a single guarded statement that drives every worker transition, with the target status passed in as a parameter.
-- claim, then later complete or fail: one guarded UPDATE
UPDATE batch_partitions
SET    status = ?,                 -- CLAIMED, then COMPLETED or FAILED
       last_updated = CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
WHERE  step_execution_id = ?
  AND  assigned_node = ?
  AND  status IN ('PENDING', 'CLAIMED');
The WHERE clause is the whole point. It explains why CLAIMED appears on both sides. It admits only a row that is still PENDING or CLAIMED, so once a partition reaches a terminal state (COMPLETED or FAILED) or is reassigned, no late write can move it. For the claim, the row starts as PENDING. Also, allowing CLAIMED makes a reclaim idempotent and allows the same statement to carry the later COMPLETED and FAILED writes, which start from CLAIMED.
Two properties then prevent double execution. First, each partition is assigned to exactly one node at partition time, so under normal operation only that node polls for its row. Second, both the worker’s write and the master’s reassignment are guarded. The worker’s write is guarded by the assigned_node and the PENDING/CLAIMED status, the reassignment is guarded by that status as it moves the row back to PENDING under a new node. So if a stalled node completes its partition just as the master reassigns it, the second write matches nothing. If the master went first, the completion fails because assigned_node no longer points to that node. If the node went first, the reassignment fails because the status is already terminal. Either way, exactly one write takes effect. This is not a contended pull-queue with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED statements. Partitions are preassigned, so the guarded update governs the lifecycle, not the dispatch. The one-partition-one-node guarantee a broker gives through its queue here comes from row-level state transitions.
Recovering From Node Failure
Figure 2. Node lifecycle and two-phase failover. (Source: created by author.)
Nodes fail. Liveness here is tracked directly rather than inferred from broker acknowledgements. Every node updates a heartbeat timestamp on an interval, using the database clock rather than its own. The staleness check compares against that same clock, so liveness is unaffected by skew between the machines’ own clocks. Detection and removal are decentralized. Every node runs the cleanup sweeps, so no single monitor’s death blinds the cluster. Reassigning a removed node’s partitions, though, is done by each affected job’s own master in the monitor loop described earlier.
Recovery is a two-phase process, as shown in Figure 2. In phase one, a node whose heartbeat is older than the unreachable threshold (ten seconds by default) is flipped from active to unreachable. In phase two, a node that is still stale past the longer cleanup threshold (thirty seconds) is removed. Its incomplete partitions are resolved by contract. Transferable partitions become eligible for reassignment and non-transferable partitions are marked as FAILED so the job fails cleanly rather than risking a second run. The gap between the thresholds is a grace period window and is there on purpose. A brief garbage collection pause or network blip marks a node as unreachable without taking its work and it recovers on its next heartbeat. Only sustained absence escalates to removal. Reassignment reuses the same compare-and-set discipline as claiming, so a partition that has reached COMPLETED in the meantime is never resurrected.
Best Practices and Gotchas: Making Database Coordination Production-Ready
Treat Transferability as a Contract, Not a Hint
The most consequential design decision is that transferability is declared, not inferred. Each partition carries one bit of metadata. If the node running the partition dies, is that work safe to rerun elsewhere? The partitioner implementation marks each partition as transferable or not, with the framework following that marking exactly rather than deciding on its own. (In the reference implementation it is a method the partitioner overrides.)
Transferable partitions assert the work is idempotent and safe to rerun, an at-least-once guarantee. On node loss, a partition is reassigned and may run twice. Non-transferable partitions assert the opposite, at-most-once. On node loss a partition is failed rather than moved and is never run elsewhere. Summing a numeric range is transferable, but appending to an external ledger or calling a pay-once API is not. This choice is a correctness contract, so decide per partition on whether the work is idempotent.
Rely on Fencing, but Do Not Trust It Alone
A node that loses its own heartbeat stops claiming work and aborts before running a claimed partition, leaving it for the master to reassign. This fencing shrinks the window in which two nodes run the same transferable partition, but it is best effort. A hard-paused JVM can wake and finish work already reassigned, so transferable work must be truly idempotent. What the system never relaxes is that no partition is silently lost. The partition either completes, or the job fails.
Design Restarts to Be Idempotent
Worker failure is automatic, but master failure is harder. When a surviving node finds a coordination row still in flight whose master has left, it atomically claims the stranded job and marks it as failed, so the job is cleanly restartable rather than being stuck forever. Recovery is fail-and-restart, not resume-in-place, so a job can restart even when its master has died after every partition completed but before finalizing. Restarts must therefore be idempotent. This requirement also binds the at-most-once guarantee to a single execution. A lost master forces a restart while its workers may still be finishing, so non-transferable work that must survive one needs a reconciliation step on restart. Automatic takeover, resuming a job without a restart, is on the roadmap. The open work is making that takeover safe when two nodes could otherwise both act as the master.
Run the Database Like a Critical Dependency
Once the database is the coordination plane, it is a hard dependency for the whole cluster, so run it replicated with backup and failover suited to the workload. The payoff for this design is that all coordination states are plain SQL. You diagnose a stuck run with a SELECT statement against the BATCH_PARTITIONS table rather than a broker console. Index the hot polling and completion-scan queries so they never fall to table scans.
Know Where the Ceiling Is
The pattern targets roughly two to twenty nodes and the ceiling is database contention, not a fixed node count. Heartbeats, polling, and status updates are all database traffic. That traffic is modest on a small-to-medium cluster, but it grows with node count and job concurrency until it competes with the batch workload for the same connection pool and I/O. Validate the range under your own load.
Trade-offs: When to Use Database Coordination and When to Reach for a Broker
Database coordination is not a universal replacement for broker-based partitioning. Choose it when the database is already present and well-managed, when operational simplicity and cost matter more than raw scale, when adding messaging middleware is impractical (constrained environments, limited operations capacity, and portability across clouds) and when the cluster sits in the small-to-medium range.
Reach for a broker when the cluster grows past that range into many dozens of nodes, when sub-second coordination latency is required, when the batch platform already shares a mature streaming backbone with other workloads, or when the work maps naturally onto the broker’s delivery and ordering semantics. The shared database also becomes a dependency you must manage at a high standard. If that approach is unrealistic, a broker’s separation of concerns may serve better.
It helps to place the database-coordinated approach against its neighbors. Spring Batch’s own remote partitioning dispatches over a broker with no built-in awareness of how many workers are live and no automatic reassignment when a worker dies after receiving a partition, which are the gaps this pattern closes. The Spring Cloud Task deployer-based partition handler is also broker-free, but it provisions a worker per partition through a platform such as Kubernetes, whereas this pattern coordinates a standing cluster of peer JVM nodes that poll for work. Database-coordinated schedulers such as Quartz, db-scheduler, and JobRunr share the instinct of coordinating through a database and failing over on node loss, but they target scheduling or general background jobs rather than Spring Batch partitioned-step execution.
Conclusion
Removing the broker from distributed Spring Batch does not delete a requirement so much as move it into SQL. The same four questions a broker answers implicitly (sizing, coordination, single ownership, and node failure) get explicit answers: a live-node count feeding the partitioner, a per-job master with no standing coordinator, compare-and-set lifecycle transitions, and a two-phase heartbeat failover. The payoff is horizontal scaling and automatic recovery with nothing in the stack beyond the database Spring Batch already required.
The database is already there and is put to work for the common case where a broker would only add moving parts. The database has a real ceiling. Knowing where that ceiling sits is most useful. The takeaway is that a relational database used as a coordination plane is enough to run correct, fault-tolerant distributed batches for the many teams whose scale never demanded a broker.
Author’s Note
The design described here is drawn from spring-batch-db-cluster-partitioning, an open-source framework the author built and maintains, which was peer-reviewed and published in the Journal of Open Source Software. It is the worked example because it is the implementation the author knows in full detail; the patterns transfer whether a reader adopts it or builds their own. The full multi-database schemas, code, and a runnable multi-node example are available in the open-source repository.

articles.title: OpenBSD 8.0 arrives with security record still intact
articles.text:
OpenBSD 8.0 is here, marking the project’s 61st release and continuing its schedule of semiannual releases dating back to 1996. What started more than 30 years ago as a fork of NetBSD has grown into one of the most security-conscious operating systems in active development. In a post to the project’s announcements mailing list, OpenBSD founder Theo de Raadt highlights a host of improvements included with the latest version and writes that the project remains “proud of OpenBSD’s record of more than thirty years with only two remote holes in the default install.”
The latest OpenBSD version brings new features and improvements across the board. These changes, particularly the new Intel Arc support and expanded virtual address space, should improve compatibility with modern graphics cards and allow the system to map more than 4GB of VRAM. Some of the major updates noted in the release newsletter are as follows:
- Added support for Intel Arc A-Series (DG2/Alchemist) graphics cards.
- 512GB kernel virtual address space on AMD64, up from 4GB, allowing VRAM mapping above 4GB.
- Added hibernation support for ARM64 systems.
- A new RPKI-to-router daemon: rtrd(8).
- RISC-V improvements including kernel support for the ‘V’ vector extension and support for Advanced Interrupt Architecture.
- Wireless network driver additions and improvements, including 802.11n and 40 MHz channels for the qwx(4) wireless driver.
- Added support for up to 64 virtual CPUs per guest virtual machine.
- Security and internal improvements for LibreSSL 4.4.0 and OpenSSH 10.6.
- Improvements to the vmm/vmd virtualization stack.
The new OpenBSD also retires support for Loongson architecture after the port stopped working with the Clang 22 compiler. If you’re interested in reading over all the changes that come with the new OpenBSD 8.0, you can take a look at the release announcement.

articles.title: Nvidia's RTX 6060 probably won't arrive until 2029, will be slower than the PS6
articles.text:
Rumor mill: Rumors had already suggested that the AI business and related memory shortages would significantly widen the traditional gap between generations of Nvidia graphics cards. Now, the latest information suggests the situation could be even worse for upcoming mainstream GPUs, which probably won't match the performance of next-generation consoles.
Prominent leaker Kepler_L2 recently suggested that Nvidia's next-generation mainstream graphics card, tentatively called the RTX 6060, could be delayed until as late as 2029. Memory supply shortages are the obvious cause.
DRAM and NAND supply constraints amid the AI data center buildout have already made currently available GPUs more expensive and harder to find. As some RTX 5090 listings march dangerously close to the $10,000 mark, Nvidia had to deny reports that it is discontinuing the flagship card.
Also see: Real Stagnation: Six Years of GeForce RTX 60 Class GPUs Tested
Meanwhile, the shortages may have already forced Nvidia to delay the previously rumored RTX 50 Super series, originally expected to debut in mid-2026. They might still arrive late this year or sometime next year to compete with a single high-end AMD RDNA 5 GPU.
The RTX 60 series is not expected until 2028, possibly extending the generational release gap to nearly four years, compared to the average gap of just over two years. A 2029 debut for the RTX 6060 would separate it from the 5060 by at least 3 years and 9 months. For comparison, the 5060 launched 4 years and 2 months after the 3060.
As for estimating the RTX 6060's relationship to the PlayStation 6, it's obviously too soon for precise predictions, but Kepler believes that Sony's upcoming console will launch sooner and with a performance advantage. The comparison roughly mirrors the relationships between prior PlayStation consoles and mainstream PC GPUs.
For example, the RTX 3060 launched about two months after the PlayStation 5, and the console's performance is comparable to that of slightly more powerful graphics cards, as per TechSpot's latest trivia question.
Assuming the 6060's performance gains follow the pattern suggested by our analysis of the last several years of mainstream GPUs, it might land somewhere near the 5060 Ti or 4070. Meanwhile, many have speculated that the PS6's 40 to 48 RDNA 5 compute units could bring it closer to the 5070 Ti.
However, price will be the main difference compared to 2020 and 2021. Kepler recently pegged the bill of materials for the PS6's memory and storage alone at $680, likely pushing the console's final price well past $1,000. It remains unclear how memory shortages will impact the RTX 6060's price. The 5060 launched with a $300 MSRP but now goes for around $470.

articles.title: ElevenLabs wants to run your voice agent. Here's what developers give up.
articles.text:
ElevenLabs wants to run your voice agent. Here’s what developers give up.
ElevenLabs launched Eleven Realtime on Tuesday, introducing two managed voice-agent models, Mini and Max, that integrate speech recognition, reasoning, turn-taking, and voice generation. Both use a cascaded architecture, but developers can’t select or independently configure the underlying models.
With this launch, the company is effectively taking over the voice-agent harness, including turn detection, interruption handling, and orchestration.
With this launch, the company is effectively taking over the voice-agent harness, including turn detection, interruption handling, and orchestration. That reduces the work required to build and maintain a voice-agent stack, but limits developers’ ability to independently troubleshoot, optimize, or replace its underlying components.
Developers can configure prompts, voices, tools, knowledge bases, and turn-taking settings, including eagerness, timeouts, and interruption handling, through ElevenAgents.
The alternative is Custom mode, which lets developers select the underlying language and speech models and configure the pipeline themselves. Realtime trades that flexibility for a managed implementation. Developers retain control over agent behavior, but not the individual models responsible for it.
Benchmarks from an outside tester
Artificial Analysis generated the performance figures by evaluating both models on speech reasoning, conversational dynamics, and human preference. On Big Bench Audio, a benchmark of 1,000 spoken reasoning questions, Max scored 98.8%, compared with 75.9% for Mini.
ElevenLabs recommends Max for agents that make frequent or complex tool calls.
The gap was even more apparent in tool use. Max completed 87.1% of tasks, while Mini managed 60.3%. ElevenLabs recommends Max for agents that make frequent or complex tool calls. Developers building agents to handle bookings, customer accounts, or other multi-step workflows will want to test that difference for themselves.
The company sets Mini as the default, saying that it is capable of handling most use cases. Mini also performed slightly better on Full-Duplex-Bench, which tests pauses, interruptions, and turn-taking, scoring 95.8% against Max’s 94.1%.
The two models are much closer on latency. Max averaged 570 milliseconds to first audio, compared with 620 milliseconds for Mini. Artificial Analysis’s June Speech-to-Speech Index recorded a faster result of 440 milliseconds for Deepslate Opal, although that earlier benchmark isn’t a direct comparison with Eleven Realtime.
Migrating from OpenAI’s Realtime API
ElevenLabs is also courting teams that already run OpenAI’s Realtime API. The migration guide says Eleven Realtime speaks the same protocol over the same WebSocket transport, so an app built on OpenAI’s SDK can point at ElevenLabs without switching SDKs. The change is the endpoint and the model name.
Migration isn’t free, though. The endpoint supports WebSocket only, so a WebRTC app has to change transports first. The SDK handles audio on its own only over WebRTC. On WebSocket, developers capture and play 24kHz PCM16 audio themselves. A WebRTC app gets that capture and playback from the SDK today, so moving over means building both.
The Realtime API also runs apart from ElevenAgents. Phone and WhatsApp channels, knowledge bases, and monitoring all sit on the platform side. The company says teams that need those features should build on ElevenAgents from the start since a team that begins with the bare API to move quickly may end up rebuilding them later.
Mini versus Max tradeoffs
According to the ElevenAgents documentation, Mini and Max agents can transfer calls between each other, but neither can transfer calls to or from agents running in Custom mode. Mini also lacks support for Zero Retention Mode and HIPAA configurations. Max supports both in the US and EU, although it isn’t available in the India or Singapore data residency environments.
Max costs more per token, but its stronger tool-use performance could make it cheaper for workloads where Mini requires more attempts to finish a task.
Both models are billed at the standard ElevenAgents per-minute rate, plus token charges. Max costs more per token, but its stronger tool-use performance could make it cheaper for workloads where Mini requires more attempts to finish a task.
Testing Before Trusting
ElevenLabs handles the underlying models and orchestration, but developers still need enough diagnostic information to figure out what went wrong when a call fails. It’s unclear how much of that information Realtime makes available.
The benchmarks are promising, but they don’t show how Realtime performs under production load. Developers will need to see whether performance holds up and whether ElevenLabs provides enough information to track down failures.
ElevenLabs did not respond to The New Stack’s request for comment by publication time.

articles.title: GPUs avaliadas em R$ 2,5 milhões somem do aeroporto de Guarulhos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
GPUs avaliadas em R$ 2,5 milhões somem do aeroporto de Guarulhos
Cada placa com RTX 5090, da Nvidia, pode custar R$ 35 mil no mercado brasileiro.
Resumo
- Duas cargas de placas de vídeo GeForce RTX 5090 da marca Zotac, avaliadas em R$ 2,5 milhões, sumiram no Aeroporto de Guarulhos.
- As placas, modelo premium da Nvidia, foram trazidas ao Brasil pelo Grupo Oderço e tinham valor aproximado de R$ 35 mil cada no mercado brasileiro.
- A GRU Airport afirmou que trabalha para solucionar o caso e que o Grupo Oderço foi orientado a pedir indenização, mas ainda não há informações sobre a resolução do caso.
Duas cargas de placas de vídeo GeForce RTX 5090 trazidas ao Brasil sumiram neste final de semana no Aeroporto de Guarulhos (GRU), em São Paulo. O caso foi denunciado pelo perfil oficial do Grupo Oderço, responsável pela importação das GPUs. Segundo o post da distribuidora, os dois pallets perdidos representam um prejuízo de R$ 2,5 milhões, o que deve representar centenas de chips gráficos.
A publicação também aponta que não há registros em vídeo do momento em que os componentes foram abduzidos. A empresa cobra um retorno da gestora GRU Airport, responsável pelas operações no aeroporto internacional de São Paulo. Os modelos que sumiram são da marca Zotac. A versão pode ser encontrada a partir de R$ 35 mil no e-commerce nacional.
Em resposta ao G1, a GRU Airport garantiu que “vem empenhando todos os esforços” para solucionar o caso, e que o sumiço das placas de vídeo já foi “reportado às autoridades competentes”. Segundo a concessionária, o Grupo Oderço já recebeu orientações para pedir indenização pela situação.
Placas de vídeo são carga preciosa
As placas RTX 5090 são artigo de luxo para quem deseja montar um PC gamer ou mesmo um computador capaz de rodar softwares de edição e trabalhos mais pesados, por exemplo. Cada unidade abduzida tem valor aproximado de R$ 35 mil no mercado brasileiro, e a Oderço fala em prejuízo de R$ 2,5 milhões considerando o preço de custo.
Modelos do tipo vêm sofrendo uma valorização no mercado por conta da crise dos chips de memória RAM. Cada Zotac RTX 5090 conta com pelo menos 32 GB de RAM GDDR7, padrão mais atual do mercado. A versão também conta com três ventoinhas para resfriamento do sistema, luzes RGB, entre outras características que vão além do componente padrão da Nvidia.
O que acontece agora?
Segundo a concessionária GRU Airport, o sumiço se deu na última quinta-feira (14/10), quando o Grupo Oderço já foi orientado sobre o procedimento para receber uma indenização pelo sumiço dos pallets.
Em nota, a administradora do aeroporto afirmou ainda que a distribuidora precisa apresentar a documentação solicitada para finalizar o processo. Vale ressaltar que a denúncia da empresa aconteceu no sábado (16/10) cobrando esclarecimentos e a localização da carga. Até o momento, não há informações sobre a resolução do caso.

articles.title: Celigo launches MCP tool management for enterprise AI assistants and agent access - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Celigo launches MCP tool management for enterprise AI assistants and agent access
Intelligent automation startup Celigo Inc. today announced its Model Context Protocol Management platform, which will let information technology and security teams govern how artificial intelligence assistants and agents act on enterprise systems.
Model Context Protocol, or MCP, has become a standard for connecting AI assistants and agents to business systems and services. Many enterprise services currently host MCP servers to provide access to business systems, and these servers expose tools that let agents interact with basic and complex controls.
Anthropic PBC introduced MCP in 2024 as an open-source standard, often described as a USB-C port for AI. It acts like a single, universal access point for AI models and agents to plug into databases, local files, search engines, business data and application programming interfaces to access resources.
Examples include looking up customer information in a customer management system, checking invoices in an enterprise resource planning system, updating an order status in a parcel tracking system or working through a ticket on a service desk. The sort of work that used to fall to integration specialists can now be completed by AI agents such as Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot and Cursor autonomously.
This opens up numerous potential security risks and access issues if these agents have access they shouldn’t or take actions outside of their role. So, it’s important to limit their activity carefully and guide them on where they operate. Although AI agents can act autonomously and provide a great deal of power, they can also hallucinate – that is, make mistakes as they work with little supervision – and they can be hijacked by malicious actors.
“AI assistants and agents are a new class of actors in the enterprise and the old model of shared credentials and broad access was never designed for them,” said Chief Product Officer Matt Graney. “Enterprises need to know who is behind every AI request, what it is authorized to do and what actions it has taken.”
Celigo MCP Management gives IT a single governed path to lock down agents and keep them within their respective domains. Graney added that every call traces back to a real person, access is approved one tool at a time and the platform runs the tools and controls them, so teams can see which system the AI has touched and maintain full transparency.
This centralized control enables broad, granular management of AI assistants and agents across the enterprise.
The company said this management interface connects MCP servers to grounded company knowledge to more than 1,000 apps built for company jobs. It lets teams control who uses which tools with an MCP Gateway and discover every MCP server through a registry.
“Celigo’s MCP was the missing piece,” said Nidecker SA Head of IT Antoine Millet. “It’s the layer in the middle connecting to all our third-party tools in the cloud. Now we get the start, the middle, and the end in one dashboard.”

articles.title: Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Fine-tuning GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod
GPT-OSS-20B is an open-weight reasoning model that thinks in English. Ask it to reason in French, German, Spanish, or Italian and it acknowledges the instruction, then produces its chain-of-thought in English anyway. On a 50-example multilingual reasoning test, the base model reasoned in the correct target language only 22 percent of the time. That 22 percent was almost entirely the English examples (English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent).
For teams deploying reasoning models for non-English users, that gap matters. A user who asks a question in French expects the model to reason and answer in French, not to switch to English mid-thought. Closing that gap is a fine-tuning problem. It raises a question every team faces once they start customizing open-weight models: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), or both?
In this post, we walk through how we fine-tuned GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod. We show when SFT alone was sufficient and when GRPO added measurable value on top. To understand more broadly when GRPO helps, we also ran a controlled Qwen2.5-7B experiment across two tasks with different capability gaps. The short answer: SFT does most of the work, GRPO refines when there is headroom to refine, and matching the technique to the capability gap is what decides the outcome.
Solution overview
This section covers the multilingual reasoning task and dataset, how SFT and GRPO complement each other, and the training stack we ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod.
The task and dataset
The dataset is HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking — a chain-of-thought reasoning dataset translated into French, Spanish, German, and Italian alongside English, roughly 949 training and 50 validation examples. The model receives a reasoning language: system-prompt instruction and must both reason and answer in that target language, overriding its strong English prior. The evaluation is 50 test cases: 10 math/logic problems across 5 languages (EN/FR/DE/ES/IT).
Two metrics matter:
- Reasoning-language correct – is the chain-of-thought in the requested language?
- Answer-language correct – is the final answer in the requested language?
How SFT and GRPO fit together
The clearest way to think about the two techniques: SFT teaches a behavior the model doesn’t have. GRPO optimizes a behavior the model can already sometimes produce. GRPO works by sampling a group of responses per prompt and pushing the policy toward the above-average ones. If the desired behavior has zero probability in the base distribution, there is very little for GRPO to reinforce. That single idea explains almost every result in this post.
The training stack
We ran on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) orchestration. For the initial SFT and GRPO runs on GPT-OSS-20B, we used the PyTorch TRL library. For the Qwen control experiment, we switched to veRL as the trainer, with Ray and KubeRay for distributed orchestration and vLLM for fast rollout generation. Checkpoints and datasets lived on Amazon FSx for Lustre, and the inter-node fabric used Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA). All fine-tuning used Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), which is parameter-efficient and well-suited to both SFT and GRPO.
The following diagram shows the training data path end-to-end. A submission from the user lands on the Amazon EKS control plane of the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster. Amazon EKS schedules a Ray head pod plus worker pods that run the veRL trainer and vLLM rollout workers. Both sets of pods mount Amazon FSx for Lustre for the base model, training data, and checkpoints. Inter-node collectives use EFA. Rollouts stream from vLLM back to the veRL trainer, and the trainer writes checkpoints back to Amazon FSx for Lustre.
The following describes each hop in more detail. The submitter starts the run from Amazon SageMaker Studio or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The Amazon EKS control plane on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod places pods on GPU nodes and starts a Ray head with worker pods for the veRL trainer and the vLLM rollout workers. Amazon FSx for Lustre provides shared, high-throughput storage for the base model, the training data, and the checkpoints. When training completes, the trainer writes the LoRA adapter back to Amazon FSx for Lustre for downstream evaluation or serving.
Prerequisites
To follow along, you need:
- An Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster with Amazon EKS orchestration. GPT-OSS SFT used 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB). The Qwen control used 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S).
- An Amazon FSx for Lustre file system mounted on the cluster with a PersistentVolumeClaim named fsx-claim at /fsx.
- EFA-enabled instances and a working NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) and aws-ofi-nccl stack for multi-node SFT.
- A container registry such as Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) to hold the training image built from the reference repository.
- A HuggingFace access token for openai/gpt-oss-20b and the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset.
- The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), kubectl, docker, and envsubst available on your workstation.
Set up the training environment
All of the commands, manifests, and scripts referenced below live in the awsome-distributed-ai GitHub repository under 3.test_cases/pytorch/trl/gpt-oss-lora-grpo/. Clone the repository and change into the test case directory:
Copy the environment template, then edit env_vars to set your ECR registry, image name, tag, and HuggingFace token:
Build the training image and push it to your registry. The image bundles PyTorch, TRL, HuggingFace Transformers, PEFT, and the training and inference scripts:
Point kubectl at your cluster and apply the FSx storage manager pod. The storage manager gives you a shell into the shared file system for checkpoint conversion and eval-log inspection:
Fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B with SFT and LoRA
We begin by measuring the base model, then configure the SFT run and examine the results.
The base-model gap
Base GPT-OSS-20B on the 50-case eval scored 22 percent reasoning-language correct (11/50). Per-language: English 100 percent, French 0 percent, German 10 percent, Spanish 0 percent, Italian 0 percent. The model defaults to English reasoning regardless of the instruction.
SFT configuration
The SFT setup used LoRA r=8, α=16, trained for 1,000 steps on 4× ml.g6e.12xlarge (16× L40S 48GB) with Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) full-shard, bf16 precision, and gradient checkpointing. The job runs as an elastic HyperPodPyTorchJob managed by Kueue, launched with hyperpodrun.
Apply the SFT manifest:
Watch training progress:
Loss and gradient norm print each step. A healthy run looks like this:
When training completes, convert the FSDP checkpoint to the Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) format that TRL’s GRPO trainer and the inference scripts expect:
SFT results and the staged learning curve
After SFT, the model reasons in the correct language 100 percent of the time (50/50) across all five languages. SFT learned this in two stages:
- Around step 200, the model learned to reason in the target language (reasoning-language metric hits 100 percent).
- Around step 1000, the model additionally learned to give the answer in the target language.
Final SFT eval (step 1000):
- Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (50/50).
- Answer-language correct: 62 percent (31/50).
- Both correct: 62 percent (31/50).
- Per-language answer accuracy: FR 60 percent, DE 60 percent, ES 30 percent, IT 60 percent, EN 100 percent.
Takeaway: SFT is not optional here. The base model can’t follow the reasoning-language instruction at all, and SFT takes reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent. The remaining gap is answer-language at 62 percent. That’s the harder half, because the final answer is short and the English prior is strongest there.
Refine answer-language with GRPO
Answer-language was the obvious target for GRPO. SFT already produced correct reasoning 100 percent of the time, and the model sometimes produced the answer in the right language, so there was a signal to reinforce.
Run GRPO on top of the SFT checkpoint
We ran GRPO with TRL’s GRPOTrainer, starting from the SFT checkpoint. The setup: load the SFT LoRA, call merge_and_unload, and add a new LoRA (r=8, α=16, about 0.068 percent trainable parameters, 13.6M of 20B). Training used K=8 generations per prompt, device_map=auto, learning rate 1e-6, and 10 epochs. The reward function scored answer-language (±5.0), reasoning-language (±1.5), and brevity (+0.5 or −1.0), for a combined range of −7.5 to +7.0.
Launch GRPO from the converted SFT checkpoint:
GRPO writes checkpoints to /fsx/checkpoints/grpo-singlenode/. Pick the best checkpoint against your held-out eval (the answer-language metric peaked early in this run) and convert it to PEFT format for inference and evaluation.
Result (from the SFT checkpoint):
- Reasoning-language correct: 100 percent (held: GRPO didn’t break what SFT taught).
- Answer-language correct: 62 to 70 percent (+8 points, 35/50).
- Both correct: 70 percent.
- Per-language answer: FR 70 percent, DE 80 percent, ES 60 percent, IT 40 percent, EN 100 percent.
GRPO delivered a real +8 point gain on the answer-language metric while holding reasoning at 100 percent. The gain came where there was headroom to gain. Answer-language was the sometimes-correct behavior that SFT had not fully converged on, and GRPO reinforced it.
Compare base, SFT, and GRPO inference side by side
To see the qualitative difference, deploy three inference pods that share the same base model but load different adapters:
Run the same French-reasoning prompt through each variant:
The base pod reasons in English despite the instruction. The SFT pod reasons in French but often answers in English. The GRPO pod reasons and answers in French. To reproduce the full 50-case eval that generated the numbers earlier, run the evaluation manifest and read the result file from the FSx storage manager:
To understand more broadly when GRPO adds value, we ran a controlled experiment on Qwen2.5-7B across two tasks with different capability gaps.
Test the pattern with a Qwen2.5-7B control
To test the “match technique to capability gap” thesis on a different model and different tasks, we ran controlled experiments on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. The first task is the same multilingual reasoning task (where headroom exists). The second task is GSM8K, where the model is already at peak accuracy. This is an internal experiment, and the public repo has not yet been released.
Infrastructure: 2× g6e.48xlarge (16× L40S), EFA 100Gbps, FSx Lustre, Ray 2.44 + KubeRay 1.4.2, veRL v0.6.1, vLLM 0.8.4.
Arms: A = base, B = SFT-only, C = SFT+GRPO.
Multilingual reasoning (50 cases)
| Metric | A base | B SFT | C SFT+GRPO | Δ GRPO | 
| Structured format | 0% | 92% | 98% | +6 | 
| Reasoning language | 0% | 96% | 98% | +2 | 
| Answer language | 0% | 38% | 44% | +6 | 
| Both correct | 0% | 38% | 44% | +6 | 
GSM8K, a task with no headroom
On GSM8K, base Qwen2.5-7B already scores 90.5 percent (181/200). GRPO at step 30 also scores 90.5 percent. When most sampled groups are all-correct, the group-relative advantage collapses to zero, so there is no learning signal. This is the other half of the thesis: GRPO needs headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) to have anything to optimize. No headroom means no gain.
Best practices
- Start with SFT. GRPO cannot teach a behavior with zero base probability. It can only reinforce responses the model already sometimes produces. SFT took reasoning-language from 22 percent to 100 percent, and every GRPO win in this work was built on that SFT checkpoint.
- Use LoRA for both SFT and GRPO. LoRA r=8/α=16 was parameter-efficient (0.068 percent trainable), and on the Qwen control it stayed numerically stable through GRPO (grad norm 0.23, about 11.7 GB per GPU). It’s a strong default when you want SFT and GRPO to share the same adapter shape.
- Match the technique to the gap. Use SFT for missing behavior. Use GRPO for refining an existing, sometimes-correct behavior. GRPO’s realistic ceiling here was +6 to +8 points.
- Check for reward headroom before spending GPU-hours. If most groups are all-correct (GSM8K 90.5 percent base), the group-relative advantage collapses to zero and GRPO gets no gradient. Verify there is headroom (pass@k >> pass@1) before starting a GRPO run.
Clean up resources
To avoid ongoing charges, delete the workload resources and then the underlying infrastructure:
- Delete the training and inference pods and jobs:
- Scale down or delete the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster or its node groups.
- Delete the Amazon FSx for Lustre file system once you have exported any checkpoints you want to keep.
- Delete any Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets or objects used for training data or checkpoint archives.
Conclusion
We showed how to fine-tune GPT-OSS-20B for multilingual reasoning on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, and how to decide between SFT and GRPO. SFT did most of the work: reasoning-language went from 22 percent to 100 percent. GRPO added a real, modest refinement on top (answer 62 percent to 70 percent) where headroom existed. A parallel Qwen2.5-7B control confirmed the pattern. GRPO added +6 percent on multilingual reasoning, where there was room to improve. It added no gain on GSM8K, where the model was already at peak accuracy (90.5 percent).
Decision framework:
- Behavior the model can’t do at all: use SFT.
- Behavior it does sometimes, with headroom: use SFT then GRPO for a few points more.
- Model already at peak accuracy, or target has zero base probability: GRPO won’t help.
To try this yourself, walk through the test cases in the awsome-distributed-ai repository. For more on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the service detail page and the Amazon SageMaker HyperPod documentation. For a walkthrough of Ray on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod, see the related post Running distributed training on Amazon SageMaker HyperPod with Ray and Amazon SageMaker Studio. The link will be added after that post is published. Share your results in the comments.

articles.title: Mods can almost double DLSS 5 performance through Foveation, reducing resolution at the edges of frames — technique makes DLSS 5 possible on high-resolution ultrawide monitors
articles.text:
Mods can almost double DLSS 5 performance through Foveation, reducing resolution at the edges of frames — technique makes DLSS 5 possible on high-resolution ultrawide monitors
This might actually make DLSS 5 more accessible.
Popular graphics post-processing injector software ReShade, commonly used to mod DLSS 5 into unsupported games, now has a foveated imaging add-on, including another standalone project that doesn't need precursor software, allowing DLSS 5 to affect only what's in view, reducing GPU load and increasing FPS.
Foveated imaging is nothing new; it's a technique that's been used in VR to increase performance. It works by only rendering what's in view, often increasing the resolution in the center and reducing it at the edges. Our eyes work in a similar way, with the clearest image in a small area in the center of your vision, blurring on the edges. With foveated rendering, you barely notice the lower-resolution edges as the peripheral vision is less concerned with fine details.
Instead of varying the resolution of the image, however, it varies the level of detail in DLSS 5 Neural Rendering. DLSS NR loads a whole AI model into your GPU and renders images in real time, making it a resource-intensive task; but the task is minimized greatly when most of the detail is only asked for in the middle of the image. That's what projects like maximedgoulet’s Foveated DLSS5 and ClarkCheekyKent’s CheekyFoveatedDLSS aim to do; with Foveated DLSS being a ReShade add-on and CheekyFoveatedDLSS capable of being a standalone integration.
Both implementations allow you to adjust the size of the center area with the highest rendering quality, with independent width and height adjustments to suit your personal situation, as some people have a larger focus area than others or have a different monitor distance. You can also adjust the render fall-off rate, so the image quality lessens more quickly or slowly past the focus area.
As Maximedgoulet's implementation is an add-on for an injector, the pipeline is quite long compared to the standalone integration of CheekyFoveatedDLSS, which Reddit comments claim is more convenient and more polished. Though both show a big improvement in performance, Maximed's Reddit post on Foveated DLSS5 claims an improvement from 48 to 80FPS in The Witcher 3 with 2x Multipass at ultrawide 7680x2160p on an RTX 4090. Considering Maximedgoulet’s 4090 could not handle DLSS-NR on an ultrawide, this implementation might genuinely be feasible to make Neural Rendering more playable.

articles.title: Native Apple Music support is finally coming to a wireless speaker system other than Sonos — has Bluesound just become the Apple-loving audiophile's ideal option?
articles.text:
There's finally a proper Sonos alternative for Apple-loving audiophiles — Bluesound is getting Apple Music as a free upgrade soon, and not just on its own devices
Good news for Apple Music aficionados: it's coming to the entire BluOS ecosystem
- Bluesound is adding fully integrated Apple Music support, on top of existing AirPlay support
- This is rare in streaming systems — Sonos has basically had a monopoly
- Available now via free software update
If you want to play Apple Music natively, in high resolution, on multi-room audio equipment the choice has largely been Sonos, Sonos or Sonos. That's now changed, and direct integration with the Apple Music service is coming to the Bluesound platform and BluOS software as a free upgrade.
That's a big deal because in addition to Bluesound's own products, the BluOS operating system also powers devices from big audio brands including NAD Electronics, PSB Speakers, DALI, Cyrus, and Monitor Audio.
It's a significant upgrade, because like Spotify and TIDAL, Apple Music is now fully integrated into the BluOS platform rather than supported indirectly via AirPlay 2. That means the audio is streaming directly to your player rather than via your phone, tablet or computer, so there's no compression, as there is over AirPlay or Bluetooth.
When is the Apple Music upgrade coming to BluOS?
The update is available from today, 20 October 2026, and you can get it by updating the BluOS software on your device. You'll then be able to use the BluOS Controller app to select your streaming, whether that's to a single device or a multi-room setup.
In the case of multi-room setups you'll be able to share Apple Music to specific rooms and audio zones, or have the same music playing everywhere.
Although the update itself is free, Apple Music is of course a subscription-based service, though you don't have to pay extra for higher quality or ad-free streaming.
It's a major win for Bluesound as the key Sonos alternative. There's obviously a lot of crossover between the the slickness the Sonos system has been known for and what people expect from Apple products.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
When Sonos had its major software issues in 2024, Bluesound and WiiM emerged as the two multi-room systems hoping to benefit most from it, but WiiM has a strange relationship with Apple. None of its products support Apple Music natively, and many of its products don't even support AirPlay.
So this is a big win for Bluesound with Apple fans, especially since it's always been considered the more audiophile-led alternative to Sonos — now Apple Music can be a source for that.
