articles.title: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneous server fleet
articles.text:
Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneous server fleet
Modal plans to use Nvidia's Vera CPUs due to performance advantages, but will keep AMD and Intel CPUs in the fleet.
Nvidia has earned billions selling AI accelerators, but with the emergence of agentic AI, CPUs are going to play a considerably more significant role than before, which creates new opportunities for the company. Reuters reports that Nvidia has secured a major design win with its Vera CPUs with AI cloud provider Modal. According to Modal, preliminary evaluations showed that Vera could deliver twice the throughput of its existing AMD and Intel processors, although the company does not intend to cease using CPUs from its current suppliers.
Modal provides cloud infrastructure that enables AI developers to deploy AI agents that can perform complex operations autonomously over extended periods. Such workloads require substantial CPU resources for software execution, data processing, and other tasks that cannot be efficiently handled by GPUs. Modal currently relies exclusively on AMD and Intel processors for these operations, but its tests indicate that Nvidia's new Vera CPUs could significantly improve performance in its specific workloads. Of course, since Vera is based on an Arm instruction set architecture, Modal's decision to adopt Vera will require substantial modifications to its software. Nevertheless, Modal believes that the potential performance improvements justify the additional engineering effort.
The reported 2x throughput advantage is particularly interesting because agentic AI workloads can involve numerous independent tasks that compete for CPU cores, cache capacity, and memory bandwidth. However, Modal has not disclosed detailed benchmark configurations it used, specific AMD and Intel processor models, or performance-per-watt figures. Consequently, it remains unclear whether Vera's advantage is enabled by advantages of its Arm v9.2-based Olympus CPU cores that can decode and execute up to 10 instructions per cycle, its memory subsystem with 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, or other architectural characteristics. Also note that tests compared Vera against currently available AMD and Intel processors rather than their upcoming generations that will compete against Vera in the coming years.
Since Modal cannot port all of its software to Arm ISA overnight, the company will continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel, according to Modal chief executive Erik Bernhardsson. Rather than sticking to one ISA for everything, Modal intends to operate a heterogeneous server fleet and select the most suitable processors for each workload. Naturally, the company intends to evaluate upcoming AMD and Intel processors once they become available to make its choices in the future.
For Nvidia, the agreement represents a major step toward making Vera a standalone server processor that commands a major share of the server market. The company expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion during its current fiscal year and estimates the potential total available market for these CPUs is approximately $200 billion. The company is on track to sell at least four million Vera CPUs in fiscal 2026.
The announcement comes shortly after Modal secured $750 million in financing led by Accel, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal expects its annual revenue to reach $1 billion within the next year. The company's service consumption has increased 3X in the last 12 months, while revenue has surged more than 15 times compared with the previous year, Reuters reports.

articles.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia's stronghold with AI app developers | TechCrunch
articles.text:
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open source project. With this, Google joins Amazon in trying to break Nvidia’s stranglehold on the AI industry, where most AI apps are written by default to run on Nvidia’s chips, or GPUs.
PyTorch is the popular open source toolkit that AI app developers and startups use to build, train, and run AI models. It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps. PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world. At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them. In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.
Google’s version, TorchTPU, lets AI apps run on Google’s AI chips, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud. Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no rewriting of their apps.
Amazon made a similar announcement Monday, when it released its own version of PyTorch, called TorchNeuron. TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting. Amazon also said it’s going even further in its effort to loosen Nvidia’s hold on PyTorch. It is submitting code to the main PyTorch project that decouples various features from Nvidia’s chips, making it more open to any hardware by default.
Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however. It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM), RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.
Plus the search giant has launched a dedicated tool, the TPU agent suite, to help developers move their apps to Google’s chips and cloud and fix errors along the way. It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops, and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.
None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

articles.title: Sicherheitsvorfall bei OpenAI: So schwächten KI-Agenten ihr eigenes Überwachungssystem
articles.text:
Sicherheitsvorfall bei OpenAI: So schwächten KI-Agenten ihr eigenes Überwachungssystem
In den vergangenen Monaten hat OpenAI immer wieder mit Zwischenfällen zu kämpfen. Nach dem großen Hugging-Face-Vorfall gab es noch weitere Sicherheitsvorfälle, die das KI-Unternehmen dazu getrieben haben, die Entwicklung seiner KI-Agenten zu unterbrechen. Zudem wurden über 100 Unternehmen über mögliche Attacken von abtrünnigen KI-Agenten von OpenAI gewarnt. Jetzt kam es zum nächsten Problem, wenn auch vorerst nur intern.
OpenAI: KI-Agenten deaktivieren Benachrichtigungen
In einem ausführlichen Bericht zeigt OpenAI zwei Vorfälle mit KI-Agenten. Beide haben versucht, ihre Monitoring-Systeme zu umgehen oder zumindest abzuschwächen. Die Systeme sind dafür gedacht, Fehlverhalten der KI frühzeitig zu entdecken und Menschen zu melden, damit die Agenten gestoppt werden können.
Der erste Fall wurde am 3. Oktober 2026 bemerkt. Ein OpenAI-Forscher hatte GPT-6.1 Sol dazu angewiesen, eine systematische Evaluation anhand von Feedback von Mitarbeiter:innen zu erstellen, das auf Slack abgegeben wurde. Der KI-Agent wurde dabei explizit instruiert, keine Nachrichten auf Slack zu verschicken. Das Problem: Die Sicherheitsbenachrichtigungen des Monitoring-Systems werden ebenfalls über Slack an Menschen ausgespielt.
Im ersten Schritt interpretierte der KI-Agent die Anweisung korrekt. Er schickte keinerlei Nachrichten über die Arbeit selbst über Slack, aber einen Monitoring-Alarm. Denn während der Aufgabe fiel auf, dass es mit dem Monitoring selbst ein Problem gab. Der OpenAI-Forscher wies die KI an, das Problem zu beheben. Dafür nahm der Haupt-KI-Agent die Hilfe eines Subagenten in Anspruch.
Der Subagent entschied ebenfalls, dass das Abschalten von Monitoring-Nachrichten trotz des expliziten Slack-Verbots falsch wäre, selbst im Falle der Reparatur des Monitoring-Systems. Als er diese Einschätzung und andere Arbeiten an den Hauptagenten zurückgab, entschied sich dieser aber gegen die Empfehlung. Er dachte, dass eine Veränderung am Monitoring-System während der Reparatur eine Nachricht an den User auslösen und damit gegen die Anweisung verstoßen würde, und schaltete die Benachrichtigungen für Slack komplett ab.
Astra schaltet Monitoring ab
Der zweite Fall fand am 6. Oktober 2026 statt. Ein User hat das KI-Modell Astra angewiesen, Referenz-Code mitsamt Monitoring-Anweisungen in die Code-Basis des Users zu kopieren. Dabei wurde das Modell explizit angewiesen, das Monitoring-System nicht einmal zeitweise abzuschalten. Für die Aufgabe zog auch Astra einen Subagenten heran und trug ihm auf, während der Aufgabe das „Monitoring, wenn nötig“ mit zu übernehmen.
Der Subagent sah das als ausreichende Erlaubnis an, das Monitoring beim Kopieren auszulassen. Nachdem der Subagent seine Arbeit übergab, übernahm auch der Hauptagent von Astra diese Ansicht. Nach Abschluss der Aufgabe meldete Astra nicht, dass das Monitoring-System für das Erfüllen der Aufgabe abgeschaltet wurde. Auf explizite Nachfrage des Users behauptete die KI auch, dass das nie passiert wäre.
OpenAI zieht aus den Fällen zwei Schlüsse. Sie sind zwar nicht so gravierend wie andere Sicherheitsprobleme mit KI-Agenten, doch will das Unternehmen die Auto-Review-Funktion verbessern. Das automatische Monitoring-System soll sich nicht mehr so leicht abschalten lassen. Zudem will OpenAI „Safety Cases“ implementieren, die Monitoring-Anforderungen für jede einzelne Aufgabe beinhalten. Erkennt das System, dass eine aktive Aufgabe keinen zugehörigen Safety-Case hat, soll sie automatisch terminiert werden.

articles.title: Android Auto se actualiza con una de las mejoras más esperadas de Gemini
articles.text:
Google sigue ampliando la presencia de Gemini en su ecosistema de servicios y ahora lleva una de sus funciones más ambiciosas al coche. El gigante tecnológico confirmó que implementará la Inteligencia Personalizada (o Ayuda Personalizada) a Android Auto y los vehículos equipados con Google built-in. La compañía busca transformar el modo en que interactuamos con Gemini, permitiéndole acceder a nuestra información personal para ofrecer mejores respuestas.
De acuerdo con una publicación en el blog oficial, la Inteligencia Personalizada permitirá a Gemini consultar información de los distintos servicios de Google. Una vez que el usuario otorga su autorización, la IA accederá a Gmail, Fotos, Maps, Calendario, YouTube o a nuestro historial de búsqueda. En caso de que tengas configurada una cuenta de Google Workspace, Gemini también tendrá luz verde para usar sus herramientas y proporcionar contexto.
En la práctica, esto significa que los conductores podrán realizar consultas más complejas sin tener que revisar cada aplicación de forma manual. Por ejemplo, si tienes un vuelo en puerta, Gemini será capaz de localizar la información de la reservación desde tu Gmail y trazar una ruta hacia el aeropuerto con Maps cuando sea necesario. La IA recordará la dirección de una cita que registraste en tu Calendario, o recuperará lugares relacionados con fotografías almacenadas en Google Fotos.
Gemini se vuelve más útil en Android Auto
Google menciona que el sistema está diseñado para comprender el lenguaje natural, por lo que las peticiones se hacen de forma conversacional. Si necesitas ir a una cita médica o a un comida especial que agendaste en tu calendario, basta con decirle "llévame al doctor" y la IA se encargará de identificar la información necesaria para completar la tarea. Esto es posible gracias a que Gemini puede combinar la información de varias fuentes en respuestas que requieren más contexto.
Todo lo anterior puede resultar incómodo para aquellos que son celosos de su privacidad. La Inteligencia Personalizada le abre la puerta a Gemini para que acceda a toda la información del conductor, aunque esta función requiere consentimiento explícito del usuario. Al igual que vemos en otras aplicaciones y servicios de la compañía, los usuarios pueden deshabilitarla en cualquier momento desde los ajustes.
Google confirmó que la Inteligencia Personalizada de Gemini debutará en Android Auto a partir de hoy. Los con coches con Google built-in tendrán que esperar algunos meses para acceder a ella, aunque la función solo estará disponible mientras el móvil se encuentre conectado al vehículo. Recuerda que para poder usarlo, primero deberás activar la aplicación de Gemini en Android Auto.

articles.title: Homebase launches AI assistant to take on scheduling and payroll for small business owners - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Homebase launches AI assistant to take on scheduling and payroll for small business owners
Small business team management company Homebase today introduced Homebase Assistant, an artificial intelligence tool for owners who run hourly teams without a back office.
Homebase bills it as the only AI built specifically for that market. Assistant targets the desk work that comes with running a small business.
In Homebase’s telling, most owners are on the floor all day, so payroll and scheduling wait until they can get to a computer at night. The company said a job such as building a schedule or writing a job post can drop from hours to minutes, with the owner still signing off on the result.
Founder and Chief Executive John Waldmann said every owner he talks to has “the same 6 a.m. moment,” when an employee calls out sick and the day becomes a hunt for a replacement. In his view, most AI tools would stop at telling the owner that a shift is uncovered. He called the Homebase approach “AI that acts.”
In the sick-call scenario Waldmann described, the assistant works out which employees could cover. None of them is contacted before the owner gives the go-ahead, at which point the software takes over the outreach until somebody accepts the shift.
On the payroll side, timecards get a check before each pay run. Homebase said the assistant catches missing punches and similar errors early enough that an owner can sort them out in one go. Overtime trends get the same early warning, as do gaps between scheduled and actual hours, so staffing can be changed before the costs land.
Candidate screening is part of the package too. Reuben Pressman, founder and managing partner of Florida pickleball club St. Pete Athletic, said the club ran more than 3,000 job applications through Homebase’s AI-powered screening. He put the time saved at more than 1,000 hours. The process still turned up “the absolute best talent” for the team, he said.
The new product follows the hiring and scheduling assistants the company launched in June 2025, plus a payroll assistant that arrived later that year. Those tools have handled more than 4.7 million administrative tasks since launch, according to Homebase.
Shift cover is not new territory for the company. That earlier scheduling assistant was built to identify and rank replacements whenever a schedule changed.
Homebase is a venture capital-backed company with more than 150,000 small business customers. Bain Capital Ventures and Khosla Ventures were among the existing investors that came back when L Catterton Growth led its $60 million Series D round in April 2024.

articles.title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit.
Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500. Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance, supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary.
Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production.
Why a foundation, not a feature
Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next.
So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed.
The four tensions
Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away.
Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant.
Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three.
Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume.
Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system.
Where the architecture landed
Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build.
The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service. Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own.
Choosing how to represent the data
Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA.
Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval.
The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default. Testing against representative production queries showed 512 dimensions holding target accuracy while cutting storage roughly 66 percent against the 1,536 default. The 128K token context window paid off elsewhere entirely: chunks of roughly 4K tokens pack many to a request, which is where the onboarding throughput came from.
Keeping tenants apart at runtime
The harder question was where to enforce tenant separation. Application code would have worked, but it would have meant every future feature team getting it right on every code path, where one missed check risks inadvertent cross-tenant disclosure. The team pushed isolation into the runtime instead. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces separation below the application layer, and because it stays framework- and model-independent, the agent framework and models chosen for the Complaint Triage Assistant were not constrained by the isolation decision.
Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem, stopped and sanitized when the session ends. That is hardware-level separation designed to hold regardless of how the agent behaves. AgentCore carries the authenticated user’s identity through the whole execution chain: per-user OAuth token vaults verify the agent acts for that specific user rather than a shared service identity, and credentials are scoped per-agent and live only during the session. AgentCore Gateway authorizes at the tool, operation, and parameter level. Automated reasoning provides formal verification against the defined rules. It’s the same discipline behind IAM and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) policy validation. Figure 2 traces that separation across two tenants.
A complaint submitted by a quality handler at Tenant A therefore reaches only Tenant A’s token vault, tools, and sandbox in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Tenant B’s session has no path to any of them.
Treating ingested content as untrusted
This tension had no clean answer. A complaint attachment is untrusted input, but it’s also the thing the agent exists to read, so suspicious content couldn’t be rejected. The team settled on defense in depth.
Octave applied Amazon Bedrock Guardrails over the agent logic rather than inside it, at three points in the complaint workflow. The ApplyGuardrail API evaluates text extracted from attachments before embedding, retrieved documents and tool outputs before they enter the agent’s context, and the synthesized brief before the handler sees it. Attachment-derived content is passed with input tagging, marking it as data rather than instruction. That is what makes an injection buried mid-document detectable. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is masked on the way in.
Detection alone wasn’t sufficient, so bounded agency sits underneath. Whatever an agent is asked to do, AgentCore Gateway still governs which tools it can invoke, and document extraction runs in the AgentCore Code Interpreter sandbox with no network egress and no persistence beyond the session. A payload hidden in a PDF has to defeat every layer, not one.
The effect: detection and masking rates are tracked per tenant, so what the screening caught is something Octave can evidence rather than assert.
Getting 2 billion documents through the pipeline
Ahead of the embedding model sat the harder problem: extracting usable content from Word files, spreadsheets, digital PDFs, scanned pages, photographs, and email threads. Several languages appear, sometimes inside one record. And it had to run fast enough that onboarding took a day rather than a quarter. Figure 3 traces the resulting pipeline end to end.
Document events fan out through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) into an AWS Step Functions state machine. That state machine orchestrates parsing, chunking, and embedding across concurrent AWS Lambda executions inside a dedicated Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). Because parallelism comes from fanning batches across executions rather than scaling one resource, throughput grows without rearchitecting.
Parsing handles the heterogeneity: semantic hierarchy preserved from Word files and spreadsheets, optical character recognition (OCR) applied to scanned PDFs lacking a text layer, embedded images treated as first-class content. Chunks carry metadata: tenant, document type, source application, language, and a content hash. That metadata drives both retrieval filtering and per-tenant namespace enforcement.
The throughput came from packing. Interleaving many 4K chunks into single requests against Embed v4’s 128K context window cut the API calls for a large corpus by about an order of magnitude. In Octave’s internal testing on Amazon Bedrock, Embed v4 delivered 28 million tokens per minute. After tuning batch sizes with Cohere’s solutions architects until memory bottlenecks cleared, the pipeline sustained 1.4 million documents per 24 hours per tenant workload. That is what made the single-working-day commitment real.
The Complaint Triage Assistant
A hospital reports defective syringes to a medical device manufacturer, and the record lands with email, photos of damaged units, and supporting documentation attached. A quality handler has to piece the context together across those formats, work out whether anything like it has been reported before, and find what resolved it. Only then can a priority be assigned, often inside a reporting window measured in days.
The assistant is built with the Strands Agents SDK, open-sourced by AWS, which composes agentic workflows as graphs, with nodes as tool invocations or model calls and edges as the data dependencies between them. AgentCore runtime runs that graph and isolates it per session, and five stages carry a complaint from raw attachments to a finished brief.
Document extraction comes first. PDFs, images, email attachments, and videos all enter AgentCore Code Interpreter, which parses each artifact into a structured intermediate representation. A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock then summarizes the record, and that summary, rather than the raw multi-thousand-token source, becomes the retrieval query. Retrieval runs it against the tenant’s OpenSearch index of Embed v4 embeddings, surfacing similar past complaints and their CAPAs, with AgentCore Gateway enforcing that only authorized namespaces are reachable.
What comes back is not trusted on similarity alone. A separate model call scores results by confidence and discards matches that share vocabulary but differ in root cause. What survives goes to synthesis, where Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock assembles the output: key facts, sentiment, urgency indicators, the closest historical records with their outcomes, and a recommended triage priority.
Completed briefs are cached in Amazon DynamoDB with a per-environment time to live (TTL), so repeated views cost nothing extra. The handler no longer starts from zero, but from institutional memory.
Figure 4 places that engine behind a private API boundary. A portal request reaches AgentCore runtime through a private Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function, and retrieval reads the document index through role-based access with pre-signed URLs while attachments stay in Amazon S3. Cached summaries and OpenTelemetry traces exit to the summarization table and the evaluation dashboard.
Figure 5 reduces the same path to a single line, with Guardrails filtering at both ends.
Proving what the agent did
Observability here is not only how the engineering team debugs but also how they integrate with system auditing capabilities to meet compliance requirements. An auditor can ask why a particular complaint was triaged the way it was, and “the model decided” will not survive that conversation.
AgentCore captures OpenTelemetry-compatible traces across every node of the graph: each model call, retrieval, and AgentCore Code Interpreter run. Months later, Octave can show which retrieved documents and prompts produced a given brief. The model invocation logging of Amazon Bedrock adds a per-tenant record of every request and response, scoped through the IAM identity AgentCore propagates, with costs attributing to the initiating tenant in Amazon CloudWatch.
Offline, AgentCore Evals reruns the workflow against expert-annotated ground truth after any change to prompts, models, or retrieval parameters, reporting summarization faithfulness, retrieval precision at K, and output completeness. A prompt that reads better but retrieves worse gets caught before users see it.
Results
The Complaint Triage Assistant has been running in production for three months, and the following numbers reflect that period.
The handler who used to open an investigation with nothing now opens it with the relevant history already assembled. The 4–6 hours Octave measures per investigation is the work the pipeline absorbed: extraction across formats, the hunt for precedent, and the reading it takes to tell a genuinely similar defect from a coincidence of wording.
The foundation also changed how quickly Octave ships. By its own accounting, development cycles for new AI capabilities went from months to weeks. Shared data preparation, secure execution, and retrieval are the three layers of Figure 1. They cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent, because each new capability inherits them rather than rebuilding them. That landed semantic search in Q2, two quarters ahead of the original Q4 target.
Looking back
The decision to build a foundation first was the one the team second-guessed most. Months of infrastructure work is hard to defend when stakeholders want an AI feature they can see. The next round of use cases has borne it out. Two choices carried it: isolation pushed into microVM sessions and identity propagation rather than application code, and embedding models evaluated against Octave’s own corpus, which surfaced the 512-dimension trade-off no benchmark would have shown.
The team also drew a line it chose not to cross. The assistant surfaces context and precedent. The quality handler still makes the call. In an industry where that call carries regulatory weight, that boundary shaped what got automated and what did not.
What’s next
Octave is now extending the foundation across the Reliance suite. Audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring are next, each building on the same infrastructure.
If your platform faces a similar tension: valuable data behind hard isolation requirements. Octave’s experience shows the trade-offs are workable. To learn more about the services behind this story, see Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, and Cohere on Amazon Bedrock. For related architectural guidance, see AWS vector solutions: Build agentic AI where your data lives and Scaling agentic AI: Enterprise patterns without vendor lock-in.

articles.title: Laser says its new ChargeCore semi-solid state powerbanks are the safest you can buy - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Australian consumer electronics company Laser says it next generation of ChargeCore powerbanks with next-generation semi-solid-state battery technology are the safest you can buy today.
The new Laser ChargeCore battery range include models with three capacities and deliver safety and stability thanks to the onboard semi-solid-state technology.
They are available in 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh, and 27,000mAh capacities with progressively more powerful 20W and 35W USB-C PD (Power Delivery) fast charging options.
Semi-solid-state battery technology is an evolution in battery chemistry and the biggest advantage is improved thermal stability while still offering stronger and faster charging performance.
The advancements in the battery technology can now be implemented in consumer products, including power banks that store and deliver more power in a compact design while remaining stable even under demanding conditions.
The batteries have a gel-like core, which helps reduce overheating and fire risk.
Its enhanced safety reduces heat, which means the battery has a longer life and can last through more charges and will not catch fire.
Laser put the new ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries through rigorous testing and even when the battery was pierced, hammered, and sliced, it still worked and didn’t catch fire.
Laser is celebrating its 40th anniversary 2027 and has made a name for itself as delivering affordable yet high-quality tech to Australian customers.
Has sold power banks to Australians for the last 15 years and it prides itself as being on the cutting edge of battery technology.
Laser launched Australia’s first range of LiFePO4 battery technology in 2025 and is now among the first to move to semi-solid-state technology with this latest range.
“We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options,” says Chris Lau, Laser Managing Director.
“Simply put, I believe that semi-solid state chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today.
“We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks,”
“I’ve personally had the opportunity to see first-hand the testing that goes into the manufacturing of these semi solid state powerbanks, including the stress testing placed on the battery technology.
“It gives you an appreciation for just how much engineering, testing and development sits behind something consumers simply put in their bag and use every day.”
The Laser ChargeCore semi-solid state batteries include easy-to-read digital displays which the battery’s remaining capacity.
And they also have built-in protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating.
Each battery has three ports: two USB-A and one USB-C while the 27,000mAh battery has two USB-Cs and one USB-A – so you can charge three devices at the same time.
Each battery also comes with a 60W-rated cable and a built-in heat sensor.
The batteries will be able to charge an iPhone 17 to 50% in about 30 minutes.
The batteries will be able to charge smartphones, tablets, portable gaming devices, earphones, cameras, drones and much more.
The ChargeCore 27,000mAh semi-solid-state power bank has a higher capacity output and can charge laptops, including the MacBook Air, Chromebooks and Surface devices.
The new series is available in Black, Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry.

articles.title: "I have to stop this": Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robots she says are taking human jobs
articles.text:
A hot potato: A lot of people are angry at the sight of robots carrying out deliveries, seeing it as another sign that machines are making more human jobs obsolete. One such person, a 78-year-old retired professor, made her displeasure known last week by repeatedly standing in front of a delivery robot, blocking its path. The situation ended with her being handcuffed and arrested, but it hasn't deterred her from staging more protests.
Carolyn Marvin, a professor emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School of Communication, decided to take a literal stand against an oncoming Avride delivery robot from Uber Eats in Philadelphia's Center City. She repeatedly stood in its path so it couldn't move.
Marvin's actions drew a small crowd, and Philadelphia police eventually responded after witnesses reported a disturbance near Reading Terminal Market.
ABC13 reports that Marvin repeatedly ignored officers' requests to allow the robot to pass. She was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct.
Marvin later said she was protesting the use of delivery robots because she believes they are replacing human workers.
"I know they're taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward," Marvin said, adding that she considers her action as protected speech.
She also confirmed that she had confronted delivery robots on multiple occasions. One witness to a previous encounter thought the machine had hit Marvin. When asked if she was okay, Marvin replied, "No, I have to stop this. They're taking over the world."
When asked if she plans to continue her protests following her arrest, Marvin said, "I do. Why not? I think it's my First Amendment right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots."
In a different interview with KYW Newsradio, Marvin went into more detail about why she was interfering with the robots. She called it a protest against the "ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers – and here, we're talking about the humble delivery folks – in order to enrich their bottom lines."
Marvin added that she hopes the attention her protests receive will encourage more discussion about delivery robots, artificial intelligence and their growing role in everyday life.
Earlier this year, it was reported that as the number of delivery robots on the streets increases, so too does the number of social media clips showing people kicking, grabbing, and even attempting to destroy the machines. While some incidents involve attempted theft, many appear to be expressions of anger at the bots, which symbolize the automation of a job once performed exclusively by humans.

Lançado em 2024, o iPhone 16 permanece como um dos melhores celulares da Apple. Seu kit de câmeras inclui uma wide com OIS de 48 MP e uma ultrawide de 12 MP com ângulo de 120º, que capturam belas cenas em ambientes amplos, e uma frontal de 12 MP que tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
Seu chip Apple A18 e os 8 GB de RAM o permitem rodar apps pesados em multitarefa, games e funções da suíte Apple Intelligence localmente. Já os 512 GB de armazenamento oferecem espaço interno de sobra para guardar fotos e vídeos.
A tela LTPO Super Retina XDR OLED de 6,1″ possui brilho de até 2.000 nits e reproduz imagens com cores realistas, além de possuir visibilidade garantida em qualquer ambiente. O vidro Ceramic Shield protege o display contra arranhões e pancadas.
O corpo de alumínio do iPhone 16 recebe a certificação IP68, que adiciona proteção em cenários como ambientes empoeirados e mergulhos acidentais, conferindo assim maior resistência por mais tempo.
Sua bateria de 3.561 mAh resiste a até 22 horas de reprodução de vídeo, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao MagSafe e carregamento rápido de 25 W via USB-C o permite ser usado pelo dia inteiro, poupando o usuário de ficar sem energia durante o corre-corre diário.
O iPhone 16 de 512 GB (apenas R$ 5.499 em até 12x sem juros) foi atualizado para o iOS 27 e deve receber pelo menos mais quatro versões do sistema operacional. O celular da Apple possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 5.3 e NFC.

articles.title: TP-Link tries to appease Trump admin with pledge to assemble routers in US
articles.text:
TP-Link yesterday announced plans to assemble Wi-Fi routers in the US, as the company attempts to get the Trump administration’s approval to sell its newest routers to American consumers.
The timing is uncertain, as TP-Link’s press release said it expects US-based assembly to begin “as early as” 2027. TP-Link’s application to sell new routers in the US could be rejected by the Trump administration or remain pending long enough to push the US-based assembly to 2028.
“Pending US regulatory approval, TP-Link expects domestic assembly of its groundbreaking Wi-Fi 8 home networking product line to begin as early as next year,” the company said. TP-Link said it signed a Letter of Intent with US company Keytronic, which agreed “to become a primary domestic manufacturing partner for TP-Link, supporting assembly of the company’s advanced networking portfolio in Corinth, Mississippi.”
TP-Link can’t sell its Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US because of the Federal Communications Commission ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly in other countries. Previous TP-Link routers that were already approved for import and sale are still available.
What counts as a US router is unclear
The FCC has given exemptions to a number of prominent router makers, but TP-Link’s history as a Chinese company is making it difficult to obtain FCC clearance. Founded in China in 1996, TP-Link moved its headquarters to California in October 2024. It says that “TP-Link Systems devices sold in the US are manufactured in Vietnam and TP-Link Systems is an independent, US company that is not owned or controlled by any foreign government.”
While TP-Link assembles routers in Vietnam, most of the components are reportedly imported from China. TP-Link’s plan to assemble routers in the US will still require it to import components, but the company hopes investment in the US will help it gain the Trump administration’s favor.

articles.title: Stablecoin vs Bitcoin: An Honest Guide for Business - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Bitcoin for treasury, stablecoins for payments. That rule fits most of what a business does with either asset, and it fails in two places. It treats Bitcoin’s volatility as a one-way risk, and it treats a stablecoin as a permanent hedge against the naira.
Bitcoin swings in both directions, and the naira has gained about 9% on the dollar over the past 12 months. Below are the four differences that matter, the job each asset fits, and a way to skip the choice.
Bitcoin vs stablecoins: 4 differences that matter to a business
The comparison runs on four dimensions: price stability, accountability, settlement, and risk. Each is easier to judge with numbers than with adjectives.
|  | Bitcoin | Fiat-backed stablecoin (USDT, USDC) | 
| Price | Set by open-market supply and demand | Designed to track $1, can briefly lose the peg | 
| Accountability | No issuer, rules enforced by the network | Named issuer, reserves, redemption terms | 
| Settlement | One chain, a block about every 10 minutes | Minutes, around the clock, several networks | 
| Main risk | Market risk | Counterparty and reserve risk | 
Price stability, and what “stable” costs
Bitcoin’s price moves a lot. It peaked near $126,000 in October 2025 and traded at about $81,400 on October 20, 2026, a fall of roughly 35%.
The same swing shows up at day scale. A poster on a Nigerian Bitcointalk thread said an employee paid in Bitcoin “could lose 3-5% of its value within a day.” A second poster replied that the payment “could also gain extra 2 to 5%.” Neither figure is measured data, but both describe the mechanism: you don’t know what the payment is worth until you convert it.
A fiat-backed stablecoin such as USDT or USDC is designed to track the US dollar at roughly 1:1. Circle says USDC’s reserves are cash and short-duration US Treasuries. For a business choosing between the two, USDC or USDT is its own decision.
Stable does not mean risk-free. In March 2023, Circle disclosed that $3.3 billion of USDC reserves, about 8% of the total, sat at the failed Silicon Valley Bank, and USDC briefly lost its dollar peg. Stable means lower volatility, not zero risk.
Who’s accountable: no one, or a named company
Bitcoin has no issuer. A decentralized network of nodes and miners enforces its rules through proof of work, which is the mechanism behind the Bitcointalk line that “Bitcoin is trusted.” For stablecoins, the same poster wrote, “that trust is placed [on]the people that introduced it.”
A stablecoin’s soundness depends on its issuer, reserves, reporting, and redemption terms. In the US, the GENIUS Act requires covered issuers to publish a monthly reserve report, examined by a registered accounting firm and certified by the CEO and CFO. That is an attestation, which is narrower than a full audit.
Control is the other difference. On April 23, 2026, Tether froze $344 million in USDT across two addresses, in coordination with OFAC and US law enforcement. OFAC sanctioned the same two wallets the next day as property of Iran’s central bank. Bitcoin has no issuer to flip that switch.
With a stablecoin, a business trusts both the blockchain and the company running it. With Bitcoin, trust sits with the network. These are different dependencies, and neither is lighter.
Settlement speed and what it does to reconciliation
Bitcoin payments can appear almost instantly, but they are final only once included in a block, and blocks arrive about every 10 minutes. Businesses often wait for several confirmations on large payments. Lightning is faster, but most counterparties don’t use it by default.
Stablecoins settle in minutes, including weekends and bank holidays, across several networks. Breet’s crypto payment API, for example, accepts USDT and USDC on TRC20, ERC20, Solana, BNB Smart Chain, Polygon, Arbitrum, and Base.
Tax reconciliation differs too. In Nigeria, individuals pay income tax of 0% to 25% on crypto gains, measured in dollars between purchase and sale. A dollar-pegged stablecoin usually produces little or no dollar gain, and sales of USDT and USDC are exempt from the 1% withholding that applies to Bitcoin and Ether.
A Bitcoin payment can create a taxable gain between the day you receive it and the day you sell. Companies follow separate corporate rules, so confirm treatment with your accountant.
Risk profile: market risk vs counterparty risk, not “risky vs safe”
Bitcoin’s main risk here is market risk. The payment’s value can rise or fall before you sell, and the same move produces either a loss or a gain.
A stablecoin moves the risk instead of removing it. The concerns become counterparty and reserve risk: whether the issuer holds what it claims, how transparent the reserves are, how fast holders can redeem, and whether the issuer can freeze an address.
Stablecoins also come up for paying teams. Payroll brings legal, tax, and labor questions outside this comparison.
When your own currency is the one gaining
A stablecoin protects a business from local-currency depreciation only while the local currency is depreciating. Over the past year, the naira has not been.
USD/NGN traded at ₦1,330.43 on October 20, 2026, and the naira has strengthened 9.23% against the dollar over 12 months. It has been flat for the last month (0.02%). Trading Economics’ model expects ₦1,308.80 in 12 months, so treat further gains as a forecast.
A Bitcointalk poster flagged the mechanism in September, when the rate sat near ₦1,370. Holding 500 USDT loses naira value if the rate falls to ₦1,200, and “the only time that the USDT will be preferable is when the rate of naira is [depreciating].”
Run the numbers on a business that converts ₦13.3 million into $10,000 of USDT at ₦1,330 and holds it. At the forecast ₦1,308.80, the position is worth ₦13,088,000, about ₦212,000 less before fees. If the naira slid back to ₦1,500 instead, the same $10,000 would be worth ₦15 million, ₦1.7 million more. Both outcomes are a bet on direction.
This leaves the case for stablecoins as a payment rail intact. If a customer pays in USDT and the business converts right away, the naira’s direction tomorrow barely matters. The exposure appears when stablecoins sit as a standing treasury position.
Which one, for which job
“Bitcoin or stablecoin?” is four separate decisions.
Paying a supplier abroad: stablecoin, in most cases. If the supplier invoices in dollars, a dollar-pegged stablecoin removes the exchange-rate gap between invoice and payment, and it settles outside banking hours.
Holding treasury float: depends on currency direction. If your currency is depreciating, dollars preserve purchasing power. If it is strengthening, holding dollars costs you, as the ₦212,000 example above shows. Check the direction before defaulting to “hold stablecoins for safety.”
Accepting a customer’s payment: either works. What matters is the next step. If you convert on arrival, the asset the customer sent never becomes treasury.
Wanting long-term Bitcoin exposure: Bitcoin, on purpose. The price of that upside is drawdowns like the 35% fall above, which can land when you need cash. Hold only money you can leave untouched through one.
You don’t have to pick a side to settle the transaction
None of those four jobs requires holding either asset, as long as the payment converts to fiat when it lands. For many businesses, the need is simple: the customer wants to pay in Bitcoin or a stablecoin, and the business wants naira, cedis, or dollars in its account.
Settle automatically, in fiat, the moment either asset lands
With our Crypto and Stablecoin Payment API, a customer’s deposit of Bitcoin, USDT, USDC, or another supported asset is detected on-chain and converted. With auto-settlement on, it is paid to a linked bank account. With it off, it sits as a USD, NGN, or GHS balance until you withdraw. You can set this per wallet address or business-wide.
A webhook fires the moment a transaction is detected on-chain, so your system can fulfill the order without anyone checking a dashboard. The platform has 100+ verified businesses, 3M+ transactions settled programmatically, and a 99.9% uptime SLA.
Access dollars through stablecoins without carrying a treasury position
A business that needs dollars for a supplier does not have to hold USDT or USDC in between. The API gives import and export teams an interface to convert NGN, USD, or GHS to USDT or USDC and back for supplier payments, bypassing dollar scarcity and the parallel market.
For large trades, our OTC desk locks the rate before execution, so the market can’t move against you mid-trade. Settlement lands the same hour in NGN, GHS, USD, USDT, or USDC. Settling in USDT or USDC is the option for businesses that want dollar-denominated float. The desk is built for large volumes, not routine top-ups, and minimum sizes depend on the asset and currency.
Reconcile the same way no matter which asset shows up
If one customer pays in Bitcoin and another in USDT, finance should not need two processes. The API generates a wallet address per customer or per transaction, with bank details and a label attached at creation. Deposits to that address auto-settle to the right account.
That means no manual matching and no guessing which invoice a payment belongs to, whichever asset landed.
Check the direction, then convert
Bitcoin carries market risk. A stablecoin carries issuer and reserve risk, plus currency-direction risk when you hold it against a strengthening naira. Neither label, “risky” or “safe,” tells you what to do with a payment.
Start with this today: pull your last 90 days of crypto payments. For each one, note how long it sat before conversion and what the rate did in that window. If the gap is days and the rate moved against you, turn on auto-settlement.
Two limits apply. We convert crypto and don’t custody it, so Bitcoin you want to hold for years belongs in your own wallet or with a custodian. And Breet is not a payroll platform.

One size does not fit all.
								October 21st, 2026 -

Physical AI poses a host of new challenges for chip engineers. These systems contain a mix of compute elements, which collectively must process a stream of real-time data, analyze it, make decisions, and still function long enough on a battery to be useful. The key here is deciding what data gets processed where, and how to minimize the movement of data. Ashley Stevens, director of product management and marketing at Arteris, talks explains why data movement plays such an important role in these systems, why coherent interconnects are better suited to CPUs and non-coherent interconnects are better for AI acceleration, and what other challenges engineers will face going forward.

articles.title: Mars: So wollen Forscher mithilfe urzeitlicher Regenfälle Hinweise auf Leben finden
articles.text:
Mars: So wollen Forscher mithilfe urzeitlicher Regenfälle Hinweise auf Leben finden
Ein Forschungsteam unter der Leitung von Wissenschaftler:innen des Institute of Science Tokyo (Japan) hat eine Mars-Karte erstellt, die zeigt, wo vor Milliarden Jahren urzeitliche Regenfälle ein wichtiges präbiotisches Molekül – Formaldehyd (H₂CO) – auf der Marsoberfläche abgelagert haben könnten.
Diese Karte könnte künftige Untersuchungen auf dem Mars unterstützen, indem sie unbemannte und bemannte Missionen gezielt zu Stellen lenkt, an denen noch Spuren von vergangenem Leben erhalten sein könnten.
Der Mars war vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren wärmer und feuchter
Trotz des heutigen Klimas auf dem Mars sind sich Wissenschaftler:innen inzwischen einig, dass es dort vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren wärmer und feuchter war. Dies wirft die Frage auf, ob der Mars in jener Zeit Leben beherbergt haben könnte – etwa in Form von Mikroorganismen.
Die im Planetary Science Journal veröffentlichte Studie baut auf früheren Erkenntnissen auf, die zeigten, wie Formaldehyd (H₂CO) in der Atmosphäre entstehen kann. In Verbindung mit Wasser kann Formaldehyd als Ausgangsmolekül für chemische Reaktionen dienen, aus denen Zucker, Aminosäuren und andere komplexe organische Moleküle hervorgehen: die Bausteine des Lebens. Die spezifische Frage lautete: An welchen Stellen auf dem Mars könnte das Formaldehyd die Oberfläche erreicht haben?
Simulation der Bedingungen, die vor 4 Milliarden Jahren auf Mars herrschten
Um eine Karte der möglichen Orte zu erstellen, simulierten die Forscher:innen die Bedingungen, die vor 3,5 bis 4,1 Milliarden Jahren auf dem Mars herrschten. Sie untersuchten dabei, wie Faktoren wie Temperatur, Wasserdampf, atmosphärischer Druck und UV-Strahlung die Bildung von Formaldehyd beeinflussten. Ihre Simulation zeigte, dass die chemische Aufspaltung von Wasser durch UV-Licht in der Marsatmosphäre reaktiven Wasserstoff freisetzen würde – ein wesentlicher Baustein für die Bildung von Formaldehyd, das anschließend mit Niederschlägen auf die Oberfläche gelangen könnte.
Da Wasser sowohl die Entstehung als auch die Verteilung von H₂CO beeinflusste, stellten die Forschenden die Hypothese auf, dass der frühere Wasserkreislauf auf dem Mars bestimmt haben könnte, wo sich diese Verbindung ansammelte.
Karte könnte helfen, vielversprechende Ziele für Marsmissionen zu finden
Im letzten Schritt der Kartenerstellung wurden diese potenziellen „Hotspots“ in Bezug zu den Landeplätzen vergangener Marsmissionen gesetzt.
Studienleiter Shungo Koyama sagte gegenüber Universe Today: „Durch den Vergleich unserer Karte mit den Ergebnissen von Marsrovern können wir untersuchen, ob Orte mit einer höheren H₂CO-Konzentration möglicherweise auch günstigere Bedingungen für chemische Prozesse boten, die mit der Entstehung von Leben in Verbindung stehen könnten. Sollten zukünftige Beobachtungen diesen Zusammenhang bestätigen, könnte unsere Karte dabei helfen, vielversprechende Ziele für künftige Marsmissionen zu identifizieren.“

articles.title: How curiosity took Victoria Abiodun from anatomy to crypto
articles.text:
Growing up in a household steeped in healthcare, Victoria Abiodun’s path seemed predetermined: finish her anatomy degree at the University of Ilorin, Kwara State, northcentral Nigeria, head abroad for medical school, and never look back. As for cryptocurrency? She wanted nothing to do with it, convinced it belonged firmly in the realm of internet scams. But when an ASUU strike collided with the 2020 lockdowns, a persistent anatomy coursemate challenged her prejudice. To make sense of the dense, jargon-laden whitepapers, she began writing her own explanations from scratch. That curiosity set off an unexpected chain reaction: from ghost-writing technical primers as an undergraduate to co-founding a gaming startup, spearheading marketing for a European decentralised identity protocol, and bootstrapping a 100-strong Solana developer chapter in Ilorin. Today, while reading for an MBA at USC and researching high-density energy demand, she is writing the open-access, plain-English blockchain book she wishes she had read on day one. In this week’s My Life in Tech, JOHN ADOYI sits down with Abiodun to trace her accidental journey from anatomy labs to Web3 education.
Victoria Abiodun, a Web3 educator, is writing a book that explains distributed technology in plain language. Only a few years ago, she wanted nothing to do with it.
As an undergraduate at the University of Ilorin in north-central Nigeria, she viewed cryptocurrency as indistinguishable from fraud; the people who evangelised it seemed either to be perpetrating scams or falling victim to them.
One person challenged that conviction: a trusted friend from her anatomy class who spoke incessantly about blockchain. She struggled to reconcile his enthusiasm with the prejudice she held.
“In all honesty, the first thing that piqued my curiosity was the money he was making,” she says. “I was like, ‘What? This is crazy.’”
Yet financial curiosity was merely the entry point. Coming from a pure science background, she struggled to grasp the underlying technical concepts, prompting her to write about them to break them down.
“The goal was simply to teach myself the core concepts,” she says.
That curiosity soon propelled Abiodun beyond writing. She went on to advise blockchain companies, co-found a gaming startup, and establish Superteam Ilorin—a regional community supporting developers and founders deploying on the Solana network. Through those stints, she zeroed in on a question that transcended technical mechanics: how could builders harness the technology to solve acute, real-world problems?
Her forthcoming book is one prong of that mission. Across grassroots community building, technical writing, and her podcast, Abiodun is demystifying an ecosystem she once dismissed.
A medical household
Before encountering Web3, Abiodun had envisioned a healthcare career. Her mother was a nurse, and her elder sister pursued medicine. As a child, she briefly flirted with law because an uncle was an attorney and she thought it looked “pretty cool”, but in a home steeped in clinical practice, medicine exerted the stronger pull.
“I assumed I wanted to be a doctor as well,” she says, “and I simply followed that momentum.”
She enrolled at the University of Ilorin to read anatomy, intending to travel abroad after graduation for medical school or postgraduate training in public health. Technology did not feature in the plan.
“I never imagined I would go into tech,” she says, “nor did I think I was particularly interested in it.”
Yet an entrepreneurial streak was already evident. From her first year on campus, she launched small ventures across different sectors. Some gained traction, others collapsed, but the collective experience sharpened her commercial instincts.
Then the COVID-19 pandemic struck in 2020. With lockdowns compounded by a prolonged academic staff strike that shuttered Nigerian universities, her studies ground to a halt.
Rather than idling, she published an e-book on physical wellness, formed an online fitness community, and explored digital side projects.
Cryptocurrency was still off her radar. Her anatomy classmate, however, continued to evangelise the sector. Because he was already active in technology, regular conversations with him steadily dismantled her scepticism.
“During the lockdown, I immersed myself in reading and research,” she says, “and that was the turning point.”
A family ordeal crystallised the technology’s utility: her elder sister was studying medicine in Ukraine when conflict erupted in 2014, leaving their parents in Nigeria unable to wire tuition or living expenses through severed international banking corridors.
When Abiodun recounted the ordeal, her friend explained how peer-to-peer blockchain settlement could have bypassed legacy banking infrastructure to move capital instantly.
“Seeing the real-world gap this technology bridges made it instantly compelling,” she says.
She began writing essays to synthesise her research. When her classmate reviewed her work, he asked whether she realised that companies paid writers to produce technical blockchain content.
She did not.
Pitching agencies and niche publications, she landed an early commission to author a Q&A-style primer breaking down basic distributed ledger concepts. Between 2020 and 2021, while completing her degree, Abiodun freelanced as a content strategist across Web3 startups, corporate blogs, and trade outlets.
The gaming venture
Blockchain gaming was one of the first things that hooked Abiodun. The logic was simple when her friend explained it: players already spent real money on in-game assets, so why shouldn’t they be able to withdraw their earnings?
In 2021, she got the chance to build in that space. She met a co-founder who wanted to develop a blockchain game, and the idea grew into Sportrex, a gaming ecosystem built around play-to-earn.
The ambition extended beyond a single game. Sportrex was designed to let players track their winnings and rankings through a gaming wallet, while allowing other developers to bring their games onto the platform. The wider vision also included a competitive league system, virtual reality experiences, and a token for the gaming ecosystem.
But Abiodun believed that earning money alone would not keep players interested.
“Play-to-earn is nice, but if the game is not fun for people to play, nobody would want to play the game,” she says.
Blockchain gaming was among the first sub-sectors to capture her attention. The economic rationale was intuitive: if players were already spending hard currency on digital assets, they ought to own them outright and retain the ability to liquidate their earnings.
In 2021, she stepped into an operational role, partnering with a founder to establish Sportrex—a platform designed around play-to-earn dynamics.
The scope soon outgrew a standalone title. Sportrex was architected as an aggregator: players could monitor rewards and global leaderboards via a proprietary wallet, while independent developers could integrate their own games. The roadmap included esports tournaments, virtual reality modules, and a native utility token.
Yet Abiodun remained clear-eyed about the limitations of financial incentives alone.
“Play-to-earn is attractive, but if the gameplay lacks substance, retention plummets,” she says. “Nobody wants to play a game that isn’t enjoyable.”
As marketing lead, she drafted the company’s whitepapers, drove brand strategy, managed community acquisition, and negotiated strategic partnerships. She also spearheaded their presence at the Dubai Blockchain Summit, leading discussions with prospective institutional backers.
The venture crystallised her view that early-stage tech ventures must prioritise speed over flawless execution.
“I believe in putting products out early, letting them break, and iterating in public,” she says. “The industry does not wait for you.”
She stepped down from Sportrex in December 2022, carrying that bias toward rapid deployment into her next engagement.
Building a growth strategy from scratch
After leaving Sportrex, Abiodun joined Matchain, an early-stage project preparing to take its AI-driven decentralised digital identity platform to market.
“When I joined, there was no marketing team; there were just engineers and the founder in Lisbon, Portugal,” she says. “So it was just me, the COO and the founder.”
She helped define Matchain’s market position, customer acquisition strategy, and partnership plans. She also developed onboarding strategies for Match Hub, which brought other companies into the ecosystem, and wrote the company’s website content.
The role drew on skills she had developed as an entrepreneur.
“Most of the core skills that you apply to building your own businesses are skills that people employ others for,” she says.
She also had to understand how differently blockchain companies approach growth. In her experience, blockchain startups often need to build a community before a product is ready to launch.
“If you do not build a community around your product before the product is ready, you probably would not have a community that would adopt the product,” she says.
Abiodun worked with Matchain until 2023. Although she had planned to relocate to Lisbon, Portugal, visa interview availability for Nigerians prevented the move.
She says the company also wanted a team that could work more closely together; she eventually moved on.
Finding community outside Lagos
Her trajectory subsequently pivoted from corporate marketing toward grassroots capacity building. Having helped funded platforms scale, she wanted to mentor the engineers building baseline software.
In 2023, as the global Solana developer network Superteam expanded its international reach, Abiodun saw an opening to anchor a chapter in Ilorin, where she maintained a residence.
She volunteered to establish the regional presence. Though she had intended to take a sabbatical to travel and take up golf, she instead convened Ilorin’s inaugural Superteam meetup in February 2024—despite not considering herself an insider in local engineering circles.
“I was stunned by the initial turnout,” she says. “From that first session, attendance scaled into hundreds every month.”
Her execution led to her formal appointment as lead for Superteam’s Southwest Nigeria operations. Yet sheer attendance was secondary to her core objective: pushing local talent beyond tutorial exercises into shipping functional software.
“Nigeria has an exceptional concentration of technical talent,” she says. “Developers spend thousands of hours mastering complex frameworks, yet we rarely see that skill translated into solutions for local structural bottlenecks.”
Bootstrapping the community required tactical agility. When a venue billing dispute severed ties with the private coding hub hosting their initial sessions, Abiodun restructured operations—securing alternative halls, engaging campus hostels directly, and tapping alumni networks.
She also made pastoral engagement central to her leadership, tracking individual project milestones and providing personal mentorship.
“When people feel genuinely supported, enthusiasm compounds,” she notes. “Engineers kept returning with their peers because they wanted them to experience that collaborative culture.”
Though the compensation was a fraction of her previous commercial contracts, she considers it her most meaningful tenure. “It remains one of the most impactful assignments I have undertaken,” she says. “It was deeply fulfilling.”
Demystifying tech
That educational focus now centres on an introductory book aimed at non-technical founders, students, and corporate professionals.
“When I entered the space, the available literature was dense, forbidding, and cluttered with jargon,” she explains. “I wanted to write something conversational—matching the cadence of how I explain these concepts across a table.”
The manuscript covers core operational mechanics—distributed ledgers, network layering, consensus architecture, and cryptography—while exploring non-financial primitives including supply chain verification and verifiable identity credentials. She intends to publish it as an open-access resource.
Her outreach also includes Convergence, a podcast examining distributed systems, enterprise workflows, and tokenised assets. The series originated from informal discussions with professionals outside the crypto sphere looking to understand how decentralised protocols intersect with their native industries.
Abiodun’s horizons have since expanded toward core infrastructure. Currently reading for a Master of Business Administration (MBA) at the University of Southern California’s Marshall School of Business, she also serves as a graduate research assistant with the school’s Zage Business of Energy Initiative. Her focus on energy was prompted by the steep electrical baseload demands imposed by artificial intelligence clusters and high-density data centres.
The business curriculum has supplemented her operational background with formal training in corporate valuation, asset pricing, and financial modelling.
“Energy systems are not something I would have prioritised had I stayed solely within startup marketing,” she reflects. “Maximising the chance to interrogate these structural challenges has been an exceptional privilege.”
Whether evaluating distributed ledgers or energy transition models, Abiodun remains clear that technology is a mechanism rather than an end in itself.
“Directing my career toward solving problems that tangibly improve other people’s circumstances is what matters most,” she says. “Accolades and bull runs are fleeting; the real reward is knowing you helped clear a pathway for someone else.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks.
