articles.title: Foxconn's latest EV push is a $727 million bet for half of Mitsubishi Electric's car parts business
articles.text:
What just happened? Foxconn has agreed to pay $727 million for a 50% stake in Mitsubishi Electric's automotive equipment business, gaining access to vehicle-control technology and software expertise for its push to develop electric vehicles for other manufacturers. The deal gives Foxconn a broader engineering base, but much of the business it is buying still serves conventional vehicles. Its success will depend on turning that expertise into products automakers want to buy.
The companies plan to combine Mitsubishi Electric's powertrain, autonomous-driving and in-car computing technology with Foxconn's manufacturing operations. They want to build EV platforms in Japan, sell them first to Japanese automakers and then seek customers overseas.
"What attracted us most was the electronic-control technology – and the substantial software resources behind them," Jun Seki, Foxconn's chief strategy officer for EVs, said at a news conference in Tokyo.
Mitsubishi Electric Mobility's products include alternators, starters, ignition coils, radar sensors and electric powertrain equipment. Its established automaker relationships also give Foxconn a route to potential customers.
But Foxconn is not buying into all of Mitsubishi Electric's EV technology. The Japanese company's power-semiconductor business is outside the agreement. That includes silicon-carbide and insulated-gate bipolar transistor power modules used in EV inverters.
The automotive deal instead covers the equipment business that Mitsubishi Electric spun off into Mitsubishi Electric Mobility in April 2024. Before closing, Mitsubishi Electric will move its remaining automotive operations, including those held by overseas subsidiaries, into that company.
Foxconn's investment arm, Lin Yin International Investment, will acquire half of the combined business. The partners expect the deal to close in October 2027, following antitrust reviews and other required approvals.
Mitsubishi Electric has been reshaping its portfolio, exiting car multimedia and fuel injectors and transferring its lighting business to Stanley Electric.
An earlier electric-powertrain partnership changed course. In May 2024, Mitsubishi Electric Mobility and Aisin agreed to establish a joint venture for traction motors, inverters and control software. Five months later, they dropped the joint-venture plan and opted for a business alliance.
The purchase gives Foxconn another way into the car industry after several years of prototypes, partnerships and setbacks.
Foxconn had planned to build Fisker's Pear EV at its Lordstown, Ohio, factory, but the vehicle never reached production. Fisker went bankrupt in 2024, and Foxconn sold the factory last year.
Foxconn has made progress elsewhere. Mitsubishi Motors, which is separate from Mitsubishi Electric, is putting its badge on the Foxtron-developed ASX VR-e for Australia and New Zealand. Foxconn also has a bus joint venture with Mitsubishi Fuso and is a partner in Saudi Arabia's Ceer EV brand.
The Mitsubishi Electric agreement adds an established automotive supplier to Foxconn's network, alongside its existing vehicle-development and manufacturing partnerships.

articles.title: Scaled Cognition targets customer service with low-cost voice model - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Scaled Cognition targets customer service with low-cost voice model
Scaled Cognition Inc., an artificial intelligence lab building models for enterprise customer service agents, is introducing a text-to-speech model today that it says provides more accurate pronunciation of account numbers, addresses and other details at a lower cost than competing services.
The product, called Voice, is available through an application programming interface or for self-hosted deployment. It supports more than 25 languages, voice cloning and can work with existing artificial intelligence agents, contact center platforms and older telephone systems. Voice cloning creates a digital replica of a given person’s voice.
The launch targets a gap between natural-sounding speech and AI that reliably communicates information customers need to complete transactions.
“Modern generative TTS models can sound fantastic, but they often stumble over the details that matter most in customer service, like reading back an alphanumeric confirmation code, a dollar amount or a street address,” Akshay Kannan, vice president of product management at Scaled Cognition, said in e-mailed comments.
Those difficulties become more pronounced in languages other than English, Kannan said. Scaled Cognition said Voice enables enterprises to get natural-sounding speech and accurate readings without paying premium prices.
Voice costs $9 per million characters through the hosted API or $1 per million characters for self-hosting. The latter figure excludes the infrastructure needed to operate it.
Kannan explained how the math works out to lower costs than competing providers. One graphics processing unit can handle about 32 simultaneous conversations using Voice. A redundant setup using two GPUs on standard cloud hardware costs roughly $6,000 a month and supports about 500 million characters, he said.
Including infrastructure, Kannan estimated costs at about $13 per million characters at that 500 million-character rate and less than $7 at 1.5 billion. He compared that to between $35 and $100 per million characters charged by other hosted voices, which he declined to name.
“Self-hosting gets economical faster than people expect,” he said.
Cloud option
At low usage, the self-hosting cost can exceed Scaled Cognition’s hosted API price. “Most of the enterprises we work with already run their own infrastructure, so Voice just drops in,” Kannan said. “For teams that don’t want to manage it, we host it for them.”
The company also claims 70 milliseconds of speech-generation latency, the time from receiving text to starting speech, rather than the total time an AI system takes to understand a caller and formulate an answer.
“Even with 16 live conversations sharing a single GPU slice, typical response time stays around 80 milliseconds,” he said. “The biggest factor customers control is distance.” Running Voice in the same cloud region as the rest of a call stack adds only a millisecond or two of latency. “That’s a big reason we let enterprises self-host it right next to their agents and telephony,” Kannan said.
One of the distinctive features of Voice is its ability to interpret meaning before generating audio, the company said. For example, its Smart Pronunciation capability determines whether abbreviations refer to titles, street names or other information and how numbers should be spoken. For example, it reads “Pay 1/2 by 1/2” as “pay half by January second.”
“Voice doesn’t just read text left to right,” Kannan said. “Before it says a word, Smart Pronunciation works out what the sentence actually means, powered by the same customer-experience-tuned intelligence behind our APT model.”
APT is the company’s model for customer-service conversations and actions in enterprise systems. When the products are paired, APT supplies conversation context that can help Voice resolve ambiguities beyond an individual sentence.
Voice doesn’t require APT or another large language model to operate. “It streams audio through a standard API and is tuned for phone audio, so anything that can send text and play back speech can use it, from modern AI agents and contact center platforms to legacy [interactive voice response systems],” Kannan said.
That compatibility could give enterprises a way to update interactive voice response systems without replacing the underlying applications.
Scaled Cognition is also offering a blind listening test that compares Voice with other models across price ranges. Kannan said early feedback favored Voice, although the supplied materials did not provide sample sizes or detailed results.
The company, which raised $100 million in Series A funding led by Khosla Ventures LLC, is positioning speech as another component of its enterprise AI platform.

articles.title: Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Access OpenAI GPT models on Amazon Bedrock from Canada with cross-Region inference
Canadian organizations building generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock often need the latest foundation models (FMs), such as OpenAI GPT-6.1, OpenAI GPT-6, and GPT-5.6, accessible from the Canadian AWS Regions. With Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference (CRIS), you can now access these models from Canada. OpenAI GPT-5.6 models (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions. Inference is processed in North America, with data-residency controls described later in this post.
Cross-Region inference is a capacity mechanism. Your application calls the Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint in your source Region. Amazon Bedrock then routes the request to a supported destination Region for processing. With this approach, you get access to a broader capacity pool that can help your application sustain throughput during demand spikes. You don’t need to manage destination Region routing in your application.
In this post, we walk through the GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 models available from Canada and the cross-Region inference profiles that serve them. We then show how to set up permissions and invoke the models with the OpenAI Responses API, Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. For the Responses API, we include streaming and tool-use examples. Finally, we cover how to request quota increases, review the observability signals available in your source Region, and clean up when you are done.
Models available from Canada
With Amazon Bedrock, you can access three families of OpenAI models in Canada through cross-Region inference. The following table summarizes each model and its positioning.
| Model | Positioning | 
| GPT-6.1 Sol | Strong reasoning and coding for tasks where both performance and cost matter | 
| GPT-6 Astra | Complex end-to-end reasoning and agentic tasks | 
| GPT-6 Sol | Strong reasoning and coding for recurring tasks with economics suited to regular use | 
| GPT-6 Luna | Fast, low-cost inference for high-volume repeated tasks with adjustable reasoning effort per request | 
| GPT-5.6 Sol | High reasoning, coding, and agentic workloads | 
| GPT-5.6 Terra | Balanced performance and cost for everyday production | 
| GPT-5.6 Luna | Fast and affordable for high-volume, latency-sensitive applications | 
These models accept text and image inputs, return text, and support a 1-million-token context window, reasoning mode, and tool calling. GPT-6.1 Sol supports the same context window and tool calling, with additional input and output modalities documented in its model card. GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 also support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock (see the Prompt caching section). These models are available through the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API on the bedrock-runtime endpoint.
For pricing, see Amazon Bedrock pricing. For per-model Region availability, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Cross-Region inference profiles from Canada
Amazon Bedrock inference profiles are logical identifiers you pass in place of a raw model ID. Each profile defines a model and the set of Regions to which Amazon Bedrock can route a request. Two profile types are available from Canada:
- US geographic (prefixed us.) routes requests to your Canadian source Region and US Regions. Choose this profile when your workload requires inference processing to remain within North America (Canada and the US).
- Global (prefixed global.) routes requests to supported commercial AWS Regions where the model is deployed. This draws on a broader capacity pool at the time of the request.
Endpoint availability differs by model and source Region, as shown in the following table.
| Model | US geographic profile | Global profile | 
| GPT-6.1 Sol | ca-central-1, ca-west-1 | ca-central-1, ca-west-1 | 
| GPT-6 Astra / Sol / Luna | ca-central-1, ca-west-1 | ca-central-1, ca-west-1 | 
| GPT-5.6 Sol / Terra / Luna | ca-central-1, ca-west-1 | ca-central-1 | 
Profile membership and model availability can change. The global profile for the GPT-5.6 models is available only from ca-central-1. From ca-west-1, use the US geographic profile for GPT-5.6. Verify the active profiles for your source Region before deployment, either with the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) or on the console (see the following section), or see the Cross-Region inference support documentation.
Getting started
The following sections walk through the setup and code needed to invoke these models from your Canadian source Region.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, confirm that you have the following:
- An AWS account with the Canada (Central) ca-central-1 or Canada West (Calgary) ca-west-1 Region enabled as your source Region.
- An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role or user with permissions to invoke the inference profiles (see Set up permissions).
- A service control policy (SCP) that allows the inference profiles in your source Region, if your organization enforces SCPs (see SCP considerations).
- Python 3.9 or later with the openai, boto3, and aws-bedrock-token-generator packages installed.
Set up permissions
For quick exploration, attach the AWS managed policy AmazonBedrockLimitedAccess. For deployed workloads with stricter access controls, use a least-privilege custom policy. The following example grants access to the GPT-6 Astra global profile from ca-central-1:
If you authenticate through the API-key path (bearer token for the OpenAI SDK), also grant bedrock:CallWithBearerToken. For the Responses API, add bedrock:InvokeModel on arn:aws:bedrock:ca-central-1:*:project/default.
SCP considerations
If your organization restricts Regions through SCPs, use the bedrock:InferenceProfileArn condition key to allow CRIS traffic while blocking direct calls to unapproved Regions. The following SCP denies Amazon Bedrock inference outside your approved source Regions unless the request uses a CRIS inference profile:
With this condition, Amazon Bedrock can route to the profile’s destination Regions even when those Regions are otherwise denied by your SCP. Every destination Region in your chosen profile must be allowed for the request to succeed. For more detail, see Set up cross-Region inference in multi-account environments.
Verify active inference profiles
Before invoking a model, you can verify which profiles are active in your source Region with the AWS CLI. The following command lists the active OpenAI profiles from ca-central-1. To run the same check from Calgary, replace ca-central-1 with ca-west-1.
The Amazon Bedrock console offers the same view. Open the console, choose Canada (Central) or Canada West (Calgary) as your Region, choose Cross-Region inference under Inference, and review the available profiles.
The following screenshot shows the active OpenAI inference profiles listed on the Amazon Bedrock console for the Canada (Central) Region.
Invoke the models through Amazon Bedrock Runtime
GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support three access paths on the bedrock-runtime endpoint: the OpenAI Responses API, the OpenAI Chat Completions API, and the Amazon Bedrock Converse API. The OpenAI-compatible APIs are called on the /openai/v1 paths of the endpoint. The endpoint accepts either AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) or an Amazon Bedrock API key.
The following examples use the Amazon Bedrock token generator for Python to create a short-term Amazon Bedrock API key from your current AWS credentials, so your application does not need to store a static key.
OpenAI Responses API
For applications that already use the OpenAI SDK with the Responses API, point the client at the Regional Amazon Bedrock Runtime endpoint and pass the inference profile ID as the model.
For streaming output, set stream=True and iterate over the response events, printing text as it arrives:
OpenAI Chat Completions API
The OpenAI Chat Completions format works through the same endpoint.
For the full list of supported parameters, including reasoning effort levels, see the model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide.
Amazon Bedrock Converse API
Use the Converse API when your application calls Amazon Bedrock through an AWS SDK. Boto3 resolves credentials through the standard AWS credential chain.
The same call works for GPT-6 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, and GPT-6.1 Sol by changing the inference profile ID. The following example uses the US geographic profile for GPT-6 Sol and the global profile for GPT-6 Luna. Both were validated from ca-central-1.
Tool use
These models support client-side tool use (function calling). Define tools in the tools parameter, and the model returns a structured tool-call request for your application to execute.
Prompt caching
GPT-5.6, GPT-6, and GPT-6.1 support prompt caching on Amazon Bedrock to reduce the cost and latency of repeated prompt prefixes. Implicit caching requires no changes to your code: Amazon Bedrock automatically caches eligible prefixes of 1,024 tokens or more. Cached tokens read on subsequent requests are billed at a discounted rate and do not count against your tokens-per-minute quota. Cached tokens appear in the response usage object and in Amazon CloudWatch metrics so you can track usage. For cache-write pricing, minimum prefix sizes, and support for explicit cache breakpoints, see the prompt caching documentation and the individual model cards.
Quota management
Cross-Region inference quotas on the bedrock-runtime endpoint are measured in tokens per minute (TPM) per model. Each quota combines input and output tokens against a single limit. US geographic and global inference profiles have separate quota allocations, so switching between them changes the pool you draw from.
Token consumption combines input tokens, cache-write input tokens, and output tokens. Output tokens are multiplied by the model’s burndown rate, so output-heavy workloads consume quota faster than raw token counts suggest. Before a production rollout, request quota increases early and monitor quota utilization. Test with representative prompts, output lengths, streaming behavior, concurrency, and peak traffic.
To request a quota increase, follow these steps:
- Open the Service Quotas console in ca-central-1 or ca-west-1.
- Choose Amazon Bedrock, then select the quota named “Cross-Region InvokeModel tokens per minute” for the model that you need.
- Choose Request increase at account level, enter your target value, and submit the request.
For details on how token usage and costs are tracked, see Track usage and costs in Amazon Bedrock.
Observability
Because these models run through the Amazon Bedrock Runtime API, requests made through an inference profile appear in your observability tooling the same way on-demand requests do. Invocation logs and Amazon CloudWatch metrics are recorded in your source Region. This holds regardless of where the request was processed. Your observability stays in one place.
- AWS CloudTrail logs every request, recording which destination Region served it in the additionalEventData.inferenceRegion field. For example:
- Amazon CloudWatch metrics are published per inference profile, covering invocation count, token count, latency, throttles, and errors.
- Model invocation logging delivers full request and response payloads to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch Logs. To activate it on the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging. You can also call the PutModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration API. It is off by default.
- AWS Data Exports itemizes spend by model and profile.
Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights
If you use these models to power AI coding assistants such as OpenAI Codex, Amazon CloudWatch Coding Agent Insights provides a dedicated dashboard. It surfaces token usage, API request counts, active users, and cost attribution across dimensions such as department, team, and environment. To activate it, configure your coding agent to export telemetry to Amazon CloudWatch. For the setup steps, see Set up OpenTelemetry for OpenAI Codex.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges after testing, remove the resources you created:
- Turn off model invocation logging. On the Amazon Bedrock console, choose Settings, then choose Model invocation logging, or call DeleteModelInvocationLoggingConfiguration. This stops delivery of logs to Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
- Delete or detach the IAM policies and any Amazon Bedrock API keys that you created for testing.
The inference profiles themselves are system-defined and incur no cost when they aren’t in use.
Security and compliance
Cross-Region inference is designed to protect your data in transit and at rest. Requests travel over the AWS private backbone encrypted with TLS 1.2+ rather than the public internet. For Canadian customers, your data at rest stays in your source Region by default. This includes invocation logs, knowledge bases, and configurations. Only the transient inference computation happens in the destination Region, and by default model providers don’t have access to your prompts or completions.
There’s one consideration specific to OpenAI models. Content flagged by automated abuse classifiers might be retained for up to 30 days in the destination Region for review. If you want to constrain processing to North America (Canada and the US), you can choose the US geographic profile. We recommend reviewing Amazon Bedrock abuse detection with your compliance team.
For a more detailed look at Canadian data residency patterns, see Cross-Region Inference and Canadian Data Residency: A Technical Architecture Guide.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how to access OpenAI GPT-5.6 (Sol, Terra, and Luna), GPT-6 (Astra, Sol, and Luna), and GPT-6.1 Sol from Canada. These models are available from the Canada (Central) and Canada West (Calgary) Regions using cross-Region inference on Amazon Bedrock. We covered the available inference profiles, how to set up permissions and an example SCP, and how to invoke the models with the Responses, Chat Completions, and Converse APIs. For the Responses API, we included streaming and tool-use examples. We also showed how to request quota increases, review usage, and clean up your test resources.
To get started, review the OpenAI model cards in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide, then open the Amazon Bedrock console and send a test prompt through an inference profile. For pricing, see the Amazon Bedrock pricing page.
If you have questions or feedback, leave a comment on this post.

articles.title: Does anyone actually want to win the medium-lift race in the United States?
articles.text:
It has been 13 years since the debut of a new medium-lift rocket in the United States, the Antares vehicle developed by Orbital Sciences Corporation.
The initial 100-series variant of the Antares rocket was kind of a hot mess. The rocket used old Soviet engines built during the era when Apollo astronauts were landing on the Moon. Decades later, in the 1990s, Aerojet acquired the engines and refurbished them for a rocket that would launch in the 2010s. Predictably, on the fifth launch of an Antares rocket in 2014, it exploded.
The Antares vehicle is the last of a dying breed of medium-lift rockets—defined as having a lift capacity of 2 to 20 metric tons—in the United States. Nearly a decade and a half later there is a new generation of medium-lift vehicles coming online, and they are starkly different from Antares, which had not just Russian engines but a core stage manufactured in Ukraine.
Four forthcoming rockets all have engines built by the rocket’s manufacturer in the United States. Each of these companies has taken various lessons from SpaceX’s successful Falcon 9 rocket, arguably the most important of which is to build as much of one’s rocket, and particularly the engines, in-house as possible to control timelines and costs.
Now, with SpaceX pulling the Falcon 9 rocket from the commercial market as soon as 2028, the “race” to bring new medium-lift capacity into service is for more than bragging rights. There are fortunes to be made, and commercial space startups to be saved.
Satellite operators legitimately don’t know who to book launches with in the 2027 to 2030 timeframe because of uncertainty over which rockets will be available. The Falcon 9 is no longer for sale. The larger Vulcan and New Glenn rockets have stacked manifests and are expensive for small- and medium-sized satellites. And no one really knows which new medium-lift vehicles will be ready and capable of scaling up their launch cadence.

articles.title: Bringing the Spark to Europe: Local Intelligence Powers Next Wave of Agents
articles.text:
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing its full lineup of local AI hardware. RTX Spark, which launched last week, powers personal agents on Windows PCs; DGX Spark supports developers building and scaling applications on Linux; and DGX Station serves enterprise teams running frontier workloads on Linux, with a Windows version arriving in December.
Announcements include:
- Underdog Desktop Agent now available for RTX Spark
- DGX Spark 64GB available on Friday, Oct. 23
- NVIDIA Sync to support eight DGX Sparks and add Model Launcher this month
- October DGX Spark software update adds Wi-Fi Assistant and updates DGX Spark Skills
- DGX Station improves manageability with seven new integrations
- DGX Station for Windows launches in December with support for many manufacturing apps and agent harnesses
- Three new open source reference workflows for robotics on DGX Station
- NVIDIA Cloud Functions is coming in early access to DGX Station
- Recursive Flint, a new local coding model, is now available for NVIDIA local hardware
- Day-0 support for new Nemotron, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax and FLUX.3 AI models
- New accelerations for llama.cpp and vLLM inference engines and a new collection of checkpoints optimized for local AI hardware.
Learn more about these local AI announcements below, and check out the demos and sessions at GTC Berlin.
RTX Spark Brings Personal Agents to the Windows PC
RTX Spark is a new beginning for the PC — running personal agents, accelerated content creation and 1440p 100 frames-per-second gaming with up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of AI compute.
Here’s what early reviewers are saying about the platform since its October 16 release:
“A dream machine for serious creators … ” — CGMag
“Designed for the future of AI … ” — The Verge
“An extremely capable, surprisingly portable and efficient machine … ” — PCMag
Underdog, a new desktop agent app built for fully local, private AI, is also bringing its experience to RTX Spark. Powered by its Husky model-specific inference engine, Underdog runs models entirely on device, so personal agents can get work done without user data ever leaving the PC. Underdog is available now for download.
To better enable developers and enthusiasts to build and customize local agents, many RTX Spark laptops come with an unlocked bootloader.
During the GTC keynote, NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang showed off how AI agents running on RTX Spark can be used to train Hugging Face’s Microduck robot using NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Hermes Agent and Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B.
ASUS, Dell Technologies, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI laptops are available today, with Acer coming soon.
Learn more about RTX Spark, and get started with the latest RTX Spark playbooks.
DGX Spark Gives Developers Room to Build
New DGX Spark 64GB systems — that can run models including Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B 24GB, Qwen3.8 27B and Gemma 4 26B-A4B — start rolling out from partners on Friday, Oct. 23.
When workloads require more capacity, developers can connect multiple DGX Spark systems via built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and NVIDIA Sync Cluster Assistant. This allows users to run advanced coding models like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, DeepSeek v4 Flash 0731 and GLM 5.3 Flash.
Now, DGX Spark supports clusters of up to eight units in manual configuration, enabling larger models, longer contexts, concurrent agents and distributed development. Ideal for small teams sharing a single cluster as a backend, with each developer running concurrent sessions against the same model, it delivers 1TB of unified memory — enough to run frontier-class models like GLM 5.3.
Get started with the DGX Spark cluster playbook.
NVIDIA Sync Model Launcher will also be available later this month. It simplifies access to local AI on a single DGX Spark or a cluster. With a few clicks, Model Launcher downloads a model and container suited to the configuration and connects the model to OpenCode. It automatically loads DGX Spark Skills for troubleshooting, device maintenance, access to official documentation and other workflow guidance.
The October DGX Spark software update brings a new Wi-Fi Assistant that lets users switch networks when DGX Spark is running in appliance mode. Plus, DGX Spark Skills provide workflow-focused guidance in troubleshooting and device maintenance directly into NVIDIA Sync via OpenCode.
DGX Spark systems are available directly from Acer, ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, HP, Lenovo, MSI and NVIDIA.
DGX Station Puts Frontier Intelligence at the Desk
For larger teams, DGX Station offers 748GB of coherent memory and up to 20 petaflops of AI performance, enabling developers to run advanced models like GLM 5.3 and serve 30+ users at speeds comparable to those provided by cloud models. Adding scale, NVIDIA Sync now supports DGX Station, simplifying connections between two Linux-based systems.
New integrations with Absolute Security, Splunk by Cisco, Fleet Device Management, Microsoft Intune, Perforce Puppet, Progress Software Chef and Tanium let IT teams manage DGX Station systems through enterprise setup, management and conformity processes, helping accelerate approvals and reduce deployment risk while minimizing time to first token.
With the upcoming Windows-based systems, developers can build workflows that harness professional applications, run on NVIDIA RTX PRO GPUs and operate from agents that run their large language models (LLMs) on NVIDIA GB300 systems — all in one machine.
DGX Station for Windows, expected from system manufacturer partners in December, extends local AI into the applications and operating environment enterprises already use. Engineers can run local models and agents in Windows-native software with access to AI models, tools and agents on the same system.
DGX Station for Windows will feature support for manufacturing applications from nTop, Dassault Systèmes, Keysight Technologies, MathWorks, Rockwell Automation, Siemens, Synopsys, Unity and Altera for AI-guided design, simulation, validation and engineering automation. Users will be able to run agents using Hermes Agent, Perplexity or Aible on premises for agentic control in enterprise environments.
The same local, controlled computing model extends to robotics. DGX Station gives robotics teams dedicated compute for post-training, simulation and evaluation, shortening iteration cycles without waiting for shared infrastructure.
NVIDIA released three open source reference workflows that bring GPT-6 Astra, NVIDIA Isaac Lab, Isaac Lab-Arena and Cosmos to NVIDIA DGX Station. Developers can use them to refine GR00T 1.7 models with reinforcement learning, train dexterous manipulation skills and post-train Cosmos world models for synthetic data generation.
NVIDIA Cloud Functions is coming in early access to Linux-based DGX Station. Teams can register local model endpoints in a shared catalog and access them through one OpenAI-compatible entry point.
Developers can upgrade the model behind an endpoint without changing application code, while teammates can use shared models without direct machine access. This turns a DGX Station into a locally controlled inference service for a team.
DGX Station brings local iteration to AI factory development. On the show floor at GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is previewing DSX OS running on DGX Station to simulate AI factory operations before full infrastructure is available. Another demo will showcase DGX Station systems powering a local token factory for more than 30 software developers.
DGX Station systems are shipping today from ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, HP, MSI, Supermicro and Exxact. DGX Station for Windows systems are expected to begin shipping later this year from ASUS, Dell Technologies, GIGABYTE, HP, MSI and Supermicro.
Introducing Recursive Flint — A New Local Coding Model Optimized for RTX Spark
Today, frontier AI lab Recursive Superintelligence released Recursive Flint, a local LLM built for fast, accurate coding. A 40-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 2.5 billion active parameters, Recursive Flint delivers fast inference — over 220 tokens per second on a 64GB RTX Spark — along with best-in-class scores in agentic coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Pro v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-bench verified.
Recursive Flint was built using Recursive’s Eureka Machine, a system for large-scale automated AI research. It automates the full research loop: proposes ideas, implements them, runs experiments to validate ideas and uses the results to decide what to try next — creating specialized kernels that boosted Flint’s generation speed on RTX Spark by 55% without changing the model’s weights.
Developers can download the open weights on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 license and run the model on RTX Spark and DGX Spark systems, as well as GeForce RTX and RTX PRO GPUs. Developers can also post-train the model with NeMo Automodel for supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation, or LoRa, as well as NeMo RL for group relative policy optimization.
New Models With Day-Zero Support
NVIDIA is also adding day-zero model support for NVIDIA Nemotron Bolt E4B 4B, GLM, DeepSeek, Qwen, MiniMax, Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-24B-A2B, plus the FLUX.3 Klein diffusion model.
Nemotron Bolt E4B 4GB packs natural conversation and multi-turn agentic skills into as little as 4GB of memory, powering fast local voice assistants, interactive game characters and embedded interfaces on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs, NVIDIA Jetson devices, and RTX and DGX Spark. Bolt E4B 4GB releases on Friday, Oct. 23.
Black Forest Labs’ FLUX 3 Image Klein is a 5.6-billion-parameter open weights image model for generation and editing. NVIDIA-optimized builds let it run on GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM and create a 1-megapixel image in about four seconds on an RTX 5090 GPU.
MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a new open model built for NVIDIA DGX Station and DGX Spark, bringing long-context AI to the desktop. Liquid AI’s LFM2.5-24B-A2B is an open weights reasoning model that activates just 2 billion of its 24 billion parameters per token, making it fast enough to run private, tool-calling AI agents directly on PCs.
Plus, NVIDIA has released a new collection of model checkpoints optimized for RAM efficiency on local AI hardware, enabling frontier-class open models to run with sufficient memory left over for KV cache. Each checkpoint is quantized while staying close to full-precision accuracy, starting with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP4-Local on a single DGX Spark 128GB or RTX PRO 6000 and GLM-5.3-Flash-FP4-Local on two systems.
Developers can post-train on day zero with NeMo AutoModel on both DGX Spark and RTX Spark, with example recipes for Nemotron Bolt E4B, Flux 3 Image Klein and more.
Accelerated AI Inference
NVIDIA continues to work with the llama.cpp and vLLM open source communities to accelerate agentic workloads on local hardware.
In llama.cpp, new speculative decoding support with MTP for Qwen 3.8 Flash Next makes end-to-end agentic tasks up to 1.4x faster on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
In vLLM, faster speculative decoding and new FlashInfer prefill kernels for Qwen’s linear-attention layers make agentic tasks with Qwen3.8 27B up to 1.3x faster on DGX Spark. On DGX Station, GLM 5.3 Flash gets up to 1.2x higher throughput.
Check out NVIDIA’s local AI inference recipes to try these latest optimizations.
Follow NVIDIA RTX Spark on X, Instagram, TikTok and Facebook — and stay informed by subscribing to the NVIDIA Local AI newsletter. Follow NVIDIA Workstation on LinkedIn and X.
See notice regarding software product information.

articles.title: La próxima Xbox no será una sola consola y Microsoft ya tiene el plan
articles.text:
Microsoft tiene planes de lanzar una consola portátil en 2027, antes de dar el salto a Project Helix. En una entrevista con Fortune, la jefa de Xbox, Asha Sharma, confirmó los planes de la compañía para los próximos años. Sharma señaló que venderán una portátil y posteriormente una consola de sobremesa, las cuales formarán parte del ecosistema de dispositivos Xbox.
Una de las cosas que ha dejado claro la nueva CEO es que quiere revertir los años que llevaron a Xbox al tercer lugar en ventas, por detrás de PlayStation y Nintendo. Parte de la estrategia de transformación combina nuevos dispositivos, una reorganización interna y una apuesta mucho más agresiva por las franquicias más rentables de la compañía. Atrás quedaron los experimentos de Game Pass y juegos que no venden, ya que ahora el foco estará en Halo, Gears of War, Fallout y otras sagas exitosas.
Uno de los pilares de esa hoja de ruta tiene que ver con el hardware. Según explicó Sharma en una entrevista con Fortune, Xbox trabaja en una consola portátil de nueva generación que llegará en la temporada navideña de 2027. Al mismo tiempo, la compañía desarrolla su próxima consola de sobremesa, cuyo debut está programado para finales de 2028 (siempre y cuando la escasez de memoria lo permita).
Sobre la portátil, Asha Sharma considera que esta consola será pieza clave en su estrategia para llegar a la marca de 1.000 millones de jugadores que se ha fijado Xbox. La entrevista no menciona detalles sobre el hardware o si Microsoft será responsable de fabricarla. Es probable que la compañía repita la dosis de la ROG Ally y se asocie con ASUS, lo cual le permitiría enfocarse en mejorar el software y ofrecer algo que vaya más en la línea de SteamOS.
Xbox lanzará su consola Project Helix en 2028
Uno de los proyectos más importantes del plan de Sharma es Project Helix, la próxima consola de sobremesa de Microsoft. A unas semanas de que asumiera la dirección de Xbox, Sharma confirmó que trabajaban en una sucesora de la Series X|S con hardware potente y compatibilidad con juegos de PC. Desde ese tiempo, poco se ha dicho de esta consola, fuera de que el equipo tuvo que replantearse el desarrollo debido a la crisis de componentes que afecta a toda la industria.
El reportaje de Fortune menciona que Xbox ha acelerado algunos plazos de desarrollo de Project Helix y que la consola podría costar entre 1.200 y 1.800 dólares. La cifra suena astronómica si la comparamos con lo que costó la PS5 o Series X cuando se lanzaron en 2020. No obstante, la escasez de memoria ha ocasionado que los precios se disparen y los analistas estiman que este fenómeno se mantendrá más allá de 2030.
En el caso de la PS6, los primeros rumores afirman que la RAM y la memoria NAND cuestan más de 680 dólares. A esa cifra tendríamos que sumar el coste del procesador y componentes, los cuales elevarían el precio por encima de los 1.000 dólares. Sony ya ha dicho que no tiene planes de vender la consola a pérdida, por lo que no subvencionará la PS6 y los usuarios tendrán que pagar el precio real.
Project Helix se lanzará a finales de 2028 y formará parte de un ecosistema de dispositivos. Es difícil creer que Microsoft podría recuperar el trono que alguna vez ostentó durante la era de la Xbox 360 si lanza una consola que cueste más de 1.200 dólares. Probablemente, la compañía esperará y hará los ajustes necesarios para ganar terreno, comenzando con una portátil.

articles.title: 3 Nigerian startups selected for MARL’s global accelerator - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startups Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax have been selected for the 14th cohort of MARL’s global accelerator programme, with each receiving US$50,000 in funding.
MARL is a US-based early-stage venture capital firm that runs an accelerator programme for tech startups around the world. Alongside funds, it gives founders hands-on help with product development, business strategy and fundraising, and connects them with its network of mentors and investors.
Three Nigerian startups have been selected for the 14th cohort. They are Solarcorp, a climate-tech company replacing diesel generators in malls and commercial clusters with shared solar-and-storage systems; Bravoo, which is building a consumer platform built around rewards and gamified experiences; and Zendtrax, which offers enterprise software for procurement, inventory and supply-chain management.
“At MARL, we believe great technology companies can emerge from anywhere. The selection of Solarcorp, Bravoo and Zendtrax into our 14th global cohort reflects the quality of innovation we’re seeing from African founders,” said Prakash Goswami, managing partner at MARL.
MARL’s vohort 14 Demo Day takes place on November 12.

articles.title: AI startup Firefly secures $20M to make the physical world a safer place - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AI startup Firefly secures $20M to make the physical world a safer place
The digital world has already become much smarter thanks to the rise of artificial intelligence, and now a startup called Firefly Technology Inc. wants to do the same for the physical world, beginning with workplace safety.
It has just raised $20 million in funding via a Series A round to make that happen. Today’s round was led by Definition Capital, which previously funded Ramp Business Corp. and Cognition Inc., developer of the AI coding assistant Devin. It was joined by BoxGroup, making its third investment in Firefly, and Susa Ventures, which led the startup’s seed round earlier this year.
Firefly’s goal is to make the world a safer place, and it believes it can do that by extending AI into the physical world to make safety systems more intelligent. Though devices such as security cameras, radios and sensors have helped make locations such as schools, hospitals and other venues safer than they used to be, there’s still a lot of disconnect between these systems. Cameras can see what’s happening, radios can facilitate communication between security personnel and sensors can trigger alarms, but these devices all work in isolation.
What this means is that when something happens, humans still need to waste valuable time understanding the situation before they can put together a response.
Firefly co-founder and Chief Executive James Batt Buckley believes AI can help to close this gap. He says the next frontier for AI is the physical world, which he wants to become as intelligent, connected and programmable as the digital one already is. His idea is to build a single, intelligent system that spans security cameras, sensors and communications, so that AI will immediately understand what’s happening and coordinate a response the moment the alarm registers within the brains of the humans tasked with executing that response.
The startup has developed a combination of purpose-built safety hardware and emergency response management software that’s designed to plug into existing hardware such as cameras and radios. The Ember Safety Management platform works by extracting intelligence from those devices and sensors to build up a clear picture of what the situation is, so it can immediately detect an incident, provide the right context and then organize the response. Firefly has also developed specialized hardware such as wearable panic buttons and AI beacons that enable panic button triangulation and detect gunshots, as well as a network gateway to ensure those systems are always connected.
Buckley said the safety technology industry has seemingly accepted a very strange contradiction. “The more important the job, the more complicated the tools seem to become,” he said. “But we now have the technology to build something fundamentally different. We’re starting with safety because it’s a problem we know deeply, but what we’re building has the potential to transform how people interact with the physical world.”
Constellation Research analyst Holger Mueller said startups such as Firefly are a reminder that AI is going to impact a lot more than just our digital experiences. “Ultimately, AI is going to have a dramatic impact on the physical world too, with one of the first being to improve physical safety in places like schools, hospitals and other large venues,” he said.
The analyst believes AI has obvious advantages over humans when it comes to monitoring a physical area for signs of danger, because it’s always on, always focused and therefore much more vigilant than any human security guard could be. “It will provide more timely and reliable alerts to any malfeasance,” Mueller said. “As with any AI innovation, a degree of cautiousness is still needed to make sure Firefly’s systems work as intended, but any teething problems can probably be ironed out. It’s good to see the innovation helping to keep schools and the kids inside them safe.”
Firefly’s platform has already been deployed by Colorado’s largest community college, Front Range Community College, where it provides unified intelligence across three expansive campuses, helping safety teams to quickly understand emergencies and take action. The startup now wants to expand its deployments, targeting educational centers, hospitals, enterprise campuses and other locations.
Definition Capital’s Teddy Citrin said the intersection of AI and hardware means organizations now have better ways to protect their people. “Firefly is building the central nervous system for physical safety, bringing together specialized hardware, existing data and coordinated action into a single platform,” he said.

articles.title: Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry
Runtime discovery with AWS Agent Registry can help address a problem that agent demos might hide. Hardcoded tools work fine for a handful, start to degrade at a few dozen, and become unmanageable beyond that. Enterprise systems expose hundreds of internal APIs for pricing, support, orders, inventory, and customer data. In these systems, the model can spend more tokens disambiguating tool names than reasoning about the user’s request. Each new capability requires a code change in the orchestrator, a redeploy, and a coordinated release across teams that would much rather ship on their own cadence.
This pattern can arise across enterprise software as a service (SaaS) engagements where teams expose large internal API surfaces to agentic consumers. Build-time wiring can become a bottleneck as the catalog expands. One approach is to change how the orchestrator accesses its tools: instead of compiling every tool into the agent, the agent can discover relevant tools at runtime.
AWS Agent Registry is a managed service for cataloging and discovering Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agents, and agent skills. Publishers register protocol-specific descriptors and searchable descriptions. At runtime, an orchestrator can search approved, discoverable records and use the returned endpoint and descriptor content to construct a client. Registry search results do not return the capability’s invocation credentials or authentication scheme.
This post walks through the Discover → Instantiate → Execute loop demonstrated by the refactored Python sample. The code deploys an order-management MCP server through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, two agent-to-agent (A2A) agents on AgentCore runtime, a Registry, and an orchestrator. The sample directory contains the deployment script, orchestrator, helper modules, and cleanup script.
Solution overview: discover, instantiate, execute
The orchestrator agent in this sample has no built-in knowledge of tools or agents.
Discover
The orchestrator sends a natural-language query to the AWS Agent Registry data plane. The search response includes record identity, name, description, record type, status, version, and protocol descriptors such as MCP server metadata or an A2A agent card. It does not include invocation credentials. The application must obtain and apply the appropriate credentials through a separate, trusted configuration path.
Instantiate
For each returned record, the orchestrator constructs a client from the descriptor type. In this sample, the registered MCP server represents tools that were first added as targets to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The MCP descriptor therefore points to the Gateway endpoint. The orchestrator fetches a Cognito OAuth access token separately and uses it when creating the MCPClient. A2A records contain an agent card whose URL identifies an AgentCore runtime endpoint. The wrapper invokes that runtime through the boto3 data-plane client, which signs the request with the caller’s AWS credentials. Registry discovery supplies connection metadata, not the authentication material.
Execute
An ephemeral inner agent is built with only the dynamically-discovered tools. The large language model (LLM) picks the right one(s) for the request, and the result is synthesized back to the user. After the turn finishes, the inner agent and its clients are torn down. The next request gets a fresh search and a fresh tool set.
The reference architecture used in the sample includes AWS Agent Registry, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon Cognito, AWS Lambda, and AWS Secrets Manager.
- AWS Agent Registry provides the governed, searchable catalog queried by the orchestrator. Only records that complete the configured approval workflow are available through the discoverable data plane.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway exposes the order-management Lambda tools as an MCP server. The sample configures Cognito JWT authorization for inbound Gateway calls and uses the Gateway AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role to invoke the Lambda target.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosts the orchestrator and the Pricing and Customer Support A2A agents. Runtime invocations use IAM-authorized Boto3 calls.
- Amazon Bedrock provides the foundation model (FM) used by the orchestrator and A2A agents. The sample currently configures an Anthropic Claude Sonnet model through a cross-Region model ID. See Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Three demo scenarios exercise the discovery loop with different capability combinations. The first is an MCP-only call (order status). The second chains MCP + A2A (pricing and discounts). The third tests a pure semantic match against ambiguous user intent: return and refund, where those words don’t appear in the matched A2A agent’s name.
Technical implementation
The linked runtime-discovery sample deploys the dependencies, creates and populates the Registry, verifies discovery, deploys the orchestrator, and runs three demos. orchestrator_agent.py contains the per-request discovery loop. utils.py parses Registry descriptors and creates MCP and A2A clients. cleanup.py removes resources.
1. The registration model
A Registry record contains a searchable description plus a protocol-specific descriptor. The sample uses the Agent Registry control-plane client for Registry and record lifecycle operations and the Agent Registry data-plane client for runtime discovery.
Creating a Registry with manual approval and IAM authorization.
The recordType field is required when creating a record. In this sample, MCP servers use recordType="MCP" and A2A-backed agents use recordType="AGENT". Protocol metadata is stored under mcpServer or a2aAgentCard in the descriptors object. An MCP descriptor contains server metadata and tool definitions. An A2A descriptor contains the agent card. The descriptors contain connection metadata but not the credentials that a consumer must present when invoking the capability.
Building current public-SDK descriptor shapes for MCP and A2A records.
Write descriptions in user-facing language that distinguishes the capability from neighboring records. Descriptor content supplies the protocol-specific server, tool, or agent-card data. Search quality should be evaluated with representative queries. This post does not assume that catalog growth automatically improves ranking.
Creating a Registry record with the current control-plane shape.
2. Approval workflow
With autoApproval set to false, a new record must move from DRAFT to PENDING_APPROVAL and then APPROVED. The submit and status-update actions are IAM-authorized, allowing publisher and approver permissions to be separated. Only approved records are returned by the discoverable Registry data plane.
The two-step approval transition.
3. The discovery layer
The data-plane client supports hybrid keyword and semantic search across discoverable records. The latest method name is search_discoverable_registry_records. Results expose normalized record fields and discoverable descriptors. They don’t expose the capability’s invocation credentials.
Searching approved, discoverable records across protocols.
In the sample scenario, a return-and-refund query retrieves the Customer Support Agent because its description captures that intent. Treat this as a demo result, not a general claim that ranking improves merely because the catalog is larger.
4. The orchestrator
The orchestrator is a Strands agent deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. It exposes discover_and_execute, which searches the Registry, parses each returned descriptor, creates the corresponding MCP or A2A client, and builds a request-scoped inner agent from only those discovered capabilities.
The core of discover_and_execute fits in a single code block:
The orchestrator’s discover/instantiate/execute loop.
The sample fans out several search queries to improve recall for its order-management domain, deduplicates records, and tears down MCP clients after the request. That fan-out is a sample-specific orchestration choice, not a Registry requirement. Authentication remains outside discovery: the Gateway OAuth token is obtained from Cognito configuration and Secrets Manager, whereas A2A runtime calls are signed through the boto3 session.
5. Running the three demos
Each demo exercises a different shape of the discovery loop.
Demo 1: Order status (MCP only)
A request that resolves to a single MCP tool call.
The Registry returns the order management MCP server. The orchestrator calls get_order_status through Gateway, the LLM synthesizes a human-readable response, and the inner agent terminates. No A2A involvement on this turn.
Demo 2: Pricing and discounts (MCP + A2A)
A request that resolves to a multi-protocol chain.
The Registry returns the order management MCP server and the pricing A2A agent: two protocols, one natural-language query. The LLM calls get_order_status to fetch line items, then calls the pricing agent on runtime for discount analysis, then synthesizes a single recommendation.
Demo 3: Return and refund (semantic match)
A request whose intent is not literally present in any tool name.
This demo shows the value of semantic discovery. The phrase ‘return refund’ doesn’t appear in the Customer Support Agent’s registered name. The hybrid search ranks it highly because its description captures the intent. Without Registry, the orchestrator would need hardcoded knowledge of which agent handles returns.
6. Observability
Instrument the discovery and invocation path using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability and Amazon CloudWatch where appropriate. Useful signals include Registry search success and failure, selected record identifiers, client-construction errors, downstream invocation outcomes, end-to-end trace correlation, and application errors. The sample grants Amazon CloudWatch Logs permissions, but it doesn’t create custom metrics or dashboards. Production teams should define the traces, logs, and alerts required for their operating model. Production deployments should also apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails as a standard control on agent responses.
What teams gain from governed runtime discovery
After the discovery loop is in place, several capabilities that were previously coupled to orchestrator releases become independent.
- Decoupled publishing. Teams can deploy and register their own MCP servers, agents, and skills. Approval policy determines when a published record becomes available to consumers.
- No orchestrator code change for newly approved records. In this pattern, adding a compatible, approved Registry record doesn’t require adding a tool-specific import or endpoint to the orchestrator. Changes to protocols, authentication setup, or orchestration policy can still require code or configuration updates.
- Governed discovery. With manual approval, only reviewed and approved records become discoverable. IAM permissions can separate record publishers from approvers.
- Separated authentication. Registry authorization can use IAM or custom JWT. Capability invocation authentication is separate: the sample uses Cognito OAuth for Gateway and Boto3/IAM signing for AgentCore runtime. Search results don’t return those credentials.
- Catalog search instead of prompt stuffing. With hybrid Registry search, the orchestrator retrieves a small candidate set instead of placing the full catalog in the model context. Search quality depends on descriptions, descriptor quality, query design, and evaluation.
When not to use runtime discovery
Runtime discovery is not necessary for every workload. Two patterns can still favor explicit build-time wiring:
- Small, stable catalogs. If the complete capability set is small and changes rarely, explicit build-time wiring might be simpler and avoid an additional discovery request.
- Fixed pipelines. When the same capabilities always run in a fixed order, implementing them as a deterministic flow is more straightforward and keeps tracing focused.
Conclusion
Discovery of assets from Registry at runtime makes the orchestrator less dependent on a fixed catalog. Against an AWS Agent Registry, it can search approved capabilities with hybrid semantic and keyword search, parse MCP or A2A descriptors, and instantiate request-scoped clients. Governance determines what is discoverable. Authentication remains an explicit concern for the Registry and each invoked capability.
AWS Agent Registry is generally available with capabilities that extend beyond this single-account sample:
- Organization-wide discovery and cross-account sharing can expose governed records across account boundaries through supported AWS Organizations and sharing mechanisms.
- Automatic capability synchronization can populate supported descriptors from a URL. Credential-provider configuration on that synchronization request is used to fetch descriptor content. It isn’t returned to runtime consumers as invocation authentication.
- Approval workflows can use Registry status APIs and IAM permissions to connect CI checks, security review, or human approval to the DRAFT → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED lifecycle.
- Tagging, AWS CloudFormation support, and infrastructure-as-code patterns can make Registry deployment and governance repeatable. Evaluation should verify search relevance and invocation behavior for the organization’s own catalog.
Run the runtime-discovery sample, then register one compatible MCP server or agent of your own. Confirm that its descriptor, approval state, authentication path, and search behavior match your production requirements.
Learn more
- AWS Agent Registry general availability announcement
- AWS Agent Registry documentation
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore console (Registry)
- AWS Agent Registry general availability technical blog post

articles.title: GPT, Claude et Gemini dans une seule app : 1min.AI Pro à vie à 35,99€
articles.text:
StackSocial affiche l’accès à vie au plan Pro de 1min.AI à 35,99 €, pour un million de crédits par mois à répartir entre GPT, Claude, Gemini et d’autres modèles. Notre test lui a attribué 7/10 : l’outil dépanne et compare bien, mais il ne remplace pas un abonnement natif.
1min.AI est un agrégateur : une seule interface donne accès à des modèles de texte d’OpenAI, d’Anthropic, de Google, de Mistral ou de Meta, ainsi qu’à des outils d’image, d’audio, de vidéo et de lecture de PDF. Plutôt qu’un abonnement mensuel, StackSocial propose son plan Pro à vie pour 35,99 €, contre un prix suggéré de 209 € affiché par le revendeur. Ce tarif est plus élevé que lors de précédentes promotions : nous avions relayé la même offre à moins de 22 € en juillet.
L’offre vise surtout les personnes qui passent d’une IA à l’autre pour écrire, résumer ou créer des visuels, sans avoir besoin des fonctions avancées de chaque service.
Le plan Pro de 1min.AI, avec un million de crédits par mois et un accès à vie, est affiché à 35,99 € au lieu de 209 € chez StackSocial.
Pourquoi choisir le 1min.AI Pro ?
- Un paiement unique : Les 35,99 € sont réglés une fois, sans renouvellement. Sur la plateforme, le même plan Pro est facturé 6,50 $ par mois en abonnement.
- Plusieurs modèles côte à côte : La fonction Multi AI Chat envoie une même question à plusieurs modèles à la fois. Vous comparez les réponses avant de retenir la plus juste.
- Un coût affiché avant chaque requête : 1min.AI estime le nombre de crédits consommés avant l’envoi. Vous voyez venir les tâches gourmandes, comme la vidéo, avant qu’elles ne vident le solde du mois.
Rédiger, résumer, créer : à quoi servent ces crédits
Le million de crédits mensuel couvre, selon les estimations de 1min.AI, jusqu’à environ 805 000 mots générés, 161 images ou 12 vidéos, des volumes qui se partagent entre les usages. En pratique, le texte coûte peu et la vidéo beaucoup : un rédacteur ou un community manager tiendra son mois, un créateur de vidéos nettement moins. Les outils annexes vont du détourage d’image à la transcription audio, en passant par le dialogue avec un PDF pour en tirer un résumé. Une connexion quotidienne rapporte en plus 15 000 crédits gratuits, soit jusqu’à 450 000 par mois.
Dans notre test de 1min.AI, deux usages ressortent nettement : le secours quand votre IA habituelle est saturée ou en panne, et la comparaison rapide de plusieurs réponses. Le service convient donc aux freelances et aux petites équipes qui alternent entre les modèles pour des tâches ponctuelles. Il est moins adapté si vous attendez une mémoire entre les conversations ou une recherche web solide, deux points faibles relevés pendant l’essai. Pour des données clients ou soumises au RGPD, sa politique de conservation des données, jusqu’à un an, l’écarte aussi.
Un agrégateur face aux abonnements ChatGPT et Claude
Un abonnement ChatGPT Plus coûte environ 23 € par mois et Claude Pro environ 21 € : 1min.AI revient moins cher dès le deuxième mois. Il n’offre pourtant ni les projets, ni les agents, ni la mémoire persistante de ces services, et les derniers modèles y arrivent avec du retard. Si vous cherchez avant tout un assistant principal, notre comparatif des meilleurs chatbots IA détaille ce que valent ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, Mistral et Gemini. 1min.AI se place à côté, comme un accès d’appoint à plusieurs d’entre eux.
✅ Les points forts
- Paiement unique de 35,99 €, sans renouvellement
- 1 000 000 de crédits par mois, plus 15 000 par connexion quotidienne
- Multi AI Chat pour comparer plusieurs modèles sur une même question
- Estimation du coût en crédits avant chaque requête
- Disponible sur le web, Windows, Mac, iOS et Android
❌ Les limites
- Derniers modèles intégrés avec du retard
- Aucune mémoire entre les conversations, recherche web limitée
- Interface cloisonnée, chaque outil dans son propre écran
- Déconseillé pour des données sensibles ou professionnelles
Le code 1min.AI Pro acheté chez StackSocial s’active dans les 30 jours ; tant qu’il n’est pas activé, il peut être retourné contre un avoir dans ce délai.
À 35,99 €, le plan Pro de 1min.AI à vie reste une dépense modeste face à un abonnement d’IA payé chaque mois. Il n’atteint pas les moins de 22 € observés cet été, et les 209 € affichés en référence sont un prix suggéré par le revendeur. Le calcul reste favorable si vous utilisez déjà plusieurs IA de façon occasionnelle.
Pour un usage d’appoint ou de comparaison, l’offre tient sa promesse, avec un volume de crédits suffisant pour du texte et des images. Si vous travaillez chaque jour avec un seul assistant, mieux vaut garder son abonnement natif, plus complet et mis à jour plus vite. Dans le doute, la version gratuite de 1min.AI permet de vérifier que l’interface vous convient avant de payer.

articles.title: Jio Platforms' anchor book draws Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids ahead of IPO
articles.text:
Jio Platforms' anchor book draws Rs 2.5 lakh crore in bids ahead of IPO
Jio Platforms allotted 7.24 crore shares at a price of Rs 1,119 per share to the anchor investors and LIC received the largest allocation
Jio Platforms has allotted shares worth Rs 8,109.85 crore to 212 anchor investors at the top end of its price band, after institutional demand for the offering exceeded Rs 2.5 lakh crore, more than 30 times the amount available in the anchor book, according to a stock exchange filing and people familiar with the matter.
The allotment of 7.24 crore shares at Rs 1,119 apiece comes ahead of the initial public offering that opens for public subscription on Wednesday.
The strong demand underscores institutional investor interest in what is expected to be India's largest IPO, although the extent to which it translates into broader public demand will become clearer once the offer opens.
Life Insurance Corporation of India received the largest allocation, worth Rs 499.98 crore, accounting for 6.17 per cent of the anchor portion.
New World Fund Inc was allotted shares worth Rs 486.27 crore, followed by the Government of Singapore at Rs 340.93 crore, SBI Focused Fund at Rs 315 crore and BNP Paribas Financial Markets - ODI at Rs 303.25 crore.
Domestic mutual funds received 2.489 crore shares worth Rs 2,784.96 crore, representing 34.34 per cent of the anchor book, through 95 schemes across 25 fund houses. Life insurers and pension funds received 97.4 lakh shares worth Rs 1,089.95 crore, or 13.44 per cent of the total.
Both categories exceeded the allocations reserved for them under the red herring prospectus dated October 14, which earmarked 33.33 per cent of the anchor portion for mutual funds and 6.67 per cent for insurers and pension funds.
Global investment firms participating in the anchor book include BlackRock, Capital Group, Fidelity, T. Rowe Price, Schroders, JPMorgan Asset Management, Franklin Templeton and Janus Henderson.
Sovereign and public investment institutions include the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, alongside other long-term institutional investors.
Some large overseas and domestic institutions bid for allocations worth $750 million to more than $1 billion each, people familiar with the matter said.
Jio Platforms is seeking to raise about Rs 30,213 crore through a fresh issue of up to 27 crore shares, at a price band of Rs 1,065 to Rs 1,119 apiece. The offering values the company at around USD 108 billion, according to the offer documents.
The IPO will open on October 21 and close on October 23.

articles.title: Zeabur shutting down after second security breach in two months
articles.text:
Development platform Zeabur has disclosed details of a cybersecurity incident in which an attacker used leaked internal credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure and steal over 3.2 million environment variable records and information for 321,810 accounts.
The attackers used stolen administrator credentials and cloud access keys to compromise Zeabur’s shared hosting infrastructure and dedicated servers, eventually gaining access to its production database.
“On October 14–15, 2026, an attacker used leaked Zeabur internal credentials to break into the shared cluster, some Dedicated Servers, and Zeabur internal systems, and eventually read the platform database,” Zeabur’s announcement reads.
Zeabur is a developer hosting and deployment platform that lets developers connect a GitHub repository and have the platform handle deployment, databases, HTTPS, and infrastructure management.
In late August 2026, the company suffered another security breach when hackers exploited a flaw in a customer’s NextChat application and then moved through poorly isolated internal systems.
This led to the theft of AWS credentials and access to the production database, exposing account information, API keys, and other secrets stored there.
In the latest incident, Zeabur says the compromise was broader, affecting shared clusters across nine regions, 321,810 accounts, and roughly 3.2 million environment-variable records.
Also, Zeabur confirmed root sign-ins on 101 GCP servers by 92 users, with the attackers adding SSH keys to 50 servers and attaching 16 customer disk copies to their own virtual machines.
The company says that attackers likely obtained the credentials they used in the second attack during the August breach, though it hasn’t confirmed this.
Beyond failing to store credentials in encrypted form, Zeabur also failed to rotate all administrator account credentials since the August incident, while administrator portals remained accessible to the public internet.
“The admin tokens had no expiry, had not been rotated since they were created in January 2024, and were not included in the post-August rotation,” explained Zeabur.
Users are urged to rotate exposed credentials and secrets immediately, revoke all active sessions, and rebuild compromised GCP servers.
Variables previously migrated exclusively to customers’ own servers as part of the August incident response escaped this latest platform database exposure, although compromised hosts could still expose them.
Zeabur announces shutdown
After discovering the latest security incident, Zeabur announced over the weekend that it will shut down its services starting December 1, 2026, and finish by December 31, 2026.
The decision comes after 3.5 years of continuous growth, including a record year in 2026, but Zeabur said scaling the project to meet market demand has made it increasingly complex and difficult to maintain, and the recent security failures reflect that.
“After the August incident, we spent a long time discussing and struggling with what to do next,” explained Zeabur.
“Following this latest incident, we reassessed what it would take to keep operating and the responsibilities our team could carry. We ultimately decided to wind down.”
On December 1, renewals will be disabled, and all running services on shared clusters will be paused. By the end of the year, all dedicated servers will expire and shut down, and all shared clusters will stop.
Users may be given additional time for data migration, though no concrete timelines on that front have been provided yet.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
