articles.title: Disney pagará USD 20 millones a Character.AI por una licencia que la protege de las demandas por daños a menores
articles.text:
Disney acordó pagar USD 20 millones a Character.AI por una licencia de su tecnología de chatbots, en un trato estructurado a través de la quiebra de la empresa que, según documentos judiciales, le permite contratar a su personal sin heredar las demandas por daños a menores que enfrenta la plataforma.
Character Technologies, la empresa detrás de Character.AI, se declaró en quiebra bajo el Capítulo 11 el 12 de octubre en un tribunal de Delaware. El expediente judicial muestra que ese paso fue parte de un plan acordado de antemano con Disney, no una consecuencia inesperada de sus problemas financieros.
La licencia que busca Disney es perpetua, mundial y no exclusiva, y cubre el código, la documentación y las patentes de Character.AI, incluidos sus sistemas de moderación y de verificación de edad. No incluye los datos de los usuarios ni el sitio web de la plataforma, que seguirán en manos de la empresa en quiebra.
El pago de USD 20 millones se divide en tres partes: USD 5,5 millones no reembolsables que Disney ya giró el 18 de septiembre, un depósito reembolsable de USD 2 millones pagado ese mismo día, y USD 12,5 millones que debe abonar al cierre de la operación. Disney actúa como “postor inicial” y otros interesados pueden superar su oferta.
Además del pago, Disney contrató a la mayoría del personal de Character.AI, entre ellos a su entonces director ejecutivo, Karandeep Anand, por una cifra estimada en USD 60 millones, según reportó Bloomberg. La empresa no asume ninguna de las deudas ni de los litigios de la plataforma que compró.
Una maniobra que esquiva las demandas
El mecanismo se conoce como “reverse acquihire”: un comprador contrata al personal clave y obtiene una licencia amplia sobre la tecnología de una empresa, sin absorberla formalmente ni asumir sus obligaciones legales. Ese formato evita, además, la obligación de notificar la operación a los reguladores antimonopolio.
John Newman, profesor de derecho de la Universidad de Memphis y ex subdirector de la Oficina de Competencia de la Comisión Federal de Comercio de Estados Unidos, dijo que “existen décadas de derecho corporativo” pensadas para que un comprador no se quede solo con los activos y descarte los pasivos, pero que el acuerdo entre Disney y Character.AI está diseñado “de una forma para la que esas protecciones legales no fueron pensadas”.
Disney también redactó un borrador de orden judicial, llamada “orden libre de cargas”, que aclararía que la operación no debe considerarse una fusión y que Character.AI seguirá siendo responsable de “cualquier obligación”, incluidas las demandas en curso.
Las demandas que Character.AI se queda sola
Según una presentación hecha por la Asociación Nacional de Procuradores Generales en nombre de 40 estados, las investigaciones encontraron capturas de pantalla de chatbots de Character.AI que alentaban a menores a ocultar autolesiones y, en algunos casos, a matar a sus padres. Al momento de la quiebra, 46 estados y territorios investigaban a la empresa.
Un vocero de Character.AI dijo que esa presentación “no es un reflejo preciso de la seguridad de nuestra plataforma”. Pensilvania había demandado por separado a la empresa en mayo, al acusar a sus chatbots de hacerse pasar por médicos con licencia.
Character.AI ya había enfrentado una demanda por el suicidio de un adolescente de 14 años en Florida, cuya familia alegó que un chatbot de la plataforma “cultivó una relación emocionalmente dependiente y sexualmente explotadora” con él. Ese caso también involucró a Google, que había pagado USD 2.700 millones en 2024 por una licencia de la tecnología de Character.AI y contrató a sus fundadores.
Google argumentó entonces que seguía siendo una empresa separada y que no era responsable del hecho, ocurrido antes de firmar ese acuerdo. El juez no aceptó el argumento y determinó que había elementos suficientes para considerar a Google responsable por complicidad. Las partes llegaron a un acuerdo extrajudicial, aprobado por un tribunal de California en julio.
Según el cronograma del expediente, otros postores tienen hasta el 20 de noviembre para presentar ofertas que superen la de Disney. La subasta está prevista para el 23 de noviembre y la audiencia judicial de aprobación de la venta, para el 24 de noviembre. Disney tiene como plazo límite el 17 de diciembre para cerrar la operación.
Según la primera declaración jurada de su director ejecutivo ante el tribunal, Character.AI generaba unos USD 2,5 millones mensuales en publicidad frente a un gasto de caja de USD 8,2 millones al mes, con cerca de 163 millones de usuarios actuales y pasados. Si ningún otro comprador supera la oferta de Disney, la empresa advirtió que la plataforma podría cerrar.

articles.title: This 3D-printed 1980s brick phone brings back the days when mobile phones were just for making calls
articles.text:
In a nutshell: A lot of people cite the 1990s Nokia 3210 as the old-school brick-like mobile phone. But for something that fits the description a lot closer, go back another decade to the 1980's and the first handheld mobile phones: brick phones. Now, a designer has 3D-printed one of these devices, retaining the originals' primary function of making and receiving calls – so there are no modern smartphone distractions.
Cologne-based designer and maker Kevin Noki created the ADHD ONE, the first part of the name being an acronym for Anti Distraction Handset Device.
The device resembles a snazzy update of 1980s brick phones sported by the likes of Wall Street's Gordon Gekko, such as the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X. There's the physical 19-key keypad, small display, and a concerning large antenna.
The phone has a much more modern set of internals. It's powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico and features an FSC-BT1026C Bluetooth module based on Qualcomm's QCC3024 chip. There's also a rechargeable lithium battery, charging controller, and custom-printed circuit board.
Unlike the 1980s originals, the ADHD ONE doesn't have its own cellular connectivity. Instead, it relies on a Bluetooth connection to an iPhone to make and receive calls, so it's not like you can completely replace your distraction-filled smartphone with one of these, but you can at least keep it hidden in a drawer.
Noki designed the phone's enclosure using Autodesk Fusion before 3D-printing the components. He's made the files available on his website for €29.99 ($33.68). The package includes 3D-printable STL files for the main housing, back panels, internal mounting frame, display cover, battery holder, and all 19 keypad buttons.
There are also three speaker grille designs (Classic, Holes, and Stripes), three antenna options (Retro, Slim, and Screw), and an alternative housing without an antenna hole. Other included files cover ready-to-flash firmware in UF2 format, Gerber and drill files for manufacturing the custom PCB, a bill of materials with component sourcing notes, and a quick-start guide to assembling the device.
The package doesn't include the firmware's source code, editable 3D/CAD files, or editable PCB design files. It's also a digital download, so no physical components are supplied. Buyers receive a ZIP file of approximately 20MB immediately after payment. The files are licensed for personal use only, meaning they cannot be redistributed or resold.
Several devices have been released in recent years promising a break from the distractions – such as depression-inducing social media apps – found on smartphones. There were the $299 Light Flip and Light Phone III, the Minimal Phone, and Commodore's Callback 8020, to name a few.

articles.title: Charge sans fil Qi2 15 W, écran LCD et capacité de 10 000 mAh : cette batterie Anker fait mieux que la concurrence et elle est à -31% — Frandroid
articles.text:
Anker est une marque qui a su se faire sa petite réputation dans le domaine de la batterie, que ce soit avec des chargeurs, des stations ou des hubs et même des câbles. La marque a su faire progresser ses appareils, notamment avec la MagGo proposée ici qui est compatible avec la charge magnétique Qi2 tout en proposant une charge rapide 15 W avec une capacité généreuse de 10 000 mAh. Donc elle est tout à fait compatible avec les iPhone dernière génération et vous pouvez l’utiliser sans souci pour redonner de l’autonomie à votre appareil sans problème. Surtout qu’elle se retrouve en promo avec 24,9 euros de réduction sur Amazon.
Les atouts de l’Anker MagGo Qi2
- Sa charge sans-fil Qi2 qui garantit une puissance de 15 W
- Sa capacité généreuse de 10 000 mAh
- Sa béquille pliable pour continuer d’utiliser le smartphone sur un bureau ou dans un train
Le prix de cette batterie Anker MagGo est de 79,99 euros, mais avec la réduction qui court jusqu’au 1er novembre 2026, vous pouvez l’avoir pour 55,09 euros.
Un équipement généreux avec écran intelligent
L’Anker MagGo est une batterie externe certifiée Qi2, la nouvelle norme universelle de charge sans fil. Contrairement aux anciennes batteries magnétiques tierces qui plafonnaient à 7,5 W, ce modèle délivre une vraie puissance de 15 W et permet ainsi d’égaliser les performances du chargeur officiel MagSafe d’Apple. C’est un argument de poids, d’autant que sa capacité de 10 000 mAh offre une réserve d’énergie confortable. Mais au-delà de la puissance brute, ce modèle MagGo intègre un véritable écran LCD qui se trouve sur la tranche et affiche le pourcentage exact de batterie restante ainsi que le temps estimé pour une charge complète.
À l’arrière, on retrouve une béquille pliable qui permet de maintenir le smartphone à la verticale ou à l’horizontale pendant la charge. Ce qui en fait un support pour continuer à regarder des vidéos ou garder un œil sur vos notifications, ce qui est pratique si vous utilisez le mode « En veille » d’iOS. Côté connectique, la batterie propose tout de même un port USB-C bidirectionnel qui sert non seulement à recharger la batterie elle-même, mais aussi un appareil en filaire avec une puissance qui peut aller jusqu’à 27 W. Et Anker a intégré la fonction pass-through qui autorise la recharge simultanée de la batterie et du téléphone branché dessus lorsqu’elle est branchée au secteur. Ce qui fait qu’elle peut être utilisée aussi bien par un iPhone qu’un smartphone sous Android, notamment s’il a une coque de protection compatible MagSafe.
Une batterie pratique qui prend un peu de place
L’intégration de la technologie Qi2, de l’écran, de la béquille et d’une grosse capacité de 10 000 mAh ne se fait pas par magie et la physique impose ses limites. Le principal défaut de ce modèle reste son gabarit massif, toutes proportions gardées quand même, puisqu’elle fait 107,3 x 68,8 x 19,8 mm pour 250 grammes. Ce qui en fait un beau bloc et quand elle est accrochée au dos d’un smartphone, elle alourdit considérablement l’appareil et rend son utilisation prolongée à une main moins évidente qu’avec des modèles d’appoint.
Face à cette MagGo 10K, Anker a récemment décliné une version Slim, la référence A1664, beaucoup plus fine (1,47 cm) et légère, mais qui fait l’impasse sur l’écran et la béquille, puisqu’il faut bien faire des compromis. Il faut donc faire un choix selon vos priorités : la finesse du modèle Slim ou la polyvalence et les gadgets avec la MagGo 10K classique. Gardez en tête que la charge sans fil à haute puissance génère toujours un peu de chaleur, même si Anker gère sur ce point avec son système de dissipation thermique ActiveShield qui régule la température en temps réel.

articles.title: Bard Santner wants to turn Zimbabwe’s diaspora remittances into a banking business
articles.text: Bard Santner , a financial services group offering asset management, corporate finance, wealth management, and remittance services, is positioning itself to capture a larger share of Zimbabwe’s $2.45 billion diaspora market . Through its newly licenced deposit-taking microfinance bank, the firm is attempting a structural shift: moving beyond zero-margin transactional transfers into high-yield lending, wealth management, and deposit mobilisation. The strategic core of this expansion is customer lifetime value. Pure-play remittance companies face severe price compression, but by bundling credit and savings onto existing cross-border flows, Bard Santner aims to convert transactional users into long-term banking clients. However, a large remittance corridor does not inherently guarantee adoption by banks, particularly given regulatory moats in South Africa and fierce competition from incumbent digital banks. Bard Santner: From Remittances to Banking The operational backdrop is defined by South Africa’s rapid surge in digital banking. A PwC analysis of major banks showed that digitally active clients rose to 27.6 million in the second half of 2025, up from 21 million in the first half. This shift has altered migrant banking habits, turning cross-border payments into an entry point for broader financial services. Digital challengers like GoTyme Bank, Bank Zero, and Discovery Bank compete aggressively on transaction costs and yields , while remittance incumbents, including Mukuru, Mama Money, and Hello Paisa, maintain deep distribution networks across primary migrant corridors. Bard Santner’s entry relies on bridging these two distinct operational models. This overlap highlights the real battleground: customer retention across borders. The key leverage point for a remittance-first bank is capital efficiency. A customer who regularly sends money to Zimbabwe represents lower customer acquisition costs for credit and savings products, provided the infrastructure can support seamless cross-border clearing. For remittance providers, expanding into deposit-taking is a defensive necessity to combat margin compression. For traditional banks, cross-border integration remains a friction-heavy gap. To succeed, new entrants must offer clear interest differentials or direct credit access tied to historical transfer data. The market’s sheer volume explains the incentive. Formal diaspora remittances reached $1.62 billion in the first seven months of 2026 , up 24% year-on-year, according to data from the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe. Yet gross inflow figures mask a structural problem: capital velocity remains strictly one-directional, with minimal retention in formal savings or investment vehicles. Converting transactional flows into sticky deposits requires overcoming deep-seated distrust of currency and a strong preference for cash. Without compelling multi-currency protections or competitive credit yields, gross remittance volume will remain an unreliable indicator of potential banking assets under management. Bard Santner’s cross-border ambition Operating across Harare, Johannesburg, and New York, Bard Santner leverages its subsidiary, TX Money Transfer, as the primary funnel. Its proposed banking suite—encompassing multi-currency accounts, SME cross-border trade finance, and diaspora-linked credit—aims to monetise both ends of the transfer corridor simultaneously. Competition for South Africa’s large migrant community is intensifying as banks, fintechs and remittance providers seek a bigger share of customers’ everyday financial activity. Image Source: Africa Business Insider. The group’s microfinance banking licence, granted by the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, took effect on October 1, 2026 . While this provides the legal framework to take deposits and issue loans within Zimbabwe, it highlights the geographic limitation of single-jurisdiction licensing in a cross-border market. The central thesis behind the strategy is serving migrants in both their host and origin economies, a positioning that larger regional banks struggle to execute efficiently due to legacy compliance and operating silos. An existing remittance base gives Bard Santner an immediate distribution channel, but conversion metrics will be the real test. Without public data on active transaction users, retention rates, or loan default projections, the size of its immediate total addressable market remains unverified. Regulatory test Building a cross-border banking proposition also means navigating different regulatory systems. Crucially, a Zimbabwean banking licence does not permit deposit-taking or credit underwriting in South Africa under South African Reserve Bank (SARB) regulations. Without local banking partnerships or a specialised license, foreign institutions cannot natively hold South African Rand deposits. This regulatory divide creates a potential bottleneck for a seamless cross-border proposition. Bard Santner must maintain clear operational separation between South African remittance origination and Zimbabwean banking execution, or face significant regulatory exposure under exchange control frameworks. It must also compete on measurable factors, including transfer fees, exchange rates, processing times and service reliability. Differences in fees and exchange rates can affect how much recipients receive, making transparent pricing important to customers sending money home. Savings and lending introduce further requirements around capital, credit assessment, affordability and consumer protection. Multi-currency products also require clarity about exchange-rate exposure and the terms governing access to funds. The key indicators to watch will be customer acquisition costs, net interest margins on multi-currency loans, capital adequacy ratios, and the formal structure of its South African partnership model. Demonstrating sustainable credit performance in a volatile macroeconomic environment will determine whether the bank can scale. Zimbabwe’s diaspora remittances provide a substantial market, but the commercial opportunity lies in building broader financial relationships around those flows. Bard Santner’s challenge is to give customers clear reasons to use its services beyond sending money home, while competing with established providers and meeting the regulatory demands of operating across borders. True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Microsoft Previews dotnetup: Toolchain Manager for .NET SDKs and Runtimes
articles.text:
Microsoft has released a public preview of dotnetup, a cross-platform toolchain manager that installs, updates, and removes .NET SDKs and runtimes inside the user's account rather than a system-managed directory. As reported on the .NET Blog, the tool was announced on October 15 by Chet Husk, program manager for the .NET SDK, and follows the model of rustup and nvm.
According to the documentation, commands and behavior may change between preview releases, and production machines should keep using the installers, package managers, or Visual Studio.
The design, as described in the announcement, tracks intent instead of versions. A developer asks for a channel such as latest, lts, preview, daily, a major like 10, a minor like 10.0, or a feature band like 10.0.1xx, and dotnetup resolves it to a release. Exact versions, as the post notes, stay pinned during updates.
Several requirements can share one managed installation, and the tool reads the nearest global.json so team builds stay deterministic. Furthermore, according to the docs, files live under the user's local data directory on Windows, macOS, and Linux, and dotnetup never writes to Program Files\dotnet or /usr/share/dotnet.
Installation uses a bootstrap script fetched from aka.ms with curl or irm. As described in the docs, it places the binary in ~/.dotnetup after checking its SHA-512 checksum, and dotnetup init then installs the latest stable SDK and configures the shell. The docs list three access modes: none runs .NET through dotnetup dotnet without touching the environment, shell edits the shell profile, and everywhere, the Windows-only default, changes the system PATH and needs elevation.
The docs also warn that everywhere mode takes precedence over machine-wide copies, including the one Visual Studio installs, so projects needing an SDK dotnetup has not installed fail to build. To avoid that, setup reportedly offers to migrate existing machine-wide installs.
As reported, monthly servicing becomes a single dotnetup update, which re-resolves every tracked channel and installs the newest matching versions. Individual runtimes can be targeted, for example dotnetup runtime install aspnetcore@10.0, and the docs list the SDK, .NET runtime, ASP.NET Core runtime, and Windows Desktop runtime as supported components. After an update, as stated in the post, dotnetup removes any component no remaining requirement needs, and sdk uninstall or runtime uninstall trigger the same cleanup.
Moreover, preview and daily builds install side by side through dotnetup sdk install preview or dotnetup runtime install daily, although the docs note that daily builds are not code-signed. dotnetup self update refreshes the tool itself. Over the dotnet-install scripts, the post claims tracking of installed components, signature and checksum validation, faster multi-version installs, and one CLI surface on every platform. The stated roadmap includes admin-level installs on Windows, replacing the script-based parts of the GitHub Actions and Azure DevOps tasks, and agent skills so AI assistants reach for the tool by default.
Meanwhile, on r/dotnet, one developer with months of use praised the simpler Linux setup, but the top comment asked why anyone would pick dotnetup over mise, which several already use.
Others criticized the curl-to-shell bootstrap, asked for winget, apt, or Homebrew packages, noted that Visual Studio does not see dotnetup installs, and wanted dotnet-ef and other CLI tools managed too. In reply on the blog, Husk stated that packages are planned after user validation.
For interested readers, full documentation, including the command reference and telemetry details, is available on Microsoft Learn, and feedback goes to the dotnetup category of the dotnet/sdk GitHub discussions.

articles.title: Revolut victime d'une panne majeure : les paiements touchés, la banque réagit
articles.text:
« Nous pouvons confirmer que tout l’argent et les données de nos clients sont en sécurité » : Revolut a posté un message sur le réseau social X, alors qu’un nombre conséquent de ses clients européens n’arrive plus à utiliser ses services. Que ce soit les paiements par carte ou l’accès à l’application, Revolut semble être à l’arrêt. L’origine de la panne se situe au niveau de l’un de ses prestataires.
Revolut victime d’une panne majeure
Depuis environ 8 heures du matin, la néobanque Revolut est victime d’une panne majeure. Un nombre conséquent de ses clients ne parviennent pas à payer par carte et à accéder à l’application. Le problème touche plusieurs pays européens, dont la France. Sur sa page de suivi de l’état du système, Revolut signale une panne touchant l’ensemble de ses 31 services surveillés.
L’origine de la panne se situe au niveau de Google Cloud, c’est-à-dire l’un de ses prestataires. Selon Sky News, Google Cloud a signalé des « problèmes » dans sa région Europe de l’Ouest affectant des dizaines de sites web, dont Revolut, Royal Mail et HSBC. Il ne s’agit donc pas d’une cyberattaque visant Revolut.
Revolut réagit
Sur le réseau social X, Revolut explique : « Nous rencontrons actuellement une interruption de service affectant plusieurs services. Nous pouvons confirmer que tout l’argent et les données de nos clients sont en sécurité. Nous travaillons à résoudre le problème depuis qu’il a été identifié ce matin et nous présentons nos excuses à toute personne touchée ainsi que pour tout désagrément causé ».
Un porte-parole de la néo banque a quant à lui confirmé l’origine de la panne : « Nous rencontrons actuellement des perturbations affectant plusieurs de nos services à la suite d’une panne survenue chez Google Cloud. Nous pouvons confirmer que les fonds et les données de tous nos clients sont en sécurité. Depuis que le problème a été identifié ce matin, nos équipes sont mobilisées pour rétablir la situation. Nous présentons nos excuses à nos clients pour la gêne occasionnée ».
Revolut semble donc en mesure d’affirmer que l’argent de ses clients et leurs données confidentielles sont en sécurité. En tout cas, bon nombre de clients Revolut ont été dans l’incapacité d’effectuer des paiements, physiques ou en ligne. En ce 21 octobre 2026, le problème semble néanmoins avoir été réglé en grande partie.

articles.title: Subaru : c'est terminé, la marque ne vendra plus aucune voiture essence en Europe dès 2028, place au 100 % électrique
articles.text:
Subaru : c'est terminé, la marque ne vendra plus aucune voiture essence en Europe dès 2028, place au 100 % électrique
Le moteur à plat qui a mené Subaru aux titres mondiaux des rallyes vit ses derniers mois sur le Vieux Continent. D'ici fin 2027, la marque n'y proposera plus que trois SUV électriques conçus avec Toyota. Et la France a pris ce virage avant tout le monde.
Le 16 octobre 2026, Subaru Deutschland a confirmé l'information au magazine auto motor und sport. Le constructeur japonais arrêtera de vendre des voitures thermiques neuves en Europe au plus tard fin 2027. La lignée née en 1966 avec la Subaru 1000, premier modèle de la marque à moteur boxer, s'éteint donc sur le continent. Dès 2028, le catalogue européen se limitera aux Solterra, Uncharted et E-Outback, cousins des Toyota bZ4X, C-HR+ et bZ4X Touring.
Outback, Forester, Crosstrek : le calendrier de sortie du boxer
L'Outback part le premier : son 2,5 litres atmosphérique de 169 ch quitte les catalogues avant la fin de l'année. Impreza, Crosstrek et Forester suivront au fil de 2027, avec leur 2 litres e-Boxer microhybride de 136 ch. Leur production pour l'Europe est déjà arrêtée, et les concessionnaires écoulent les derniers stocks.
Subaru met en cause les plafonds de CO2 que Bruxelles impose aux flottes des constructeurs. Il cite aussi la liste croissante des aides à la conduite et des équipements de sécurité obligatoires. Pour une marque de niche, chaque homologation coûte très cher. Le boxer hybride complet de 197 ch, vendu sur les Crosstrek et Forester américains, ne fait l'objet d'aucun projet concret pour l'Europe.
Le revirement est brutal. En juillet 2025, Subaru Europe présentait encore ses trois électriques comme un complément à la gamme thermique.
En France, Subaru vend déjà uniquement des voitures électriques
Pour les automobilistes français, le décor reste le même. Après cinq années de quasi-absence, la marque est revenue en 2026 avec Emil Frey France et une gamme exclusivement électrique. Le Solterra démarre à 48 990 €, l'Uncharted à 36 990 €, et l'E-Outback a rejoint le réseau en juin. La fiscalité française avait déjà eu raison du boxer. Pierre Guignot, président de Subaru France, vise 550 immatriculations cette année.
	
Nous allons étoffer notre offre avec d'autres modèles 100 % électriques en 2027 et 2028, issus de la toute dernière génération technologique.
En Suisse, la demande progresse. D'après Blick, le Solterra et l'Uncharted cumulent 277 immatriculations depuis janvier, contre 327 pour le seul Crosstrek. Subaru prépare aussi son émancipation. Sa première plateforme électrique maison, avec des batteries Panasonic et des moteurs Aisin, doit arriver vers 2029.

articles.title: How to review AI code without reading the code
articles.text:
How to review AI code without reading the code
The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.
Faros AI’s new report shows a 76.3% increase in pull requests merged without review since their last report in April. Many companies now run AI reviews on 50% to 80% of their PRs. AI review took over bug-finding. But it didn’t take over the conversation where a team debates what it decided and why, and that is the part I missed too.
The part AI review doesn’t solve
Most teams are stuck in one of two modes. They review every line and become the bottleneck, or they rubber-stamp and lose track of what changed and why. There is no middle ground yet.
“The argument over whether engineers should stop reading code is over, because we already have.”
AI review is good at the mechanical half of the job. It never gets tired, it reads every line, and it holds the same standard on every PR. But it never saw what was decided. It won’t tell you not to build something, and it can’t be accountable for the result. A better model won’t fix that, because the tool reads the wrong artifact at the wrong time.
As I wrote in “Kill the code review theater, keep the review,” code review is how a team builds a mental model of its system. That has been the only scheduled moment for engineers to talk to each other about that system. Teams that hand code reviews to AI tools rarely notice they’ve also given up that moment.
I didn’t notice either. The five layers of trust I proposed in March for replacing code review all checked the code. Four asked, “Is it right?” One asked, “Is that what we meant?” None asked, “Are we building the right thing?”
Debating decisions replaces reading the code
A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way: a token bucket or a sliding window, fail open or fail closed, one limit for every customer or one each. An AI-written PR is full of them, and almost none of them show up in the diff.
My new framework for the review bottleneck also has five layers.
- Challenge. Before the PR exists, a second agent on a different model pushes back on the coding agent’s approach. The output records what was proposed, what was rejected and why, and which agent gave ground. Settled points stay on the record too, because two agents can also agree to look the other way.
- Capture. The intent (why we’re making the change) and the acceptance criteria (how it should behave) get captured from coding with the agent and go onto the PR. You need both: intent without criteria can’t be checked, and criteria without intent can’t be judged.
- Codify. Review comments your team keeps repeating, like “use the Money type, not float,” go into an AI slop registry, and become invariants, standing rules checked on every change.
- Debate. People discuss the decisions the agents surfaced and couldn’t settle, and leave the line-by-line checking to the machines. It’s the only layer that asks whether we’re building the right thing.
- Own. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so a named team owns the invariants and the mental model behind them, and signs off on the change.
The first three are work for machines, and tools for them exist today. Debate and Own are work for people, and Debate is the layer that was missing.
“The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide.”
The principle we designed around is simple: agents verify, people decide. People are better at judging whether a change is right, weighing trade-offs and risks, and owning the decision. Invariants are rules for agents. Decisions are judgment calls for people, and the calls that keep coming back become rules.
Debate also ends the argument over whether engineers should read AI-generated code.
I recently spoke to Robert ‘Uncle Bob’ Martin, the author of “Clean Code,” who recently said that he doesn’t read the code anymore. But he did say that humans should take responsibility for the systems, just above the code. Decisions sit at that level.
A reviewer who has debated the decisions doesn’t have to read code line by line to explain a change.
Should we just review specs?
The obvious objection is that this just moves the reading somewhere else, and at some point that place was specs. My issue with reviewing specs is that it seems backward. A spec takes time to write, gets written before the work teaches you anything, and drifts the moment implementation starts.
Decisions come out of the work itself. They are generated live, they are short, and each one exists because the change could have gone another way. That is also why Capture pulls the intent and acceptance criteria out of the coding session after the work, instead of asking anyone to write them up front.
How I see decision review working
Here is how I see it working, based on what we’ve been building at Aviator.
Where decisions come from
Most decisions already happen on the author’s machine, and today we throw them away.
- A capture skill pulls intent, acceptance criteria, and decisions out of the coding agent session. Every time the agent stops to ask and the engineer makes a call, it records that call.
- A review skill runs an adversarial review agent that argues with the coding agent before the PR is submitted. It records what they disagreed about and how they settled it. What they couldn’t settle is what the team debates.
What a decision looks like
This example uses a PR that adds a per-installation rate limit to webhook ingest.
The intent is one sentence: throttle webhook bursts per GitHub installation so one noisy customer can’t starve the broker, without dropping events or breaking their order.
The PR carries six decisions. The one still open is a product call, not a code one: the burst limit is one value for every customer. Two are accepted risks: a Redis outage fails open, and deferred events hold their payload in the broker. Exposing limiter metrics on the on-prem Grafana board became a follow-up with a linked ticket. The other two were argued out between the author, the reviewer, and the agents and settled.
Take one of the settled ones, “token bucket, not a sliding window.” The author’s agent explains it in the thread: one Lua call per event instead of a sorted-set scan, chosen after profiling a replay of a webhook storm. A reviewer who disagrees can push back in the same thread or ask the agent directly.
None of that is visible in the diff.
What the reviewer does
The reviewer’s part comes down to three steps:
- Read the intent and what’s changing.
- Go through the decisions and argue where you disagree.
- Check what isn’t passing, then approve.
That is enough to understand the change, build a mental model, and argue about what matters, without reading line by line.
Each decision is its own thread, with humans and agents labeled separately, so you know who made which call. A reviewer can agree, challenge, override, or turn a decision into a tracked follow-up. The code is still there. You open it where a decision sends you, and comments on the code join the same record.
What happens after the merge
The decisions outlive the review.
- Your team’s week. You see the key decisions made in your part of the codebase over the last day or week, without reading the PRs. That is what knowledge-sharing code review was always for.
- Memory for agents. Coding and review agents pull past decisions for the code they touch, so they don’t re-argue settled trade-offs.
- Follow-ups that stick. “Do it later” becomes a linked ticket, not a line in a PR description nobody reads again.
- Rules from patterns. When a decision keeps recurring, propose it as an invariant; it becomes a rule only after someone approves it.
Someone still has to sign. A model has no reputation and can’t be asked why, so every debated decision ends with a named person who agreed to it. That is where Debate hands off to the last layer, Own.
“If AI already reviews most of your PRs, try one question on your team: what did we decide last week, and who agreed to it?”

articles.title: Fuse Energy bets on NVIDIA GPUs as it expands from energy supply into AI infrastructure | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Fuse Energy, a British energy company, has opened reservations for Fuse Compute, its first commercial AI product, offering access to NVIDIA GPUs in UK data centres powered by Fuse – marking a new step into AI infrastructure by the EnergyTech startup.
Interested parties can register interest and reserve capacity today, with the first GPUs slated to come online in December 2026. The ambition here is to own the full AI stack: power, land, data centres and AI compute.
“Power is the biggest hurdle to building AI infrastructure, and it’s the part we already know how to do,” says Alan Chang, CEO and co-founder of Fuse Energy. “Every AI company is fighting for the same scarce GPUs, and the grid can’t connect data centres fast enough to keep up. Fuse Compute puts that expertise to work for the companies building the future of intelligence, and makes sure that future is built in Britain.”
This is an interesting new direction for an energy company whose focus is simplyfying gas and electricity management. Fuse has raised €178 million ($199 million) since its founding in 2022.
Our earlier coverage traces Fuse’s expansion from supplying 50,000 UK homes in July 2025, when it reported €76 million in annualised revenue and raised €8.5 million, to more than 200,000 households and €341 million in annual recurring revenue by December, when it secured another €59 million.
By June 2026, Fuse was supplying more than 300,000 households and had closed a €25 million Series B extension, while reporting monthly EBITDA profitability since December 2025.
Its expansion into AI compute comes amid significant funding for companies developing the underlying infrastructure. In the UK, Nscale raised €1.7 billion for vertically integrated AI compute, Volta reportedly secured €259.8 million across two rounds to develop AI factories, and Orbital Industries raised €43 million for industrial hardware including data-centre technologies.
Elsewhere, Finland’s Verda raised €164.8 million for AI cloud expansion and Spain’s iPronics secured €107.6 million for optical networking. These 2026 infrastructure financing announcements totalled approximately €2.4 billion, excluding Fuse’s historical funding.
The company says that AI is creating more demand for compute than the UK can supply. The UK Government’s Compute Roadmap estimates the country will need at least 6GW of AI-capable data centre capacity by 2030, yet new data centres face waits of up to a decade for a grid connection.
Power has become the main constraint on how quickly that capacity can be built. The Government aims to expand the UK’s public compute capacity 20x by 2030, but the country has few home-grown providers of large-scale compute, leaving many British AI companies reliant on capacity hosted overseas.
Fuse’s move into compute builds on its experience in power. Its most recent solar site was built at around 30% below the industry average cost per megawatt. It holds a power generation pipeline of more than 1GW and a data centre connection pipeline of 142MW across 15 projects. This will allow it to energise and construct high-density AI sites quickly and cheaply.
Fuse Compute will offer bare-metal, single-tenant NVIDIA GPU nodes in UK data centres, with UK jurisdiction and a UK data path. The first 128 NVIDIA B300 GPUs are due to come online in December 2026, followed by 1,024 in Q2 2027, a further 22MW in Q4 2027 and 116MW from 2028.
In energy, Fuse already supplies 470,000 UK homes and holds both supplier and meter operator licences.
On the supply side, Fuse owns and operates low carbon generation assets, with 22 MW active and over 1 GW in the pipeline across the UK, US, and Europe.
For the company, keeping compute onshore means that the data will stay under UK jurisdiction, and that British AI companies will no longer need to rely on overseas capacity.
Fuse’s near-term data centre projects will also reportedly bring 250 construction and operational jobs to the UK, and represent €1.1 billion (£1 billion) of investment in UK infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine’s drone rescue of wounded soldier puts much touted idea into practice
articles.text:
Ukraine’s unprecedented drone rescue of a wounded soldier from the battlefield has shown once again how battlefield necessity can spur innovation. The operation was revealed just days after separate Ukrainian drones designed for casualty evacuation were deployed for frontline testing—taking a step beyond the US military’s decades of experimentation with similar concepts.
The drone evacuation of the injured soldier took place at an undisclosed time and place on the frontline where the presence of Russian drones and landmines made it impractical to send in a wheeled ground robot, according to The Kyiv Independent. On October 19, Ukraine’s Army shared a video of the drone evacuation, showing the wounded soldier securing himself in a harness suspended beneath a heavy hexacopter drone with six rotors before being flown to safety.
“This is a historic event, the next stage of evacuating the wounded, which we will all come to,” said Napalm, a programmer of the 92nd separate assault brigade’s unmanned ground systems company, who went by his callsign per Ukrainian military practice, in a statement. “Now the serious systematic work begins, so that such missions are carried out constantly.”
Flying out the wounded
To perform the improvised aerial evacuation, the 92nd brigade prepared and tested a heavy hexacopter drone—the Heavy Shot AYUDAG 6 model—provided for free by the Ukrainian manufacturer Gurzuf Defence. Special carabiners were first delivered to the wounded soldier so he could attach himself to the drone that was equipped with a winch, according to a blog post by Gurzuf Defence.
The wounded soldier, who serves with Ukraine’s 30th separate mechanized brigade, had already spent nearly 500 days at a frontline position while under threat of Russian fire, according to Gurzuf Defence. Like many soldiers at frontline positions, he had been relying on friendly drone deliveries for ammunition and other supplies.
The drone evacuation flight took 1 hour and 14 minutes from start to finish while covering a distance of nearly 39 miles (62 kilometers). This particular hexacopter can reportedly carry up to 200 pounds (90 kilograms).

articles.title: Google Cloud and NVIDIA Announce General Availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin Infrastructure
articles.text:
General availability of the instances is coming next month, with planned expansion of availability to Europe — bringing an integrated platform for training, inference and large-scale reinforcement learning to cloud customers.
A5X instances bring together NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72, NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNICs, Google Cloud Virgo Network and Google Cloud’s fourth-generation advanced liquid-cooling technology for demanding agentic inference and reinforcement learning workloads at scale. Google Cloud plans to scale its Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to as many as 960,000 Rubin GPUs across multiple sites.
Ineffable Intelligence, a London-based technology company founded by AlphaGo creator David Silver, was the first customer to access A5X. Ineffable is using the platform to advance large-scale reinforcement learning and shape “superlearner” systems that learn continuously from experience.
Learning through interaction requires a continuous cycle of generating experience, evaluating outcomes and updating models, requiring infrastructure that can support the entire process at scale. A5X brings Vera Rubin into Google Cloud’s AI Hypercomputer as an integrated system, combining compute, networking and storage to support experience-driven learning at scale.
“We’re building superlearners that continually improve through their own experience,” said David Silver, founder and CEO of Ineffable Intelligence. “That demands both substantial compute and a tight connection between generating experience and training on it, so each improvement in the agent can quickly shape its next experience. Vera Rubin’s combination of compute performance and high-bandwidth connectivity, between the Vera CPU and Rubin GPUs and between the Rubin GPUs within the rack, allow us to push the scale and ambition of our reinforcement learning research further.”
WPP, a London-based marketing and communications company, has also demonstrated its creative agent reference architecture on NVIDIA Vera Rubin-based A5X instances using NVIDIA Nemotron models and NVIDIA OpenShell, part of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for safe AI agents.
The agents turn conversational requests into multistep creative workflows, such as video generation, upscaling and restyling, with human approval before execution. OpenShell provides governed sandboxes for agent execution, helping control access to sensitive brand assets and creative tools. In WPP’s initial tests, workloads that typically required a multi-node cluster ran on a single A5X instance.
As organizations deploy agentic systems, they need to protect the proprietary models and sensitive data that power these systems — even when running on infrastructure they don’t own.
Google Cloud will be among the first cloud providers to offer NVIDIA Confidential Computing at rack scale on bare metal instances such as A4X Max instances powered by NVIDIA GB300 NVL72. Additionally, Google Cloud is making Confidential Computing generally available on G4 VMs powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, offering a flexible platform for confidential inference and fine-tuning. Customers including Vertebrae, Polaris Cloud and Confidential Core AI are using Confidential G4 for conversational privacy, verifiable agent execution and policy-governed enterprise intelligence.
To support energy-efficient deployment at scale, Google Cloud and NVIDIA are exploring NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS capabilities for Vera Rubin-based infrastructure to help optimize performance per watt and expand capacity within available data-center power budgets.

articles.title: Browsers Block eMudhra Intermediate CAs Over Recoverable Private Keys
articles.text:
The private keys associated with eight intermediate certificates issued by Indian certificate authority (CA) eMudhra have been compromised, and root programs and trust stores have started blocking them.
The certificates were issued in April 2025, and some of the compromised keys could allow attackers to generate fraudulent certificates and impersonate any website.
On October 17, Mozilla and Google blocked the certificates in Firefox and Chrome. Apple and Microsoft blocked them on October 19 and October 20, respectively. Sectigo took revocation steps too, and Cloudflare patched its services.
eMudhra revoked the compromised certificates, and the issue was communicated to downstream trust stores.
“The private keys for these certificates were generated with insufficient randomness (i.e., weak cryptographic entropy), enabling anyone to forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not yet removed trust in those CAs,” Google explains.
Although the certificates have been blocked and revoked, some clients may require software updates to ensure that the compromised intermediates are no longer trusted.
Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has published a tool to check whether clients still trust the compromised certificates. He also explains that the private keys were incorrectly generated and could be retrieved from the certificates.
In fact, Jackson warned that several individuals have independently retrieved the keys, as the process is fairly easy and fast.
“The private keys are effectively all-zeroes apart from the last byte. They can be recovered near instantly via the baby-step giant-step discrete log algorithm,” Jackson said.
There appears to be no evidence in Certificate Transparency (CT) logs that the keys were used maliciously before revocation, but not all clients enforce CT, and threat actors may have used them to impersonate those clients.
According to eMudhra, a flaw in the script used during the key generation ceremony created a second, weaker key pair, which was mistakenly used to create the certificate signing requests because its labels were similar to those of the original keys.
“Some additional context – these issuers created were meant for export to our US and European data centers to solve data sovereignty issues for some of our customers (but never ended up operationally in production except for one),” the CA said.
“There were human errors in multiple steps of the process that resulted in significant flaws in the key lifecycle integrity process for this KGC. We are now digging deeper for code flaws, process gaps, and maker/checker controls specific to this issue. Over the next week, we will reverify every key ceremony we have done,” eMudhra added.

articles.title: Ce télescope découvre une comète inconnue, alors que ce n'est pas du tout sa mission
articles.text:
Au moment de partir dans l’espace en juillet 2023, la feuille de route d’Euclid était particulièrement chargée. Le télescope mis en orbite par l’Agence spatiale européenne (ESA) devait retracer l’histoire de l’expansion de l’Univers, identifier des galaxies extrêmement lointaines pour mieux comprendre le Big Bang, percer les secrets de la matière noire et de l’énergie noire et mettre à l’épreuve la relativité générale à l’échelle du cosmos et le modèle standard de la cosmologie, rien que ça !
Autant dire que ce qui se passe dans le Système solaire ne présente pas un intérêt particulier pour ce télescope qui vise beaucoup plus loin. L’ESA a pourtant annoncé, ce lundi 19 octobre, qu’Euclid avait découvert sa première comète. Le télescope en avait déjà photographié, mais toutes étaient déjà connues. Baptisée C/2026 S1 (Euclid), elle a été aperçue lors d’une série d’observations qui ont eu lieu entre le 16 et le 24 septembre.
Un télescope fait pour ne pas trouver de comètes
Repérer des objets proches qui se déplacent vite ne fait pas partie des missions d’Euclid. Euclid évite même délibérément la bande du ciel qui suit le plan du Système solaire, là où se concentrent astéroïdes et comètes, car la lumière renvoyée par leur poussière gênerait ses images du ciel profond. Cette comète a en plus été repérée alors qu’elle était encore loin du Soleil, donc peu brillante. Enfin, Euclid ne photographie en général chaque portion du ciel qu’une seule fois. Il ne peut donc pas y revenir à la demande pour confirmer la nature d’un objet.
La découverte revient à Mikko Pöntinen, doctorant à l’Université d’Helsinki, et au groupe de travail du consortium Euclid consacré aux objets du Système solaire. Il a passé les images d’Euclid dans un logiciel qu’il a lui-même conçu pour repérer les objets rapides comme des comètes ou des astéroïdes. C’est là qu’ils ont trouvé cet astre entouré d’un halo luminescent et qu’on ne trouvait dans aucun catalogue d’objets connus. Il a alors transmis ses observations au Minor Planet Center, l’organisme de l’Union astronomique internationale qui recense comètes et astéroïdes. L’alerte a permis à des astronomes au sol de suivre l’objet, et le Minor Planet Center a confirmé le 8 octobre qu’il s’agissait d’une comète inconnue.
Un heureux hasard prometteur
C/2026 S1 (Euclid) se trouve à environ 1,3 milliard de kilomètres de la Terre, soit à peu près la distance qui sépare le Soleil de la zone comprise entre les orbites de Jupiter et de Saturne. Elle ne se trouve pas pour autant dans le plan où tournent les planètes. Vue depuis le Soleil, elle passe « au-dessus » de ce plan, sur une orbite qu’elle met des milliers d’années à parcourir.
La comète n’a été trouvée que grâce à une suite de coïncidences : sa trajectoire l’a menée devant l’objectif d’Euclid pile au moment où il photographiait cette partie du ciel, plusieurs jours de suite.
« Très peu de comètes devraient être découvertes par Euclid », reconnaît Bruno Altieri, scientifique chargé des archives d’Euclid et membre de l’équipe de découverte.
Cette découverte a quand même servi de répétition. « Cette comète n’est pas une candidate adaptée pour Comet Interceptor, mais le processus de découverte et d’alerte nous donne un vrai cas test », explique Valeria Pettorino, responsable scientifique d’Euclid.
Cette coordination servira à la mission Comet Interceptor. Son lancement est prévu en 2029, et ses trois sondes devront aller à la rencontre d’une comète qui ne s’est jamais approchée du Soleil. Sauf si une cible est repérée avant le lancement, les sondes attendront au point de Lagrange L2, à 1,5 million de kilomètres de la Terre, qu’une comète adaptée soit découverte. Plus elle sera repérée tôt, loin du Soleil, plus la mission aura le temps de la rejoindre. Euclid vient de montrer qu’il peut faire ce type de détection précoce.

articles.title: YouTube quiere ponértelo más difícil para dar 'No me gusta' a un vídeo
articles.text:
Ponerle No me gusta a un vídeo en YouTube estaría por volverse algo más complicado. La plataforma de Google ha comenzado a probar cambios en su interfaz que esconden el botón del pulgar abajo, obligando a los usuarios a completar un paso extra para usarlo.
En primera instancia puede no parecer algo demasiado relevante, pero la historia es bastante diferente. Después de todo, YouTube lleva algunos años experimentando con el No me gusta con cambios que no han sido del agrado de la mayoría de los usuarios.
Según ha publicado TheBobPony en X (Twitter), YouTube está probando mover el botón de No me gusta al menú de tres puntos que aparece en cada vídeo. De esta manera, el citado control ya no es visible junto con las opciones de dar like, compartir, guardar o preguntar a Gemini, sino que queda oculta en segundo plano.
Desde YouTube no se han pronunciado en público respecto de este experimento. Tampoco se sabe qué tan amplia es el test que se está realizando, aunque es bastante común que Google realice pruebas limitadas a un número reducido de usuarios. De allí a que se concreten en el producto final, es una historia diferente.
No obstante, no deja de llamar la atención el empecinamiento de YouTube con cambiar el modo de usar el No me gusta. Tengamos en cuenta que la compañía ya había modificado la forma de mostrar el uso de dicha reacción hacia el público general, y a finales del año pasado optó por quitarlo definitivamente de los Shorts.
YouTube podría ocultar el botón de No me gusta en todos los vídeos
Como ya indicamos, no es la primera vez que YouTube experimenta con el botón No me gusta. La compañía quedó envuelta en una polémica en 2021 cuando optó por dejar de mostrar públicamente el conteo de pulgares abajo en un vídeo. Según la explicación oficial, el objetivo detrás de esa decisión fue para evitar el mal uso de la característica, especialmente en campañas de review bombing.
La determinación se dio en un momento clave, cuando el mundo poco a poco regresaba a la normalidad tras el tramo más duro de la pandemia de COVID-19. Por entonces, la explosión en la creación y el consumo de contenidos disparó la popularidad de gran cantidad de creadores, pero también llevó al rápido desaliento de muchos que, con razón o no, veían que el conteo de No me gusta en sus vídeos era más alto que el de Me gusta.
YouTube habló por entonces de velar por el bienestar de los creadores más pequeños y de evitar que campañas de calificaciones injustas terminen sesgando la recepción del público general. A finales del año pasado, en tanto, quitó el No me gusta de los Shorts, como parte de la adopción de un sistema de corazones como el de TikTok e Instagram.
Ya veremos qué sucede con esta cuestión, pero es difícil pensar que ocultar el No me gusta pueda tener una utilidad real. A no ser que YouTube tenga datos muy concluyentes de que el botón se está usando mal o con fines pura y exclusivamente dañinos, es curioso que la compañía se tome la molestia de quitarlo u ocultarlo de su UI.

articles.title: Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
articles.text:
Intel asks FCC for waiver to buy foreign robots — chipmaker’s automated guided vehicles could run afoul of agency’s sweeping robot ban
These robots move chips between tools and sections of the fab.
Intel has asked the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to make an exception for the automated guided vehicles (AGVs) that the company uses to transport the sensitive silicon wafers and other materials, containers, and supplies needed to make the most advanced chips in its fabs. According to Bloomberg, the American chipmaker fears that its AGVs would fall under the blanket prohibition against foreign-made robots after they were added to the FCC’s Covered List.
AGVs are niche machines that chip fabs use to transport materials and supplies between tools and sections of the fab, helping ensure that the cleanroom conditions required for each manufacturing process are maintained. This makes them critical equipment for U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, but, apparently, there are no suitable domestic alternatives for these devices at the moment. Intel’s current fleet of AGVs requires continuous maintenance, including software and firmware updates, and if it’s forced to find a local supplier for its AGVs, the company says that it would take years, crippling the United States’ chipmaking efforts.
The biggest AGV suppliers are Japanese companies like Murata Machinery and Daifuku Co., while a few smaller businesses from South Korea and Taiwan are also trying to break into the market. It’s unclear why these companies haven’t applied for a conditional approval yet, which would allow them to continue selling these products in the U.S. while also promising Washington that they’ll set up a manufacturing base in the country. This is something that Netgear has already done, allowing it to continue selling its foreign-made routers despite being an American company.
Intel says that it remains unclear if updates to its AGVs would break compliance with the FCC, and that it’s asking the agency to issue a conditional waiver “out of an abundance of caution to ensure the ongoing operation of these specific AGV units.” While Team Blue is the only company concerned about AGVs at the moment, other chip manufacturers would likely need a similar waiver in the near future, especially as they build more fabs in the U.S. This includes TSMC, which is planning to build 12 more fabs and four packaging facilities in Arizona, Samsung, with its new Taylor, Texas, fab, and even Elon Musk’s Terafab, which has already begun construction.
Washington has been using the FCC to force companies to invest in American manufacturing. Its blanket bans on foreign-made products like drones and routers have affected some of the biggest brands in the U.S., including DJI and TP-Link. While these bans do not outright ban the sale of all products made by these companies, especially those that have already been approved before, they make it impossible for them to introduce new products and even release software updates to their existing product line. The FCC eventually walked back on the software update ban, but they still would not be able to register new products unless they build them in the U.S.

articles.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.
Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time.
The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat.
The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations. Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.
OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting.
Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.
With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.
OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.
Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings.
Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users.

articles.title: The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
articles.text:
The Download: introducing the Impossible issue
Plus: Elon Musk reportedly ordered the recent Starlink slowdown in Ukraine.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Introducing: the Impossible issue
We wanted our last print edition of 2026 to include a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s fun to dream about living on other planets or uploading our brains. But also because scientists and engineers who won’t give up on daring endeavors remind us what technology is supposed to do: make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful.
That’s the ambition behind the stories in our new Impossible issue. We explore bold attempts to make synthetic blood, build cities on the moon, and attain cognitive immortality. We investigate AI’s ability to say no, a bionic eye that can restore sight, and high hopes for blended meat. Plus, we check in on six technologies that have been “coming soon” for years.
This issue is for the folks with the audacity to try, and refuse to let anyone—themselves included— tell them no. We hope you enjoy the ride.
Subscribe now to read the full print issue.
Astrolab’s upcoming rover will run the first LLMs on the moon
Large language models are set to go lunar. A computer capable of running AI software is one of the payloads aboard Astrolab’s FLIP lunar rover, which is slated to head to the moon as early as next month.
The mission will test whether LLMs can enable greater autonomy and real-time intelligent decision-making in the extreme lunar environment. But the moon will present formidable challenges, from extreme temperatures to intense cosmic radiation.
Find out how the lunar rover could change the future of space exploration.
—Tereza Pultarova
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
In Alaska’s Denali National Park, a 2013 lightning fire burned nearly 35,000 acres, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves permafrost. It’s given scientists a rare opportunity to study how fires reshape permafrost and carbon storage over time.
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects. As warming temperatures fuel fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires and permafrost loss. Their observations are revealing worrisome signs about what lies ahead.
Discover what their fieldwork is revealing about a cascading climate disaster.
—James Temple
MIT Technology Review Narrated: the explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the industry on its head.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.
MIT Technology Review spoke to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He explained what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

They’ve formed special committees to discuss a deal. (BBC)
+ Elon Musk, the CEO of both companies, said it’s “a good idea.” (Axios)

The UN says the 1.5°C climate target is now out of reach. (Nature)

+ Climate tech companies offer rays of hope. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Ukraine says it’s carried out the world’s first drone evacuation
A heavy hexacopter flew a soldier to safety. (Ars Technica)

Quote of the day

—GPT-6 Astra, an OpenAI coding agent, tells its user it hasn’t disabled a safeguard after doing exactly that, the company reveals in a new misalignment report.

This giant microwave may change the future of war
US armed forces are hunting for a weapon that disables drones en masse—and they want it fast.
One solution focuses on microwaves: high-powered electronic devices that push out kilowatts of power to zap the circuits of a drone as if it were the tinfoil you forgot to take off your leftovers when you heated them up.
Defense tech startup Epirus may have the winning formula. The company has developed a cutting-edge, cost-efficient drone zapper that’s sparking the interest of the US military—and drones are just one of its targets. Peer into its crosshairs.

articles.title: So hat es sich angefühlt, im Jahr 2026 nochmal mit Windows 7 zu arbeiten
articles.text:
Vier Dinge, die Windows 7 bis heute besser löst als Windows 11
Es begab sich also, dass ich im Jahr 2026 für einige Zeit wieder Windows 7 genutzt habe, um damit zu arbeiten. Grund dafür war ein alter Laptop, den ich mir auf Ebay für wenig Geld ersteigert habe, um damit weniger abgelenkt arbeiten zu können. Wie genau das abgelaufen ist, könnt ihr hier nachlesen. Auf diesem Laptop war noch Windows 7 installiert.
Also dachte ich mir: Wieso nicht schauen, wie sich dieses Betriebssystem aus dem Jahr 2009 heute anfühlt. Dabei ging es mir aber nicht darum, wie performant Windows 7 heute noch ist. Denn natürlich laufen viele moderne Programme nicht mehr auf diesem OS. Aber gibt es Features oder grundlegende Strukturen, die anders als heute sind – und vielleicht sogar besser?
Dabei sind mir vor allem vier Dinge aufgefallen, die in Windows 7 meiner Meinung nach noch deutlich angenehmer waren, als es heute bei Windows 11 der Fall ist.
Windows 7 sollte heute nicht mehr einfach so genutzt werden, denn das Betriebssystem erhält seit Jahren keine Sicherheitsupdates mehr. Schwachstellen bleiben also ungepatcht, weshalb das System ein leichtes Ziel für Schadsoftware und Angreifer im Netz ist. Zudem haben aktuelle Browser den Support eingestellt, was das Surfen riskant macht. Wir haben Windows 7 auf einem Rechner genutzt, der nicht mit dem Internet verbunden war.
Es geht auch ohne Microsoft-Account
Einen der größten Unterschiede bemerke ich direkt schon beim Start. In Windows 7 konnte man noch ein lokales Benutzerkonto anlegen. Es war also nicht nötig, ein Microsoft-Konto zu haben und sich damit anzumelden. Oder mit anderen Worten: Es war nicht erforderlich, Teil des Microsoft-Ökosystems zu sein.
Ein lokales Profil existiert isoliert auf dem Rechner: Zugangsdaten, persönliche Angaben und Dateien bleiben physisch auf der Festplatte, ohne mit den Servern von Microsoft synchronisiert zu werden. Für die Inbetriebnahme von Windows 7 war weder eine E-Mail-Adresse noch eine bestehende Internetverbindung erforderlich.
Bei den neueren Versionen von Windows (und bei Apples sowieso) ist Microsoft sehr darauf bedacht, nicht nur ein Betriebssystem zu verkaufen, sondern die User direkt an ihre Plattform zu binden. Oftmals zulasten von Privatsphäre, Offline-Fähigkeiten und der Kontrolle über die eigene Hardware.
Ein Betriebssystem, kein Vertriebskanal
Freilich war es schon immer so, dass Microsoft ein großes Interesse daran hatte, den Windows-Usern auch ihre andere Software zu verkaufen. Bei Windows 7 war das aber noch verhältnismäßig dezent. Nach dem Start finde ich da ein eher reduziertes System vor. Paint, der Editor, Windows Media Player, das Snipping Tool oder Minesweeper wecken in mir heute beinahe nostalgische Gefühle – und ich kann sie auch einfach ignorieren, wenn ich möchte. Selbst Standardprogramme wie Windows Mail sind damals noch optional und mussten erst mit dem „Windows Live Essentials“-Paket, manuell heruntergeladen werden.
Heute sind zahlreiche Microsoft-Dienste fest im System verankert: Onedrive startet automatisch und synchronisiert ungefragt Nutzerordner. Microsoft Teams soll das Standard-Tool für Kommunikation sein. Edge will nicht nur mein Browser sein, sondern auch jedes PDF öffnen – und schiebt sich auch sonst ständig ungefragt in den Vordergrund. Dazu kommen noch die Web-Apps von Microsoft 365, die Xbox-App oder der inzwischen auch allgegenwärtige Copilot. Kurzum: Das Betriebssystem fungiert heute als Vertriebskanal für Microsofts Cloud-Ökosystem.
Keine ständigen „Empfehlungen“
Was mir in Windows 7 nicht an jeder Ecke begegnet: Reklame, die als „Tipps“ oder „Empfehlungen“ getarnt ist. Das Startmenü listet nur das auf, was tatsächlich auf meiner Festplatte installiert ist. Weder gibt es Pop-ups, die für andere Produkte werben, noch muss ich mich erst durch die Datenschutzeinstellungen klicken, um Banner abzuschalten.
In Windows 11 tauchen hingegen im Startmenü Vorschläge für Apps und Abonnements auf, der Sperrbildschirm bewirbt Games oder Microsoft-Produkte, die Widget-Leiste ist vom MSN-Newsfeed dominiert, der wiederum auch Werbung ausspielt. Selbst in der Einstellungen-App finden sich Banner, die zum Kauf von Onedrive-Speicher oder Microsoft 365 bewegen wollen.
Windows 7 fühlt sich noch deutlich mehr wie ein Werkzeug an, das mich in Ruhe arbeiten lässt, anstatt den Desktop als fortlaufende Werbefläche zu monetarisieren.
Die Taskleiste ist in Windows 7 noch wirklich flexibel: Sie lässt sich einfach entsperren und an jeden Bildschirmrand verschieben. Ich kann die Schaltflächen selbst beschriften, gruppieren oder einzeln anzeigen lassen. Auch Drag-and-Drop funktioniert nahtlos: Ich kann eine Datei einfach auf ein Programm-Icon in der Leiste ziehen, um das Fenster in den Vordergrund zu holen oder die Datei direkt darin zu öffnen. Außerdem reicht ein kurzer Rechtsklick, um schnell auf zuletzt geöffnete Dokumente oder angeheftete Favoriten zuzugreifen.
Auch das Kontextmenü funktioniert einfach. Ein Rechtsklick auf eine Datei zeigt direkt alle verfügbaren Einstellungen und Befehle in einer einzigen, nachvollziehbar gegliederten Liste. In Windows 11 ist das ein zweistufiges Menü, das viele gängige Optionen wie Packprogramme, Text-Editoren oder Druckbefehle hinter dem Punkt „Weitere Optionen anzeigen“ versteckt. Häufig benötigte Aktionen wie Kopieren oder Löschen wurden zu kleinen, unbeschrifteten Icons am Menürand.
Was in Windows 7 oft ein einziger Klick ist, braucht in Windows 11 oft zwei Schritte oder den Griff zur Tastenkombination „Shift + F10“. Das Design mag zwar moderner und aufgeräumter aussehen, opfert dafür aber die praktische Direktheit von Windows 7.
Alternativen für Windows 7
Wer Optik und Funktionen von Windows 7 vermisst, für den können einige Linux-Distributionen eine gute Alternative sein. Denn eines ist klar: Im Jahr 2026 sollte niemand mehr mit einem veralteten Betriebssystem, das diverse Sicherheitslücken hat, durch das Internet surfen. Wie ihr Linux einfach installieren könnt, erklären wir euch hier.
Linux Mint ist für viele das Betriebssystem, das Windows 7 am ähnlichsten ist, etwa durch das klassische Startmenü links unten, oder die anpassbare Taskleiste. Beim Wechsel von Windows 7 auf Linux Mint fühlt sich vieles intuitiv und vertraut an. Ähnlich einsteigerfreundlich ist Zorin OS, das extra für Wechsler entwickelt wurde und per Knopfdruck ein Windows-typisches Layout bietet, inklusive praktischer Hilfen zur Ausführung von Windows-Programmen.
Für User, die Wert auf große Flexibilität und transparente Aero-Glass-Effekte wie bei Windows 7 legen, empfiehlt sich Kubuntu. Diese Distribution arbeitet mit einem rein lokalen Benutzerkonto, erzwingt keine Cloud-Anbindung und überlässt den Usern die Kontrolle über ihre Updates.

articles.title: Spotify is busting free of CarPlay with the launch of its first native car app
articles.text:
Spotify announced Wednesday the launch of its next-generation, fully native in-car app, built directly on Google’s Android Automotive operating system. The standalone app, which is launching today in select Audi models, runs directly on the vehicle’s infotainment hardware — eliminating the need for phone tethering, Bluetooth connections, or aux cables.
Spotify is busting free of CarPlay with the launch of its first native car app
Say goodbye to those aux cables. Spotify’s new in-car app is here, and it’s rolling out to Audi vehicles today.
It’s the clearest sign yet that Spotify is ready to move beyond Apple CarPlay and Android, popular phone projection systems that currently dominate the way most people consume media in their cars. And with 34 percent of Spotify’s monthly active users and 77 percent of Premium subscribers streaming music in their cars, the platform they use to listen has never been more important.
Spotify’s new native app will launch with several Audi models, including the electric A6 e-tron and Q6 e-tron, as well as the gas-powered A5, Q5, and A6. Jonathan Tarlton, Spotify’s automotive business development lead, said the app, which has been in development for a little more than a year, is about delivering a more inviting experience to users — and specifically one that’s completely controlled by Spotify.
Spotify’s standard Android Automotive app operated as a “headless” integration, meaning that Spotify supplied the underlying backend data, playlists, and music catalog, but Google’s templates dictated how the interface was drawn and structured onscreen. The new Audi application is “headful,” allowing Spotify to draw and render its own native UI directly on the vehicle’s screens from scratch.
“We’re drawing all the pixels,” Tarlton said in an interview. “We own the user experience. So we’re not in a template or a framework. It’s 100 percent Spotify.”
To be sure, Spotify isn’t turning its back on Apple CarPlay and Android Auto; the company is still “heavily invested” in phone projection, Tarlton assured us. That said, the native Spotify app is being set up to compete directly with phone mirroring. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto remain the default way many people listen to music or podcasts in their vehicles: Drivers get in, connect their phones automatically, and tap into their familiar mobile interface. A native Spotify app could encourage people to listen through the car’s own operating system instead of projecting their phones — a scenario that Tarlton says he welcomes.
“We’re drawing all the pixels. We own the user experience. So we’re not in a template or a framework. It’s 100 percent Spotify.”
— Jonathan Tarlton, head of automotive business development at Spotify
“We want to give users choice,” he said. “We want to be wherever they are and we want to make sure that they’re accessing Spotify in the way they want to access it, whether they’re locked into the iOS ecosystem … or Android on the phone as well.”
People may love their CarPlay, but the experience is not without its tradeoffs. Wireless connection, in particular, can be spotty depending on your vehicle. Tarlton said the new app is aimed at reducing some of those headaches, like “a cold start in the morning,” he said. “You’re not having to wait to boot. You’re not having to wait for a screen to load. You’re not having to plug your phone in.”
There are other benefits to using the native Spotify app over a projected one from your phone. Passengers can scan a QR code displayed on the screen to join a wireless “Spotify Jam” session and add songs directly to the queue from their smartphones. On vehicles with a dedicated secondary passenger display, front passengers can browse, view lyrics, and watch video content without disturbing the driver. And while the vehicle is parked or charging, those motion graphics, like video podcasts and lyrics, move to the central display so everyone can enjoy.
With these features in particular, Spotify feels like it’s doing its part in helping to bring car passengers together again, Tarlton said. Often today you’ll find parents rocking out to their favorite hits in the front while kids are wearing their headphones in the back. The new app aims to correct that dynamic. “I’m excited that we can bring joy to the cabin again,” he said. “It’s not just technology.”
The rollout of the new Spotify app will focus in particular on cars with Android-based operating systems, he said. In that way, Spotifty can avoid having to build separate, bespoke applications for every individual automaker. Rather, the company can use a standard Android Automotive APK that it can then distribute through multiple app stores, whether it’s the Google Play Store or proprietary automaker stores like the Audi Application Store.
“Our number one goal was to prevent fragmentation, not just for our sake, but for the sake of the whole industry,” Tarlton said, “because we believe in having an open and fair place for apps to play — and the car is such a great place for that.”
