articles.title: ChatGPT ya programa en COBOL, un lenguaje más viejo que muchos de sus usuarios
articles.text:
Cuando pensamos en la IA y vibe coding, lo primero que nos viene a la mente es la programación con lenguajes modernos como Python o JavaScript. Si bien esto es útil, una parte importante de la infraestructura tecnológica mundial sigue ligada a tecnologías mucho más antiguas. Sistemas bancarios o aplicaciones gubernamentales se crearon con lenguajes que ya no se usan, por lo que OpenAI ha entrenado a ChatGPT para que pueda trabajar con ellos.
En una publicación de su blog, la compañía anunció que sus modelos de IA mejoraron notablemente en tareas relacionadas con tecnología antigua. Lenguajes como COBOL, Fortran, OCaml y Visual Basic, que hoy reciben menos atención que JavaScript y otros lenguajes modernos, siguen siendo fundamentales para el funcionamiento de empresas y gobiernos. Debido a ello, OpenAI entrenó a sus modelos para programar y migrar código en estos lenguajes.
Para medir los avances, la empresa desarrolló una herramienta conocida como MultiLangBench, en donde la IA debe construir un motor compatible con SQLite en 20 lenguajes de programación distintos. A eso se suma un benchmark de migración de COBOL, que mide si el modelo puede trasladar aplicaciones heredadas a otros lenguajes manteniendo su comportamiento.
Según los primeros datos, GPT-6 Astra logró una tasa media de éxito del 87,4% en MultiLangBench, que representa un salto notable si comparamos el 26,8% que lograba GPT‑5.6 Sol. En COBOL, Astra pasó del 10,9% al 72,1%, mientras que en Fortran aumentó del 21,4% al 83,5%. En el caso de Visual Basic, la IA registró una tasa de éxito cercana al 90%, lo que significa que el modelo más reciente de ChatGPT puede comprender este lenguaje que en su momento fue muy utilizado.
ChatGPT ya es capaz de migrar aplicaciones de COBOL a otro lenguaje
Lejos de los números, la verdadera prueba de fuego fue la de modernizar las aplicaciones antiguas. Este es uno de los principales cuellos de botella para muchas empresas y organizaciones, que tienen que mantener programas desarrollados hace décadas. En algunos casos, los empleados que los implementaron ya no laboran ahí o la documentación se perdió, lo que incrementa el coste de manutención.
Al intentar migrar una aplicación de COBOL a lenguajes como C++, Java, Kotlin, Python o Rust manteniendo la misma funcionalidad, GPT-6.1 Sol consiguió una tasa de éxito del 86,6% con bajo esfuerzo de razonamiento. Cuando se le permitió emplear un proceso más exhaustivo, la IA logró una precisión del 97,9%.
“Para comprobar si estos comportamientos se conservan, evaluamos nuestros modelos en pruebas ocultas que requieren paridad byte por byte en salidas observables”, mencionó la compañía. “Una migración solo se considera exitosa si todas las pruebas pasan”.
Según OpenAI, estos resultados sugieren que ChatGPT podría convertirse en una herramienta para actualizar infraestructuras tecnológicas heredadas. Lejos de limitarse a resolver errores o generar fragmentos de código, la IA ya es capaz de comprender sistemas construidos sobre lenguajes antiguos. Esto ayudaría a que los nuevos programadores que no crecieron con COBOL o Visual Basic puedan modernizar las viejas aplicaciones.
La compañía ha liberado MultiLangBench en GitHub para que los desarrolladores puedan revisar la metodología y analizar el rendimiento por lenguaje.

articles.title: Building Physical AI Systems That Can Work in the Real World - EE Times
articles.text:
Physical AI brings AI into machines that must sense their surroundings, make decisions, and act in the physical world. The market opportunity is substantial: McKinsey estimates that AI-powered agents and robots could unlock about $2.9 trillion in annual economic value in the U.S. by 2030. However, realizing this opportunity depends on moving from working prototypes to products that can operate reliably, safely, and economically at scale.
That exposes a different engineering problem. In a prototype, teams can often add more compute, sensors, cooling, or power to prove that a capability works. In deployment, every added capability must fit within the size, weight, power, and cost budget, often abbreviated to SWaP-C, of the system.
Those constraints shape how a robot performs: How long it can operate between charges, how much productive payload it can carry, and how reliably it operates over time. The challenge is not simply adding more intelligence but integrating it effectively into deployable products.
A robot must continuously interpret its surroundings, decide how to respond, and translate those decisions into physical action. Doing that requires capabilities from perception and AI inference to planning and motion control to work together, while meeting different compute and timing requirements.
System constraints shape intelligence
Every physical AI system has a finite design envelope. Processors, batteries, cooling, sensors, actuators, and mechanical components all compete for space, power, thermal headroom, and cost.
In a deployable robot, every gram matters. A larger battery may extend operating time but adds weight and takes up space. More compute can enable more advanced AI models, but places greater demands on cooling and energy.
Consider a quadruped robot navigating challenging terrain. Much of its onboard energy and weight budget must support the basic demands of locomotion, while the same system needs sensing, perception, navigation, and control to operate autonomously. More sophisticated reasoning cannot be added in isolation. It has to fit alongside motors, batteries, sensors, and other components within the same finite system envelope.
This makes physical AI a capability integration exercise. As Arm’s Federico Pecora explains in a recent paper titled The Missing Science of Robotic Systems: Capability Integration in the Model-Centric Era, robot intelligence depends on how perception, planning, control, safety, and orchestration work together across different timing, compute, and memory requirements. The “robot brain” is not only the largest model that runs on an accelerator, but the system architecture that enables these capabilities to work together at the right rates and with the right level of assurance.
The tradeoffs also vary significantly by machine. A quadruped navigating rough terrain, a humanoid manipulating objects, and a stationary industrial robot may all be described as robots, but they require different combinations of capabilities—and different levels of compute performance, energy efficiency, responsiveness, and safety.
As robotic systems become more capable, the industry needs more consistent ways to describe those capabilities and connect them to the underlying system requirements. That is why we are working with the ecosystem to establish a Robotics Capability Framework, which seeks to establish a common language to define and compare intelligent robotic systems.
AI changes the design equation
AI is changing how robotic and autonomous systems are designed. These machines increasingly need to interpret changing environments, respond to live data, and operate predictably as conditions change.
Doing that efficiently requires compute, software, memory, sensors, and safety functions to be planned together. Multiple workloads operate simultaneously with different timing requirements and priorities.
Heterogeneous compute gives engineering teams flexibility to match each workload to the right processing resource. Demanding AI workloads may run on dedicated accelerators, for example, while CPUs coordinate the wider system and microcontrollers handle low-latency control close to the hardware.
The value comes from designing these components as one coordinated system, with workloads running in the right place at the right time, with the right level of priority and isolation.
Deployment makes compute architecture a competitive advantage
Scaling physical AI is about more than raw performance. Every new model, sensor, reasoning layer, or safety function must fit within the available size, weight, power, thermal, memory, and cost envelope.
The systems that scale will extract more intelligence from every watt, coordinate diverse workloads efficiently, and keep safety-critical behavior predictable as AI demands increase. Managing these constraints can extend operating time, preserve productive payload, and make fleets more practical and economical to deploy.
Physical AI will be defined by products that are capable enough to be useful, efficient enough to scale, and predictable enough to trust.
Read also:
Physical AI Needs An Ecosystem
What Robots Show Us: Display and Data in Physical AI
Physical AI Isn’t Just Bigger AI; It’s a Systems Architecture Challenge
Dear Dermot,
At UNER AI (https://uner.ai/), our approach aligns closely with the article’s conclusion: physical AI requires coordinated hardware and software within real-world power, timing and cost constraints. We provide and deploy Autoware-based AI solutions across Renesas R-Car V4M, NVIDIA Orin and AMD Xilinx FPGA platforms, combining AI acceleration, MCU orchestration and Digital Twin validation to address these requirements.
I would conclude that successful physical AI depends on the entire system working together within real-world constraints.
Regards
CEO
Sergey Christ

articles.title: Blog Review: Oct. 21
articles.text:
From server to rack; AMBA CXS; digital twins; edge AI development loop; satellite power; global talent challenges.
Synopsys’ Neeraj Paliwal considers how AI workloads are shifting key design and optimization considerations from the server to the rack, with designs starting from the target workload and working backward to optimize for useful AI work per watt and dollar.
Cadence’s Ravi Vora demonstrates how AMBA CXS evolves a wide, credited link into a scalable shared transport for multi-protocol and multi-node traffic that enables controlled interleaving while preserving stream ordering, route identity, packet reconstruction, and required contiguity.
In a podcast, Siemens’ Conor Peick and Katherina Westrich chat about the adoption of digital twins in the semiconductor industry, ranging from chip design and verification to fab construction and automation.
Arm’s Christopher Seidl shows how to create a development loop for edge AI in which target information and evidence from real execution flow back into the next iteration.
Keysight’s Nancy Friedrich explores the trends driving rising requirements for satellite power generation and distribution and how lab-based power-emulation configurations can be leveraged to assess system performance in scenarios that affect the performance of satellite solar arrays and battery packs.
In a blog for SEMI, Stanton Chase’s Jan-Bart Smits compares semiconductor talent shortages across North America, EMEA, and Southeast Asia, warning that while causes differ by region, government subsidies alone cannot buy the expertise needed for desired buildouts.
Plus, check out the blogs featured in the latest Low Power-High Performance newsletter:
Rambus’ Paul Karazuba examines multiple interacting factors impacting PCIe retimer reach, including silicon design, controller intelligence, channel quality, and the transmission medium.
Siemens EDA’s Shehab Ashraf looks at short-resilient via insertion and its effect on reliability and performance.
Cadence’s Mayank Bhatnagar shows how open interfaces and interoperability let designers choose technologies based on system needs.
Arm’s Francisco Socal outlines extending chiplet connectivity across AXI and CHI with scalable protocol subsets, interoperability, and flexible transport support.
Ayar Labs’ Vladimir Stojanovic and Global Unichip’s Igor Elkanovich explain how optical engines can operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors in multi-chip packages.

articles.title: Her Startup opens applications for 2nd cohort of African women-led tech startups - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Her Startup, an accelerator for women-led technology startups in Africa, has opened applications for the second cohort of its programme.
The Her Startup initiative, a partnership between the KSH Foundation, Tomorrow Foundation and EHA Impact Ventures, will select 10 early-stage women founders and help them build investment-ready tech businesses. The training component will be delivered by Founder Institute, which bills itself as the world’s largest pre-seed startup accelerator.
Women-founded startups continue to struggle for funding in Africa. According to Disrupt Africa’s latest Diversity Dividend report, only 9.6 per cent of ventures funded in 2025 were led by a female CEO.
Her Startup was set up to tackle that gap by giving women entrepreneurs training, capital and networks through a single, integrated programme.
Selected founders will take part in a 12-week intensive training programme with Founder Institute, with fees covered by Her Startup, and will receive a monthly stipend so they can commit to the programme full-time.
They will also get the chance to pitch to Her Startup’s investment committee for funding through convertible revenue-based financing, as well as 12 months of sector-matched mentoring and access to Founder Institute’s global network.
The programme is open to women founders or CEOs aged between 18 and 35 who run a tech-enabled business that has been operating for at least six months and generates at least US$500 in monthly gross revenue. Founders from Francophone Africa are strongly encouraged to apply for the 2026/2027 cohort.
The second cohort follows a 2024/2025 pilot that drew more than 200 applications from 18 African countries. Ten founders were selected for training, and three ventures won funding at the programme’s Pitch Day in Lagos in April 2025. Alumni have since gone on to win grants and awards and attract investor interest.
One of them is Nigerian healthtech startup Dynalimb Technologies, which makes affordable 3D-printed prosthetics.
“Since Her Startup, we’ve seen a steady rise in customer adoption and product sales, as more amputees experience the comfort and mobility that Dynalimb’s affordable 3D-printed prosthetics provide,” said Blessing Aniefiok, the startup’s COO.
Her Startup’s funding model sets it apart, with repayments on its convertible, revenue-based financing linked to each company’s revenue.
“It’s not enough to just give these companies financing. It’s about giving them financing that will truly help them succeed. We chose a convertible, revenue-based loan, an innovative financing mechanism that is just starting to enter the market. It is incredibly founder-friendly, and it will help the women in this programme succeed,” said Evelyn Castle, co-founder of Her Startup and co-founder of EHA Impact Ventures.
Applications are open here until October 26.

articles.title: OYO-parent PRISM to nearly halve IPO fresh issue size to up to Rs 3,350 cr: Sources
articles.text:
OYO-parent PRISM to nearly halve IPO fresh issue size to up to Rs 3,350 cr: Sources
People familiar with the matter said the reduction in the issue size follows continued strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, which has lowered the amount of capital the company needs to raise compared with what was originally envisaged.
OYO parent PRISM is planning to nearly halve the size of the fresh issue in its proposed initial public offering (IPO) to up to Rs 3,350 crore from almost Rs 6,650 crore, sources said.
People familiar with the matter told PTI the reduction in the issue size follows continued strong cash generation and an improving balance-sheet position, which has lowered the amount of capital the company needs to raise compared with what was originally envisaged.
"The original issue was sized before the company's more recent financial performance came through. With cash generation remaining strong and the balance sheet improving, the funding requirement has come down, allowing the company to reduce the amount of primary capital it raises.
"The objective is to raise what the business needs while keeping the capital structure efficient. The plan is to repay the residual debt over the next two to three years through cash flows generated by the business," a person familiar with the matter said.
Earlier, OYO had planned to raise up to Rs 6,650 crore through an IPO, of which around Rs 5,000 crore was intended for debt repayment.
The revised issue size comes with PRISM continuing to focus on reducing its outstanding debt.
Under the revised structure, most of the issue proceeds are proposed to be used towards repayment or prepayment, in part or full, of certain borrowings.
The revised issue comes as PRISM moves towards the next stage of its proposed IPO following its earlier filing of the uUpdated draft herring prospectus.
Moody's Ratings has revised the outlook on PRISM to 'positive' from 'stable', while reaffirming the travel tech unicorn's B2 corporate family rating.
Explaining the rationale behind ratings, Moody's said, "We expect OYO's EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation) to grow to around Rs 3,000 crore ($315 million) over the next 12-18 months as the company continues to scale and add new storefronts to its platform.
For FY26, OYO's EBITDA more than doubled to Rs 2,630 crore from Rs 1,080 crore in FY25.
OYO was founded in 2013 by Ritesh Agarwal, who currently holds a 30.52 per cent stake in the company. SVF India Holdings (Cayman) Ltd, a subsidiary of SoftBank Group Corp is the largest shareholder in the company, with a 40.04% stake.

articles.title: Smartphones Samsung : bonne nouvelle si vous avez un Galaxy A36
articles.text:
Pour son Galaxy A36 5G, Samsung a promis 6 ans de mises à jour, ce qui est désormais le minimum pour les téléphones du géant coréen. La patience des utilisateurs de ce modèle est aujourd’hui récompensée avec la mise à jour stable de One UI 9, basé sur Android 17 qui commence à être déployé.
Le Samsung Galaxy A36 5G passe à One UI 9
C’est sous le numéro de build A366BXXUCDZIF que le fichier de mise à jour vient de pointer le bout de son nez. Il pèse environ 2,4 Go et plusieurs utilisateurs européens ont indiqué l’avoir reçu, comme en Grèce et en Turquie, pour ne citer que ces deux pays.
Cette version intègre également le patch de sécurité de septembre 2026. Pour vérifier si la mise à jour Android est disponible chez vous, il suffit de se rendre dans le menu des paramètres de votre téléphone, puis dans la section dédiée aux mises à jour logicielles.
Les nouveautés de One UI 9 et Android 17
Côté interface, One UI 9 apporte son lot d’améliorations, notamment côté personnalisation de l’interface. Le panneau des paramètres rapides peut par exemple être redimensionné et les commandes réorganisées. De son côté, la barre d’état accueille un nouvel indicateur affichant la vitesse du réseau. En revanche, pas certains que toutes les nouveautés IA de Samsung soient de la partie.
À lire : Samsung : One UI 9 (Android 17) débarque sur les derniers téléphones haut de gamme éligibles
Une nouvelle rubrique « Garantie et entretien » fait également son apparition dans les réglages, entre autres nouveautés. Comme toujours, le déploiement se fait par vagues progressives selon les régions (du monde). Si vous êtes l’heureux possesseur d’un Galaxy A36 5G, vous devriez donc recevoir une notification dans les prochains jours.

articles.title: ByteDance, Alibaba et Tencent commandent à nouveau pour 35 milliards de dollars de puces NVIDIA
articles.text:
Malgré les difficultés d'accès aux produits NVIDIA, les géants chinois de la tech continuent de commander en masse tout ce qu'ils peuvent. La preuve avec ces commandes d'un montant exceptionnel.
NVIDIA, c'est le nec plus ultra des GPU que l'on installe dans des data centers afin d'entraîner et faire fonctionner des modèles IA. Malheuresement pour les géants chinois du secteur, il est difficile voire impossible de s'offrir les GPU les plus avancés de la firme de Jensen Huang, à cause de la rivalité américano-chinoise. Pourtant, ils continuent de mettre des milliards dans les produits auxquels ils ont encore accès !
Alibaba, Tencent et Bytedance ont ensemble commandé pour 35 milliards de RTX PRO 5500
Malgré son fort recul sur le marché chinois des accélérateurs IA, NVIDIA continue d'être particulièrement sexy pour les entreprises locales. La preuve, comme nous le rapporte Reuters, avec ces commandes folles passées par les plus grandes entreprises locales de la tech.
Ainsi, selon le média anglophone, Alibaba, Tencent et ByteDance auraient à eux trois placé pour 35 milliards de dollars de commande chez NVIDIA. Celles-ci concernent la carte graphique RTX PRO 5500. Un produit qui est ici une sorte de substitut pour les firmes chinoises.
Les géants chinois ne veulent pas lâcher NVIDIA
Car les géants chinois cités ne peuvent accéder au meilleur composant de NVIDIA, le GPU B300, à cause de l'interdiction d'export imposée par les États-Unis. En dessous, la puce H200 est elle accessible, mais les commandes sont soumises à des conditions d'octroi de licence, avec un examen au cas par cas.
Les entreprises chinoises ont donc décidé de se rabattre sur la RTX PRO 5500, et ce alors que Huawei est pourtant en pleine ascension en Chine - signe que les produits NVIDIA restent pour le moment incontournables. À noter d'ailleurs que les commandes passées représentent plus de 3 millions de RTX PRO 5500, et que les sources de Reuters indiquent ne pas être sûres de la capacité de NVIDIA à pouvoir répondre à l'ensemble de la demande. NVIDIA pourrait ainsi en 2027 ne pas pouvoir produire plus de 3 millions de ces GPU pour l'ensemble du marché mondial.
Source : Reuters

articles.title: Un développeur réussit l’impossible : faire tourner le vrai iOS sur un Android grâce à l'IA — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les lanceurs d’applications et les thèmes qui imitent iOS ne manquent pas sur Android. Icônes arrondies, Centre de contrôle imité au pixel près, horloge géante sur l’écran de verrouillage : l’illusion fonctionne jusqu’au premier passage dans les paramètres, où l’interface Android reprend immédiatement ses droits.
Le Redmi qui fait le tour de X depuis le 18 octobre ne joue pas dans cette catégorie. Lorsqu’on ouvre ses Réglages, c’est bien la véritable application d’Apple qui s’affiche, et qui présente le téléphone comme un iPhone X sous iOS 16.7.16.
Cette vidéo de deux minutes et demie, vue plusieurs millions de fois, présente ios-topaz, un projet publié sur GitHub par le développeur Makr. Il s’agit d’un portage d’ios-sweet, un projet distinct de l’équipe dipa studio, qui faisait déjà démarrer iOS 16 sur un Redmi Note 10 Pro.
Makr n’en est pas à son premier portage sur ce smartphone. Avec un autre projet publié sur GitHub, topaz-woa, il fait déjà démarrer Windows 11 pour processeurs ARM sur le même Redmi Note 12 4G. Début octobre, le bureau de Windows s’affichait, avec l’écran tactile et le stockage fonctionnels.
Makr fait tourner directement XNU, le noyau d’iOS et de macOS dont Apple publie une partie du code en open source, sur la puce Snapdragon 685 du Redmi, un smartphone lancé en France en mars 2023 à partir de 199,90 euros.
Le développeur y greffe ensuite le système officiel de l’iPhone X, à quelques ajustements près. Aucun émulateur n’intervient. Les services système et SpringBoard, le gestionnaire de l’écran d’accueil d’Apple, s’exécutent nativement après environ trois minutes de démarrage. Makr indique avoir ajouté la prise en charge du Wi-Fi (réseaux WPA2) ce mardi 20 octobre.
Pourquoi iOS est si difficile à sortir de l’iPhone
Le chemin inverse est balisé depuis longtemps. Dès 2010, le projet iDroid faisait démarrer Android sur les premiers iPhone, suivi dix ans plus tard par l’entreprise Corellium et son Project Sandcastle sur les modèles équipés d’une puce A10. L’écart tient à la conception des deux systèmes. Android repose sur un noyau Linux conçu pour s’adapter à des milliers de composants différents, alors qu’iOS est taillé sur mesure pour le matériel d’Apple. Pour faire tourner iOS ailleurs, Makr a donc dû adapter dans le noyau XNU, en partant du travail d’ios-sweet, les pilotes indispensables au Redmi, de la gestion de l’écran tactile au stockage UFS, jusqu’à l’amorçage manuel du modem Qualcomm pour activer le Wi-Fi.
L’architecture du processeur réserve elle aussi son lot de casse-têtes matériels. D’un côté, iOS découpe la mémoire vive en pages de 16 Ko, un format que les quatre cœurs économes du Snapdragon 685 (habitués aux 4 Ko d’Android) sont incapables de lire, ce qui oblige le téléphone à ne tourner que sur la moitié de ses huit cœurs.
Le système de l’iPhone X fait aussi appel à des instructions processeur modernes que l’ancienne architecture ARMv8.0 du Redmi ignore totalement : le noyau doit alors les intercepter à la volée pour les simuler une par une, au prix d’une lourde perte de vitesse. Pour abattre ce travail titanesque, le développeur ne s’est d’ailleurs pas appuyé que sur ses propres nuits blanches. Les journaux du dépôt GitHub révèlent des modifications cosignées par Claude, l’assistant de programmation d’Anthropic. Makr ne précise pas quelle part du travail il a confiée à l’IA.
Pour l’instant, un iPhone X de vitrine
En l’état, inutile d’espérer faire de ce Redmi modifié son smartphone du quotidien. L’appareil est privé de Bluetooth, de données mobiles, de GPS, de son et d’appareil photo, tandis que l’horloge interne non reconnue réinitialise la date au 31 décembre à chaque redémarrage. Plus handicapant encore, la version publique est dépourvue d’accélération matérielle pour la partie graphique : le processeur central doit dessiner chaque élément de l’interface à la main et le navigateur Safari se contente d’afficher des pages blanches. HackiOS, un projet concurrent du groupe OOSexGang, montre en vidéo iOS 16.5 sur un Poco X5 Pro et un Xiaomi Mi 11 Lite 5G. Ses auteurs promettent d’ouvrir leur code, mais n’ont publié ni code source ni version installable, et personne n’a pu vérifier leurs démonstrations.
La suite est déjà annoncée. Dans la documentation du projet, Makr détaille depuis le 19 octobre son plan pour la partie graphique : écrire un pilote pour la puce Adreno 610 du Redmi, afin que l’interface d’iOS soit calculée par le GPU et non plus par le processeur. Il n’avance aucune date.
Un laboratoire réservé aux bidouilleurs et sous l’œil d’Apple
Sans Secure Enclave (le coprocesseur de sécurité des iPhone) et avec la plupart des protections d’Apple désactivées, mieux vaut n’y stocker aucune donnée personnelle. L’expérience s’adresse donc uniquement aux bidouilleurs disposant d’un PC sous Linux, d’une solide maîtrise des lignes de commande et d’un Redmi Note 12 4G au démarrage déverrouillé (bootloader) dont ils acceptent d’effacer intégralement la mémoire. Sur le plan légal, Makr prend soin de ne distribuer aucun fichier appartenant à Apple, obligeant chaque curieux à récupérer lui-même l’image officielle d’iOS sur les serveurs de la marque avant de la modifier.
L’installation n’écrit rien sur les partitions de démarrage. Le noyau est lancé depuis la mémoire vive avec la commande fastboot, et les autres systèmes installés sur le téléphone ne sont pas touchés. En revanche, iOS s’installe à la place des données utilisateur d’Android, qui sont effacées.
Ne distribuer aucun fichier d’Apple ne garantit toutefois pas l’immunité face aux avocats de Cupertino, dont le contrat de licence d’iOS réserve son installation aux appareils de la marque.
En 2019, la firme avait ainsi poursuivi la société Corellium pour ses iPhone virtuels destinés aux chercheurs en sécurité, avant que la justice américaine ne reconnaisse un « usage loyal » (fair use) et que le litige ne se solde par un accord confidentiel en 2023. Personne ne remplacera son iPhone par un Xiaomi muet qui met trois minutes à s’allumer. Le projet montre surtout qu’un amateur, aidé d’un assistant IA et du travail déjà publié par ios-sweet, peut désormais faire démarrer le vrai iOS sur un smartphone Android de milieu de gamme.

articles.title: Starlink bridé en Ukraine : le gouvernement américain jette Elon Musk sous le bus
articles.text:
Quelqu’un, vraisemblablement, ment. Interrogé par des journalistes en Inde ce mercredi 21 octobre, Marco Rubio, le secrétaire d’État américain, a lâché Elon Musk. Le responsable a en effet renvoyé au PDG de SpaceX la responsabilité de Starlink en Ukraine. Ce dernier disait de son côté qu’il fallait plutôt voir du côté de Washington.
« Starlink est une entreprise privée. Ils ont un contrat. Ils ont des conditions contractuelles sur la façon dont cette technologie peut être utilisée. Le point important est que nous ne pouvons pas dicter à une entreprise privée les décisions qu’elle prend ou ne prend pas », a déclaré Marco Rubio, ajoutant que, selon lui, la Maison-Blanche n’a pas son mot à dire.
« Ce que je peux vous dire avec certitude, c’est que ni le président des États-Unis, ni personne dans notre système, n’a jamais demandé que des modifications soient apportées à ce système. Et c’est ce que nous avons dit à plusieurs reprises », a-t-il ajouté. Ce serait donc Elon Musk qui aurait pris cette décision de ralentir l’emploi de Starlink en Ukraine.
Ici, Marco Rubio s’exprimait au lendemain d’une révélation du Wall Street Journal. Le journal avance qu’Elon Musk aurait lui-même donné l’ordre de brider Starshield, la version militaire de Starlink avec laquelle l’armée ukrainienne pilote ses drones. Elon Musk et Donald Trump en auraient même parlé avant la décision.
CBS News affirme aussi, sources à l’appui, que le patron de SpaceX a parlé à plusieurs responsables de l’administration avant de donner l’ordre. Au sujet de l’article du WSJ, Marco Rubio a indiqué ne pas être « familier avec l’histoire », ajoutant ignorer « ce que l’article reflète ». L’article du Wall Street Journal est sorti le jour de l’annonce des résultats de SpaceX.
Tout le monde se renvoie la balle
Le 14 octobre, Elon Musk avait rejeté la faute sur Donald Trump : selon lui, toute limite était décidée « par l’armée américaine et, au final, par le président ». Le même jour, le ministre des Affaires étrangères de Pologne l’accusait de faire de la politique avec ses produits. Le Telegraph pointait la responsabilité sur Elon Musk.
L’argument du contrat privé tient assez mal : le gouvernement américain paie Starshield et décide qui y a accès. Sur CNN, sur le plateau de la journaliste Kaitlan Collins, le républicain Brian Fitzpatrick a estimé qu’aucun civil ne devait décider de l’usage de cet outil militaire. Dans tous les cas, cela mérite des investigations.
D’ailleurs, le sénateur démocrate Adam Schiff réclame une enquête du Sénat, puisque soit Donald Trump, soit Elon Musk a menti. Le journaliste Ronan Farrow avait enquêté dès 2023 pour le New Yorker sur l’emprise d’Elon Musk en Ukraine. Le reporter a réagi sur cette nouvelle affaire dans une série de messages sur X.

articles.title: Un agricultor halló en su campo de maíz en Minnesota los restos de un cohete chino de 3,35 metros
articles.text:
Un agricultor del condado de Stevens, en Minnesota, encontró un objeto metálico circular de 3,35 metros de diámetro mientras cosechaba maíz el 14 de octubre. El análisis de Ars Technica concluyó que se trata de la etapa superior de un cohete chino Zhuque-2E.
La Oficina del Sheriff del condado de Stevens recibió el aviso ese mismo día y confirmó el hallazgo en Scott Township, una zona rural al oeste del estado. “Los agentes confirmaron que había un objeto metálico grande, de unos 3,35 metros de diámetro, presuntamente un objeto espacial”, informó la oficina en un comunicado.
Las autoridades trabajan junto a agencias estatales y federales para identificar al dueño del objeto y coordinar su retiro del campo, aunque no precisaron una fecha para completar esa tarea. Según informaron, el objeto no representó ningún peligro para la población mientras permaneció en el terreno.
Un cohete que recorrió medio planeta antes de caer
El 15 de septiembre, un cohete Zhuque-2E de la empresa china LandSpace despegó desde Dongfeng, una zona de lanzamientos comerciales ubicada junto al centro militar de Jiuquan, en el noroeste de China. Media hora después del despegue, liberó diez satélites en una órbita polar circular de unos 900 kilómetros de altitud.
Los satélites pertenecen a la red Qianfan, también llamada “Mil Velas”, el proyecto con el que China busca competir con Starlink, la constelación de SpaceX. Desde 2024, el país lanzó 258 satélites Qianfan, con el objetivo de llegar a 1.296 unidades y, a largo plazo, superar los 15.000.
Después de soltar su carga, la etapa superior del cohete encendió otra vez su motor para reducir la velocidad y salir de órbita, sin completar una vuelta entera a la Tierra. El vuelo duró entre 75 y 80 minutos y recorrió medio planeta: despegó en el desierto de Gobi, sobrevoló la Antártida y cruzó América.
Esa misma noche, usuarios de redes sociales registraron estelas de fuego que cruzaban el cielo sobre Kansas rumbo a Minnesota, visibles también desde Wisconsin. Según Ars Technica, el horario, la trayectoria y la dirección de esos registros permitieron vincular la caída con el lanzamiento del Zhuque-2E.
El diámetro de la etapa superior del cohete coincide de forma exacta con el del objeto hallado en el campo de maíz.
Un diseño pensado para caer en el océano
Lo inusual del caso, según el sitio especializado, es el tamaño del resto recuperado, mayor al de la mayoría de los objetos que sobreviven a la reentrada, y el hecho de que haya caído el mismo día del lanzamiento.
Nunca antes una persona sufrió heridas graves por la caída de basura espacial, aunque sí existen antecedentes de daños materiales. El derecho internacional establece que el país responsable de un lanzamiento debe responder por los daños que un objeto espacial cause en tierra.
La práctica habitual para desechar una etapa de cohete es dirigirla hacia una reentrada controlada sobre el océano, lo que sugiere que lo ocurrido el 15 de septiembre fue resultado de una maniobra de desorbitado fallida. LandSpace no se pronunció públicamente sobre la caída del resto en Minnesota.
En teoría, deshacerse de una etapa gastada apenas termina su misión es una práctica responsable que limita la generación de basura espacial. Pero los cohetes chinos ya habían generado inconvenientes similares.
La etapa superior del vuelo anterior del Zhuque-2E, en junio, se fragmentó tras cumplir su misión y dejó decenas de piezas de basura en una zona de la órbita baja terrestre muy transitada, donde operan la Estación Espacial Internacional y buena parte de los satélites Starlink.
Los cohetes estadounidenses que cumplen misiones en órbita baja suelen reservar combustible para una disposición guiada hacia el reingreso, algo que no ocurrió con el vuelo de septiembre del Zhuque-2E.

articles.title: OpenAI says GPT-6.1 Sol is dramatically better at migrating legacy code
articles.text:
OpenAI confirmed that its newer models are much better at writing and migrating software in older programming languages.
The company lists programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic as a few examples where it has seen significant improvements.
OpenAI says COBOL supports more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions, and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is still used in areas such as weather forecasting and nuclear reactor safety analysis.
"These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world," OpenAI explained in a blog post.
To measure progress, OpenAI created MultiLangBench, which asks models to build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 programming languages.
GPT-6 Astra reached an average test pass rate of 87.4%, up from 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol. In COBOL specifically, Astra jumped from 10.9% to 72.1%, while Fortran improved from 21.4% to 83.5%.
"Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%)," OpenAI noted.
GPT-6.1 Sol is much better at migrating COBOL
OpenAI also tested whether its models could migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust without changing their behaviour.
"GPT-6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT-5.6 Sol's 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost," OpenAI said. "At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation."
This work could help companies modernize older software, although production migrations would still require expert review and testing.

articles.title: Can a Simple App Really Fix PC Game Stutters?
articles.text:
Shader compilation stutter has plagued PC gaming for years, and a new application called Shader Compilation Stutter Killer, or SCSKiller for short, promises to do something about it. The idea is simple enough: compile shaders before launching a game rather than waiting for them to be compiled during gameplay. But does it actually work?
That's what we set out to find out, testing the application across several notoriously stutter-prone games. Along the way, we also discovered something rather interesting about shader compilation on Radeon GPUs. Something that could be a pretty big deal, and that we hadn't heard about before.
What's SCSKiller?
SCSKiller is a free and open-source application, so if you're interested, we recommend downloading it and giving it a shot for yourself. For those unfamiliar with shader compilation stutter, it's a common issue in modern PC gaming where a game briefly freezes or hitches the first time a new visual effect appears.
Some games attempt to address this by precompiling shaders before gameplay begins. The Last of Us Part I, for example, is famous for its lengthy shader compilation process.
Unfortunately, even games that precompile shaders can still suffer from horrific shader compilation stutter, while others don't bother precompiling much of anything, which can also lead to a poor experience.
Rather than relying on a game to compile shaders, either beforehand or on the fly, SCSKiller attempts to do the work before you launch it. The application scans game files, extracts the necessary shader code, and compiles as many shader pipelines as possible into the GPU driver's cache. The idea is that when you launch the game, those shaders are already compiled, so the driver doesn't have to interrupt gameplay to process new visual effects.
SCSKiller doesn't rely on a whitelist of specific games. Instead, it works at the engine level, with support for games built using Unreal Engine 4 and 5, Unity, RE Engine, and FromSoftware's engines, alongside a more generic approach for other DirectX 12 titles. It also supports DirectX 11 games on Nvidia GPUs.
For games where shader pipelines can't easily be extracted from the game files, SCSKiller includes an optional recorder. This allows you to play for a few minutes with recording enabled, after which the application can use the collected data to compile additional shaders.
It's important to understand that SCSKiller doesn't solve all forms of stuttering, because not every stutter you encounter is related to shader compilation. One of the biggest issues, particularly with Unreal Engine 5 games, has been traversal stutter, and SCSKiller can't address that.
In our opinion, traversal stuttering is generally more disruptive, as it can result in longer pauses when new environmental assets are loaded from local storage. This typically happens as you cross an invisible boundary within the game world, triggering the loading of additional assets. Perhaps we'll get a Shader Traversal Stutter Killer, or STSKiller, in the future. Fingers crossed.
The Drawbacks: Compilation Time, Storage, and Memory
There are some drawbacks to SCSKiller, though they're largely unavoidable consequences of how the application works. For starters, brute-forcing thousands of shader pipelines can take considerable time, depending on how many shaders need compiling and the performance of your CPU.
Of course, the advantage is that you can run the compilation process when you're not actively using your PC. Just be aware that it can pin CPU usage at 100% for extended periods, though with a properly configured system, that shouldn't be an issue.
SCSKiller also consumes additional storage space, and with SSDs at a premium right now, that's something worth considering. Compiling thousands of shaders increases the size of the GPU driver's shader cache. As a result, you may need to increase the cache size to prevent older compiled shaders from being removed.
Nvidia users can adjust this through the driver settings. The standard limit is typically 10 GB, but you can increase it to 100 GB or even set it to unlimited, preventing older shaders from being deleted as new ones are added.
Unfortunately, things are more restrictive for Radeon users. According to SCSKiller, AMD's driver has a fixed shader cache limit of 16 GB. We haven't independently confirmed that limit with AMD, but if accurate, it means Radeon owners can't simply increase the cache size. Once the cache reaches its limit, older entries are removed to make room for new ones. SCSKiller will then identify previously optimized games as needing to be compiled again.
This potentially limits the usefulness of SCSKiller on Radeon GPUs, particularly if you're trying to optimize a large library of games. That said, there's no need to panic. As we discovered during testing, AMD has some pretty interesting shader compilation behavior of its own, and we'll explore that shortly.
Test System and Methodology
For all of this initial testing, we used our Ryzen 7 9800X3D test system with 32 GB of RAM, initially paired with the GeForce RTX 5090. Later, we also tested the Radeon RX 9070 XT and GeForce RTX 5070 to investigate some interesting differences in shader compilation behavior.
We may explore additional hardware configurations in the future, particularly slower CPUs. For now, though, the goal was simply to determine whether SCSKiller actually works. As it turns out, we were able to demonstrate that quite clearly using the 9800X3D. So, let's get into the results.
Test System Specs
| CPU | AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D | 
| Motherboard | MSI MPG X870E Carbon WiFi [BIOS 7E49v1AA7] | 
| Memory | G.Skill Trident Z5 RGB DDR5-6000 32GB CL30 [CL30-38-38-96] | 
| Graphics Card | GeForce RTX 5090, GeForce RTX 5070, Radeon RX 9070 XT | 
| ATX Case | MSI Prospect 700R | 
| Power Supply | Kolink Regulator Gold ATX 3.0 1200W | 
| Storage | TeamGroup T-Force Cardea A440 M.2 PCIe Gen4 NVMe SSD 4TB | 
| Operating System | Windows 11 25H2 | 
| Display Driver | AMD Radeon Adrenalin 26.9.2 Nvidia GeForce Game Ready Driver 617.42 | 
Gaming Benchmarks
Star Wars Jedi: Survivor
We'll start with Star Wars Jedi: Survivor, a game famous for its numerous stuttering issues. Jedi: Survivor precompiles shaders when loading for the first time. For this initial test, both configurations were running the game for the first time immediately after completing that initial shader compilation process.
There are quite a few interesting things to note here. First, performance was substantially better with SCSKiller enabled, boosting the average frame rate by 25%, with a similar improvement to the 1% lows. However, you might have also noticed that the standard configuration was consuming around 60% more GPU power, at least at the beginning of the test. That difference gradually decreased to just under 40% by the end of our run.
Despite the game precompiling shaders when initially loading, there appears to be considerable additional shader compilation work taking place during gameplay, particularly in the early stages. This can reduce frame rates and increase the processing overhead associated with rendering new effects.
Something else worth noting is that SCSKiller increased system memory usage. We're looking at around 7% more RAM consumption in this example, apparently due to the additional precompiled shader data being buffered into system memory.
For our second Jedi: Survivor test, we loaded an earlier section of the game immediately after completing the first run. By this point, the game had already been running for quite some time. In terms of performance, the SCSKiller configuration was around 14% faster, though neither configuration suffered from what we'd consider shader compilation stutter.
Interestingly, SCSKiller was now consuming around 30% more system memory, representing almost 7 GB of additional RAM usage. That wasn't a problem for our 32 GB configuration, but it's certainly something to consider if you have less than 32 GB of system memory.
GPU power consumption also increased with SCSKiller this time, which makes sense given that we were rendering more frames. It also suggests the RTX 5090 was spending less time dealing with shader compilation work during gameplay. Although SCSKiller wasn't solving any noticeable shader compilation stutter in this particular example, since the standard configuration wasn't stuttering to begin with, it still managed to improve performance substantially.
It's possible that slower hardware would have exhibited more obvious stuttering with the standard configuration, but that's something we'll need to explore in future testing. It's also worth noting that despite consuming more system memory, SCSKiller didn't always improve frame rates. In another section of the game, performance was much the same between the two configurations. And as we mentioned earlier, SCSKiller can't fix traversal stutter, which remained clearly visible at several points throughout our testing.
Grounded 2
Another game reportedly affected by shader compilation stutter is Grounded 2, so we decided to take a look. However, with the hardware configuration we were testing, we didn't encounter any significant stuttering issues, at least in the sections of the game we examined.
Despite SCSKiller increasing system memory usage by around 5 to 6 GB, there were no measurable performance improvements. In this case, the application simply didn't provide any meaningful benefit.
Hogwarts Legacy
Another game we were particularly keen to investigate was Hogwarts Legacy, especially since the developer of SCSKiller specifically highlights performance improvements in this title. Unfortunately, we couldn't reproduce those improvements in our testing. Initially, we tested using the Ultra quality preset at 4K with Performance upscaling and ray tracing enabled.
Performance remained pretty poor even after running SCSKiller, particularly the 1% lows, and we couldn't identify any meaningful improvements to frame times. What we did see, however, was a substantial increase in system memory usage of over 20%, effectively maxing out our 32 GB capacity.
Concerned that the additional memory consumption might be preventing SCSKiller from delivering an improvement, we decided to retest with ray tracing disabled, which reduced overall memory usage. Unfortunately, that didn't change much. Performance was virtually identical between the two configurations. If anything, the standard configuration was slightly faster, while SCSKiller was now consuming over 50% more system memory without providing any measurable advantage.
Frame pacing was also largely unchanged. In a final attempt to reduce system memory usage, we dropped to the Medium quality preset, again with ray tracing disabled. But once again, frame rates and frame pacing were essentially identical between the two configurations. This time, SCSKiller increased system memory usage by around 25%, still without delivering any meaningful improvement.
So, what's going on here?
It's possible that our hardware configuration was influencing the results, though the SCSKiller developer also reported improvements using an RTX 5090. Alternatively, it could simply be that the section of the game we tested wasn't particularly affected by shader compilation stutter. Either way, we weren't able to reproduce the improvements claimed by the developer, despite testing several graphics configurations.
The Blood of Dawnwalker
The Blood of Dawnwalker is another game we've heard suffers from shader compilation stutter, though in our testing, the issue didn't seem particularly problematic. That said, SCSKiller did manage to deliver a reasonable performance improvement, presumably by making additional compiled shader data available in system memory.
By the end of our test, the 1% lows had improved by 15%, accompanied by a 6% increase in the average frame rate. That's a pretty decent improvement considering the application is free, assuming you have enough storage space and system memory available.
In this example, system memory usage increased by 33%, with SCSKiller consuming approximately 5 GB of additional RAM.
Silent Hill: Townfall
Another relatively new game we decided to examine was Silent Hill: Townfall. Unfortunately, performance was much the same between the two configurations, and SCSKiller wasn't able to eliminate the stuttering we encountered.
In fact, we observed more stuttering with SCSKiller enabled, though it's important to note that this was based on a single pass through the game. That's one limitation of this type of side-by-side testing, as stuttering behavior can vary between runs, so we wouldn't read too much into that particular result. Still, there was no evidence of a meaningful improvement in the section we tested.
Tiny Tina's Wonderlands: A Dramatic Improvement
Now, here's a game we know stutters like absolute buggery. Tiny Tina's Wonderlands is an Unreal Engine 4 title with so much shader compilation stutter that it's almost unplayable at times. And keep in mind, we're testing with a Ryzen 7 9800X3D and GeForce RTX 5090 here. The average frame rate looks pretty impressive, but the 1% lows tell a very different story. They're absolutely horrid.
The game does precompile shaders before you start playing, and while things improve as you spend more time in the same area, moving somewhere new often means it's Stutter City all over again. For example, we left our initial test area for a few minutes before returning. Despite having already explored that section of the game, it didn't take long for the shader compilation stutters to return.
Admittedly, they weren't quite as severe as before, but they remained pretty annoying, especially considering the hardware we were using. This is where SCSKiller really comes into its own. It transformed Tiny Tina's Wonderlands from a stuttery mess into an exceptionally smooth experience, eliminating the constant hitching we had been experiencing.
By the end of our test, the 1% lows had improved from just 45 fps to an incredible 147 fps. More importantly, the constant stuttering and hitching were completely gone in the section we tested. This was one of the most impressive results we'd seen so far, demonstrating SCSKiller can be effective when shader compilation is responsible for poor performance.
However, what happened next was arguably even more interesting.
AMD's Background Shader Compilation: An Unexpected Discovery
Having seen how dramatically SCSKiller improved performance on the RTX 5090 in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, we decided to swap out the GeForce GPU for a Radeon RX 9070 XT. And we're glad we did, because the results were rather puzzling, but in a good way. What we observed was the first few seconds of gameplay after freshly installing the RX 9070 XT along with AMD's latest display driver. SCSKiller hadn't been used at all.
We simply allowed the game to perform its usual shader precompilation process before loading our save file. Yet, despite everything we'd just seen with the RTX 5090, the game ran perfectly smoothly. There was no noticeable stuttering whatsoever. We couldn't quite believe what we were seeing, especially after spending so much time testing the GeForce GPU, where the experience had been a complete mess.
We continued playing, exploring several new areas, but at no point did the game exhibit the same stuttering problems. This left us looking for answers. That's when we came across an extremely brief article on AMD's website titled AMD Software: Adrenalin Edition 26.9.2 Background Shader Compilation. This was the exact driver we were using for our testing. The article explains that AMD has expanded its DirectX 12 background shader processing support to Unreal Engine 5 games.
According to AMD, the functionality was already enabled for Unreal Engine 4 titles, along with several specifically named games, including Borderlands 3, Dirt 5, Cyberpunk 2077, Guardians of the Galaxy, Halo Infinite, and Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. AMD also notes that background shader compilation can reduce initial game loading times, though performance may be temporarily reduced while compilation is taking place. Because shader compilation is CPU-intensive, the time required to complete the process depends on the processor and overall system load.
For benchmarking purposes, AMD recommends allowing approximately 15 minutes of gameplay for background compilation to finish before recording performance measurements. The company also recommends excluding the first run of each new session when using an in-game benchmark. Based on that explanation, AMD appears to be saying that background shader compilation has already been supported in Unreal Engine 4 titles for some time, with Unreal Engine 5 support arriving more recently.
So the bigger news for Radeon owners is that AMD has been working on background shader compilation at the driver level, and its latest update expands that functionality to Unreal Engine 5 games. This was news to us. Admittedly, shader compilation performance isn't something we've investigated in detail for quite some time. There didn't appear to be much progress on the issue, so it had become one of those unfortunate realities of PC gaming that we'd more or less accepted.
But based on what we're seeing in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, AMD appears to have effectively solved shader compilation stutter in this particular game. And what's particularly impressive is how quickly it happens. After a brief shader preparation process, we could simply load into the game and start playing without encountering any noticeable stutters. Meanwhile, the same game remained a complete mess on our GeForce GPUs without SCSKiller.
Tiny Tina's Wonderlands: Radeon vs. GeForce
Despite Tiny Tina's Wonderlands already running perfectly smoothly on the RX 9070 XT, we still wanted to see what would happen if we used SCSKiller. This was also when we discovered the apparent 16 GB shader cache limitation on Radeon GPUs. After precompiling the game's shaders using SCSKiller, we ran the test again and found virtually identical performance. SCSKiller increased system memory usage by approximately 2 GB, but this had no measurable effect on frame rates or frame pacing. In other words, AMD's standard driver configuration was already doing everything we needed.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
For comparison, we also tested the GeForce RTX 5070 under identical conditions, both with the standard driver configuration and after using SCSKiller. As expected, the RTX 5070 suffered from severe shader compilation stutter when running the game normally. However, after using SCSKiller, those issues were completely eliminated in our test. The application also increased VRAM usage by around 4 GB, bringing it roughly in line with what we observed on the Radeon RX 9070 XT.
Comparing the two GPUs with their standard driver configurations reveals how significant AMD's advantage was in this particular game. Although average frame rates were similar, the 1% and 0.1% lows were substantially better on the Radeon GPU, with AMD's background shader compilation apparently doing an excellent job of preventing the constant interruptions we encountered on GeForce.
For a better representation of image quality comparisons, check out the HUB video below:
Now, compare the standard RX 9070 XT configuration against the RTX 5070 after using SCSKiller. Both GPUs delivered exceptionally smooth performance at roughly the same frame rates, with the GeForce GPU actually coming out ever so slightly ahead. That's a good result for SCSKiller, but it's also a demonstration of what AMD's driver is already doing.
What makes this particularly interesting is the amount of preparation required. For the RX 9070 XT, we literally installed the driver, restarted the system, loaded into Windows, and immediately launched Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. After the game's brief initial shader preparation process, we were playing without any issues.
For the RTX 5070 to deliver the same kind of smooth performance, we first had to install SCSKiller and then spend around 30 minutes precompiling shaders. Only after completing that process were we able to achieve the results shown here. So, at least in Tiny Tina's Wonderlands, AMD's driver implementation appears considerably more efficient at preparing shaders and avoiding compilation stutter. Very impressive stuff.
Final Fantasy VII Rebirth: Another Stutter-Filled Experience
Finally, we wanted to compare the RTX 5070 and RX 9070 XT in Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, another game we've heard suffers from severe shader compilation stutter. And unfortunately, those reports appear to be accurate. Starting with the RX 9070 XT, we compared the standard driver configuration against SCSKiller. Neither configuration was flawless.
It's worth noting that Final Fantasy VII Rebirth has a hard 120 fps frame rate cap, which is a little annoying for this type of testing. However, we're primarily interested in the 1% and 0.1% lows anyway, so the cap isn't a major concern. With the standard Radeon driver configuration, 1% lows remained above 60 fps, but there were still noticeable stutters, reflected in the 0.1% low results. SCSKiller certainly helped, though it wasn't able to eliminate every stuttering issue in this particular title.
While the RX 9070 XT wasn't perfect, its performance was considerably better than what we observed with the RTX 5070. In fact, the situation was remarkably similar to Tiny Tina's Wonderlands. With the standard GeForce driver configuration, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth was a stuttery mess. Whereas the Radeon GPU managed to keep its 1% lows above 60 fps, the RTX 5070 suffered from severe performance drops, with its 1% lows falling into single digits. Average frame rates were very similar between the two GPUs, but the 1% and 0.1% lows on the GeForce GPU were terrible.
Then we enabled SCSKiller. After precompiling shaders, the RTX 5070's performance problems were essentially eliminated. The jarring stutters disappeared, 1% lows remained well above 60 fps throughout our testing, and even the 0.1% lows were very good. Frame pacing was excellent, resulting in a completely transformed gaming experience.
We initially captured several minutes of gameplay, but continued playing beyond that and didn't encounter any further issues in the areas we explored. Comparing the RX 9070 XT and RTX 5070 with SCSKiller enabled on both GPUs produced very similar results. Interestingly, SCSKiller consumed more system memory with the RTX 5070 than with the RX 9070 XT. It's possible that this relates to the Radeon driver's more restrictive on-disk shader cache capacity.
Overall, SCSKiller helped improve performance on both GPUs, though the most dramatic improvement was clearly seen on the GeForce side.
Conclusion: Does SCSKiller Actually Work?
SCSKiller certainly took us down a rabbit hole we weren't expecting. At some point, we might conduct a more extensive investigation comparing Radeon and GeForce GPUs across a broader range of hardware configurations and games. For now, though, we can conclude that SCSKiller is genuinely useful and it can improve performance in games affected by shader compilation stutter.
That doesn't mean it's a universal solution. It doesn't address traversal stutter, and even in games where shader compilation is an issue, the benefits can vary significantly depending on the hardware and the sections being tested. In some titles, such as Hogwarts Legacy, we couldn't reproduce the developer's claimed improvements at all. In others, such as Star Wars Jedi: Survivor and The Blood of Dawnwalker, we observed respectable performance gains, even when the standard configuration wasn't exhibiting particularly severe stuttering.
Then there are games like Tiny Tina's Wonderlands and Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, where SCSKiller completely transformed the experience on our GeForce GPUs.
Of course, there are some practical considerations. Compiling shaders can take considerable time, particularly when dealing with thousands of pipelines. You may also need to repeat the process after driver or game updates, and the resulting shader cache can consume a substantial amount of local storage. SCSKiller can also increase system memory consumption considerably, which may or may not be a problem depending on your PC's configuration.
But the good news is that the application itself is free, and there's little downside to trying it in a game you're already having trouble with, provided you're mindful of storage requirements and anti-cheat compatibility. It's straightforward to download and use, and based on our results, certainly worth experimenting with if you're experiencing shader-related stutters.
The Radeon results, however, are a different story, and potentially the more interesting discovery to come out of this testing. Initially, the inability to increase AMD's on-disk shader cache size seemed like a bit of a Radeon fail. And while we'd still like to see AMD provide more control over that limit, if the company continues improving background shader compilation, perhaps it won't be such a significant limitation after all.
We actually spoke with AMD about this, and the company said that while it appreciates third-party applications such as SCSKiller, it also considers itself an industry leader in supporting DirectX 12 Advanced Shader Delivery, which aims to address the same underlying problems through an officially supported approach.
Advanced Shader Delivery is a separate technology developed by Microsoft for Windows 11 and DirectX 12. It allows supported games to download precompiled shaders, reducing the need for compilation on the player's PC and helping prevent stuttering. AMD has been an early supporter of this technology, though its benefits depend on game and platform support.
In any case, there's clearly more testing to be done. We're particularly interested in seeing how AMD's background shader compilation performs across more games, different CPU configurations, and older Radeon hardware. Likewise, SCSKiller deserves a closer look with slower processors, where shader compilation stutter may be even more disruptive. For now, though, we've learned two things: SCSKiller really can work, and AMD's shader compilation improvements might be a bigger deal than we initially realized.

articles.title: TornadoVM 7 Enables GPU-Native Workloads From Java Applications
articles.text:
TornadoVM, an open-source heterogeneous GPU programming framework for Java has reached version 7.3, a major milestone for the project.
InfoQ previously covered the project in December 2025 and in 2022.
TornadoVM automatically accelerates Java programs on multi-core CPUs and GPUs. Rather than replacing existing JVMs, it works alongside them and provides a rich GPU programming ecosystem in Java that you can use with any mainstream JDK distribution such as OpenJDK, Graalvm, Temurin, or Zulu.
It offloads Java code to hardware backends, manages memory between the Java heap and accelerators, and runs the resulting compute kernels. This makes it a useful building block for modern cloud and machine learning workloads.
During development, TornadoVM compiles the source Java code to OpenCL and Apple Metal backends. The idea is that you can develop locally on your laptop and use the hardware available locally, and then deploy into a server that has Nvidia GPUs, and achieve major performance improvements - a form of "Write Once, Run Anywhere" for modern ML workloads.
Version 7 brings several architectural changes. The backends now use the Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API in place of the Java Native Interface (JNI). The experimental JVM Compiler Interface (JVMCI) dependency has also been removed. According to the team, TornadoVM now sources "all compiler metadata through a reflection + ASM + Unsafe layer" which is the single, uniform path on every supported JDK (21, 25, 26 and 27).
The release also deepens integration with the Nvidia ecosystem through an optimized CUDA backend. This includes support for the cuTile programming model (via a new TileContext) and the ability to call CUDA libraries such as cuBLAS and CUTLASS directly from within TornadoVM TaskGraphs. Developers can swap JIT-generated kernels for CUDA library calls, or chain the two together, depending on their performance and portability needs. Similarly, TornadoVM adds the same functionality for Apple's MXL library again via the hybrid API. Finally, support for multi-GPU execution has been added.
Not every Java computation benefits from offloading. The best candidates are data-parallel workloads, such as loops with no dependencies between iterations, because their iterations can run in parallel on the accelerator.
One of the goals of recent TornadoVM versions is to produce an idiomatic JVM environment for accessing the libraries that Nvidia have been tuning for different hardware platforms. The aim is for Java developers to tap into things like Linear Algebra, Fast Fourier Transforms (for Signal Analysis), Deep Neural Networks and hand-optimized matrix multiplication for sparse matrices. TornadoVM has library integrations with Quarkus, Lang4j, Flink, Spring AI and others and is also available through SDKMan.
For example, consider the integration of Apache Flink with TornadoVM - the main idea is that the developer writes a standard query as they normally would with the Table API. A configuration flag is used to indicate that this query should potentially be accelerated on a GPU.
Then, when the computation reaches the task manager, the framework checks if there is a GPU available in the node it is executing on and, if so, it connects to a library provider - which analyzes the intermediate representation (IR) of the query to see if the computation is actually suitable for GPU execution.
In total, TornadoVM offers four ways to program Nvidia GPUs as a Java programmer - Firstly, the parallel API which is really just an annotation that annotates a loop, and provides a hint for the compiler that this loop can be potentially paralyzed. This simple API did not prove to be sufficient in the long-term to get the desired performance for production applications, so additional APIs were added - such as the kernel context API and the already-mentioned TileContext.
Alongside the 7.3 release, the TornadoVM team introduced jitLLM v2.0, its next-generation Java AI inference engine built on TornadoVM. The team positions jitLLM as a direct competitor to llama.cpp and Ollama in performance, and it ships as a single JAR file.
Both TornadoVM and jitLLM are being commercialized through Beestream.ai, a spin-off founded by the TornadoVM team.
Further details can be found on the TornadoVM site, and also in recent videos from Devoxx Belgium, including: "Tap into the NVIDIA Ecosystem from Java with TornadoVM's Hybrid API".

articles.title: Miura 5 entra en fase de ensayos a nivel de sistema y apunta a su primer vuelo de prueba ya en 2027
articles.text:
La compañía española PLD Space acaba de anunciar el comienzo de la fase de ensayos a nivel de sistema de su lanzador Miura 5, con el objetivo de hacer el primer lanzamiento de prueba en 2027. Será el paso inicial hacia la puesta en marcha de este primer lanzador español, que se encargará de poner satélites en órbita de forma recurrente.
Tres vehículos. PLD Space cuenta con tres vehículos relacionados con la preparación de Miura 5. Los dos primeros son unidades de calificación, dirigidas a la realización de ensayos a nivel de sistema. El tercero, en cambio, es el lanzador de vuelo, que actualmente se encuentra en proceso de integración.
Lo ensayado y por ensayar. En un comunicado de prensa, la compañía ha anunciado que, de momento, se ha finalizado el ensayo de la separación de etapas en sus instalaciones de Teruel. Ahora, llega el momento de probar la carga de propelentes y el encendido estático de la segunda etapa, cuyas estructuras y sistemas de aviónica, alimentación, control y propulsión ya se han integrado.
Motores. También se están empezando los ensayos con las primeras unidades de vuelo de los Teprel-C y Teprel-C Vac. De momento se han fabricado e integrado siete motores completos, además de 35 cámaras de combustión, 40 generadores de gas y 15 turbobombas.
Otras piezas que ya están listas. Hay varias piezas de los distintos sistemas de Miura 5 que ya están fabricadas. Es el caso de los tanques de oxígeno líquido de ambas etapas y la mayoría de las placas electrónicas del primer vehículo. También se han terminado los ensayos de los dos modelos de calificación de la cofia. Además, hay 13 tanques completos fabricados, la aviónica de vuelo está al 100% y hay conjuntos para cuatro cohetes.
Operaciones de lanzamiento. Si todo va bien, Miura 5 se lanzará en 2027, desde el Puerto Espacial de Kourou, en la Guayana Francesa. Estas instalaciones están ya en fase de obras y preparación para el lanzamiento. No obstante, si se esperase a probar las operaciones de lanzamiento directamente allí, sería más complicado reparar los posibles fallos que se detectasen. Por eso, ya se están probado los tres equipos que se encargarán de preparar y sujetar el cohete hasta su despegue.
Estos son el strongback, el hold-down y los sistemas umbilicales. El primero se encarga de pasar la nave de posición horizontal a vertical y después sigue sujetándola durante la preparación. Por su parte, el segundo consiste en una serie de anclajes que mantienen el cohete fijo a la base mientras los motores arrancan. Se sueltan justo en el momento del despegue. Finalmente, los sistemas umbilicales son las conexiones por las que el cohete recibe electricidad, datos y fluidos, como los propelentes, hasta justo antes de despegar.
Lo que queda por venir. Cuando se finalicen todas las pruebas en Teruel, ya podría llevarse el cohete a la Guayana Francesa. En declaraciones a Xataka de 2025, el CEO de PLD Space, Raúl Torres, señaló que allí comenzaría una nueva fase de pruebas combinadas con la agencia espacial francesa (CNES). Si todo esto sale bien, Miura 5 estaría listo para el lanzamiento, en el que se intentará ya la reentrada de la primera etapa con el objetivo de recoger datos, sin esperar recuperarla . Es cierto que las fechas han cambiado respecto a las previstas inicialmente, pero ese debería ser el orden de los acontecimientos. Por ahora, todo progresa adecuadamente.

articles.title: DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
articles.text:
DeepSeek open-sources the inference engine behind its API. And Huawei gets equal billing with Nvidia.
DeepSeek has open-sourced the inference engine it uses to serve its models in production, a step it said last year wasn’t yet practical.
Dubbed DeepInfer, the framework is designed to let developers run DeepSeek’s V4.1 Flash model on their own infrastructure, with many of the same optimizations the company uses behind its API. Support for future DeepSeek models is also planned.
“Running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether.”
DeepSeek has, of course, long made its model weights available for developers to download and run using third-party software such as vLLM. But running a model efficiently is a different matter altogether. The software that manages requests, distributes work across chips, and generates responses can have a significant impact on speed, throughput and computing costs. And so DeepInfer essentially gives developers access to DeepSeek’s own approach to those challenges.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable.”
‘Making AI more affordable’
Taking to X on Tuesday, DeepSeek said it was making its internal inference technology available to outside developers in an effort to bring down the expense of running large AI models.
“We’re sharing our production stack to help the community lower compute costs, reduce energy use, and make AI more affordable,” the company writes.
Released under the Apache 2.0 license, DeepInfer includes optimized computing kernels and communication libraries, including DeepSeek’s previously open-sourced FlashMLA, DeepGEMM, and DeepEP, alongside mechanisms for distributing inference across multiple chips. It also supports speculative decoding, a technique that speeds up response generation by predicting and verifying multiple tokens at once, and asynchronous scheduling to reduce the time processors spend waiting for new work. The framework also supports structured outputs, allowing developers to specify how model responses should be formatted.
Alongside DeepInfer, the company is also open-sourcing deepseek-recipe, a companion library that handles how API requests are converted into model inputs, and how the resulting output is processed into responses. Available for Rust and Python, it’s designed to help developers reproduce the behavior of DeepSeek’s official API when running their own deployments. The library was quietly released in September, with an updated version published on Tuesday.
The announcement comes just days after DeepSeek released an updated version of V4.1 Flash, called DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017, touting improvements in coding performance and efficiency. That release coincided with the company making its in-house web search technology available to developers through new Search and Fetch APIs, as per The New Stack‘s report on Monday.
Why DeepSeek held back in 2025
DeepInfer goes further than DeepSeek’s previous plans to share its inference technology. Back in April 2025, the company published a document outlining its plans for its inference engine, explaining that it had considered releasing the entire system before deciding to contribute individual components and improvements to existing projects instead.
At the time, DeepSeek identified several obstacles. Its inference software had evolved from an early version of vLLM into a highly customized system, and the company questioned whether its relatively small research team could maintain another major open-source project. There were also practical difficulties in making the software usable outside DeepSeek’s own infrastructure.
“The engine is tightly coupled with our internal infrastructure, including cluster management tools, making it impractical for public deployment without significant modifications,” the company wrote at the time.
So what’s changed now, exactly? Well, DeepSeek hasn’t explained how it overcame those earlier difficulties, although the scope of the new release offers some clues. The DeepInfer documentation makes clear that the publicly available software currently supports offline inference, with “the core features needed for serving at scale,” as the company puts it. However, several components needed to operate a complete production service are still missing. These include a KV cache management system, infrastructure for separating different stages of inference across machines, and load balancing across replicas.
In other words, DeepSeek has opened up much of the engine responsible for running its models, while leaving developers to supply some of the surrounding infrastructure required to operate a full-fledged service. That narrower release may help explain how the company has made its technology available despite the challenges it identified last year.
Nvidia and Huawei, side by side
While the release of DeepSeek’s inference engine is significant enough in its own right, arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.
“Arguably the more interesting tidbit is the hardware supported from day one.”
Nvidia is included, as expected, though support is restricted to its SM100 architecture, used in Blackwell data center GPUs. Notably, the other supported platform is Huawei’s Ascend 950 NPU series, putting the Chinese chipmaker alongside Nvidia in DeepSeek’s list of compatible hardware. Older Nvidia architectures, including Hopper, are conspicuously absent.
This also ties back to DeepSeek’s published open-source plans from 2025. While the company was reluctant to release its entire inference engine at the time, it committed to working with hardware manufacturers ahead of future model launches, with the aim of making its models available across different chip architectures from day one.
US export restrictions have complicated Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips, adding another dimension to DeepSeek’s growing ties with Huawei. In September, Bloomberg reported that DeepSeek was planning to deploy at least 160,000 Huawei Ascend 950DT chips at a new data center in Inner Mongolia, specifically to run its models. The company has largely relied on Nvidia for training, although The Information reported in September that DeepSeek also plans to increase its use of Huawei chips for training, with deliveries expected as early as the fourth quarter.
Later that month, Reuters reported that DeepSeek and Huawei were collaborating on software tools intended to make Ascend processors easier to program, further underlining the company’s investment in Chinese AI hardware.
The Huawei inclusion has already attracted attention among the wider developer community. In a discussion on Reddit, one commenter singled out the two supported hardware platforms as a highlight of the news, while another pointed to DeepSeek’s origins in quantitative finance as a possible explanation for its technical expertise.
“Once again Deepseek shows how good high-frequency traders are at optimizing performance… On Ascend NPUs nonetheless!!,” the commenter wrote.
Another user seemingly poked fun at Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, following reports that requests involving kernel programming for Huawei’s AI chips could trigger safeguards that redirect certain advanced AI development tasks to an older model.
“Don’t let Opus 5.5 see this! It will delete the Ascend support,” the user joked.
It is worth noting that feature support differs between the Nvidia and Huawei implementations. DeepInfer’s batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling features, which help ensure reproducible outputs under specified conditions, are available only on Nvidia hardware. DeepSeek’s published performance measurements also use Nvidia GPUs, with four SM100 GPUs used for prefill and 64 for decoding, leaving open the question of how the framework performs on Huawei’s chips by comparison.
For developers without access to either chip family, the immediate value may lie in studying the newly available code and adapting its optimizations to other inference engines. For now, DeepSeek has given the wider open-source community considerably more of its inference technology to experiment with.
