Netflix said it has worked with more than 30 local production companies, supported over 8,000 jobs, and carried more than 300 South African titles since 2016. In October, Williams said Netflix now commissions 15 to 20 South African titles annually, up from eight to 12. In September, Netflix announced another large South African slate , and local productions can still travel. Spiro, Africa’s most-funded e-mobility company, has launched its first 100 bikes in Accra, Ghana. The company announced on Tuesday that it is introducing the Ekon 450 M1 v3 motorcycle and a battery-swapping system. Spiro is the latest electric motorcycle company to expand into a new market, after ARC Mobility, the Kenyan-focused e-bike maker, entered South Africa in September. Explain like I’m new here: Spiro’s expansion push is coming amid its fundraising haul. Since the start of 2026, it has raised over $300 million and turned its focus to a battery-swapping network as a moat. With large networks, Spiro makes money from subscriptions, helping it lock in riders. To support its manufacturing ambitions, it acquired UK-based engineering firm Coexlion in May to bring production in-house. This helps it control inventory costs, offering it a predictable way to assess risks for its asset-financing business. articles.title: China Defends DeepSeek After US Ban of Its AI From Government Systems
articles.text:
China hit back Tuesday at a U.S. ban on the use of Chinese artificial intelligence startup DeepSeek’s products by federal civilian agencies and warned of retaliatory measures as the two AI powers race to develop the technology.
The Department of Homeland Security said the agencies should remove DeepSeek products as well as third-party products and services developed using DeepSeek from their IT systems, according to a notice made public on Monday.
The latest warnings reflect “the depth of strategic distrust between Beijing and Washington” even as U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping work hard to keep their personal relationship “warm and constructive,” said George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at Washington-based The Asia Group consultancy.
The Homeland Security order, dating back to late July, also blocks civilian agencies from procuring DeepSeek products and services.
DeepSeek’s open-source models are widely available in countries including the United States, and are mostly free to use.
The notice in the Federal Register alleges that DeepSeek’s models “present multiple threat vectors.” Concerns include that DeepSeek’s servers are located in China and that Chinese authorities could potentially access private company infrastructure and sensitive U.S. data, the order says.
Asked in Beijing about the U.S. ban, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China “will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies.”
“China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security,” she told reporters.
China’s Ministry of Commerce also expressed “strong dissatisfaction and firm opposition” against the U.S.’s move, saying late Tuesday that the U.S. side disregarded the consensus reached between Xi and Trump and ignored the broader landscape of China-U.S. economic and trade relations.
Through discriminatory restrictions under “the guise of national security,” the U.S. is trying to suppress and contain China, the commerce ministry statement said. “China will closely monitor the situation and take all necessary measures to firmly defend its legitimate rights and interests.”
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
China and the U.S. have recently made progress in some collaboration on AI governance, including a U.S. proposal for setting up a notification system on national security-related incidents, but they remain at odds on many issues.
AI is expected to be on the agenda when Trump and Xi meet again in mid-November on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China. The two leaders last met in September as Xi made a state visit to Washington.
U.S.-led restrictions still ban China from accessing some of the world’s most advanced AI chips and the machines that make them.
The U.S. also has said Chinese AI startups including DeepSeek had engaged in large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American AI models, claims that Beijing has dismissed.
And last week, Beijing rolled out its own proposals to restrict exports of certain advanced AI models.
Related: Chinese AI Model Writes More Hackable Code When Told It’s for US Contractor
Related: US Agencies Detail Incident Response Practices for Rogue AI Agents
Related: Think You’ve Eliminated Chinese AI? Check the Model’s Lineage, Cisco Says

articles.title: Thought Industries' Lens checks product knowledge for conflicts before customers see it - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Thought Industries’ Lens checks product knowledge for conflicts before customers see it
Customer learning software company Thought Industries Inc. today launched Lens, an artificial intelligence product that checks a business’ product knowledge for conflicts before it reaches customers.
Thought Industries Academy, its existing course software, joins Lens in a new Customer Knowledge AI Platform.
The launch is seeking to take on the problem of knowledge silos. At many companies, customer and product knowledge lives wherever the team that produced it happens to work. Because AI tools now answer queries from customers from many of those separate sources, the same question can draw two different answers. Customers who get stuck between those answers adopt less of the product, the company said.
Lens connects to the places where business already keeps that material, the help center and product documentation among them. None of it has to move. On top sits what the company calls a governed knowledge layer, where agents inside Lens look for sources that disagree. The business sets the trust rules in plain language. When a product changes, the agents work to bring the affected guidance up to date.
Customers can get answers from Lens inside the product itself or through whatever AI assistant they prefer. The agents can also complete workflows. Logged questions show businesses which parts of a product keep tripping customers up.
Checking for conflicts between sources is what Thought Industries says existing tools lack. It sees Model Context Protocol connectors and the AI built into individual systems as mostly finding information. Chief Executive Irana Wasti said search and retrieval alone do not settle which source is right.
“When every agent is working from a different version of product knowledge, they can simply spread wrong answers faster,” she said. Customers who do get what they need “use more, buy more and stay longer,” according to Wasti.
The Linux Foundation, which runs training and certification programs for open-source software, plans to use Lens. Clyde Seepersad, senior vice president and general manager of education there, said the information its users search for often sits in systems beyond the courseware. The foundation keeps control over what gets surfaced, he said, and the questions coming in should give it “a much clearer picture of what customers need.”
Thought Industries is also changing how it describes its own business. Customer and product leaders are now the stated audience, and the pitch centers on turning scattered knowledge into a competitive advantage. Academy remains the piece that runs courses, learning paths and certifications, with AI recommending what a learner should take next.
Lens is available now in beta. Thought Industries is a private equity-backed company that has sold customer training software since 2013, and Luminate Capital Partners made a strategic growth investment in it in 2019.

articles.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand.
Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization.
In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents.
The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK. While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
About Keyfactor EJBCA
Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance.
EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).
The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments.
Solution overview
The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table.
| Layer | Trust boundary | Mechanism | Validates | 
| 1. User Auth | User to System | OAuth + X.509 cert + delegation minting | User identity, credential binding | 
| 2. Agent-to-Agent | Agent to Agent | Signed envelopes (PoP + nonce + timestamp) | Caller identity, request freshness, no replay | 
| 3. MCP Auth | Agent to Tool Server | Scoped token + envelope + delegation | All identities, authorization chain, OCSP | 
Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them.
Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup.
AWS services used
The following AWS services form the foundation of the reference architecture.
| Service | Purpose | 
| Amazon Bedrock | LLM inference through Strands Agents SDK | 
| Amazon RDS for MySQL | Application database accessed through MCP tools | 
| Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) | Email delivery for the Email Agent | 
| AWS Secrets Manager | Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata | 
| Amazon EC2 | Hosts Keycloak IDP and EJBCA PKI server | 
Solution walkthrough
The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution.
Prerequisites
- An active AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon SES, and AWS Secrets Manager.
- Keycloak 26.2 or later (required for RFC 8693 standard token exchange. Previous versions use a legacy exchange that is incompatible).
- Keyfactor EJBCA Enterprise with REST API V1 and an OCSP responder configured.
- EJBCA API administrator certificate (api-admin.p12) for REST API authentication.
- Python 3.9+ development environment.
- Familiarity with X.509 certificates, OCSP, OAuth 2.0, RSA digital signatures, and PKCS#12 key stores.
Step 1: User login, certificate issuance, and delegation minting
The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token.
First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization.
Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role.
Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate.
Step 2: Agent-to-agent signed envelopes
When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with RSA-PSS-SHA256. The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.
The receiving agent performs six validation checks on the envelope before processing the request:
- Signature verification: Proves the sender possesses the private key (proof-of-possession).
- Timestamp freshness: The envelope must be within ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (default 60 seconds) of the current time.
- Nonce uniqueness: The ReplayCache rejects any previously seen nonce, preventing request replay.
- CA chain validation: The sender’s certificate must chain to the trusted CA (UserCA.pem).
- Role authorization: The certificate CN’s role suffix must be in ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES for this agent.
- OCSP revocation check: A real-time check against EJBCA confirms the certificate has not been revoked.
If the orchestrator needs to re-send the same prompt (for example, after a transient failure), it must create a new envelope with a fresh nonce. Old envelopes can’t be replayed, even by the legitimate sender.
Step 3: MCP server authentication
The MCP server (FastMCP) is the final trust boundary before any database operation runs. It performs four validation checks on every tool invocation, implementing defense-in-depth. Even if one credential is subject to unauthorized access, the remaining checks prevent unauthorized operations.
The authentication sequence:
- Token introspection: A POST to the Keycloak /token/introspect endpoint verifies the token is active and its audience contains “mcp-server”. A full-session token without the correct audience is rejected.
- Envelope verification: The agent’s signed envelope is validated for signature correctness, timestamp freshness, nonce uniqueness, CA chain trust, role match (mysql-agent), and OCSP non-revocation.
- Delegation verification: The user’s delegation assertion is validated. The signature proves the user’s key holder authorized this delegation, the calling agent’s certificate fingerprint appears in the authorized list, and the user’s certificate is checked through OCSP.
- Identity cross-check: The token username, the delegation subject, and the agent certificate CN prefix must all match. This confirms a single consistent identity chain from user through to tool execution.
Step 4: Replay prevention
Every signed envelope carries a unique nonce, a 128-bit cryptographically random hex string generated with Python’s secrets module. The ReplayCache is a thread-safe in-memory store that remembers every nonce until its freshness window expires (2x ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS). If the same nonce appears in a second request, the envelope is immediately rejected, even if its signature is valid and the timestamp is fresh.
The timestamp validation complements the nonce check. An envelope’s timestamp must be within ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (default 60 seconds) of the server’s current time. Together, these mechanisms address four unauthorized access scenarios:
- Recorded replay: An unauthorized user captures a valid envelope and resubmits it later. The nonce was already seen.
- Delayed delivery: An envelope intercepted in transit arrives after the freshness window. The timestamp check fails.
- Stale request reuse: An old envelope cached by a proxy is resubmitted. Both nonce and timestamp checks fail.
- Precomputed forgery: An unauthorized user cannot predict future nonces to pre-sign envelopes.
Step 5: Client-side key generation
A critical security property of this architecture is that private keys are generated locally and never transmitted to any external system. The application generates RSA 2048+ key pairs using the Python cryptography library. It constructs a CSR containing only the public key and subject information, and sends only the CSR to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll endpoint.
EJBCA validates the CSR, applies the certificate profile (7-day validity, key usage constraints), signs it with the CA key, and returns the issued certificate. The application then bundles the locally held private key with the returned certificate into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager.
This design provides several security properties:
- The user’s private key is used only at login to sign the delegation assertion. It’s never shared with agents.
- Each agent’s private key is used only by that agent to sign envelopes. It’s never shared between agents.
- EJBCA never sees or stores private keys. It operates purely as a certificate authority.
- If Secrets Manager is subject to unauthorized access, the PKCS12 password (stored separately) adds an additional layer.
- Key material can be rotated independently by re-enrolling with a new CSR at next login.
Step 6: Complete logout and credential revocation
Logout triggers a revocation cascade that immediately invalidates all outstanding credentials. The sequence results in no remaining valid credentials after completion:
- Revoke user certificate in EJBCA: This immediately invalidates all outstanding delegations, because delegation verification checks the user’s certificate through OCSP in real time.
- Revoke all three agent certificates: This invalidates all outstanding signed envelopes, since envelope verification includes OCSP.
- Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager: Using ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery for immediate removal with no recovery window.
- Terminate Keycloak session: Invalidates the downscoped token through the session termination endpoint.
The revocation cascade is the key security property. Revoking a single user certificate at the PKI layer promptly revokes all downstream agent authority without needing to individually revoke tokens, delete sessions, or contact each agent. OCSP provides the propagation mechanism, and because every request checks OCSP, the effect is immediate.
Security considerations
The design choices in this architecture address several security properties that are important for production multi-agent deployments.
Private key isolation. The user’s private key exists only during the login flow and is used solely to sign the delegation. Agent keys are scoped per-agent and never shared. No key material crosses trust boundaries.
Delegation compared to credential sharing. Agents prove their authority through a cryptographic chain (delegation to agent fingerprint to envelope signature) without ever holding user credentials. If an agent key is exposed, only that agent’s key is revealed, not the user’s.
Audience-scoped tokens. RFC 8693 token exchange produces a token accepted only by the MCP server. An inadvertently disclosed downscoped token cannot authenticate against Keycloak admin APIs, other services, or even a different MCP server instance.
Replay prevention. The combination of per-request nonces and a 60-second freshness window confirms that every request is single-use and time-bound. The ReplayCache is thread-safe and self-cleaning.
Fail-closed design. Every validation failure results in immediate denial. OCSP unreachable: deny. Invalid signature: deny. Expired timestamp: deny. Replayed nonce: deny. Wrong audience: deny. There’s no graceful degradation for security checks.
Revocation cascade. Revoking one user certificate promptly invalidates all delegations, all agent authority, and all outstanding envelopes. This is propagated through real-time OCSP without requiring individual credential cleanup.
Forward-only trust chain. The ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES map enforces that only orchestrator-agent can call mysql-agent and email-agent. Sub-agents cannot call each other, can’t call upward to the orchestrator, and cannot impersonate the user.
AI governance considerations
The PKI architecture provides built-in behavior boundaries for the AI agents in this system. Production deployments should use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering, topic avoidance, and grounding checks on agent responses, alongside the PKI-based access controls described in this post.
- Tool boundaries: The AI agent operates under strict tool constraints. It can only invoke pre-defined MCP tools (execute_sql, describe_table, list_tables). The agent can’t execute arbitrary code or access resources outside its certificate scope.
- Human oversight: All agent actions are logged and auditable. AWS CloudTrail captures AWS API calls, and the MCP server logs every validated tool invocation with the full identity chain (user, agent, timestamp, and operation).
- Data handling: User queries and results stay within the authenticated session boundary. The audience-scoped token confines data access to the specific MCP server instance.
- Certificate-based behavior boundaries: Agents can only invoke tools they hold valid certificates for. An agent without a mysql-agent certificate cannot access the database, regardless of what the LLM might generate as instructions.
Extending the architecture
You can extend this architecture to support additional agent types, horizontal scaling, and multi-tenant isolation. The following paragraphs describe the most common extension points.
- To add new agent types, you only need to add an entry in ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES. Certificates are automatically issued at login, and the delegation assertion dynamically includes the new agent’s fingerprint. No infrastructure changes are required.
- For horizontal scaling, you can deploy EJBCA’s OCSP responder in high-availability mode behind a load balancer. AWS Secrets Manager supports high request rates suitable for this workload. The ReplayCache can be backed by Amazon ElastiCache for distributed deployments.
- To harden the architecture for production, you can use hardware security module (HSM)-backed EJBCA signing keys through AWS CloudHSM or an on-premises HSM. OCSP response stapling reduces validation latency, and Certificate Transparency logs provide a full audit trail of issued certificates.
- For multi-tenant deployments, you can create per-tenant Certificate Authorities or per-tenant delegation authorities for cryptographic tenant isolation. Combined with per-tenant AWS accounts, this delivers strong isolation between tenants.
- You can also complement PKI-based agent identity with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Use PKI for agent-to-agent authentication and IAM for AWS service authorization. The two systems work independently, providing defense in depth.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources created during this walkthrough:
- Delete the Amazon RDS for MySQL instance (or the AWS CloudFormation stack if you used the scripted setup).
- Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, including user certificates and agent certificates under the mcp/ prefix.
- Remove the verified sender email address from Amazon SES.
- Terminate the Amazon EC2 instances running Keycloak and EJBCA (if deployed for this demonstration).
- Revoke and delete all test certificates in EJBCA by using the EJBCA admin console or REST API.
- Remove the Keycloak realm (mcp-realm) and associated clients.
- If you used the scripted setup, run ./scripts/cleanup.sh (Linux) or ./scripts/cleanup.bat (Windows) to automate these steps.
Conclusion
In this post, we demonstrated a reference architecture for securing AI agent communications using X.509 PKI with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. The architecture addresses the fundamental identity gap in multi-agent AI systems through four complementary mechanisms:
- Signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every inter-agent call, making it significantly harder for an unauthorized party to forge an agent’s identity or replay its requests.
- User-signed delegation assertions decouple authorization from credential sharing. Agents prove they are authorized to act on the user’s behalf without holding the user’s private key or full-session token.
- RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any token disclosure to a single service boundary.
- Real-time OCSP revocation checking confirms that credential revocation takes immediate effect across the entire system. Revoking one user certificate promptly ends all downstream agent authority.
This architecture is framework-agnostic. While we demonstrated it with the AWS Strands Agents SDK and FastMCP, the same PKI patterns apply to LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, or any other multi-agent framework that uses tool protocols. As AI agents proliferate and gain access to increasingly sensitive operations, agent identity infrastructure moves from optional to essential.
To get started with this reference architecture, see the accompanying GitHub repository. For more information about the services used, see the following resources:

articles.title: Eindhoven-based Photon Bridge raises €10 million to build optical engines for AI and telecom | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Photon Bridge (formerly Photon IP), an Eindhoven-based startup building optical engines for AI and telecom, has raised €10 million to tackle an emerging bottleneck in AI infrastructure: producing the millions of lasers needed to connect increasingly large clusters of AI processors.
New investors, the Amadeus APEX Technology Fund and 360 Capital, co-led the round, while existing investors Innovation Industries, Faber, and Brabant Development Agency (BOM) also increased their investment. In January 2025, the company announced it had secured a €4.75 million Seed round led by Innovation Industries.
“Every new wave of compute creates new bottlenecks further down the supply chain, and lasers are the next one. Photon Bridge is addressing this with a technology that combines deep photonics expertise with a credible path towards manufacturing at very large scale,” said Ion Hauer, Investment Partner at APEX Ventures.
Photon Bridge was founded in 2020 in Eindhoven by Rui Santos and Xaveer Leijtens to rethink how high-performance photonic systems are built at scale. The company says it is building laser sources for a market expected to need millions of units as optical connections move closer to AI chips.
It develops high-power, multi-wavelength laser-source technology for next-generation optical interconnects in AI data centres.
According to the startup, data transfer between processors is becoming a performance constraint as AI clusters expand from thousands to hundreds of thousands of chips. It notes that optical connections can move enormous amounts of data faster and more efficiently than conventional electrical interconnects, prompting their integration closer to processors.
It also notes that this shift is accelerating with the emergence of co-packaged optics, which integrates optical connectivity directly alongside the chips that move data through AI systems. The startup says that this, in turn, drives demand for the lasers that supply light to these connections.
“Today’s high-power laser supply chain was largely built for telecom and subsea networks, where volumes are far lower. AI could transform the laser from a specialist photonics component into something that has to be manufactured at semiconductor scale. Photon Bridge has designed its technology around that transition,” the company mentioned in the press release
Rather than generating the required optical power using a small number of increasingly powerful lasers, Photon Bridge claims that it combines and multiplexes light from multiple lower-power semiconductor lasers.
The Dutch startup says this approach reduces power densities, making individual lasers less sensitive to manufacturing defects, improving production yield and allowing Photon Bridge’s architecture to scale more efficiently as volumes increase.
The platform is designed to deliver high wavelength counts with up to 40 mW of optical power per wavelength per fibre, while enabling production across multiple indium phosphide (InP) foundries.
In September 2025, Photon IP rebranded as Photon Bridge and appointed Paul Marchal as CEO.
Marchal, CEO of Photon Bridge, said, “AI is fundamentally changing the way computing infrastructure is built. We are moving towards enormous systems in which hundreds of thousands of processors have to operate together, and moving data between them is becoming one of the defining constraints on performance.
“That means optics has to move closer to the compute. But it also creates an entirely different manufacturing challenge. The industry will soon need millions of these laser sources every year. Instead of making individual lasers increasingly powerful and difficult to manufacture, we move that scaling challenge into the architecture.”
Photon Bridge highlights that its approach is designed around manufacturing yield, a consideration that becomes increasingly important as laser production shifts from traditional telecom volumes to the scale required by AI infrastructure.
“AI is turning lasers from a telecom component into a semiconductor-scale product. Once you start talking about millions of units a year, manufacturing yield becomes fundamental. Photon Bridge has designed its architecture from the beginning around the volumes this market is going to require,” said Cesare Maifredi, Partner at 360 Capital.
The company plans to use this capital to accelerate product development and customer qualification, deliver its first samples in 2027, and prepare for volume manufacturing from 2028. Photon Bridge will also expand its Eindhoven team as it moves toward commercialisation.

articles.title: Quantum error correction goes well beyond breakeven
articles.text:
Running complicated algorithms on quantum computing hardware is going to require the use of logical qubits, where collections of hardware qubits are linked together in ways that allow errors to be detected and corrected. In general, the more hardware qubits you dedicate to each logical qubit, the better the chances are of identifying errors. But, given that the hardware qubits are prone to errors, adding more of them also increases the probability that errors will occur. If the hardware error rate is too high, then growing the logical qubit will only make matters worse.
Fortunately, several companies have demonstrated hardware where the error rate is not too high. Several demonstrations show logical qubits are beyond the breakeven point, where adding more qubits improves performance. The problem is that the improvement isn’t very dramatic. To lower error rates to levels we’ll need to run complex algorithms, we’d have to add a completely impractical number of qubits to each logical qubit.
On Monday, Quantinuum announced that its current generation of hardware is capable of scaling well beyond the breakeven point. Each step up in the size of logical qubits improved some measures of their performance by a factor of over 10.
Error correction codes and scaling
To understand the results, we must take a little detour through the ideas behind error correction. A logical qubit consists of a set of qubits that hold data, and another set that is used for measurements, all of them entangled to others. There are various error correction “codes,” each of which has a different geometry of entangled connections among its constituent qubits. During operations, measurements of the appropriate qubits produce what’s called “syndrome data,” which can be interpreted to provide an indication of whether an error has occurred within the logical qubit, as well as where and its nature.
Depending on their geometry, error codes have a number of key properties: how many hardware qubits are needed for it to work, how many individual logical qubits it hosts, and something called the distance, which is a rough measure of how many errors can occur simultaneously before the logical qubit fails.
Members of some families of error correction codes differ in a fairly simple way: Each step up in size (which may require multiple hardware qubits) means a greater distance. So by adding more hardware qubits, you can create a similar geometry while providing a greater distance.
These sorts of codes can be used to measure how well a given quantum processor’s error correction scales. You start by measuring the error rate of the logical qubit with a small distance, say three. Then you can devote more hardware qubits to the text and measure it at a distance of five, repeat the process for a distance of seven, and so on until you run out of hardware qubits to add.
If the hardware is past the breakeven point, then the error rate will be lower with each step up in distance. And the scaling factor—how much better the error rate gets at each step—gives you a sense of how far beyond breakeven it is. This matters a great deal for practical reasons. If each step up in size cuts the error rate by a factor of 10, then you only have to step up in distance a few times to get the error rate down by a considerable amount. If, by contrast, the scaling factor is closer to two, then you have to go up in distance many, many times to get the same effect.
So far, most demonstrations of scaling beyond the breakeven point have seen the error rate drop by something much closer to two than 10. Which may mean that we’d need to add many thousands of hardware qubits to the logical qubit just to get the error rate down to what we’d need to run a complex algorithm.
Meet Helios
Quantinuum builds what are called trapped ion quantum computers. As their name implies, each qubit is stored in an ion, an atom that has lost one or more of its electrons. Because they are charged, it’s possible to manipulate these using electrical fields generated by electronics, moving them around and rearranging them. The company’s latest hardware, called Helios, rotates the ions around a ring, selectively shifting the appropriate ones into one of two arms where measurements and operations of the ions’ quantum states can be performed using lasers. Because any two ions can be brought into these arms at the same time, it’s possible to entangle any ion with any other, providing Helios the ability to host essentially any error code.
In general, the company’s hardware has relatively low error rates. But previous iterations didn’t have enough qubits to increase the distance of logical qubits very much. But with Helios, the company finally had the ability to use versions of an error correction code (called a color code) with distances of three, five, and seven (though it only has enough hardware qubits to host a single distance of seven logical qubits at a time).
In addition, Quantinuum has made a key change in how its processor operates. A significant number of errors in earlier Quantinuum processors occurred through what’s called “leakage.” This occurs when a qubit, instead of occupying one of the two energy states used for calculations, ends up in a nearby energy state that’s not normally used. Now, the company is using a scheme that uses laser light to selectively manipulate those qubits that have leaked into other energy states and bring them back to one of the two used for computation. This suppresses leakage errors by a factor of 6.5 and can be done at the same time the system is using lasers to cool the ions.
It has also developed a software-based system that can take any leaked data-holding qubits and swap them out for measurement qubits, which can then be reset and reused.
Color coding
For one of the two experiments the company is announcing today, the company was able to use 13 hardware qubits to build a distance three color code, 37 for distance five, and 73 hardware qubits to get a distance seven logical qubit. These were then used to estimate the error rate that occurs when the logical qubits are simply used to hold onto the same state, essentially acting as a form of quantum memory. The performance of the hardware is good enough now, however, that just doing one round of error correction and measuring can’t provide an accurate measure of how often problems occur—errors are too rare. So instead, the team did 20 rounds of error correction before measuring to determine whether the memory had been maintained.
To get this to work, the system had to take the syndrome data obtained from querying the measurement qubits and figure out the nature of any errors that were detected. As the distance of the error correction code goes up, it gets increasingly challenging to perform this analysis rapidly enough to keep it from becoming a bottleneck. The Quantinuum team showed that they had three different pieces of software, each able to operate in real time: a standard algorithm, a convolutional neural network, and a transformer-based neural network.
For the distance three color code, the logical error rate was about 5 x 10-4. Stepping up to the distance five code brought that down to about 4 x 10-5, and the distance seven code saw another order-of-magnitude drop, down to 5 x 10-6. Overall, each step up in distance reduced the logical error rate by roughly a factor of 12. That is, to my knowledge, the best scaling seen yet.
Another important step that was done here is showing that the syndrome data from one round only correlates with the data from the one immediately before and immediately after. This indicates that there are no systemic sources of error that are biasing the error-detection process.
Of course, performing actual operations involves doing considerably more to the logical qubits than allowing them to just sit still and hold their state. So, the researchers also looked at the logical error rate associated with performing a relatively simple two-qubit gate operation. Unfortunately, this requires using two logical qubits, and the Helios processor isn’t able to hold more than one distance seven error code at a time. So instead, the researchers compared using hardware qubits directly and using distance three and five color codes.
Running these two-qubit gates directly on the hardware produced an error rate of about 10-3, and the distance three code didn’t improve things dramatically. But the distance five code dropped the logical error rate to about 7 x 10-5. So, the hardware seems to be well beyond breakeven, even when it’s being asked to perform relatively complicated tasks.
That other scaling
These results can be viewed a couple of different ways. From the “no big deal” perspective, even the best logical error rate is still too high to perform complicated algorithms, and getting there had some major drawbacks: it was only seen when operations weren’t being performed on the qubit, and the system is only big enough to host one of these. We still have a long way to go before we’re ready to perform lots of error-corrected operations at a potentially useful error rate.
From a more optimistic perspective, this is the best scaling I’m aware of, and the performance suggests that getting the hardware error rate down a bit further could have significant payoffs. The logical error rate depends on the hardware error rate in a way that means that, once things get good enough, then small improvements can have very large impacts on the logical error rate. The scaling seen here doesn’t tell us that we’re at that point, but it is suggestive that we’re getting close.
The main question for Quantinuum is whether it can scale its qubit counts as effectively as its roadmap suggests it will. If so, it may not need to drop its hardware error rate much to start being able to generate useful logical qubits. That may mean solving somewhat different problems than some of its competitors, who will need to do different combinations of dropping the hardware error rate, boosting qubit counts, or figuring out how to integrate multiple functional units into a single computer.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

articles.title: NVIDIA Cloud Partners Scale Across Europe — Sovereign, Open and Built for Safe AI Agents
articles.text:
Demand from AI-natives is pulling the European AI cloud ecosystem forward faster than ever. Developers need compute closer to their data, open models they can customize and serve at scale, and full-stack infrastructure that is secure by design.
NVIDIA Cloud Partners across Europe, the Nordics, Africa, and Central Asia are expanding regional compute capacity for model training and inference, helping developers build agentic and physical AI applications, and establishing boundaries around what agents can access and do.
Together, they’re turning Europe’s energy, data, research and industrial expertise into productive intelligence — supporting new models, applications, organizations and jobs while giving people more control over where and how they develop and deploy AI.
Sovereign: AI Clouds Building European AI Infrastructure
Europe is home to world-class research, engineering talent, industrial expertise, data, the next generation of models and applications that requires large-scale computing close to where that knowledge resides. Regional AI clouds provide the infrastructure foundation on which model builders, enterprises and entire industries can grow.
As AI factories scale, power becomes a constraint which makes it critical for every watt to produce more intelligence. Nscale is using the NVIDIA DSX Platform to coordinate power allocation with workload requirements. In tests using NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems, Nscale demonstrated that NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS enabled 37% more GPUs and nearly 50% higher aggregate inference throughput within the same provisioned power budget.
Nscale also plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure for frontier-model training and production workloads to support leading model and application builders using its full-stack, vertically integrated platform with expansion across five European markets.
Crusoe is developing Spark, its liquid-cooled modular AI factories designed for the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, to bring Crusoe Cloud capacity closer to users for low-latency AI inference. Crusoe Cloud serves leading model and application builders across EMEA, including Base44, Gradium, LTX and Wonderful.
Aleria, Cassava Technologies, Firebird, G42, Radiant, SWI Compute and Vultr are also developing and expanding NVIDIA-powered AI infrastructure across Europe, the Nordics, Africa and Central Asia.
Regional capacity from AI clouds combines the full-stack NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform, including NVIDIA Vera Rubin, NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, giving customers greater choice and control over where workloads and data reside while advancing sovereign computing services and economic growth.
Open: Models and Libraries, From Training to Inference
Across the ecosystem, AI clouds are expanding NVIDIA-powered infrastructure and services for developers to build applications with open models and libraries. This new capacity supports model training, fine-tuning for specialized tasks and inference at scale, including applications deployed at the edge.
For production inference, Nebius has adopted NVIDIA Groq 3 LPX, using Spectrum-X Ethernet networking to integrate it with Vera Rubin NVL72 on Nebius Token Factory. The combination will bring faster token generation to latency-sensitive applications and agentic systems through the platform’s managed serverless and dedicated endpoints and familiar application programming interfaces.
For robotics and physical AI, Nebius offers a purpose-built AI cloud solution that includes its full-stack Physical AI Workbench. Robotics companies including Rhoda AI, RoboForce and Sereact are building on the platform. The company also launched three NVIDIA retail agent blueprints — covering inventory, store operations, and fine-tuning —- into early access on Nebius infrastructure.
Nebius is expanding its cloud services widely across the continent with its Physical AI Living Lab, and in Germany as a computer supplier for the Next Frontier Challenge of SPRIND, the Federal Agency for Breakthrough Innovation.
Baseten has developed a specialized model for code-review routing with Nemotron 3.5 Lightning used by CodeRabbit. Through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, CodeRabbit improved routing agreement from 75.8% to 80.7% while reducing estimated inference costs by 50% for the evaluated workload. The results demonstrate how AI developers can customize NVIDIA open models for specialized tasks while improving accuracy and inference efficiency.
Fireworks and Era4 are partnering to bring open models to enterprises across the U.K. and Europe. The collaboration combines Fireworks’ model training and inference platform with direct liquid-cooled capacity powered by NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at Era4’s Chesterfield facility, supporting plans for enterprise AI solutions in financial services, insurance and life sciences.
Mistral is expanding its NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure to support model training, customization and inference. The expansion includes NVIDIA Vera Rubin infrastructure planned for delivery in 2027. Trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral-operated European data centers, Mistral Large 4 is the company’s latest frontier multimodal model, advancing capabilities across coding, agentic workflows and multimodal understanding.
Verda plans to deploy NVIDIA Vera Rubin, continuing to promote open weight models with NVIDIA Nemotron and NVIDIA Cosmos already in production, and using the NVIDIA Dynamo open source framework for inference optimization.
Safe: Secure Boundaries for AI Agents, From Silicon to Software
As developers connect models to tools and business systems, they also need controls over what agents can access and do.
Announced at GTC Berlin, the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture with support from AI cloud ecosystem partners. Built on the foundation of NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software, the architecture is designed to give organizations full-stack control to deploy AI agents with clear boundaries around what agents can access and do.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 for model inference, NVIDIA Vera CPUs with OpenShell for agent harnesses and tool use, and NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs running NVIDIA Sentry for in-silicon enforcement. Each play a distinct role in delivering that control, working together so agents can achieve what they’re meant to do without moving beyond the boundaries people set for them.
Partners including Aleria, Baseten, Cassava, CoreWeave, Crusoe, DigitalOcean, Firebird, Fireworks, Firmus, G42, GMI Cloud, IREN, Lambda, Lightning AI, Nebius, Nscale, Radiant Verda and Vultr are supporting the OpenShell Reference Architecture to enable secure agentic deployments for their customers.
Together, European AI clouds are connecting regional infrastructure investment with the work of building and deploying AI. Expanded capacity gives builders more places to run workloads. Model and inference services help them put that capacity to use. Agent controls address what applications are allowed to do as they move into production.
Explore NVIDIA Cloud Partners for infrastructure and services, and the OpenShell Reference Architecture for agent deployment controls.

articles.title: Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
articles.text:
Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
If you've ever wanted to run Windows 98 SE on your mid-2010s or newer PC with fast USB hub support, here's your chance.
Windows 98 SE devotees can now enjoy (experimental) support for USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4. Developer and maker Yeo Kheng Meng, who also enjoys retrocomputing, recently released the vibe-coded xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, enabling the practical use of generic USB 3.x, USB4, and Thunderbolt 3/4 host controllers on systems running Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. An extensive blog post by the dev provides further reading about the driver, compatibility, its creation, and usage.
Demo video “shows many different USB devices being hotplugged to a modern 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 with only xHCI controller.”
Some of you will be wondering why a project to bring USB4 (Thunderbolt 3 and 4) to PCs running Windows 98 SE exists. Retro computing fan Meng explains on his GitHub that this project should appeal directly to users of PCs from the mid-2010s that have xHCI-only (USB 3.x) chipsets and no legacy EHCI controller. However, older OSes don’t have xHCI drivers, and that’s where xHCI98 steps in. “Without xHCI support, even keyboards, mice, and flash drives need the BIOS's legacy support, cannot be hotplugged, and devices such as Ethernet and audio do not work at all,” explains Meng, revealing his motivation. “This project fills that gap.”
Impressively, xHCI98 drives a lot more than USB storage. It replaces Windows’ own USB port and hub drivers to facilitate the connection and use of USB 1.1 and 2.0 and SuperSpeed (USB 3.x) devices and hubs, UAS (USB Attached SCSI) storage through a second driver (xhciuas.sys), and Thunderbolt 3 and USB4 docks and NVMe enclosures through a third driver (xhcicm.sys).
Meng has developed and tested xHCI98 mostly on Intel hardware, as that is what he owns. Candidly, he admits “this is a solo human's project with AI assistance, so bugs are not unexpected,” even if you do have the same hardware as the dev - a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 (Comet Lake xHCI, no EHCI). It stands up pretty well during the plug/unplug video demo above, though the test rig used is not quite the USB cart of death.
As a solo developer, Meng isn't shy to admit he leaned heavily on AI assistance to prepare the xHCI98 release. His vibe coding adventure was supported by Claude Fable 5.1 for planning, Claude Opus 5.5 for coding, and Codex GPT 6 Astra as an adversarial reviewer.
In addition to a few bug warnings, there are some other things to know about using this driver with the various older versions of Windows it supports, standby and hibernation, and more. The dev helpfully sketches out a process for checking your hardware, outlines various install methods, discusses updating, and talks about tuning the driver for those who will be jumping in at the deep end with this project.

articles.title: Lucasfilm VP suggests more Star Wars games could be in the cards following Galactic Racer and Zero Company's success, says 'huge triple-A games like Battlefront' are 'essential' but not 'the goal' — 'Good ideas can come from a lot of different places. You don’t have to necessarily be a top five publisher to make a great Star Wars game'
articles.text:
'One of the great things about Star Wars is it has all kinds of other opportunities to tell stories in different genres' — Lucasfilm VP says 'the goal' is 'to find the best partner' to make more games like Galactic Racer and Zero Company
The VP says, "Good ideas can come from a lot of different places," including indie studios
- Lucasfilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly suggests more Star Wars games could be made following the success of Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Star Wars: Zero Company
- Reilly says that while "huge triple-A games like Battlefront are always going to be an essential part of the strategy," the "goal" is to find "the best partner"
- This goes for both triple-A and smaller independent studios
It sounds like Lucasfilm Games wants to release more Star Wars games following the success of Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Star Wars: Zero Company, but it's not necessarily looking for triple-A studio pitches.
That's according to Lucasfilm Games vice president Douglas Reilly, who told The Game Business that games developed by independent studios "very much is part of the strategy."
"Obviously, huge triple-A games like Battlefront are always going to be an essential part of the strategy," Reilly added. "But one of the great things about Star Wars is it has all kinds of other opportunities to tell stories in different genres.
Reilly said, "The goal has been to find the best partner who makes that experience come alive inside the galaxy far, far away," and it doesn't necessarily "have to always be triple-A."
"Sometimes it can be double-A, and it’s really about the experience that we’re delivering and the fantasy we’re fulfilling," he said, adding that Lucasfilm Games has "tried to be more flexible about who we’re willing to take pitches from."
Saber Interactive is quietly working on its Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic remake, which it confirmed is still in development, while a new game from Arcnaut Studios and Mass Effect trilogy director Casey Hudson, Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic, is now in the works.
In addition, a new report has now claimed that Destiny developer Bungie and DICE are "aggressively" pursuing a Star Wars: Battlefront 3 project, but official confirmation has yet to come in.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
"Good ideas can come from a lot of different places," Reilly continued. "You don’t have to necessarily be a top five publisher to make a great Star Wars game. There are some hurdles.
"We have a high-quality bar, and that means typically we work with more experienced teams than ones with no track record. But we’re exploring all kinds of things, large and small, with partners that are going to surprise folks."
I reviewed both Star Wars: Galactic Racer and Star Wars: Zero Company, and they're among the best games of the year. Galactic Racer is the Star Wars racing game I've always wanted and an exhilarating roguelike racer with endless customization, while Zero Company acts as an excellent companion story to the Clone Wars era with immensely fun turn-based tactics gameplay.

articles.title: Eric Schmidt reportedly owns about half as much of Anthropic as CEO Dario Amodei | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Eric Schmidt’s fortune is about to get even bigger. The former Google CEO is reported to own about 1% of Anthropic after investing tens of millions of dollars in the leading AI lab’s Series A round in 2021, per Bloomberg. The startup was valued at $461 million at the time, according to PitchBook data.
If Bloomberg’s estimate is accurate, Schmidt’s stake is remarkably large compared with the 2% of the company that co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei holds. Anthropic is widely expected to go public before the end of the year, with top-end market estimates valuing the company at as much as $2 trillion. At that valuation, Schmidt would add as much as $20 billion to his net worth, which Bloomberg currently puts at $57.5 billion.
Schmidt has been an active tech investor since stepping down as Google CEO in 2011. He deploys capital through multiple entities, including Tomorrow Ventures, Innovation Endeavors Management, and his family office, Hillspire. His other AI bets include Mistral, General Intuition, and Reflection AI.
Schmidt and Anthropic didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment.

articles.title: We can do impossible things
articles.text:
We can do impossible things
It’s all too easy to lose sight of ambition when we’re busy playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems.
I’d wager everyone has a rehearsed response to what’s absolutely one of the world’s worst interview questions: “What’s your biggest weakness?” Whenever I’ve gotten it, I take a slow—even pensive—breath and rattle off my line: “I say no to myself too much.”
I won’t lie. It’s a bit shameless—a definite humblebrag. I’m a systems thinker: When an idea pops up, I immediately spin up a feasibility assessment in my head. I run lists, plot timelines, and tally budget line items. Sometimes a rough Gantt chart starts to take shape. (I’m a gas at parties, as you can surely tell.)
My brain, throughout my 20-plus-year career as a science and tech journalist, has played host to a near constant tug-of-war between ambition and reality. Learning to find that balance is a big part of what’s helped me survive in this industry and, ultimately, led me here. This past spring, I had the great privilege of joining the incredible team of journalists behind MIT Technology Review to take the reins of the print magazine.
If you’ve been reading along with us for the last handful of issues, you may have noticed a few changes starting to materialize. We’ve brought back a regular roster of lists and infographics (both things that magazines do particularly well). But the biggest change is only just beginning to take shape, which is why Mat Honan, our editor in chief, asked me to hop in to introduce myself—and the issue you’re holding in your hands right now.
We’re giving ourselves permission to play around and experiment. To be a little … audacious.
Because, practical though I may be, I do still have plenty of ideas. It’s just that I sometimes need a reminder to stop blocking myself and do the thing. That’s the spirit driving this issue in particular.
We wanted to end 2026 with a slate of stories that check in on impossible ideas. Why? Because it’s frankly a lot of fun to dream about living on the moon or uploading our brains. Because losing sight of ambition is all too easy when it feels as if we’re playing whack-a-mole with the world’s problems. But also because the scientists and engineers who absolutely refuse to give up on even the most daring endeavors—like making synthetic blood or decoding animals’ speech—remind us what this whole technology thing is supposed to do to begin with.
It’s supposed to take cutting-edge research and development and apply it to make life better, safer, healthier, even more joyful. And when we eff up and make things worse (see: forever chemicals, traffic deaths, and AI that encourages potentially dangerous user behavior), we’re supposed to dig back in, assess the damage, and find ways to fix what we’ve broken. Even when unraveling the mess might itself seem impossible.
Right before I came to MIT Technology Review, I edited a newsletter about individual actions that can help address the climate crisis, which some would call—and have called—a fool’s errand, given the sheer scale of the problem. They might say it’s as implausible as an AI kill switch, practical nuclear fusion, or a superconductor that works at room temperature. But if I learned nothing else from three years spent finding ways for li’l old me (or li’l old you!) to chip away at one of humanity’s biggest existential threats, it’s that focusing on what we can’t do only makes the darkness darker.
So yeah, this one’s for the folks who have the audacity to try, and who refuse to let anyone—themselves included—tell them no.
I hope you enjoy the ride.

articles.title: Dunkle Energie: So könnten schwache Radiowellen ihr Geheimnis lüften
articles.text:
70 Prozent des Universums unerklärt: Wie schwache Radiosignale das Rätsel der Dunklen Energie lösen sollen
Was steckt hinter Dunkler Energie? Dies ist eines der großen Rätsel der Kosmologie. Die unsichtbare, hypothetische Form der Energie gilt als verantwortlich für die Ausdehnung des Universums, nachdem der erste Schub durch den Big Bang abgeklungen war.
Neuer Weg zum Verständnis von Dunkler Energie?
Direkt nachgewiesen werden konnte die Dunkle Energie, die fast 70 Prozent der Energiedichte des Universums ausmachen soll, noch nicht. Ein Forschungsteam könnte aber nun einen Weg gefunden haben, Dunkle Energie künftig besser zu verstehen.
Die Resultate ihrer Forschung haben die Wissenschaftler:innen in gleich zwei Papern vorgestellt, die beide in der Fachzeitschrift The Astrophysical Journal erschienen sind.
Analyse von neutralem Wasserstoff
Die Forschenden haben mit dem Radioteleskop Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment (CHIME) nach Spuren von kosmischem Wasserstoff gesucht. Genauer gesagt nach neutralem atomaren Wasserstoff, der nicht ionisiert und also elektrisch ungeladen ist.
Neutraler Wasserstoff sendet eine Radiostrahlung mit einer Wellenlänge von etwa 21 Zentimetern aus. Durch die Expansion des Universums wird die Strahlung auf dem Weg zur Erde zu niedrigeren Frequenzen verschoben.
Je stärker die Verzerrung im Vergleich zur ursprünglichen Wellenlänge ist, desto länger waren die Strahlen unterwegs. Daraus kann man ablesen, aus welcher Zeit die Signale stammen. Die Strahlung des neutralen Wasserstoffs, die CHIME auffing, wurde vor acht bis neun Milliarden Jahren ausgesendet. Sie stammt also aus dem relativ jungen Universum.
CHIME beobachtete erstmals direkt neutralen Wasserstoff
Bei der Analyse von neutralem Wasserstoff gibt es eine Schwierigkeit. Sein Signal ist so schwach, dass es von anderen Radioquellen überlagert wird.
Bisher konnten Forschende mit CHIME Wasserstoff nur indirekt wahrnehmen. Sie mussten die empfangenen Signale mit bereits kartierten Galaxien abgleichen.
Mit Hilfe neuer Algorithmen ist es den Wissenschaftler:innen nun gelungen, mit CHIME die Wellenlängen des Wasserstoffs unmittelbar zu erkennen. Das Radioteleskop konnte eigenständig Störsignale erkennen und ausblenden. So soll die Detektion von neutralem Wasserstoff künftig einfacher werden.
Verteilung von Wasserstoff gibt Aufschluss über Ausdehnung des Universums
Was hat dies alles nun mit Dunkler Energie zu tun? Um diese mysteriöse Kraft zu verstehen, ist es wichtig, die Verteilung von Materie im Universum zu unterschiedlichen Zeiten zu kennen.
Nur daraus kann man ablesen, wie schnell sich das Weltall ausgedehnt hat und welche Rolle die Dunkle Energie dabei gespielt hat. Und da Wasserstoff das häufigste Element im Universum ist, ist es der beste Marker, um die Verteilung von Materie und ihre Veränderung zu analysieren.

articles.title: I can’t get enough of the iPhone Duo’s matte inner display
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo has all the messiness of a first-gen product. And while I’m not sure I love all of the decisions Apple made around its design, it got one thing right: the matte finish on the inner screen. I’ve been using it for the past week to watch movies on a plane, peruse my photo gallery, and catch up on a little reading, and I’m convinced. The matte screen is the best thing about the Duo, and I hope every other foldable maker copies it.
I can’t get enough of the iPhone Duo’s matte inner display
Nano-texture was the right move.
Nano-texture was the right move.
When we first got our hands on the Duo, the nano-texture finish on the 7.6-inch inner screen was genuinely a surprise. I’ve used a dozen or so book-style foldables over the past five years, and every one of them came with a glossy inner display. Aside from occasionally noting that they can be hard to see in direct sun, I never really questioned it. That’s just how screens are, I figured. But opening up the Duo for the first time, it clicked. Matte makes sense.
The benefits proved out while I used the phone for the past seven days. I propped it up on my tray table to watch an episode of Widow’s Bay. The matte screen effectively fought off the glare from the open window in my row. Reading a longer article felt a little easier on the eyes, and that’s what the inner screen is really there for. And there’s something about that slight matte finish that signals to my brain that it’s time to read. I can sort of fool myself into thinking that I’m holding an e-reader when I open the Kindle app and turn the phone sideways to its portrait orientation. It’s cute to imagine using your reading app in the landscape-oriented, partway-closed posture like a physical book. But I wouldn’t actually read anything like that; portrait all the way.
The thing to know about the Duo’s matte finish is that it’s pretty subtle. You don’t feel it under your finger quite as much as the more paperlike finish on TCL’s Nxtpaper devices. My colleague Dominic Preston wondered if it would be jarring flipping between the glossy cover screen and the matte display, and personally it hasn’t bothered me. The fact that the Duo’s big screen isn’t full-on e-reader matte probably helps ease that transition.
In fact, changing between the two screens somehow feels nice in both directions. Opening up to the inner screen feels like a welcome break from the reflections on the outer screen. When closing it and going back to the outer screen, the richer blacks and colors feel inviting.
I can concede that if you’re watching something with a lot of dark, shadowy scenes, the matte might feel like it obscures a bit of the detail that would otherwise stand out. It didn’t really bother me. But the bottom line is that this is a device that you will, by its nature, take outside. You’ll use it in ideal lighting conditions and crappy ones. I’ll take a slight hit in richness and detail for a more comfortable overall viewing experience. When my seatmate throws the window shade open, I’ll be ready for it.

articles.title: El Galaxy S27 traería pésimas noticias: Samsung recortaría la RAM de su próximo tope de gama
articles.text:
Los Samsung Galaxy S27 podrían llegar con una sorpresa desagradable. Según recoge 9to5Google, nuevas filtraciones apuntan a que la firma coreana podría disminuir la cantidad de memoria RAM a implementar en las variantes de entrada de su próxima línea de topes de gama.
Puntualmente, se indica que el Galaxy S27 y el S27+ tendrían 8 GB de RAM, y no solo los 12 GB que han sido el estándar en los S25 y S26. Si esto se confirma será una pésima noticia para los compradores, pues la reducción en la cantidad de memoria instalada no necesariamente implicaría salvarse de pagar precios más altos que en la actualidad.
La información es para tomar con pinzas, por supuesto. Pero la crisis de la RAM ha dejado señales bastante evidentes de su impacto en toda la electrónica de consumo, y en el pasado analistas han barajado la posibilidad de que los móviles de alta gama comiencen a recular en su elección de hardware para mitigar la escasez y el encarecimiento de este componente.
De acuerdo con la nueva filtración, el Galaxy S27 podría volver a una configuración segmentada como la que Samsung usó por última vez en el S24. Si esto se confirma, tanto el S27 estándar como la variante Plus llegarían con 8 GB en sus opciones de 256 GB de espacio interno y mantendrían los 12 GB para las versiones de 512 GB.
Samsung podría volver a los 8 GB de RAM con el Galaxy S27
El citado reporte indica que Samsung no habría tomado una decisión final sobre qué configuraciones ofrecería con el nuevo S27 Pro. Dicho modelo llegaría seguro con 12 GB de RAM, pero también estaría "en consideración" la posibilidad de ofrecer alguna opción con 16 GB.
En el caso del Galaxy S27 Ultra, Samsung mantendría la estrategia ya existente de equipar sus versiones de 256 y 512 GB con 12 GB de RAM, mientras que la de 1 TB seguiría siendo la única con 16 GB de memoria. Ya veremos si esto realmente es así o si se trata de meros supuestos relacionados con la actualidad de la industria.
Que el mercado de la electrónica de consumo transita uno de sus períodos más complejos por la escasez y el encarecimiento de componentes cruciales, es verdad. Aunque también hay mucha especulación que se debe tomar con cautela.
Pocos días atrás se conoció el rumor de que Samsung supuestamente analizaría no lanzar los Galaxy S27 con el chip Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 de Qualcomm, por presuntos problemas de sobrecalentamiento. Claro que la compañía coreana no ha revelado nada oficialmente en tal sentido, así que por ahora hay que tomarlo como un rumor y no mucho más.

articles.title: India-New Zealand trade pact kicks in
articles.text:
India-New Zealand trade pact kicks in
The agreement provides duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather.
The India-New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (FTA), signed on April 27, came into effect on Tuesday, providing duty-free access to a range of Indian goods, including products from labour-intensive sectors such as textiles and leather.
It is the seventh trade pact to come into force in the last five years. The others are agreements with the UAE, Mauritius, the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) bloc, the UK, Oman and Australia.
Signed on April 27, 2026, the agreement follows negotiations launched in 2010, stalled in 2015 and revived in March 2025. The pact becomes India's 17th operational FTA.
According to experts, the sectors benefiting from the FTA are textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, engineering goods and auto components, gems and jewellery, agriculture and processed foods, pharmaceuticals, and other manufacturing industries.
Gulzar Didwania, Partner, Deloitte India, said the deal is expected to support higher FDI inflows into India, but the scale of any increase remains uncertain and will depend on private-sector investment decisions.
New Zealand has committed FDI worth USD 20 billion in over 15 years.
"The FTA's provisions on duty-free access for certain inputs, bilateral cumulation, customs facilitation, and investment-promotion mechanisms may encourage deeper value-chain integration and improve investment conditions," he said.
He added that the pact has significance beyond trade, strengthening India's strategic position in the Indo-Pacific, expanding its network of FTAs with developed economies.
At a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules. Its target of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 sets an ambitious agenda for both countries.
What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses.
With 100 per cent of Indian exports gaining duty-free access to New Zealand from day one, the agreement gives Indian exporters a significant competitive advantage. MSMEs in textiles, leather, footwear and engineering goods are particularly well placed to benefit.
Economic think tank Chintan Research Foundation (CRF India) President Shishir Priyadarshi said that at a time of growing global trade uncertainty, the India-New Zealand FTA is a strong endorsement of open markets and predictable trade rules.
"What makes this FTA particularly valuable is that it goes beyond goods to cover services, investment, skills and mobility, creating fresh opportunities for Indian professionals and businesses," he said.
Trade expert and Hi-Tech Gears Chairman Deep Kapuria said the FTA operationalisation with New Zealand completes India's preferential market access in all major countries of the Asia-Pacific region.
"New Zealand is a very open economy; India has very well crafted this trade deal by securing market access for new services such as Ayush, yoga instructors and student mobility, including post-study work visa," he said.
Bilateral trade declined by about 11 per cent to USD 1.15 billion in 2025-26 from USD 1.3 billion in the previous fiscal year. India's exports stood at USD 566.51 million, while imports were USD 589.1 million, resulting in a meagre trade deficit of USD 22.59 million for India.
Rani Singh, Indian-origin New Zealander, said the deal is an important step forward for both countries as it is not just about trade; it is about bringing the two countries closer, creating opportunities for businesses and people, and building a stronger relationship for the future.
"India now has an opportunity to build its own strong partnership with New Zealand. With duty-free access to New Zealand for all Indian export tariff lines from day one, Indian businesses can become more competitive in this market," she said.
Singh added that the benefits are not limited to goods as there is also scope for greater cooperation in education, tourism, technology, professional services and investment.
Greater opportunities for eligible skilled professionals and young people can further strengthen these connections, she said.

articles.title: AuxoAI raises over $20M to bring AI expertise to the enterprise and redesign how work gets done - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AuxoAI raises over $20M to bring AI expertise to the enterprise and redesign how work gets done
AuxoAI Inc., an enterprise engineering and consulting company that helps large businesses build and deploy artificial intelligence systems, today announced it has raised $20.7 million in a Series A funding to accelerate growth and scale its enterprise AI consulting model.
The company said it has spent over three years working with Global 2000 enterprises and strategic partners, bringing AI into the core of their operations. It focuses on combining business-process expertise, data engineering and AI agents – autonomous systems that use artificial intelligence to work with little or no human oversight, with deep insight into company data to complete long-term tasks.
AuxoAI builds AI solutions by sending on-site engineers and strategy teams to understand enterprise culture, data, workflow automation and customer engagement to tailor experiences to business and employee needs.
At the core of the company’s platform is Damia, which the company describes as an FDE Workbench, or “forward-deployed engineer” toolkit that also transforms data into applications and licenses for customers. It combines reusable agent capacities with tools for capturing a company’s business knowledge and processes.
The company said that over the years, it has learned how to work with customers to encode relevant knowledge and relationships and use that to create AI agents around the company’s processes. This preserves what the team learns in software and structured knowledge, rather than only interviews or paper documents, but in living software that can work alongside employees.
The company calls this effect “intelligence embedded in the work itself,” where consulting treats AI as a lever or tool for the customer rather than an end product.
AuxoAI partners with companies that businesses already know and trust, including Google LLC, Amazon Web Services Inc., Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and Microsoft Corp., allowing the company to provide enterprise-ready AI, cloud, data and productivity via these platforms.
NTT Venture Capital, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm backed by Japanese technology conglomerate NTT Inc., led the funding round. The round also included participation from prominent industry executives and strategic investors, such as George Still Jr., partner emeritus at Norwest Venture Partners; Amit Zavery, president, chief product officer and chief operating officer at ServiceNow Inc.; and Giacomo Sonnino, managing director at Charlesbank Capital Partners and former chief operating officer of Quantum Black North America.
NTTVC’s portfolio includes Anthropic PBC, which will bring on another major artificial intelligence leader to extend AuxoAI’s capabilities.
The company said the new funding will serve to accelerate the next phase of its journey to expand its global reach. It aims to provide onsite consulting talent for enterprise AI transformation, invest in proprietary technology and AI-native delivery capabilities, and scale up its presence and strategic ecosystem.
