articles.title: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This is a guest post co-written with Roei Zavida from Eon.
Independent software vendors (ISVs) building AI-powered products need to connect agents and humans to dozens of operational tools across clouds, each with different authentication models, network boundaries, and access policies. When those tools span AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously, the integration surface multiplies.
This post describes how Eon used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Eon used it to replace per-tool credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) processes with a single authenticated gateway. The result gives developers and autonomous agents unified access to investigation tooling across three clouds. New engineers now reach all their investigation tools in about two minutes instead of the two days it previously took to configure credentials and local MCP servers.
About Eon
Eon provides the Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era. The platform discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP. It provides continuous deduplicated backup that reduces storage costs by up to 50 percent in Eon’s internal measurements. It also detects ransomware and rogue-agent damage and delivers live grounded context for AI agents. All of this runs from a single read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, storing data in Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg formats. Founded by former AWS engineers, Eon runs its software as a service (SaaS) infrastructure on AWS.
The challenge
Eon’s internal engineering team investigates production incidents across multiple clouds and dozens of operational systems. A crashed Kubernetes pod requires checking container logs, Grafana metrics, the deployment’s GitHub pull request (PR), and cloud-provider health status within the same session.
Eon needed to address several key requirements:
- Credential consolidation — Each new tool added another integration to configure, secure, and rotate, which got harder to keep consistent as the toolset grew.
- Eliminate local MCP processes — Each developer ran several MCP servers locally, which was hard to standardize and keep current.
- Identity separation — Engineers accessed each system with role-based permissions, but there was no single place to decide which tools each person or agent could call.
- Cross-account access without networking overhead — Hosting MCP servers across multiple AWS accounts required virtual private cloud (VPC) peering or AWS PrivateLink per account, multiplying operational cost and setup time.
- Developer onboarding — New engineers spent roughly 2 days configuring credentials and local MCP servers before investigating their first incident.
- Agent access — Eon’s autonomous site reliability engineering (SRE) agent (running Claude on Amazon Bedrock) needed the same tool access as humans, but with different permissions.
Growing engineering headcount combined with a fast-expanding set of AI tools and MCPs made maintaining credentials and local MCP servers increasingly costly. This pushed Eon toward a centralized solution.
Approaches considered
Before building on AgentCore, Eon evaluated alternatives:
Option 1: Centralized proxy with custom auth
Every harness had its own proxy configuration with all the targets. A single reverse proxy aggregating all tools, with a custom authentication layer. This handled credential consolidation but only supported remote MCP and required building and maintaining tool protocol translation, session management, and authorization logic from scratch. The implementation and maintenance burden was significant.
Option 2: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is a managed gateway with built-in identity federation, Cedar-based authorization policies, and Runtime hosting that converts local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints. This addressed all requirements without custom infrastructure.
Eon chose Option 2 because it provided identity separation, cross-account connectivity, and policy enforcement as managed capabilities rather than code they would need to build and maintain. These were the only two options on the table.
Solution overview
Eon deployed the full Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack: AgentCore Gateway, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AgentCore Runtime, and AgentCore Identity, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows how client requests flow through the authentication layer to a single gateway. The gateway routes authorized tool calls to targets hosted on AgentCore Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts.
The architecture has five layers:
Clients
Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenAI Codex connect to a single MCP URL. An autonomous SRE agent running Claude on Amazon Bedrock connects to the same gateway with a different identity.
Identity plane
Corporate single sign-on (SSO) federates through Amazon Cognito, which mints the JSON Web Token (JWT) and hands it to the gateway. Amazon API Gateway sits in front as the OAuth entry point for humans, proxying the MCP session. Agents authenticate with Cognito client_credentials grants directly against the gateway.
One gateway, least-privilege access
A single AgentCore MCP Gateway serves as the company-wide front door. Cedar policies in ENFORCE mode control which principals can invoke which tools. Read operations are available to selected groups, not every authenticated user. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only.
Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Cedar policies map each principal to permitted tools. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. The gateway evaluates every tools/call request against Cedar before forwarding to the target.
Targets
Dozens of target MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools on the one gateway, served by AgentCore Runtimes distributed across multiple AWS accounts. Each Runtime converts local stdio-based MCP servers into Streamable HTTP endpoints accessible through the gateway.
A developer opens their integrated development environment (IDE), configures one MCP URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and the gateway aggregates hundreds of tools into a single tools/list response. No local setup and no per-tool tokens.
Identity and access separation
The core security decision was enforcing read and write boundaries through Cedar policy at the gateway level.
Single gateway, policy-enforced separation:
The gateway accepts both JWT tokens (humans through corporate SSO and Cognito) and client_credentials tokens (agents). Cedar policies determine what each principal can do. Humans in approved groups get read access. Write operations require explicit Cedar permits granted only to specific agent identities.
Cedar reinforces per-tool granularity:
Cedar policies are managed as code through GitHub PRs with review comments, giving the team version control and audit trail on every permission change.
Within the gateway, Cedar policies scope tool access by SSO group, and groups map to job role. Engineers have access to development and testing environments by default. Production access follows Eon’s security and compliance controls: it is read-only, granted just-in-time through an approval process, and audited. A new team member’s group is scoped the same way, by role rather than by which service they happen to own. Because every agent action is checked against Cedar in ENFORCE mode and scoped to a least-privilege tool set, the autonomous agent operates within safe, bounded limits. It can only invoke the specific tools its identity is explicitly permitted to call.
        “Before, our internal agent couldn’t reach the same investigation tools developers used. After, it uses the same Gateway with its own identity and a tighter tool set.”
— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon
Cross-account connectivity
Eon runs Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts, organized by environment or service boundary. AgentCore Gateway reaches each Runtime through IAM cross-account role assumption. The Runtime in Account B trusts the AgentCore Gateway execution role in Account A through a standard IAM trust policy.
What this eliminated:
- VPC peering configuration and route table management across multiple AWS accounts.
- PrivateLink endpoint costs per account.
- Security group coordination between accounts.
- Days of setup per new account (replaced by one IAM trust policy, deployable in minutes).
Target attachment patterns:
Depending on each tool’s authentication and hosting model, Eon uses two primary attachment patterns. The following table summarizes when to use each pattern and gives an example.
| Pattern | When to use | Example | 
| Runtime + IAM | Tool needs a cloud hop through IAM credentials | Grafana queries, Kubernetes API calls | 
| Runtime wrapping remote MCP | Tool surface needs filtering or credential translation | Linear | 
Most targets use Runtime + IAM. Eon only wraps a remote MCP to shrink its catalog or slot in a credential the gateway cannot otherwise supply.
Investigation session flow
The following flow traces a developer investigating a production incident:
- Authentication. The developer opens Claude Code (or Cursor/Codex) and connects to the gateway MCP URL. The IDE initiates OAuth through corporate SSO. Cognito issues a JWT carrying the developer’s identity and group memberships.
- Tool discovery. The gateway aggregates `tools/list` from dozens of connected targets and returns a unified manifest of hundreds of tools to the IDE. The developer sees all available investigation tools in one list.
- Tool invocation. The developer asks: “Show me the error rate spike for the payments service in the last hour.” The IDE’s agent selects the Grafana query tool and sends a `tools/call` request.
- Policy evaluation. The gateway evaluates the request against Cedar. The developer’s group membership grants access to the Grafana tool. The request passes.
- Runtime execution. The gateway forwards the request to the Runtime hosting the Grafana MCP server (running in a separate AWS account). The Runtime authenticates to Grafana using a service credential stored in the AgentCore Identity vault, executes the query, and returns results.
- Cross-tool correlation. The agent follows up by checking the Kubernetes deployment status and the related GitHub PR, each routed to different Runtimes. The developer sees correlated results without switching tools or re-authenticating.
Lessons learned at scale
Deploying to 100+ developers and approximately 10,000 sessions surfaced production challenges:
Managing Cedar policy size
Every tool schema that the gateway pre-indexes contributes to Cedar policy size. With dozens of targets exposing extensive tool manifests, Eon’s policy grew toward the size quota. The fix: DYNAMIC listing mode for high-tool-count targets. In DYNAMIC mode, the gateway forwards tools/list calls to the MCP server at request time instead of pre-indexing schemas, adding zero bytes to the policy.
The trade-off is that semantic tool search is unavailable for DYNAMIC targets. Eon runs a hybrid configuration: DEFAULT mode for targets requiring per-user OAuth (smaller tool counts, need pre-indexed schemas for the consent flow) and DYNAMIC mode for large-catalog targets.
OAuth session binding for standard MCP clients
Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex expect the OAuth state parameter for cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection. AgentCore uses session-URI binding. Eon built an Amazon API Gateway shim that translates between the two protocols so standard MCP clients can complete the OAuth flow without modification.
Filtering tool surfaces
Some MCP servers expose hundreds of tools. Individual developers need only a subset for their service. Eon built a Runtime wrapper that filters the tool manifest at the Runtime layer, reducing noise in tools/list responses and preventing accidental invocation of irrelevant operations. This approach also keeps those targets on DEFAULT mode, preserving semantic search and embedded features that DYNAMIC mode sacrifices.
Results
| Metric | Before AgentCore | After AgentCore | 
| Credential sets per developer | One per system/MCP server (GitHub, Grafana, cloud accounts, etc.) | 0 (one SSO login) | 
| Local MCP processes per machine | 10 | 0 | 
| Developer onboarding time | 2 days | 2 minutes | 
| Cross-account networking configs | VPC peering per account | 0 (IAM-only) | 
| Tool authorization | Configured per tool | One Cedar policy for humans and agents | 
| Developers on the platform | — | 100+ | 
| Tools accessible from one URL | — | Hundreds (across dozens of targets) | 
| Sessions processed | — | ~10,000 | 
The single-gateway architecture has run in production for Eon’s internal engineering team for several months. The clearest outcome is developer onboarding. Setting up access to the full tool set dropped from roughly two days of configuring credentials and local MCP servers to about two minutes. A new engineer connects one gateway URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and immediately sees the tools their role allows.
The internal agent accounts for most of the time saved, because it gains access to more context through the gateway, improving investigation accuracy. Engineers save the time previously spent on AI tool setup, because they only need to connect to the gateway URL.
Eon is exploring how the same patterns can support AI capabilities in its own product.
        “AgentCore gave us one authenticated MCP Gateway instead of per-tool tokens and local MCP processes. Developers and our internal agent now reach Kubernetes, Grafana, GitHub, and our cloud accounts from a single URL.”
— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon
Conclusion
This post described how Eon replaced per-tool credentials and local MCP processes with a single Amazon Bedrock AgentCore MCP Gateway. The result is Cedar-based identity separation, cross-account connectivity without VPC peering, and unified tool access for more than 100 developers and autonomous agents across three clouds. The single-gateway architecture, Cedar least-privilege enforcement, and hybrid DEFAULT and DYNAMIC policy mode are reusable patterns for ISVs connecting agents and developers to tools across multiple clouds.
To learn more about building on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, review these resources:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway documentation.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime documentation.
- Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Workshop.

articles.title: Scaling CPO Testing Beyond A Single Die
articles.text:
Fiber alignment, connector durability, and simultaneous optical and electrical testing pose challenges for high-volume manufacturing.
Key Takeaways:
Experts At The Table: The industry is forging a path from single-site to multi-site testing while system architectures and connector types continue to evolve. Semiconductor Engineering sat down with Matt Griffin, senior product manager for optoelectronics test at Teradyne; Ira Leventhal, vice president of research and venture at Advantest America; Dave Armstrong, fellow at ISE Labs, a subsidiary of ASE Group; and Kazuo Yamaguchi, silicon photonics researcher and engineer at Keysight Technologies. What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one, click here.
Fig. 1: (L-R): Teradyne’s Griffin; Keysight’s Yamaguchi; ISE Labs’ Armstrong; Advantest’s Leventhal.
SE: Is it true that you can only test one die at a time today?
Armstrong: I would hope some insertions will go away over time, but right now there are more things being added than being subtracted. It’s a hard one. In terms of testing one die, that depends on the die. If an 8 kW GPU is your main ASIC, and you have multiple connectors around multiple sides of the part from a tester resource standpoint, and the amount of power a tester can deliver and take out of the part, it’s pretty challenging to get beyond one die. But if you look down the NPO-versus-CPO path, NPO is typically a single connector device. You’re going to have to be able to go to multi-site to scale that to high volume. Insertions two and three are the fertile ground for multi-site. Those are longer more complex test insertions. PIC wafer testing tends to be single-site today. From my experience, there is some hope on the horizon to bring it up a little bit higher with some capabilities in the probe card area, notably from Technoprobe.
Griffin: I agree with Dave. Most production solutions today are single-site, and when you talk about the optical engine, the main bottleneck is fiber alignment. Many companies are working on multi-site solutions, and I hope they succeed and take off because that only helps the whole industry ramp faster. But we’ve got a little bit longer to go there.
SE: For these alignment ports, can you repeatedly test at that site?
Griffin: Ideally, you’re able to repeatedly test almost infinitely because you should never be contacting the device with the optical probe or the fiber array unit (FAU). When you’re bringing up a new test solution, you do sometimes crash FAUs on first systems. In reality, the bigger concern is contamination on the FAU, so cleaning is needed. On the connector side, at the module level or for optical engines with receptacles attached, the optical connector lifecycle is where we need more effort, because the device-side connector is designed to be attached once and, hopefully, never disconnected. And every new connector generation changes both the connector recipe and the automation recipe.
Leventhal: In a sense, this is nothing new. For instance, with BGAs, if you socket at the device too many times, then you start worrying about damaging the balls on the BGA. It’s a similar problem and the industry will gravitate toward connector designs that are more robust. Matt made a really important point about how your test side connector needs to be some sort of a hardened connector that doesn’t wear out easily after 20 to 50 insertions. It needs to last for tens of thousands or 100,000 insertions. So you’ve got to go to a hardened metal, and then you’ve got a hardened metal going against the receptacle on the device, which is not going to be that hardened metal. If you’re not careful, you could damage that connector sooner than the spec lifetime. So as the industry evolves to the winning connector designs, robustness on the device side is going to be a really important part of that.
SE: What are the challenges with making simultaneous electrical and optical connections?
Armstrong: It’s just a question of time.
Yamaguchi: Beyond DC and optical probing, the harder part of simultaneous electrical and optical connection is characterizing electro-optic devices in RF. Modulator and photodetector performance is ultimately validated through S-parameters, so you need optical and high-frequency RF contact at the same time. Probe cards can only fit a limited number of RF lines, and their bandwidth is also limited, while today’s devices are characterized beyond 200 GHz. At wafer and die insertions, simultaneous connection is really an RF probing challenge.
Leventhal: Warpage is going to create additional challenges on top of just trying to solve the problem in an ideal case. You need to be able to align in multiple axes. And the BGA has a crazy amount of pins that you have to make reliable contact with, so that problem is getting more challenging. Adding to that is being able to do the right level of alignment, either coming from the top or coming from the side. It’s significantly challenging. I agree with Dave, it’s a question of time in multiple senses. Each insertion takes time, although there are ways of minimizing that by integrating certain operations together. But also, it’s going to take time for all of this to mature to the point that it’s going to be easier to test at scale.
Griffin: At its core, there’s an optical and an electrical interface to the device at every insertion, and sometimes those interfaces are on the top side of the device, sometimes the bottom side, and sometimes both. And then when you talk about module level, they’re on two to four sides of the package across some number of optical engines. So if you look at optical alignment on its own, it’s not that big of a challenge. But when you start combining it with all the different, I’ll say, flavors of architecture that we’re seeing, and trying to design a scalable test system that can handle as many of those flavors as possible for your customers, that’s really where some of the fun challenges are.
Armstrong: I also chair the IPSR test roadmap for photonics, and in our latest report we highlight a test methodology for AC testing. AC testing, bit error rate testing, will be one of the bigger time sinks. If we had good DFT, we could just do loopback on the optical side and loopback on the electrical side at the same time. And technically, there’s no reason you couldn’t combine those two tests. But today, most people are saying, “Okay, I’ll do loopback on one side or the other side, and a bit error rate test of some nature on the other side, so that becomes a very expensive setup that doubles the effective test time. The more DFT and concurrent testing we do, the better off we’ll be in the long run.
Griffin: The automation challenge is still there, but I agree with Dave’s point. Most customers going to volume will have some sort of loopback capability — electrical, optical, or a combination — but it remains to be seen what wins out there.
SE: Which measurements dominate production test — optical power, insertion loss, or bit error rate?
Armstrong: In terms of test time, it seems like a lot of people are very concerned with insertion loss just because of how often it’s done, but I don’t think that should be number one. Eye quality would be number one, and high-quality receiver sensitivity would also be high on the list, and bit error rate.
Griffin: I agree. I’ll add wavelength sweeps for optical engines. Those can take a significant amount of time, depending on customer requirements.
Yamaguchi: I also agree, but we need to be mindful of correlating such performance with not only ‘known good die,’ but also ‘known good and reliable die.’ It’s the probability of surviving integration and service life, because defects that escape pre-assembly are largely integration-induced effects such as fiber/FAU coupling loss after attach, resonance drift versus laser tunability, thermal and packaging effects. In the end, overall transmitter and receiver performance are defined by standards, using metrics such as TDECQ (Transmitter and Dispersion Eye Closure Quaternary) and receiver sensitivity.
Leventhal: Going forward, the main issue is whether your data transmission is working correctly in both directions — electrical to optical, optical to electrical — and how are you going to root-cause problems when the system is not working? We will need to gather key information as early as possible to determine what causes data transmission issues.

articles.title: Eva Ngigi Sarwari, Equity’s head of payments, dies at 45
articles.text:
Eva Ngigi Sarwari, managing director of Finserve Africa and Equity Group’s director of payments and international banking, has died aged 45 while on a business trip to China, according to a statement from her colleagues.
Her death cuts short a career that spanned over two decades in banking and payments, from introducing customers to electronic banking at Co-operative Bank of Kenya to leading Visa’s business across three East African markets.
“It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of our dear friend and colleague, Eva Ngigi Sarwari,” her colleagues said in the statement on Tuesday.
They described the news as a “sudden and profound shock” and said they would make further updates as details became available. The statement did not disclose the cause or date of her death.
Sarwari joined Equity in January 2025 as group director for payments and international banking, with responsibility for executing the bank’s payments strategy across Africa. In April 2026, she became managing director of Finserve Africa, the group’s payments and digital financial services subsidiary, overseeing its strategy, commercial direction and operations.
The roles brought her back into a banking group after more than four years at Visa, where she served as senior director and country manager from September 2020 to December 2024. Her role covered three neighbouring markets, including Kenya, South Sudan and Somalia.
The appointments brought together experience accumulated across local banks, an international banking group and one of the world’s largest card networks.
Before Equity, Sarwari spent more than four years at Visa as senior director and country manager for Kenya, South Sudan and Somalia. From September 2020 to December 2024, she was responsible for developing and implementing the company’s growth strategy in those markets.
She joined Visa from SC Ventures, Standard Chartered’s venture-building arm, where she served as a venture lead during 2020. That role followed more than seven years in Standard Chartered’s transaction banking business.
As head of transaction banking for commercial banking from July 2017 to January 2020, she helped shape the bank’s strategy for Kenya and East Africa, with responsibility for revenue growth, product relevance and digital transformation. Previously, as a principal in transaction banking, she worked with development organisations and public-sector clients across East Africa.
Sarwari moved to Standard Chartered in November 2012 after just over two years at Stanbic Bank Kenya, where she managed sales of transactional products and services.
She began her banking career at Co-operative Bank of Kenya in June 2005. As a relationship manager, she helped bring customers onto electronic banking systems, demonstrating products, overseeing installations and training users. It was practical work that would run through her subsequent career.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with Eva’s family, friends and colleagues during this difficult time,” the statement added.

articles.title: Musk ordenou restrição do Starlink usado pela Ucrânia, diz jornal
articles.text:
Elon Musk ordenou a redução da velocidade de uma versão militar do Starlink utilizada pela Ucrânia, prejudicando operações com drones de ataque e interceptação. A medida, iniciada em 14 de outubro, provocou preocupação em Kiev e confusão no governo de Donald Trump, segundo o The Wall Street Journal.
A decisão ampliou as tensões entre Washington e Kiev e levantou dúvidas sobre o papel do governo americano na restrição. Enquanto autoridades divergem sobre o envolvimento de Trump, as forças ucranianas tentam esclarecer quando terão acesso normal à rede.
Restrição afeta operações militares
O limite imposto à conexão via satélite comprometeu o uso de drones ucranianos em ataques contra posições russas e na interceptação de ameaças aéreas. Autoridades da Ucrânia também afirmaram que a mudança permitiu que mísseis russos escapassem de suas defesas.
A restrição ocorreu em meio a críticas de Trump e Musk ao presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky. Os dois demonstraram irritação com ataques a refinarias russas de diesel. Trump atribuiu às ofensivas a alta dos preços da energia, embora analistas citados na reportagem apontem que a guerra no Irã teve impacto maior.
Em 10 de outubro, quatro dias antes de os operadores ucranianos relatarem problemas com o Starlink, Trump havia criticado Zelensky por atacar instalações de combustível na Rússia. Musk reagiu a um vídeo das declarações publicado pela Casa Branca no X: “Zelensky foi longe demais”.
Segundo pessoas ouvidas pelo Wall Street Journal, Musk conversou com Trump sobre a restrição. Uma delas afirmou que a conversa ocorreu antes da decisão. Outros funcionários americanos, porém, disseram acreditar que o empresário agiu por conta própria.
Governo americano nega envolvimento
A falta de clareza sobre quem autorizou a mudança levou a Casa Branca a investigar informalmente o caso. Representantes da SpaceX também procuraram integrantes do governo para alinhar o entendimento sobre a decisão e a comunicação pública.
Horas depois de a restrição se tornar conhecida, Musk publicou no X: “Quaisquer limites de velocidade ou uso são decididos pelos militares dos EUA e, em última instância, pelo presidente dos Estados Unidos”.
Na segunda-feira, Trump afirmou não saber quem havia determinado a redução. “Gostaria de descobrir”, disse.
Na quarta-feira, o secretário de Estado americano, Marco Rubio, negou que o governo tivesse solicitado a medida. “Não houve conhecimento prévio”, declarou durante uma visita à Índia. O secretário de Defesa, Pete Hegseth, também disse que o Pentágono não havia emitido ordens para retirar recursos da Ucrânia, mas ressaltou que a SpaceX pode decidir sobre seus próprios termos de serviço.
Kiev aguarda esclarecimentos
A Ucrânia ainda buscava respostas sobre o alcance da restrição. Na terça-feira, Denys Sienik, principal diplomata ucraniano em Washington, afirmou que o país aguardava uma posição oficial do Pentágono e da SpaceX para entender o que havia acontecido e se o serviço seria restabelecido.
O especialista militar Michael Kofman, da Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, disse que as limitações continuavam prejudicando as operações ucranianas. Segundo ele, a conexão disponível estava abaixo de 130 km/h, diante de um limite citado de 160 km/h para drones de ataque e interceptação. Como esses valores são incomuns para descrever conexões, a unidade de medida merece conferência no texto original antes da publicação.
O caso também envolve acusações de Zelensky de que os Estados Unidos teriam interrompido temporariamente o compartilhamento de informações de inteligência com a Ucrânia. Autoridades americanas negaram a denúncia.
Entre os principais desdobramentos estão:
- Impacto operacional: a limitação do Starlink dificultou o emprego de drones em missões de ataque e defesa.
- Divergência política: fontes ouvidas pelo jornal discordam sobre o conhecimento prévio de Trump e o grau de envolvimento do governo.
- Dependência tecnológica: a Ucrânia precisa de esclarecimentos da SpaceX e do Pentágono sobre a continuidade do serviço.
O impasse evidencia como o acesso a uma rede privada de comunicação pode afetar operações militares. Para a Ucrânia, esclarecer as condições de uso do Starlink é essencial para avaliar a capacidade de manter suas ações na linha de frente.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Meta tries to scapegoat staff who downloaded torrents to spare execs
articles.text:
In copyright lawsuits over AI training, Meta has spent weeks blaming staff for downloading torrents. The company has now been ordered to name executives who authorized decisions to pirate books from shadow libraries like Anna’s Archive and LibGen, TorrentFreak reported.
In a discovery order impacting a class action raised by book authors—including Richard Kadrey and Sarah Silverman—as well as a lawsuit from publisher Entrepreneur Media, Magistrate Judge Thomas Hixon largely agreed that Meta must clearly identify key decision-makers. Following testimony from Meta staff who downloaded torrents, the order could expose a wider range of supervisors, managers, and executives whom staffers said greenlit the piracy.
Meta had been hoping to avoid detailing the chain of command, particularly for leadership involved in early AI training. According to a Meta court filing, its initial efforts to compile massive AI datasets were managed through an “informal approach” where supposedly nobody with authority made any decisions. Instead, Meta insisted that a “decision” was “made only in the sense” that some staffers “technically” downloaded torrents.
Zuckerberg could be roped in
Authors and publishers have argued that Meta made a willful choice to induce infringement by downloading and illegally distributing their copyrighted works. Since torrenting depends on a swarm of users, Meta could not have quickly downloaded 80.6 terabytes of data from LibGen or 35.7 terabytes through Anna’s Archive if the company wasn’t also seeding, authors have argued. (Meta has argued that it relied on “mitigations” to prevent seeding.)
Meta’s efforts to scapegoat staff seem to ignore that staff expressed discomfort in being directed to pirate work. In the past year, authors’ lawsuits have exposed internal messages in which staff pushed back or rejected directions on torrenting, including one worker who commented that “torrenting from a corporate laptop doesn’t feel right.” Another staffer testified that he initiated downloads that “required some director or VP level approval to use for training,” a joint letter from Entrepreneur Media and Meta noted. There was also a time when leadership halted, then resumed, downloading torrents sourced from Anna’s Archive, another staffer testified. And while Meta has argued that communications that might identify who specifically authorized certain torrenting instances are privileged, at least one string of unredacted messages unsealed early last year allegedly showed that the decision to download from LibGen, for example, occurred after “a prior escalation to MZ” (Mark Zuckerberg).

articles.title: Meta's Muse hits 10M US downloads in 40 days, a milestone reached by only 11 other apps | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meta’s AI companion, Muse, is now one of only a dozen mobile apps to have reached 10 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. According to new data from market intelligence provider Sensor Tower, Muse has seen 10.9 million downloads since its September debut, 10.2 million of which were in the United States.
Only 11 other apps to date have reached this type of post-launch milestone, said Sensor Tower’s senior insights analyst Kara Lee. The most recent of these was Meta’s Threads, back in July 2023.
Other apps that saw this kind of scale were largely mobile games, Lee noted, like Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Pokémon GO, and others. Besides Threads, Disney+ was the only other nongame app to make it into the exclusive club.
Meta’s success is tied to the company’s ability to scale its new apps by marketing them across its other services, which it has done with both Threads and Muse. Threads was built on top of Instagram’s social graph, and its content has been integrated into both Facebook and Instagram. However, Muse isn’t only benefiting from Meta’s ability to market the AI agent across its family of apps, which today includes 3.6 billion daily active users; the company is also heavily investing in advertising to drive new users to Muse.
Per Sensor Tower’s data, Meta has allocated 39% of its total advertising spend to market Muse in October, up from 23% last month. In addition, Muse now ranks as the 21st largest brand in the U.S. by advertising impressions this month, up from 73rd in September.
Still, marketing an app and retaining users after the initial shine wears off are two different things. In this case, Muse is seeing better retention rates than its AI competitors like ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok.
In the U.S., the app had a 30% retention rate after 7 days and a 23% retention rate after 14 days. By comparison, its rivals saw an average of a 19% 7-day retention rate and a 16% 14-day retention rate, according to the firm’s data.
Muse also hit another milestone that demonstrates active engagement with the AI app. Its daily active users reached 2.5 million for the first time on October 16, a 15% week-over-week increase.
Meta’s latest AI app, which can handle various tasks on users’ behalf, has seen breakout success since its debut. It shot up to No. 1 on the App Store and at one point even outpaced some of the metrics ChatGPT saw following its launch. Its latest milestone sees it topping its rivals again, as ChatGPT saw 3.7 million U.S. downloads in its first 40 days on the market. Grok and Claude saw only 500,000 and 200,000 U.S. downloads, respectively, in their first 40 days.
Globally, ChatGPT beat out Muse, having scaled to around 15 million global downloads in its first 40 days. But this isn’t a fair comparison, as ChatGPT benefited from a wider reach. Muse is only available in the U.S. and Canada for now, while ChatGPT’s app attracted attention from markets like Japan, Brazil, and Germany, too. (Japan, for instance, accounted for 25% of its global installs during its first 40 days.)
Since launching, Muse has retained its No. 1 rank on the U.S. App Store for all days except October 19, when streaming app Kick briefly beat it out. It has since reclaimed the top spot as of Tuesday. Muse has also been No. 1 on Google Play over the past 30 days.

articles.title: Europe’s Industrial Leaders Reinvent Engineering and Manufacturing With NVIDIA
articles.text:
To increase productivity, accelerate innovation and create new opportunities for economic growth, Europe’s industrial leaders are tapping NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries, as well as NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron open models, across the engineering and manufacturing lifecycle.
Bringing those capabilities together on the factory floor, the NVIDIA Factory Operations Blueprint (FOX) is now available in early access on GitHub, providing a path for developers to build and deploy always-on factory manager agents that coordinate work across machines, and specialist agents focused on use cases such as visual inspection, root cause analysis, report generation and fleet management.
These agents can connect to frontier models, including NVIDIA Cosmos and Nemotron, and foundational knowledge including computer-aided design, product lifecycle management, simulation software, and IT and operational technology systems.
Building on the FOX blueprint enables the ecosystem to build industrial agents that monitor factory operations in real time, correlate visual findings and machine logs to investigate problems, and coordinate responses. With Cosmos in-context learning, these agents can adapt using examples and documentation, without fine-tuning.
Siemens is integrating agents built using FOX into Intelligence Center X, its agentic enterprise system, to help identify root causes and coordinate factory operations, for estimated cost savings of 20%. Siemens’ Process Preparation X agents use NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory tools and skills to generate defect images for circuit-board inspection. At its Erlangen electronics factory, Siemens used this approach to reduce calibration time of inspection processes by 40%.
Accelerating Engineering From the First Design
NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries accelerate simulation, giving engineers faster feedback to explore design alternatives before committing to physical prototypes. At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is releasing cuDSS for general availability, accelerating the demanding calculations behind the complex simulations of structural stress, fluid flow, electromagnetic fields and semiconductor device behavior.
Mercedes-Benz uses Siemens’ Simcenter STAR-CCM+ running on NVIDIA GPUs to compare vehicle designs through faster aerodynamic simulations. In factories, the company applies NVIDIA Cosmos 3 and the Metropolis VSS blueprint to build agents for vehicle inspection and windshield assembly verification, detecting deviations and ensuring consistently high quality.
Cadence is benchmarking automotive fluid-dynamics workloads on NVIDIA GPUs to assess opportunities for faster design iteration, while Autodesk brings the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo and Warp frameworks into NavPack, integrated with Autodesk Alias, to help designers like those at Bentley’s predict vehicle performance and iterate faster using simulation-trained AI.
imec and Infineon are accelerating semiconductor simulation with Synopsys software and NVIDIA accelerated computing. Benchmarks of S-Litho on imec’s model show up to 40x speedup, while Infineon uses Sentaurus Device with NVIDIA CUDA libraries to achieve a 12x speedup in 3D breakdown simulation for next-generation power devices.
Leonardo is working with Neural Concept on AI-driven aircraft design, tapping NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bring aircraft geometry and aerodynamic simulation results together.
Car manufacturers use Dassault Systèmes’ LEO & AURA Virtual Companions, powered by NVIDIA Nemotron, and orchestrating CATIA AI Agents & SIMULIA AI Agents with SIMULIA solvers, accelerated by NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, to rapidly design and virtually test vehicle doors before building physical prototypes.
UniversalAGI is working with Saab to protect sailors from life-threatending wave impacts at sea, using UniversalAGI’s Latent Interaction Field Transformer physics AI foundation models with accelerated processing by NVIDIA Warp to evaluate thousands of wave conditions and headings in real time instead of days. These capabilities enable vessels to anticipate dangerous motion and autonomously select safer routes to avoid putting sailors at risk, while NVIDIA Omniverse libraries help visualize vessel behavior at sea.
PhysicsX is working with GB1, Britain’s America’s Cup team, on AI-powered yacht design, using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to visualize hull geometry and pressure fields, while Fermioniq’s Sofia agent helps Deltares and Dutch ministries model river flow by translating natural-language requests into simulation solvers built on NVIDIA Warp.
Mistral plans to use CUDA-X, Warp and Omniverse libraries to accelerate physics simulation and generate training data for engineering AI models.
Testing Factories and Robots Virtually
NVIDIA Omniverse and Isaac libraries enable digital twins and robotics simulation, helping manufacturers evaluate production systems and robot behavior before making changes on the factory floor.
Audi uses a battery-production digital twin built with NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to test production concepts before physical equipment is available. The company is also working with Dassault Systèmes and Agile Robots to simulate and validate mobile humanoid robots and logistics processes in DELMIA virtual twins built with Omniverse libraries.
Schaeffler is integrating digital twins of its humanoid actuators — components that move robot joints — with NVIDIA Isaac simulation frameworks, helping its robotics partners evaluate component behavior in simulation and reduce physical testing.
Wandelbots uses NOVA with Isaac Sim, built on Omniverse and OpenUSD, to validate assembly workflows digitally and prepare applications for physical robots.
Falkor, a KONGSBERG company, is integrating agents and NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into its platform. With Microsoft Azure NCv6 virtual machines powered by NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, agents with spatial intelligence combine engineering data, operating information and 3D equipment geometry to see, simulate and reason over industrial facilities, supporting inspection and maintenance use cases across the process and energy industries.
The same simulation approach extends to AI infrastructure. Schneider Electric, together with AVEVA, is developing an AI factory digital twin built for Nscale with Omniverse libraries to help engineers compare power, cooling and equipment configurations before making physical changes.

articles.title: Motorola desafía a Xiaomi: su próximo móvil tendrá una batería gigante y precio rompedor
articles.text:
Motorola prepara el lanzamiento de un nuevo móvil de gama media con gran autonomía. A unos meses de presentar el Moto G47, el fabricante tiene todo listo para desvelar el Moto G47 Power, la variante que llega con una batería de mayor capacidad. Tal y como ha ocurrido con las generaciones anteriores, Motorola tomará como base el G47, por lo que este terminal comparte muchas de sus características.
Una filtración reciente ha revelado todas las especificaciones, incluido el precio. De acuerdo con GSMArena, el Moto G47 Power llegará con una batería de 7.000 mAh que es prácticamente idéntica a la que vimos en el G37 Power. Esta garantiza hasta dos días completos de uso sin necesidad de conectarlo y admite carga rápida TurboPower de 30 W por cable.
Por fuera, el Moto G47 Power ofrece una pantalla LCD de 6,67 pulgadas con resolución de 1604 x 720 píxeles y tasa de refresco de 120 Hz y recubrimiento Gorilla Glass 7i. Bajo el capó encontraremos un procesador MediaTek Dimensity 6300 de ocho núcleos junto con una configuración de 4 GB de RAM y 128 GB de almacenamiento interno. La filtración no menciona otras variantes, aunque podríamos esperar una de 8 GB + 128 GB, si es que la escasez de memoria lo permite.
En el apartado fotográfico tampoco habrá muchos cambios, ya que el Moto G47 Power usaría la misma configuración que su hermano menor. El módulo trasero incluye una cámara principal de 108 megapíxeles con zoom de 3 aumentos sin pérdida de calidad y una lente macro dedicada para fotografía de cerca. Este modelo no incluye gran angular y la cámara frontal solo alcanza los 8 MP, que son suficientes para las selfies y las videollamadas.
Moto G47 Power vs Moto G47: ¿qué cambia?
La diferencia fundamental entre ambos modelos está en la autonomía. El Moto G47 Power eleva la capacidad de la batería hasta los 7.000 mAh, mientras que el Moto G47 se queda en los 5.200 mAh. Otro ajuste importante lo vemos en la carga rápida, que pasa de 20 W a 30 W por cable. El resto de especificaciones se mantiene idéntico, incluidas las cámaras y el procesador.
Si lo comparamos con el G37 Power que se presentó en abril de este año, la única diferencia es el tiempo adicional de soporte que obtendrás. A juzgar por las filtraciones, el Moto G47 Power sería prácticamente idéntico, por lo que podrías comprar esta variante y ahorrarte unos cuantos euros.
De acuerdo con el último rumor, el Moto G47 Power tendría un precio de salida cercano a los 270 euros para la versión de 4 GB + 128 GB. El móvil se venderá en dos acabados: uno negro y otro verde turquesa con el acabado fino de Pantone que caracteriza a la marca. Por el momento no hay detalles sobre su disponibilidad, aunque está confirmado que lo veremos en España, puesto que Motorola publicó su documentación sobre la Etiqueta Energética Europea hace unos días.

articles.title: Mit Videos und Beratung: Experten sollen bald direkt auf Linkedin Geld verdienen können
articles.text:
Mit Videos und Beratung: Experten sollen bald direkt auf Linkedin Geld verdienen können
Immer mehr Menschen nutzen Linkedin nicht nur für ihre berufliche Karriere, sondern auch für eigene Projekte und zusätzliche Einnahmequellen. Laut dem Business-Netzwerk ist die Zahl der Gründer:innen auf Linkedin um 70 Prozent gestiegen. In welchem Zeitraum, ist aber unklar. Im Vergleich zu 2019 hat zudem der Anteil der Nutzer:innen, die mehr als eine berufliche Position angeben, um 26 Prozent zugenommen. Auch mehr als 80 Prozent der Creator veröffentlichen ihre Inhalte neben einer weiteren beruflichen Tätigkeit. Für die Gründer:innenzahl nennt Linkedin allerdings keinen konkreten Vergleichszeitraum.
Mit den jetzt angekündigten Funktionen will Linkedin diesen Entwicklungen Rechnung tragen und Nutzer:innen neue Möglichkeiten bieten, ihre beruflichen Kontakte zu pflegen und mit ihren Inhalten sowie ihrem Fachwissen Geld zu verdienen. Geplant sind unter anderem kostenpflichtige Beratungsgespräche über das eigene Profil, Werbeeinnahmen für Video-Creator und ein neues Creator-Dashboard. Außerdem testet das Business-Netzwerk einen eigenen Network-Feed und führt digitale Visitenkarten sowie persönliche Notizen für Kontakte ein.
Advice-Sessions: Beratungen über das Linkedin-Profil verkaufen
Mit dem neuen Feature Advice-Sessions können Expert:innen kostenpflichtige Einzelberatungen über ihr LinkedIn-Profil anbieten. Interessierte können dort Termine buchen, bezahlen und die Beratung per Video wahrnehmen. Linkedin übernimmt damit auch die Abwicklung von Beratungsleistungen, für die Berater:innen und andere Selbstständige bisher auf externe Buchungs- und Zahlungsdienste angewiesen waren.
Vorerst steht das Feature allerdings nur Business-Premium-Abonnent:innen in den USA zur Verfügung. Weitere Länder sollen folgen. Wann Advice-Sessions in Deutschland starten und welche Gebühren anfallen, hat Linkedin noch nicht mitgeteilt.
Mit In-Stream-Ads auf Linkedin Geld verdienen
Creator wiederum können mit ihren Videos auf Linkedin Geld verdienen. Über das In-Stream-Ads-Programm erhalten ausgewählte Nutzer:innen Werbeeinnahmen, wenn vor ihren Videos sogenannte Pre-Roll-Ads ausgespielt werden. Die Teilnahme am Programm soll künftig über das neue Creator-Dashboard möglich sein.
Mit der Monetarisierung von Videoinhalten beschäftigt sich Linkedin bereits seit einiger Zeit. So führte das Unternehmen 2025 mit BrandLink neue Werbeformate für Videos ein. Nun sollen weitere Creator von den Werbeeinnahmen profitieren können. Vorerst testet Linkedin das In-Stream-Ads-Programm allerdings nur mit ausgewählten Creatorn und Advertisern in den USA. Eine Ausweitung ist geplant.
Das neue Creator-Dashboard soll außerdem die Verwaltung von Inhalten erleichtern und einen Überblick über die Content-Performance sowie verfügbare Einnahmemöglichkeiten bieten. Linkedin will es in den kommenden Wochen weltweit einführen. In der mobilen App ist es dann über das Profilbild oben links erreichbar. Welche Monetarisierungsfunktionen dort angezeigt werden, hängt allerdings von der jeweiligen Verfügbarkeit ab. So bleibt das In-Stream-Ads-Programm zunächst auf ausgewählte Teilnehmer:innen in den USA beschränkt.
Linkedin testet neuen Network-Feed und führt digitale Visitenkarten ein
Neben den Einnahmemöglichkeiten gibt es auch Neuerungen beim Networking. Linkedin testet einen eigenen Network-Feed, in dem Beiträge von Kontakten und abonnierten Profilen zusammengeführt werden. Nutzer:innen sollen so leichter verfolgen können, was Menschen aus ihrem beruflichen Umfeld veröffentlichen, statt sich ausschließlich auf die Auswahl des bisherigen Feeds verlassen zu müssen. Der Test startet zunächst in den USA, Indien, Großbritannien und Australien. Wann die neue Ansicht in Deutschland verfügbar sein wird, ist noch offen.
Außerdem führt Linkedin personalisierbare digitale Visitenkarten ein, die sich im Smartphone-Wallet speichern und bei persönlichen Treffen teilen lassen. Die Funktion soll in den kommenden Monaten weltweit verfügbar werden. Premiumabonnent:innen können bereits jetzt private Notizen zu anderen Profilen hinterlegen und beispielsweise festhalten, wo sie jemanden kennengelernt haben, worüber gesprochen wurde oder wann ein erneuter Austausch ansteht.
Autor:innen können zudem Kommentare künftig anpinnen und damit etwa besonders hilfreiche Ergänzungen oder Antworten hervorheben. Linkedin reagiert mit den neuen Networking-Funktionen nach eigenen Angaben auch auf Unsicherheiten beim Aufbau beruflicher Beziehungen. Laut einer Untersuchung des Unternehmens weiß mehr als die Hälfte der befragten Angehörigen der Generation Z nicht genau, wie sie nach dem ersten Vernetzen eine berufliche Beziehung weiterentwickeln soll.
Linkedin will mehr Geschäft über das eigene Netzwerk abwickeln
Linkedin arbeitet schon länger daran, aus beruflicher Reichweite neue Einnahmemöglichkeiten zu schaffen. Im Juni 2026 führte das Unternehmen einen eigenen Creator-Marketplace für Kooperationen zwischen Marken und B2B‑Influencern ein. Hinzu kommen Funktionen wie die Collaborative-Posts, mit denen sich Inhalte gemeinsam veröffentlichen lassen. Mit Advice-Sessions nimmt Linkedin nun auch den Verkauf von Beratungsleistungen in den Blick und will neben der Kund:innengewinnung künftig deren Buchung, Bezahlung und Durchführung ermöglichen.
Für Selbstständige liegt der Vorteil vor allem darin, dass sie ihre Beratungsleistungen dort anbieten können, wo sie bereits Kontakte pflegen, Reichweite aufbauen und potenzielle Kund:innen erreichen. Linkedin könnte damit einen Teil jener Geschäftsprozesse übernehmen, die bisher über externe Anbieter:innen abgewickelt werden. Das spart möglicherweise Aufwand, macht Selbstständige aber auch stärker von dem Business-Netzwerk abhängig, das nicht nur die Sichtbarkeit ihrer Angebote beeinflusst, sondern künftig auch Buchungen und Zahlungen verarbeitet.
Wie attraktiv die neuen Einnahmemöglichkeiten wirtschaftlich sind, lässt sich noch nicht beurteilen. Linkedin hat weder mögliche Gebühren für Advice-Sessions noch konkrete Verdienstmöglichkeiten durch In-Stream-Ads genannt. Für Nutzer:innen in Deutschland bleibt die Frage vorerst ohnehin theoretisch, denn während das Creator-Dashboard und die digitalen Visitenkarten weltweit eingeführt werden sollen, sind die beiden Monetarisierungsangebote zunächst auf die USA beschränkt.
Der Artikel stammt von Larissa Ceccio aus der OnlineMarketing.de-Redaktion und wird im Rahmen einer Content-Kooperation auf t3n veröffentlicht.

articles.title: Egyptian fintech MNT-Halan begins trading on EGX after heavily oversubscribed IPO - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian fintech company MNT-Halan has begun trading on the Egyptian Exchange (EGX) following a strong response to its initial public offering (IPO).
Founded in 2018, MNT-Halan was created to digitally bank the unbanked and substitute cash with electronic solutions. The MNT-Halan digital ecosystem includes small and micro business lending, payments, consumer finance, and e-commerce.
Since inception, MNT-Halan has disbursed over US$15.5 billion in loans and served more than 8 million customers globally. Through its subsidiaries, including Halan and Tasaheel, the group has served around 7.9 million customers since launch and has roughly 1.9 million active customers annually. It had disbursed more than EGP178 billion (US$3.3 billion) in financing.
In the meantime, the company has also become a unicorn, raising several significant funding rounds, most recently earlier this month, and it has now listed on the EGX. MNT-Halan, which lists under the ticker HALN.CA, marked the milestone with a bell-ringing ceremony in Cairo yesterday (October 20), attended by government officials, regulators, EGX leadership and representatives of the banks and advisors involved in the deal.
The IPO saw MNT Investments B.V. sell 320 million existing shares, equal to 20 per cent of MNT-Halan’s issued share capital. Of these, 272 million shares went to the private tranche and 48 million to the public tranche.
Demand was strong across the board. The private tranche was 11.2 times oversubscribed, rising to 19.4 times when cornerstone investors are excluded. The public tranche was 43.6 times oversubscribed, with more than 41,500 subscription orders received.
“The strong demand for our IPO reflects investors’ confidence in Egypt, the financial ecosystem we have built, and our growth trajectory,” said Mounir Nakhla, founder and CEO of MNT-Halan.
“As we enter this next phase, we remain focused on broadening our product ecosystem, deepening customer engagement and leveraging our proprietary technology to reach more customers and drive sustainable growth.”

articles.title: Un vecino valló su plaza de garaje con una red pensando que la Ley de Propiedad Horizontal le daría la razón. La Justicia ha hablado
articles.text:
Pocas cosas hay tan españolas como una junta de vecinos. La convivencia es un plato que se sirve caliente y los juzgados españoles tienen que ver multitud de situaciones de lo más estrambóticas. Algunas, incluso, han tenido que llegar al Tribunal Supremo para que sea el máximo órgano judicial el que decida. En otras no ha hecho falta
Y de ello podemos sacar algunas conclusiones.
Una valla. Es lo que instalaron unos vecinos vecinos de Huelva en su plaza de garaje. Concretamente, una vaya con una malla metálica para que nadie pudiera entrar en la misma y una instalación eléctrica para ver mejor lo que tenían que hacer dentro.
Las obras se llevaron a cabo pese a que no informaron de esta decisión a la comunidad de propietarios. Ésta decidió dar plenos poderes al presidente de la comunidad de vecinos para, llegado el caso, denunciar a estos vecinos si no retiraban la instalación.
Como esto no se produjo, los vecinos fueron demandados por la comunidad de vecinos. Era 2013.
¿Qué paso? Durante los siguientes años, vecinos y comunidad de propietarios mantuvieron una guerra abierta en los tribunales. El resultado es que el Juzgado de Primera Instancia de Moguer (Huelva) resolvió que la instalación, no permitida por la comunidad de propietarios, era ilegal y por tanto tenían que desmantelar la valla metálica y la instalación eléctrica.
La decisión, que no había llegado antes de 2016, fue recurrida por los demandantes ya que no contemplaba que los demandados tuvieran que pagar las costas del juicio. Dos años más tarde, ya en 2018, la Audiencia Provincial de Huelva tuvo que confirmar la decisión tomada por el juzgado anterior, recalcando que aunque el acuerdo de rechazo a la instalación hubiera sido impugnado por los vecinos afectados, eso no era suficiente para saltarse dicho veto Sin unas medidas cautelares de un juez no cabía el encaje jurídico para seguir adelante con la obra.
¿Por qué? La Ley de Propiedad Horizontal señala en su artículo 7.1 lo siguiente:
El propietario de cada piso o local podrá modificar los elementos arquitectónicos, instalaciones o servicios de aquél cuando no menoscabe o altere la seguridad del edificio, su estructura general, su configuración o estado exteriores, o perjudique los derechos de otro propietario, debiendo dar cuenta de tales obras previamente a quien represente a la comunidad
En este caso, los vecinos habrían incurrido en más de una ilegalidad. Y es que estarían alterando la configuración o estado exteriores pero, además, no habían remitido el aviso de que iban a realizar obras a la comunidad de vecinos o su representante. Por lo tanto, los tribunales determinaron que estaban realizando una alteración unilateral de la configuración del garaje.
Más casos. Aunque el vallado con una red metálica de una plaza de garaje es llamativo, no es el único caso donde la modificación de las instalaciones del garaje ha terminado con demandas cruzadas entre vecinos y comunidades de propietarios.
Este mismo año, los compañeros de Xataka Home nos traían el caso de un vecino que se había construido un trastero sobre su plaza de garaje. En la zona inferior guardaba la furgoneta y justo encima había ideado una suerte de almacén.
Los hay que utilizan el espacio justo al revés. En 2024 contábamos en Xataka que el Tribunal Supremo se pronunciaba sobre un caso más o menos parecido. En este caso se acusaba al vecino de utilizar su trastero como garaje. Aprovechando que ambos espacios eran contiguos, tiró el muro que los separaba para crearse un una plaza de garaje doble donde meter dos coches.
Una cuestión estructural. Lo que hay que tener en cuenta en este caso es que estas modificaciones suponen una modificación sustancial de lo que nos encontramos en la plaza de garaje. Y es que, como han confirmado los expertos a Xataka, podemos montar una barandilla en la plaza para que el vecino no raye el coche pero sólo si no impedimos su entrada y salida del coche y mantengamos el uso de la plaza.
Lo que se dirimía en este caso es el uso de la plaza como trastero. Esto está prohibido porque no se estaría utilizando el espacio para lo que ha sido concebido. Cualquier modificación de este tipo tiene que respetar las condiciones de seguridad del edificio y, si así fuera, tener el visto bueno de los vecinos. En el caso onubense, de lo segundo no hay ni rastro.

articles.title: Chinese crime ring steals more than $5 million in gift cards from Staples customer service — more than 15,000 gift cards acquired through internal Nexus system, nearly $500,000 spent before being deactivated
articles.text:
Chinese crime ring steals more than $5 million in gift cards from Staples customer service — more than 15,000 gift cards acquired through internal Nexus system, nearly $500,000 spent before being deactivated
Over $5 million worth of gift cards for retailers like Target and Sephora were stolen when thieves gained access to a system called Nexus.
Millions of dollars worth of gift cards were stolen and then used to buy high-value tech gear at retailers like Target, Sephora, and Lowe's after a Chinese crime ring gained access to an internal Staples system and then used it to issue more than 15,000 cards to itself. While the hack hasn't been made public to date, a 404 Media report notes that it actually took place back in 2023.
The outlet reviewed court records that show that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) was told about the hack in October of that year. The hack came to light after it led to a search warrant that was unsealed last week. And while the document doesn't specifically name Staples as the victim of the hack, 404 Media has confirmed that it was the company affected based on other information. Such information includes the fact that the victim company is headquartered in Massachusetts, that it uses Blackhawk Networks to fulfill gift card orders, and that the company uses an internal customer support system called Nexus. The report notes that a reference to Nexus can be found on a former Staples executive's LinkedIn profile.
While Staples was under the impression that Nexus could not be accessed from beyond its own network, hackers found that not to be the case. They then "performed multiple heap dump requests," a process that captures all of the data held in an app's memory. That information gave the hackers the tools they needed to hijack logged-in sessions of Staples customer service employees. From there, they were able to issue gift cards at will.
Once the gift cards had been issued, the crime group sent runners to physical retail stores to spend them before they were identified and canceled. Target found that 35 gift cards were used at a New Hampshire store, with high-value products from Apple, Bose, and Beats all bought. All 35 cards were used within a period of just a single hour, although not all of them were obtained via this hack.
In total, Target told investigators that 3,850 gift cards worth over $140,000 were used across 85 different stores in just two days. Sephora was hit for $58,600 worth of sales, while Lowe's saw $226,000 spent across online and in-store purchases. In total, 4,630 stolen gift cards were used with a value of around $425,000.
This hack was just the tip of the iceberg, too. Last April, a Department of Justice announcement confirmed that three Chinese nationals had been sentenced for their part in a gift card fraud conspiracy. Including the Staples hack, the crime group stole more than $100 million worth of gift cards.
Chinese organized crime groups often pop up on the radar of U.S.-based law enforcement. Earlier this year, a Chinese phishing service that was used to generate scam websites using AI was dismantled. The service was linked to almost $2 billion in losses.

articles.title: Disrupt Africa, Touch Inspiration launch accelerator to help non-technical founders build and launch apps - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Disrupt Africa has partnered with Kenya-based digital product and technology company Touch Inspiration to launch Disrupt Launchpad, an app development accelerator that helps non-technical founders turn their ideas into working applications and bring them to market.
Founded in 2014, Disrupt Africa is the leading news platform dedicated to the African tech startup ecosystem, and a producer of research publications and podcasts.
Touch Inspiration was founded in 2017 and helps entrepreneurs and businesses turn their ideas into working digital products. The company specialises in developing web and mobile applications, AI-powered solutions and business platforms, taking products from defined requirements through development and launch.
The two organisations have joined forces to launch Disrupt Launchpad, a programme designed for entrepreneurs who have a clear app idea but lack the technical skills, team or resources to bring it to life. Through Touch Inspiration, founders can get their apps professionally built and launched at startup-friendly rates, while Disrupt Africa helps put those products in front of a wider audience of potential users, customers and investors.
“We meet so many people who are inspired to create something, but don’t know how to bring it to life. What makes this partnership with Disrupt Africa so exciting is that we get to help those people build their apps and, just as importantly, get them in front of the people who will actually use them. It’s one thing to have a great idea, but seeing it come to life and reach the market is where the real value is realised,” said Robert M., founder of Touch Inspiration.
“The whole point of Disrupt Africa has always been to make entrepreneurship accessible to everyone, and with this partnership with Robert M. and the amazing team at Touch Inspiration we’re going right in at the start. Funding is important, networking is key, but being able to build your great idea in the first place is absolutely essential,” said Tom Jackson, co-founder of Disrupt Africa. “This programme will help you build, and launch, and put you in a strong position to turn it into a success.”
Aspiring entrepreneurs and existing startups with clear app ideas are invited to apply through Disrupt Launchpad. The programme offers startup-friendly development rates, while selected ventures may even qualify for an equity-based partnership, reducing the upfront cost of getting their applications built.

articles.title: AI companies don't know how to fix the problems they're creating, so they're throwing money at kids — which still won't fix the problem
articles.text:
Elon Musk's stock grants and Anthropic's public fund are band-aids on an open sore and do not address AI's most fundamental and pressing problems
Money for... something
AI development and expansion is rocketing across our society, sparkling and bright like a Roman candle, but with its tail on fire. The disruptions are coming so fast, and the concerns are rising so quickly, that no one, not even those running the biggest AI companies, knows what to do. Instead of addressing issues like AI slop, job loss, self-replicating and developing AI running amok, and data centers, these AI bosses have come up with a better solution: cold, hard cash.
On Monday, Elon Musk casually posted on his X platform that he would give one of his SpaceX shares to every child in America, with the promise of more to come. Over at Anthropic, Dario Amodei proposed a public fund built on the value of 5% of his company's shares when it goes public next month.
Of the two offers, Anthropic has the most obvious value. The company might be worth a trillion dollars when it goes public in November, which means the fund will be close to $50 billion. That's a lot of money.
Whether it's $150 (the approximate value of a SpaceX share) or $5 billion, neither offer actually addresses AI's myriad issues. None of this equals regulation, oversight, a pause, or a concrete global discussion about a technology that may in 12 months' time be able to do any of our jobs, access most of our systems, and start making decisions on our behalf. None address the real-time, growing cybersecurity threats posed by AI that can crack any encryption and set off Denial of Service attacks at unimaginable scales.
But how?
Let’s leave aside all that for a moment and talk about the nuts and bolts of these proposals.
First of all, there’s the question of how Elon Musk is going to give every one of the 72 million children in America a stock grant (assuming — a big assumption — he follows through). There are ways of doing this (custodial accounts, transfer to a brokerage, even platforms like GiveaShare that support stock gifts for children). Trump Account recently did something similar (sort of tiny Individual Retirement Accounts for pint-sized people). However, when those stocks go in there, they're not something the children will access now or in the near future.
What would be the value of $150? A couple of toys, a few outfits? More likely, what’s going to happen here is those SpaceX shares will sit and maybe accumulate value (maybe not), and then, when the child is an adult looking for one of the few jobs AI has not taken over, they’ll use it to help support themselves for a little while. Maybe buy a meal.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As for Amodei's Anthropic offer, well, it is a lot of money, but once you set up the fund, you’d figure out how to manage it and allocate it. Who is going to control that fund, and how will it be parceled out? Will it, for instance, go to every individual state? Will it go to schools, grade schools, maybe high schools, maybe universities? Will it be used to set up AI curriculum? If so, what curriculum built now will be useful a decade from now? Those billions could be used, but they’ll have to be sort of churned and replenished so that new curriculum could be built (probably by AI).
I’m not saying that’s what’s going to happen because it could just be for job training centers, retraining for new jobs that people have never done before, but that AI cannot reasonably do. Maybe Anthropic will be funding trade schools. I have yet to see an AI plumber or electrician, though I guess eventually the robots will be skilled enough to run a pipe or fix a circuit.
Of the two plans, I have far less confidence in Musk to hand over those 72 million shares because he’s made promises like this before and has not carried through. It becomes a bit of a show, a flurry of hands and a digital wink to convince people that he actually cares, but there’s no indication that he really does beyond the growth of his company and personal wealth.
Money for something
Now, these things are not mutually exclusive. I do believe we need money to help retrain vast workforces in this AI age, and that should happen sooner as opposed to later. And sure, you know, giving a child a share is not a terrible gesture, a little something to put aside for later, for a rainy day, or a day when they realize that the AI is in control and the only way they can buy food is directly from another person because the AI is running the grocery store.
Maybe though, Anthropic's Fund could be used to figure out a better, more environmentally and community-friendly way to build data centres, perhaps in places where both people and wildlife don’t need to live (space, underground). I don’t know what the answer is to that, but that research needs to happen.
It’s unclear if either one of these monetary plans will actually come through, but one thing I can guarantee is that AI is not slowing down. Yes, there’s probably a coming correction, and there may be more consolidation, but the trajectory is set. It will continue, and if we don’t get people together to actually talk about how we’re managing this revolution, no amount of money is going to solve our AI problems.

articles.title: NVIDIA cuDSS Now Generally Available to Accelerate Engineering and Scientific Simulations
articles.text:
NVIDIA cuDSS, launched today in general availability, is an NVIDIA CUDA-X library that shifts a critical part of engineering and scientific simulations onto GPUs.
Complex engineering feats — from advanced chips to aircraft to industrial systems —– depend on simulation to predict how designs will perform before they’re built. As designs become more complex, simulations take longer to run, increasing computing demands and limiting the number of ideas teams can test.
NVIDIA cuDSS accelerates solving large sparse systems — the math-heavy step that repeats throughout engineering and scientific simulations and often limits how many designs a team can test — by tapping into GPUs. This lets applications reduce time to results and increase simulation throughput, enabling end users to explore larger more realistic models, more accurate representations and a wider design space at a reduced cost.
Industry leaders are already integrating NVIDIA cuDSS into their tools to transform workflows for their end customers:
- Applied Materials: With cuDSS, Applied Materials accelerated sparse solves in Ginestra, its physics-based, defect-centric simulation platform, by up to 10x versus CPU-only approaches, speeding exploration of semiconductor materials and device reliability.
- COMSOL: Using COMSOL Multiphysics with NVIDIA cuDSS on NVIDIA accelerated computing, ZEISS SMT achieved a measured 4x speedup in an EUV lithography plasma simulation benchmark, completing the full simulation in six days and 14 hours.
- Cadence: Uses cuDSS in its Celsius software to accelerate simulations of heat, structural stress and warpage in advanced chips and 3D chip designs, helping customers including Nokia analyze complex designs faster.
- Dassault Systèmes: Dassault Systèmes reports an 8-10x speedup using cuDSS within its Abaqus structural and computer simulation technology electromagnetic solvers for performance-critical simulations across industries.
- Siemens: Siemens uses cuDSS in Simcenter STAR-CCM+ to accelerate simulations of structures in fluid-structure interaction workflows.
- Synopsys: Synopsys uses cuDSS in its Sentaurus Device simulator tool to accelerate simulations of advanced logic, memory and power chips, helping Infineon model increasingly complex devices faster.
Accelerated Simulation at Scale
As simulation workloads grow in size and complexity, cuDSS can scale out of the box from individual workstations to large computing clusters.
Developers can integrate cuDSS into existing engineering, scientific and optimization software offerings, bringing GPU acceleration to tools already used by engineers and researchers. They can use cuDSS through C, C++, Python and Fortran interfaces.
Learn more about cuDSS by visiting the NVIDIA demo booth and Dassault Systèmes booth at GTC Berlin.
