articles.title: Britain’s Skyfly raises €8.91 million to bring its two-seat Axe eVTOL to market and develop Longbow for defence | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Skyfly Technologies, a British developer of electric and hybrid-electric vertical take-off aircraft, has closed an €8.91 million ($10 million) Seed round.
The round was led by HICO Investment Group, a specialist growth equity investor, with participation from Archangel, a €50 million early-stage fund and Europe’s only dedicated next-generation defence technology venture fund.
“What Skyfly’s team has achieved with so little is remarkable: a new aircraft, designed and built from scratch, flying and now leading the way through a brand-new certification pathway. We’re excited to back a team with a big vision and relentless drive to execute,” said Chris Hartnoll, Managing Director, HICO Investment Group.
Founded in 2019 and based in Thorpe Mandeville, Oxfordshire, Skyfly develops manned and unmanned aircraft and systems for civilian and defence markets. Its flagship product, the Axe, is a two-seat, fully electric, vertically-capable aircraft with a range of more than 100 miles and a cruise speed of 100mph, requiring no runway for take-off or landing. The Longbow is its hybrid-electric unmanned derivative for defence and government customers.
The Axe is developed under the leadership of CTO Dr. William Brooks, who has spent over three decades in light aircraft development and has certified more than 2,000 aircraft currently in service. Axe takes off like a helicopter using eight fixed-angle electric motors, transitions to forward flight where its wings generate aerodynamic lift and can operate from conventional runways.
Since there are no tilting motors or rotary wings, Axe is designed to eliminate the mechanical complexity and potential points of failure that characterise many eVTOL concepts. In an emergency power loss scenario, the winged design allows the aircraft to glide rather than fall.
The Axe offers a range of over 100 miles, a flight time of 60 to 90 minutes, a cruising speed of 100mph and a 200kg payload capacity. Skyfly projects an operating cost of around €83.57 (£70) per flight, which gives it a favourable standing against the likes of legacy two-seater aircrafts such as Robinson R22 or Cessna 152.
Longbow, Skyfly’s second aircraft, is a hybrid-electric unmanned aircraft with a range exceeding 400 miles and the same 200kg payload. It is designed for cargo resupply, intelligence and surveillance, medevac, and ship-to-shore logistics missions. The company says both the aircraft will be manufactured at Skyfly’s 10,000 sq.ft. facility in Thorpe Mandeville, Oxfordshire.
“Longbow addresses a clear requirement for unmanned systems that can move meaningful payloads over significant distances without relying on a runway. Archangel invests exclusively in defence-first companies, and our backing of Skyfly reflects the potential we see in its technology to deliver mission necessary capability for the modern battlespace,” said Nicholas Nelson, General Partner at Archangel Ventures.
Skyfly says its Axe prototype has completed more than 100 piloted flights, including Europe’s first airfield-to-airfield eVTOL flight. It holds experimental flight permits in both the UK and the US, and sixty-one private customers globally have already placed orders.
The fundraise comes amid a regulatory shift, with the FAA’s MOSAIC reforms taking effect in July 2026. The MOSAIC reforms rewrote the rules governing Light Sport Aircraft to admit electric propulsion, multi-motor architectures and vertical take-off aircraft into a category that has been historically restricted to private owners rather than commercial operators. Skyfly says its Axe, a two-seat electric Vertically Capable Aircraft (eVCA) classified as Light Sport-class, was designed precisely for this rulebook.
Michael Thompson, founder and CEO of Skyfly, said, “This investment gives us the resources to take the Axe from a flying prototype to a certified aircraft in customers’ hands. The FAA’s MOSAIC rules have opened a route to market that simply did not exist for electric aircraft before, and the Axe was designed for exactly this category. HICO and Archangel understood that timing, and their backing lets us move at the pace the opportunity demands: completing certification and standing up series production.”
The fresh capital will be deployed across three areas: completing FAA Light Sport Aircraft certification for the Axe under the MOSAIC rules, scaling manufacturing capacity on both sides of the Atlantic, and accelerating development of the Longbow.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo is a messy, expensive, good time
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo is the riskiest Apple product in years. It’s a huge rethink of what an iPhone is and could be, and it contains the seeds of many fascinating ideas that might be great in the future.
The iPhone Duo is a messy, expensive, good time
Apple’s first foldable is an early adopter special.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
But that future is yet to come. The iPhone Duo is also one of Apple’s messiest first-generation products in a long time, and right now it will delight gadget nerds and early adopters and likely frustrate everyone else.
It’s been a minute since the iPhone has looked or worked significantly differently. The last major change was the iPhone X, which dropped the home button almost a decade ago, and even that was a fairly subtle improvement. In fact, “subtle improvement” is really the entire story of the iPhone — it’s the foundation of Apple’s entire business, after all, and there’s a lot of risk in just up and changing it. You can see it in this year’s iPhone 18 Pro: It’s been refined in many ways, with better thermals and an interesting variable aperture lens, but it’s barely different than the iPhone 17 Pro.
But you can’t play it safe designing a foldable. You have to make some big decisions about screen sizes and what the inner and outer displays are for, and then make an even bigger set of decisions about how that big inner screen should work. All of those decisions are risky, and Apple’s riskiest decision was the Duo’s size and shape.
iPhone Duo
The Good
- Fun to play with
- Matte inner display is very cool
- You will watch less TikTok on it
The Bad
- You will watch less TikTok on it because the cover display is too small
- Heavier and bulkier than a standard phone
- Gets hot
- Cameras are just OK
Hardware and design
Apple’s single most important design decision for the Duo was to make it shaped like a passport.
The wide aspect ratio makes the inner screen friendlier for 16:9 YouTube videos, but it also marks a departure from the taller foldable design phone makers have embraced over the past five years. Prior to 2026, most folding phones opted for a tall-and-narrow shape to optimize for using vertical apps on the cover screen. But rumors started pointing to Apple going with its landscape-first form factor, and other foldable makers shifted gears — seemingly to get ahead of Apple. Now that the iPhone and a handful of competitors have adopted the wide format, they have to solve a new problem: designing a cover screen that will work well enough for vertically oriented apps.
The Duo’s 5.4-inch outer display is glossy, while the 7.6-inch inner display has a striking nano-texture matte coating. Apple’s very proud of this inner matte display, and for good reason — it looks and feels incredibly solid, a big step up from foldables with glossy, seemingly soft screens with glaringly obvious creases, like the Pixel Fold, and even the more subtle but still visible crease of the Galaxy Fold 8.
The matte display is indeed there to help hide the crease, which Apple keeps calling “perceptually flat” because it’s more fun to invent science-y marketing phrases than just saying “you mostly don’t see it.” But it’s true: You mostly can’t see the display crease, although you can definitely feel it. If you’re looking at a white image off-axis, you can see it, and there are moments in some lighting where it’s much more obvious. It definitely shows up more prominently on camera than it does to your eyes.
What you will see is the under-display camera, which reflects light in a more glossy way if you’re outdoors or in a bright area. Overall, though, the camera and display crease stopped being noticeable after a while. The crease also wasn’t any more noticeable after a week of constant flipping and folding, although we’ll see how it holds up over time.
That’ll be a real test, because Duo owners are going to be constantly flipping this thing open. Between Apple’s display aspect ratio and iOS design choices, the outer screen feels like much more of a status display than you’d expect — everything about the Duo gently nudges you to flip it open and use it in tablet mode. And not just tablet mode, but portrait tablet mode. That’s because iPhone apps are largely portrait, and the Duo is still very much an iPhone, even though its shape makes it fight all that history.
iPhones have gotten bigger over the years, but they’ve mostly stuck to the same basic rectangular aspect ratios: 2:3 from the first iPhone through the 4S, 16:9 from the iPhone 5 through the 8, and 19.5:9 from the iPhone X on to today’s iPhone 18 Pro. Basically, the iPhone has mostly gotten taller over time.
It’s wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places
The Duo changes all of that — it’s the first iPhone that’s gotten shorter and wider. Both the inner and outer displays have a 1.4:1 aspect ratio, which was a very deliberate choice on Apple’s part, because they’re the same shape open and closed. This is clever in terms of display math and potentially great for app developers, but in practice it means that the outer display is really quite small, especially compared to modern Max-sized phones. If you’re texting someone in Messages with the keyboard onscreen, you’re lucky to be able to see two or three texts at once.
Apple has tried to reclaim some vertical space by scooting the UI elements of updated apps off to the right, but if you’re left-handed, that means using the phone closed with one hand can be challenging, even for someone with big hands. Having that strip of real estate along the right side occupied by navigation controls also means that using the Duo single-handed in your right forces you to reach farther when there’s something on the left side of the screen you need to tap. This means that you’re sometimes holding a fairly heavy phone, stretching for a small target that’s just out of reach, which isn’t particularly confidence-inspiring.
It’s also wild to have iPhone apps with controls in all kinds of different places; reaching for the back button in Apple’s Mail app and realizing it’s moved from the top left to the right is kind of disorienting. A lot of using the Duo is just figuring out how to use an iPhone again, which hasn’t happened in a long time.
If you’re using an app that isn’t updated for the Duo, you’ll see a black bar along the right side of the cover screen where those navigation controls would otherwise live. But even updated apps don’t feel particularly useful for anything other than a quick check-in on the cover screen. Apple says you’re getting 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro, but that’s pretty small for today’s apps. It’s like having an iPhone 5 in a world of iPhone Pro Maxes.
This means that when you pull the Duo out of your pocket, you’ll almost always be looking at a tiny amount of information. And the second you want to really do anything, you’ll find yourself unfolding the phone to use the vastly larger and more useful inner display.
But you don’t get any additional height when you open the Duo up. Switching from a tiny portrait display to a bigger landscape view isn’t useful for most phone apps, which are all designed around big portrait displays. Most phone apps look silly this way, especially those still running as standard iPhone apps, which look normal but with lots of black padding on either side. It’s either cramped and tiny on the outer screen or a little silly and awkward when you open the Duo.
This means almost every time you open the phone you instinctively rotate it, and while it will work no matter how it’s rotated, it’s better to rotate it counterclockwise so the cameras are on top and the volume buttons are on the top left. Over our week of testing, this started feeling more natural, but it’s exactly the opposite of what you’d initially expect. It’s especially odd in Apple’s bumper case, which has a large notch to expose the Touch ID sensor and camera control, and it looks for all the world like it belongs at the bottom.
You might think this is a little thing, but it’s strange to find yourself slightly unsure of how to hold a smartphone. A nontrivial part of the Duo experience is just reorienting yourself to where the volume buttons are as you flip the thing around. When closed, they’re on top of the phone, but if you rotate the Duo clockwise, they end up on the bottom right, and it’s the top button that turns the volume down because they don’t change orientation with the display. There’s a buried setting in iOS that makes the volume buttons reorient themselves as you turn the Duo around; Apple needs to set it so it works right by default.
One other thing to get used to is simply unlocking the phone. Touch ID is integrated into the wake button on the side of the phone. There’s no Face ID at all, and it might take a minute to remember that when you stare at your phone for a beat and wonder why your notifications aren’t unfurling. Ask us how we know. But a week is long enough to get used to Touch ID life again, and it’s mostly painless once you remember you’re supposed to be using it.
Now, here’s the thing: This is all pretty fun! The iPhone has been the same for so long that being forced to come up with little moves and tricks and ways to think about holding the Duo is a gadget nerd thrill. Other foldables do this too — Samsung and Google and Huawei have been pushing the envelope of gadget-y smartphones for ages — but Apple’s played it so safe for so long that the Duo is legitimately surprising. But Apple hasn’t found some magical software solution to making a product with this much inherent complexity any less chaotic. It just happens to be the kind of first-generation chaos that will delight early adopters and lead most everyone else back to their regular old iPhones.
Software
That first-generation wonkiness is most obvious in the software, especially in how the Duo supports third-party apps. Almost everyone who sees the Duo assumes that it simply opens up into being an iPad, but that’s not how it works at all. In classic Apple fashion, the company decided to throw everything out and start over.
That means getting rid of a lot of weird iPad baggage, but it also means that solved problems on the iPad are back on the Duo. It’s big stuff and little stuff: For whatever reason, the Duo doesn’t support pinching the keyboard to make it smaller and friendlier to use one-handed — a feature iPads have had for ages. It also means there are new ways to think about multitasking, and sometimes you’ll be unsure what will happen when you swipe around the screen because apps interact with iOS and each other in very different ways.
If you want to run two apps at once on the Duo, you swipe up and over to pin an app to one side, and then pin another app to the other side. If you tap on the little divider, you connect the apps into a set, and you can come right back to it in the app switcher. It’s neat, but it only works in landscape. If you want to have two apps open when you’re holding the Duo in portrait mode, you’re basically out of luck — unless what you want is to watch a video on the top while scrolling an app on the bottom. In that case, you need to make sure you have an app that supports background video, open that app, start the video, close that app to initiate the floating video window, open your other app, and then (and only then!) find a little button in the floating video window and hit that to pop everything into place.
This is legitimately cool once you figure it out. But you will note that this is a totally different approach to multitasking than any previous iPhone or iPad, and nothing about the Duo’s interface makes it obvious that it can work this way. It’s a lot of these little moments of figuring it out for yourself that really solidify the Duo as an early adopter special — especially since some features only work in some apps sometimes. That floating video feature? Yeah, it works with YouTube TV, but it doesn’t seem to work with regular YouTube.
This is initially surprising, because the YouTube app appears to be at least a little updated for the Duo. But it turns out that right now there are basically three ways apps work on the Duo.
iPhone Duo AMA
Got more questions about the Duo? Verge subscribers can post their questions over to our AMA where senior reviewer Allison Johnson will be answering them starting at 11:30AM ET.
First, there are regular iPhone apps that haven’t been updated at all. As with an iPad, you can zoom and rotate these apps to make things a little more useful, but they look pretty silly. This is the vast majority of apps right now, although we saw lots of apps get updated to the second category during the course of our review.
The second category is what you might call the messy middle: apps that have been updated for iOS 27. They get some automatic layout fixes so they’ll automatically expand to fill the inner screen in landscape orientation and don’t look quite as silly as standard iPhone apps. But you can tell they haven’t actually been designed for these displays, and those rough edges are super obvious. The telltale sign of these apps is the black bar on the right when you use them on the cover screen — proper Duo apps add controls to that space, but these in-between apps don’t.
Then there are fully updated Duo apps built for the Duo-specific iOS 27.1 — we got to test a few of these, and they can be pretty good. Instagram’s Edits app is a perfect example of why a folding phone is useful. It opens into a full video editor with a big timeline and nice preview window, and you can just get things done. And even in the span of the past week that we’ve been using the Duo, we’ve seen some apps, like Slack, go from the messy middle to fully updated. This makes a big difference in how useful they feel on the inner screen, but obviously doesn’t address the reality of the small outer-screen real estate.
Developers will need to have either a lot of energy to create neat stuff that takes advantage of the Duo’s form factor or a lot of encouragement from Apple. Maybe both. Either way, we have to hand it to the Deck-Man app, which reformats Apple Music into a little virtual Walkman. The page-turn animation in Books is terrific. And if you’ve ever dreamed of reading PDFs on a big screen in the back of an Uber, know that they look particularly great on the matte display.
But the reality is you’re going to see a lot of tiny iPhone apps and apps in the weird unoptimized middle zone for a while. It’s all just messy, in a lot of the same ways Android foldables are. That’s particularly surprising because the Android tablet app story has always been messy, but Apple had the whole ecosystem of iPad apps waiting at the ready. For whatever reason, the company just didn’t go that way, and that means it will take a while for the Duo’s app story to settle down.
Versus the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8
The Duo’s most obvious competitor is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which Samsung managed to sneak out a few months ahead of the Duo. They’re both wide folds, but they’re not exactly the same. The Fold 8’s front screen is slightly taller and narrower, and the Duo is noticeably thicker and heavier. Those details add up to a big difference in how it feels to use the cover screen, especially one-handed. The Duo is pretty hard to use single-handed, but it feels doable with the Fold 8.
Apple also insists on preserving the more narrow vertical aspect ratio when you use an app on the cover screen by reserving that strip on the side for controls, whereas Samsung lets content occupy the entire width of the screen. On the larger inner display, Samsung offers a couple of options to make the keyboard friendlier to use. You can switch to a one-handed option that’s easier to reach or a floating keyboard you can move around and resize. And lots more Android apps readily take advantage of the full inner screen because foldables have been a thing on Android for quite a while now.
Apple is really emphasizing the ability to use the Duo in a variety of postures, including that kind of “I’m reading a book” situation where it’s partially closed. You can prop the phone up in tent mode and use it as a clock or digital photo frame. If you use it as an alarm, you’ll get a nice glow from the inner screen that’s supposed to help gently wake you up. You can watch videos on half of the inner screen in laptop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. Weirdly, Apple is actually more liberal in this than Samsung. The half-open position is called Flex mode on other Galaxy foldables, but the Z Fold 8 doesn’t let you use it, probably because the hinge isn’t stiff enough all the way through its range of motion.
Another important difference: The Duo is rated IP68 for full water and dust resistance, while the Z Fold 8 is IP48, so it isn’t fully dust-resistant. Neither phone should be used carelessly at the beach, but that higher dust rating offers a little more peace of mind.
Overall, these feel like pretty familiar moves for both of these companies. Apple wants you to use its phone its way. Samsung is less hung up on details like aspect ratios and where the keyboard can be. As always, Apple’s phone works best the deeper you are in the walled garden. The Duo feels a little more polished, but the Z Fold 8 has the better cover screen experience. Given how much of the experience of a foldable is reliant on the cover screen, that counts for a lot.
Performance and battery life
We each tested our own review units under pretty different circumstances over the past week, so it’s not surprising our battery life experiences differed. Nilay used the Duo just like he would during any other workday, using Slack, Google Docs, and Safari, and watching YouTube TV, Instagram, and TikTok. He needed to charge the Duo at least once to get through the day. This matched his usual experience with regular Pro iPhones, although the MagSafe battery packs he uses to get through the day are made for taller iPhones and don’t fit the Duo very well.
Allison was traveling more with the Duo, and spent more time watching video on Wi-Fi on her flights and scrolling social media. She had about 30 percent left after about 6.5 hours of screen-on time, which is decent. But as ever, iPhone battery life tends to vary dramatically for everyone, and change a lot over time. That’s even more so the case with a foldable — the more you use the inner screen, the worse of a time you’ll have with the battery.
Performance-wise, the Duo has an A20 Pro chip, and Apple says it has the same improved vapor chamber thermal management system as the iPhone 18 Pro. For most things it’s plenty fast, but the reality is that it’s also a thin phone driving two big displays, and it definitely gets warm, and sometimes hot. We saw this happen in two places: third-party apps, particularly video apps and Google’s apps, caused things to get hot. The first-generation nature of the Duo really came through here, and it’s something we would hope would improve as various apps get updated.
The phone also heats up when you use the camera for a long time — especially features that use the camera and both displays at once, like Duo Preview and Kid Cue. You can just feel the phone getting significantly hotter when this happens. Add in processor-intensive camera features like Smart Take, which automatically hits the shutter button, and the phone gets hot enough to start noticeably lagging after a while.
You’d hope Apple can improve battery life and thermal management over time — it has certainly done that with other iPhones in the past. But the Duo today gets hot, and doesn’t seem ready to last a full day of heavy use. Those are real compromises on a phone that starts at $2,000.
Camera
The Duo’s other big compromise is camera quality. It has a smaller main camera sensor than the one you’ll find in the 18 Pro and is instead on par with what you get from the iPhone Air. That’s fine for grabbing everyday shots, but it’s fundamentally a notch below flagship tier. The Duo relies on heavier sharpening to make up for its weaker hardware, so fine details look a little crunchier than they do on the 18 Pro. The Duo retains a bit less color detail in low light too, though Night Mode kind of evens out the playing field between them.
Some of the manual controls on the 18 Pro are absent here, too. There’s no shutter speed and no moving aperture, but you do get white balance and manual focus controls. The biggest concession is that there’s no telephoto camera here. You get that 2x crop zoom and up to just 10x digital zoom. There’s a 48-megapixel ultrawide that’s fine, but you just don’t have the flexibility you’ll find on basically every slab phone that costs half as much as the Duo.
The 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the front screen is a little worse than the 18-megapixel one on the 18 Pro — again, it looks like it’s compensating for its lower resolution by oversharpening details. There’s also an under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen that’s okay in good light but really quite bad in dim light. (Apple won’t say the FaceTime camera’s resolution, but it’s just 4 megapixels.) Overall, it’s serviceable for a video call, but not much else.
But the good thing about a folding phone is that every camera on this thing is a selfie camera. You can open it up and preview your image on the front display while you use the much better main camera to take a photo of yourself. You’ll actually want to use the camera control button on purpose for a change, because it’s the only sensible way to press the shutter when you have the phone facing you like this — there’s no on-screen shutter and the volume controls are right next to the lens.
Apple’s Kid Cue takes a page out of Google’s book by using the front screen to play animations designed to get your kid looking at the camera. It works, but your subject will be looking off to the side since the Duo (wisely) uses the better main camera lens rather than the selfie camera for this. But if you’ve ever tried to get a young kid to look at a camera and make a normal face, you’ll probably agree that this is close enough.
Outside of that, the form factor lets you do a couple of fun things with the camera. You can set it up in laptop mode or standing up like a book to shoot a time-lapse. There’s a feature called Smart Take that will automatically snap photos when it senses that subjects in the frame are striking a pose that’s kinda fun. (It would be cool if you could switch the image preview to the other panel to use it halfway open like a waist-level viewfinder, but you can’t.)
The main camera records up to 4K/120 video and it will let you apply Cinematic mode to your clips after capture like the 18 Pro does. You also get the new texture controls in Photographic Styles if you want your foldable phone camera to act more like a film camera. Still, you’re definitely not getting the latest and greatest iPhone camera, which is weird on a $2,000 phone — though that’s certainly not unusual for a foldable.
On the other side of the aisle, Samsung basically split its Fold series into two models: the wide one with less-good cameras and the portrait-oriented one with a better main camera. You can’t have everything — unless you have access to foldables sold in China, in which case, yeah you can. The bottom line is that the Duo offers a totally acceptable camera for a new iPhone, but it’s far from the best iPhone camera you can get.
Bits and bobs
There’s a lot of other little stuff to say about the Duo — it’s full of new ideas and weird little details keep coming up the more you use it. The Duo has MagSafe, unlike the Z Fold 8, which is a big quality-of-life improvement. Allison found that a PopSocket made the Duo way easier to hold, while Nilay had a less-good time trying to use his existing MagSafe battery packs on the phone. He also has MagSafe mounts around his house and stuck the phone up all over the place, with entertaining results. Who hasn’t dreamed of having a tablet in the shower?
You can use the Duo like a tiny little laptop, which is adorable, and it connects to a portable keyboard for some purse computer action. You can also watch movies and TV shows with it slightly bent, so it stays open on a table in tent mode. (It takes a second for the phone to figure out that you want to do this, but it gets there.) If all of this sounds stressful, then the first-gen foldable life might not be for you. But if you’re itching to try some of this out for yourself, then you just might be the kind of early adopter who will have a good time with the Duo.
The wrap-up
The hard rule at The Verge for 15 years now is that you have to review the product that’s in the box — not the idea of the product, or all of our hopes and dreams, or even the promise of software updates to come. (And boy, does the Duo have a lot of software and app updates to come.) There’s a lot of potential in the Duo, but right now it is a first-gen device in every possible way.
It is expensive, it’s full of compromises, and it can be incredibly frustrating to use. Switching from the Duo back to one of our standard slab phones to get something done often felt like a relief. Sometimes you just need your iPhone to do what you need it to do — that’s why Apple has been so risk-averse in changing it.
It is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios
But all of the risk and weirdness of the Duo is also fun, in the way the best early adopter devices are fun. It’s incomplete as a product, but complete enough as an idea that you can see where things are going. It’s reminiscent of the very first MacBook Air, which took exactly no one by storm — it took a full redesign for Apple to get it right, and then it took over the entire industry.
We’ll see what happens with the Duo, but as it stands, it is very much an open question whether Apple made the right choices about the Duo’s screen sizes and aspect ratios. Most Duo owners will find that the cover display is simply too small to use all the time. Avoiding the entire iPad app ecosystem is another choice that might not age well; so is asking developers to jump on board with a device that’s clearly destined to eventually run into the iPad. Apple also made some very real compromises around the camera, and we’ll need to do a lot more testing to understand the Duo’s performance and thermal management story.
But the Duo is a more cohesive idea about foldables than most of its Android competition, precisely because Apple has a better app and developer story to lean on. Right now the problem for most Android foldables is that the inner screens aren’t that useful so there’s no super compelling reason to open them. The problem with the Duo is that the outer screen isn’t useful enough, so you want to open it all the time, and Apple’s ecosystem means that eventually the apps will be useful on the inner screen.
But the real answer is somewhere in the middle — for both screens to be interesting and useful. Someone’s going to get there, and we’ll see if Apple can be the first.

articles.title: Del horno al iPhone Duo: así se fabrica el titanio del primer teléfono plegable de Apple
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo es el primer teléfono plegable de Apple. En un video que compartieron en sus redes sociales, la empresa dio a conocer cómo es que se fabrica el titanio que luego termina en su nuevo producto estrella
El titanio que Apple utilizará en el iPhone Duo parte de un proceso industrial que comienza a temperaturas extremas y continúa con varias etapas de transformación. En su planta de Houston, Pensilvania, Perryman Company fundirá, forjará y laminará el material antes de suministrarlo para productos de Apple, incluido el nuevo teléfono plegable.
La compañía indicó que el titanio destinado al iPhone Duo tendrá al menos un 80 % de contenido reciclado. Apple se comprometió a aportar hasta 100 millones de dólares durante los próximos tres años para trabajar con Perryman, una empresa familiar especializada en productos de titanio. El anuncio forma parte de su American Manufacturing Program.
La noticia también llegó a las redes sociales: Apple publicó un carrusel en su cuenta verificada de Instagram, @helloapple, con imágenes del metal al rojo vivo, trabajadores de Perryman y el producto terminado. La publicación presenta la cadena de fabricación como parte de la historia del iPhone Duo y destaca el uso del titanio estadounidense.
Del material reciclado al lingote
El titanio es abundante en la corteza terrestre, pero no suele encontrarse como metal puro. Está unido a otros elementos en minerales y su extracción y procesamiento requieren varias fases. El Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos señala que, aunque el metal puro se aisló en 1910, la producción comercial mediante el proceso Kroll comenzó en 1948.
Para el suministro anunciado, Apple destaca el contenido reciclado y las operaciones de Perryman en Pensilvania. La empresa se presenta como fabricante integrado: controla distintas etapas, desde la fundición del titanio hasta la producción de barras, alambre y otras formas.
Su historia industrial se remonta a 1988; incorporó instalaciones automatizadas de laminado en caliente en 1997, amplió sus procesos de forja y fabricación en 2012 y agregó hornos de fusión por haz de electrones y arco al vacío en 2019 y 2020.
En la fundición, el material se lleva a temperaturas muy elevadas para producir metal que después puede convertirse en lingotes. Perryman emplea hornos de arco al vacío y de haz de electrones para ampliar sus capacidades de fusión.
A partir del lingote, la forja aplica presión para modificar su forma y estructura; luego, el laminado en caliente comprime el metal entre rodillos mientras conserva suficiente temperatura para trabajarlo. De esas fases salen productos intermedios que pueden transformarse en barras, bobinas u otras formas industriales.
Qué significa que sea titanio grado 5
Apple identificó el material como titanio grado 5, una aleación conocida en la industria como Ti-6Al-4V, compuesta principalmente por titanio, aluminio y vanadio. Es una de las aleaciones de titanio más utilizadas en sectores como el aeroespacial y el médico por su combinación de resistencia, bajo peso y resistencia a la corrosión.
Apple sostiene que esta resistencia resulta relevante para el iPhone Duo, cuya estructura debe acompañar un diseño plegable. El teléfono, presentado por la compañía como su primer iPhone plegable, tiene un marco de titanio grado 5 y una cubierta de bisagra hecha con titanio reciclado impreso en 3D, según el anuncio de lanzamiento.
Un recorrido industrial que continúa
La fundición, la forja y el laminado no son el último paso para obtener una pieza lista para un teléfono. Después, el material debe convertirse en componentes con las dimensiones y acabados requeridos. Apple no detalló en su anuncio todas las operaciones posteriores ni el recorrido exacto entre la planta de Perryman y el ensamblaje de la estructura del iPhone Duo.
La alianza conecta una aleación empleada durante décadas en industrias de alta exigencia con un dispositivo de consumo masivo. En las imágenes difundidas por Apple, el titanio aparece primero como metal incandescente y luego como rollos y barras, una manera de mostrar cómo el material atraviesa distintas etapas antes de formar parte del teléfono. La empresa presenta esa fabricación como parte de la historia del iPhone Duo: una estructura resistente concebida para un producto con pantalla plegable.

articles.title: GitHub Actions Runner Controller 0.15.0 Targets Reliability at Scale
articles.text:
GitHub has released Actions Runner Controller (ARC) 0.15.0, introducing reliability, scalability, and observability improvements for organisations running self-hosted GitHub Actions runners on Kubernetes. The October 1 release focuses on reducing unnecessary Kubernetes API requests, improving controller throughput and making upgrades and shutdowns more predictable, particularly for environments managing large numbers of runner scale sets.
ARC is a Kubernetes operator that automatically scales self-hosted runners in response to workflow demand. It allows organisations to run their own execution infrastructure while creating and removing runner instances as jobs arrive and finish. This is particularly useful for enterprises that need control over build environments, network access, compute resources, or workload isolation without maintaining a permanently provisioned pool of runners.
One of the main themes in version 0.15.0 is reducing the work the controller performs to keep runner resources in sync. Controller updates now use Kubernetes patch requests instead of full update requests, reducing the size of API payloads. Runner status aggregation has also moved to metrics for EphemeralRunnerSet and AutoscalingRunnerSet, reducing the number of status updates sent to the Kubernetes API.
The controllers now filter incoming events to avoid unnecessary reconciliation, while listener API client rate limits can be configured through queries-per-second and burst settings. Teams can also configure reconciliation concurrency globally or for individual controllers using max-concurrent-reconciles flags. Together, these changes give platform teams more control over how ARC behaves under load and should help reduce avoidable processing and API traffic in larger deployments.
The release also addresses lifecycle management. Patch-version upgrades now update resources in place, maintaining a one-to-one mapping between autoscaling runner sets and ephemeral runner sets and reducing disruption during upgrades.
Controller shutdown behaviour has also been improved. The terminationGracePeriodSeconds setting is now configurable and aligned with the controller manager's graceful-shutdown timeout, allowing operators to better control how the controller exits during restarts or upgrades.
ARC can also re-register a runner scale set when its recorded counterpart no longer exists in the GitHub Actions service. This helps the controller recover from a mismatch between its local Kubernetes state and the scale-set state maintained by GitHub.
Finally, ephemeral runners can be deleted faster when their runner pods exit successfully because ARC skips an additional server-side check for runner removal. While individually small, these changes address the operational details that become increasingly important when runner environments are created and destroyed continuously.
Moving runner status aggregation into metrics is particularly relevant to teams operating ARC as shared CI infrastructure. Large runner fleets generate frequent lifecycle events as jobs are queued, runners are provisioned, workloads execute, and ephemeral environments are removed. Reducing status patches can ease pressure on the Kubernetes API, while metrics provide a more suitable basis for monitoring aggregate controller and runner behaviour.
Configurable reconciliation concurrency and listener rate limits also help operators tune the balance between throughput and API pressure. However, these settings are not simply performance switches: increasing concurrency can increase the rate at which the controller interacts with Kubernetes and GitHub services. Teams should therefore validate changes against their workload patterns and cluster capacity rather than assuming higher concurrency is always better.
ARC is part of a broader move towards dynamically managed CI execution infrastructure. CircleCI's Machine Runner Orchestrator, for example, focuses on scaling machine-based runners and supports different resource classes, including CPU, GPU, and ARM workloads. ARC instead integrates directly with Kubernetes to manage GitHub Actions runner scale sets, commonly using ephemeral runner environments. The two approaches address the same broad challenge, matching execution capacity to CI demand, but differ in their platform integration and runner execution models
For organisations already standardised on GitHub Actions and Kubernetes, ARC provides a native way to manage runner capacity alongside other cluster resources. Its trade-off is that platform teams must also operate the controller, manage Kubernetes capacity and understand how runner scaling interacts with cluster scheduling, API limits and workflow demand.
ARC 0.15.0 is an incremental release, but its emphasis reflects a significant engineering concern: once CI infrastructure serves many repositories and teams, controller efficiency and lifecycle reliability become delivery concerns in their own right.

articles.title: Inside Gabon’s first angel investor network
articles.text:
20 octobre 2026
Hello 👋,
Welcome back to Francophone Weekly by TechCabal, your weekly deep dive into the tech ecosystem across French-speaking Africa. For readers who want to understand Francophone Africa beyond headlines—through markets, startups, and systems. New editions of the newsletter will land directly in your inbox every Tuesday at 12 PM WAT.
By default, this newsletter is in French. If you’re reading this in your email inbox, click the “Read in English” button below to switch to the English version. If you’re reading on our website, you can either click the button below or toggle the language selector at the top right-hand side of the page to view the English edition.
Le premier réseau structuré d’investisseurs providentiels du Gabon a déployé 67,3 millions de FCFA (118 000 dollars) dans quatre entreprises. La façon dont il y est parvenu en dit plus long sur les écosystèmes naissants que le chiffre lui-même.
En 2025, le Gabon a enregistré une seule opération de capital-risque, d’une valeur d’environ 1 million de dollars, selon l’Association africaine du capital-investissement et du capital-risque (AVCA). Le Cameroun, son voisin au sein du même bloc économique, a comptabilisé huit opérations pour 26 millions de dollars. L’Afrique centrale dans son ensemble n’a concentré que 10 opérations et 27 millions de dollars, faisant de cette région le plus petit marché de capital-risque du continent.
C’est dans ce contexte qu’est né le Gabon Angel Investor Network (GAIN), premier réseau structuré de business angels du pays. Cinq fondateurs l’ont lancé en 2021. Le réseau a réalisé son premier investissement en 2022. Depuis, il a injecté 67 345 000 FCFA (118 000 dollars) dans quatre entreprises, et son ticket moyen est passé de 11,5 millions de FCFA (19 000 dollars) à 25 millions de FCFA (43 000 dollars).
Ces chiffres paraissent modestes au regard des standards du marché du capital-risque nigérian — et c’est précisément là l’enjeu. Le GAIN construit simultanément une base d’investisseurs et un pipeline de startups, dans un marché où moins de 10 % des startups accèdent au crédit bancaire à un stade précoce.
Selon des données de la Banque des États de l’Afrique Centrale (BEAC) citées par le GAIN, le Gabon a capté 18,25 % des nouveaux crédits de la Communauté Économique et Monétaire de l’Afrique Centrale (CEMAC) au quatrième trimestre 2025, contre 63,93 % pour le Cameroun.
Des échanges avec Fabrice Nze Bekale, président du réseau, et Vanessa Adande, membre fondatrice et trésorière, en marge du sommet Africa’s Early Stage Investor Summit (AESIS) 2026 organisé par le GAIN à Libreville, la capitale gabonaise, ce mois-ci, révèlent que construire depuis zéro exige une flexibilité sur presque toutes les variables qu’un investisseur tient ordinairement pour fixes.
1. Recruter des investisseurs, une affaire de confiance
            Les participants au Libreville AESIS 2026 Investor MeetUp, la dernière rencontre du GAIN consacrée aux échanges entre investisseurs et entrepreneurs au Gabon. Source de l’image : GAIN.
       
        
    
Le GAIN a d’abord recruté dans l’entourage de ses fondateurs. Des cinq membres fondateurs, seuls Fabrice Nze Bekale et Vanessa Adande sont restés. Le déclic est venu en 2024, avec une première sortie (le remboursement intégral d’une facilité accordée à un entrepreneur) et la première édition de l’AESIS au Gabon. Cette visibilité a presque doublé le nombre de membres en 18 mois. Le GAIN en compte aujourd’hui 36.
La moitié sont des femmes, et ce résultat n’a rien d’un hasard. Adande a constaté que le rôle d’investisseur paraissait trop risqué aux femmes, vu de l’extérieur. Elle a donc appelé celles qu’elle connaissait pour leur expliquer le fonctionnement du GAIN au quotidien, et les a rassurées : investir dans un dossier identifié n’est jamais obligatoire.
Elle a aussi avancé un argument de pipeline : une entrepreneure a plus de chances d’être financée si d’autres femmes font partie du groupe d’investisseurs.
« Les hommes de l’association étaient d’ailleurs étonnés que ça demande autant d’effort. Pas moi », confie-t-elle. « Tout ce qui concerne l’argent demande de la confiance. On a confiance dans ce qu’on connaît. »
Le point dépasse largement le cas gabonais. L’AVCA classe l’Afrique centrale parmi les régions où les fondatrices ont levé la plus faible part du capital en 2025 : 8 %.
Dit Adande, l’intérêt des membres féminines s’est ravivé depuis la masterclass d’octobre, plusieurs d’entre elles ayant demandé comment fonctionnent les opérations en pratique. Le GAIN prévoit également un événement plus large dédié à l’investissement providentiel en 2027, afin d’élargir son vivier de cibles d’investissement.
La sortie de 2024 était un remboursement de prêt. Pour un réseau jeune, démontrer que les investisseurs ont récupéré leur mise fait davantage pour attirer de nouveaux membres qu’une valorisation sur le papier.
La spécialisation sectorielle est un luxe
Les réseaux d’angels matures se spécialisent. Le GAIN ne le peut pas encore.
« Dans nos pays, c’est toujours très nouveau, en particulier au Gabon, explique Fabrice Nze Bekale. On est encore à un stade où on fait des réseaux de business angels multisectoriels. On ne peut pas trop se spécialiser, un peu comme DNA [le Dakar Network of Angels] l’a fait au Sénégal, parce que ça reflète l’état de développement et de sophistication de l’écosystème entrepreneurial. »
Au Sénégal, le DNA se concentre sur les startups technologiques. Les quatre investissements du GAIN couvrent l’import-export, une marketplace, la santé et l’agro-industrie, et un dossier dans la santé est en due diligence.
Avec environ 150 startups actives au Gabon, selon la société d’incubation numérique SING, un mandat limité à la tech laisserait les membres avec presque rien à examiner. Le GAIN investit dans des startups tech et non-tech, et peut également considérer des petites et moyennes entreprises (PME) à fort potentiel de croissance. Chaque candidat doit être légalement constitué, avoir au moins un an d’existence, démontrer une traction réelle et présenter un plan d’affaires structuré.
Attendre des entreprises logicielles à l’échelle du capital-risque dans un marché de 150 startups, c’est s’exposer à des années de réunions sans jamais sortir un seul chèque. Le revers de la médaille, c’est qu’un petit groupe doit alors évaluer des profils de risque très hétérogènes — ce qui renvoie directement au problème de due diligence du GAIN.
La newsletter continue après cette publicité.
Fondateurs. Investisseurs. Décideurs politiques. Leaders d’entreprise. Moonshot 2026 rassemble les personnes qui façonnent l’écosystème technologique africain en matière d’IA, de commerce, de climat, d’entreprise et de culture. Mettez votre marque en avant dès aujourd’hui.
2. Moins de fonds propres, plus de dette
            Le Gabon Angel Investor Network (GAIN) s’emploie à connecter les entrepreneurs locaux avec des investisseurs capables d’apporter des financements, une expertise et des contacts d’affaires. Source de l’image : GAIN/LinkedIn.
       
        
    
« L’idéal, c’est toujours de faire des investissements en equity,” Nze Bekale dit. « Mais on est souvent contraints de prendre un peu d’equity pour mettre beaucoup de dette, ou bien de faire de la dette convertible dès le départ, parce que les entrepreneurs ne veulent pas ouvrir leur capital. »
La réticence à la dilution est profonde en Afrique francophone, où beaucoup d’entreprises sont familiales. Le GAIN calibre chaque opération selon la maturité de l’entreprise et sa capacité de remboursement : fonds propres, dette ou financement hybride.
Le continent évolue dans le même sens : la dette a représenté 41 % des 4,1 milliards de dollars levés par les startups africaines en 2025, un record, selon le rapport Partech 2025 Africa Tech Venture Capital.
Cette flexibilité exige une rédaction rigoureuse, car les obligations convertibles échouent en silence. Dans un cas anonymisé présenté lors de la masterclass de l’AESIS, un BSA AIR — l’équivalent français du SAFE (Simple Agreement for Future Equity) — est arrivé à échéance sans avoir converti, et la cession de l’entreprise s’est transformée en une longue négociation sur les droits des investisseurs.
Un convertible doit prévoir dès la signature son échéance, son taux, ses déclencheurs de conversion et le cas de cession. Des angels qui détiennent surtout de la dette doivent aussi évaluer la capacité de remboursement réelle d’aujourd’hui, pas celle des projections.
Expliquer ce qu’est un business angel
Un autre front se situe hors de la salle de négociation.
« On doit faire de la sensibilisation auprès des investisseurs potentiels, auprès des entrepreneurs, et surtout faire de l’advocacy auprès des autorités pour leur expliquer notre rôle, qui n’est pas celui d’une banque et qui n’est pas celui d’un incubateur, » insiste Nze Bekale.
Les autorités ont encore tendance à assimiler les business angels à des financeurs d’activités génératrices de revenus : un plombier ou un chauffeur de taxi qui s’installe à son compte, avec des budgets de 500 000 à 1 million de FCFA (900 à 1 750 dollars).
« On se regroupe pour financer des projets pour lesquels on a besoin de se regrouper, et pas des projets à 500 000 ou un million de francs CFA », précise-t-il.
Si l’État classe l’investissement providentiel dans l’appui à la micro-entreprise, il concevra ses incitations pour le mauvais segment. Le GAIN, qui travaille déjà avec le Centre gabonais de l’innovation (CGI) et le ministère des PME et des PMI, a besoin que l’investissement providentiel soit reconnu comme une catégorie à part entière.
La due diligence, goulot d’étranglement caché
Le GAIN veut augmenter ses financements cette année. C’est la due diligence qui le freine. Pour son premier deal, le réseau a rémunéré un consultant externe à hauteur de 1 à 2 % du montant levé. Pour les suivants, Nze Bekale a mené les DD lui-même.
« Comme ça a commencé à trop peser sur moi, cette année on a décidé de tester un autre modèle », raconte-t-il. Des volontaires parmi les investisseurs potentiels forment désormais une équipe et conduisent le processus.
Pourtant, cela n’a pas bien fonctionné.
« Tout le monde a des activités professionnelles principales, et donc ils ont très peu de temps à consacrer aux DD. Ce n’est même pas secondaire, c’est peut-être tertiaire ou quaternaire, » Nze Bekale dit.
Sur le dossier en cours dans la santé, l’équipe travaille depuis six ou sept mois. Un processus early-stage classique prend deux à quatre mois entre le premier rendez-vous et le décaissement.
Le GAIN envisage de revenir au consultant rémunéré. En attendant, les analystes d’ACT Afrique, le cabinet de conseil de Nze Bekale, portent une grande partie du travail.
« Je n’ai pas de problème à le faire parce que je suis le président, mais si je n’étais pas le président, la question se poserait autrement. »
Il a raison de s’inquiéter. Une due diligence qui repose sur le cabinet d’un seul membre crée un point de défaillance unique et un conflit d’intérêts latent. Le modèle de frais a son propre défaut : 2 % d’une levée de 25 millions de FCFA (43 000 dollars), c’est 500 000 FCFA (860 dollars), tout au plus quelques jours de travail d’analyste.
Deux correctifs seraient utiles. D’abord, standardiser les modèles et les listes de vérification pour réduire le nombre d’heures par opération. Ensuite, traiter la due diligence comme une infrastructure d’écosystème : les institutions de financement du développement financent déjà l’incubation, et un pool d’analystes mutualisé entre les réseaux de business angels de la CEMAC ne coûterait pas grand-chose.
L’épreuve de 2027
Le GAIN a démontré sa capacité à recruter des investisseurs, et la moitié de ses membres sont des femmes. Son prochain défi est de professionnaliser la due diligence sans s’appuyer sur le cabinet de son président. S’il y parvient, ses 36 membres pourront commencer à signer des chèques de 50 millions de FCFA (86 000 dollars) — le plafond que leur mandat autorise.
La newsletter se termine ici.
Touchez les acteurs qui font bouger l’écosystème technologique et commercial francophone. articles.title: Sólo hay una forma de que la nueva Xbox Helix no cueste entre 1.200 y 1.800 dólares y es que Microsoft venda a pérdidas
articles.text:
Asha Sharma, CEO de Xbox, lleva unas semanas de gira por varios medios que no suelen estar ligados a videojuegos y en los que está comentando el 'Reset de Xbox'. Básicamente, es un nombre de marketing para algo mucho más oscuro: una brutal ronda de despidos dentro de la división de juegos de Xbox.
En estos artículos el tono es extraño, ya que se pasan más tiempo detallando qué tiene Sharma sobre el escritorio que comentando las vagas declaraciones de la directiva, pero de vez en cuando aflora un tema interesante como que Xbox no está en venta. Ahora, de otra peculiar entrevista en Fortune, Sharma dibuja el paisaje de la Xbox Helix, la máquina de nueva generación de la que ya se nos avisó de que no sería barata.
Y si se cumple, llegará a un precio de entre 1.200 y 1.800 dólares a no ser que Microsoft mueva una ficha que rompe con el objetivo de que Xbox empiece a dar dinero: vender a pérdidas.
Xbox Helix superando todas las barreras psicológicas de precio
Xbox Helix en su forma actual se ha proyectado internamente a un precio para consumidores de entre 1.200 y 1.800 dólares. Es un precio que pulveriza esa barrera de los 1.000 dólares por una consola y que se hace especialmente cuesta arriba teniendo en cuenta que las de actual generación salieron por 500 euros.
Pero bueno, la crisis de componentes provocada por la IA y las compañías como la propia Microsoft ha destruido el mercado de consumo, y la PlayStation 6 también apunta a ser carísima (de hecho, un reputado insider ya ha comentado que sólo la RAM y el almacenamiento de la nueva PlayStation costaría unos 680 dólares). Sólo habría una forma de que Xbox Helix no se vaya a esa cantidad de dinero, y es que Microsoft decida 'subsidiar' la consola.
Esto es lo que siempre se ha conocido como vender la máquina a pérdidas. En el segmento de las consolas, hay ocasiones en las que los fabricantes han vendido por debajo del precio de producción (componentes + fabricación + logística) porque recuperan el dinero gracias a las regalías de los juegos y, en la época en la que estamos, también de los servicios.
Sin embargo, la situación no parece la misma que la de Xbox 360 y PS3 y, como ya expusieron desde Sony hace unos meses, vendiendo consolas más caras puede que pierdas usuarios, pero lo que hay que hacer es exprimir más los beneficios por cada usuario que se quede en tu sistema.
Está por ver eso de que Microsoft decida vender a pérdidas confiando en recuperar por otra parte, sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que los jhuegos y servicios de Xbox no están en su mejor momento. El propio Satya Nadella comentó este verano que se acabó lo de financiar Xbox, que llevaban décadas sin ser rentables y que la división debía empezar a generar dinero al ritmo que querían. Según los cálculos, Xbox representa el 6% de las ganancias del grupo y hay que aumentar el porcentaje.
Pero bueno, hay que hacer mucho scroll en el curioso artículo de Fortune hasta dar con el dato, y tampoco se profundiza mucho en él. Por descontado, no se insinúa nada de la nueva máquina más allá del precio, pero sí se apunta que llegaría en navidades de 2028 y que formará parte de una de las estrategias para ser la "compañía de entretenimiento número 1" en la industria.
Más despidos antes de Navidad
Hay otro elemento interesante en el artículo de Fortune. Tras dos párrafos en los que se detalla cómo Sharma paseó con miembros de Blizzard, equipo que aún no ha sido afectado por el bestial recorte de personal en Xbox, disfrutando de los fans que se acercaron a la BlizzCon, el artículo recuerda que Xbox tiene como objetivo entretener a 1.000 millones de personas al día.
Esto no implica que haya 1.000 millones de jugadores al día, ya que es algo que está extremadamente lejos de cualquier plataforma y, de hecho, ya calculamos que es lo que hacen 25 Steam en su mejor día. Lo que busca Sharma y la nueva directiva es que haya 1.000 personas entretenidas con algo de Xbox, que pueden ser videojuegos, pero también series, películas o cualquier producto que tenga la licencia de la marca.
En Fortune exponen que, actualmente, están por los 100 millones diarios, aunque habría que ver qué juegos meten en la ecuación porque recordemos que 'Candy Crush' es de Xbox y tiene más de eso. Siguiendo con Fortune, Sharma les comentó que, tras años difíciles, espera que ese 'Reset' empiece a dar sus frutos para el año que viene.
Esto implica que las mejoras financieras deberían empezar a asomar en el año fiscal 2027. Ahí da igual que sea porque los juegos vendan más, porque Game Pass consiga más suscriptores o simplemente por la lógica de que los 3.200 despidos en el año fiscal 2026 impliquen que hay que pagar menos nóminas. Xbox debe empezar a ser rentable para seguir las directrices de la dirección de Microsoft.
En el mismo artículo se comenta que la nueva ronda de despidos llegaría en noviembre, y debe ser un infierno ser un trabajador de uno de los estudios de Xbox que aún no han sido desmantelados sabiendo que antes de navidades te puedes ir a la calle en un momento complicadísimo en la industria.
Se estima que se han despedido a casi 1.900 personas dentro de estudios de Xbox desde julio de este año y quedan unos 1.300 empleos que recortar hasta verano de 2027, y ya hemos visto que da igual que hagan uno de los mejores contenidos del año como la expansión de 'Doom Eternal' o un juego tan redondo como 'Gears of War E-Day' porque ninguno está a salvo. Quizá en Activision sí puedan dormir tranquilos.
Veremos cómo se convierten en la mayor fuente de entretenimiento del planeta ahora que no compiten sólo contra las consolas o Netflix, sino contra algo como TikTok y similares en una competencia, en definitiva, por nuestra atención.

articles.title: Chinese AI Model Writes More Hackable Code When Told It’s for US Contractor
articles.text:
AI models that have a pro-China lean may systematically generate more vulnerable code when writing applications for Western organizations, cybersecurity firm Hirundo has discovered.
The fact that geopolitical triggers lead to more vulnerable code being produced by Chinese AI is not new: CrowdStrike reached a similar conclusion in November 2025, and so did Booz Allen Hamilton in May 2026 (PDF).
Both organizations said that the bias occurred when the AI was prompted to code for an organization in a country of interest to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Hirundo has verified that on its own.
It instructed Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder to build a web service that allows users to sign up, log in, and store secrets. The model built over 1,000 applications, and the test clearly showed the bias, Hirundo notes in a report shared with SecurityWeek ahead of publication.
“We ran every request through two models. The first is Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct as Alibaba ships it. The second is Hirundo’s Westernized Qwen3-Coder: the same model after we removed its CCP alignment from the weights with behavioral unlearning,” the company says.
Both were instructed to build apps for a US defense contractor, a Chinese defense contractor, and a Hong Kong democracy advocacy group.
Each application was checked for secret leakage and for vulnerabilities that would make it hackable, using Semgrep with Meta’s PurpleLlama security rules and ETH Zurich’s open benchmark BaxBench. Of a total of 1,840 apps, BaxBench’s attacks broke into 1,144.
The original Qwen3-Coder model built more vulnerable apps for the US contractor (70% of them were hackable) than for the Chinese contractor (59%).
Furthermore, the apps it built for the Hong Kong entity were more likely to expose secrets (47% would leak) compared to those built for a neutral entity, such as a local football fan club (37% would leak).
Telling the model to build secure applications does not change the bias. In fact, when instructed to do so, Qwen3-Coder made 74% of the US contractors’ apps hackable compared to only 59% of the neutral entity’s apps.
According to Hirundo, the bias can be eliminated by removing the model’s CCP political alignment. Its modified Qwen3-Coder model gave the same treatment to the US and Chinese contractors and did not make the Hong Kong democracy advocacy group’s apps more vulnerable.
“Bottom line: in the original model, a security instruction couldn’t override a behavior that lives in the weights. After the weights were fixed, the same instruction closed the gap,” the company says.
Looking at the code, Hirundo observed that the models often introduced broken access control flows, letting users read other users’ data. The behavior is similar for both cloud-hosted and locally deployed models.
“Code generated on an air-gapped workstation doesn’t stay there. It ships, goes into production, faces the internet, and often stays in service for years. An app that lets any user read everyone else’s secrets is exactly as exploitable whether it was written in the cloud or on-premises,” the company noted.
But the bigger issue is that Chinese models have become increasingly popular, they are the basis of many new models, they can also be found inside US products, and they are proven pro-CCP biased.
In March, HuggingFace said Chinese models accounted for 41% of downloads on the platform. In April, Cisco warned that AI models’ components could often be traced back to China, and May research from ATOM Report showed that China had a 70% share of new model derivatives in February.
According to Hirundo, an Israeli cybersecurity startup that raised $8 million last year to eliminate AI’s bad behavior, an AI’s tilt can be solved by controlling the model’s weights so that nothing sits between the prompt and the model.
It claims that the Westernized Qwen3-Coder it used to test Alibaba’s Qwen3-Coder pro-China lean is proof that this solves the problem: not only is the corrected model unbiased, but it also produces working apps about as often as the original.
“The tilt isn’t a fixed property of Chinese models. It lives in the weights, and that’s where we closed the US-China gap. Any defense, government or advocacy organization using a Chinese-origin coding model should test it under its own name, and fix it before it writes production code,” Hirundo says.

articles.title: Galaxy S25 despenca e recebe descontão no Mercado Livre • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy S25 despenca e recebe descontão no Mercado Livre
Celular premium da Samsung equipado pelo chip Snapdragon 8 Elite, 12 GB de RAM e sistema de câmeras com vídeos em 8K fica 54% mais barato no Pix
O Galaxy S25 (256 GB) está em promoção no Mercado Livre com 54% de desconto em relação ao preço original. O celular premium anunciado em 2025 por R$ 7.499,00 sai por R$ 3.476,16 no Pix com o cupom de 10% OFF na página do produto.
