articles.title: Polestar tries to quantify what it’s like to drive a performance car
articles.text:
The human desire to go fast is old, dating back at least as far as the first time some adventurous Yamnaya saw a horse on the Pontic-Caspian steppe and thought, “I bet if I jumped on that thing’s back, it would be faster than walking.”
A thousand years later, someone else invented the wheel—and the chariot—and humanity was ready to roll. Now, about five millennia since that first horseback ride, equestrianism is mostly a leisure activity, and we drive cars, propelled by motors with more power than an entire herd of beasts could muster.
Acceleration, top speed, and lap times are the usual ways we quantify that performance, and performance electric vehicles are currently in an arms race to see which one can hit 60 mph in the least amount of time. But measuring a car’s performance is easy—all you need is a stopwatch and a track. How about measuring the effect of car performance on the driver? That’s a question Polestar is trying to answer with researchers at the University of Oxford.
“As electric cars redefine what performance can be, we wanted to understand something that can’t be captured by a specification sheet alone: the human experience behind the wheel,” said Christian Samson, Polestar’s head of product attributes. “Working with University of Oxford allows us to look at performance through a different lens—connecting the engineering of the car with the experience of the person driving it.”
The pilot study involved 12 drivers who track-tested both rear- and all-wheel-drive versions of the Polestar 4 at a track in Sweden. The Polestar 4 is the OEM’s midsize crossover, a compelling Porsche Macan alternative that you can sadly no longer buy here in the US. The drivers were instrumented with heart rate monitors and skullcaps studded with electrodes, plus the cars’ gaze-tracking driver monitoring system to gather physiological data, which was combined with telemetry from the cars and subjective interview assessments after the fact. While being measured, drivers lapped the Gotland Ring circuit gently, then dynamically.

articles.title: Ex-Nvidia-turned-VC Amulya Vishwanath: 'Physical AI is in its LEGO era' | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s the moment everyone is waiting for — the ChatGPT moment for robotics, Amulya Vishwanath explained to TechCrunch’s Equity.
She is the founder and managing partner of Techable Ventures, a VC firm focused on physical AI, which she started after spending nearly seven years as a product marketer at Nvidia. Before that, she held the same role at a company that was later bought by Intel and was a digital signal processing engineer at Interconnect Systems, which was later bought by the electronics manufacturer Molex.
She stopped by Equity to talk about the future of physical AI — one of the industry’s latest buzzwords.
“A lot of companies and experts have been talking about the ChatGPT moment for robotics,” she said, adding that right now the industry was more in a “LEGO era.”
“There are a lot of foundational software and building blocks for robotics that are being rethought right now as we speak, and it’s super important in order for innovation to scale,” she continued.
Right now, people are building the basics — the robotic hands or the actuators — that can one day come together and build that big-ticket-item, like a bunch of LEGOs coming together. There’s general- and special-purpose robots being built right now, too, and eventually, as people continue building them, they will get better and more advanced.
“We’ve done this during the internet era,” she said. “We’ve done this long, long time ago with the Industrial Revolution. I think it’s just a matter of time before things fall into place.”
“Talent is also going to be very critical,” she continued, adding elsewhere in the convo that talent is still a key definer of the U.S. market. This is one of the “moats” of her firm, she said, helping connect founders to top talent so they can stay competitive right now, as so much talent is going to big companies like Anthropic and Nvidia. She pointed out that she’s built up a strong network to help founders from her years of working in this space.
“This just makes it a lot easier for me to be the strength or the first call for founders,” she said.

articles.title: Menino que só fala francês é levado para casa com ajuda do ChatGPT
articles.text:
Um menino haitiano de 9 anos que fala apenas francês foi encontrado sozinho em Farroupilha, na Serra Gaúcha. Policiais militares usaram o ChatGPT para traduzir perguntas, obter pistas sobre o endereço e ajudá-lo a voltar para casa, segundo o g1.
O caso aconteceu na tarde de sábado (17), depois que um morador acionou a Brigada Militar pelo telefone 190. Assustado e sem falar português, o menino precisou de tempo para confiar nos agentes e conseguir se comunicar.
ChatGPT ajudou os policiais a conversar com o menino
O soldado Rafael Tondollo e o sargento Jeferson Maurício Espinoza Carrets atenderam à ocorrência. Ao perceberem que a barreira do idioma dificultava a conversa, recorreram ao ChatGPT para traduzir perguntas em áudio, entre elas: “Em qual escola você estuda?”.
A resposta ajudou a equipe a identificar um ponto de referência para procurar a residência. Os policiais seguiram até a região da escola e, durante o trajeto, o menino reconheceu as ruas e começou a indicar o caminho.
Tondollo contou que conquistar a confiança da criança foi uma das principais dificuldades no início da abordagem. “Como ele estava muito assustado, foi bem difícil e demorado conseguir iniciar um diálogo, precisamos de algum tempo para que ele tivesse confiança em nós e se sentisse seguro falar”, relatou o soldado.
Menino reconheceu o caminho de casa
A criança identificou a própria casa quando a viatura ainda estava a quase uma quadra do local. “Quando chegamos na rua da casa dele, ele abriu a porta da viatura faltando quase uma quadra da casa. Ficou muito feliz ao voltar para casa”, contou Tondollo ao g1.
Os pais não estavam na residência, mas um vizinho conseguiu entrar em contato com o pai, que voltou pouco depois. Segundo o policial, a família fazia compras em uma frutaria no centro da cidade quando o menino disse que iria ao banheiro e saiu correndo pela porta em direção à rua.
Ao perceberem que o filho havia desaparecido, os pais começaram a procurá-lo. Depois de esgotarem as possibilidades de busca, seguiram a pé para casa, onde conseguiram reencontrá-lo.
Criança ficou sozinha por cerca de uma hora
De acordo com a Brigada Militar, o menino foi encontrado a aproximadamente 1,5 quilômetro do comércio onde estava com os pais. Ele ficou sozinho por cerca de uma hora e não sofreu ferimentos.
A ferramenta de inteligência artificial não identificou automaticamente o endereço da criança. O ChatGPT ajudou os policiais a traduzir perguntas e obter a informação sobre a escola; a partir dessa referência, o deslocamento e o reconhecimento das ruas pelo próprio menino permitiram chegar à casa da família.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Apple restringe las reservas del iPhone Duo para combatir la reventa
articles.text:
Apple parece haber tomado medida para combatir la reventa del iPhone Duo. En las últimas horas, la firma de Cupertino ha implementado un límite a la cantidad de unidades de su móvil plegable que un mismo cliente puede reservar. Esto, luego de que las fechas de entrega se demoraran hasta enero de 2027 apenas minutos después del inicio de la preventa.
Según se observa en las versiones online de la Apple Store, las reservas del iPhone Duo se han limitado a un máximo de 2 unidades por cliente. Si intentas cargar una cantidad mayor, la tienda muestra un mensaje informando de la restricción y obligando a respetar el tope para poder continuar con el procedimiento de compra.
El nuevo límite de dos iPhone Duo por comprador impacta sobre todas las variantes del smartphone. Esto da a entender que el objetivo de Apple es limitar el impacto que los scalpers tienen sobre la disponibilidad de su primer smartphone plegable, si bien ya estuvieron haciendo estragos durante la primera jornada de reservas.
La preventa del iPhone Duo se puso en marcha el pasado viernes 16, con un alto nivel de demanda. Esto, combinado con la poca cantidad de unidades del móvil que se han producido hasta la fecha, resultó en una combinación fatal para la mayoría de los compradores que apostaban a recibirlo el primer día.
Las unidades disponibles para entregar el viernes 23 de octubre se agotaron en apenas minutos, de modo que un gran número de compradores debió conformarse con fechas esparcidas entre noviembre y diciembre próximo, y también en enero de 2027. La situación no fue puntual de un mercado, sino que afectó a todas las versiones de la Apple Store.
Apple restringe las reservas del iPhone Duo: solo 2 por comprador
Más allá de la demanda genuina del público, el lanzamiento del iPhone Duo ha padecido el accionar de los scalpers. Esto no solo ha derivado en la aparición de unidades del plegable en eBay, revendiéndose a precios infladísimos (y ridículos), sino que también expuso operaciones para obtener el móvil usando sistemas total o parcialmente automatizados.
Es cierto que el uso de bots para comprar productos de escasa disponibilidad ni bien se habilita su venta, no es algo nuevo. Sin embargo, con el iPhone Duo generó todavía más ruido por la expectación generada entre el público y porque el responsable de una de las maniobras de scalping no tuvo mejor idea que salir a presumirlo en X (Twitter).
Que Apple ahora limite las reservas del iPhone Duo es una señal de que se están tomando medidas para evitar que la situación se repita. Claro que el daño inicial de los revendedores ya está hecho y nunca se va a dar respuesta definitiva a este tipo de problemas. Por lo pronto, el plegable de la manzana mantiene su fecha de entrega más temprana para el 22 de enero del próximo año.
Lo que todavía es un misterio es si el iPhone Duo se podrá comprar sin reserva previa y de forma presencial en las Apple Store físicas. Los de Cupertino no han brindado detalles sobre cómo piensan lidiar con este asunto cuando se formen largas colas en sus tiendas alrededor del mundo.

articles.title: Getting old is hard. This age-tech housing aims to make it easier. | BetaKit
articles.text:
My grandmother was a commanding woman. In her 92 years, she raised three children and a grandchild, mostly by herself. She helped manage a series of successful restaurants and nightclubs; in her little spare time, she hiked and skied. She was decidedly capable.
But when I unexpectedly knocked on her door one autumn when I was 19, something was different: she asked me the same questions, different only in sentence structure, again and again.
What brought me to town?
Where was I going to school?
What was I doing in town?
What college was I enrolled in?
Over the years, she lost more of her faculties. Eventually, she left the stovetop on for so long that a steel pot melted into molten coagulant. That was the boiling point: a week later she moved in with my parents.
My grandmother’s experience was not abnormal. Like many seniors, she was caught between her desire to remain independent and the limitations of her advancing age; she didn’t want to leave her home, but could also no longer live safely on her own. With little money to afford in-home care, those years put untold pressure on my parents and left my grandmother in a sort of purgatory: she wasn’t independent, but she also didn’t have round-the-clock care.
If Calgary’s Garden Loft had been around back then, might things have been different?
“The world’s first full-stack house”
The small, loft-styled suites Garden Loft builds look like the type of in-fills you might see in a trendy Calgary neighbourhood: angular, with glassy entranceways and teak-wood finish. But inside, they’re full of cutting-edge tech masquerading as modern decor.
Garden Loft was founded in 2022 by University of Calgary dean of architecture John Brown, his wife and fellow co-founder Carina van Olm Brown, and third co-founder, Matthew North. The company builds modular, prefabricated housing for older people and others with differing abilities. Its tech is imbued with “gerontechnology,” more commonly called age-tech. Age-tech is digital technology used to improve or manage the health, well-being, and independence of seniors.
“This is more than a smart home. It’s a new model of care.”
Garden Loft evolved out of the trio’s previous business, a boutique design and construction firm called Housebrand. In its capacity as a custom builder, Housebrand had been receiving customer commissions asking for housing that could adapt to their needs as they aged.
“The costs of [renovating] all of that makes sense for a person that needs it, but it doesn’t make sense for the larger housing market,” Brown told me last July when I visited the industrial Calgary workshop where he and his partners are building Garden Loft’s homes. “We started to think about a separate solution: What if we had a house that already had everything in it?” he said.
That notion led to a research partnership in 2014 between Brown, in his capacity as dean of the U of C’s School of Architecture, Planning, and Landscape, and the Cumming School of Medicine. Its purpose was to explore the potential of integrating medical technology into backyard suite housing that could be leased, installed, and removed as a person’s health needs change.
Fast forward a decade and Garden Loft now describes itself as the Tesla of housing: a full-stack alternative to expensive in-home care and assisted living facilities that are often underfunded.
“Tesla, notwithstanding Elon Musk being crazy, was the first full-stack car. Deeply integrated technology on all kinds of levels,” Brown said, claiming that Garden Lofts is the “world’s first full-stack house.”
A mix of built-in tech and digital infrastructure, Garden Loft attempts to set itself apart from its peers in the seniors-housing space by the breadth of the technology it integrates into its products. Think injury-resistant flooring that Brown says can dampen fall impacts by as much as 43 percent, digital sensor technology to monitor activity levels, and a digital community platform with curated service delivery for users.
For its efforts, the company was awarded the City of Calgary’s 2023 accessibility award.
But where Garden Loft really makes its stand is in its use of software. Building on a proprietary digital platform, a Garden Loft suite can continuously measure 37 different data streams, looking for deviations in metrics like sleep quality, hydration, stability, gait speed, toilet use, activity levels, and more. That data runs through an algorithm that identifies potential early warning signals of declining health and compiles them along a gradient: green for good, yellow when three or four indicators emerge, and so on. All of this can be accessed by residents via Garden Loft’s digital platform.
If all of that data collection sounds a little Big Brother, Brown maintains that Garden Loft’s clients, most of whom are in their mid-80s or older, retain agency over how their data is used and shared.
RELATED: Canada’s housing supply is in crisis. Can robots help?
“You have control over your data. You can cede it; give access to your family or your healthcare provider,” Brown told me, adding that residents must choose what data, if any, they want to share with healthcare providers or supports like friends or family.
While Brown was clear that the data measured by Garden Loft’s systems is technically behavioural, not medical, information he recognized that it would still be sensitive. He said the company is working on ways to protect that data, though he didn’t explain exactly what those protections would look like.
“We generate the data, and we have control over it, and we’re just working right now around data privacy,” he said last August.
After our initial conversation, I reached out to Brown to follow up on the issue of data privacy. He told me that Garden Loft would house the data it generates on private, domestically located servers and that user data “will not be sold or otherwise shared.”
It takes a village
Garden Loft has spent the last few years incubating with the support of Calgary funding catalyst and growth studio Thin Air Labs (James Lochrie, a Thin Air managing partner, now sits on the company’s board). In that time, the company has deployed several prototype properties: three in Calgary, three in Edmonton, one in Airdrie, Alta., and one in Ottawa.
Currently, Garden Loft is working on several projects to build 10-to-30-unit “village” style housing that Brown thinks has the potential to upend the assisted-living model in Canada.
“You get 80 percent of what’s delivered in a supported living environment or long-term care facility at 50 percent of the cost, and you stay in the housing market rather than entering the care industry,” Brown claimed.
A 10-unit prototype village is under construction in Bassano, Alta., with four additional village projects in development, including in an as-of-yet-undisclosed Northern Alberta Indigenous community. The village design concept can include a different care model than the standalone homes the company currently has in the market. In the village scenario, Garden Loft is leaning into a telehealth model of care, integrating clinical and pharmaceutical support services that residents can contact on an as-needed basis. Those resident healthcare providers can in turn access residents’ real-time biometrics if they choose to make that data available.
The Bassano village project, which Brown says will open next year, is partnering with the Dr. Barrie Strafford Centre for Learning, Innovation, and Quality (CLIQ) on an Alberta Innovates-funded research project that will evaluate health outcomes over two years to fine-tune the company’s wellness monitoring platform.
A new kind of care
Much like Garden Loft’s village project aims to change what congregated supportive living looks like, age-tech is changing what supportive care looks like broadly at a moment when healthcare for older people in Canada is buckling.
Laura Tamblyn Watts is the CEO of CanAge, Canada’s national seniors’ advocacy organization. She’s also a board member of AgeWell, a national centre of excellence that studies aging and technology. Tamblyn Watts said that in the current senior-care environment, technology is playing a growing role in expanding the continuum of what care looks like as people get older.
“When you read statistics that say things like 90 percent of people want to remain in their own home—well, of course they do because the questions being asked are: ‘Do you want to move into long-term care or do you want to live in your home as long as you want?’ Those aren’t very good questions. They set up this false dichotomy [between long-term care and living alone].
“You get 80 percent of what’s delivered in a supported living environment or long-term care facility at 50 percent of the cost, and you stay in the housing market rather than entering the care industry.”
“There’s a continuum in between,” Tamblyn Watts said. “That idea of integrated age technology is so critically important; it’s part of a broader trend to look at prefabricated housing supports where they are both integrated, as well as accessible, affordable, and inclusive.”
That matters because regardless of where a person lives on that continuum of care, prices are steep. Retirement home costs average just over $3,000 per month, and can spike into the tens of thousands. In-home care isn’t much better, according to Tamblyn Watts, who said hiring a caregiver with only six weeks of formal education—far less than a registered nurse requires—can cost in the hundreds of thousands per year.
Put the soaring prices aside for a moment, and there is another chokepoint: capacity. According to the Canadian Institute for Health Information (CIHI), Canada has just shy of 200,000 long-term care beds. Meanwhile, Canadians 85 and older are among the country’s fastest-growing demographics, with researchers projecting that capacity in long-term care will need to double in the next decade to meet demand.
As I walked through Garden Loft’s warehouse last summer, its dual bays littered with halfway finished homes, my mind kept returning to my grandmother and the ways that as her cognition declined, the space she inhabited, and the life she had built for herself, diminished, too. Could such futuristic housing have slowed the pace at which her world shrunk? Might it have eased the burden of care as she transitioned from capable to dependent?
RELATED: AlayaCare raises $51 million CAD to scale homecare provider platform
Against that backdrop, Brown believes new caregiving models like the one he and his partners are building now will come to serve as a necessary release valve for the long-term care industry, the governments funding it, and the people whose health and dignity rely on these systems of care.
“Governments in North America realize they can’t provide the level of healthcare [needed], that we can’t keep everyone in a facility or hospital. There has to be home care,” Brown said, adding that what Garden Loft is building constitutes a new kind of supportive living.
“This is more than a smart home. It’s a new model of care,” he said. “We have to try to age people in place, and what we’re doing is providing a technical, digital, and physical framework to enable that to happen to a higher degree.”
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Garden Loft.

articles.title: Nuclear-powered spaceships
articles.text:
Nuclear-powered spaceships
A new era of spaceflight could save astronauts time and cut exposure to cosmic radiation as they rocket to Mars—and beyond.
Just before the Artemis II crew began its historic slingshot around the moon this past April, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom. SR-1, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, is meant to fly an uncrewed mission to Mars by the end of 2028, arriving in 2029. A successful mission would herald a new era of more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight—saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation as they travel to Mars and beyond. “You wake up to that announcement, and it puts a big smile on your face,” says Simon Middleburgh, co-director of the Nuclear Futures Institute at Bangor University in Wales.
The sticking points
Running a nuclear reactor in space may sound like lunacy, but it’s not. The Soviet Union sent dozens of reactors into orbit, often to power spy satellites. And experts say there aren’t any major technical obstacles to making nuclear space propulsion happen. “I think it’s a very doable technology,” says Philip Metzger, a spaceflight engineering researcher at the Florida Space Institute.“I’m happy to see them finally doing this.”
Still, developing space propulsion using reactors has been slow going. The US has started—and terminated—several programs looking into it over the past 75 years. The latest casualty was DRACO, a collaboration between NASA and the Department of Defense, which ended in 2025. The project was canceled because of high experimentation costs, an inability to compete with conventional rocket propulsion on price, and difficulty ensuring that ground tests could be performed safely and effectively. (You are creating an incredibly powerful nuclear reaction, after all.)
The progress
After much wavering, it now appears that nuclear-powered interplanetary travel is a $2 billion bet NASA is willing to make. The agency is pursuing an approach called nuclear electric propulsion, which uses the neutrons produced in a self-sustaining, uranium-atom-splitting reaction to create heat and ultimately electricity. The electricity is used to ionize a gas, which is blasted out of the spacecraft with the help of magnetic fields, generating thrust. The approach “is very low thrust, but very efficient,” says Sebastian Corbisiero, the US Department of Energy’s national technical director of space reactor programs. “So you can use it for a long period of time.”
What might such a rocket look like? A presentation by Steve Sinacore, program director of NASA’s SR-1 program, offers some clues. So far, the concept art makes the craft look like a colossal fletched arrow. The back will house the power-and-propulsion system, while the tip will hold a uranium-filled nuclear reactor with a capacity of at least 20 kilowatts. (For context, a typical nuclear plant on Earth is about 50,000 times more powerful.) The “fletches” on SR-1 are large fins that help cool the reactor by radiating heat into space.
Like many other pieces of space hardware, the reactor will need to be put through its paces on the ground before it’s cleared for the rough rocket trip to space. “Going through the launch safely is going to be a challenge,” says Middleburgh. “You are being shaken, rattled, and rolled.” For safety reasons, the reactor will be switched on around two days post-launch, when it’s comfortably far from Earth. Uranium isn’t tremendously dangerous by itself, but that can’t be said of the waste products that emerge when the reactor is running. If SR-1 works as planned, its journey to Mars will take about a year.
Will this novel form of space propulsion actually reach the Red Planet by 2029? It’s possible. NASA says the Idaho National Laboratory, which is building SR-1’s reactor, is making progress and is on target for a late-2028 launch. “Procurement of major components is underway, and integration work on the power and propulsion element is advancing steadily,” Sinacore told MIT Technology Review. The outlook will get even sunnier if the Artemis program, which aims to start laying the foundations for a base on the lunar south pole by the decade’s end, keeps to its own bold deadline.
“It’s an aggressive timeline,” says Lindsey Holmes, who is vice president of advanced projects at Analytical Mechanics Associates, an aerospace company in Virginia. She suspects the push is being driven partly by China’s and Russia’s own deep-space nuclear ambitions. The two countries have spoken about plans to place a reactor on the moon’s surface in the mid-2030s to power a jointly operated lunar base. Whether it flies or fails in space, SR-1’s development should help NASA put its own reactor on the moon; the technology involved in the two projects is broadly similar, given that the lunar surface, like space itself, is a vacuum. If an interplanetary nuclear-powered spacecraft works, a nuclear reactor on the moon should too.
Progress meter . . . . . . . . . . . . 6
Most of the technology for SR-1 already exists; it’s going to come down to piecing it all together and then seeing how it performs in space.

articles.title: Electronics hobbyist converts $120 DDR5 SODIMM kit into ‘$1000’ desktop kit to fight RAM crisis — ICs from SK hynix DDR5-5600 16GB modules used to create DDR5-7800 desktop sticks
articles.text:
Electronics hobbyist converts $120 DDR5 SODIMM kit into ‘$1000’ desktop kit to fight RAM crisis — ICs from SK hynix DDR5-5600 16GB modules used to create DDR5-7800 desktop sticks
You have to be lucky to find such cheap DDR5 SODIMMs, and specialist equipment and skills are required for success.
What if you could buy a cheap used DDR5 SODIMM (laptop memory) kit and transform it into a super-fast DDR5 desktop kit? That’s what electronics hobbyist Blighted Agent recently did when they succeeded in converting a SK hynix 2x 16GB DDR5-5600 SODIMM kit they got from Facebook Marketplace for $120 into a 2x 16GB DDR5-7800 desktop kit, claimed to be worth around $1,000. They also had to buy some blank DDR5 desktop memory PCBs from AliExpress for around $16 each, and a set of heatsinks for around $18.
In the above video, our hero says they bought the donor laptop 2x 16GB DDR5-5600 sticks for just $120, which is a bargain. With extra bits and pieces from AliExpress (desktop DDR5 PCBs, etc.), the total bill of materials came to $175. Blighted Agent comments that the SODIMMs used what he believed to be SK hynix A-die modules, which are the same as the ICs used in expensive desktop DDR5 modules like the G.Skill Trident Royal line.
The process began with taking the memory ICs from the donor modules using a hot air station. Then they were cleaned and had 0.45mm leaded solder balls added, using a DDR5 stencil, reballing jig, and hot air. Next, the blank desktop DDR5 PCBs were prepared. A little solder was added to the plethora of BGA connectors to be ready for the memory chips to connect to.
The old DDR5 ICs and the new desktop modules could now be mated, using flux, the preheater, hot air, and watching and prodding carefully with a dental pick. Blighted Agent’s experience lets him know when the BGA chips have successfully mated with the PCB. You can eyeball when they pop precisely into place due to surface tension, and offer up a modicum of resistance to pick prodding.
Finally, the enthusiast added the SPD chip and BIOS chip from the SODIMMs to the new desktop DIMMs. These new desktop DIMMs were quickly tested in a PC before they were finished off with carefully applied thermal pads and the fancy-looking heatsinks.
Blighted Agent felt lucky that there were no issues with the newly created desktop modules. There’s a lot of intricate things that can go wrong during such a process. The initial boot verification showed them recognized in his Asus ROG Maximus Z790 Apex Encore motherboard as two “SK hynix 16,384MB 5600MHz” modules, which was correct. Some tuning resulted in rock-steady performance at DDR5-7800 CL38 and 1.40V. This was verified by stress testing for 90 minutes, which the enthusiast reckons was ample for a gaming PC. It is very likely a better result than using those mechanical SODIMM-to-DIMM converters you can buy, which can be problematic.
Blighted Agent seems to specialize in BGA soldering work, and has also successfully upgraded several graphics cards with double the VRAM. Though videos like this are edited to be brief, and they make the process look easy, the TechTuber admits there is a lot that can go wrong during this kind of rework. Moreover, with RAM modules, they lack the testing equipment to locate an issue with any particular IC on the PCB. So, if this module didn’t work, they might have ended up in a world of pain, not knowing which memory chip had an issue due to either an internal fault or a BGA soldering glitch.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Looking around at used DDR5 SODIMMs, it looks like Blighted Agent was very lucky to get a used working 32GB kit for $120. I just checked eBay U.S., and the best deal there was $320. Meanwhile, the best price for a new 32GB DDR5-6000 kit seems to be $449 at the time of writing.
We reported on Russian enthusiast VIK-on succeeding in a similar project earlier this year, but all their costing was in Rubles, and they went the extra mile in flashing custom firmware so the remade modules would be auto-detected with 6400 MT/s XMP support on most motherboards. In late 2026, DDR5 RAM continues to be too expensive.

Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: Comment équiper le parc informatique d'une PME ?
articles.text:
Ordinateurs, écrans, périphériques, solutions d’impression… Équiper une entreprise demande aujourd’hui de penser au-delà du simple choix des PC. Les usages, le renouvellement du matériel, le budget et l’accompagnement doivent être pris en compte pour construire un parc cohérent et durable.
La première étape consiste à partir des usages plutôt que des seules caractéristiques techniques. Un ordinateur destiné à un commercial régulièrement en déplacement n'aura pas les mêmes contraintes qu'un poste utilisé quotidiennement au bureau. De la même manière, un développeur, un graphiste ou un collaborateur principalement tourné vers la bureautique n'auront pas nécessairement besoin du même niveau de performances.
Comment choisir les équipements adaptés à une entreprise ?
L’objectif n’est pas de choisir systématiquement la configuration la plus puissante, mais bien celle qui répond aux besoins sans générer de dépenses inutiles. Processeur, mémoire vive, stockage, autonomie, qualité de l’écran et autres connectiques sont donc les éléments capitaux à considérer en fonction des métiers.
C'est dans cette logique que BELTA accompagne les entreprises, avec une offre qui ne se limite pas aux ordinateurs portables ou fixes. Son catalogue couvre également les stations de travail, écrans, stations d'accueil, claviers, souris et autres périphériques nécessaires à la constitution d'un environnement de travail complet.
L'entreprise propose également des solutions d'impression, avec une approche qui permet de regrouper plusieurs besoins auprès d'un même interlocuteur.
Pourquoi anticiper le renouvellement du parc informatique ?
Attendre la panne d'un équipement pour le remplacer peut rapidement devenir problématique. Un renouvellement planifié permet de mieux maîtriser les dépenses, de limiter les interruptions de travail et de conserver un parc homogène.
Cette anticipation passe également par une réflexion sur les configurations. Une entreprise peut, par exemple, standardiser certains modèles tout en prévoyant des configurations plus spécifiques pour les métiers qui nécessitent davantage de puissance. C'est aussi sur ce terrain que l'accompagnement d'un revendeur B2B expert prend tout son sens.
BELTA propose notamment des configurations sur mesure, ainsi que des cotations dédiées négociées en partenariat avec les constructeurs. L'entreprise peut également assurer le stockage du matériel pour ses clients, afin de faciliter le déploiement progressif des équipements lorsque plusieurs collaborateurs doivent être renouvelés ou équipés.
Enfin, chaque entreprise peut bénéficier d'un commercial dédié, avec un interlocuteur qui connaît ses besoins, qui peut le conseiller grâce à son expertise dans la durée.
Revendeur B2B ou grande distribution : quelle différence ?
Pour un achat standard, la grande distribution peut satisfaire la demande. La problématique est différente lorsqu'une entreprise a besoin de conseil pour équiper plusieurs collaborateurs, renouveler régulièrement son parc ou déployer des configurations particulières.
Un revendeur informatique B2B spécialisé peut alors apporter un accompagnement plus large : identification des besoins, configuration des machines, négociation des tarifs, stockage, livraison, suivi commercial dédié… L'intérêt est également de pouvoir centraliser plusieurs familles d'équipements et de services auprès d'un même partenaire.
BELTA s'inscrit dans cette approche depuis plus de 40 ans. 'entreprise compte aujourd'hui 120 collaborateurs et 30 000 clients, avec une activité qui couvre à la fois l'informatique professionnelle, les périphériques, le matériel et consommables d’impression. Elle met également en avant des offres et des services pensés pour simplifier la gestion des équipements, notamment avec son offre forfait, qui permet aux entreprises de disposer d'une solution simple mais personnalisable sur-mesure en fonction de chaque besoin spécifique d'impression.
L’entreprise accompagne des organisations issues de secteurs d’activité très variés, notamment l’industrie, la santé, la finance, le commerce, les collectivités ou encore l’administration. Une diversité qui lui permet de répondre à des besoins informatiques multiples, en tenant compte des spécificités et des contraintes propres à chaque structure.
« Notre offre propose l’ensemble des équipements nécessaires à un environnement de travail professionnel : ordinateurs portables et fixes, stations de travail, écrans, accessoires, périphériques informatiques associés et solutions d’impression. Elle permet ainsi aux entreprises de constituer un parc informatique cohérent, adapté à leurs usages. » explique Antoine Chevalier, responsable de l’offre de la société BELTA.
Pour une entreprise, un bon parc informatique repose avant tout sur des équipements réellement adaptés aux besoins des collaborateurs, mais aussi suffisamment évolutifs pour accompagner son développement.
Bien identifier les usages, anticiper le renouvellement, harmoniser les configurations lorsque cela se justifie et s’appuyer sur un interlocuteur spécialisé sont autant de leviers pour construire un parc informatique aussi fiable que maîtrisé. Pour aller plus loin et bénéficier d’un accompagnement adapté à votre parc informatique, découvrez les solutions proposées sur Belta.fr.

articles.title: FreightTech unicorn sennder targets €1 billion in annual revenue as C.H. Robinson integration completes | EU-Startups
articles.text:
sennder, a German digital road freight forwarder, today announced that it will hit €1 billion in annual revenue for this year, as well as completing the integration of C.H. Robinson’s European operations.
The delivery scale-up has raised over €340 million in funding and is now on track to deliver IFRS EBITDA profitability for the full year of 2026. sennder now operates as one business on one platform, sennOS, moving more than 150,000 shipments a month through a network of more than 40,000 vetted carriers.
“Continued operational momentum and sustained profitability puts us in an even stronger position to invest in the digital transformation of freight,” says David Nothacker, co-founder and CEO of sennder. “We brought two large businesses onto one platform and lifted operator productivity by 45% in the process, and this milestone reinforces sennder’s role as a dependable partner for customers and carriers alike and enables us to keep raising the standard for reliability, efficiency and innovation in European road freight.”
To understand sennder’s landmark, it is important to look at the wider transport/cargo sector in Europe and the developing competition – as well as the funding being distributed in 2026.
These include Berlin-based cargo.one with nearly €17 million for multimodal freight software and Ukraine-based Cargofy with €5.2 million in primary funding for AI-powered freight operations.
In Germany, FRYTE Mobility raised €3.5 million for electric truck charging coordination and NexDash secured €2.5 million for road-freight electrification, while Belgium’s Vectrix raised €1.15 million for transport-order automation.
These announcements represent approximately €29.4 million in new company funding.
EU-Startups previously covered sennder’s €131.2 million Series D in 2021 and CEO David Nothacker’s discussion of the C.H. Robinson transaction in 2025.
Founded in 2015, sennder is a digital road freight forwarder, leveraging data and technology to increase efficiency and transparency in road logistics, with the aim of reducing empty miles and optimising transport flows.
sennder connects shippers with a broad network of carriers, with the goal of enabling low-emission, cost-effective transport while supporting carriers in navigating a traditionally fragmented industry.
Over the past 12 months, these initiatives have prevented more than 31,000 tonnes of CO2e emissions.
For sennder, today’s achievement is driven by putting profitability and revenue quality ahead of volume growth, actively optimising its customer portfolio.
Operator productivity, measured as gross profit per operator, rose 45% YoY. sennder attributes the increase to scale, the single integrated platform and its growing use of reasoning AI agents which work alongside teams, supporting them in serving customers at scale.
The AI agents reason across vast volumes of live network data to match loads with the right capacity, price shipments in real time and resolve issues before they escalate, streamlining operations further.
With profitability established, sennder will continue to invest in its platform, its AI agents and its European carrier network. The focus is profitable growth: growing volume that is sustainable and supports reliable service for customers and carriers.

articles.title: Exercise in a pill
articles.text:
Exercise in a pill
In unraveling the pathways by which movement helps the body, we could develop medicines that offer some of the same benefits, without the workout.
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks—without the workout. The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.
The sticking points
It will take a lot of experimentation to untangle the myriad pathways by which exercise promotes health. But IDing the cascade of hormones, enzymes, and other molecules related to physical activity is just the first step. Scientists need to figure out how to turn that knowledge into safe and effective drugs. That’s a tall order: More than 90% of treatments that enter human studies fail.
There are regulatory hurdles too. The FDA approves medications to treat diseases, not to enhance wellness, says Thomas Burris, a pharmacologist at the University of Florida whose work focuses on diseases that respond to exercise, like obesity, type 2 diabetes, and dementia.
The progress
There may never be a pill that delivers all the benefits of exercise, but research could lead to new medicines that mimic some aspects of working out. Scientists have already identified many important exercise-related signals and have even developed compounds to regulate them. (Some preliminary results have been so promising that doping authorities have proactively banned the compounds.)
Burris and his colleagues are focused on a receptor that’s always switched on, even without exercise. Working out appears to boost that receptor in muscle cells, which in turn helps bolster endurance over time. Burris’s lab has spent years designing a drug that cranks up the receptor’s activity directly, and mice treated with the drug ran longer and farther than mice that weren’t. They “become marathon mice without having to do any type of exercise,” Burris says. There are even indications—also in mice—that the compound mimics some of the cognitive benefits of exercise and could help treat heart failure. Burris founded a company called Pelagos to carry the work forward into a clinical trial.
Other workout-mimicking drugs have already entered human studies. In June, the biotech firm Cambrian Bio reported that its experimental drug ATX-304 boosted metabolism and reduced liver and belly fat in people with obesity and prediabetes. It activates a metabolic switch that helps cells sense when energy supplies dip and coordinates the production of more fuel—the same switch that helps us sustain long sessions jumping rope or swimming laps. Cambrian hopes it will help people lose weight without losing muscle, a common concern with GLP-1 medicines.
Progress meter ............ 5
Our understanding of how exercise benefits the body is still coming into focus, and drug development is prone to failure.

articles.title: Design Proteins with RFD4-Proteina Using Reward-Guided Inference-Time Search | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Protein design is a search problem. Choose amino acids for an eight-residue protein sequence and more than 25 billion combinations are possible. Choose amino acids for a 100-residue protein sequence and the number of possibilities exceeds the number of atoms in the observable universe. Somewhere in that space is a protein that opens a path to a new therapy. There are too many combinations to search exhaustively, so finding it depends on knowing where to look.
RFD4-Proteina, an NVIDIA BioNeMo open model co-developed with the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington’s School of Medicine, navigates that space using patterns learned from nature. It co-designs protein sequences and all-atom structures, and uses reward-guided inference-time search to focus compute on the most promising candidates.
This tutorial shows computational biologists, ML engineers and drug discovery researchers how to design protein binder candidates against PD-L1, an oncology target, using reward-guided inference-time search and introduces experimental validation results across design tasks.
You can access RFD4-Proteina in two ways:
- Choose the open model for training, inference, method development, and direct control over sampling code or
- Choose the NIM microservice for rapid inference deployment with an HTTP interface
Building on Proteina-Complexa’s partially latent approach, RFD4-Proteina combines explicit backbone coordinates with latent representation, learned sequence and atomistic variables. Its autoencoder decoder produces the sequence and all-atom structure together, removing the separate inverse-folding handoff to a model such as ProteinMPNN.
Prerequisites
- Open model
  - Supported Linux GPU host and Python 3.12; follow the repository setup guide and use a supported NVIDIA GPU.
  - Model cache: Setup downloads the Hugging Face bundle automatically; set HF_HOME only if you want a different cache directory.
- NIM
  - Self-host: x86_64 or arm64 Linux meeting the NIM prerequisites, Docker, NVIDIA Driver, NVIDIA Container Toolkit, and an NGC API key.
  - NIM API endpoint (not recommended for production runs): HTTP access through NVIDIA build.nvidia.com via Shell and Python scripts, no local GPU or model installation required.
About RFD4-Proteina
The search loop shown in Figure 1, above, is where RFD4-Proteina focuses its compute.
During inference-time reasoning search, the model denoises generation trajectories to obtain structures, scores these designs, retains and branches promising partial states, and continues until the generation criteria are reached.
Rewards can measure geometry, interactions, or independent prediction confidence. This kind of extra search optimizes designs against a specified objective to yield higher-scoring designs. Later in this tutorial, you will see how a user can enable this functionality through the open model and the NIM.
RFD4-Proteina is faster and uses less memory than RFD3 for several reasons:
- It works on a residue-level latent representation instead of atom-level, which avoids memory blow-up.
- Engineering of the diffusion process cuts sampling from about 400 steps in Proteina-Complexa to 60, and computation is concentrated on the parts of the process that matter most thanks to reasoning capabilities in the model.
- Inference-time search is also faster, since the oracles (OF3 and physics methods like tmol) are CUDA-accelerated.
- The model and kernels were co-designed with the cuEquivariance and BioNeMo Inference Runtime (BIR) teams for speed and scalability.
From a molecular design idea to candidate designs
The workflow in Figure 3, above, demonstrates how to use RFD4-Proteina to go from a scientific objective to candidates for experimental testing. An agent can coordinate these tools and track results, while scientists define the objectives and use experimental evidence to guide the next round.
Preparing the molecular inputs and environment
Begin by defining the criteria and requirements for generation. For example, RFD4-Proteina expects users to define what may change, what must remain fixed, and computational and experimental success criteria.
Use AtomWorks to generate /manipulate the input data. AtomWorks is the molecular data layer used to prepare structures and design annotations for RFD4-Proteina. Its Python and PyMOL workflows prepare fixed atoms, designable residues, hotspots, and molecular context. Preserve the supplied ligand or motif chemistry when designing surrounding protein.
Both the open model and NIM accept annotated CIFs or a condition specification plus its source structure. The specification below fixes the target and defines the new binder.
The repository’s cropped PD-L1 structure from PDB 5O45 serves as the target. Fix the target’s sequence and backbone coordinates, allow its side chains to repack, and direct binder generation toward hotspot atoms on Tyr56, Met115, and Tyr123. The new binder has 100–150 residues, with free sequence and coordinates.
Clone the repository, then run the examples from its root. This writes pdl1.json; both paths use the same target CIF and conditions.
git clone https://github.com/RosettaCommons/RFD4-Proteina.git
cd RFD4-Proteina
cat > pdl1.json <<'JSON'
{
  "pdl1_binder": {
    "input": "docs/examples/inputs/5o45_cropped.cif",
    "contig": "100-150, /0, A17-131",
    "conditions": {
      "C_CRD": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A') and is_protein_backbone"}]},
      "C_SEQ": {"true": [{"select": "sel('A')"}]},
      "C_HOT": {"true": [
        {"select": "sel('A/*/56/[CG,OH]')"},
        {"select": "sel('A/*/115/[CG,SD]')"},
        {"select": "sel('A/*/123/[CD2,OH]')"}
      ]}
    }
  }
}
JSON
Open model setup
On a supported Linux/CUDA system, install the repository environment with a current uv release (validated with 0.12.24). If uv is already installed, update it first so it recognizes CUDA 13.2. Setup caches the Hugging Face model bundle, including the paired autoencoder. While the model repository is private, authenticate with hf auth login using an account with access.
bash setup.sh --native
source .venv/bin/activate
NIM environment setup
To host the NIM, run this block in Bash on a supported GPU host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit installed.
read -rsp 'NGC API key: ' NGC_API_KEY; echo
export NGC_API_KEY
printf '%s' "$NGC_API_KEY" | docker login nvcr.io \
  -u '$oauthtoken' --password-stdin
image=nvcr.io/nim/ipd/rfd4-proteina:latest
docker pull "$image"
export RFD4_NIM_IMAGE="$(docker image inspect \
  --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' "$image")"
printf '%s\n' "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE" > nim-image.txt
export LOCAL_NIM_CACHE="$HOME/.cache/nim"
mkdir -p "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE"
docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \
  --runtime=nvidia --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 \
  -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE":/opt/nim/.cache \
  --shm-size=16g "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE"
Generate sequences and structures
Open-model generation
Save the following as design.py in the repository root. The same script supports generation and search. Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina") loads the current Hugging Face model and paired autoencoder checkpoints.
import hydra
from rfd4_proteina import Proteina
from rfproteina.generate import run_generation
@hydra.main(config_path="configs", config_name="inference", version_base="1.3")
def main(cfg):
    model = Proteina.from_pretrained("nvidia/RFD4-Proteina")
    run_generation(cfg, model=model)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
Generate one candidate from the repository root:
python design.py inputs=pdl1.json out_dir=runs/pdl1-open seed=42 compile_lengths=null
Outputs are saved under runs/pdl1-open/inference_samples/. Add num_replicates=10 for ten candidates and choose a new out_dir for each run. Hugging Face caches downloads; add revision=”<commit>” to from_pretrained to reproduce a particular model version.
NIM generation
Save this as nim_client.py. It sends the PD-L1 condition spec and target CIF to the NIM, then saves generated structures and response metrics.
import json
from pathlib import Path
import requests
spec = json.loads(Path("pdl1.json").read_text())["pdl1_binder"]
target = Path(spec["input"])
spec["input"] = target.name
payload = {
    "task": "motif_scaffolding",
    "input": {"format": "condition_spec", "example_id": "pdl1_binder",
              "spec": spec, "files": [{"filename": target.name, "content": target.read_text()}]},
    "sampling": {"num_replicates": 1, "seed": 42},
    "metrics": {"tags": ["design", "hotspot_conditioning"]},
}
def submit(payload, out):
    out.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    response = requests.post("http://localhost:8000/biology/ipd/rfd4-proteina/generative",
                             json=payload, timeout=1800)
    response.raise_for_status()
    result = response.json()
    (out / "response.json").write_text(json.dumps(result, indent=2))
    for i, design in enumerate(result["designs"]):
        dest = out / f"design-{i}.cif"
        dest.write_text(design["structure"]["content"])
        print(design["design_id"], dest)
if __name__ == "__main__":
    submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim"))
Install requests and run the client from the repository root. Keep pdl1.json beside the target CIF.
python -m pip install requests
python nim_client.py
Performance optimizations across open model and NIM
For faster design iteration, the BioIR backend accelerates RFD4-Proteina by 1.37–1.73× over the default compiled backend across six tested Hopper GPU configurations (see Figure 4, below). On H100 PCIe, total suite time drops from 161 to 111 seconds, about 31% less runtime. The benchmark uses batch size 1 and sums warm end-to-end timings across 15 sequence lengths (128–1,024 tokens).
Inference-time search with external oracles
Open-model search with OpenFold3
Install the optional OpenFold3 runtime and weights with ./scripts/download_example_data.sh ./data_path. Set OF3_IMAGE, OF3_MODEL_DIR, and OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR to the paths it prints, then run mkdir -p "$OF3_JAX_CACHE_DIR". Apptainer must be available on the GPU host.
This example uses the AlphaFold3 codebase, which is released under the open-source Apache 2.0 license, and the OpenFold3 model weights, which are also released under the Apache 2.0 license.
Reuse design.py with the search preset:
python design.py inference_experiment=inference_beam_example \
  metrics/refolding_oracles=of3 inputs=pdl1.json subset_to_examples=null \
  num_replicates=1 out_dir=runs/pdl1-open-search seed=42 compile_lengths=null
The preset uses two branches, a beam width of three, and scoring at steps 20, 40, 50 and 60. It rewards the designed chain’s OpenFold3 pLDDT (oracle.plddt_coi), with a floor of 50, and saves qualifying rollouts at reward 80. This measures confidence in the binder, not evidence of binding; inspect interface and refolding metrics separately. Outputs are under runs/pdl1-open-search/.
NIM search with OpenFold3
Save this as nim_search_request.py. It reuses the PD-L1 input and submits a reward-guided OpenFold3 search.
from pathlib import Path
from nim_client import payload, submit
key = "oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt"
payload["sampling"]["num_steps"] = 60
payload["search"] = {
    "step_checkpoints": [0, 20, 40, 50, 60],
    "n_branch": 2, "beam_width": 3,
    "reward_metrics_tags": ["unconditional_refolding"],
    "weights": {key: 1.0}, "clip_values": {key: {"min": 50.0}},
    "intermediate_save_min_reward": 80.0,
}
payload["metrics"] = {"tags": ["design", "unconditional_refolding"]}
submit(payload, Path("runs/pdl1-nim-search"))
Enable the NIM oracle
Mount the OpenFold3 reward.py callback as described in the oracle guide. It reports oracle_of3_nvcf.overall_plddt for the whole complex; evaluate the binder interface separately.
Save the OpenFold3 NVCF callback from the oracle guide as reward.py and export OF3_NIM_API_KEY with an NVCF invoke credential. Relaunch the service with this callback:
docker stop rfd4-proteina
docker run -d --rm --name rfd4-proteina \
  --gpus 'device=0' -p 8000:8000 --shm-size=16g \
  -e NGC_API_KEY -v "$LOCAL_NIM_CACHE:/opt/nim/.cache" \
  -v "$PWD/reward.py:/opt/nim/reward.py:ro" \
  -e NIM_ALLOW_ORACLE_PLUGIN=true -e OF3_NIM_API_KEY \
  "$RFD4_NIM_IMAGE"
Run the search script. It saves designs and response metrics under runs/pdl1-nim-search/.
python nim_search_request.py
This request uses two branches, checkpoints [0, 20, 40, 50, 60], and a beam width of three. It sets a reward floor of 50 and saves intermediate designs with scores of at least 80. These are example thresholds for OpenFold3 overall pLDDT, a prediction-confidence metric for the whole complex. Search-time reward tags and final reporting tags are separate.
Search output counts vary. Inspect the generated CIFs and retained metrics before selecting candidates. Include refolding and scoring in compute comparisons.
Filter and rank candidates
Check constraints, motif preservation, clashes, interfaces, refolding consistency, and structural diversity metrics. OpenFold3, and RoseTTAFold3 provide prediction options; TMol provides Rosetta-inspired all-atom scoring and optimization.
Common metrics include ipTM (interface Predicted Template Modeling), ipSAE (interaction prediction Score from Aligned Errors), and RMSD (Root Mean Square Deviation) scores from protein structure prediction models like OpenFold 3, along with interaction energies from physics-based models like TMol.
Test experimentally and refine
Table 1, above, highlights RFD4-Proteina’s broad range of capabilities across molecular tasks. It not only supports this variety of tasks, in the accompanying manuscript it is demonstrated that the model is also the state-of-the-art model across this breadth of molecular tasks, both in terms of output quality and throughput.
Turn that throughput into scientific progress by selecting diverse candidates for synthesis, expression, and task-specific assays. Feed experimental outcomes back into the objective, constraints, and ranking criteria for the next round.
Run a campaign with an AI agent
Use the rfd4-proteina-campaign skill to coordinate generation, search and evaluation with a record of inputs, model versions and compute use. The rfd4-proteina-package skill produces a results archive with structures, metrics and a filtering report.
Use rfd4-proteina-campaign to design 100–150-residue PD-L1 binders from pdl1.json, preserving its target and hotspot constraints. Use the Hugging Face model via from_pretrained and OpenFold3. Agree on criteria and a compute budget, then compare generation with reward-guided search and run a campaign via rfd4-proteina-campaign. Return up to ten diverse candidates with scores and compute usage; package the results with rfd4-proteina-package.
Apply the workflow to your design problem
RFD4-Proteina combines fast generation, smart search, and agent programmability in one workflow. Joint sequence and all-atom structure generation streamlines candidate creation, while reward-guided search focuses compute on task-specific objectives. Shared condition specifications connect both form factors to common evaluation tools, and NIM’s HTTP API lets agents submit requests and inspect results.
Use the open model for method development and NIM for application integration with optional BioIR acceleration, bringing computational exploration and experimental feedback into an iterative design campaign.
Get started with the RFD4-Proteina NIM microservice, explore the open model on GitHub, or point your agent at BioNeMo Agent Toolkit skills.

articles.title: Warum in Windows 11 ein Relikt aus Windows 95 steckt - und was SimCity damit zu tun hat.
articles.text:
SimCity sei Dank: Warum in Windows 11 immer noch ein Stück Windows 95 steckt
Der offizielle Support von Windows 95 endete am 31. Dezember 2001. Doch auch 25 Jahre später ist ein Teil des Betriebssystems von Microsoft im Nachfolger Windows 11 aktiv. Selbst in dessen aktuellem Funktionsupdate 26H2, das Microsoft am 26. September 2026 veröffentlichte.
EmulateHeap als Relikt von Windows 95
Bei dem Relikt handelt es sich laut Windows Latest um EmulateHeap. Dieser Kompatibilitäts-Patch ermöglicht es den Nutzer:innen von modernen Microsoft-Betriebssystemen, alte Software oder Spiele aus der Ära von Windows 95 zum Laufen zu bringen.
EmulateHeap kopiert die Eigenschaften des Speichermanagers von Windows 95 für neuere Systeme. Denn der hält gerade für Games Vorteile bereit, die spätere Inkarnationen von Windows nicht haben.
Microsoft änderte für SimCity Code von Windows 95
Wenn Windows Programme ausführt, greifen die temporär auf Speicherkapazitäten zurück. Sobald man die Applikation beendet, wird der Speicherplatz wieder freigegeben.
Doch manchmal kann es zu einem Bug namens Use-after-free kommen. Dabei greift ein Programm auf einen Speicherbereich zu, nachdem der bereits freigegeben wurde. Dies kann zu einem Absturz führen.
Einen dieser Softwarefehler enthielt SimCity, das 1989 auf den Markt kam. Doch auf Rechnern, die mit Betriebssystemen aus der 1990 gestarteten Windows 3.x-Familie liefen, fiel dies nicht auf. Windows 3.0 und Co. funktionierten mit einer anderen Speicherarchitektur.
Doch als SimCity auf der Beta von Windows 95 getestet wurde, stürzte die Städtebausimulation ab. Anstatt auf einen Patch vonseiten der Macher von SimCity zu warten, änderten die Verantwortlichen bei Microsoft kurzerhand den Code von Windows 95 und ermöglichten dem Spiel den Zugriff auf eigentlich wieder freigegebenen Speicher.
Darum erschuf Microsoft EmulateHeap
Der Fix von Windows 95 war als Ausnahme für SimCity gedacht. Doch später zeigte sich, dass auch andere Spiele und Programme auf die Eigenheit des Speichersystems vertrauten. Bei späteren Versionen von Windows stürzten diese Apps ab. Als Lösung für dieses Problem schuf Microsoft EmulateHeap. Der Patch leitet Befehle wie HeapCreate oder LocalLock auf die simulierte Speicherverwaltung von Windows 95 weiter.
Bei Windows 11 findet man EmulateHeap in den Systemdateien. Um es zu finden, muss man laut der Lernplattform Microsoft Ignite bei alten Spielen oder Programmen einen Rechtsklick auf die .exe-Datei machen. Danach „Eigenschaften“ den Reiter „Kompatibilität“ auswählen. Dort dann einen Haken bei „Programm im Kompatibilitätsmodus ausführen für: Windows 95“ setzen.

articles.title: « Il a fait dérailler la saga », Resident Evil: Code Veronica est-il à l’origine du virage controversé de la série ?
articles.text:
Avant la sortie de Resident Evil 7 en 2017, qui a relancé la série, beaucoup pensaient que la licence de Capcom était dans une sacrée impasse. Entre plusieurs épisodes mal accueillis et des films qui tenaient davantage du nanar que du chef-d’œuvre, tout ou presque donnait l’impression que la saga était en fin de vie.
Depuis, la série a retrouvé une seconde jeunesse et enchaîne les succès, jusqu’à Resident Evil Requiem, mais ce n’était pas gagné. Pour Miguel Corti, ancien responsable chez Capcom, la dérive a commencé dès Resident Evil Code: Veronica, le fameux épisode sur Dreamcast. Il l’a expliqué sur Bluesky, dans des messages relayés ce mardi 20 octobre par GamesRadar.
À sa sortie en 2000 sur la console de Sega, le jeu avait pourtant été encensé par la critique, avec une moyenne de 94/100 sur Metacritic. Les tests saluaient ses graphismes et l’audace de Capcom, qui abandonnait les décors en 2D précalculés des premiers épisodes au profit d’environnements modélisés en 3D. Pour autant, les déplacements rigides et les commandes peu précises étaient également critiqués, ainsi que l’ambiance édulcorée.
Dans une série de messages publiés sur Bluesky, puis supprimés, Miguel Corti a livré de nombreuses informations sur le développement de Resident Evil 7, et en a profité pour laisser entendre que Resident Evil 5 et 6, les épisodes les plus décriés de la licence, n’auraient jamais vu le jour sans Code: Veronica.
« Tout le monde évoque systématiquement les trois premiers jeux Resident Evil, mais on semble oublier Code Veronica », explique Miguel Corti dans l’un de ces messages. « Il existe un lien direct entre Code Veronica et les épisodes 5 et 6 ; c’est avec Code Veronica que la série a dérapé, en cherchant à entasser autant de lieux et d’intrigues que la capacité d’un disque Dreamcast le permettait. »
Pour Miguel Corti, Code: Veronica a ouvert la voie à trop d’action
Pour l’ancien responsable de Capcom, Code: Veronica n’est ni plus ni moins que la note d’intention de ce que deviendront Resident Evil 5 et 6 : des jeux boursouflés par une action omniprésente, qui délaissent peu à peu l’horreur. Pour appuyer son propos, il prend en exemple la scène d’introduction de Code: Veronica, qui est, selon lui, « un pur pastiche de Die Hard ou des films de John Woo, sans la moindre trace d’horreur ».
Resident Evil 4, sorti en 2005, avait pourtant déjà largement renforcé la dimension action de la série, avec des affrontements plus dynamiques et des séquences spectaculaires. Mais le jeu de Shinji Mikami conservait une atmosphère oppressante. Il avait trouvé entre action et horreur un équilibre que ses successeurs n’ont pas réussi à préserver.
« Je ne cherche pas à dénigrer les fans de Code Veronica, mais comme ce titre a eu une incidence directe et négative sur l’évolution de la franchise, j’ai un parti pris assez marqué à son encontre », termine Miguel Corti. Quant à savoir si c’est bien l’épisode Dreamcast qui a fait basculer la saga dans l’action débridée, le débat reste ouvert. C’est une évolution que Capcom aurait peut-être fini par adopter tôt ou tard, alors que le survival horror connaissait lui aussi un tournant au début des années 2000.
Ces critiques arrivent alors que Capcom prépare le retour du jeu. Annoncé au Summer Game Fest 2026, Resident Evil Veronica, remake de Code: Veronica, doit sortir en 2027 sur PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2 et PC.

articles.title: Une photo du visage suffit à cette IA pour repérer les patients atteints de cancer les plus à risque
articles.text:
Une simple photo du visage pourrait-elle aider les médecins à mieux évaluer l'état de santé d'un patient atteint de cancer ? Une étude montre qu'une intelligence artificielle peut identifier dans les traits du visage des signes associés au risque de mortalité, parfois difficiles à apprécier à l'œil nu.
Un visage fatigué, des traits creusés, une apparence plus âgée que l'âge réel… Les médecins savent depuis longtemps que l'apparence physique peut donner des indications sur l'état général d'un patient. Mais une IA pourrait aller plus loin, en quantifiant des signes dont l'importance est difficile à apprécier pour un observateur humain.
C'est ce qu'explorent des chercheurs américains du Mass General Brigham, qui ont développé un système capable d'analyser une photographie du visage pour évaluer le risque de mortalité chez des personnes atteintes de cancer. Leurs résultats ont été publiés le 19 octobre dans The Lancet Digital Health.
Plus de 40 millions de visages pour apprendre à repérer les signes
Baptisée FAHR-Face, cette IA a été entraînée sur plus de 40 millions de photographies issues d'un jeu de données constitué à partir d'images collectées sur Internet. Sa particularité ? Elle a d'abord appris à reconnaître les caractéristiques des visages sans disposer de diagnostics médicaux associés aux photographies. Les chercheurs l'ont ensuite adaptée à deux tâches : estimer "l'âge facial" d'une personne et évaluer le pronostic de patients atteints de cancer.
Pour cette seconde application, l'IA a été entraînée sur 34 389 photographies de patients. Le quart des patients présentant les scores de risque les plus élevés affichait un risque instantané de décès plus de trois fois supérieur à celui du quart le moins à risque, après ajustement statistique tenant compte d'autres facteurs cliniques connus.
Ce résultat ne signifie pas que l'IA peut prédire combien de temps il reste à vivre à quelqu'un. Elle établit des associations statistiques entre certaines caractéristiques du visage et la mortalité observée chez les patients étudiés.
Les chercheurs ont également constaté que leur outil d'estimation de l'âge résistait plutôt bien aux changements d'éclairage, de pose ou de maquillage. Même certaines interventions de chirurgie esthétique modifiaient peu ses résultats.
Un simple selfie pour aider les médecins ? Pas si vite
L'objectif est d'apporter aux oncologues un indicateur supplémentaire pour évaluer la fragilité d'un patient avant de lui proposer une opération ou un traitement particulièrement éprouvant.
Mais cette IA ne permet pas de diagnostiquer un cancer à partir d'un selfie. Les patients évalués dans les études cliniques étaient déjà atteints de la maladie. L'outil cherche à estimer leur pronostic, pas à détecter une tumeur.
Les chercheurs ont obtenu des résultats encourageants sur des cohortes indépendantes, avec des performances étudiées selon l'âge, le sexe, l'origine ethnique et différents types de cancers. Il reste toutefois à démontrer que cette technologie améliore réellement les décisions médicales, au-delà des méthodes d'évaluation existantes.
L'utilisation de millions de visages collectés sur Internet soulève également des questions sur l'origine et la réutilisation des données personnelles.
Déjà présentés sous forme de prépublication en 2025, ces travaux franchissent une nouvelle étape avec leur publication dans une revue scientifique. Ils suggèrent qu'une photographie ordinaire pourrait, un jour, apporter aux médecins des informations supplémentaires sur l'état de santé de leurs patients.

articles.title: Berlin-based YGO raises €8 million to make travel inventory bookable through AI agents | EU-Startups
articles.text:
YGO, a Berlin-based startup building an AI infrastructure layer for the travel industry, raised €8 million in a Series A round.
The round was led by Ventech, with participation from Sake Bosch, Caesar and Business Angels. In August 2024, the company announced it had secured €2.5 million in funding led by GetAway Group.
“Online travel booking is undergoing its biggest structural shift in decades but most of the industry’s infrastructure was never built for it. YGO’s customers are already re-owning their customer relationships with AI and putting real KPI uplifts on the board to prove it. That’s why we believe YGO’s neutral infrastructure will become critical to how travel operates in an AI-first world,” said Nicolas Barthalon, Partner at Ventech.
Founded in 2023 by Julian Kögel, Sebastian Kreutzberger, and Willi Ibbeken, YGO sits at the intersection of legacy travel technology and the emerging ecosystem of AI agents. The company’s platform connects travel companies, including tour operators, online travel agencies, and travel agencies, directly with airlines, hotels, and tour operator inventory, without the need to restructure their existing booking infrastructure.
YGO does this by structuring and enriching fragmented hotel and product data, giving it the depth and accuracy that AI agents need to reliably discover, compare and recommend travel products. Its content enrichment product automatically generates verified, structured hotel data and delivers it across a company’s own digital channels and to external AI assistants via MCP (Model Context Protocol).
Its Hotel Q&A product embeds an AI-powered question-and-answer layer directly onto hotel pages, allowing travellers to ask any question and receive verified answers in real time and in their own language. Its AI Distribution product, on the other hand, makes a travel company’s entire hotel portfolio accessible and bookable through AI agents such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.
YGO says online travel agencies and metasearch platforms have captured 15-25% of every booking, acting as intermediaries between travellers and suppliers. With AI assistants becoming the starting point for travel planning and booking, suppliers are looking for ways to reclaim direct relationships with their customers.
The platform already processes bookings for major European travel players including Condor, Bentour, and GetAway Group. YGO says their collaboration has led to a 90% reduction in manual operations and a 20% improvement in conversion for one airline client, and a 2.4x increase in average order value with no additional headcount for another.
“Travel is one of the last major industries still built on infrastructure that was never designed for an AI-first world. We built YGO to change that: to give the travel industry the infrastructure to make its inventory accessible, bookable and ready for AI – whether through their own platforms or through external AI agents,” said Kögel, co-founder and CEO of YGO.
YGO has grown its recurring ARR into seven figures within six months and has processed more than €15 million in bookings through its infrastructure to date. The fresh capital will be utilised to scale go-to-market and sales operations, deepen its AI orchestration platform, and expand the company’s customer base beyond the DACH region, targeting both enterprise accounts and mid-sized travel companies.
“This funding allows us to build on the strong business we already have with some of Europe’s leading travel players and become the AI infrastructure layer connecting the industry to the next generation of travel,” added Kögel.

articles.title: Interspecies communication
articles.text:
Interspecies communication
Decoding how animals communicate could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world.
Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could offer a window into the inner lives of other species and help humans realize that “animals are sentient creatures who think, who have hopes and dreams of their own,” says Con Slobodchikoff, the founder of Zoolingua, a company working on dog-to-human speech.
The sticking points
Teasing all this out is complex. To decipher howls, squeaks, and clicks, researchers must match the creatures making sounds with what’s happening around them. Prairie dogs, for example, utter a different series of yips when a coyote approaches than when a hawk is nearby. It’s painstaking work, especially for difficult-to-observe species, like deep-diving whales or subterranean mole rats.
There are other hurdles. Many animals communicate not just through sound but through visual cues, touch, pheromones, or a combination of signals, some of which might be difficult for us to perceive. And without a multispecies Rosetta stone, it’s hard to know if translations are accurate.
The progress
Over the past 50 years, a growing arsenal of devices has made it easier to observe the sophisticated ways animals communicate. Hydrophones at the bottom of the ocean can capture humpback whale song, and tiny wearable “biologgers” can record a bat’s every squeak.
In the last decade, advances in AI have leveled up our ability to make sense of it all. The technology can detect different calls, distinguish which sounds belong to which animal, and spot patterns. Researchers at the Earth Species Project (ESP), a nonprofit founded in 2018 to decode animal communication, recently used machine learning to detect vocalizations of carrion crows and determine which bird made which call.
They suspect that more advanced AI could translate critters’ chatter. Large language models like Claude and ChatGPT excel at finding relationships between words, explains Sara Keen, one of ESP’s behavioral ecologists. ESP hopes its own NatureLM—trained on human speech, music, and animal sounds—will be able to interpret the vocalizations of a variety of species.
That promise, however, is still theoretical. Yossi Yovel, a neuroecologist at Tel Aviv University, worries that these models will put too much emphasis on acoustic similarities and make mistakes—like lumping together similar sounds that have different meanings.
As for a two-way convo? It’s not clear when—or whether—that will happen. Still, “a lot of animals have an evolutionary structure that is similar enough that we should be able to understand what they’re saying,” Slobodchikoff says.
