articles.title: AI’s Midas problem: When code is free, features are worthless
articles.text:
AI’s Midas problem: When code is free, features are worthless
Every team that adopted Claude Code, Cursor, or Copilot to produce more code has the same problem: When output is free, offering volume stops being a viable strategy. In fact, teams accelerating their software development with AI may be giving up the very thing that makes their software valuable.
It’s time to remember what makes software valuable and why racing to produce a mountain of code and features leads to failure.
The Midas touch
In Ovid’s tale, Midas, king of Phrygia, took in the missing satyr Silenus, whom Phrygian peasants had found drunk, granted him ten days of hospitality, and then returned him to Dionysus. In return, he was offered the reward of his choice: whatever he wished for. Famously, he wished that everything he touched would turn to gold.
Testing his new ability on an oak twig and then a stone, Midas was delighted. Nathaniel Hawthorne, who retold the myth for children in 1851, added a rose garden: His Midas turns every bloom to gold, still delighted, though his daughter Marygold mourns that the roses no longer smell sweet. In both versions, the celebration ends at the table, where food and drink turn to gold in his hands. That’s when Midas realized his reward was a bane, not a blessing, and asked to be rid of it.
Many leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now coming to a realization similar to that of Midas.
Though the process is gradual, many organizations and leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now reaching a similar conclusion. Reports show organizations slashing budgets and limiting tool use.
With Microsoft and Meta reportedly cutting internal spending on Anthropic’s Claude, and Uber and Accenture capping what employees can spend on AI tools, it’s time to acknowledge that the return on investment might not be there — McKinsey’s own 2026 research found record AI spending hasn’t moved earnings for 94% of enterprises — and it’s easy to see why.
The economics of plenty
If Midas had depended on the value of gold, perhaps hoping to trade the gold he created to fund his lavish lifestyle of hosting ten-day-long parties, he would have quickly learned that his gold was no longer valuable. His touch would cause hyperinflation, and gold’s price would plummet. His skill would be as useful as turning everything you touch to ash.
In the modern, non-mythical world, everything you touch with AI becomes a commodity. If you can get Claude or ChatGPT to create something for you, then everyone else can. They have access to the same tools. Whether you’re building software or writing a book, when you use AI, its perceived value is little more than the cost of the tokens you used.
When coding looked like magic to most people, basic coding competence was sufficient value. You could build a career translating human-language requirements into code. This value rolled up to the team, department, and organization level, with code magicians performing their arcane translations in return for money, whether the software was internal, built for a customer, or sold as a product.
If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless.
If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless. We know that a page that adds nothing beyond the AI summary is worthless, and software built by translating a user’s wants into code is the same.
How to avoid incinerating your software’s value
There is hope for us, though. When Midas asked to be rid of his power, he had to wash in the Pactolus River. Our touch isn’t directly connected to the generation machine, so it won’t inevitably turn our work to ash.
The answer is conceptually simple, though it takes a lot of effort in practice, which seems to be exactly what people want to avoid. Nevertheless, for your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription.
For your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription.
That means moving away from the feature-factory model of software development, where the value is primarily in the translation of “human wants” into code. Instead, teams building software must develop a deeper understanding of the jobs users do and the challenges they face, so they can generate novel ideas and commercial insights users wouldn’t reach on their own.
This second mode of building means you may deliver something completely different from what users ask for, yet one that gracefully solves many of the challenges they face in their work. Combining deep business domain knowledge with an understanding of abstract, reusable solutions lets you deliver something exceptional.
DORA’s State of DevOps research has highlighted this need for user-centricity. That doesn’t mean doing whatever users ask; it means understanding their work and challenges so you can provide software they value. DORA’s 2024 report says this approach improves product performance, regardless of delivery speed.
We are living through a time of excess code, sentences, and images. The path forward isn’t more; it’s better.

articles.title: One month of Netflix is a miniscule price to pay for the anime gloriousness that is Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2
articles.text:
Cyberpunk Edgerunners Season 2: Studio Trigger delivers yet another animated masterpiece
Night City never sleeps
When you create a smash-hit like Season 1 of Cyberpunk Edgerunners, returning for a second outing was never going to be easy. Setting the bar so high you’ll need top-shelf cybernetics to make that leap — but with Edgerunners Season 2, Studio Trigger yet again proves why it stands alone as master animators of high-octane action that is as visually stunning as it is visceral.
The story itself will be familiar in theme and setting to fans of Edgerunner's first outing, but the series is more of an anthology than direct follow-ons to what came before. The events of the first season are referenced — David is a known Night City legend by characters in the show — but don’t expect to see any follow-ups on Lucy or other stories.
Instead Edgerunners gives us a whole new cast — focused on budding videographer Roman, the chrome-obsessed renegade Talia, cyberpsychosis-survivor King, and revenge-fuelled netrunner D — whose individual stories cross and diverge as the events of Season 2 unfold.
Don’t worry, things are easy to follow, and the plots develop at an excellent pace — keeping you engaged while also making sure characters aren’t abandoned for longer than you want.
To some extent, you *could* start here considering the disconnect to Season 1, but (1) you’ll be missing out on a phenomenal season of animated TV, and (2) while the characters don’t make a return, the world of Cyberpunk and Night City and its factions do.
More generally, Season 2 is fuelled by the same themes as its predecessor, and there are familiarities between the new cast and Maine’s crew. There’s naivety and dreams of a different world to what exists, grizzled veterans and long-standing grudges between factions, and a looming sense of inevitable tragedy that seems to eventually catch up with everyone in Night City.
The context of Season 1 will help you better appreciate Season 2, even if it isn’t necessarily required reading (though required or not, you’re depriving yourself if you skip it).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
I’m aiming to keep things spoiler-lite for this preview, so I’ll cut myself off here before I get into more specific plot details and shift gear to the animation.
Simply put: it’s sublime.
Studio Trigger is well known for its dazzling action — delivering artistically beautiful scenes of violence, but also graphically gory fight scenes that make it clear you never want to be on the wrong side of a gunfight.
Each combat encounter is unique too, with Studio Trigger finding ways to keep its action constantly feeling fresh rather than just repetitive brawls and shootouts, thanks to engaging set pieces and aesthetic flashes that make every gory execution different from the last.
This was showcased in Season 1, and that same mastery is present in Season 2. But I love the artistic approaches taken in the show’s calmer moments too. The grainy film footage effect of Roman’s recordings gives the technofuturistic events an appropriately vintage quality; D’s traumatic and hazy flashbacks are rendered with minimal, blocky colors and silhouettes.
There are also playful ‘anime moments.’ Roman’s over-the-top visual reaction to hearing of a rare 35mm camera almost doesn’t fit the gritty reality around him, but helps to cement his position of child-like wonder — one that has yet to be corrupted by the harsh reality of Night City.
In every case these artistic choices don’t add to a frenetic chaos — they emphasise moments both in and out of action, provide a deeper insight into the psyche of the characters, and bring the world of Cyberpunk Edgerunners to life in all its technofuturistic glory.
If you have a Netflix subscription and haven’t experienced Cyberpunk Edgerunners yet, you’re doing yourself a disservice — stop reading and get over there. Season 1 and now Season 2 are masterclasses in animated excellence that are sure to delight fans and non-fans of anime alike.
Heck, they’re worth subscribing to Netflix if you don’t already for a month to catch it all. It’ll be the best binge-watch of your life.

articles.title: Egypt’s Tactful AI gets backing from former e& CEO Hatem Dowidar - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian agentic AI customer experience (CX) startup Tactful AI has secured investment from Hatem Dowidar, the former group CEO of e&, as part of an extension of its pre-Series A funding round.
Founded by Mohamed Elmasry, Mohammad Hassan and Sherif Khairallah, Tactful is a unified customer experience platform that provides businesses with a single dashboard through which to manage, engage, augment, and understand customers’ journeys across various touch points.
In 2022, the company was acquired by Dstny, a leading European company that offers a series of interactive communication tools that brings employees and customers closer together, but it was reacquired by its founders in July 2025.
Disrupt Africa reported in February Tactful AI had raised US$1 million in a pre-Series A funding round co-led by Foras AI and M Empire, and it has now extended that round with the investment from Dowidar, the size of which is undisclosed.
Dowidar has spent more than 25 years in telecoms and technology. He led e& as group CEO from 2020 until March 2026, after joining the company as chief operating officer in 2015. Before e&, he spent 16 years in executive roles at Vodafone, including as CEO of Vodafone Egypt.
The extra funding is a boost for Tactful AI at a time when it is about to launch a next-generation version of its technology, which aims to let enterprises build, modify and evolve end-to-end CX workflows in-house, cutting development cycles from months to hours while keeping human sign-off at every step.
The startup has been growing fast. Since January 2025, its annual recurring revenue (ARR) has risen 11.7 times, and the number of monthly customer conversations processed through its platform has increased 32-fold. Its clients include Elaraby Group, Raneen, 2B, Lucky One, Erada Finance and Simplex.
“Enterprises across the region are actively seeking practical, reliable solutions to integrate AI into their customer operations safely and at scale. Tactful has successfully deployed this infrastructure in live production environments,” Dowidar said. “Seeing the capabilities of their next-generation technology convinced me that this team has everything it takes to set the industry benchmark, both regionally and globally.”
Elmasry said few leaders understood as well as Dowidar what large enterprises need before they trust new customer-facing technologies.
“His support and trust come at a pivotal moment as we take our boldest step yet toward defining a new era of agentic AI-driven customer experience,” he said.
Tactful AI plans to raise a Series A round in 2027.

articles.title: IBM-backed llm-d framework adds controls for running AI models in-house - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
IBM-backed llm-d framework adds controls for running AI models in-house
IBM Corp. and several other contributors to the open-source llm-d project are releasing version 1.0 of their distributed artificial intelligence inference framework, adding operational controls intended to help enterprises run large models reliably on their own infrastructure.
The release, announced ahead of the PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose today and tomorrow, focuses on managing competing workloads, maintaining service during upgrades and improving hardware efficiency as AI agents generate growing volumes of model requests.
Built for Kubernetes, llm-d coordinates model serving across computing infrastructure. IBM, its Red Hat subsidiary and Google LLC are its lead maintainers. They co-founded the project last year with CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia Corp. Other contributors include Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Cisco Systems Inc., Hugging Face Inc., Intel Corp. and Mistral AI SAS.
The project offers organizations seeking more control over inference costs and infrastructure choices a way to reduce dependence on a single model provider, cloud or hardware platform.
“At IBM Research, we are seeing that open large language models and llm-d can greatly lower the costs of inference in computationally demanding problems such as designing hardware for quantum error correction, helping achieve a 11.8X efficiency advantage,” Ruchir Puri, IBM Research’s chief scientist, vice president of IBM’s Technology & Technical Community and IBM Fellow, wrote in e-mailed comments. “Llm-d 1.0 extends these savings by delivering the operational readiness needed for enterprises to extract more out of their computational capacity.”
The project is focused on what happens after deployment. A production inference service must handle changing traffic, hardware failures, software updates and users competing for resources while maintaining acceptable response times.
Version 1.0 adds support for quality of service across multiple tenants, zero-downtime operations and serving patterns tailored to AI agents. Flow controls and prioritization are designed to keep bursts of agent activity from overwhelming services that require fast responses, such as coding assistants used by people.
The release “adds the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable [application programming interface], multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure and upgrades that don’t interrupt operations,” said Carlos Costa, distinguished engineer at IBM Research and a project co-founder and lead maintainer.
Workloads can behave differently even when they reach models through the same endpoint. An agent may issue many requests, pause to use an external tool and return for additional model calls.
The framework can keep requests directed to appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns, increasing opportunities to reuse previously processed context. That matters because agents repeatedly consult the same code, documents, instructions and conversation history while completing assignments.
A routing system directs requests toward replicas that already hold relevant cached context. Another capability moves cached information among graphics processing unit memory, CPU memory and storage, preserving reusable information when GPU capacity becomes constrained.
These techniques were previously available, but version 1.0 integrates them with operational controls, along with methods that separate prompt processing from response generation, optimize work batches and distribute large mixture-of-experts models across accelerators. IBM cited a recent agentic coding test in which the framework’s router captured 97% of available cache reuse.
In a separate demonstration, IBM and Red Hat said they ran 3,000 software-engineering agents concurrently on self-hosted infrastructure at a cost five to 10 times lower than serving the same open model through a hosted service.
The economics become more significant as agents perform multiple rounds of reasoning, tool use and revision for a single assignment, IBM said. Reprocessing identical material at each step consumes additional computing resources.
Llm-d works with inference engines including vLLM and SGLang, supplying distributed routing and operational capabilities around model servers. It is currently hosted as a sandbox project by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.
“It delivers high-performance, distributed inference with the reliability and scale enterprises need within an operational model they already know,” said Stephen Watt, vice president in Red Hat’s chief technology officer’s office.

articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy.
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer.
Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources. Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks. Operational databases include Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), Oracle, and SQL Server. Analytical engines include Amazon Athena, Trino, and SAP HANA, and software as a service (SaaS) sources include Salesforce. The linked-model pattern extends beyond the Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora pair this walkthrough uses. In this walkthrough, a Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reaches Mosaic through the MCP endpoint. The joins, metric definitions, and per-caller row and column filters live inside Mosaic, not in the agent prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series. If any of it is new, the Stardog post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to model a C360 domain in Strategy Mosaic across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora using two linked models, with no ETL.
- How Mosaic’s metric syntax (base, advanced with named filter objects, level qualifiers, and compound) captures the business definitions the agent must reason over.
- How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP server, and how user identity propagates so per-user Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) hold end-to-end.
- How to choose between live pushdown and in-memory execution for agent traffic.
- How to publish the same governed definitions to Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, and custom apps, and how to export them in Apache Ossie format for tools outside Mosaic.
The source of truth for the walkthrough is Strategy One (March 2026), the release when Mosaic access through the MCP server became available by default.
Strategy Mosaic terms used in this post
A short reference before we get to the model.
- Mosaic Schema and Mosaic Models. Two modeling paths within one universal semantic layer. Mosaic Schema is the centrally governed enterprise model. Mosaic Models is the self-service, AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio. Models can map to Schema attributes and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS. This walkthrough uses Mosaic Models.
- Model. The top-level artifact within either modeling path. Publishes attributes, metrics, hierarchies, and security rules over physical tables. The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, one over Amazon Redshift and one over Aurora, linked together.
- Attribute. A business entity such as Customer. Carries multiple forms: an ID form for joining and a display form for reading. Mosaic uses forms to resolve names like “Carolyn Inworth” to the underlying cid.
- Hierarchy. A parent-child relationship between attributes. Category rolls up through parent to Department. Address rolls up to City to State.
- Fact and metric. A fact is a numeric column. A metric aggregates it. Purchase Amount = price * quantity is a base metric. Metrics can also be advanced (an aggregation qualified by a named condition) or compound (a formula over other metrics).
- Filter object. A named condition referenced from metrics in angle brackets. [Large Orders] is a filter whose qualification is Purchase Amount > 500. A metric references <[Large Orders]> without inlining the predicate.
- Level qualifier. Metric expression syntax that pins aggregation grain. {~+, !Customer+} sets the grain to Customer regardless of how the query is sliced.
- Model linking. Composition across models on shared attributes (Customer, Time). Mosaic pushes aggregates to each source and joins intermediate results on the linking attributes.
- Certified model. Only certified models are reachable through the MCP server.
- Live or in-memory. Two per-model execution modes: live pushdown to the source, or answers from a Mosaic-resident cube. Details later in this post.
The example: Customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora
The C360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. The schema is adapted from Stardog’s C360 Knowledge Kit, so a reader following the series sees the same entities, keys, and anchor question answered by a different semantic layer. A retail organization has customer records, addresses, credit cards, and rewards enrollment sitting on the operational side, and orders, products, and product categories sitting in the warehouse. Business users want answers that span both without knowing which system holds which fact.
Where this post differs is how Mosaic reaches the two sources. Mosaic does not federate rows across engines at query time. It plans one query per source, pushes native SQL down, and joins the intermediate result sets in the Mosaic engine on the shared attributes declared through model linking. The C360 walkthrough models the analytical side as a Purchase model over Amazon Redshift and the operational side as a Customer model over Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible edition.
The schema across the two databases:
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible (operational)
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
Amazon Redshift (analytical)
| Table | Key columns | 
| purchase | id (PK), cid, pid, date, quantity, price, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
| category | id (PK), dept_name, parent | 
| vendor | id (PK), vendor_name, industry | 
The shared ID is cid, an integer that appears as the primary key in customer on Aurora and as a plain column in purchase on Amazon Redshift. There is no SQL constraint linking them, and there can’t be, because they live in different engines. Every question that joins a customer to their orders must reconcile that integer somewhere. Mosaic absorbs it through model linking rather than a materialized cross-engine join.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post. It needs customer profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from Aurora, ranked and filtered on definitions that live in the semantic layer.
Reference architecture
Figure 1 shows the end-to-end runtime. The inbound authentication path runs from the client through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the runtime. The outbound query path runs from the Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP endpoint to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora.
The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP). It then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent. The agent invokes Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, its MCP tool connects directly to the Mosaic MCP endpoint at https://<env-domain>/collaboration/mcp/mosaic over HTTPS. The agent presents an OAuth 2.0 access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Mosaic validates the token against its bundled OAuth authorization server and resolves the caller to a Strategy user. It then applies the Use MCP Server privilege and certified-model gate, evaluates row-level and column-level security for that user, and plans the query across the linked Purchase and Customer models. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora respond to source-native SQL that the Mosaic engine emits per source.
Two properties matter for the rest of the walkthrough. Cross-source joins happen because a modeler declared a link, not because two sources happen to be reachable. The agent can only traverse links that exist in the model. The token that reaches Mosaic represents the human user, not a service account, so RLS and OLS evaluate against the caller’s identity end-to-end. AWS Secrets Manager holds the caller’s refresh token between calls, and the Governed access section walks the full identity chain.
Build the semantic layer
The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, the self-service AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio, linked on shared attributes. Mosaic Studio is the authoring suite, and the screenshots in this post come from its Design Center modeling workspace. Three passes: datasets and joins on each side, attributes and hierarchies, then metrics that carry the business logic. A team with an existing centrally governed Mosaic Schema can map the model’s attributes to it and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS from the enterprise schema without a parallel security review. Do this early if your data architects already maintain a governed schema.
Two linked models
Each Mosaic model connects to one live source. Model linking composes them.
- Purchase: Live against Amazon Redshift. Facts on the purchase table (price * quantity), dimensions on product, category, vendor, and the purchase date.
- Customer: Live against Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible. Dimensions on customer, address, credit_card, rewards_account.
Inside each model, the physical joins are declared once against the source schema. The Purchase model resolves purchase.pid = product.id, product.dept = category.id, and product.brand = vendor.id, plus a self-reference on category.parent = category.id for the department rollup. The Customer model resolves customer.location = address.id, customer.cid = credit_card.cid, and customer.cid = rewards_account.cid. These are the relationships Mosaic uses to plan the source-native SQL it pushes down. Nothing physical crosses between Purchase and Customer.
The two models link on Customer and Time. When a question needs both (for example top spenders in Wisconsin pulls state from address and spend from purchase), Mosaic pushes the appropriate aggregation to each source and combines the results on the linking attributes. No ETL, no third copy.
Domain ownership follows the model boundary. The CRM team owns Customer, and the data system team owns Purchase. Neither hands over its source. They agree on the linking attributes, and security propagates from the underlying models automatically. There’s no materialized cross-engine join and no shared physical schema between Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora. The join is the linking-attribute agreement.
Attributes and hierarchies
Attributes carry multiple forms. Customer uses cid as the ID form and first_name + last_name as the display form, so an agent can ask about “Carolyn Inworth” and Mosaic resolves it to the right key on both sides of the link. Figure 2 shows the Customer attribute authored in Mosaic Studio, with cid as the ID form and Full Name, First Name, and Last Name as display forms.
Two hierarchies matter for C360:
- The Category hierarchy rolls up through parent to Department. The category.parent self-reference means a department-level question aggregates consistently.
- Address rolls up through City to State in the same pattern. That makes State = 'WI' a single attribute qualification rather than a join the agent must construct.
Figure 3 shows the geography hierarchy authored in Design Center, chaining State through City and ZIP Code down to Customer.
The agent asks for State = 'WI', not for address.state. Physical column names don’t leave the model. Every consumer of the semantic layer sees the attribute form and its display forms, and the hierarchy carries the rollup automatically.
Metrics: Base, advanced, compound, time-intelligence
A base metric applies a group function to a fact. Purchase Amount is Sum(price * quantity) on the purchase table.
Figure 4 shows the Purchase Amount base metric authored in Mosaic Studio: the formula Price * Quantity, with a description field that tells the agent what the metric means in business terms.
The interesting C360 concepts are advanced metrics: an aggregation qualified by a named condition. In Strategy, conditions are references to filter objects in angle brackets, not inline predicates. Filter objects are model objects with their own name, description, and permissions, so they are reusable and auditable across metrics that share a definition.
Define the filters once:
| Filter object | Qualification | 
| [Large Orders] | Purchase Amount > 500 | 
| [Sports Category] | Category = "Sports" | 
| [Rewards Members] | Rewards Account is not null | 
| [Card Present] | Purchase Card is not null | 
| [Big Spender] | Customer Lifetime Spend > 10000 | 
Each filter object carries a name, description, qualification, and access permissions. The shape a modeler authors or exports for [Large Orders] looks like this:
Then reference the filters in metric expressions. Each of these is an advanced metric: a base aggregation qualified by a named filter.
Figure 5 shows the Design Center view of an advanced metric with a filter condition applied. It uses the same authoring pattern as the preceding Large Order Spend.
Customer Lifetime Spend also needs a level qualifier, because lifetime means the whole history regardless of how the current question is sliced:
The ! before Customer sets grouping to none, so the metric returns each customer’s full total on every row rather than collapsing to one row per customer. See Strategy Metric Level Symbols for the full syntax.
Notice that [Big Spender] in the filter table qualifies on a metric expression rather than an attribute predicate. Filter objects can gate on either. Share of wallet is a compound metric, built from other metrics:
Levels and conditions carry through from the components unchanged. Share of wallet is a ratio, so it doesn’t add or average. The share across an AWS Region isn’t the average of each customer’s share, and the metric description tells the agent that. See Strategy Conditional Metrics.
Beyond base, advanced, and compound, Mosaic ships governed time-intelligence metrics as first-class expressions. Previous Year, Previous Quarter, Year-to-Date, and Quarter-to-Date are declared once on the model and preserved through slice, so a question like how does Sports spend this year compare with last year becomes an attribute pick and two metric references rather than a hand-written SQL date filter. Custom calendars attach at the model level, so the same year-over-year expression works for a fiscal year that ends in September and a calendar year that ends in December. See Governed Time-Intelligence Metrics in Mosaic.
Edit the filter object once and the Power BI dashboard, the SQL extract, and the agent all move together. That is what a named, governed model artifact gets you that an inline SQL predicate cannot.
How Mosaic plans and executes queries
The Mosaic engine parses each MCP query call as Trino-dialect SQL, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying Purchase and Customer models, applies the RLS or OLS that the caller is subject to, and plans physical SQL per source. The dialect matches what Strategy publishes for the MCP query tool, so the SQL the agent emits is portable across MCP clients connecting to the same certified model.
For the auto-enrollment question, planning unfolds like this:
- Push down to Amazon Aurora: a join of customer and rewards_account on cid, projecting profile and rewards_account.create_date, filtered where enrollment is null. Returns one row per unenrolled customer.
- Push down to Amazon Redshift: SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid. Returns one row per customer with total spend.
- Combine inside Mosaic: join the two intermediate result sets on cid (the linking attribute), rank by lifetime spend, and return the top 20.
Aurora runs a transactional profile join. Amazon Redshift runs the fact aggregation. Mosaic handles the cross-engine join on a small intermediate set (one row per customer, not one row per order). A hand-written pipeline approximates the same shape and then must be kept in sync forever.
One SQL detail matters. Metrics are governed values, but Trino treats them as selected columns, so when a query uses GROUP BY, metrics need an aggregation wrapper such as SUM(metric_name). The metric’s definition, conditions, and join paths are still resolved by Mosaic. The outer aggregation is the caller’s. A non-additive ratio like share of wallet therefore needs to say so in its description.
Live pushdown or in-memory
Every Mosaic model runs in one of two modes.
| Mode | Behavior | Best fit | 
| Live | Pushdown to Redshift or Aurora at query time | Consistently-current data. Source security applies directly | 
| In-memory | Answered from a Mosaic-resident cube | Bounded recent windows. Predictable latency. No per-query warehouse compute | 
Both modes enforce the same security rules. RLS and OLS are set once on the model and evaluated regardless of where the answer comes from. The choice is a performance and cost question.
Agent traffic is repetitive and bursty. An agent decomposing top spenders in Wisconsin into several exploratory follow-ups fires many small queries over the same recent slice. Serving that from memory turns variable per-query warehouse spend into fixed Mosaic capacity, and it’s usually faster. For interactive agent workloads over a bounded window, in-memory is often both quicker and cheaper. Configure Mosaic-side entitlements before switching a model to in-memory, and validate them in the same test pass you use to validate the numbers.
One definition, four interfaces
The metrics, attributes, hierarchies, and security rules built in the previous section reach every consumer through native protocols. No connector translation, no metric re-implementation, no drift.
| Protocol | Typical consumer | What it uses Mosaic for | 
| MCP | AI agents (Strands, Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) | Semantic discovery + governed query | 
| SQL / JDBC / ODBC (Trino) | Tableau, SQL clients, Python notebooks | Flexibility and ad-hoc analysis | 
| DAX / XMLA | Power BI, Excel PivotTables | Semantic fidelity for BI | 
| REST | Custom applications, data science | Programmatic access | 
The same certified Mosaic model that the Strands agent in this walkthrough consumes also serves a business analyst working in Amazon Quick, which registers Mosaic MCP as an OAuth-authenticated connector. No second integration is required.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Mosaic enforces access in the semantic layer, before a query reaches Amazon Redshift or Aurora. HR and fraud roles see personally identifiable information (PII) fields like ssn and card_num. Marketing and analytics roles do not. Enforcement is identical whether the caller is a Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One set of RLS and OLS objects, one certified-model gate, one privilege check. Attributes and metrics marked as sensitive also feed Mosaic Sentinel Risk Management, which alerts on queries that touch flagged objects and detects behavioral anomalies as a defense-in-depth layer next to OLS.
Figure 6 shows the identity propagation chain across two lanes: the front-door OAuth handshake that runs once per user, and the per-request path that runs on every agent tool call. Each lane carries the user’s identity end-to-end so Mosaic can enforce RLS and OLS on the caller rather than a service account.
The chain follows two lanes.
Front-door OAuth handshake (once per user). The human user authenticates against the enterprise IdP. The application starts an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow against Strategy Library at /collaboration/authorize with scope offline_access. Strategy Library, federated to the same IdP through SAML or OIDC, returns a refresh and access token pair at /collaboration/token. The app persists the refresh token to AWS Secrets Manager, keyed by the user’s IdP sub claim.
Per-request path (every agent tool call). AgentCore Gateway validates the IdP JWT and routes to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent invoking Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. The agent’s MCP tool retrieves the user’s refresh token from Secrets Manager, exchanges it for a fresh access token, and presents Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to /collaboration/mcp/mosaic. Mosaic resolves the token to a Strategy user, enforces the Use MCP Server privilege, certified-model gate, and RLS and OLS, then plans and executes against Purchase and Customer. A marketing analyst doesn’t see ssn or card_num. A fraud analyst does.
Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Governance evaluates on the caller’s identity from IdP to Mosaic engine.
Expose the layer through the Mosaic MCP server
Strategy Library exposes two MCP endpoints:
| Endpoint | Path | What it does | 
| Agents MCP | /collaboration/mcp/agent | Routes a question to a certified Strategy agent, which answers using its own data and instructions | 
| Mosaic MCP | /collaboration/mcp/mosaic | Queries Mosaic models and AI-enabled cubes directly, no Strategy agent required | 
Both work independently. This walkthrough uses Mosaic MCP. Putting the semantic layer directly in front of the Strands agent skips an inference hop.
The tool chain
Four tools, chained from project to model to semantics to query.
| Tool | What it does | Parameters | 
| get_projects | Lists Strategy projects the caller can access | none | 
| get_models | Lists certified Mosaic models and datasets in a project | project | 
| get_semantics | Returns a model’s full definition: attributes and metrics with data types, descriptions, and metric formulas | model | 
| query | Runs a read-only Trino SQL query. Writes and DDL rejected with MOSAIC_SQL_WRITE_REJECTED | sql | 
The agent chains these calls automatically. get_projects and get_models narrow to the right model by description before the agent reads a column name. get_semantics returns the governed definitions the agent then uses to compose SQL against real object names: Sports Share of Wallet as a compound metric, Customer Lifetime Spend scoped to Customer, the Category hierarchy, and the formula for every metric.
Two Mosaic-specific SQL conventions matter. Column identifiers follow a <form>__<name> pattern and must be wrapped in double quotes ("customer__customer name"). Time attributes are exposed both as base columns and as pre-bucketed interval columns ((day interval), (month interval)), and the docs explicitly say to use the interval columns for time-grouped aggregations rather than date_trunc.
Metadata is what makes it accurate
get_semantics returns definitions, but the agent still must choose the right metric. Without descriptions, Total Spend and Customer Lifetime Spend look interchangeable, and they aren’t. Four properties do most of the work: object descriptions (what the metric means and when not to use it, including aggregation behavior for non-additive metrics), semantic definitions (how compound metrics compose), relationships (which attributes are valid slices), and governance context (so the agent can say what it can’t see rather than presenting a filtered number as complete). The model description is the first thing get_models returns and it’s how the agent picks the right model. Mosaic can import metadata from upstream catalogs, so column descriptions already maintained flow in rather than being retyped.
Deploy the agent
Strands is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the Mosaic MCP endpoint as a tool source. The AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and forwards the human user’s JWT.
The system prompt matters. Give the agent explicit instructions to follow the three-step call pattern before writing SQL: get_projects, then get_models, then get_semantics on the target model. Tell it to reference only attribute and metric names that get_semantics returned. Include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (Customer Lifetime Spend is the customer’s total across their history regardless of the current slice. Sports Share of Wallet is a ratio. And so on). This is the prompt engineering that pays the most in accuracy.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The get_semantics payload runs to a few thousand tokens and doesn’t change within a model version, so caching drops the input-token cost per call on repeated invocations. Agent traffic against a stable semantic layer is exactly the repetitive, bursty pattern that benefits most.
Two effects compound on the MCP path. First, get_semantics returns compressed business context (metric definitions, hierarchies, attribute forms) instead of raw schema DDL, so the model reasons over a smaller, higher-signal payload. Strategy’s published benchmark measures the input-token and per-query cost impact of serving semantic context versus raw schema. Second, Bedrock prompt caching keeps that already-compressed payload warm across calls. For repetitive agent traffic, both effects apply per call: the model reasons over compressed context, and repeat calls hit the cache.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three query categories through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them as a different role.
Query 1, Aurora-only. List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a query against the Customer model that projects the display forms of Customer and City and filters state to WI:
Mosaic pushes a single query to Aurora and returns the rows. Amazon Redshift is not touched.
Query 2, Amazon Redshift only. What are our top 10 products by units sold?
The entire query pushes to Amazon Redshift. Aurora is not touched.
Query 3, cross-model. Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?
Mosaic plans across both models. Profile and enrollment status come from Aurora, spend aggregation from Amazon Redshift, joined on the Customer linking attribute inside the Mosaic engine, then filtered and top-N’d. The agent did not need to define Customer Lifetime Spend. It referenced the metric by name and Mosaic resolved the formula, level qualifier, and linking paths.
Governance rerun. We ran Query 1 with ssn added to the projection as two callers. As a fraud analyst, get_semantics returned the SSN attribute and the query returned the values. As a marketing analyst, get_semantics returned a Customer attribute without ssn at all, so the agent had no attribute to project. Same request, same query text, two correct answers from one definition.
Cross-interface confirmation. We opened the same certified Customer model in Excel through the Mosaic XMLA endpoint and dragged State and Customer Lifetime Spend onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals matched the agent’s numbers exactly.
Early in the run, the agent averaged share of wallet across customers, the classic non-additive mistake. Adding one line to the metric description (“ratio metric. Do not average across customers, recompute from components”) stopped it. That’s the case for writing metric descriptions in the first sprint rather than the last.
Extending across data sources
The same linking mechanism extends to a third source: clickstream events in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) queried through Amazon Athena, tables in Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon S3, or a SaaS source such as a CRM. Model the source in Mosaic, link it on Customer and Time, and browse-to-buy questions compose into the same customer view without a third pipeline. Adding a source doesn’t change the metric definitions that already exist. The agent can only travel paths a modeler declared. AWS Lake Formation governs access to the underlying lake tables. Mosaic’s RLS and OLS apply on top.
The same live-source pattern applies to every system in Strategy’s supported data source catalog, covering on-premises databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL alongside the warehouses and engines already named in this post.
Interoperability with Apache Ossie
Some tools will not take a dependency on a single semantic layer. Apache Ossie (incubating) is the open specification for that gap, launched as the Open Semantic Interchange on September 23, 2025 and now in the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie (incubating). It defines a vendor-neutral format for metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business concepts so definitions move between tools without being retyped. Strategy participates alongside Snowflake, Dremio, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and others.
Mosaic exports and imports Ossie artifacts. Metric and dimension definitions modeled over Amazon Redshift publish as Ossie YAML consumable by Ossie-aware tools without a Mosaic connector. Definitions authored elsewhere (a metric maintained in dbt, a dimension standardized in a catalog) flow into Mosaic instead of being re-implemented. The artifacts are plain text, so they live in Git and promote through environments like other code.
Apache Ossie is early. Use it where portability matters most and fidelity matters least, for example formulas, dimensions, descriptions, and ownership metadata, while keeping governance policy, execution strategy, and security configuration native to Mosaic.
Deployment: Strategy Cloud
Mosaic runs as a managed service on Strategy Cloud. Strategy operates the application. Connections to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora go over the network from Strategy Cloud egress. You allow-list the Strategy Cloud CIDRs on the source security groups.
Observability
Two observability planes cover the path from question to answer.
Sentinel and Platform Analytics cover the query side. Sentinel captures near real-time query duration, slow queries, and usage by user, tool, and model.
AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, covers the agent side: planning steps, tool calls, latency per turn. Sentinel and Platform Analytics show what happened once the request reached Mosaic. AgentCore Observability shows what the agent was doing before it got there.
Conclusion
Reliable agentic analytics combines strong reasoning, trusted business context, and secure execution. Amazon Bedrock provides the model, Strategy Mosaic provides the governed semantic layer over live data, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent and terminates authentication. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not to Amazon Redshift or Aurora directly. Schemas evolve, the semantic model absorbs the change, and the same definitions serve Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, the Strands agent, and Amazon Quick. Through Apache Ossie, they also reach tools that do not connect to Mosaic.
Where to start
- Pick one metric currently argued about (NRR, contribution margin, active customer are common candidates). One metric with more than one definition in circulation.
- Write three to five business questions about it. These become your acceptance tests.
- Model your primary source in Mosaic and get the metric returning a defensible number.
- Link additional sources incrementally, one at a time, on the attributes that already exist in the model.
- Author descriptions on every metric and attribute the agent will see. This is where accuracy moves most.
- Connect the Strands agent over Mosaic MCP and run your acceptance questions.
- Observe real query patterns for a couple of weeks, then move what’s hot to in-memory.
- Export stable definitions to Apache Ossie and put them under version control.

articles.title: Inside NVIDIA Sentry: Secure AI Agents at Runtime | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
An AI agent can complete its assignment and still cross a security boundary. Recent incidents show that agents can circumvent security controls while using tools, credentials, and services to pursue their assigned goals. Monitoring and enforcement need to operate outside the agent’s reach so that it can’t alter or disable them.
NVIDIA Sentry is a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture announced at GTC Berlin, it’s built on NVIDIA DOCA, runs on NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs, and provides host-isolated runtime protection for AI agents. NVIDIA Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and within its defined operational boundaries.
Trusted even when host resources can’t be trusted, it controls the agent’s only path to the model, providing tamper-evident traceability of agent activity while enforcing granular security controls on agent access in silicon. In addition to inspecting agent communications, NVIDIA Sentry uses out-of-band observability to establish real-time situational awareness, continuously evaluating agents’ runtime security and behavior to validate their security and integrity.
This post explains how NVIDIA Sentry evaluates agent requests, detects threats, and enforces security policies independently of host software.
An independent security layer for agent runtime protection
An earlier agentic AI security post described how NVIDIA BlueField runs security services in a hardware trust domain independent from the host.
NVIDIA Sentry builds on that foundation to continuously monitor AI agent behavior and enforce access policies independently of host software, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain outside the agent’s reach to keep agents operating within their designed intent.
Software runtime boundaries remain essential. NVIDIA OpenShell is a secure runtime for autonomous agents that governs what an agent can do. OpenShell separates policy enforcement from the agent workload, so a compromised agent can’t change its own restrictions. NVIDIA Sentry adds an independent hardware safeguard out of band, running on BlueField-4, beyond the agent’s reach and knowledge.
In the OpenShell reference architecture, agents execute on NVIDIA Vera CPUs, while BlueField-4 sits on the node’s only path to the model. NVIDIA Sentry inspects agent-to-model communications and enforces access policies without relying on the agent to report its own behavior. Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment, such as a container or microVM, to help detect external threats and agent misbehavior.
Governing agent communications
DOCA Tower is NVIDIA Sentry’s AI security gateway. Built on Envoy, the open source edge and service proxy, it operates as a transparent proxy for agent traffic, placing a bidirectional inspection layer between an agent and the external environment.
Agent network traffic reaches BlueField-4 through a direct network I/O path that bypasses host OS/hypervisor packet processing. All of the agent’s network communications are governed by NVIDIA Sentry as BlueField-4 sits on the only path to the model and to the outside world.
An agent’s network access boundary is controlled using DOCA Flow and DOCA Tower, which work in concert to restrict agent access to approved resources. DOCA Flow is used to implement a layer-4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon on BlueField-4. The firewall blocks connections to unauthorized destinations and forwards permitted traffic to DOCA Tower for layer-7 (application layer) inspection, authorization, and additional security checks.
DOCA Tower acts as a transparent proxy, performing Transport Layer Security (TLS) termination using built-in, in-silicon TLS acceleration. For connections configured for inspection, it decrypts the agent traffic permitted by the layer-4 firewall to inspect and control agent communications.
NVIDIA Sentry uses the Open Policy Agent (OPA), an open source policy engine, to evaluate access requests against defined policies. OPA uses Rego, a declarative domain-specific language designed to evaluate complex hierarchical data structures. OPA runs locally in memory and can evaluate requests in under a millisecond, depending on policy complexity and configuration.
DOCA Tower is compatible with OpenShell policies, using OPA to extend network access policies and runtime controls into BlueField-4 and to the infrastructure.
Enforcing agent access policies with runtime context
An agent’s network communications provide only part of the information needed to assess its security and integrity. Visibility into the agent’s execution environment adds context for evaluating access requests that go beyond a traditional resource access policy.
DOCA Argus provides real-time visibility into an agent’s execution environment and operational state, giving NVIDIA Sentry additional context about agent access requests.
It uses live memory introspection to analyze selected regions of volatile host memory and obtain independent evidence of the system’s operational state.
DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing host memory on BlueField-4 without host-resident agents. This agentless design provides independent runtime visibility while preserving host compute resources. By operating outside the host in its own isolated trust domain, DOCA Argus remains beyond the reach of host software even if the host is compromised.
DOCA Argus maps the execution environment in real time—for example, containers to their respective pods and sandboxes to microVMs—and identifies the running processes and their properties within each environment. It also maps relationships between processes and threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, memory, and other system resources. DOCA Argus tracks containers, processes, and loaded libraries using their associated hashes.
This runtime context enables NVIDIA Sentry to connect agent access requests to the processes and execution environments behind them, enforcing policies that consider both the requested action and the security and integrity of the agent making it.
Using runtime context to evaluate agent access
NVIDIA Sentry correlates network connection information from DOCA Tower with runtime context from DOCA Argus to evaluate access requests. NVIDIA Sentry uses this context to enforce policies based on additional attributes and assertions provided by DOCA Argus. It also enriches tamper-evident records of agent activity with runtime context, reducing the need for downstream correlation.
Figure 1 shows how these checks work. DOCA Tower uses its policy engine to correlate a network connection with the agent’s process that initiated it, its properties, and the container it belongs to. A network access policy can, for example, require that the container’s hash match a list of approved container hashes. It can also require that the initiating process, identified by its hash, appear in the container software bill of materials (SBOM), have permission to initiate network connections, and use an approved execution path and command-line arguments. DOCA Tower then checks whether policy permits the requested access—for example, access to an API and permission to perform the requested action.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Argus real-time observations and alerts to continuously evaluate agent security. Potential warning signs include executing unapproved tools; using ptrace to attack another process or spawn a process that attacks the agent; excessive outbound traffic suggesting data leakage; unauthorized file access or changes; CPU spikes; excessive writes to temporary folders; and large-scale file deletion. When NVIDIA Sentry detects any deviation, it can request millisecond-scale in-silicon containment.
Extending controls to agent interactions
Agent security policies need to govern both what leaves the sandbox and what comes back. Requests can expose sensitive information or initiate unauthorized operations. Responses can introduce malicious instructions or other content that redirects an agent from its assigned goals.
NVIDIA Sentry uses DOCA Tower’s extensible inspection capabilities to apply controls to requests and responses. These controls can:
- Apply IP-, URL-, and protocol-level restrictions to agent communications.
- Capture tamper-evident records of agent requests, responses, and data flows for behavioral analysis and investigation.
- Govern agent-to-agent (A2A) and Model Context Protocol (MCP) traffic.
- Detect and redact personally identifiable information and secrets, including API keys, tokens, and passwords.
- Identify and block content prohibited by policy.
NVIDIA Sentry evaluates inspected requests and responses throughout an agent’s session, applying policy as the agent accesses models, tools, APIs, and services.
Evaluating agent behavior using specialized models
NVIDIA Sentry integrates with specialized AI models to analyze agent communications and classify agent behavior using tool calls and available reasoning traces. These models run locally or remotely on dedicated GPU-accelerated systems. The classifiers assess whether an agent’s behavior remains consistent with an agent’s designed intent or indicates behavioral drift.
The models can classify agent communications inline or out of band. Inline classification can trigger blocking before potentially harmful content reaches its destination. Out-of-band classification can trigger a response action after detecting agent misbehavior.
Tamper-evident activity records and detection results provide forensic evidence for further incident investigations.
Agent communications require continuous classification to detect misbehavior. DOCA Argus complements this classification with ongoing analysis of the agent’s operational environment to evaluate runtime security and behavior.
NVIDIA Sentry can contain and quarantine agents within milliseconds using BlueField-4 in-silicon enforcement capabilities without the cooperation of the agent or the host software.
These independent controls matter when software boundaries fail. Even if an agent escapes its sandbox, NVIDIA Sentry retains its monitoring and enforcement capabilities as it operates from BlueField-4’s isolated trust domain.
Enterprise security platforms can also use NVIDIA Sentry telemetry to correlate detections and request response actions. The protected record preserves the observed activity and policy context that led to enforcement for subsequent review.
Using agent identity in access decisions
Security controls must connect an agent’s identity with its permissions and requested action. NVIDIA Sentry uses this identity context in application-layer policy evaluation. DOCA Tower integrates with SPIFFE/SPIRE to support verifiable workload identity and supports integration with partner identity systems.
Identity establishes who is making a request. Authorization policies determine which resources an identity may access and which operations are permitted. Runtime evidence adds context about the execution environment associated with the request.
This approach connects identity and runtime security. If an agent’s behavior or integrity changes, NVIDIA Sentry can use that context when evaluating subsequent access requests, applying the organization’s defined policies.
Preserving a trusted record of agent activity
Security teams need evidence for incident investigations, even when an agent has escaped its sandbox or altered host-based logs.
NVIDIA Sentry produces attested telemetry and tamper-evident records using BlueField-4’s independent trust domain. DOCA Tower records inspected communications and policy decisions outside the reach of the agent and host software, while DOCA Argus contributes independently observed runtime signals.
An agent that changes a log inside its own environment cannot make the same change to the protected record maintained on BlueField-4.
Attestation provides verifiable evidence of telemetry’s source and integrity. Security teams can use these records to reconstruct observed interactions, review enforcement decisions, and support audits.
NVIDIA Sentry can supply this telemetry to enterprise security platforms, such as XDR and SIEM platforms and security data lakes, connecting agent activity with broader threat intelligence, detection logic, and incident-response workflows.
Extending NVIDIA Sentry with enterprise security capabilities
NVIDIA Sentry enables developers and cybersecurity providers to extend monitoring, governance, and enforcement through DOCA libraries and microservices.
DOCA Tower uses Envoy’s extensibility, enabling partners to adapt existing plugins or develop new ones to run on BlueField. This provides a familiar foundation for integrating access controls, content inspection, telemetry, and specialized detection logic into the application-layer path.
NVIDIA plans to publish core plugins to accelerate development, including a plugin that exposes agent communications for further analysis of available reasoning traces.
Partners can combine these capabilities with their identity services, AI classifiers, threat intelligence, and security operations platforms. NVIDIA Sentry contributes independent runtime visibility and infrastructure enforcement, while connected platforms add enterprise context and coordinate investigation and response.
Building layered protection for AI agents
Scaling agentic AI requires continuous visibility into and control over what agents can access and do throughout execution. NVIDIA Sentry brings that control into an independent infrastructure domain, combining application-layer inspection through DOCA Tower with runtime evidence and visibility from DOCA Argus and in-silicon enforcement on BlueField-4.
Alongside NVIDIA OpenShell, NVIDIA Sentry extends protection from software execution boundaries to a hardware-isolated safeguard. It enables security teams to evaluate agent identity, authority, interactions, and runtime integrity together—and act when behavior crosses defined boundaries.
Developers and cybersecurity teams can begin exploring these foundations with NVIDIA DOCA. Available libraries and microservices, including DOCA Argus, DOCA Flow, and OVS-DOCA, provide a starting point for experimenting with out-of-band observability and infrastructure enforcement ahead of NVIDIA Sentry’s planned availability early next year.

articles.title: CJIS v6.1 Compliance: 5 Practical Priorities for Agencies
articles.text:
For agencies responsible for protecting Criminal Justice Information (CJI), meeting CJIS requirements means more than putting security controls in place. Those controls need to work across the systems staff use every day, and agencies need to be able to prove they're effective.
But, between legacy systems, stretched IT teams, and constantly changing access needs, even agencies with strong security practices can struggle to apply controls consistently and keep the evidence auditors expect.
So, where should you focus your efforts? In this article, we'll walk through five key areas agencies should be paying attention to under CJIS v6.1, with practical advice to make compliance easier to manage.
Multi-Factor Authentication
CJIS v6.1 requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged accounts under controls IA-2(1) and IA-2(2), covering local, network, and remote access. The challenge is making sure no accounts slip through the cracks.
Start by reviewing MFA coverage across your environment, paying particular attention to legacy applications and administrative accounts. When implementing MFA, consider phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys.
You'll also need reliable processes for enrolling, replacing, and revoking authenticators.
Solutions like Specops Secure Access help agencies comply by extending MFA protection to Windows logons, RDP, RADIUS, and offline access, with flexible options including authenticator apps and YubiKeys. Its event API integrations also help provide evidence for compliance audits.
Remember, MFA isn't a one-time fix. Revisit your configurations as systems and access needs change.
Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy
Verizon’s Data Breach Investigation Report found stolen credentials are involved in 44.7% of breaches. 
Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
Account Management and Privileges
Access permissions can quickly become outdated as employees change roles or leave, a risk which CJIS v6.1 aims to reduce by enforcing effective account management and least privilege.
Start by keeping an accurate inventory of user, administrative, service, and temporary accounts. Limit permissions to what is needed for each role, separate administrative privileges from everyday activities, and automate account provisioning and removal where possible.
Review accounts and privileges at least annually. Temporary and emergency accounts must be removed within 72 hours, while accounts inactive for 90 days must be disabled within one week. The key is making access reviews an ongoing process, not just an annual exercise.
Passwords
IA-5 sets an eight-character password minimum and is a Priority 1 control, so has been sanctionable since October 2024. Aligning with NIST recommendations, agencies should encourage longer, unique passphrases and use approved password managers to reduce reuse.
Agencies should also:
- Screen for compromised passwords, updating password blocklists at least quarterly and whenever compromise is suspected.
- Block weak or reused passwords during creation or reset.
- Limit failed login attempts to no more than five per account.
This is where Specops Password Policy can help. It simplifies password policy management across Active Directory, continuously checking against over 6 billion compromised passwords and scanning daily for newly exposed credentials.
Customizable grace periods help reduce unnecessary lockouts when a compromised password is found, while compliance templates and reporting make it easier to track your progress.
Finally, check annual password change requirements with your CJIS Systems Agency, as IA-5 still specifies a yearly change or refresh despite guidance discouraging unnecessary resets.
Logging
Audit logs help agencies detect suspicious activity and investigate security incidents. However, collecting logs isn't enough. Agencies also need to capture the right events, review records regularly, and protect them against tampering.
Start by checking logging coverage across systems handling CJI. Make sure records capture who did what and when, as well as the outcome. Centralizing logs in a SIEM can make suspicious activity easier to spot.
Audit Readiness
Agencies are audited at least once every three years, but you’re expected to maintain compliance between audits. Rather than scrambling to pull evidence together at the last minute, it’s better to treat CJIS compliance as an ongoing responsibility.
Some best practices include:
- Maintaining an inventory of applicable security controls and identifying who is responsible for implementing, reviewing, and documenting each one.
- Keeping evidence organized, including records of MFA configurations, access reviews, audit logs, security policies, training, and assessment results. That makes it easier to demonstrate compliance.
- Documenting identified weaknesses and setting deadlines for resolving them. In line with CA-5, you should update remediation plans at least every six months or when new information becomes available.
- Conducting internal assessments to identify issues before a formal assessment.
- Building security monitoring and compliance reviews into everyday IT operations, so changes or new risks don't go unnoticed.
By making audit preparation part of routine security management, agencies can identify gaps earlier, reduce the work involved in formal assessments, and maintain a stronger compliance posture between audits.
Strengthen Your CJIS Compliance Posture
CJIS compliance isn't a one-and-done exercise. As systems and security risks change, agencies need to make sure their controls keep pace. By regularly reviewing controls and keeping evidence organized, you can make compliance easier to manage while strengthening your agency's security.
Passwords are a good place to start when assessing your CJIS compliance. But how do you know where the gaps are?

articles.title: Le gouvernement américain banni DeepSeek : l'IA chinoise est accusée de surveillance de masse
articles.text:
Ce lundi 19 octobre, une mesure du secrétaire à la Sécurité intérieure américaine Markwayne Mullin, a été publiée. Elle interdit aux agences civiles du pays d’acheter et d’utiliser les produits de DeepSeek. Une mesure qui vise directement l’État chinois, accusé de plusieurs méfaits via cette intelligence artificielle.
Les États-Unis ne veulent plus de DeepSeek chez eux
C’est le Département de la Sécurité intérieure (DHS) qui a pris cette mesure au titre du Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act de 2018. Une loi qui permet d’exclure les fournisseurs jugés risqués de la chaîne d’approvisionnement fédérale, ce qui concerne aussi les applications et systèmes informatiques. L’ordre a donc été signé par le secrétaire de ce département, Markwayne Mullin : il était initialement daté du 24 juillet, avant sa publication publique ce 19 octobre au Federal Register, rapporte la BBC. Une étape de plus après que l’Agence d’information de la défense américaine (DISA) avait bloqué DeepSeek sur les réseaux du Pentagone en janvier 2025, comme le précise CyberScoop. En mai 2025, c’est Microsoft qui avait interdit à ses employés d’utiliser cette IA.
Cette mesure impose deux obligations aux agences civiles : supprimer tous les usages de DeepSeek en vigueur et renoncer à l’installer à nouveau. Elle couvre directement la version de DeepSeek distribuée par Hangzhou DeepSeek Artrificial Intelligence Co., l’entreprise chinoise qui l’édite, mais pas que. Cela concerne également toutes les applications tierces qui se basent sur DeepSeek. Y compris celles qui utilisent la version open source du chatbot, que n’importe qui peut télécharger, modifier et utiliser. Seules les agences relevant du département de la Défense peuvent continuer à utiliser cette IA : elles relèvent d’un cadre différent aux yeux du gouvernement.
Pourquoi Washington vise cette IA chinoise
Le DHS justifie cette exclusion par plusieurs risques de cybersécurité et de souveraineté des données. Il explique que les serveurs de DeepSeek étant en Chine, le gouvernement pourrait collecter massivement des données gouvernementales américaines. c’est le cœur de l’argumentaire du DHS : le gouvernement chinois pourrait obliger DeepSeek à lui laisser accès à ses serveurs et à surveiller des utilisateurs. De quoi produire des renseignements exploitables sur des citoyens américains comme sur des programmes gouvernementaux.
Selon l’agence, les modèles de DeepSeek présentent « plusieurs vecteurs de menace » : collecte possible de données personnelles, suivi des utilisateurs, vulnérabilités de sécurité et même présence potentielle de malwares. Autre argument en faveur du blocage : avec son modèle R1, le chatbot avait bousculé Washington et la Silicon Valley, puisque ce modèle avait des performances similaires aux meilleurs modèles américains (GPT, Gemini, etc.) tout en revendiquant un coût de développement bien plus faible. Par la suite, DeepSeek avait été accusé de s’être servi de LLM américains pour s’entraîner, notamment par la Maison Blanche. Un argument hypothétique, puisqu’il n’a pas été revendiqué par le Département de la Sécurité intérieure.
Ce n’est pas la première fois qu’un service numérique chinois est banni par le gouvernement américain en interne. Une loi adoptée en 2022 et entrée en vigueur en 2023 avait banni TikTok des téléphones fédéraux. Une interdiction qui a été levée cette année : le ministère de la Justice a estimé que la version américaine de TikTok ne relevait plus de la loi, puisqu’elle fonctionne indépendamment de ByteDance, son éditeur chinois.
