articles.title: Most AI incident tools still leave a key decision to humans
articles.text:
Most AI incident tools still leave a key decision to humans
An AI SRE agent can help troubleshoot an incident. But can you trust it to decide on its own when something needs attention?
Most teams treat agent autonomy as a yes or no question. For incident response, it is a progression with three phases, and many agents in production sit earlier on it than the teams running them realize. Most AI SRE tools still stop short of the final phase.
On Thursday, October 22, The New Stack hosts a live webinar with Raaz Dwivedi, co-founder and CTO of Traversal and an assistant professor at Cornell Tech. His team applies causal AI and agentic reasoning to production incidents. He will walk through where the industry sits on that progression and what it takes to move up.
You have successfully registered for the webinar.
The three phases of agent autonomy
Invoked: copilots, chat interfaces, and CLIs that wait for an on-call engineer to open them and ask a question mid-incident.
Background: scheduled jobs, alert rules, and triggers that fire on conditions someone predicted in advance.
Proactive: agents that decide for themselves when an incident needs attention, without waiting to be invoked or scheduled.
The first two phases share a limit. Each depends on a person noticing that something is wrong, or on someone predicting the right condition ahead of time. Proactive agents remove that dependency.
What it takes to trust an AI SRE agent
Moving to the third phase raises a trust question. An agent that waits to be asked can be wrong without much consequence, because an engineer reviews the answer. An agent that decides when to engage also has to judge when to stay quiet. Dwivedi will cover what separates an agent that responds from one that acts on its own, why many AI SRE tools stall in the first two phases, and what has to be true before a team lets an agent make that call.
What changes once agents act on their own
Dwivedi will also discuss where the shift is already happening, drawing on Traversal Workers, agents that already operate at the proactive end of the progression. He will explore what changes for engineering teams once the agent in their stack stops waiting to be asked.
The session closes with live Q&A, so you can ask him your questions directly.
Join us on Thursday, October 22, 2026 at 1 p.m. Eastern / 10 a.m. Pacific, to learn where your team stands in the progression and what it would take to move up. Register today.

articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer.
AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language, an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions.
The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git.
- How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates.
- How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time.
- How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository.
The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release. Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation.
The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift
The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table.
Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path (AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables.
The schema in Amazon Redshift:
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
| purchase | id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
| category | id (PK), dept_name, parent | 
| vendor | id (PK), vendor_name, industry | 
Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities.
AtScale terms used in this post
AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. The AtScale documentation and the SML specification use a specific set of primitives that come up throughout this post. A short reference is useful before we get to the walkthrough.
- Semantic Modeling Language (SML) – An open, YAML-based specification for describing semantic models. Every SML object (model, dataset, dimension, hierarchy, metric, calculation, perspective, row security) is a YAML file. The specification lives at github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML.
- Model – The top-level artifact. A model references datasets, dimensions, facts, and metrics, and exposes them through the AtScale query engine.
- Dimension and hierarchy – A dimension groups related attributes (customer, product, date). A hierarchy inside a dimension organizes those attributes into levels (product → category → department, or year → quarter → month → day).
- Fact and measure – A fact is a dataset that holds measurable events joined to dimensions on key columns. A measure is a quantity aggregated from a fact column, for example SUM(price * quantity) for revenue.
- Calculation – A derived measure expressed as a formula against other measures.
- Perspective – A publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. Perspectives are how AtScale controls which dimensions and measures a caller can see.
- Row security – A model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes.
- Autonomous aggregate management – AtScale watches query patterns across consumers and materializes summary tables in the warehouse when a pattern is expensive enough to justify one. Subsequent queries that match the pattern route to the aggregate transparently.
- Design Center – The AtScale authoring surface. A modeler edits SML through a visual canvas or a text editor. Either way the artifact on disk is SML YAML in Git.
- AtScale MCP server – The in-product MCP endpoint at <atscale-host>/mcp that exposes the semantic model to any MCP client.
Where more detail is useful, the AtScale documentation and the SML specification are the authoritative references.
Reference architecture
The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path, following the same shape as the Stardog and Denodo posts.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to AgentCore runtime (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), which hosts the agent process. The agent invokes Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, it invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server. AgentCore Gateway serves as the outbound proxy: the AtScale MCP server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls route through Gateway and AgentCore Identity injects the credential at that hop. AtScale’s MCP endpoint accepts either a bearer token (for development and single-identity scenarios) or an OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak instance (the production path). The AtScale engine validates the token, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query against the deployed C360 model.
The query request travels down through the AtScale engine, and the results travel back up. There’s no ETL job that pre-materializes cross-database joins. The analytical copy in Amazon Redshift is the source of truth for the semantic model, kept fresh from Aurora by the upstream replication path.
The architecture is deliberately opinionated on identity. Gateway and Identity hold the tokens at the runtime edges. The agent doesn’t see them and only orchestrates the conversation and the tool calls.
Build the semantic layer
AtScale’s semantic model is a collection of SML objects (datasets, dimensions, facts, measures, calculations, perspectives, row security) versioned in Git. A working model has a shape a data engineer will recognize from a star schema, but every object is expressed as YAML rather than data definition language (DDL), and every object is a separate file. Building the C360 model happens in three passes: datasets over the Amazon Redshift tables, dimensions and hierarchies with the joins between them, and measures and calculations that express the business logic.
Datasets. Each Amazon Redshift table becomes an SML dataset. A dataset declares the physical connection, the schema, the table, and the columns AtScale will surface. Datasets can be authored visually in Design Center or edited directly as YAML. Either surface writes the same SML file to Git.
Dimensions and hierarchies. The C360 model has seven dimensions. dim_customer holds customer profile attributes and joins to dim_address through the location key and to dim_rewards through cid. dim_product holds product attributes and organizes them into a hierarchy through dim_category. dim_date supports date-based analysis. dim_vendor groups products by supplier. dim_rewards holds one row per enrolled customer with account_id and create_date, and snowflakes off dim_customer so that never-enrolled customers surface as null in the enrollment attributes.
AtScale’s hierarchy primitive is the concise expression of the product-to-category relationship. A query against the model can navigate product → category → parent category without a recursive SQL common table expression, and the large language model (LLM) sees a single dimensional path rather than a join graph.
A representative SML fragment for the product hierarchy:
Facts and measures. The fact table for C360 is fact_purchase, mapped to the Amazon Redshift purchase table. It joins to dim_customer on cid, to dim_product on pid, and to dim_date on purchase_date. Measures come off the fact: total_revenue as SUM(price * quantity), order_count as COUNT(id), and units_sold as SUM(quantity).
Calculated measures. Business logic that lives in the model rather than in the query. customer_lifetime_value is total_revenue evaluated at customer grain, the same formula applied to a coarser slice of the fact. Segments like big_spender and spend_tier are calculated measures with conditional expressions:
The expression is evaluated at query time. A column would hold one answer at one grain. The expression recomputes for whatever slice the query asks about, by customer, by customer and year, or by region. When the definition changes (the threshold moves from $10,000 to $15,000), the update happens in one YAML file, gets reviewed as a pull request, and deploys through the AtScale CI hook. Each consumer picks up the new definition on the next query, whether that is the agent, Excel over XMLA, or Tableau over Multidimensional Expressions (MDX).
The artifact on the right of Figure 3 is not a description of the model. It is the model. Design Center’s visual canvas and the YAML editor are two views of the same file, and the Git diff is the authoritative record of every change. The files conform to the open-source SML specification, so the repository can be read without the engine.
After it’s deployed, the model is simultaneously reachable over SQL (for JDBC-based BI tools and notebooks), XMLA (for Excel and Power BI), and MCP (for the agent). The total_revenue calculation returns the same number to Claude Sonnet 4.6 as it does to an Excel PivotTable pointed at the same XMLA endpoint. We confirm this match in Verification.
How AtScale plans and pushes down queries
When the agent asks a question against the semantic model, AtScale’s AI Computation Engine (ACE) does the planning. The steps a query goes through are the same for a dimensional SQL request from the MCP run_query tool and for an XMLA request from Excel. Only the parser at the front differs.
Take the auto-enrollment question: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent, prompted with the model context returned by describe_model, composes a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model. ACE parses that query into a logical plan, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying fact_purchase, dim_customer, dim_address, and dim_rewards datasets, applies any row security the caller is subject to, and then plans the physical query against Amazon Redshift.
Two things happen at the physical-planning stage that separate AtScale from a hand-written pipeline. First, the join is pushed to Amazon Redshift as a native SQL join rather than materialized in the semantic layer. The Amazon Redshift optimizer sees a single SQL statement with a filter and an aggregate, and executes it accordingly. Second, AtScale’s aggregate manager checks its registry for a pre-built aggregate that matches the query pattern. If a summary table exists that groups purchases by customer at the right grain, AtScale rewrites the query to hit the aggregate instead of scanning fact_purchase. The query returns in a fraction of the time it would take against the raw fact table, without the agent or the modeler doing any manual work to route it.
The aggregate manager is what makes an agent-driven workload economically feasible. LLM-driven analysis fires more queries than a human analyst would, and open-ended prompts like Tell me something interesting about our sales can spawn a dozen. AtScale watches the query pattern, materializes aggregates in the warehouse itself (not a separate cache), and routes matching queries transparently. Aggregate creation is demand-defined against observed traffic across consumers, not only the agent.
The audit record for the query captures both the dimensional SQL the LLM wrote and the warehouse-native SQL AtScale rewrote it into, along with whether an aggregate served the query. That record is available to an operator through the AtScale Queries page in Design Center, and it’s what the following governance section builds on.
A note on multi-source and interoperability
AtScale connects to warehouses over JDBC. The C360 walkthrough targets Amazon Redshift Serverless. The same SML model works over Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and AtScale documents the connection pattern for each. What changes when you swap the connection is the SQL dialect AtScale emits, not the SML in Git.
One architectural property is worth stating explicitly because it differs from the first two posts in this series. A single AtScale query resolves in one warehouse engine. If the C360 model spans two warehouses (dimensions on Snowflake, facts on Amazon Redshift, say), a query that touches both must be reconciled in one of two ways. The first is upstream, by consolidating an analytical copy in one warehouse through a replication path. The second is by the warehouse itself, using engine-level federation such as Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or Apache Iceberg tables that both engines can read. AtScale plans a dimensional query and pushes it to one engine. The cross-engine story lives one layer down.
That choice cuts both ways. It rules out the live cross-engine federation Stardog and Denodo perform at query time, but it lets AtScale’s planner and aggregate manager work against a single-engine execution model, which is what makes the aggregate story load-bearing at scale. Enterprises that already run a warehouse-centric analytical architecture with change data capture (CDC) pipelines from operational systems reuse that architecture. Enterprises whose answers require live federation across engines are better served by the semantic layers in the first two posts.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Customer 360 data is regulated. Some users (HR, fraud) need to see personally identifiable information such as Social Security numbers and card numbers. Most users (marketing, analytics) must not. Row-level filters restrict analysts by geography, and a per-user audit trail must survive from the human’s browser through to the warehouse.
AtScale enforces these requirements at the semantic layer, before any query reaches the warehouse. Enforcement happens identically whether the caller is the Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One row-security object in SML, one perspective, one set of role bindings, applied to each consumer of the model.
Identity propagation from the user to AtScale
The chain follows the same shape as the one in the Denodo post, with the terminal hop landing at the AtScale engine rather than continuing to the warehouse.
- The human authenticates to the application against the enterprise IdP and receives a JWT.
- The application forwards the JWT as a bearer token to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway, which validates it (issuer, audience, signature) and routes the request to AgentCore runtime.
- When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code.
- The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager.
RBAC, row security, and perspectives
AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group.
For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles.
- hr_user: sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num.
- marketing_user: sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer.
When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn, the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn. The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt.
Audit fidelity
Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record.
An audit record for a governed query looks like this:
The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran.
Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server
The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at <atscale-host>/mcp. It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model.
The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are:
- list_models: Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts.
- describe_model: Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries.
- search_columns: Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window.
- validate_query: Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for.
- run_query: Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows.
- run_queries: Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel.
- get_version: Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema.
The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp, documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity.
Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop.
Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling
The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset.
AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable.
The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today.
Deploy and run the agent
Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models.
The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment.
Query 1, single dimension
List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name, last_name, and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI'. AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows.
Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit
What are our top 10 products by units sold?
The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase. The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side.
Query 3, cross-domain
Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?
The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, and fact_purchase, and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query.
Governance rerun
We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection (Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN) as two different callers. As hr_user, describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user, describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn. The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched.
Cross-consumer confirmation
We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number.
Extending across data sources
Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are:
- Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables.
- Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object.
- Add or extend a dimension (dim_ticket) and add the join to dim_customer on cid.
- Add any new measures the model needs (open_ticket_count, avg_resolution_time).
- Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook.
Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model, it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note.
Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS
AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS. AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale, and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation.
The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI (atscale-sml-api, atscale-sml-web), PostgreSQL metadata storage (atscale-db), the query cache (atscale-redis), and ingress (atscale-ingress, typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer).
The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials.
Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer.
AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier.
Conclusion
Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.
The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query.
Where to start
Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand.
- Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today.
- Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one.
- Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data.
- Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions.
- Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it.
Further reading
- AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI
- AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com
- AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation)
- AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints
- Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
- Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
- Strands Agents on AWS Prescriptive Guidance
- Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (first post in this series)
- Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series)

articles.title: How NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture Secures and Governs AI Agent Workloads at Scale | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Autonomous agents can work for hours on complex tasks, accessing files, tools, the internet, and spawning other agents to collaborate with. Executing complex tasks over long time horizons leads to compounding risk: the agents may download code, build new tools, request additional privileges, and touch more of the underlying infrastructure.
The agents’ action paths are determined as they work and reason through the steps needed to complete their goals. As they interact with the tools and systems around them, they adapt their reasoning and behavior to achieve their task.
The adaptability of agents is what makes them so powerful, but they are goal-oriented and may not prioritize safety in pursuit of their objectives. In order for agents to work both autonomously and safely, we need to build environments that provide control and visibility in what the agent is doing.
An agent cannot govern itself. Security and governance belong in the infrastructure the agent operates in.
OpenShell provides deterministic governance outside of the agent’s reach
NVIDIA OpenShell is an open-source runtime to build the security and governance needed for agentic systems into the computing infrastructure. OpenShell defines and enforces which systems and data an agent can access, from files and internet services to systems that interact with physical devices.
It is the foundation of the NVIDIA OpenShell Reference Architecture for building safe AI agents. OpenShell treats agent workloads as untrusted throughout execution. An agent is given access to what it needs, when it needs it.
OpenShell has four key components:
- Gateway: The control plane that manages sandbox lifecycles and policies
- Supervisor: Checks outbound requests against policy and mediates access to credentials. This runs completely separate to the sandbox
- Sandbox: Isolates the agent workload and restricts filesystem and process access
- Policy prover: Adds formal verification, checking whether a policy’s permissions stay within an organization-defined ceiling.
As the agents evolve, these components provide the infrastructure controls that allow them to work safely.
Extending and integrating OpenShell
Extensibility is a core principle of OpenShell’s design. Supervisor middleware lets you inspect, block, or change the content that an agent sends and receives over the network as an additional enforcement layer. Gateway interceptors let operators add deployment-specific governance to OpenShell control-plane operations without modifying the gateway.
Organizations also need to establish who an agent acts for, what authority it holds, and whether an action fits the task. Identity, authorization, data protection, and auditing each address part of that problem. OpenShell provides enforcement points where those systems can be integrated.
In the reference architecture, OpenShell runs on NVIDIA Vera CPUs.
NVIDIA Vera, the compute layer beneath the controls
OpenShell defines what agents can do. Vera determines how fast they can do it. Agents operate through loops of dependent steps where each step must complete before the next begins: reasoning, calling tools, executing code, querying data.
AI factories run thousands of these loops concurrently, placing new demands on CPU architecture across five dimensions:
- They need massive core counts to run many concurrent workflows, and fast individual cores to shorten each sequential step.
- They need high-bandwidth fabric and memory to keep those cores fed with the live data agents depend on.
- They need massive I/O to move data at speed between CPUs, GPUs, storage, and network.
- They need hardware-enforced security, because agents increasingly operate on sensitive enterprise data and must be isolated from each other and the host.
- They need to deliver all of this within the power envelope of a modern data center (more agent work per watt, not just more raw performance).
NVIDIA calls this combination the max single-threaded CPU at scale, and NVIDIA Vera is built for it: massive Olympus cores, a second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric, LPDDR5X memory, Gen 6 I/O, confidential computing, and an energy-efficient design purpose-built for power-limited data centers.
Three architectural properties make Vera fast for agent workloads
- First, 88 NVIDIA-designed Olympus cores with a 10-wide front end, neural branch predictor, and deep out-of-order execution deliver up to 2x performance on critical agentic workloads versus x86, shortening each tool call, code execution, and evaluation.
- Second, Vera’s second-generation Scalable Coherency Fabric provides up to 3x core-to-core bandwidth and up to 50% lower core-to-core latency than x86 alternatives, keeping data moving predictably under load. Vera also integrates 96 lanes of PCIe Gen 6, delivering the I/O bandwidth to connect GPUs, high-speed storage, and network at the throughput agentic infrastructure demands.
- Third, up to 1.2 TB/s of LPDDR5X memory bandwidth, with up to 40% lower loaded memory latency than chiplet-based designs, keeps agents supplied with the live context they need without stalling on memory access. LPDDR5X also makes Vera dramatically more efficient: Vera delivers 2x more performance per watt than x86 CPUs, while the LPDDR5X memory subsystem itself draws an order of magnitude less power than competing DDR5-based memory configurations, enabling more agent work within the same power envelope.
Agent workloads depend on sandboxes: isolated execution environments where agents run code, invoke tools, and complete tasks without interfering with each other or the host system. The denser and faster those sandboxes spin up, the more agent work a given infrastructure footprint can sustain.
CoreWeave, the AI cloud platform purpose-built for training and serving models at scale, found sandbox startup to be more than 3x faster on Vera than on x86, with a single rack supporting more than 11,000 concurrent agent environments.
Running Terminal Bench, which measures CPU performance across real agentic loop tasks, CoreWeave found Vera delivered 1.8x faster performance versus x86, across agentic tasks ranging from scripting to database recovery. That density and performance under load is what agent infrastructure actually requires.
NVIDIA BlueField and NVIDIA Sentry for hardware-enforced protection
OpenShell places authority outside the agent. For deployments that require additional protection, that separation can also extend into purpose-built silicon.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs provide a hardware-isolated trust domain outside the agent’s reach. In the OpenShell reference architecture, BlueField-4 sits in the I/O path between agents running on Vera and the models they access. NVIDIA Sentry, a security software framework built on NVIDIA DOCA, runs in this independent domain to continuously monitor agent behavior and enforce runtime policy.
NVIDIA Sentry observes requests and responses, networking and file activities, verifies identity and delegated authority, and analyzes selected host memory to detect deviations from authorized behavior without relying on agent self-reporting.
When it detects a threat or policy violation, BlueField-4 enforces policy in silicon, allowing NVIDIA Sentry to quarantine the agent within milliseconds. Together, they add an optional hardware safeguard alongside OpenShell’s software boundaries. Learn more about NVIDIA Sentry in this technical deep-dive.
Bringing secure agent runtimes to scale
Running agents in production requires infrastructure that can keep thousands of workflows moving while governing every action they take. Vera provides the compute, memory bandwidth, and I/O to sustain those workflows. OpenShell supplies the runtime boundaries that determine which actions execute and which resources agents can reach.
Together, Vera and OpenShell make secure agent execution a foundation for scale. Agents can run longer, use tools, and work with enterprise data within policies enforced outside their control. For deployments that require additional protection, NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 adds independent monitoring and in-silicon enforcement.
The NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, where LLMs run, together with OpenShell and NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4, are the pillars of the OpenShell reference architecture. They form the complete stack for safe AI agents: a complete, hardware-rooted foundation that gives organizations the performance to make agents productive and the controls to keep their work within authorized boundaries.
Get started
To implement secure agent governance in your organization, begin with NVIDIA OpenShell, follow the documentation, and explore how NVIDIA Vera CPUs accelerate agent workloads.

articles.title: Transport for biological material helps Cellbox raise a €5 million Series A | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cellbox Solutions, a German warm-chain logistics technology company, has completed the final closing of its Series A financing, bringing the total to €5 million – the company will develop its business model and expand its offering to include integrated logistics solutions for sensitive biological materials.
Following the first closing of approximately €3.5 million in March 2026 (as covered by EU-Startups), Cellbox Solutions has attracted additional investors. Among them are members of the Baltic Business Angels Invest GmbH. Existing investors NRW.BANK and Fraunhofer Venture also participated in the financing.
“Over the past years, we have built a strong foundation for the controlled transport of living biological materials,” says Prof. Dr. Kathrin Adlkofer, founder and CEO of Cellbox Solutions. “With the successful completion of our Series A round, we are now expanding our established warm-chain technology platform into a broader offering for physiological logistics. This will allow us to support customers more comprehensively across their logistics workflows and expand our presence in key international markets.”
This financing follows several other 2026 funding announcements in Europe’s cell-therapy and life sciences technology sectors.
In the Netherlands, Scinus Group secured €3 million to commercialise its cell-expansion platform, while Italy’s Cellply raised €7.15 million for cell-therapy quality-control technologies and the UK’s Tozaro attracted €6.9 million to improve cell and gene therapy manufacturing.
In Germany, Leipzig-based Primogene secured €4.1 million for enzymatic biomanufacturing, with related investments also recorded by Dutch startup QT Sense (€4 million) and Switzerland’s ALP Bio (€1.9 million).
Together with Cellbox Solutions’ €5 million Series A, these 2026 financings amount to approximately €32 million across related but distinct life sciences technologies, including grant funding.
“Completion of the Series A gives us additional resources to scale the commercial model behind our technology. By expanding rental and recurring service offerings and combining them with transportation, monitoring, and complementary logistics services, we can build longer-term customer relationships and a more scalable service model across markets. Our focus is now on translating the strength of the Cellbox platform into sustainable commercial growth,” adds Dr. Bernd Muehlenweg, CBO and CFO of Cellbox Solutions.
Founded in 2017, Cellbox Solutions is a Cologne-based warm-chain logistics technology company providing solutions for the global healthcare and life sciences industries to transport sensitive biological materials and therapeutics that cannot be frozen and require controlled physiological conditions.
The company’s portable CO₂ incubator platform, Cellbox, creates a regulated environment for the transport of living cells, organoids, tissues, and other advanced biological materials. Temperature and CO₂ levels are individually adjustable to ensure reproducible incubation conditions throughout shipment. Cellbox systems are deployed globally and support research, clinical, and advanced therapy applications.
Today’s financing marks the next phase in the company’s commercial growth, and will help leverage the established technological, product-related, and regulatory advances Cellbox Solutions has achieved in recent years.
A key focus is building on the company’s specialized transport capabilities to link controlled transport under physiological conditions even more closely with additional logistics and service offerings.
Cellbox Go and Cellbox Shipper make up the core of the company’s technology platform. Both incubators provide controlled temperature and CO₂ conditions during ground and air transport and are already used internationally in research and cell therapy applications.
With over 400 Cellbox systems currently on the market, a growing number of customer relationships and a regulatory foundation that includes Drug Master Files for the CellboxTM product family, the company believes they are well positioned to expand its commercial offering.
This includes combining CellboxTM systems with rental and transport options, as well as recurring services such as monitoring, fleet management, and shipment coordination.
To this end, the company is continuing to expand its activities in Europe, Asia, and North America and is increasingly focusing on strategic partnerships with logistics providers.

articles.title: Tempestades e frio de 12 °C chegam a estados do Sul e do Sudeste
articles.text:
A chuva volta a ganhar força pelo oeste da Região Sul nesta quarta-feira (21) e deve avançar sobre áreas do Sudeste e do Centro-Oeste na quinta-feira (22), segundo o Inmet. A previsão inclui tempestades e queda de temperatura em algumas capitais.
Enquanto a chuva se espalha pelo centro-sul do país, o interior do Nordeste terá sol forte, calor de até 40 °C e baixa umidade do ar. No oeste da Região Norte, as precipitações continuam.
Onde há risco de tempestades
No Sul, a chuva deve atingir áreas cada vez maiores ao longo dos dois dias. Na quinta-feira, os três estados estarão sob aviso amarelo de perigo potencial para tempestades. As precipitações podem ser mais intensas no sul e leste do Paraná, em grande parte de Santa Catarina e no oeste e norte do Rio Grande do Sul.
A instabilidade também aumenta no Sudeste. Na quinta-feira, são esperadas pancadas de chuva com trovoadas em partes de São Paulo, Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro e Espírito Santo. No Centro-Oeste, a chuva ganha força em áreas de Mato Grosso, Goiás e Mato Grosso do Sul.
Para entender onde os avisos merecem mais atenção, o Inmet destaca:
- Sul: aviso amarelo para tempestades nos três estados na quinta-feira.
- Sudeste: aviso amarelo para tempestades em partes dos quatro estados na quinta-feira.
- Mato Grosso: aviso amarelo para tempestades no oeste e norte do estado nesta quarta-feira.
- Nordeste: aviso amarelo para baixa umidade do ar em áreas de sete estados: Maranhão, Piauí, Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba, Pernambuco e Bahia.
Nordeste terá calor de até 40 °C
A mudança no tempo está ligada à alteração na circulação dos ventos sobre a América do Sul. A faixa de nuvens que vinha favorecendo a chuva em partes do oeste e sul do Nordeste deve perder força nesta quarta-feira. Com o avanço de uma massa de ar seco pelo interior, a chuva diminui e o sol predomina em boa parte da região.
O calor será intenso. Teresina (PI) pode chegar a 40 °C na quinta-feira. A previsão é de máxima de 33 °C em São Luís (MA) e de 32 °C em Fortaleza (CE) e Maceió (AL).
Com pouca chuva e predomínio de sol, a umidade do ar pode cair principalmente à tarde. No litoral nordestino, ainda há possibilidade de precipitações isoladas entre o Ceará e a Bahia. Na região de Porto Seguro, no sul baiano, a chuva pode ocorrer com mais frequência.
Temperaturas mais amenas no Sul e Sudeste
A maior presença de nuvens e a chuva devem limitar a elevação das temperaturas em algumas capitais. São Paulo (SP) tem máxima prevista de 24 °C na quinta-feira. Curitiba (PR) e Florianópolis (SC) não devem passar de 21 °C.
No Norte, o calor continua mesmo nas áreas com previsão de chuva. Boa Vista (RR) pode registrar 37 °C na quinta-feira, enquanto Rio Branco (AC) tem mínima prevista de 23 °C.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Visiting Slate’s first showroom as its $25,000 electric truck nears production
articles.text:
As I sat in the cab of the pickup truck and manually rolled down the windows, I closed my eyes and, for the briefest moment, flashed back to opening the windows on a cold, winter day in my dad’s 1975 Ford Ranger to let more cigarette smoke escape. I opened my eyes and looked through the windshield at a wall in the Slate Customer Experience Center studded with bright color chips.
Last week, in a former Tesla store staffed by some former Tesla employees, Slate opened its first showroom. Located in the Fulton Market District just northwest of the Chicago Loop, the Slate Experience Center is a place for would-be buyers to poke around a prototype, check out customization options, buy some Slate merch, and even preorder a new Slate Truck with a $300 deposit.
Designed for the American obsession with pickup trucks, the Slate Truck is a bare-bones electric pickup truck retailing for $24,950. It sports plastic panels, a minimalist interior design sensibility, actual window winders, and a projected range of 205 miles. Ars went for a ride in a Slate Truck over the summer, but we haven’t had a chance to shop for one. So I stopped by the Slate Experience Center so I could, er, experience the Slate.

Upon walking into the showroom on a Monday morning, the first thing I noticed was a marquee-style sign on the wall boldly and brightly serving as a price tag for the black truck parked in the middle of the showroom. The vibe was industrial-barn-chic-meets-SoHo-loft. Three other people were there, and another shopper entered as I left. One man alternated between sitting in the cab, peering at the truck as he walked around it, and peppering Manager of Customer Experience Steve Purdy with questions.
The showroom has been open since October 15, launching with a three-day event that offered ridealongs. Interest has been strong, Purdy told me, and while he couldn’t provide sales numbers, he said the response has been “incredible.”
“We’re really happy with the number of [$300] deposits we’ve gotten since we opened,” Purdy said.
I was hoping there would be at least two Slate Trucks on site so I could compare build quality between trucks and check things like panel gaps, window operation, and chassis creaks. But only one truck was on display. And it wasn’t close to a production model; rather, the black Slate Truck was a hand-built older prototype with a black wrap (the Slate Truck base color is gray). The bed and passenger sides were cordoned off, but the driver-side door was open so shoppers could hop in and check out the interior.
It was bigger than I expected—to my eye, roughly the size of a Hyundai Santa Cruz. The tailgate was down, and it felt reassuringly sturdy when I pressed down on it. The 5-foot-long (152.4 cm) bed floor looked and felt durable, not much different from any other pickup on the market.
I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
I really wanted to jump up and down on the tailgate. But I couldn’t even sit on it.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
You roll down the windows the old way.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The early prototype on display in the showroom.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
The exterior passed the eye test, with the panels appearing well-fitted. The doors sat flush with the surrounding body panels when closed. Of course, I was looking at a prototype carefully built to be poked and prodded by automotive reporters and the general public, so the level of fit and finish was no surprise. The challenge for Slate will be getting consistent build quality with minimal panel gaps, watertight seals, consistent door-to-fender transitions, and hood/frunk alignment. The Slate assembly line in Warsaw, Indiana, is still making prototyping runs at this point, Purdy told me, and the company is hoping to start on production models “soon.”
I hopped inside the cab once I got the opportunity, and the door closed with a solid-sounding “thunk.” It’s spartan inside, with a small screen for the instrument panel, a phone holder, physical climate controls, and window winders. The seats were both supportive and comfortable, and, after moving my seat, I had ample legroom. While the seat slid back and forth smoothly, the seatback recline lever on the side didn’t work.
The shopping experience
Beyond the default Blank Slate body style, Slate offers two SUV options—the Squareback SUV and Fastback SUV—and an open-air kit. I asked Purdy if they were selling any of the SUVs. “Most customers are going with the truck configuration,” he said. “And then they’re customizing their trucks in the Slate Garage.”
Being able to order online and have the truck delivered is a major attraction for those who can’t stand “the kabuki dance of f***ery at a dealership,” as one of my colleagues put it. But if you want to do all that at the Slate Experience Center, staffers will sit down and help you configure your customized Slate. There is a wall with removable dashboard panels across the color spectrum and a couple of miniature models of the cab with tiny, colored panels to help customers decide on the details.
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
All the headlight and taillight options for the Slate Truck are on display.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Miniature interior models help customers visualize what their Slate Truck will look like.
Eric Bangeman/Ars Technica
Purdy told me that Slate is staying the course with the $24,950 sticker price. But will customers actually get their Slate Trucks this year as the company promised? “We will ship some trucks by the end of the year,” Purdy said. “Those will go to investors and employees, with early orderers receiving their Slate Trucks in early 2027.
For service, Slate will be using RepairPal. Owners will be able to choose from 4,000 shops, some of which can service the high-voltage electrical systems and others limited to body damage, Purdy said. For scratches or minor dings from fender benders, owners can replace the exterior body panels themselves. Pricing for replacement parts has yet to be finalized. And Slate is confident the plastic body panels will weather climate extremes without a hitch. “We’re a Michigan company,” Purdy reminded me.
Monday morning is not exactly prime time for dealership traffic, but a handful of prospective customers were in the showroom, which is a promising sign. While there is no shortage of electrified pickup trucks on the market, there is a shortage of affordable ones. At $25,000, the Slate Truck costs far less than a Rivian R1T, Tesla Cybertruck, Chevy Silverado EV, or any currently shipping battery-electric truck. It could be a breakout hit—especially if Slate can beat Ford’s sub-$30,000 Fathom pickup to market.
But the sleek-looking showroom and an attractive prototype still face a production reality check. Tesla had significant quality-control problems with early Model Ys, with customers receiving cars with loose seats and broken seatbelts, and some Cybertrucks have shipped with misaligned panel gaps. A new player is entering the game, but production is still on the (near) horizon, and no one knows if the Slate Trucks delivered to customers will live up to the promise of the carefully hand-built prototypes. People are definitely very interested in Slate. Now it’s time to deliver.
Eric Bangeman is the Managing Editor of Ars Technica. He lives in the northwest suburbs of Chicago, where he enjoys road cycling and plays bass in a band.
The black truck featured in this article was one of their earlier prototypes. The Slate guy I talked to at the event indicated that the other vehicles there were more recent. In addition to the roped off one, there was a grey truck (which I believe was the true base model) as well as an SUV configuration with a wrap. The SUV you could get in and sit and adjust the seats and look all over. I found the legroom quite good front and rear even with the seat fully retracted. Back seat access is only available from the passenger side. Seats are limited manually adjusted and acceptable moderately firm.
I did a ride-along, I’d compare the ride quality to a classic Ford Ranger. It handled the uneven Chicago road fine. No complaints. There wasn’t any opportunity to test its acceleration really due to lunch hour traffic.
The crowd did skew older, probably on account of it being a Thursday.
Regarding the manual windows, I tried them in the SUV and honestly the mechanism felt really good. Better than my old Rangers I’ve had.
The frunk is spacious, I think probably an entire shopping cart full of groceries can fit easily. Not quite Costco sized but not far off. The truck config has very little space behind the seats so I think the frunk will actually be used.
The SUV config is literally a roll cage and capper stuck in between the truck rear glass panel, with the bolster removed. Slate Guy told me it is possible to buy the SUV config and convert it to truck again if you buy the bolster, but final details on that aren’t finished.
Fasteners, at least on the outside, are generally exposed Torx T30 and imo panels look easy to swap. The actual panels seem really sturdy, more so than the super thin aluminum/steel common to normal cars. It’s like a composite and Slate Guy said the grey color is the actual material color all the way through.
The only downside I found is the heat is resistive, not a heat pump.
If I can I’ll try to post pictures I took.

articles.title: The newest AdGuard VPN update makes catching discounts and toggling connections faster than ever
articles.text:
The newest AdGuard VPN update makes catching discounts and toggling connections faster than ever
Hands-free Siri commands, widget controls, and smarter website exclusions to your daily browsing.
- AdGuard VPN's v2.17 update improves both iOS and Android platforms simultaneously.
- iOS users get revamped Shortcuts, allowing one-tap connections, Home Screen widgets, and Siri voice commands.
- Android users can now spot promotional discounts directly inside the app, while both platforms benefit from expanded non-Latin script domain exclusions.
AdGuard has just launched version 2.17 of its virtual private network app, and this time, the privacy company is taking a unified approach.
For the first time, the release rolls out simultaneously for both iOS and Android devices. Moving forward, the provider says it will "keep updates for both platforms in sync to bring you key features and improvements faster."
For iPhone and iPad users, the standout feature is a revamped Shortcuts integration that lets you control your secure connection with just one tap or a simple voice command.
Meanwhile, Android users are getting a streamlined way to snag cheaper subscription deals, alongside improved split-tunneling exclusions for international websites across both operating systems.
Speeding up your connection on iOS
If you regularly toggle your VPN on and off to use local services, the process can quickly become tedious.
As AdGuard points out in its official release post, jumping between your privacy tunnel and restrictive local services can be a chore: "You start the day with AdGuard VPN on. Then you need it off for a few minutes to check your bank account, so you open the app, tap Disconnect, open the banking app, close the banking app, open the AdGuard VPN app again, and tap Connect."
To bypass this daily annoyance, version 2.17 introduces improved Shortcuts for iOS. Users can now place a Connect, Disconnect, or Toggle button directly on their Home Screen or within their phone's Control Center.
You can even set up background automations to ensure the VPN turns itself on the moment you open a specific application or connect to an unfamiliar public Wi-Fi network.
If tapping a widget is still too much effort, the update also brings full Siri integration to the table. By diving into the app's settings menu, you can record custom voice triggers, such as "Hey Siri, connect to AdGuard VPN", to control your privacy completely hands-free.
While we noted in our latest AdGuard VPN review that the service had room to grow against industry giants, quality-of-life updates like these certainly push it in the right direction.
Smarter exclusions and easier savings
While Apple users get the flashy widgets, the Android camp hasn't been entirely left out.
Finding a good deal on a digital privacy subscription usually requires hunting through promotional emails or constantly refreshing a provider's website. Now, AdGuard VPN will display active promotions and discounts directly on the purchase screen inside the Android app.
Finally, the v2.17 update brings a highly requested technical tweak to both the iOS and Android platforms. AdGuard's Exclusions feature, which allows you to choose which websites automatically bypass the encrypted tunnel, now fully supports domains written in non-Latin scripts. This means users can seamlessly whitelist domains like *.рф for Russia and *.中国 for China without the application returning an error.
The version 2.17 update is available to download right now. If you spot any bugs, the provider encourages users to submit feedback directly through its social media channels or via its GitHub repositories.

With over two decades of experience as a reporter and editor, he specializes in making complex topics like cybersecurity, VPNs, and enterprise software accessible and engaging.

articles.title: Google DeepMind says four AI agents beat Minecraft in 27 hours by writing 2,783 programs of their own — AI team died 605 times on Easy difficulty and ran up an estimated $520 in tokens
articles.text:
Google DeepMind says four AI agents beat Minecraft in 27 hours by writing 2,783 programs of their own — AI team died 605 times on Easy difficulty and ran up an estimated $520 in tokens
About half the run was spent fighting the dragon, solved by stacking dirt to reach its crystals.
The game of Minecraft is no match for a team of four Gemini 4 Argon agents, as they were able to defeat it in 27 hours with 2,783 self-written programs, a paper from Google DeepMind reveals. The agents did die 605 times, even on Easy, and about half the run was spent fighting the Ender Dragon, the final boss of the game. The run finally came to completion when the End was solved by stacking dirt to reach the boss’s crystals, at an estimated cost of around $520 in tokens.
The experimental run was designed from the get-go with one goal: kill the Ender Dragon. The playthrough involved a random, shared survival world on Easy with four agents — a fifth agent existed only for reporting — from Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s latest frontier model. Each agent had its own player through the open-source Mineflayer JavaScript library for Minecraft bots, but they were able to coordinate through in-game chat and shared notes. Every program used in the run was written by the agents themselves, and the emphasis is on coding and teamwork rather than game-playing.
The authors say this is the “first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents,” at least “to our knowledge,” qualified by the use of Mineflayer “without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans.” Mineflayer tells the agents where blocks and creatures are, with a pathfinding plugin to plan routes. There was “no human input during the run” and “no one assigned roles or wrote game logic.” The run, starting with the first program and ending with the dragon's death, took 27 hours and 14 minutes.
Although the agents were not given roles, within about 10 minutes a division of labor was proposed in chat by bot janesick. Bot Auratian offered an alternative plan while Bot Gyldenia acknowledged it. The roles ended up being: Gyldenia for food, beds, and flint; Bulicame for diamonds; Janesick for iron and tools; Auratian for the Nether portal. Moments of losses, such as a Ghast fireball destroying dropped items, led the team to diagnose the cause and write rules to prevent it in the future.
Finding the stronghold involved janesick, who threw two Eyes of Ender from different spots and sampled each eye’s flight once every 50 ms, triangulating the location. Carrying the eyes involved its own dire moment when Auratian drowned during the task, but the spot was noted, and the eyes were rescued.
The eventual fight with the dragon led to 69 deaths, and the ten crystals kept regenerating the boss until Auratian discovered they could use dirt pillars to reach the crystals. Four hours and 40 minutes later, all ten crystals were downed, and the dragon was dead 39 minutes after that.
The agents operated by writing short JavaScript programs, almost 2,800 in total, with 42 helper functions kept alive between programs, while a Mineflayer bot ran them in the shared world. Text was returned with status data, not pictures. This is a shared approach to the non-screenshot GPT-6 Astra clear of the Orc starting zone in World of Warcraft earlier this month. AI agents playing games is an ongoing trend, with Pokémon Red probably being the most popular, a game defeated in multiple ways, including with a Jev decision model layer.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Minecraft has also been a popular target, and the authors admit this, highlighting two earlier community dragon kills: a planner with an action-selection model on a fixed speedrun seed in Peaceful mode, and a single Claude Opus 5 agent that used 37 ready-made, high-level tools on Normal, versus Mineflayer alone for the Gemini team. AI Bengineering’s Claude run, relying mostly on Opus 5 at high effort, took 3 hours and 56 minutes from start — “no human input after the prompt” — to kill with 388 tool calls and only one death. The cost in that case, at API-equivalent rates, was about $93.
Google’s Minecraft run, using Gemini 4 Argon’s 50% introductory pricing, which runs from initial API access that followed the model announcement through Nov. 30, cost more than half a grand; at normal pricing, that’s more than a grand. A GPT-6 Astra Portal run last month, which took about 24 hours, came in at $571 in tokens.
Google’s run took about 1.35 billion input tokens with 91% served from cache. About 24,000 model calls involved around 16 million output tokens, a quarter of them thinking. In total, if we’re also including the observer agent, the session would be estimated at $810, or $1,620 after the promotion, at list prices.
Each player is driven by a “general-purpose Gemini 4 Argon coding agent,” which is a fancy way of saying that it’s not specialized for Minecraft. Gemini 4 Argon itself is a frontier model for “real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense,” according to a company blog. With Minecraft, 22% of the agents’ programs ended in an error, with more than 600 deaths.
Although the model was used for a game here, the run was designed to show that Argon is capable of “complex, long-horizon workflows” for complex real-world tasks and agent coordination. Such long projects can involve decompiling a game back into source code, as we covered recently with a Modern Warfare 2 rebuild that now has 83% of its functions matching the original byte for byte.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.
