articles.title: La generación Z no puede escapar de la IA. Tiene que aprender a dominarla
articles.text:
Casi ocho de cada diez estadounidenses pertenecientes a las generaciones Z y millennial afirman, según una encuesta de Operation HOPE y Beyond Finance que se ha hecho entre el 16 y el 18 de marzo de 2026 a 2.000 personas que nacieron entre 1981 y 2008, que suelen aplicar la estrategia de “gasto de supervivencia” (gasta ahora, ahorra más tarde) y que consideran que la creación de patrimonio es cada vez menos alcanzable (en concreto, un 71 %).
Conviene recordar que Beyond Finance es una empresa de consolidación de deudas. Sabiendo este dato, David Carroll Orr, un creador multidisciplinar con intereses en medios digitales, poesía, arquitectura y narrativa (así se define), argumenta que los jóvenes no actúan por apatía, sino que hacen una evaluación racional de un sistema que no les da dónde agarrarse, y que la inteligencia artificial está eliminando los puestos de entrada.
¿Se está cerrando el paso a la primera oferta de trabajo de forma definitiva?
Orr recurre a los datos del Burning Glass Institute sobre la contratación en puestos de nivel de entrada, que se ha ralentizado, y cita a responsables del sector de la inteligencia artificial que afirman que la mitad de los puestos de nivel júnior se automatizará.
No menciona nombres, pero la opinión más conocida al respecto es la de Dario Amodei, director ejecutivo de Anthropic, quien en una entrevista concedida ya avisó de que la IA podría eliminar la mitad de los empleos de oficina de nivel inicial en el plazo de entre uno y cinco años y de que el paro en Estados Unidos podría subir al 10-20 %.
El propio Burning Glass Institute había publicado en julio de 2025 el informe The Expertise Upheaval, donde identificó el impacto de la inteligencia artificial en la pérdida de los primeros peldaños de la escalera de la experiencia. Era aquel espacio en el que, según Orr, el becario redactaba memorandos, revisaba documentos o escribía código y aprendía equivocándose.
Para Orr, esos peldaños corresponden al Lore (en inglés, el ensayo y error de la experiencia humana), en contraposición al Ledger (libro mayor), el registro rígido de la administración. Los puestos de entrada son el Lore de una carrera profesional, mientras que la IA generativa sería una nueva evolución del Ledger.
“Lanzar proyectiles contra la fábrica automatizada no nos devolverá los puestos de trabajo en los peldaños más bajos”, escribe Orr. Basándose en sus investigaciones sobre los archivos de la frontera estadounidense del siglo XIX, propone una salida, la “persistencia forense”: aquellas comunidades aprendieron a moverse entre los registros de tierras y los juzgados para ganar margen dentro del sistema.
Así pues, tanto la educación universitaria como la formación en el trabajo tienen que dejar de preparar a los jóvenes para comportarse como “software humano” y enseñarles a dirigir y auditar las herramientas automatizadas. “Estamos utilizando tecnología del siglo XXI para imponer una perspectiva del siglo XIX sobre el valor humano”, remata.
Las nóminas revelan, con cifras reales, los efectos de los que habla la columna. El Stanford Digital Economy Lab trabaja con datos de nóminas que ADP pone a disposición de los investigadores. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar y Ruyu Chen publicaron el 12 de agosto de 2026 una actualización de su estudio que calcula que los trabajadores júnior (22-25 años) en los puestos más expuestos a la inteligencia artificial tienen un nivel de empleo un 19 % inferior al esperado frente a sus homólogos en áreas menos expuestas. Con datos de julio de 2025, esa brecha era del 15 %.
Según el estudio, el empleo de esos trabajadores jóvenes en los puestos más expuestos cayó casi un 11 % entre noviembre de 2022 (lanzamiento de ChatGPT) y junio de 2026, en contraste con un aumento de alrededor del 10 % en los empleos menos expuestos. En el caso de los trabajadores más experimentados, no se aprecia una brecha comparable. En el conjunto de datos, los cambios observados se deben principalmente a que se contrata a menos gente, y no a despidos.
Los autores no son catastrofistas: no ven un desplazamiento generalizado del empleo y advierten de que sus datos describen un patrón, pero no demuestran que la inteligencia artificial lo cause. Además, el nivel educativo desempeña un papel significativo, ya que la brecha se reduce al tenerlo en cuenta. Y hay un matiz que encaja con lo que defiende Orr: en los casos en los que la inteligencia artificial refuerza a los trabajadores en lugar de sustituirlos, el empleo se mantiene o crece.
En España, los datos sobre la reducción de oportunidades en puestos de entrada también son evidentes. Según el Barómetro de Talento Digital 2026 del Observatorio del Talento Digital de DIGITALENT Group, presentado el 24 de septiembre de 2026, el 51,7 % de las empresas prevé que se reduzcan las oportunidades para perfiles júnior debido a la inteligencia artificial.
El 39,6 % sitúa el pensamiento crítico y el criterio profesional como prioridad, y solo el 2,4 % señala la programación. Solo el 20,8 % de las organizaciones considera que su plantilla está bastante o muy preparada para trabajar con IA, y solo el 29,5 % cuenta con un marco formal y comunicado sobre el uso de la inteligencia artificial.
Estos datos revelan, en línea con lo que plantea Orr, una brecha significativa en la preparación de las empresas para trabajar con inteligencia artificial. Las personas sin experiencia, aquellas que entran en el mercado laboral para adquirir el Lore en la empresa, se encuentran en una situación de incertidumbre. Según datos de la patronal DigitalES de mayo de 2026, las ofertas de trabajo para programadores júnior se han reducido un 33 % en España en un año, en comparación con un aumento del 13 % en las de perfiles sénior.
La capacitación en inteligencia artificial en el trabajo ya está regulada
En Europa, existe un reglamento que establece que las empresas que utilicen sistemas de inteligencia artificial deben ocuparse de formar a sus trabajadores en el tema desde el 2 de febrero de 2025, fecha en la que empezó a aplicarse el artículo 4 del Reglamento de IA. Esta disposición ha sido modificada por el Reglamento (UE) 2026/1744 de 8 de julio de 2026, en vigor desde el 27 de julio de 2026. Ya no exige a las empresas que garanticen un nivel concreto de capacitación, sino simplemente que adopten medidas para apoyar la formación de su plantilla y de quienes usan los sistemas en su nombre.
Las empresas ya no están obligadas a garantizar el logro de objetivos de aprendizaje, pero la obligación de poner medios sigue existiendo. Si su empresa utiliza asistentes de inteligencia artificial en el trabajo, pregunte qué formación ofrece y solicítela. Ninguno de los estudios mencionados resuelve quién formará dentro de diez años a los perfiles sénior si se reduce el número de personas que aprenden el oficio en los puestos de nivel bajo.

articles.text: Un taxi sin conductor Waymo circula por lower Manhattan, en Nueva York. Los coches eléctricos y totalmente autónomos Waymo , de Alphabet (empresa matriz de Google), desembarcarán en los próximos días en la Comunidad de Madrid. articles.title: European Leaders Turn to NVIDIA Vera CPUs to Build Local Infrastructure
articles.text:
Nebius and Nscale are among global technology partners looking to NVIDIA Vera CPUs to build the next wave of infrastructure.
Their momentum reflects rapid advancements in agentic computing.
Agents do more than generate answers: they retrieve information, run software tools, execute code and evaluate results. Each step depends on fast CPU processing.
Vera accelerates that work, helping agents respond faster and enabling data centers to make better use of computing capacity. Vera is designed to sustain that speed even when running thousands of tasks simultaneously, helping organizations expand services without trading responsiveness for scale.
Building Europe’s Computing Capacity
AI cloud providers Nebius, Nscale and Verda are building with Vera to support the growing computing needs of businesses and developers. High-performance, energy-efficient CPUs help these providers scale the data processing and software execution behind services, alongside the GPUs running models.
The broader sovereign AI ecosystem also includes Aleria, a sovereign AI infrastructure and platform provider, supporting demand for infrastructure that keeps data and operations under customers’ control.
More Ways to Put Vera to Work
Server manufacturers Bull, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro are building Vera-based systems, giving customers more deployment options for their high-performance computing and AI data centers. Vera can power standalone CPU servers or work alongside NVIDIA GPUs in accelerated systems, supporting different workloads and deployment needs.
Data processing companies ClickHouse, Cloudera, Duck Labs, Elastic, Polars, Redpanda, SAP and Starburst observed strong results on Vera for analytical, extract-transform-and-load and semantic search workloads in early testing. Vera’s per-core performance, LPDDR5X memory bandwidth and NVIDIA Scalable Coherency Fabric help achieve performance gains across the board.
Software and developer-platform companies Atlassian, Inherent and Nous Research are adopting Vera for environments where AI agents work alongside developers and researchers. Atlassian is looking to Vera to accelerate the data processing that builds semantic search indexes for its AI-powered products; Inherent has tested Vera and is looking to adopt it for environments where AI agents work alongside engineers on novel scientific research; and Nous Research uses Vera to authenticate agent identities and validate every action before it executes, keeping deployments secure as agent fleets grow.
Baseten-Blaxel, Daytona, E2B, Modal, Prime Intellect and Vercel provide cloud-based sandboxes, which serve as computers for AI agents, and are building on Vera to power the infrastructure agents depend on to execute code, run tools and test results.
Every agent needs a secure, isolated sandbox that can be provisioned instantly, and because sandboxes spin up millions of times a day, the speed of each individual startup cycle compounds at scale. Vera’s fast per-core performance and high-bandwidth memory make it well suited to this pattern, giving sandbox providers the throughput not only to spin up sandboxes but to run agentic workloads at maximum scale without interruption.

articles.title: EIF commits €20 million to Swedish VC BackingMinds to support underrepresented entrepreneurs | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Swedish VC firm BackingMinds has received around €20 million from the European Investment Fund (EIF) for BackingMinds Invest III in order to seek out promising entrepreneurs and businesses often overlooked by traditional investors.
The EIF, which is part of the Luxembourg-based European Investment Bank (EIB) Group, will be the first institutional investor in the fund – backed by the EU’s InvestEU programme. This follows their €50 million fund close in 2022 and its investment in Swedish entrepreneurship platform Techarena in 2025.
“The future is never where you expect it, and neither are the founders building it,” says BackingMinds Founding Partner Sara Wimmercranz. “Some of the most innovative companies in the Nordics are being built where venture capital rarely reaches. A network is a filter. It lets through what already looks like the network and repeats the patterns of the past. As investors, we need to be more open and seek founders out. The EIF’s commitment lets us do that on a larger scale.”
BackingMinds’ EIF commitment comes amid further institutional backing for specialised European venture funds in 2026.
In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve closed a €62 million pre-Seed fund, while Turbine Capital reached a €54 million final close for Nordic DeepTech investments, both with EIF backing.
Elsewhere, Berlin-based Auxxo closed its €33.3 million Female Catalyst Fund II, Copenhagen’s Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech, including €40 million from the EIF, and Munich-based Ananda Impact Ventures raised €73 million at first close for impact investments.
Together, these fund closings represent approximately €282.3 million, excluding BackingMinds’ separate €20 million EIF commitment.
“Europe cannot afford to leave talented entrepreneurs undiscovered simply because they are outside the traditional venture capital networks,” adds EIF Deputy Chief Executive Merete Clausen. “BackingMinds has shown that promising businesses can be found in places and among founders that investors too often miss. By supporting this fund, we are helping to unlock that potential and bring more capital to companies tackling some of Europe’s most pressing challenges.”
Founded in 2016, BackingMinds is a Stockholm-based VC firm, founded by Sara Wimmercranz and Susanne Najafi to address the gaps in capital distribution. Through its two earlier funds, BackingMinds has invested in 23 companies.
Of these, 46% have had at least one female founder, 43% have had founders with immigrant backgrounds and 71% were established outside a capital city.
The new fund will finance early-stage companies primarily in Sweden and across the Nordic region, aiming to find entrepreneurial talent beyond established venture capital networks. It will seek out businesses founded by women as well as by people with immigrant backgrounds and based outside capital cities.
The focus will also be on commercially promising companies that address environmental or social challenges ranging from reducing carbon emissions and upgrading energy efficiency to improving healthcare and bolstering education.
According to the EIF, their support is aimed at helping BackingMinds Invest III attract other institutional investors.

articles.title: Achieve Productive AI Capacity Faster and More Predictably with NVIDIA DSX POD | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
AI factories turn energy into intelligence. But before an AI workload can produce its first token, operators must bring an interconnected system of compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, and software online as one productive unit.
In a conventional data center build, teams must first select the site, design power and cooling for the deployment, lay out the data center, and plan and install racks and cables. Then they can validate the network and cluster incrementally and bring service online. This work requires coordinated specialized labor, with critical dependencies among installation, infrastructure readiness, and system testing. Delays can push back bring-up and the date the infrastructure begins producing tokens.
NVIDIA DSX POD shifts more of this work into a controlled factory environment. One of multiple AI factory implementation models supported by NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is the standardized, factory-built implementation. It enables partners to build standardized containers that pre-integrate AI infrastructure, complete critical validation before shipment, and connect to prepared site infrastructure after delivery. The result is a repeatable approach designed to reduce onsite integration complexity and help operators reach productive AI capacity faster and more predictably.
This post explains the foundation of NVIDIA DSX POD, how the reference design aligns with the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform, and how NVIDIA and its ecosystem partners work through product engineering, deployment, and support.
A design foundation for moving AI factory integration upstream
Modular and prefabricated data centers already exist. The engineering challenge for an AI factory extends beyond placing conventional IT equipment in an enclosure.
Rack-scale AI systems combine high-density compute, high-speed scale-up and scale-out networking, liquid cooling, power delivery, telemetry, and management software. These elements behave as one system. Their mechanical, electrical, thermal, and network requirements must remain within specification during factory integration, transportation, installation, and operation.
NVIDIA DSX POD provides the design foundation for partners to install rack-scale systems in containers at the factory, functionally test the integrated unit, transport it, and bring it online safely through repeatable processes at the destination. NVIDIA’s investment spans the engineering disciplines required to make that possible, including rack layout, structural loading, power, cooling, cabling, service access, reliability, and validation.
This work extends the progression toward greater factory integration to reduce installation complexity and accelerate deployment. NVIDIA has moved from chips and boards to complete rack-scale systems, and large-scale reference architectures like NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD.
NVIDIA DSX POD carries this approach into a factory-built AI factory implementation, moving most component integration from the customer site into a controlled manufacturing environment. The reference design does not make containerization mandatory for every AI factory. Conventional data center construction and onsite-integrated designs remain important options. NVIDIA DSX POD adds a standardized path for large-scale deployments where schedule predictability, repeatability, and reduced onsite work are priorities.
Architecture aligned with NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform
NVIDIA DSX is the broad design framework for co-designed AI infrastructure. It brings compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, facility controls, and software together at the data center level. Customers and partners can implement that framework in different physical forms.
NVIDIA DSX POD is a specific realization of that broader design: a standardized AI factory architecture composed of factory-built container types and defined interfaces between them. The architecture is designed around the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform and its rack-scale systems.
The reference design describes a complete AI factory rather than a compute enclosure in isolation. It accounts for compute, service and management functions, scale-out networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, and other supporting infrastructure.
Technical requirements for factory-integrated deployment
The central purpose of the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design is to make the full deployment process repeatable. That requires coordinated requirements across the following areas: compute integration, networking and storage, cabling and controls, power delivery, liquid cooling, and mechanical design and transportation.
Compute integration
The NVIDIA DSX POD compute container is designed for NVIDIA Vera Rubin rack scale infrastructure. The design defines how compute and supporting racks fit within the enclosure and how partners address structural support, weight distribution, equipment restraint, service clearances, airflow and liquid-cooling access, rack-level power, and network connectivity.
Factory integration also changes the validation boundary. Instead of treating each rack as an independent shipment that will be assembled into a cluster onsite, partners validate the installed compute environment as a deployment unit. The validation plan can cover rack inventory, firmware and configuration baselines, power-on checks, fabric connectivity, sensor operation, cooling integrity, and system-level functional tests before the container leaves the factory.
Networking and storage
AI workloads depend on predictable movement of model data, training data, checkpoint data, and inference context across the AI factory. The reference design therefore treats networking and storage as part of the system architecture rather than as site-specific additions made after compute arrives.
The design defines the connectivity required within a compute container, between containers, and from the modular system to the customer’s external network. It accounts for scale-out fabrics, service and management networks, fiber entry points, trunk cabling, cable routing, labeling, bend radius, service access, and validation of factory-installed link before shipment.
Storage requirements follow the same principle. The architecture defines the required capacity, performance, connectivity, management, and service characteristics while allowing the final equipment implementation to reflect the deployment scale and partner solution. This enables storage and networking to arrive as coordinated parts of the AI factory instead of independent systems that must be reconciled late in site integration.
Cabling and controls
NVIDIA DSX POD reduces the onsite work of cabling in a rack-scale deployment, moving rack-to-rack network cabling, power wiring, control wiring, and sensor integration into the factory wherever practical.
The reference design clearly defines cable paths, separation requirements, termination points, labeling conventions, test procedures, and serviceability requirements to help partners easily install and test these connections under controlled conditions to reduce the number of field terminations required after delivery.
Power delivery
DSX POD makes power delivery seamless with a standard input 800 VDC power design that begins with the electrical input to the core containers and continues through protection, distribution, grounding, rack connections, controls, and telemetry. The reference design defines the power characteristics and interfaces required by the installed AI infrastructure. Partners then engineer the upstream generation, conversion, and regional electrical solution for the customer site.
This separation is important because utility conditions, codes, equipment availability, and grid architectures differ across regions. A common interface at the container boundary enables repeatable core designs while preserving flexibility in how ecosystem partners deliver power to each deployment.
NVIDIA software can complement the physical design by helping operators manage workloads within available power limits. Policy-driven power control, workload orchestration, and high-fidelity telemetry can help an AI factory convert a fixed power envelope into more productive computing.
Liquid cooling
Vera Rubin rack-scale systems require coordinated liquid-cooling infrastructure. Within the container, the design covers the plumbing that connects racks to the container cooling interface, including routing, manifolds, isolation, instrumentation, leak detection, pressure integrity, and service access.
Partners can assemble, flush, pressure-test, and validate the internal cooling loop at the factory. At the site, they connect the container to prepared water and heat-rejection infrastructure, commission the complete loop, and verify performance under operating conditions.
NVIDIA DSX POD changes where integration occurs. It does not eliminate the supporting facility infrastructure.
Mechanical design and transportation
Shipping high-value rack-scale systems already installed in an enclosure requires a design that treats logistics as an engineering requirement. The container structure, equipment restraints, weight distribution, center of gravity, lifting and handling points, access paths, and transport conditions must work together.
The reference design also connects transportation requirements to factory quality gates. Partners inspect the integrated unit before shipment, document its configuration and test status, secure it for transport, and repeat defined checks after arrival. This process helps establish that the system delivered to the site matches the system validated at the factory.
Parallelizing factory integration and site preparation
The factory-built model changes the deployment sequence. Site teams can prepare land, foundations, power, and external connectivity while partners manufacture and integrate the containers in parallel.
At the factory, partners install the rack-scale systems, complete internal cabling and plumbing, integrate controls, load approved configuration baselines, and run functional tests. At the deployment site, construction teams prepare the physical and utility interfaces that the containers require.
After delivery, the work focuses on placement, inter-container connections, and hookup to external power, cooling, and networking. Teams then confirm transport integrity, validate the site connections, and complete system commissioning.
This model does not remove onsite work. It reduces the amount of complex, repeatable integration performed in the field and moves it into an environment designed for consistent tooling, quality controls, and parallel production.
Scaling with standardized deployment units
A standardized container architecture gives operators a repeatable unit for planning and expansion. After preparing the supporting site infrastructure, an operator can add compute and supporting capacity using the same defined interfaces and validation process.
Standardization also creates a consistent foundation for software optimization. When the underlying compute, network, power, cooling, and telemetry architecture is known software and operational practices for that environment can be tuned easily. Partners can still adapt each implementation to local codes, site conditions, customer requirements, and regional supply chains.
This balance is central to NVIDIA DSX POD. The reference design supplies reusable NVIDIA engineering and validation. The ecosystem supplies manufacturing capacity, site expertise, regional engineering, customization, deployment, service, and support.
A partner-led delivery model
NVIDIA provides the validated AI infrastructure design foundation and works with the ecosystem to prove that rack-scale systems can be integrated, tested, transported, and deployed as repeatable factory-built units.
OEMs and ODMs integrate the computing systems. Mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and infrastructure specialists adapt power and cooling to the site. Modular solution providers manufacture the enclosures and integrate the subsystems. Site partners prepare the location, complete installation, and support commissioning. Together, these partners turn the reference design into a customer-specific AI factory.
The model expands the modular data center market rather than replacing existing offerings. Partners can continue to deliver different levels of integration, from modular infrastructure that customers populate onsite to fully factory-integrated deployments. NVIDIA DSX POD gives the ecosystem a validated path for the latter while preserving room for differentiation in implementation and service.
Learn more about NVIDIA DSX POD
The value of an AI factory begins when the infrastructure starts producing tokens. By moving repeatable integration and validation into the factory, NVIDIA DSX POD is designed to reduce schedule exposure late in the build, simplify onsite work, and make deployment more predictable.
The reference design brings NVIDIA Vera Rubin compute, networking, storage, power, cooling, cabling, controls, and validation into one coordinated architecture. NVIDIA DSX POD provides the engineering foundation. Partners build, customize, deliver, and support the resulting solutions.
Learn more about how the NVIDIA DSX POD reference design can help turn available land, power, and prepared site infrastructure into productive AI capacity faster and more predictably.

articles.title: AOMEI Backupper Compromised in Short-Burst Supply Chain Campaign
articles.text:
Between April and July, AOMEI Backupper served malware to its users multiple times in short-burst supply chain compromises, security researchers warn.
AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup, sync, and disk cloning software, available in free and paid editions for home users, businesses, and Windows Server environments. AOMEI says its products are used by more than 186 million people worldwide.
Unlike typical supply chain attacks, this campaign relied on short-lived tampering windows to serve the CrossRoad downloader and the ShinyRoad backdoor.
“Each tampering window remained active for only five to ten minutes before reverting to authentic versions,” report Google Cloud’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, which investigated the attack alongside ManageEngine Threat Analysis Lab (METAL).
The attacks hit all systems that fetched the modified AOMEI Backupper packages during the attack windows, suggesting an opportunistic campaign rather than a targeted one.
However, throughout the investigation, Google Cloud identified higher education, IT services, and telecommunications entities in Australia, Brazil, India, Pakistan, Portugal, Singapore, South Africa, Spain, Switzerland, Türkiye, and the United States that have been compromised.
“We confirmed several tampering windows in 2026, alongside related malware samples observed in the wild starting in late April. However, given the short duration of these windows, it is probable that additional tampering occurred throughout the campaign that remained outside our visibility,” Google Cloud notes.
During the very short attack windows, the threat actor, tracked as UNC7017, tampered with the update server’s update settings file to redirect to a malicious ZIP archive and modified the server’s automatic notification service to force systems into automatically executing the malware.
METAL’s analysis of the incident shows that the hackers abused AOMEI Backupper’s promotional content channel for malware distribution. The channel runs background services that poll AOMEI’s servers for content and includes two configuration paths that deliver content to a directory and execute it.
“The two paths converge on the same location. One controls what lands in html\; the other controls what can be executed from it. Neither configuration file is cryptographically authenticated by the client, and the checksum used to validate the archive is declared inside the same unauthenticated file that names it,” METAL explains.
ManageEngine’s threat analysts caught a glimpse of the potential attack path on May 28, and observed in real time the change in payloads served by AOMEI on July 16. On July 20, the short-burst tampering was also caught by Mandiant.
Analysis of the payload showed the delivery of a legitimate version of the Radmin Server remote administration tool alongside a malicious DLL loaded through it that would establish a reverse TCP connection to the attackers’ command-and-control (C&C) server.
Google Cloud’s researchers also observed UNC7017 introducing a secondary exploitation vector, replacing a legitimate banner with a 1×1 pixel window assigned maximum execution priority that forced the AOMEI client to request a remote resource via WebDAV, thus sending NetNTLMv2 authentication hashes to the attackers.
Throughout the various stages of the campaign, the threat actor delivered multiple payloads, including the CrossRoad dropper, a modified version of Radmin Server, and the Adaptix C&C framework.
CrossRoad was seen performing system validation, cleanup, and payload staging, establishing persistence for the late-stage backdoor, and deleting itself from the disk. The final payload was the ShinyRoad modular backdoor framework.
In July, after the successful deployment of ShinyRoad, UNC7017 was seen dropping AdaptAgent, which is part of the Adaptix C2 post-exploitation framework.
“This campaign highlights a broader evolution in software supply chain attack methodologies. Supply chain intrusions have historically focused on inserting backdoors into software source code or tampering with developer build pipelines. UNC7017’s use of ephemeral configuration tampering represents a lower-overhead, higher-stealth alternative,” Google Cloud notes.
METAL says it initially notified AOMEI Technology of the potential tampering in early June, but the vendor dismissed the report, claiming the content was likely intercepted and modified in transit. Google Cloud notified it again in mid-July, and the company said in late July that it had taken corrective actions.

articles.title: It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
articles.text:
It’s a bird, it’s a plane … it’s a robo-puffin?
MIT engineers’ design for a robot that both swims and flies could lead to a new class of vehicles for ocean exploration.
Given that water is 1,000 times denser than air, moving through those two mediums requires very different mechanics—or so one might assume. Yet birds like gulls and puffins can plunge into the sea, swim underwater, and leap back into the air to fly away. And now engineers at MIT and EPFL in Lausanne, Switzerland, have designed a robot that can do likewise.
The “flapping-wing aerial-aquatic vehicle,” or FAAV, weighs less than 300 grams (about half a pound) and is equipped with a central fuselage, two flexible wings, and a steerable tail. The body contains a battery and a waterproof electric motor that drives a crankshaft, which pumps the wings up and down at preset frequencies. The wings are made of thin membranes that are coated with hydrophobic nanoparticles to help wick away water. And the tail is motorized, enabling it to change its angle to help the robot fly up or dive down.
In experiments carried out in a water tank and at Lake Geneva, a team led by Raphael Zufferey, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at MIT, identified combinations of wing size, flapping frequency, and tail angle that enable the robot to smoothly transition from swimming to flying.
The best results came with medium-size wings that were flexible enough to minimize flapping amplitude in water and also firm enough to keep the robot aloft in the air. The speeds and flapping frequencies were similar to those used by actual birds, and a pitch of 70 degrees—a relatively steep angle—allowed the robot to make the leap from water to air. Interestingly, although many diving birds paddle their feet to help them take off from the water’s surface, the team found that the bot didn’t need feet at all.
The engineers’ results could help pave the way for a new class of drones and vehicles that could fly to and sample from aquatic regions too dangerous for traditional vessels to access.
“Our dream vision is for oceanographers, marine biologists, and members of coastal communities to launch this robot from a boat, or from shore, and it would fly close to the area of interest, such as an iceberg or a port facility, or over a pod of whales,” says Zufferey. “It would dive into the water to take a measurement or collect a sample, and fly back to deliver the data at a fraction of the cost of traditional methods. Then it could go back out to dive for more.”
The researchers are now trying to design wings that can turn as well as flap. They will also test the robot’s performance under turbulent conditions, such as swimming in choppy waters and flying through wind. Then they hope to deploy the vehicle to help answer questions in ocean science.
“One of the major challenges in ocean science is collecting data both frequently and across many locations, which is something this robot could do in the future,” Zufferey says. “You could send this out not just every week, but every hour. It could fly out at high speeds, dive in, fly back, deliver its data, and go back out, multiple times.”

articles.title: Lua hoje: confira a fase da Lua desta quarta-feira 21/10/2026
articles.text:
Hoje, 21 de outubro de 2026, a Lua está na fase crescente e 80% visível. Confira o calendário completo de fases da Lua deste mês, de acordo com o Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet).
Confira as próximas fases
As fases da Lua no mês de outubro de 2026 começam no dia 3 com a chegada da Lua Minguante, às 10h26 (horário de Brasília). Depois disso, no dia 10, foi a vez da Lua Nova, que chegou às 12h50. A Lua Crescente surgiu às 13h13 do dia 18. Por fim, vem a Lua Cheia, dia 26, à 1h13.
Leia mais:
- Entenda o que é a Lua, como e quando ela se formou
- Saiba como tirar a melhor foto possível com uma câmera de celular
- 7 dicas para fotografar a lua com seu celular
Calendário fases da Lua em outubro de 2026
- Lua Minguante: dia 3, às 10h26
- Lua Nova: dia 10, às 12h50
- Lua Crescente: dia 18, às 13h13
- Lua Cheia: dia 26, à 1h13
O que é o ciclo lunar?
Uma lunação ou ciclo lunar, como é chamado o intervalo de tempo entre luas novas, é sutilmente variável, com média de duração de 29,5 dias. Durante esse período, ela passa pelas quatro fases principais (nova, crescente, cheia e minguante), e cada uma se prolonga por aproximadamente sete dias.
Também existem as “interfases”: quarto crescente e crescente gibosa (entre as fases nova e cheia) e minguante gibosa e quarto minguante (entre a cheia e a minguante).
Entenda cada fase da Lua
Lua Nova
Na Lua Nova, o satélite se posiciona entre a Terra e o Sol. Isso faz com que o lado iluminado da Lua fique voltado para o Sol, enquanto o lado escuro fica voltado para nós. Por esse motivo, a Lua não é visível no céu noturno. Essa fase marca o início de um novo ciclo lunar e está relacionada ao recomeço e a novas possibilidades.
Lua Crescente
Depois da Lua Nova, surge a fase Crescente. Aos poucos, uma pequena faixa iluminada começa a aparecer no céu, aumentando noite após noite. No início, vemos apenas um fino arco de luz, mas com o passar dos dias a parte iluminada cresce até que metade da Lua esteja visível, momento chamado de Quarto Crescente. Essa fase simboliza crescimento, desenvolvimento e a construção de novos caminhos.
Lua Cheia
Na Lua Cheia, a Terra se encontra entre o Sol e a Lua. Isso permite que o lado lunar voltado para nós receba luz por completo, tornando-se totalmente visível e brilhante no céu. É o período de maior intensidade luminosa, quando a Lua nasce no horizonte exatamente no momento em que o Sol se põe. A Lua Cheia é associada à plenitude, ao auge de processos e à energia em seu ponto máximo.
Lua Minguante
Após a Lua Cheia, a luz da Lua começa a diminuir gradualmente. A cada noite, vemos menos da sua superfície iluminada. Quando apenas metade dela está visível, ocorre o Quarto Minguante, fase oposta ao Quarto Crescente. A Lua continua a perder luminosidade até chegar novamente à Lua Nova, reiniciando o ciclo. A fase Minguante simboliza reflexão, encerramento e preparação para novos começos.
Qual a fase da Lua hoje?
Hoje a Lua está na fase Crescente.
Flávia Correia é jornalista do Olhar Digital, cobrindo Ciência e Espaço.

articles.title: SpaceX alum's aviation startup, Reliable Robotics, lands $115M, topping $1B valuation | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Reliable Robotics has been working for nearly a decade to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft. Now, with a $115 million funding boost, the Mountain View, California-based startup has a longer runway as it pushes to get its autonomous flight system certified by the Federal Aviation Administration — a critical milestone that co-founder and CEO Robert Rose said the startup is inching toward.
The financing is an extension of its Series D round and includes $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round, which now totals $275 million, has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark. Other investors include Gideon Strategic Partners, RockCreek, Geek Ventures, Gold Hill Capital, Sparkwave Capital, and others. Reliable has raised $380 million to date.
“We continue to make steady progress and deliver evidence to the FAA and every day, we inch closer and closer,” said Rose, a former director of flight software at SpaceX who has also had stints at Tesla and Google. Reliable co-founder and CTO Juerg Frefel is also a SpaceX veteran who spent nearly a decade there as an engineer.
And in aviation — one of the most regulated industries in the world — moving toward certification of new technology is progress.
Reliable Robotics is working to gain FAA certification on four fronts, all of which are linked to its goal of autonomous flight.
Its first product, called continuous autopilot engagement, handles the engine startup, taxiing, takeoff, and landing for the pilot, who remains in the aircraft and interacts with the autonomous flight system through a touchscreen. Rose expects to receive certification for this critical first system in 18 to 24 months.
The second certification, which Rose says is at least three years away, removes the pilot from the cockpit and moves them to a ground-control station.
Reliable is also working toward certification of a collision-avoidance radar, which the company has developed in-house after failing to attract legacy suppliers to take on the project. Most conventional radar systems use an antenna that moves to scan the surrounding airspace. Reliable has developed a solid-state radar that has no moving parts and scans the sky at a longer range and at much higher resolution, according to Rose. It’s also easier to maintain because there are no moving parts and it costs less, he added.
“This is of great interest to operators these days, given the collisions that we’ve had recently in commercial aviation,” he said, adding that the radar also works on the ground to prevent collisions with other aircraft or infrastructure. Rose expects the solid-state radar to be certified by the end of 2027.
The final certification is for its airline, called Reliable Airlines, which will be the first airline certified to use the autonomous flying technology. The airline is based in Albuquerque and uses six Cessna Caravans — workhorses of the aviation industry — to fly cargo six days a week. (The FAA certifies equipment, but the agency also must certify the airline operations under a separate set of regulations.)
While the certification process is lengthy, Nimble Partners founder John Burbank said the benefits will be broad and significant.
“It’s a much bigger effort and much bigger opportunity than to just build one plane,” Burbank said, noting that Reliable is building a system that can be adopted by any airframe. “They had a really big vision nine years ago, and saw this as something needed and essential. Once they get the first one approved, then everyone will realize this is going to be the path for the industry, just as we’re seeing the path for the auto industry being autonomous.”

articles.title: Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
articles.text:
Google is bringing Personal Intelligence to Gemini AI in your car. With this update, Gemini in Android Auto and cars with Google built-in can tap into your information across Google apps, including Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, YouTube, and Search.
Google’s more personalized Gemini AI is heading to your car
Gemini AI can now draw from Gmail, Calendar, Maps, Photos, and other apps while you drive.
As an example, Google says you can ask Gemini about your flight status if you’re driving to the airport. The AI assistant can pull your flight details from a confirmation message in Gmail and then use that information to look up the status. You can also ask Gemini to “take me to my doctor’s appointment” instead of pulling up directions manually, or ask it to “find the car wash from the photo I took last week and navigate there.”
Google brought its Gemini assistant to Android Auto last year before rolling it out to cars with Google built-in in April. Several carmakers—including Ford, GM, Honda, Nissan, Volvo, and Polestar—have shipped newer cars with Google built-in, which adds support for native Android apps.
Google says it will connect your apps to Gemini only if you enable its Personal Intelligence setting. It will also share personalized responses only if you have your phone connected to your car. “If you don’t use Personal Intelligence, everything in the car still works: You can use navigation, listen to music, make calls, and ask questions, but the answers won’t be tailored to you,” Google says.
Personal Intelligence is rolling out to Android Auto today, with support coming to cars with Google built-in in the coming months.

articles.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
articles.text:
How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results.
AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.
To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.
Here are the tips they shared with us.
Vlad Mihalcea
GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea
How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?
I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.
For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.
What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?
I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.
It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.
I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.
Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?
I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.
This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.
Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.
One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.
Patrick Baumgartner
GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner
Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?
A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.
Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering.
The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner.
And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that.
Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently?
There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot.
Let’s start with the first one.
One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom.
Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work.
With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details.
The really important part was verification.
We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs.
That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence.
The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed.
For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result.
Can you share the second example?
A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell.
And then a real user did.
They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it.
We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged.
During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical.
That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution. It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent.
How about the third example?
The third example is completely different again.
Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app?
It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns.
Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary.
So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English.
It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition.
I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages.
What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product.
That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building.
How do you typically use Copilot?
I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore.
My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows.
I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go.
For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need.
I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction.
By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked.
That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed.
I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro.
But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me.
The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed.
Context is king.
Can you share some tips and best practices?
The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting.
For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit.
A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper.
I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful.
The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate.
Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work?
The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates.
“Done” should not mean that the model says it is done.
For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness.
The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done.
I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts.
The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills.
I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill.
The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there.
One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit, inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards.
The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain.
I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts.
The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model.
I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate:
change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again.
It continues until there are no findings left.
That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter.
I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly.
More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process.
That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck.
But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential.
How do you think AI is changing our profession?
I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another.
The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented.
So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution.
In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering.
And I like that.
Frank Delporte
GitHub profile: @FDelporte
How did you get started in tech?
I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-).
How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?
It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports.
One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected. Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button.
This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer.
So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect.
Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.”
What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail:
I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi?
Check the pull request for the full conversation. Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation.
Can you share some tips and best practices?
- Tell it where to look: For the Pi4J issue #622, I added two file paths. That is a tiny bit of effort that removes a huge amount of searching in a large codebase. You usually have a hunch about the neighbourhood even when you have no idea about the bug. Give it to the tool so it doesn’t need to investigate the complete code.
- Ask for proof and tests: “Add a unit test to validate the change” is something I ask a lot these days. Well, asked, because it has now become a rule in my instructions file. It also prevents cases where the diagnosis was wrong, because the test won’t fail on the old code.
- Ask why: If you don’t understand a fix, say so and ask. The explanation is a deliverable too and should be added into your project documentation or inside the ticket or pull request. It teaches everyone who reads the info later. For example, this also triggered more questions within the Pi4J team about virtual thread pinning on native calls.
- Stay in control: All of these pull requests in Pi4J were reviewed and approved by maintainers before they went in. That’s the model that works best in this project: the agent does the investigation, the humans stay responsible for what ships. But also for my other projects I always do a review of the code that was generated by the tool. I always want to keep code readable and maintainable. Too often, a tool creates duplicate methods or recreates something which is already available in another place and should be combined. That’s your responsibility. You can go very fast these days with AI-assisted coding, which also means you can very fast create a mess. Don’t do that, keep your code manageable, your colleagues and future-self will thank you if they have to investigate bugs or make improvements later.

articles.title: UniUni go-public deal falls through as SPAC terminates agreement | BetaKit
articles.text:
Richmond, BC-based last-mile delivery company UniUni will need to find a new path to the public markets after its deal with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) was terminated.
The news: MAK Acquisition, a Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX)-listed SPAC led by ex-Dye & Durham CEO Matthew Proud, announced on Tuesday morning that it terminated its merger agreement with UniUni. Earlier this year, UniUni signed the deal to merge with MAK and trade on the TSX; a deal that would’ve valued the combined entity at more than $1 billion USD ($1.4 billion CAD).
The termination followed MAK warning UniUni nearly one month ago that it was in breach of its interim covenant, meaning UniUni wasn’t meeting a certain standard in the lead-up to the deal closing, as its business and financial performance had deteriorated. BetaKit has reached out to UniUni for comment.
From the source: “Under the Purchase Agreement, UniUni had 15 business days following receipt of the notice of breach to cure the breach, however the breach was incurable as UniUni exceeded its maximum cumulative pre-tax loss,” MAK said in its release. “As a result, MAK has exercised its right to terminate the Purchase Agreement, and the Proposed Transaction will not proceed.”
The context: The day after MAK warned UniUni of the breach, UniUni announced it was entering into a term sheet for a private funding round led by an undisclosed existing investor. It’s unclear if this funding was intended to improve its fiscal position for the SPAC deal, or as an alternative source of liquidity in preparation for the deal to fall through. UniUni said at the time that the funding was meant to support its continued growth across North America and strengthen its financial position heading into peak delivery season.
Final thought: Based out of Richmond, BC, UniUni uses gig workers and passenger vehicles to deliver goods to consumers. It has partnered with outlets like Temu, Shein, and AliExpress, and in 2025 claimed a network of more than 100,000 registered drivers across Canada and the US. While the company has raised multiple large funding rounds, recent reporting has suggested the company is “deeply unprofitable” as it faces several lawsuits, including class action allegations of unfair labour practices.
Feature image courtesy UniUni.

articles.title: RHEL for NVIDIA delivers trusted foundation for next-gen AI workloads
articles.text:
New NVIDIA GPUs typically arrive before a standard enterprise Linux release can carry every driver, kernel change, and virtualization patch those systems need. The usual result is a bad choice: wait, or stand the first cluster up on an operating system the team does not intend to keep.
Red Hat Enterprise Linux for NVIDIA 26.03 is the other choice. It is a partner-optimized edition of Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) for the latest NVIDIA hardware, included with a RHEL for ARM 64 subscription. It is how you start on enterprise Linux now and it is the edition ready to support the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform as part of Red Hat AI Factory with NVIDIA.
Red Hat Enterprise Linux for NVIDIA 26.03
RHEL for NVIDIA 26.03 is built on the latest version of RHEL, modifying a strictly limited set of core packages—the Linux kernel, QEMU, and libvirt—to enable launch-day hardware support. The rest of the userspace matches standard RHEL. Once those hardware enablement patches mature and merge into the upstream Linux kernel, organizations can seamlessly transition back to mainline RHEL via an off-ramp without reinstalling. That is the fast lane. It is not a separate product, and it is not a permanent fork of RHEL. The result is your ability to stay on an operating system your team already knows, instead of building the first AI cluster on a placeholder OS and planning to re-engineer it later.
Grace Blackwell was supported in the initial release, and Vera Rubin is the next platform RHEL for NVIDIA is ready for. Built for that moment, 26.03 can take driver and platform enablement for upcoming NVIDIA systems, so the operating system is not a year behind the rack.
The platform above the operating system
The host operating system matters because of the platform that has to run on it. Red Hat OpenShift ships dedicated node payloads built on RHEL for NVIDIA, providing the low-level hardware enablement required for Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization and Red Hat AI to orchestrate workloads and serve high-performance inference on Day 0.
Security is part of the foundation
As mentioned earlier, the rest of the userspace matches RHEL. This means the controls you already use on RHEL are the controls on this edition, including SELinux. You get that baseline on the fast lane, rather than inheriting whatever security posture came with a temporary operating system.
While RHEL is pre-hardened with multiple security capabilities built in to help mitigate risk and exposure, it’s always important to maintain a proactive posture.
Don’t forget to maintain key guardrails when using AI
You wouldn’t hand a contractor your production credentials on their first afternoon. Yet when an AI coding assistant offers a fix to a problem you are dealing with and asks for credentials, it’s very easy to click ‘allow’. 
Clicking the ‘allow’ button just skipped every check you would require of a human contractor. Are they on the roster? Who are they? Who built this, and can we prove it? What are they allowed to touch? Is anyone watching? Can we prove it later? None of that ran. You clicked ‘allow’.
The same scenario can be said about allowing an AI agent access to key information and what actions it can perform with that information.
There is a better path. You can still use the assistant. Give it a narrow policy: read-only access in staging, a short-lived credential, and a limit on where it can send data. The MCP server for RHEL, in developer preview, can add a different guardrail for system troubleshooting: it can require a check before a generated command runs. With those controls in place, your team can still use the assistant, with a smaller set of permissions and a check before a generated command runs.
Leverage new technologies, while maintaining security best practices
The acceptance of cutting a corner with security is often easiest to do on new infrastructure. People are excited to install assistants and plugins in the first week because they want value out of the box. That excitement is what can cloud judgement.
RHEL is pre-hardened with multiple security capabilities built in to help mitigate risk and exposure. These same security capabilities are in RHEL for NVIDIA which is available now. As you deploy next-generation architectures like Vera Rubin, your OS is already waiting—allowing you to innovate at hardware speed on a foundation you can trust.

articles.title: This program is pushing startups to plan for security sooner | BetaKit
articles.text:
Startup founders spend plenty of time thinking about their product, customers, and capital. Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst wants security added to the top of that list.
The Catalyst’s upcoming Cyber for Startups program aims to show that cybersecurity can play an outsized role in the most critical stages of company-building. The no-cost program will offer online and in-person cohorts this fall. Participating early- and mid-stage Canadian technology startups will have access to assessments, workshops, tools, templates, and coaching, all aimed at building security into products, operations, and growth plans, from the beginning.
“Cybersecurity doesn’t have to be overwhelming or prohibitively expensive.”
Charles Finlay,
Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst
“For startups, cybersecurity isn’t just about protecting against threats but about creating opportunities,” said Charles Finlay, founding executive director at Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst. “Strong security practices can help founders win customers’ confidence, attract investment, and compete for larger contracts. When security is treated as an afterthought, startups risk closing doors to opportunities they’ve worked hard to create.”
According to Finlay, strong security practices should be considered part of best practices, as those practices help startups with customer trust, enterprise procurement, investment readiness, and access to regulated markets. It also helps companies avoid technical debt, which becomes more costly to address as they grow. Cyber for Startups is geared toward companies that are building or scaling technology products, preparing to sell into enterprise or regulated markets, or looking to strengthen their cybersecurity posture as they grow. These companies face security expectations across several important parts of the business.
Enterprise buyers and regulators, for example, usually want to understand how a startup protects sensitive information, and often ask about controls, policies, or even SOC 2 attestation. Investors may also scrutinize security practices as part of due diligence. Security can also reach back into product development itself, influencing decisions around architecture and how data is handled within a product.
Cyber for Startups is designed to help companies work through each of those challenges in a structured way. During the program, participants will assess their current security posture, identify gaps, and turn those findings into a tailored, long-term roadmap that details which issues need attention now and which should become a milestone later. Crucially, the program focuses on how to communicate security posture to potential clients, helping founders gain trust even when the work is in progress.
“One of the biggest challenges comes when a startup moves from building a product to selling it,” Finlay added. “Suddenly, prospective customers are asking detailed questions about how their data will be protected, what security controls are in place, and how risks are managed. Founders can find themselves scrambling to meet expectations they hadn’t anticipated. We want to help companies prepare for those conversations well before they’re sitting across the table from a potential customer.”
Cyber for Startups is designed to help founders build security into their product development and go-to-market strategies from the outset because cybersecurity requirements need to inform how a product is built, who it will be sold to, and which markets the company plans to enter. Startups that put off these critical decisions risk accumulating technical debt, leaving them with costly and complex security problems to untangle as the business grows.
“Decisions about how data is collected and stored, who has access to systems, and how security is built into a product can seem relatively minor when a company is small,” Finlay said. “But those decisions become much harder and more expensive to reverse as the business grows. Getting the fundamentals right early on can save founders from having to rebuild critical parts of their technology down the road.”
The program is targeted toward the people making these decisions, including technical founders, product leaders, and executives responsible for compliance, risk, or growth. No prior formal cybersecurity training is required.
Cyber for Startups will be delivered across several cohorts across Canada this fall, both virtually and in person. The first in-person cohort will take place in Brampton, Ont., on Nov. 12, in partnership with the City of Brampton, Brampton Innovation District, and the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange, with funding provided in part by the Government of Ontario. Applications for the Brampton cohort are open until Oct. 30.
“When security is treated as an afterthought, startups risk closing doors to opportunities they’ve worked hard to create.”
Charles Finlay,
Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst
RBC will support two other offerings: an online cohort running through November and December, and an in-person Vancouver cohort scheduled for February. Rolling registration will be available for both.
Offering both formats is intended to make the program more accessible to startups in different regions and stages of growth in Canada. In-person cohorts will run over a single day and prioritize networking and coaching, while the online version spreads the program across four weeks, focusing on roadmapping work.
As startups grow, the financial stakes of cybersecurity can grow with them. Data from the Canadian Internet Registration Authority found that 39 percent of Canadian organizations surveyed this year had experienced a cyber attack in the last 12 months.
The costs of these incidents can also be significant. Statistics Canada’s most recent survey on the topic found that Canadian businesses spent roughly $1.2 billion recovering from cybersecurity incidents in 2023, nearly double the amount reported in 2021.
Cyber for Startups is designed to make security an early decision for founders, before growth turns it into a more expensive one.
“I want founders to leave understanding that they don’t need to have everything figured out on day one, but they do need a plan,” Finlay said. “Cybersecurity doesn’t have to be overwhelming or prohibitively expensive. It’s about understanding your risks, making informed decisions, and taking practical steps as your business grows. That’s exactly what we’re trying to help startups do through this program.”

Build security into your startup from the start. Apply for the next cohort of Cyber for Startups.
Feature image courtesy Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst.
