articles.title: Dyson se proposer d'aspirer et laver en un seul passage avec le V15s Detect Submarine en promo à -33%
articles.text:
Le Dyson V15s Detect Submarine est un aspirateur balai qui aspire et passe aussi la serpillère, que vous retrouvez en promo à 589 euros au lieu de 879 euros sur Fnac.
Le Dyson V15s Detect Submarine marque l'entrée très attendue du constructeur britannique sur le marché des aspirateurs laveurs. Si l'on devait faire une analogie facile, nous dirions que Dyson est aux aspirateurs ce qu'Apple est aux smartphones. Un produit luxueux, haut de gamme, qu'on aime utiliser autant qu'afficher. Ici, il combine l'aspiration cyclonique du V15 avec une tête de lavage à l'eau claire. Comme tout appareil Dyson, son prix de base est onéreux mais il bénéficie de 290 euros de réduction sur Fnac, ce qui peut permettre de sauter plus facilement le pas.
Voici le Dyson V15s Detect Submarine à 589 € au lieu de 879 € sur Fnac
Pourquoi choisir le Dyson V15s Detect Submarine ?
- Pour son aspiration sans compromis typique de Dyson avec une puissance de 240 AW avec une brosse Optic Fluffy pour traquer la poussière invisible à l'œil nu.
- Le lavage efficace des tâches avec la brosse Submarine humidifiée qui vient à bout des tâches incrustées et liquides sur les sols durs.
- Son écosystème modulaire livré avec une pléthore d'accessoires pour passer du nettoyage d'une salle de bain à l'aspiration des poils d'animaux en un clic.
Un nettoyage hybride efficace qui se mérite
Si vous connaissez les Dyson, vous ne serez pas surpris de leur efficacité en aspiration, et ce modèle ne fait pas exception à la règle. Avec sa puissance de 12 500 Pa, il peut aspirer toute la poussière sur son chemin pour l'engranger dans son réservoir de 0,76 l. Ce n'est pas tout puisqu'il est doté d'une tête Submarine qui lave mais attention : elle peut faire l'un ou l'autre, pas les deux en même temps. Et il faut avoir une petite condition physique pour le manier parce qu'il est quand même 4,1 kg et qu'il faut garder en permanence le doigt sur la gâchette. Il est quand même silencieux en mode lavage, avec 60 dB mesurés, ce qui contraste avec l'autonomie de ses petits réservoirs (300 ml d'eau propre) qui imposent des allers-retours fréquents au robinet. Il se destine avant tout aux profils avec des surfaces dures, de taille modérée (environ 40m²) qui ont l'habitude d'aspirer avant de passer la serpillère.
Une approche modulaire face aux aspirateurs tout-en-un
Contrairement aux aspirateurs laveurs massifs comme le Dreame H12 Pro, ce modèle Dyson apporte de la polyvalence en conservant le format passe-partout et les accessoires dédiés d'un aspirateur balai premium : un suceur long, une brosse Digital Motorbar, une mini brosse motorisée auto démêlante et la station murale qui va avec. C'est juste dommage qu'il ne sache pas aspirer et laver en même temps, et que son autonomie ne fasse pas un peu de progrès : 60 minutes en mode Eco, une poignée de minutes en mode Boost. Et il n'y a pas de station d'auto nettoyage, donc ça implique un entretien de votre part.
✅ Les points forts
- Sa puissance d'aspiration de 240 AW sur tous les types de sols
- Son lavage qui vient à bout des tâches aussi bien fraîches qu'incrustées
- Sa polyvalence avec sa panoplie complète d'accessoires
- So niveau sonore maîtrisé et agréable en mode lavage de 60 dB
❌ Les limites
- Impossible d'aspirer et laver en même temps avec la brosse Submarine
- Ses réservoirs d'eau sous-dimensionnés qui poussent à des remplissages fréquents
- Un collecteur d'eau sale mal conçu qui fuit si la brosse est inclinée
- Son poids important et le maintien de la gâchette obligatoire
- Un seul rouleau fourni
L'aspirateur balai laveur Dyson V15s Detect Submarine est bradé à 589 € sur Fnac
Le Dyson V15s Detect Submarine est une bonne affaire si vous êtes fan de la marque et que vous cherchez un modèle capable de ponctuellement laver en profondeur les sols de vos petites pièces. C'est l'outil idéal pour centraliser le matériel d'entretien au sein d'un appartement ou pour un ménage par zone de la maison.
Si vous avez de grandes surfaces carrelées à traiter en une seule passe, les petits réservoirs d'eau vont rendre l'expérience trop fastidieuse. Et un dernier conseil pratique : pensez à bien transporter la brosse Submarine à l'horizontale jusqu'à votre évier : le bac d'eau sale étant ouvert, il risque de fuir s'il est trop incliné quand vous le manipulez.

articles.title: Por qué la IA podría poner fin al futuro de las consolas de PlayStation, Xbox y Nintendo
articles.text:
Las consolas de videojuegos podrían dejar de ser un producto de masas en la próxima década, según un informe de Bloomberg Intelligence, la división de análisis financiero de la agencia estadounidense. El documento sostiene que la inteligencia artificial, lejos de ser ajena al mundo del entretenimiento doméstico, terminará redefiniendo el modo en que millones de personas juegan.
La proyección central es que el mercado de videojuegos a través de streaming o la nube alcanzará los 38.000 millones de dólares en 2035. Ese crecimiento convertiría a las máquinas de sobremesa, como PlayStation, Xbox o Switch, en dispositivos de nicho para una porción menor de usuarios.
Qué se dice sobre el fin de las consolas de videojuegos
El informe, liderado por el analista Nathan Naidu, plantea una paradoja. Las inversiones multimillonarias que las compañías tecnológicas destinan a centros de datos para inteligencia artificial están absorbiendo capacidad de fabricación de memoria y encareciendo los componentes electrónicos en el corto plazo.
Sin embargo, esa misma expansión dejará disponible, con el tiempo, una cantidad mayor de GPU (unidades de procesamiento gráfico). Según Bloomberg Intelligence, ese excedente intensificará la competencia entre los proveedores de cómputo en la nube y reducirá el costo de esos servicios.
El mercado del juego en la nube crecerá porque la infraestructura de IA dejará disponible más capacidad de cómputo, lo que abaratará el acceso a videojuegos sin necesidad de comprar hardware costoso. Esa es la lógica de fondo que atraviesa todo el informe.
A esto se suma otro factor: los títulos AAA exigen cada vez hardware más potente, lo que compromete el rendimiento de las consolas actuales y acorta su vida comercial. Para Bloomberg Intelligence, ese desgaste técnico empuja a los jugadores hacia alternativas de transmisión por internet.
Cómo el precio de las consolas ya refleja la crisis de componentes
El declive proyectado no depende únicamente de una estimación a diez años. Ya existen señales concretas en el mercado actual.
En esta generación, los usuarios debieron afrontar subidas de precio en lugar de las habituales rebajas que suelen acompañar el paso del tiempo. Hoy, comprar una PlayStation 5, una Xbox Series X o S, o una Switch 2 cuesta más que cuando esas máquinas llegaron a las tiendas.
La escasez de memoria, impulsada por el auge de los centros de datos para IA, golpeó directamente a fabricantes como Microsoft y Sony, que debieron ajustar precios de sus consolas durante este año. Todo indica que las próximas generaciones de ambas compañías llegarán con un costo superior al de sus predecesoras.
A ese escenario se suma la desaparición progresiva del formato físico. Sony mantiene su decisión de dejar de fabricar juegos físicos para PlayStation a partir de enero de 2028, lo que deja ese segmento prácticamente en manos de Nintendo, mientras Microsoft refuerza su apuesta por la distribución a través de internet.
Cómo podría cambiar el reemplazo de las consolas
El escenario que describe Bloomberg Intelligence no implica la desaparición inmediata de las consolas, sino un cambio de rol: de puerta de entrada obligatoria al entretenimiento a dispositivo reservado para quienes busquen la mejor experiencia local posible.
El reemplazo vendría de la mano del juego en la nube, un modelo en el que el usuario transmite el videojuego desde servidores remotos sin necesidad de hardware potente en su hogar. La combinación de consolas más caras, fin del formato físico y conexiones de fibra óptica cada vez más veloces configura, según el análisis, un terreno favorable para esa transición.
El antecedente más citado para cuestionar este pronóstico es lo que sucedió con Google Stadia, el servicio de transmisión de videojuegos que la compañía cerró en enero de 2023. Sin embargo, el propio análisis advierte que la coyuntura actual es distinta a la que llevó al cierre de ese servicio.
En aquel momento, la infraestructura de nube para videojuegos resultaba mucho más costosa y la latencia seguía siendo un obstáculo sin resolver. Los recursos de computación en la nube son hoy mayores, y la propia expansión de la IA podría terminar liberando espacio en los centros de datos para servicios como el juego en streaming.
A mediano plazo, el informe no anticipa la desaparición de las consolas de videojuegos. Lo que plantea es un desplazamiento gradual: mientras el hardware físico se encarece y pierde margen de maniobra frente a las exigencias técnicas de los juegos más recientes, la infraestructura de cómputo en la nube avanza en sentido contrario, con costos a la baja y mayor disponibilidad de capacidad de procesamiento.

articles.title: The Key to AI Software Security Isn’t Speed, It’s Maturity
articles.text:
Agentic artificial intelligence software development has all the traits of a summer blockbuster, with the prospects of Godzilla-sized productivity gains thrilling business leaders and security implications sending chills down the spines of developers and SOC teams. One difference, though, is that those thrills and chills are going to last longer than a summer, and the fallout could be a lot more serious than some spilled popcorn.
The proliferation of large language models, whether for software development or general use, alongside both sanctioned tools and shadow AI brought in by employees, is expanding the attack surface too quickly for traditional controls to keep up, particularly with the growing use of agentic AI. And the increased risks are coming home to roost, with Gartner predicting that the costs of incidents driven by agentic AI will increase fourfold through 2027.
The impact of agentic AI is a particularly sharp double-edged sword, with SonarSource noting that the frontier LLMs such as Claude and Gemini that write the best, most functional code also produce the most severe security vulnerabilities.
Organizations are aware of the need to gain control over agentic AI’s risk factors, but the protections implemented so far may well be insufficient. Governance is the go-to concept for reigning in AI-driven software development, and with good reason. It’s critical for maintaining control over what AI agents can and can’t do. Along with the improved observability of AI tool use and commits, this can help organizations limit the risk levels of AI while reaping the rewards of improved productivity.
But governance and Governance only go so far when organizations are in other critical ways still working in the dark regarding security controls. Specifically, they may not know where they are on the ascending scale of AI adoption and as a result may not understand what they need at their current stage. Without a clear understanding of the capabilities of their current AI projects, the risks involved and the level of developer skills required to manage AI, they can fall far short in implementing security best practices. They need a governance plan that fully addresses the new reality of software development.
Know the Different Stages of AI Adoption and Maturity
Organizations can navigate the AI implementation puzzle without losing control of risk management, with the context provided by a three-phase, eight-stage AI Adoption Model that mirrors the steps you’ll take along the AI path, from relatively bare-bones AI assistants performing routine tasks to AI agents capable of initiating and finishing tasks completely on their own.
The model is highly detailed in describing each stage, but to summarize it briefly, it consists of eight observable stages defining activity, risk levels and developer skill requirements across the three phases of AI implementation: AI Assisted, AI Native and Agentic.
Phase 1. AI Assisted
The first phase includes stages 1 (Minimal AI Use) and 2 (Supervised Assistance) and covers organizations in the foothills of AI implementation, using AI models that work directly for developers and present low to moderate risk levels. These early stages are an ideal time to establish governance policies. Developers, meanwhile, should receive upskilling on topics ranging from secure coding to code review, and these skills should be verifiable using a tool to establish baselines and track developer performance.
Phase 2: AI Native
Applying to stages 3 (Unsupervised Assistance) and 4 (AI-Primary Development), this is the phase where developers are allowing AI models to work more on their own without close supervision. Productivity can skyrocket with agents taking advantage of information-sharing standards such as Model Context Protocol (MCP), but risk levels run high. A major risk arises when developers trust AI too much, but tools are available to detect over-trust and track MCP activity. Stage 4 begins the transition from AI Native to Agentic. Developers have become code reviewers rather than authors, a significant shift that requires effective education and upskilling.
Phase 3: Agentic
This phase is what every organization is shooting for, but it comes with risk levels ranging from very high and critical to extreme and maximum. The stages steadily climb the ladder of both capability and risk. At Stage 5 (Single Agent), Command Line Interface (CLI) agents, such as Claude Code or Gemini CLI, perform operations from start to finish on their own. At Stage 6 (Multi-agent Parallel), AI can scale quickly as multiple agents work together. Stage 7 (Scaled Agent Management) takes it to the next level, with multiple agents operating at scale, and Stage 8 (Autonomous Orchestration) requires developers to coordinate agents as a unified team. Developer education should cover policy enforcement, the use of application risk scorecards, and the ability to track commits for audit purposes.
As the progression of these stages makes clear, establishing governance and a comprehensive learning program early on is essential because risk levels can quickly get out of hand as AI agents perform more complex, autonomous and unsupervised operations. Failing to establish a governance foundation early can come back to bite you in a big way.
Fortunately, most developers are somewhere between stages 2 through 4 right now, so it’s not too late for organizations to implement the guardrails, oversight and education programs necessary to manage the entirely new world of the Agentic Development Lifecycle (ADLC).
Where to Start, How to Proceed
As with many a new technology, adoption of AI is running well ahead of organizations’ abilities to secure it. The headlong rush into AI, compounded by unskilled employees bringing their own LLMs into the network without understanding how to manage security assessments or perform contextual reviews, has left organizations lacking visibility into who is using AI, how they are using it and the impact it has on production code. They may be flying fast with AI adoption but in many ways are also flying blind without the oversight, guardrails and developer-level observability they need to ensure that AI is being used safely.
Establishing effective AI governance can feel daunting. Organizations can reasonably ask, “Where do we start?” The answer is to understand where they are in the first place. It helps organizations identify the security controls and developer skill levels needed at their current stage of adoption, as well as what will be required at the next one.
No matter where an organization is in AI adoption, the next level of both capability and risk will arrive faster than expected.

articles.title: 8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
articles.text:
8 eMudhra certificates are compromised. Here's what you need to know
On October 19, 2026, at approximately 17:00 UTC, Cloudflare became aware that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised. These certificates were widely trusted by browsers, operating systems, and also within Cloudflare. Because the keys themselves are weak, an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic. This is a serious security incident with implications across the Internet. For reference, here is a link to more information about how SSL certificates work and why they are so critical to the operation of the Internet.
We immediately prioritized patching critical services across Cloudflare to protect our customers ahead of the public disclosure of the vulnerability. Our security review has not identified active exploitation of this issue on Cloudflare services.
We have released updates for the Cloudflare One Clients, also known as WARP or the 1.1.1.1 app, and Cloudflare Tunnel, also known as cloudflared. We have also deployed mitigations across our CDN, Developer, and Zero Trust products. If you are using Cloudflare Zero Trust with Gateway and an up-to-date client (see below), you are automatically protected.
Our response
We prioritized updating services that use public certificates to authenticate remote endpoints, including proxies connecting to origins and applications calling external APIs. In parallel, we updated shared trust stores, base images, and other shared foundations, providing a common mitigation path for services that inherit their certificate trust from those sources. We paired these updates with reloads, restarts, and image deployments needed to activate them. Applications with bundled or custom trust stores received separate assessment and updates. This work addresses certificate-based authentication, not a weakness in TLS’s encryption algorithms.
Teams across Cloudflare are presently working on further remediation. We are making progress, but there's much work still to be done. Some customers will need to take action on software or trust configurations that they operate, especially on their origin servers. The recommended actions are summarized below.
What customers should do
| Users of these software or services | Action the customer should take | 
| Cloudflare One/WARP | Cloudflare One Client: Upgrade to: v2.5.7 (Android), v1.12.7 (iOS), Windows Desktop (2026.8.2115.0), macOS (2026.8.2115.0), Linux (2026.8.2115.0) 1.1.1.1 app: Upgrade to: v6.38.11 (Android), v6.31.8 (iOS), Windows Desktop (2026.8.2115.0), macOS (2026.8.2115.0), Linux (2026.8.2115.0) | 
| Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) | Upgrade to 2026.10.2. For container deployments, update and redeploy the fixed image | 
| Customer-configured TLS client authentication | Review and update your mutual TLS trust store/uploaded CAs used to verify client certificates | 
| Customer Origin TLS Servers configuration | Review your custom origin certificates and server configurations if using Full (strict) encryption mode or Strict mode. We are updating Automatic SSL/TLS to automatically notify you if you still use these distrusted certificates, which would cause breakages. | 
| Cloudflare Containers | Customers using Cloudflare Containers, including Sandboxes, should review their container images and application dependencies for affected certificate trust stores and apply updates based on your deployed image. Customers can also enable HTTPS egress interception to route outbound HTTPS requests through Cloudflare, moving remote-server certificate validation from the application to Cloudflare-managed infrastructure. This allows Cloudflare’s trust-store mitigations to protect intercepted connections. Containers that have this enabled are already protected. | 
Developer guidance
For developers, look beneath the SDK.
An API client may delegate certificate verification to an HTTP library, a language runtime, the operating system, or a custom trust configuration. Updating the SDK alone may not change the underlying policy.
Once you patch, you may notice certificate errors in your dashboards. It's important to not resolve these errors by disabling verification. That would remove the authentication protection these updates are intended to restore.
This incident affects many software stacks that rely on the WebPKI for authentication. Mozilla’s Dennis Jackson has crowdsourced a list of commonly used packages that have been patched. We advise readers to upgrade as soon as possible. (Note that some of these may be indirect dependencies of your software stack, so look at the dependency tree.) Apply the relevant dependency updates, rebuild affected images, and confirm whether applications require a reload, restart, or redeployment.
Dennis Jackson’s test site provides browser checks, non-browser testing instructions, and package update information. Results apply to the verification path being tested, not every application on the device. Validate through the application’s actual TLS path. A successful browser test does not prove that a background service is protected. Neither does a curl test if the application uses a different verifier.
Timeline
The timeline of events so far is below.
| Date and Time | Event | 
| October 19, approximately 17:00 UTC | Cloudflare becomes aware of the compromise and begins assessment. | 
| October 20, 02:00 UTC | Cloudflare One Client and WARP app security updates published across platforms (except Cloudflare One Agent on iOS, for which app review is still pending). | 
| October 20 09:15 UTC | Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) security update published. | 
| October 20 19:20 UTC | CDN and server-side Zero Trust mitigations fully deployed. | 
Looking forward
The impact of this incident is not felt equally. Browser maintainers were able to remediate the issue with a flip of a switch. They of course have just one application to update, instead of hundreds, but they do have a neat trick up their sleeves: most browsers use quick-revocation mechanisms (like Chrome CRLSets). At Cloudflare we also use such a mechanism for some of our products. To bring it to more systems at Cloudflare and industry, we’re excited about projects like upki that understand a trust store can’t be a static list of root certificate authorities, but needs the ability to be quickly updated with information like revocation and certificate transparency keys.

articles.title: Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
articles.text:
Tesla and SpaceX have formed special committees to discuss a possible merger, Elon Musk said during the latter’s third quarter earnings call Tuesday.
Tesla and SpaceX are discussing a possible merger, Musk says
Musk called the merger “a good idea,” though he cautioned it wasn’t a guarantee.
Musk, who serves as CEO of both companies, said the special committees were formed at the request of shareholders and consist of independent directors (though he did not name them). He also noted that he is not a member of either committee, nor involved in any of the discussions.
“Because I’m a conflicted party, I can’t actually be in the discussions of the special committees,” Musk said. “So it’s an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking and I can’t be in the conversation.”
The groups have not reached agreement on the terms of any transaction — and there’s no guarantee that they will. “At the end of the day, the shareholders have to be supportive of this,” he continued. “And particularly on the Tesla side, we will need a 50 percent vote of all shares, not just those who vote, but of all shareholders. And that’s quite a high hurdle to try to achieve.”
That said, Musk called the possibility of a Tesla-SpaceX merger a “good idea.” He continued:
I do think there’s a lot of merit to combining companies as we are pretty much in the superintelligence singularity. And there’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software, chip design, the TeraFab, obviously robotics, mass to orbit with the Starmind constellation, connectivity. So I think it would be a good idea, but it’s really up to the special committees of both companies. They’ve got to come up with something and then that’s going to be put to the shareholders as a vote.
A Tesla-SpaceX merger would be a blockbuster corporate deal creating a mega-entity valued upwards of $3.6 trillion. But combining Musk’s car and energy company with his AI and rocket company would not be without its tradeoffs. A lot depends on which company absorbs the other. To buy SpaceX, Tesla would have to create millions of new stock shares, which for current Tesla owners would mean owning a smaller slice of a much larger pie. SpaceX’s launch goals require tens of billions of dollars every year — extra spending that could drain Tesla’s ability to build new car factories and battery plants.
That said, most Wall Street analysts and legal experts believe SpaceX would acquire Tesla (or absorb it through a stock swap) rather than vice versa. Since its IPO, SpaceX has maintained a higher valuation than Tesla. A merger in that direction would allow SpaceX shareholders to hold the majority control of the combined mega-entity. Some Tesla shareholders may balk at this deal.
But it would also create one company for those who believe in Musk’s vision of the future — robot cars, humanoid robots, AI super-intelligence, and human habitats on Mars — in which to place their investments. And Tesla shareholder approved Musk’s enormous pay package last year — even after a Delaware judge tossed it over lack of independence.
Earlier this month, Barclays published a client note suggesting a potential Tesla-SpaceX combination could be announced ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting scheduled for December 3, 2026.

articles.title: Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust
articles.text:
Introducing tsrs: A port of TypeScript to Rust
Cloudflare and VoidZero are now working with Max Schwenk of Owner.com on tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler. We are doing this work in close collaboration with the TypeScript team, and incubating tsrs as part of the Oxc JavaScript compiler toolchain.
Our goal is to help developers spend less time waiting for their code to be checked and more time building. Making TypeScript faster and more memory-efficient also helps bring complete development environments to more places, including right in your browser.
To be clear, we are not forking TypeScript. We believe the TypeScript team should remain in full control of the language’s design and direction. They have maintained a long-term vision while guiding TypeScript’s adoption across the JavaScript community. We do not want to change that.
The TypeScript team can move quite fast on many things, but for some features they may spend years intentionally exploring options and making prototypes before picking the right implementation. A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible. We have to preserve the TypeScript language strictly based on its original implementation – and the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like.
Performance and memory improvements
Early benchmarks of our Rust port of TypeScript are promising: tsrs is up to 8x faster and uses ~70% less memory compared to TypeScript 7.0 when using the same number of type check workers:
As you can see, the next version of TypeScript already brings many performance improvements, making TypeScript 7.1 beta up to 2.5x faster than TypeScript 7.0. Some of these optimizations were upstreamed from tsrs, and we’re hoping to find more.
You may have seen recent benchmarks of different TypeScript ports with various performance claims, often due to using larger machine types and different options compared to TypeScript’s defaults. We worked with the TypeScript team to ensure the above benchmarks are comparing the same configuration.
By default, tsrs ships with an adaptive configuration dependent on the machine type that uses more memory but is even faster:
Try tsrs
TypeScript in Rust aims to be a faithful port of TypeScript. You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm:
npm install tsrs
npx tsrs
Why now?
We’ve seen many attempts at porting TypeScript to other languages over the years. Because of the complexity involved, only one of the ports succeeded: the TypeScript team’s port of TypeScript from JavaScript to Go.
However, frontier AI models can now do large-scale ports almost independently in a matter of days. We have now seen slopforks, faithful ports, and completely re-architected versions of TypeScript in Rust or C++. There is clearly a demand for even faster TypeScript.
Why Rust?
You might be thinking: “TypeScript’s Go port already made TypeScript 10x faster and far more memory efficient than the previous version written in TypeScript. Why isn’t that enough?”
However, it’s not just about speed. Rust offers some unique advantages: running in WebAssembly. The Rust + Wasm story has always been strong, and one of the reasons comes down to the fundamentals of Rust’s language design. When you compile a Go program to Wasm, you have to compile Go’s garbage collector along with it. But Rust’s memory management model enables straightforward memory interactions between a WebAssembly guest and host. This is one of the key things that makes Rust a much better fit for the WebAssembly use-case: memory efficiency.
Cloudflare Workers have supported Wasm for a long time. Just a few weeks ago we announced supporting native Rust in Workers with the new Emscripten target for wasm-bindgen. When you run entire software build and deployment systems in tight loops on Workers, the benefits of a small memory footprint pay off quickly. It means you can run these workloads so efficiently that it’s now possible to run fully encapsulated development systems in places where they couldn’t have been run before.
This enables new possibilities when combined with agents: You are now able to run a development toolchain end-to-end in a fully sandboxed environment on Cloudflare. But with Wasm, you can also run those environments safely client-side in your browser, or on an embedded device, or an IoT application.
How will the tsrs port be maintained?
First, we are working with Theo Browne to merge tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package that supports all of TypeScript’s features including Language Server Protocol (LSP) and content mappers. Second, we’ve seen a lot of success with how we maintain Vinext in sync with its upstream, Next.js. We explained how we do this in a recent blog post:
Each morning, an agent reviews the changes, fetches diffs, and opens tracking issues for anything that could affect Vinext. Every night, the compatibility matrix is regenerated as we run the Next.js test suite against Vinext. When one of these tests or issues reveals a gap, agents are now in the position where they can identify the change across both codebases, build a reproduction, port any relevant tests, and propose a fix.
We will apply the same process to TypeScript, taking extreme care that we don’t introduce diverging behaviors from upstream TypeScript. When we come across performance improvements, we’ll attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase so everyone wins.
Finally, we recognize that there are some differences to the upstream version of TypeScript right now, like for example the order in which diagnostics are printed. We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release.
What’s next?
Cloudflare is already the home of many free and open source Rust tools that power the JavaScript ecosystem, such as Vite, Rolldown, Oxlint, and Oxfmt. With more than 10 million developers building on Cloudflare, we care a lot about making the underlying developer toolchain faster, more portable, and easier to run in more places. We are excited to experiment with deeper tsrs integrations into our stack, for example for type-aware lint rules in Oxlint.
Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project — without getting in the way of TypeScript itself. The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable. We know the TypeScript team is taking this seriously – they are experimenting with memory and performance improvements for tsc. We are excited to collaborate with the TypeScript team and the JavaScript community to build the best and fastest implementations of TypeScript together.

articles.title: Here’s the tea
articles.text:
Here’s the tea
An MIT historian uncovers the true origins of an artifact once thought to be a relic of the Boston Tea Party.
When Tristan Brown, an associate professor of history at MIT, first examined a Chinese tea chest label displayed at Old South Meeting House, he had no reason to doubt its story. Descendants of the Boston blacksmith Thomas Wells had donated the label in 1987, saying it had been recovered after colonial protesters threw tea into Boston Harbor in 1773.
But after a year of research, Brown reached a different conclusion: The label was made nearly a century later. The decisive clue came when he read the Chinese text in Cantonese rather than Mandarin, as previous scholars had done. He found that the characters had been used phonetically, in slightly variant forms across contemporary sources, to represent the name of Smith, Archer & Co., a US firm that acquired Asian tea for shipment to American markets during the 1860s and 1870s.
Working with the Wells family, he traced the label to a relative who traveled from Michigan to California during the Gold Rush era before returning and operating a business known as the California Tea Store. Brown argues that claims for its revolutionary pedigree probably developed later, amid the centennial commemorations of the 1870s.
The discovery does not make the label historically insignificant, he says. Instead, what began as an inquiry into a supposed artifact of the Boston Tea Party became a study of how ordinary objects acquire historical authority, and how historical memory itself is made.
“History is never finished,” he says. “Even objects that have sat in museums for decades can reveal entirely new stories when we ask new questions.”

articles.title: OPINION: Europe needs more than just successful exits | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The acquisition of Berlin-based Talon.One by Dutch payments provider Adyen in July 2026 offers a useful perspective on European technology investing. A company founded in Germany developed technology valuable to a global payments business, and its next chapter is being written within Europe. This is a significant outcome for the founders and investors. However, it also raises a larger question: how can Europe turn individual successes into an ecosystem capable of producing them repeatedly?
The answer is not simply to encourage more European acquisitions. Successful startups need access to the best opportunities available, whether their future lies with a European buyer, an international technology group or the public markets. What matters is that these decisions reflect commercial potential rather than a lack of viable alternatives. For Europe, the challenge is to create the conditions in which successful companies can scale, attract investment and generate lasting economic value.
Exits are a measure of maturity, not the final destination
From a venture capital perspective, exits matter because they return capital to investors and founders, establish reference points for valuations, and help to finance the next generation of start-ups. Therefore, an acquisition is more than just the end of an investment cycle. The wider impact of an acquisition depends on whether experienced founders start again, whether employees launch new businesses, whether investors reinvest, and whether specialist knowledge remains accessible to the local ecosystem.
The Talon.One transaction is particularly interesting in this respect. Adyen paid €750 million for the loyalty and incentives platform, combining complementary European technologies together in a business with international reach. The company’s founders also reinvested some of their proceeds in Adyen shares. This is one possible model for maintaining continuity, although the long-term consequences for jobs, innovation and further investment will only become apparent over time.
Yet a European buyer does not automatically guarantee a better outcome. An acquisition by a US technology group can also give European innovation access to new markets, capital and expertise. The relevant questions concern what happens after the transaction: where future investment takes place, whether technological capabilities continue to develop and how much value flows back into the startup ecosystem. While the identity of the buyer is important, the industrial logic and long-term consequences also deserve equal attention.
Germany’s progress reveals the next challenge
Germany is a useful test case for Europe’s progress. According to the German Startup Monitor 2026, the country added ten unicorns in 2026, indicating that more companies are achieving significant valuations. Yet 62% of respondents considering a stock market listing favour the US. These figures measure different things, but together they capture a tension: Germany is producing ambitious technology companies while many founders still see stronger exit opportunities outside its domestic market.
This preference is not irrational. Founders and their investors have a responsibility to consider factors such as access to capital, market depth, suitable buyers, and prospects for future growth. US markets can offer genuine advantages. Rather than persuading companies to reject opportunities abroad, Europe needs to build more competitive options.
This is important long before a potential exit. Investors assess the availability of future funding and realistic exit routes when deciding whether to back a company. If these options appear limited, promising businesses may struggle to attract the necessary capital to reach their full potential. Therefore, a stronger exit environment can support investment across the entire startup lifecycle.
What a stronger European exit market would require
Three priorities stand out:
- Deeper growth capital: European startups need access to substantial later-stage funding and patient institutional investors, without having to reshape their strategy around capital availability elsewhere. This would also give founders greater flexibility over when and how they pursue an exit.
- More strategic buyers: Acquisitions can provide distribution, customers and resources for expansion. Talon.One and Adyen illustrate the potential of cross-border European combinations. A broader base of established technology companies willing to acquire and develop innovative businesses would create additional exit opportunities.
- Earlier exit planning: Founders should consider which investors could fund the next round, which buyers could offer strategic value, and the potential impact of a transaction on teams, research and future ventures. Investor nationality alone is no substitute for that assessment.
The objective is choice
Europe’s ambition should not be to keep every company, every shareholder or every exit within its borders. International capital and global customers are essential for building competitive businesses. In my experience, a European startup acquired by a US company can still create substantial value for its founders, employees and investors, and a European acquisition can likewise bolster a regional technology group.
The more meaningful test is whether European founders have real alternatives, such as sufficient capital to scale up, credible paths to public markets and a strong base of strategic acquirers and investors who can recycle returns into new ventures.
Successful exits show what European technology can achieve. A mature ecosystem makes those successes less exceptional. This requires a joint effort by founders, investors, established companies and policymakers alike.
Editor’s note: IRIS was an investor in Talon.One.

articles.title: Drei Monate statt drei Jahre: Dieser Entwickler ließ 15 KI-Agenten im Schlaf für sich programmieren
articles.text:
Wie ein Entwickler mit 15 KI-Agenten einen digitalen Zwilling von Genf baute
Der Schweizer Entwickler Arnaud Ricci hat seit Juli 2026 in seiner Freizeit mit Genève 3D einen digitalen Zwilling des Kantons Genf aufgebaut. Die interaktive Browser-Anwendung bildet nicht nur Gebäude, Straßen und Bäume dreidimensional ab, sondern stellt auch fahrende Straßenbahnen, Züge, Flugzeuge sowie das aktuelle Wetter dar.
Eigentlich wollte Ricci lediglich das Liniennetz der Genfer Verkehrsbetriebe nachbauen, wie das in Lausanne ansässige Fachmagazin ICT-Journal berichtet. Dass daraus innerhalb von rund drei Monaten ein kantonsweites Modell hervorging, führt der Entwickler auf den Einsatz von KI-Agenten zurück, ohne die ein solches Vorhaben nach seiner Einschätzung zwei bis drei Jahre gedauert hätte.
Claude von Anthropic im Schichtbetrieb: Wie Arnaud Ricci 15 KI-Agenten steuert
Für die Entwicklungsarbeit testete Ricci zunächst verschiedene Sprachmodelle von OpenAI und dem ebenfalls im kalifornischen San Francisco ansässigen KI-Unternehmen Anthropic. Schließlich entschied er sich vor allem für Anthropics Modell Claude und zog andere Systeme nur noch punktuell heran, um die gelieferten Ergebnisse gegenzuprüfen.
Bei der Programmierung schrieb Ricci den Code meist nicht mehr selbst, sondern gab die Ziele vor, woraufhin ein leitender KI-Agent die Aufgaben in Teilschritte zerlegte und an untergeordnete Agenten verteilte. „Im Grunde habe ich wie ein Manager gearbeitet“, sagte der Entwickler dem Fachmagazin und verwies darauf, dass zeitweise bis zu 15 Agenten gleichzeitig arbeiteten, selbst während er schlief.
Ohne menschliche Nachkontrolle funktioniert dieser Ansatz allerdings nicht, zumal Fehlentscheidungen bei autonomen KI-Agenten von Anthropic und OpenAI schnell zu Folgeschäden im Code führen können. Zwar überprüfen die Agenten ihre Arbeit anhand von Bildschirmfotos selbst, doch das zeitliche Verhalten von Echtzeit-Animationen oder komplexe Schattenwürfe lassen sich über Standbilder kaum beurteilen.
Ricci musste die grafische Darstellung deshalb immer wieder selbst kontrollieren und über angepasste Anweisungen nachbessern lassen. Damit die Agenten behobene Fehler bei späteren Arbeitsschritten nicht wiederholen, hält er jedes gelöste Problem schriftlich für künftige Durchläufe fest und unterzieht den Programmcode vor der Veröffentlichung automatisierten Tests sowie Sicherheitsprüfungen.
Open Data in Genève 3D: Datenströme von Meteoschweiz, Nasa und Eumetsat
Die inhaltliche Basis der Plattform bilden frei verfügbare Datensätze von mehr als 15 Behörden und Institutionen, die in der Dokumentation von Genève 3D aufgeschlüsselt sind. Neben dem Genfer Geoinformationssystem SITG und dem freien Kartenprojekt Openstreetmap bezieht die Anwendung unter anderem Daten vom Schweizer Bundesamt für Meteorologie und Klimatologie (Meteoschweiz) in Zürich, vom Bundesamt für Landestopografie (Swisstopo) im bernischen Wabern, von der europäischen Wettersatelliten-Organisation EUMETSAT im südhessischen Darmstadt sowie von der US-Raumfahrtbehörde Nasa.
Bei der Zusammenführung dieser Quellen zeigten sich jedoch deutliche Hürden, weil viele Streckenverläufe des öffentlichen Nahverkehrs ursprünglich nur für flache 2D-Karten gedacht waren und mithilfe von Openstreetmap für das 3D-Gelände überarbeitet werden mussten. Zudem verfügen die dargestellten Busse, Straßenbahnen und Züge über keine Live-Ortung per GPS: Ihre Positionen werden lediglich aus den offiziellen Fahrplänen und den gemeldeten Verspätungen errechnet, weshalb sich die Karte nicht für die reale Reiseplanung eignet.
Erschwerend kommt hinzu, dass die beteiligten Stellen ihre Daten in völlig unterschiedlichen Abständen aktualisieren, die von wenigen Minuten bei Gewitter- und Verkehrsdaten bis zu mehreren Monaten bei Gebäudegeometrien reichen. Um unnötige Rechenprozesse zu vermeiden, baute Ricci zusammen mit seinen KI-Agenten eine Prüfroutine, die vor einer Neuberechnung der 3D-Ebenen kontrolliert, ob sich ein Datensatz tatsächlich inhaltlich verändert hat oder ob der Anbieter lediglich das Datum erneuert hat.
Three.js im Browser: Hohe Hardware-Last und historische Ansicht Genève 1850
Damit das Modell ohne Zusatzsoftware direkt im Webbrowser läuft, entwickelte Ricci eine eigene Javascript-Engine auf Grundlage der freien Grafikbibliothek Three.js. Weil die Anwendung mit wachsendem Funktionsumfang unübersichtlich zu werden drohte, musste er das Grundgerüst des Programmcodes mehrfach umbauen.
Um die eigenen Server zu entlasten, lädt die Plattform benötigte Daten nach Bedarf herunter, legt bis zu 80 Megabyte an Gebäudegeometrien lokal im Browser ab und überlässt die Grafikberechnung vollständig dem Endgerät der Nutzer:innen. Dieser Ansatz spart zwar Betriebskosten für den Entwickler, führt aber auf Smartphones und leistungsschwächeren Computern schnell zu einer hohen Hardware-Last, weshalb für solche Geräte eine optisch deutlich reduzierte Qualitätsstufe nötig ist.
Beim Datenschutz verzichtet die Seite auf Cookies und externe Analyse-Dienste und nutzt stattdessen einen eigenen Zähler, der weder IP-Adressen noch eingegebene Suchbegriffe erfasst. Während die Plattform derzeit vor allem zum Erkunden dient, sieht Ricci künftige Einsatzmöglichkeiten im Unterricht, im Tourismus oder in der Stadtplanung, wo Behörden geplante Bauprojekte und geänderte Verkehrsführungen für Bürger:innen vorab im 3D-Modell sichtbar machen könnten.
Parallel zur Gegenwartskarte hat Ricci mit Genève 1850 auch das historische Stadtrelief des Genfer Architekten Auguste Magnin als begehbare Simulation mit Fußgänger:innen und Pferdekutschen neu umgesetzt. Das ursprüngliche Digitalprojekt der Stadt Genf lief im längst eingestellten Flash Player des kalifornischen Softwareherstellers Adobe und war in modernen Browsern nicht mehr abrufbar. In Riccis Neuauflage lässt sich das Modell wie auch die aktuelle Stadtkarte kostenfrei im Browser sowie versuchsweise mit Virtual-Reality-Brillen der Facebook-Mutter Meta aus dem kalifornischen Menlo Park betrachten.

articles.title: Reaction Dynamics plans rapid expansion to launch new medium-lift rocket by 2031
articles.text:
Reaction Dynamics is looking to raise hundreds of millions in funding and add nearly 300 employees over the next five years to send a new, more powerful rocket toward the stars.
At the SpaceBound Conference in Ottawa on Tuesday morning, the Longueuil, Que.-based rocket maker revealed its plans to develop and send a new medium-lift rocket to space by 2031. Dubbed Borealis, the medium-lift rocket is the larger sibling of Reaction Dynamics’ light-lift Aurora rocket. While Aurora is meant for payloads below half a tonne, Borealis is designed to haul a six-tonne payload to low Earth orbit for larger spacecraft deployments, satellite constellation launches, and other large space missions, similar to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”
SpaceX’s rocket is so popular for shipping satellites to space that it’s started turning away customers past 2028. This has opened the door for Canada’s burgeoning space industry, including Reaction Dynamics. The company said it’s already signed 10 agreements and letters of intent with undisclosed prospective launch customers across Canada, the United States, and Europe.
“We see an opportunity to serve Canadian demand while providing additional dedicated launch capacity for customers in the United States, Europe, and allied countries,” Jesse Mikelberg, Reaction Dynamics’ director of business development and strategy, said in an email to BetaKit. “As a result, customers would have greater control over their launch schedule and destination orbit.”
To give those prospective customers a ride to space, Reaction Dynamics has set some big-time goals. First, the company wants to launch Aurora into orbit from Canadian soil by 2028. The company will then build on that base of manufacturing investments, equipment, processes, and expertise to get Borealis into space by 2031, Mikelberg explained.
“Aurora will give us flight experience and practical knowledge of manufacturing, transporting, integrating, and launching an orbital vehicle,” Mikelberg said. “It will also help us establish customer relationships, spaceport operations, and credibility through execution.”
While Mikelberg makes it sound simple, it is literally rocket science. This requires a lot of manpower and capital. Reaction Dynamics is planning for a large influx of both.
Over the next five years, the company aims to increase its headcount from 68 employees to 350. To accommodate all the new staff, Reaction Dynamics is also looking to increase its manufacturing and testing footprint from 60,000 square feet to 375,000 square feet. The company sees a “strong foundation” for this expansion in Québec, Mikelberg said, but it’s also eyeing land in Ontario or Nova Scotia.
RELATED: First Canada, then the world: nation’s rocket builders see a bigger opening in space
Expanding a business like this, let alone one that builds rockets, isn’t cheap. Reaction Dynamics is planning to raise around $350 million CAD in new private investment across two rounds over the next five years: a Series B targeting between $70 million and 100 million CAD to support Aurora’s first orbital launch in 2028, and then a Series C, or a similar funding instrument, targeting between $200 million and 250 million CAD to aid development for Borealis’ first launch in 2031.
This funding would come in addition to the $50 million Reaction Dynamics has already raised to date from private investors and non-dilutive government funding sources.
“Our approach is to broaden the investor base as we demonstrate propulsion performance, establish manufacturing capacity, secure customers, and gain flight experience,” Mikelberg said.
Founded in 2017, Reaction Dynamics has been building rocket propulsion systems since long before space became one of the “key sovereign capabilities” in the federal government’s Defence Industrial Strategy. Under the DIS, the 2025 federal budget committed $182.6 million over three years to the Department of National Defence (DND) to establish a sovereign space launch capability.
Reaction Dynamics benefitted from Canada’s renewed focus on space earlier this year when the company was awarded an $8.3 million grant under the first round of the DND’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security (IDEaS) Launch the North contest to build out its rocket launch capabilities. Reaction’s younger Canadian rocket-building peers, Canada Rocket Company and NordSpace, also received that funding.
The IDEaS funding was announced alongside the federal government signing a $200 million lease with Maritime Launch Services to establish a government spaceport in Nova Scotia. Reaction Dynamics has also invested in MLS, and its spaceport just outside Canso, NS, is the planned location for Aurora’s first orbital launch.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” Reaction Dynamics founder and CEO Bachar Elzein said in a statement. “Aurora is how we get there in 2028. Borealis is how we build on that foundation to deliver medium lift by 2031. Nearly a decade of propulsion development and engineering, right here in Quebec, has brought us to this point.”
CLARIFICATION (10/20/2026): This story has been updated to note Jesse Mikelberg’s current title.
Feature image courtesy Reaction Dynamics.

articles.title: Android Auto : Gemini peut fouiller dans vos mails et photos, mais pas en France — Frandroid
articles.text:
Vous l’avez sans doute constaté, les écrans prennent une place de plus en plus grande dans notre vie. On pense aux smartphones, qui sont omniprésents, mais ce n’est pas tout. Dans nos voitures aussi, les dalles numériques sont partout, et elles sont de plus en plus imposantes. Trouver son chemin, régler la climatisation ou la ventilation : tout ou presque passe par l’écran tactile, ce qui n’est pas l’idéal en roulant.
Google veut aller un peu plus loin avec une nouvelle fonctionnalité, dévoilée ce mardi 20 octobre. La firme américaine propose depuis novembre dernier son intelligence artificielle Gemini dans certaines voitures. C’est le cas chez Renault et Volvo, mais aussi bientôt chez Xpeng et Geely. Elle est aussi déjà présente sur les smartphones fonctionnant sous Android. Mais voilà que la société californienne franchit une nouvelle étape, comme elle l’indique sur son site officiel.
Baptisée Personal Intelligence, cette fonctionnalité a été lancée en janvier aux États-Unis dans l’application Gemini, comme le détaillait Numerama. Elle permet à l’assistant d’aller fouiller dans les applications Google associées au compte du conducteur. La liste comprend Maps, Photos, YouTube et la recherche Google, mais aussi l’écosystème Workspace, dont Gmail ou Agenda. Mais quel est réellement l’intérêt ? Google en met deux en avant.
Deux usages mis en avant par Google
Tout d’abord, ce nouveau système est capable d’aller chercher une information précise dans un mail, une photo ou un lieu enregistré dans Google Maps, afin de répondre plus précisément à une question. Ensuite, Gemini est capable d’assurer un « raisonnement à partir de sources complexes », en croisant plusieurs de ces informations pour répondre à une seule demande. Google cite quelques exemples assez parlants : vous pouvez demander à l’assistant de vous trouver un restaurant sur votre itinéraire qui correspond à vos habitudes (végétarien, par exemple), ou encore de vous guider jusqu’à votre rendez-vous chez le médecin, sans avoir à chercher l’adresse.
En lisant vos mails, l’IA sait à quelle heure est votre rendez-vous, et à quelle adresse. Mieux encore, cette dernière peut analyser votre galerie d’images pour répondre à des demandes complexes telles que « trouve la station de lavage auto de la photo que j’ai prise la semaine dernière et lance l’itinéraire ». Sur la route de l’aéroport, une seule question suffit aussi pour connaître sa porte d’embarquement, tirée du mail de confirmation, et savoir si le vol part à l’heure. Côté confidentialité, Google précise que Personal Intelligence n’accède qu’aux applications que vous avez autorisées : rien n’est connecté tant que vous n’avez pas activé la fonction, et elle se coupe à tout moment dans les réglages de Gemini.
Les véhicules équipés de Google intégré, eux, « ne partagent des réponses personnalisées que lorsque vous êtes à bord et que votre téléphone est connecté ». Personal Intelligence est déployée depuis ce mardi, d’abord sur Android Auto. Puis, elle arrivera sur les véhicules équipés de Google intégré au cours des prochains mois. Si vous avez déjà activé Personal Intelligence dans l’application Gemini, la fonction vous suit automatiquement en voiture ; sinon, il faut l’activer dans les réglages de Gemini.
Les conducteurs français devront en revanche patienter. En bas de son annonce, Google précise que Personal Intelligence n’est pas proposée dans l’Espace économique européen, en Suisse, au Royaume-Uni ni au Nigeria. Ailleurs, elle est réservée aux comptes Google personnels des plus de 18 ans, les comptes Workspace professionnels ou scolaires étant exclus. En France, Gemini reste bien utilisable dans Android Auto, mais sans ces réponses personnalisées, et Google n’a donné aucune date pour l’Europe.

articles.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, and covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from U.S. government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the U.S. and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.
China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.
The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.
Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.
The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off of Nvidia shares.
The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.
In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

articles.title: Fausses cagnottes : attention aux arnaques qui profitent des pillages du 17 octobre
articles.text:
Les pillages survenus ce week-end à travers la France ont laissé un certain nombre de commerçants complètement dévastés. Marchandises volées, investissements partis en fumée, vitrines cassées, agressions physiques : les conséquences sont lourdes pour les commerçants touchés, qui doivent désormais faire face aux dégâts, aussi bien matériels que psychologiques. Face à cette situation, les cagnottes de soutien se sont multipliées. Certaines ont été mises en place par les commerçants eux-mêmes, tandis que d’autres sont mises en ligne à l’initiative de personnes désirant aider. Malheureusement, certains lancent aussi de fausses cagnottes, autrement dit, des arnaques.
Des escrocs profitent de la détresse des commerçants
Un gérant d’un magasin Micromania situé à Nice a été victime de pilleurs. Il a été agressé physiquement, tandis que son magasin a été pillé et ses vitrines cassées. Face aux images de l’agression et du pillage, mais aussi du courage dont l’homme a fait preuve, plusieurs personnes ont lancé des cagnottes afin de lui venir en aide. Cependant, le gérant a alerté sur la prolifération de fausses cagnottes en ligne.
Il explique dans une story Instagram : « Mon équipe et moi, on est très touchés par le soutien, merci pour ce que vous faites. Maintenant, je vois des cagnottes en ligne, je ne suis au courant de rien, personne ne m’a contacté, elles ne sont pas de mon fait. Prenez soin de vous. Évitez ce genre d’arnaque, ne vous faites pas avoir. Pour le moment, rien n’est fait. Si vous voulez de mes nouvelles, peut-être que j’en donnerai ici ».
Le problème est que nous n’avons aucune garantie que l’argent versé sur une cagnotte en ligne non officielle sera bel et bien reversé à un commerçant en difficulté. Un escroc peut profiter de l’empathie des personnes pour tout simplement détourner les fonds collectés. À noter que le gérant du magasin Micromania a depuis sa dernière story Instagram validé une cagnotte officielle (et sûre) disponible ici.
Comment éviter les fausses cagnottes en ligne ?
Si vous désirez aider un commerçant impacté par les pillages de ce week-end, le premier réflexe à adopter est d’aller sur l’un de ses moyens de communication officiels (page Instagram, site web, compte Facebook, etc.). Si un commerçant n’en propose aucun, vérifiez l’identité du bénéficiaire et l’origine de la collecte. Pour rappel, le fait qu’une collecte soit hébergée sur une plateforme connue (Leetchi, GoFundMe, etc.) ne constitue en aucun cas une garantie absolue de fiabilité.
Méfiez-vous également des collectes dont le créateur reste anonyme, dont l’utilisation des fonds est floue ou qui ne fournissent aucun élément permettant de vérifier le lien avec le commerçant concerné.

articles.title: Après avoir vendu sa maison, une famille française transforme un bus en véhicule électrique alimenté par des batteries de Tesla pour voyager partout dans le monde
articles.text:
Après avoir vendu sa maison, une famille française transforme un bus en véhicule électrique alimenté par des batteries de Tesla pour voyager partout dans le monde
Rien ne se perd, tout se transforme. Et la famille Guillemot nous le rappelle avec son bus électrique alimenté par trois batteries Tesla. C’est la famille Guillemot qui a créé Chouchou, un bus électrique qui stocke 225 kWh dans trois batteries Tesla. Résultat, 90 mètres² de panneaux solaires pour le trajet comme la maison. Un projet lancé après la pandémie de coronavirus qui accompagne leur vie nomade.
Chouchou utilise le moteur d’une Tesla Model S Performance et l’énergie est stockée dans trois batteries de Model 3 Long Range pour un total de 225 kWh. Quant au bus qui transporte la famille (Jean-Philippe et Laure avec leurs enfants Clara et Lisa) appelé Chouchou, il s’agit d’un Temsa Safari de 12 mètres de long, 2,50 mètres de large et 3,85 mètres de haut. Autrefois, il était équipé d’un moteur diesel de 12 litres pour une consommation de 35 litres aux 100 km.
Des batteries Tesla pour alimenter ce bus électrique
C’est finalement en 2022 que la famille Guillemot modifie ce véhicule pour le transformer en bus électrique. Mais tout ne fut pas aisé. En 2022, un premier moteur de Tesla utilisé est tombé en panne après 250 km à cause d’une erreur électrique. Il a fallu un mois de réparation.
Pour l’autonomie, les trois batteries Tesla permettent de parcourir 400 km sur un terrain plat à vitesse modérée selon la famille. La famille Guillemot a ajouté 90 mètres² de panneaux solaires pour réduire sa dépendance aux bornes de recharge.
Quand le bus est garé, deux grandes parties se déploient pour laisser place à ces panneaux solaires. La production atteint environ 16 kW quand les conditions sont idéales. Lors des premiers voyages de la famille Guillemot, une seule journée ensoleillée permettait de récupérer environ 37 % de batterie.
La réserve d’énergie alimente aussi la maison de 30 mètres² avec douche, WC, cuisine équipée d’un four et d’un lave-vaisselle, lave-linge et sèche-linge. Bref, la totale, avec un espace de travail qui complète l’ensemble. Il y a également de petites chambres pour que chacun ait son espace privé et son propre couchage.
La famille Guillemot a aussi décoré sa maison avec des meubles trouvés lors de leurs voyages, comme un canapé à Montpellier et des meubles à Barcelone. Mais bien évidemment, cette totale liberté en bus électrique a demandé beaucoup de travail.
La famille compte transmettre son expérience
Jean-Philippe Guillemot, le père de la famille, est un autodidacte et a fait lui-même la plupart des travaux de conversion. Parmi les installations effectuées, la récupération d’énergie au freinage et une prise pour les bornes. Si le soleil permet une grande partie de l’alimentation, la recharge permet de repartir quand la météo n’est pas idéale.
Et ce bus électrique personnalisé a beaucoup voyagé entre la France, mais aussi le Maroc, l’Italie, la Grèce, la Turquie, la Bulgarie et la Roumanie. À l’automne 2026, le couple prévoit un nouveau départ vers une destination après un an stationné à Toulouse. Quant aux deux enfants, elles sont étudiantes et ne prévoient plus de suivre le prochain trajet.
Le père de la famille Guillemot prépare également un second véhicule électrique et solaire sous la forme d’un chantier collectif. Le but est de transmettre quatre années d’apprentissage et de voyages à d’autres personnes pour convertir un poids lourd diesel en habitation électrique et solaire.

articles.title: Sans Huawei, que reste-t-il à la marque Aito pour conquérir l’Europe ? - Numerama
articles.text:
Présente au Mondial de l’automobile de Paris 2026, la marque chinoise Aito s’est fait remarquer avec son stand XXL, l’un des trois plus grands du salon. La marque ambitionne un lancement en Europe à l’automne 2027. Il y aurait cependant un grand changement entre les modèles proposés en Chine et ceux disponibles dans les pays européens : la technologie Huawei serait absente.
Selon les médias chinois, comme Carnewschina le 20 octobre 2026, la marque n’embarquerait pas les technologies de conduite autonome et de cockpit signées Huawei, mais celles de Bosch. Sans les technologies Huawei qui ont contribué à son succès en Chine, que reste-t-il à Aito pour convaincre les automobilistes européens ?
« Huawei inside » en Chine contre « Bosch inside » en Europe
La notoriété de la marque Aito – dont le nom signifie « Adding Intelligence To Auto » (littéralement, ajouter de l’intelligence à l’automobile) – repose presque intégralement en Chine sur son intégration des technologies Huawei. Le constructeur Seres, derrière la marque Aito, a choisi une autre approche pour son expansion européenne.
Les futures Aito 6, 7, 8 et 9 feront l’impasse sur les logiciels et matériels signés Huawei. À la place, Seres se serait associé à l’équipementier allemand Bosch pour développer les aides à la conduite (ADAS), le cockpit intelligent et la gestion du châssis.
Sur le papier, cette décision industrielle apparaît logique. En s’appuyant sur Bosch, la marque s’assure que les ADAS de ses modèles sont correctement calibrées pour nos routes. Cela permet aussi à la marque de montrer patte blanche en impliquant un équipementier local. Mais que reste-t-il à Aito pour se démarquer des autres concurrents chinois ?
Aito a-t-elle encore un avantage concurrentiel ?
En Chine, ce qui a permis à Aito de vendre des véhicules à plus de 300 000 yuans (plus de 40 000 euros) et de rivaliser avec d’autres acteurs premium, ce n’est ni le design, ni la conception technique du modèle par Seres. C’était l’écosystème HarmonyOS développé par Huawei, ainsi que toutes les technologies de conduite autonome avancée et l’image de marque du géant de la tech.
Aito est l’une des réussites de l’alliance Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance (HIMA) avec Huawei comme moteur du succès. En retirant la technologie Huawei pour la remplacer par celle de Bosch, Aito perd son unique facteur de différenciation. Sur un marché ultra-concurrentiel pour les nouveaux entrants, la marque se retrouve un peu le bec dans l’eau : sans image de marque, sans réseau et sans l’argument tech qui fait sa force en Chine.
On peut néanmoins imaginer que les solutions développées en Chine par Huawei ne fonctionnent pas correctement en Europe, et que le choix de l’équipementier Bosch, qui équipe de très nombreux constructeurs occidentaux, évite la catastrophe de systèmes inadaptés.
Aito, une marque fragilisée en Chine
Il n’y a pas que dans le cadre de son expansion européenne que la relation entre Seres et Huawei a du plomb dans l’aile. La relation entre les deux marques s’est déjà considérablement refroidie en Chine. Alors que le rôle de Huawei a toujours été plus que celui de simple équipementier technologique, la situation a changé le 15 septembre 2026. Seres a récupéré le pilotage et la définition produit, le design, le marketing, les canaux de vente et le réseau de service, tandis que Huawei passe à un rôle de soutien technologique, un partenariat (plus limité) renouvelé pour cinq ans.
Le désengagement progressif de Huawei dans la marque Aito a déjà provoqué une vague d’inquiétude chez les propriétaires de véhicules de la marque en Chine. Certains propriétaires, inquiets de voir Huawei prendre ses distances avec Aito, ont même remplacé le logo de leur SUV par celui de DFSK, une marque d’utilitaires et véhicules urbains low cost du groupe Seres. Une manière ironique d’exprimer leurs craintes quant au maintien du positionnement premium et à la valeur de revente de leur véhicule. Ils craignent qu’Aito ne devienne un constructeur de seconde zone.
En abandonnant la seule brique technologique qui faisait sa valeur ajoutée au profit d’une solution plus commune, Seres prend le risque de débarquer en Europe avec une coquille un peu trop vide. Et ce, au moment même où sa crédibilité s’effrite également en Chine. En outre, ce ne serait pas vraiment la première déconvenue de la marque Seres en Europe.

articles.title: Revolut outage disrupts online banking operations worldwide
articles.text:
Fintech company Revolut is working to resolve a massive outage that disrupted most of its services worldwide earlier today.
Since the incident began, thousands of users on the Downdetector outage tracking platform have reported issues with the Revolut app, mobile banking services, and transferring funds between accounts.
In a statement today, the company said the outage has affected its services since Tuesday morning and added that customers' data and funds are safe.
"We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," Revolut said.
"We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused."
On its official status page, the company says the outage affects 28 services, including sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading, and live support chat, which are now flagged as partially unavailable.
According to Reuters, the Revolut outage is reportedly linked to ongoing service disruptions affecting Google Cloud's London-based europe-west2 data center after a "power event."
A Revolut spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer reached out earlier about the root cause of today's outage.
Last month, Revolut also disclosed a data breach after it shared personally identifiable information (PII) from an undisclosed number of customers with a threat actor who was impersonating a government agency.
Four years ago, Revolut disclosed another data breach after threat actors stole the personal, contact, and financial information of more than 50,000 customers in September 2022.
Revolut provides banking, money management, and investment services to more than 80 million customers across 160+ countries and regions, including 800,000 business customers.
Update October 20, 13:52 EDT: Revolut has linked today's outage to the Google Cloud incident and said that all services have now been restored.
"Due to a recent Google Cloud outage, customers may have experienced temporary service disruption on the Revolut app today," the company said.
"The issue has now been fixed, and services are now restored. All our customers’ money and data is safe, and has remained safe throughout this incident. We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

articles.title: Mozilla asks UK CMA to consult on browser choice screens now | The Mozilla Blog
articles.text:
Why is the CMA asking us to choose the furniture before the house? The UK’s search choice screens need browser choice screens alongside them
Mobile browsers are a key gateway to the internet for 56 million people in the UK. Smartphone users spend around half an hour a day in these apps, and opening a browser is the most common way they look up information online.
Yet most people are using a smartphone browser that was preinstalled and set as the default for them, without ever being asked which browser they would actually prefer.
Mozilla believes people deserve an active choice in the tools they depend on every day, which is why the latest proposals from the UK Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) matter. We welcome the CMA’s plans to give people a choice of search service and are asking it to consult on browser choice now, so both screens can launch together.
On September 23rd, the CMA published updated plans that would require Google to show people in the UK a choice of search service on new Android devices, covering the default search app and home-screen search widget as well as Chrome. Search choice screens would also appear in Chrome on other platforms, including through a major update for existing users. Some AI assistants would also be eligible to appear alongside search engines.
The proposals are well designed, but solve only half the problem
The CMA’s mobile browser investigation found that preinstallation, prominent placement and default settings restrict browser competition. Mozilla’s innovative 2023 experiment showed that properly designed browser choice screens can help people choose a browser they expect to keep using, and can be an effective tool for giving people agency over their online life. It also showed that an overwhelming majority of people (98%!) want to see them.
The EU Digital Markets Act has since demonstrated their impact in practice. We welcome the CMA’s work on search choice, but people in the UK deserve browser choice too. Asking people to pick a search service inside a browser that most of them never actively chose in the first place leaves some of the biggest issues identified in the CMA’s own mobile browser investigation unaddressed.
The CMA commissioned user research on search choice screens to refine and improve the proposals it first consulted on in January. Providers’ positions on the choice screen would be fully randomised. Users would have to scroll to the bottom before confirming, and could “test drive” a search provider for at least a week.
The CMA has also recognized that search is changing. Its research found that many people were already using AI assistants to search alongside traditional search services. Under the revised, more technology-neutral eligibility criteria, an AI assistant could also qualify to appear on the search choice screen if it meets the requirements, including being able to search the web and attribute its sources. But browser choice should not be left behind.
Why the two choices belong together
- Less confusion. The CMA’s new research found that participants often confused browsers with search services and were unsure what their search choice would change. Mozilla’s research has revealed similar confusion. These findings support designing and testing the two screens together, with clear explanations of each decision.
- Less duplication. The CMA’s work on search choice can also inform browser choice. Developing the two together would allow the design, order and timing to be tested as one journey, helping to avoid separate rounds of changes and interruptions for users.
- Order matters. Nobody chooses the furniture before the house. Browsers have their own search defaults, which is why we recommend showing the browser choice screen first, followed by the search screen, with wording that makes clear these are two separate decisions.
The EU and Japan already show both screens
The EU’s Digital Markets Act introduced browser choice screens on iOS for the first time and brought browser and search choice together during Android set-up.
Browser first, then search, so the relationship between the two makes sense. In Japan, search and browser choice screens are presented on both Android and iOS.
And people are making use of the browser screen to select alternatives. In May, we reported Firefox is selected through a DMA choice screen once every ten seconds, with retention five times higher than for organic downloads. Other independent browsers have also reported substantial growth.
Choice matters more as AI moves into the browser
The CMA’s proposals recognize that AI is changing how people search. AI is also changing what browsers offer, adding to the ways they compete on features, privacy and user control. Firefox already lets people on desktop pick which AI assistant sits in the sidebar, and our Smart Window beta extends that choice to the model behind the browser’s own assistant. There are meaningful differences between browsers. AI is the latest example of why giving people an active choice matters.
When people aren’t offered an active browser choice, they may be choosing search and AI services within a browser someone else picked. One decision taken at the factory can end up shaping the ones that follow. A search choice screen gives people a say over their search provider; offering browser choice alongside it would give them a say over that first decision too.
Our ask of the CMA
We’re asking the CMA to consult now on browser choice screens for Apple’s and Google’s mobile platforms, so they can launch alongside the search screens. Apple and Google already offer browser choice screens in the EU and Japan. The CMA can draw on that experience and its own research to give people in the UK an active choice of both browser and search service.
Mozilla’s response to the consultation is available here.
