Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (256 GB) alcança menor preço em meses com cupom
Galaxy Tab S10 Lite com tela LCD, S Pen e chip intermediário fica mais barato ao combinar cupom e pagamento via Pix no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (256 GB) está disponível por R$ 2.199,12 no Pix com o cupom OFFSOHJ no Mercado Livre. O tablet intermediário da Samsung com tela de 10,9 polegadas e bateria de até 16 horas, lançado por R$ 3.199, recebe um desconto de 31% e atinge o menor preço desde agosto.
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite traz uma tela LCD de 10,9 polegadas com resolução Full HD+ e taxa de atualização de 90 Hz. O painel com ampla área de trabalho é recomendado para estudos e consumo de mídia, oferecendo mais conforto visual para os usuários.
Apesar da configuração inferior ao S10 e S10 FE, o dispositivo com o chip Samsung Exynos 1380 e 8 GB GB de RAM entrega um desempenho equilibrado para tarefas leves e o uso dos recursos do Galaxy AI. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno trazem um espaço satisfatório, mas a memória pode chegar até 2 TB utilizando cartões microSD.
Seguindo os padrões dos tablets Samsung, o Galaxy Tab S10 Lite traz a caneta S Pen como parte do kit inicial. Além de facilitar a digitalização de anotações e desenhos à mão, ele permite usar recursos de IA (Apagador de Objetos) e de pesquisa (Circule para pesquisar) para agilizar o dia a dia.
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite oferece suporte ao Samsung Dex, função que transforma o tablet em um desktop ao ser conectado a um monitor. Ele ainda traz uma câmera frontal de 5 MP para videochamadas em Full HD e uma câmera traseira de 8 MP para fotografar documentos e outros cliques mais simples.
A bateria de 8.000 mAh garante uma autonomia de até 16 horas de reprodução de vídeo, variando conforme o uso das conexões sem fio Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3. Em relação ao software, ele vem de fábrica com o Android 15 e receberá atualizações do sistema operacional até 2032.
Pensando para o transporte em bolsas e mochilas, o Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (R$ 2.199,12 no Pix com cupom OFFSOHJ) é fabricado com corpo em Armor Alumínio com 6,6 mm de espessura e pesa 524 gramas. Por fim, o certificado IP42 de resistência à poeira e à água protege o aparelho de respingos de água.

articles.title: Pourquoi désactiver l’accès à distance de votre Freebox ne protège pas totalement votre réseau — Frandroid
articles.text:
Freebox OS, l’interface d’administration des Freebox, peut s’ouvrir depuis n’importe quelle connexion : on retrouve alors les réglages de sa box sans être chez soi. C’est pratique, mais beaucoup d’abonnés n’en ont pas l’usage et préfèrent couper cet accès. Une interface d’administration n’a pas de raison d’être visible depuis Internet quand on ne s’en sert pas.
Le problème, c’est que le réglage qu’on vérifie spontanément pour cela est trompeur. Les failles PHP d’octobre 2026 m’ont forcé à aller fouiller dans les réglages de la Freebox, même si a priori, ces box ne sont pas impactées par ces failles.
Le réglage qu’on croit suffisant
Le premier réflexe consiste à ouvrir Freebox OS, à passer les paramètres en « Mode avancé » et à se rendre dans « Gestion des accès ». On y trouve une case « Activer l’authentification par mot de passe » : décochée, elle donne l’impression que l’accès à distance est coupé.
Ce n’est pas le cas. Cette case empêche seulement de se connecter à distance avec le mot de passe administrateur. Elle ne ferme pas le port. L’interface l’indique d’ailleurs, en petits caractères, juste au-dessus : « Lorsque vous utilisez des applications ou des liens de partage, l’accès à votre Freebox est rendu possible automatiquement », puis, en orange : « L’accès distant est possible pour les applications et les liens de partages ».
Ce que nous avons constaté
Nous avons fait le test sur une Freebox Ultra (Freebox Server v9), sous la version 4.13.1 du firmware. L’accès par mot de passe était décoché et aucun lien de partage n’était actif. Pourtant, depuis un smartphone en 5G, Wi-Fi coupé (pour simuler une personne située en dehors de notre réseau local), la page de connexion de Freebox OS s’affichait sans difficulté à l’adresse personnelle de la box.
    Pour aller plus loin
Faille PHP : les abonnés Free peuvent souffler, leur Freebox n’est pas concernée
            
Elle n’a cessé de répondre qu’une fois toutes les applications associées à la box révoquées. Nous en avons ensuite associé une seule, en ne lui laissant qu’une permission, « Modification des réglages de la Freebox » : la page est aussitôt redevenue accessible depuis Internet. Les droits accordés à l’application ne changent donc rien, c’est sa présence qui compte. Une seule suffit, qu’il s’agisse de Freebox Connect, de l’application Freebox de votre iPhone ou d’un logiciel tiers associé il y a des années et oublié depuis.
Ce fonctionnement n’a rien d’une faille : les applications ont besoin de joindre la box depuis l’extérieur, et l’accès leur est donc ouvert. Mais rien dans le réglage ne le laisse deviner au premier coup d’œil. Voir la page de connexion ne veut pas dire qu’on peut entrer. C’est néanmoins une interface d’administration visible par des personnes qui connaîtraient son adresse. Nous n’avons pas pu vérifier ce comportement sur les Freebox Delta, Pop ou Révolution.
Vérifiez si votre box est visible de l’extérieur
- Depuis un appareil connecté à votre Freebox, ouvrez l’adresse mafreebox.freebox.fr/api_version. Une petite fiche de texte s’affiche. Notez deux valeurs : api_domain (une adresse qui se termine par fbxos.fr) et https_port (un nombre à cinq chiffres).
- Sur votre smartphone, coupez le Wi-Fi pour passer en 4G ou 5G. C’est indispensable : depuis chez vous, la box répond toujours, et le test ne prouverait rien.
- Ouvrez https:// + l’adresse api_domain + : + le port, suivi de /login.php. Par exemple : https://abcd1234.fbxos.fr:12345/login.php.
Si la page « Freebox OS :: Identification » s’affiche, votre interface est visible depuis Internet. Si le navigateur finit par afficher une erreur de connexion, elle ne l’est pas.
Comment la fermer
Dans Freebox OS, en mode avancé, ouvrez « Gestion des accès », puis l’onglet « Applications ». La liste montre tout ce qui est associé à votre box, avec la date du dernier accès. Vous y trouverez sans doute des appareils oubliés.
- Pour fermer la porte complètement, cliquez sur « Révoquer tous les accès », puis vérifiez dans la fenêtre « Liens de partage » qu’aucun partage n’est actif. Refaites ensuite le test en 5G : la page ne doit plus répondre.
- Si vous tenez à Freebox Connect, supprimez au moins les applications que vous n’utilisez plus, avec l’icône de corbeille. Sachez toutefois que tant qu’il en subsiste une, l’interface reste visible depuis Internet.
La contrepartie est simple : les applications révoquées ne fonctionnent plus. Rien n’est définitif pour autant. Si vous avez de nouveau besoin de l’une d’elles, vous pouvez l’associer à tout moment, en validant la demande directement sur l’écran du Freebox Server.
On vous l’accorde : ces précautions seront sûrement inutiles pour la plupart des personnes, et du tant que les Freebox n’ont pas de faille de vulnérabilité. Mais pour les personnes qui aiment bien que leur réseau local vive en totale autarcie, ce réglage pourrait être utile.

articles.title: Eka is worth $1.45B thanks to a physical AI model that has experts raving | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Robots still aren’t that good at picking things up, despite billions of dollars of investment and endless videos fed into deep learning models.
That may be about to change, thanks to a manipulation architecture built by Eka Robotics, which encompasses a force-sensitive gripper and a new kind of deep-learning model. Founded by MIT professor Pulkit Agrawal and former Google DeepMind researcher Tuomas Haarnoja, the startup just closed an $150 million Series A round that values it at $1.45 billion post-money, led by venture funds a16z and F-Prime.
“They are already exceeding superhuman performance for certain tasks, and so we think over the next few months there will be superhuman performance in many dexterous manipulation tasks,” Raghu Raghuram, the a16z general partner who co-led the fundraising round, told TechCrunch.
In an era of never-ending robotic demonstrations, Eka’s capabilities are shocking veteran robot builders.
Kris Hauser, a professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, said it had a “wow factor” compared to other robot demos he saw recently. The Eka robot “was able to adapt to a large number of different objects without retraining,” Hauser said, adding that it also had an aspect of “humanness, creepy humanness that it would try over and over again if it failed the first time.”
Another roboticist, who asked for anonymity because of their work at a frontier lab, told TechCrunch that seeing Eka’s robot in action was an emotional experience, comparable to when robots first achieved reliable legged locomotion five to 10 years ago. Take a look for yourself:
What’s notable here? How smoothly and rapidly the robot moves. It can pick up about 1,500 objects that weigh up to 1 kg in an hour, compared to about 600 for a human; Eka says it reliably picks up objects more than 95% of the time. And the robot arm is strong enough to hurt itself as it moves that quickly. That indicates, per the frontier lab observer, that “they have a lot of trust in their algorithm not breaking the robot. I wonder how many robots they broke along the way?”
When the frontier lab roboticist met Eka’s robot, they handed it a raspberry, the lab’s apparent favorite test item. “The experience of a big, heavy robot rushing towards my arm and then slowing down just in time and very gently touching me is a feeling that I am, as we speak, carrying this feeling in my body,” they told TechCrunch.
How not to squish the raspberry
These capabilities are a consequence of how the foundational model was built. Rather than a vision-language-action model — which is trained to understand the relationship between language, visual inputs, and actions — the schema here is a vision-force-action model, which focuses on the relationship between language, force inputs, and actions. Critics of the current direction of generative AI robotics models, like Rodney Brooks, say that they will fail without an attempt to represent force and touch; Eka’s results suggest such critics have a point.
“Vision is not the primary way in which you close this last millimeter problem,” Eka co-founder Agrawal told TechCrunch. “Vision tells you roughly where the object is, what the pose is, but the actual grabbing, the actual searching is happening through forces.”
Eka had to design a unique robotic hand that was more flexible than traditional grippers, and included more force sensors; it reacts to contact, which is why it doesn’t crush the raspberry. The founders are cagey about how they achieved that for obvious competitive reasons, but it comes down to using a physics simulator to model the multiple forces the robot will encounter as it attempts to grasp something, and using that to create a reinforcement learning environment that can be run at scale. They say they can generate thousands of hours of robot experience in minutes.
“Rather than being limited to the data that you’re collecting from, say, human demonstrations, Eka is pushing through reinforcement learning this approach where the robot can surpass any kind of demonstrations that are given to it,” Hauser said. “What’s really exciting is that they’re able to not be limited to the data that is presented to them for training.”
Agrawal and Haarnoja, who first met in graduate school at the University of California–Berkeley, are leading researchers in the field of reinforcement learning for robotics control. Eka’s key bet was that this technique could be done at scale through simulation, rather than relying on videos collected by gig workers or robot operators performing tasks over many hours. Simulation was key to achieving their robot’s reliable manipulation, a feat that in the past has proven more difficult for tasks that require interacting with objects, rather than avoiding them.
“What EKA is bridging is the generality-performance gap, which plagues a lot of modern robotics,” Agrawal argues.
Making a general-purpose robot useful
Right now, the most generalizable physical AI models — the ones that can attempt lots of different tasks — aren’t particularly good at them. But AI models trained to be highly capable at a single task may not close the business case for a company: The promise of generative AI is that robots can quickly learn multiple tasks, even novel ones.
The current approaches are good at producing robots that are more generally intelligent than before — Astra, ChatGPT’s latest LLM, can operate a robot in an unfamiliar setting and perform tasks with it, but slowly and at a high cost. The promise of a model like Eka’s is that it handles the physicality while a more general model makes decisions about how to solve a problem. Astra, for example, might know that plates get stacked in a cupboard when they come out of the dishwasher, but Eka’s model is capable of picking up a dish without breaking it.
“Most of the field has been focusing on the planning,” Eka co-founder Haarnoja says, “so they approach from the top: high-level intelligence, pushing that down towards the physical. Whereas we think about it from the bottom up.”
Eka still needs to prove itself in the field, though. The company is working in secretive pilots with a number of industrial customers doing pick-and-place and wire manipulation, but the leap from lab to line is almost as big as the gap between sim and real.
“What’s going to be a big challenge is when they work with integrators on real assembly lines, and it needs to run without breaking for an entire year,” Hauser said. The other open question is “‘how generalizable these techniques can be to different tasks?’ What I’ve seen is pick and place, but many industry tasks that are value added involve more than just pick-and-place.”
Agrawal is also focused on deployability; right now, he says Eka’s gripper hardware — which costs less than $1,000 — is rated for 5 million duty cycles, but the ultimate goal is to hit the 20 million cycle bar set by standard industrial arms.
“What we are building is that engineering of how to design entire workflows, but we are starting off being very pragmatic, and saying here are two verticals in pick, arrange, place, and wire handling, let’s make them be home runs,” Agrawal said. “Once we have made home runs on them, the sky is the limit in how much we can do with the approach we are developing.”
